n-f-s-grundtvig: Grundtvig was born at Udby, the son of the Lutheran pastor Johan Ottosen Grundtvig, and was called Frederik by those close to him. His mother respected old Norse legends and traditions, and he was schooled in the European Enlightenment but also influenced by German romanticism and the ancient history of the Nordic countries. At nine he was sent to the pastor Laurids Svindt Feld at Thyregod, then attended the cathedral school of Aarhus from 1798. He entered the University of Copenhagen in 1801, and near the end of his studies began to read Icelandic and the sagas.

After working as a tutor on Langeland from 1805, he returned to Copenhagen in 1808 and had success with Northern Mythology and a long drama in 1809. His first sermon, in 1810, denounced the city's clergy and offended the church authorities. In 1810 he went through a religious crisis and converted to a strongly held Lutheranism, retiring to his father's parish at Udby as chaplain. His rate of publication in the following years was staggering, including two more world histories and, from 1816 to 1819, the journal Danne-Virke, which he almost wrote alone.

His 1825 pamphlet against the theologian Henrik Nicolai Clausen led to a conviction for libel, a fine and a seven-year ban on preaching. During it he visited England three times between 1829 and 1831 and studied Anglo-Saxon.

In 1839 he became pastor of the Vartov hospital church in Copenhagen, which he held until his death. From 1844 he took part in politics, and in 1848 he sat in the Constituent Assembly that wrote Denmark's first constitution. He received the titular rank of bishop in 1861, without a see. He wrote or translated about 1,500 hymns, and his hymn book replaced the slow measures of orthodox Lutheranism with the national poets' hymns.

Grundtvig called himself a pastor, not a theologian. His theology put the authority of the living word in place of the apostolic commentaries, and he wished each congregation to be a practically independent community. He coined the name Asatro for the pre-Christian Scandinavian faith, known until then as the old customs.

He is regarded as the ideological father of the folk high school, though his own plan was to reform Sorø Academy into a popular school teaching practical skills as well as national poetry and history. The plan nearly succeeded under Christian VIII but ended with the king's death in 1848. One of his followers, Kristen Kold, had already founded the first folk high school. He opposed compulsion in education, including examinations. In 1820 he published Bjovulfs Drape, the first full translation of Beowulf into a modern language.
naacp: The Race Riot of 1908 in Springfield, Illinois, the state capital and the hometown of Abraham Lincoln, showed the need for an effective civil rights organisation. Lynchings of Black Americans, particularly men, were then at an all-time high. In January 1909 Mary White Ovington, the journalist William English Walling and Henry Moskowitz met in New York City and sent appeals for support to more than 60 prominent Americans. They set a meeting for 12 February 1909, the hundredth anniversary of Lincoln's birth. The first large meeting did not take place for another three months, but February is often cited as the founding date.

The first branches were added in 1912, in Boston and Chicago. By 1915 there were 50 branches with 6,000 members, and the First World War brought a surge: by 1920 there were 395 branches and more than 90,000 members, including 74 in the South. By 1945 it claimed 894 branches and 351,000 members.

In its early years the association was based in New York City and concentrated on litigation against the disenfranchisement of Black voters, which every southern state had established by 1908, and against the Jim Crow statutes. In 1913 it organised opposition to President Woodrow Wilson's introduction of racial segregation into federal workplaces and hiring. It helped win the right of African Americans to serve as officers in the First World War, when 600 were commissioned, and in 1915 organised a nationwide protest against D. W. Griffith's film The Birth of a Nation.
Its legal department pursued segregation in the courts. Charles Hamilton Houston's victory in Missouri ex rel. Gaines v. Canada in 1938 led to the creation of the Legal Defense Fund in 1939.

For decades in the first half of the twentieth century the organisation was effectively led by its executive secretary, who acted as chief operating officer. James Weldon Johnson and Walter F. White held the post in succession from 1920 to 1958 and were much more widely known than the presidents of those years. Local branches carried the national campaigns into communities: they carried out the boycotts of The Birth of a Nation and took the campaign against lynching to hundreds of places.
nabadwip: Nabadwip, historically also called Nadia, lies on the western bank of the Hooghly at its confluence with the Jalangi. The name joins the Bengali naba, new, and dwipa, island, and refers to an island formed from the silt the Ganges carried down. A reading of the name as nine islands, spread by a book called Bhakti Ratnakar, has no ground, historians say. The Bhagirathi once ran west of the town and has since shifted its course, cutting it off from the rest of the district.

Nabadwip was the capital of the Sena dynasty under Ballal Sen and Lakshman Sen, who ruled Bengal from here between 1159 and 1206. Bakhtiyar Khalji invaded and plundered the town and defeated Lakshman Sen, a victory that led to Muslim rule in Bengal and badly damaged the town's prosperity.

Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was born in 1486, and with him Vaishnava culture became established. When the local ruler Chand Kazi ordered Vaishnavas to stop chanting, Chaitanya went to his house with companions and persuaded him to allow it, an episode called the first civil disobedience in India. Scholars such as Basudev Sarvabhauma and Raghunath Shiromani made the town the main centre of Sanskrit learning; in the time of Raja Rudra Roy it had four thousand students and six hundred professors, and was called the Oxford of Bengal.

In the 18th century the scholars Buno Ramnath and Shankara Tarkabagish made its name widely known, and the Navya Nyaya school of logic reached its peak here. Under Raja Krishnachandra of Nadia, Shakta worship spread.

Nabadwip's urban agglomeration had 175,474 inhabitants in the 2011 census, and the town is still noted for its traditional Sanskrit schools. It is a pilgrimage centre for Vaishnavas, who gather for Gaura-purnima, Chaitanya's birthday on the full moon of February or March, and for Dol Jatra and Rash purnima. The Shakta Rash, with its huge images of goddesses, is the most popular festival.
nabeshima-clan: The early origins of the family are uncertain, and its genealogies give two accounts. One traces it to the Uda Genji through the Sasaki clan: Nagaoka Tsunehide, a descendant of the Sasaki, settled at Nabeshima in Hizen and took the place-name as his surname. The other links the family with the Shōni clan, which claimed descent from Fujiwara no Hidesato, a Shōni member having succeeded to the Nabeshima line through his mother's relatives.

By the 16th century the Nabeshima were bound to the Ryūzōji by marriage as well as service. Nabeshima Naoshige, born in 1538 at the family residence in Honjō, was a cousin of Ryūzōji Takanobu through his mother and became his stepbrother when Takanobu's mother, Keigin-ni, married Naoshige's father, Nabeshima Kiyofusa.

After Takanobu was killed at the Battle of Okitanawate in 1584, the change of power was gradual. His son Ryūzōji Masaie stayed head of the family, and when Masaie retired in 1590 his five-year-old son Takafusa succeeded him, while Naoshige governed the lands in fact. Only after Takafusa and Masaie both died in 1607 did Naoshige's son Nabeshima Katsushige take the former Ryūzōji position as the first lord of Saga.

Under Katsushige and his successors three branch houses came to rule domains of their own, Ogi, Hasunoike and Kashima, which the Tokugawa shogunate recognised while Saga treated their lords as subordinate to the main house. Disputes over their status under the second lord, Nabeshima Mitsushige, led to the Sanke kakushiki regulations of 1683. Former Ryūzōji retainers and related families kept their own estates inside the domain throughout the Edo period.

Nabeshima Naomasa, lord from 1830, reformed the domain's finances and administration, expanded its school, the Kōdōkan, and strengthened the defence of Nagasaki. From 1850 Saga built reverberatory furnaces for casting cannon and promoted Western medicine and education. Saga forces fought for the new imperial government in the Boshin War of 1868–1869.

With the abolition of the han system in 1871 the four domains became prefectures. The last lord, Nabeshima Naohiro, studied in England, served as Japanese minister plenipotentiary to Italy from 1880 and sat in the House of Peers; under the Peerage Ordinance of 1884 the head of the house was made a marquess. The family remained in the peerage until the kazoku was abolished in 1947. A foundation set up in 1940 by Marquess Nabeshima Naomitsu runs the Chokokan museum in Saga, which keeps the family's documents and works of art.
nabeshima-naomasa: Naomasa was born the 17th son of Nabeshima Narinao, the 9th daimyo of Saga Domain in Hizen Province. His wife was the 18th daughter of the shogun Tokugawa Ienari, who on his accession let him use a character of his own name, so that he wrote his name Narimasa until the end of the Edo period. His honorary title was Hizen-no-Kami, and Western accounts sometimes called him Prince Hizen.

He inherited a domain close to bankruptcy, burdened by the cost of guarding the foreign settlement at Dejima and by his father's spending; creditors besieged his Edo residence before he could leave for Saga. His retired father blocked his reforms, and he took full control only after the fire at Saga Castle in 1835.

Citing the need to rebuild the castle, he cut the samurai supported by the domain to one fifth, made weapons, charcoal and tea domain monopolies, and invested in the domain academy, the Kodokan. Through Nagasaki he imported Armstrong cannon and had Saga armouries copy them, invited swordsmiths and metal casters from across Japan regardless of rank, and sponsored steam engines and steam warships. He introduced smallpox vaccination into Japan, testing it first on his own son.

After the arrival of Commodore Matthew Perry in 1853 he first backed the Sonno joi faction and helped build coastal batteries around Edo Bay, while secretly negotiating with Great Britain, and later argued for opening the country to trade. Retired from 1861, he kept Saga neutral between the factions of the Bakumatsu period. In the Boshin War he joined the Satcho Alliance, and his forces fought at the Battle of Ueno and against the Ouetsu Reppan Domei.

He became a councillor of the Meiji government and governor of Saga until the domain was absorbed into Saga Prefecture in July 1871, and with Shimazu Yoshitake was made Commissioner of Colonial Affairs for the settlement of Ezo. He died that year at the Saga residence in Tokyo. A reconstruction of his Kakurin-tei tea house stands in Kono Park in Saga City.
nabeshima-naoshige: Naoshige was born on 12 April 1538, the second son of Nabeshima Kiyofusa; his mother was a daughter of Ryūzōji Iesumi. He served the Ryūzōji clan as a vassal and became chief retainer of Ryūzōji Takanobu of Hizen. In 1570, when an Ōtomo clan army of 60,000 surrounded Takanobu at Saga Castle, Naoshige, with only 5,000 troops, proposed a night raid on the enemy camp, which routed the besiegers. In 1575 he attacked Suko Castle in western Hizen and forced its commander, Hirai Tsuneharu, to commit suicide.

After Takanobu's death at Okitanawate in 1584, Naoshige took over Saga Castle. In 1585 he joined the alliance under Ryūzōji Ieharu that invaded Ōtomo lands, but its siege near Kurume collapsed on 23 April before the Ōtomo generals Tachibana Dōsetsu and Takahashi Shigetane. In 1587, with the Ryūzōji led by a weak heir, he left them to support Toyotomi Hideyoshi in his campaign in Kyūshū. In 1592 he led over 12,000 men to Korea in the first of Hideyoshi's Korean campaigns, where he struck up a friendship with Katō Kiyomasa.

In 1600 he fought on the Tokugawa side at the sieges of Udo and Yanagawa, and at the Battle of Sekigahara he sent his son Nabeshima Katsushige to assist Tokugawa Ieyasu. After the Tokugawa victory the family's fief of 357,000 koku was left untouched. Naoshige died on 24 July 1618. He is remembered for resettling potters from Korea in Hizen, and his deeds and sayings fill the third chapter of the Hagakure by Tsunetomo Yamamoto, a close attendant of his grandson Mitsushige.
nablus: Nablus stands about 49 kilometres north of Jerusalem, at an elevation of around 550 metres in a narrow east-west valley between Mount Ebal to the north and Mount Gerizim to the south. It lies at a junction of two ancient commercial roads, one linking the Sharon coastal plain to the Jordan valley and the other joining the Galilee in the north to Judea in the south. Abundant water from nearby springs helped the city prosper. Ancient Shechem is now identified with the nearby site of Tell Balata.

Flavia Neapolis was named in 72 CE by the Roman emperor Vespasian and applied to an older Samaritan village. It lay 2 kilometres west of the biblical city of Shechem, which the Romans destroyed that year during the First Jewish-Roman War. In the Byzantine period conflict between the Samaritan and Christian inhabitants peaked in the Samaritan revolts, put down by 573, which greatly reduced the Samaritan population. The Muslim general Khalid ibn al-Walid took the city in 636, and its name was kept in the Arabic form Nabulus.

The Crusaders captured it in 1099 under Prince Tancred and called it Naples. They did not sack it, presumably because of its large Christian population, and Muslims, Orthodox Christians and Samaritans stayed. In 1120 the Council of Nablus issued the first written laws of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Saladin's Ayyubids ended Crusader rule in 1187 and restored the Great Mosque, which had been a church. The Ottomans took the city in 1517, and Nablus became the administrative and commercial centre of what is now the northern West Bank.

British forces took the area in the First World War, in the Battle of Nablus of 19 to 25 September 1918, and the city became part of Mandatory Palestine in 1922. During the 1948 Arab-Israeli War it came under Jordanian occupation, and thousands of refugees settled in camps in and around it, doubling its population. Jordan annexed it in 1950.

Much of the city's history survives in its Old City, which holds more than 100 monumental buildings and is divided into six quarters. It has the Great Mosque, the 15th-century Khan al-Tujjar caravanserai and the Abd al-Hadi Palace. Nabulsi soap, made of virgin olive oil, water and a sodium compound, has been known for its quality since the 10th century, though the factories have fallen from thirty in the 19th century to two. A small Samaritan community remains.
nabonassar: Nabonassar, Nabû-nāṣir, meaning Nabu is protector, was king of Babylon from 747 to 734 BCE. Nothing is known of his origin, though he appears to have been a native Mesopotamian. His three predecessors came from the Chaldean tribes settled in the far south east of Babylonia since the 9th century BCE. He deposed the last of them, Nabu-shuma-ishkun, bringing native rule back to Babylon after twenty-three years of Chaldean rule. The country he took over was divided by conflicts with the immigrant Aramean and Chaldean tribes, and central authority was greatly diminished.

In his third year the Assyrian general Tiglath-Pileser III came to power and invaded Babylonia in 745 BCE, sacking Rabbilu and Hamranu, subjugating the Aramean and Chaldean tribes and destroying Sarrabanu, the capital of the Bit-Shilani, whose leader he impaled. Whether or not Nabonassar asked for Assyrian help, he seems to have been the main beneficiary: his regime was stabilised, and he put down a revolt in Borsippa. His hold on Uruk stayed uncertain. Twenty-three tablets from his first to his fourteenth year record agriculture, herding, weaving and sales, and seem to show an economic recovery. He died of illness in his palace in the fourteenth year of his reign.

His son Nabu-nadin-zeri succeeded him, the only known hereditary succession in Babylonia between 810 BCE and the rise of the Neo-Babylonian Empire in 626 BCE. His reign saw a calendar reform that introduced calculated intercalary months and the eighteen-year cycle texts. Berossus reported that records of the stars were kept from his reign onward, and that he gathered and destroyed the records of his predecessors so that the history of the Chaldean kings began with him. Ptolemy’s Almagest dates an era from noon on 26 February 747 BCE, though before the Hellenistic period there is no trace of it. Both the Babylonian Chronicle and the Ptolemaic Canon begin with his accession.
nabonidus: Nabonidus's origins are obscure. He made no claim of kinship to earlier Babylonian kings, and one inscription has him say: I am Nabonidus, the only son, who has nobody. In my mind there was no thought of kingship. His mother, Adad-guppi, was of Assyrian ancestry, and his father, Nabu-balatsu-iqbi, whom he calls a learned counsellor and prince, may have been Assyrian or Babylonian. Some scholars think he married a daughter of Nebuchadnezzar II. He had a prominent career of some kind before becoming king, and he adopted Assyrian royal titles such as king of the Universe.

Nabonidus was proclaimed king after the murder of Labashi-Marduk in 556 BCE, in a plot likely led by his son Belshazzar. In his first autumn he campaigned in eastern Cilicia and brought back prisoners and booty, including 2,850 people given to the temples as slaves. He reorganised the offerings in the Eanna temple at Uruk. His inscriptions suggest he raised the moon god Sîn and lowered Marduk, the traditional national deity of Babylon, though how far this amounted to reform is debated, and it met considerable opposition.

In 553 BCE he campaigned in Arabia, defeated the king of Dadanu and captured Tayma, which he made a provisional seat by the summer of 552 BCE. He stayed there for about a decade, returning in 543 or 542 BCE, and the reason is unknown; one suggestion is disagreement with the Babylonian clergy and oligarchy. Belshazzar acted as regent in Babylonia meanwhile, and Nabonidus was still recognised as king.

On returning he rebuilt the Eḫulḫul, Sîn's temple at Harran, directly on its old foundation and counted it his major achievement. There is some evidence of famine in his later reign. His excavations of temple foundations have led some to call him the first archaeologist.

After the battle of Opis, Cyrus the Great's Persians entered Babylon without a fight in 539 BCE. Accounts of Nabonidus's fate differ: Berossus says he surrendered at Borsippa and was spared and settled in Carmania, while Xenophon says Ugbaru killed him, though he may have meant Belshazzar. He was the last native ruler of ancient Mesopotamia. Cyrus justified his conquest by presenting himself as chosen by Marduk and by writing accounts of Nabonidus's heretical acts.
nabonidus-chronicle: The chronicle belongs to the series of Babylonian Chronicles, which record year by year the accessions and deaths of kings, major campaigns and notable religious events, reporting only what mattered directly to Babylonia. It survives on a single clay tablet, 14 cm by 14 cm, written in two columns on each side and once holding some 300 to 400 lines, of which little more than 75 are still legible. The surviving copy was probably made by a scribe in the Seleucid period, but the original was probably written in the late 6th or early 5th century BCE, perhaps by the same scribe as the Nabonassar to Shamash-shum-ukin Chronicle.

The text probably began with Nabonidus's accession in 556 BCE, and it mentions his campaigns against a place called Hume and in the West. In his sixth year it records Cyrus the Great's plunder of Ecbatana, the capital of the Median king Astyages, and in several entries it describes the king's stay at the Arabian oasis of Tema. Another campaign of Cyrus in the ninth year may be his attack on Lydia.

A long passage on the seventeenth and final year tells of the gods of other cities being brought into Babylon, the Persian victory at the Battle of Opis, the capture of Sippar and Babylon without further fighting, and Cyrus's welcome and appointment of governors. It ends with mourning for a king's wife and a mention of Cambyses II.

The British Museum bought the tablet in 1879 from the dealers Spartali & Co. Its findspot is unknown, though it is presumed to have come from Babylon. Sir Henry Rawlinson first discussed it, as the Annals of Nabonidus, in the Athenaeum of 14 February 1880, and T. G. Pinches published the first English translation in 1882; Sidney Smith, A. Leo Oppenheim, Albert Kirk Grayson and others have translated it since.

Scholars see it as the work of the priests of Marduk and part of a group of pro-Persian texts, with the Cyrus Cylinder and the Verse Account of Nabonidus, that attack the king for religious infidelity. Julye Bidmead links the priests' hostility to his attempts to promote the moon god Sîn. Even so, Amélie Kuhrt calls it the most reliable and sober ancient account of the fall of Babylon.
nabopolassar: Nabopolassar's origins are unclear. In his own inscriptions he calls himself a son of a nobody, a descriptor known from no other Mesopotamian king. The later kings Neriglissar and Nabonidus also had no blood tie to earlier royalty but named their fathers with pride. Historians have variously identified him as a Chaldean, an Assyrian or a Babylonian. Near-contemporary texts such as the Uruk prophecy call him king of the sea, meaning southernmost Babylonia, and a letter of the Assyrian king Sinsharishkun calls him a man from the lower sea. The term Chaldean dynasty remains in common use for the family he founded.

In the middle of the seventh century BCE the Neo-Assyrian Empire ruled the entire Near East. Babylonia was divided among native Babylonians, Chaldean tribes and Arameans, and the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III had conquered Babylon in 729 BCE.

Nabopolassar probably held high office in Uruk before he rebelled against Sinsharishkun in early 626 BCE. He took Babylon and Nippur from their Assyrian garrisons. In October 626 BCE the Assyrians retook Nippur and besieged both Uruk and Babylon, but Nabopolassar repelled both sieges. He was crowned king of Babylon on 22 or 23 November 626 BCE. Fighting for Babylonia lasted about ten years, and Sinsharishkun recaptured Uruk in 623 BCE.

In 616 BCE Nabopolassar marched up the Euphrates into Assyrian lands, took the city of Hindanu and defeated an Assyrian force near Gablinu. Pharaoh Psamtik I of Egypt aided Assyria, but the Babylonians kept the middle Euphrates. In May 615 BCE they attacked Assur. The Medes under Cyaxares entered Assyria soon after, and in 614 BCE sacked Assur. In 612 BCE the Medes and Babylonians took and burned Nineveh, and Sinsharishkun probably died defending it. Babylonian chronicles lament the sackings, and Nabopolassar's own inscriptions sometimes ascribe the victory to the gods and sometimes boast of the destruction.

Egypt under Pharaoh Necho II fought for several years to restore Assyria until his defeat at the Battle of Carchemish in 605 BCE. Nabopolassar died that year and was succeeded by his son Nebuchadnezzar II. Babylon, neglected during the wars, needed a new wall and restored temples such as the Esagila. Babylonians long remembered him as the avenger of Akkad, and Hellenistic authors, who called him Belesys or Bupolasaros, cast him as a pious and just king ordered by Marduk to free his homeland.
nabu-apla-iddina: Nabû-apla-iddina was the sixth king of the dynasty of E and the second of four generations of one family to rule Babylon: his father Nabû-šuma-ukin I preceded him and his son Marduk-zakir-šumi I followed. His reign came after a hundred and fifty years of instability in which Aramaean tribes had raided Mesopotamia. The Suteans had sacked Uruk and Nippur in the 11th century and so destroyed the temples of Sippar that the cult image of Šamaš was lost, and a votive disc had served in its place.

Assyria under Ashurnasirpal II was a powerful rival, but he avoided open war and any great loss of territory. In 878 BCE he sent troops to Suḫu on the middle Euphrates when its governor Kudurru refused tribute to Assyria; the army of 3,000, led by his brother Zabdanu and the diviner Bel-apli-iddina, was defeated and its leaders taken prisoner. Late in his reign the treaty with Shalmaneser III helped to secure his son's rule against the revolt of Marduk-bēl-ušati. Kassites held high positions at his court, the province of Chaldea is first mentioned in his time, and the king's feathered crown gave way to a peaked dome.

The Sun God Tablet shows him led by the priest Nabû-nadin-shum and the goddess Aa before the seated Šamaš, and celebrates his victory over the Sutû. He was the first Babylonian king in over two centuries, since Nabû-kudurrī-uṣur I, to claim a military title.

His reign saw something of a literary revival: new editions of the Utukkū Lemnūtu series and the Sakikkū texts were prepared, and Kabti-ilani-Marduk's Epic of Erra is sometimes dated to it. About 250 years later Nabû-apal-usur found the Sun God Tablet already broken and placed it in a clay box with his own inscription, where it was discovered in the 19th century. Inscriptions of his time survive on perhaps five kudurrus, and Assyrian king lists and chronicles name him.
nabu-mukin-apli: His name, usually written dAG-DU-A, means Nabû is establisher of a legitimate heir. He founded Babylon's eighth dynasty, the so-called Dynasty of E, and ruled for thirty-six years; the Synchronistic Kinglist makes him a contemporary of the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser II. His reign falls in the Babylonian dark age, and the sources for it are meagre. The Eclectic Chronicle names him but preserves no events, and the Religious Chronicle gives the most detail.

According to that chronicle the Akitu, the New Year festival of Marduk and Nabû, was interrupted several times, once for nine years in a row, because the Aramaeans were belligerent and Babylon was cut off from its farmland. The festival seems to have involved carrying the cult statues from Nabû's shrine in neighbouring Borsippa to Babylon.

Boundary stones are the chief documents of his reign. A kudurru from Sippar, dated to his 25th year, records the settlement of a feud over an estate near the city of Sha-mamitu. The land had belonged to the provincial governor Arad-Sibitti and his Kassite family, the bīt-Abi-Rattaš, and had passed by marriage to the family of the bow-maker Buruša, whose slave Arad-Sibitti had once killed with an arrow by accident. Buruša paid 887 shekels to clear his title of the creditors' claims, and the king's three sons witnessed the settlement.

Another kudurru, from the Diyala region east of the Tigris, is dated to his 16th year and records the sale of two plots of land. His younger son Rīmūt-ilī served as overseer of the temples. After Ninurta-kudurri-uṣur II's reign of eight months, another son, Mar-biti-aḫḫe-idinna, took the throne. The Chaldeans settled in the far south-east of Babylonia just after his reign.
nabu-mukin-zeri: Nabû-mukin-zēri, also known as Mukin-zēri, was the chief of the Chaldean Amukanu tribe of southern Babylonia, called Bīt-Amukanu in the Babylonian chronicle. He took advantage of the instability that followed the revolt against Nabû-nādin-zēri, deposing the revolt's leader, Nabû-šuma-ukîn II, and seizing the throne for himself. His name is written in cuneiform as mdAG-DU-NUMUN, and the Ptolemaic Canon gives it as Chinzēros.

Much of what is known of his reign comes from a cache of diplomatic letters found in 1952 by archaeologists led by Max Mallowan in the Northwest Palace at Kalhu, modern Nimrud. Of more than three hundred tablets, over twenty letters and fragments concern Babylonia, and they show a land split by rivalries among Aramaic, Babylonian and Chaldean factions. One reports a mission by two Assyrian officers, Šamaš-bunaya and Nabû-namir, who had to address the elders of Babylon outside the city gates, in view of Nabû-mukin-zēri's representative Asinu, urging them that only the Assyrian king could uphold their civic privileges.

The invasion of 731 BCE by Tiglath-pileser III drove him from Babylon to his southern stronghold of Šapia, where he held out while the Assyrians devastated the surrounding land and cut down its date palms. Other Chaldean leaders paid tribute, among them Marduk-apla-iddina II of the Bīt-Yakin and Balassu of the Bīt-Dakuri, while Zakiru of the Bīt-Ša'alli was taken to Assyria in chains and Nabû-ušabši of the Bīt-Šilani was impaled. Nippur and Dilbat sided with Assyria, and Dilbat suffered reprisals from his allies among the religious establishment of Babylon.

Fear of the usurper kept some Assyrian sympathisers from helping the invaders or accepting their offers of amnesty, and the Assyrian cavalry commander Iasubaya reported that he had failed to draw the Arameans away from him. Nabû-mukin-zēri answered Assyrian propaganda by trying to divide their allies, reminding Marduk-apla-iddina of the changing fortunes of his uncle Balassu.

The Chronicle on the Reigns from Nabû-Nasir to Šamaš-šuma-ukin records that in the third year the Assyrian king came down to Akkad, ravaged Bīt-Amukanu and captured Nabû-mukin-zēri. A contemporary letter to Tiglath-pileser III gives a different end, reporting that Mukin-zēri and his son Šumu-ukin had both been killed and the city conquered. Tiglath-pileser then took the throne of Babylon himself and presided over two successive Akītu festivals, as Assyria annexed the region around 730 BCE.
nadaun: Nadaun lies on the banks of the Beas in the foothills of the Sivalik range, at an average elevation of 508 metres, midway between Jwalamukhi, 12 km away, and Hamirpur, 28 km away. It borders the districts of Kangra and Una. Its climate is sub-tropical, with monsoon rains in July and August and summer temperatures that rarely exceed 40 degrees Celsius.

In the 1690s, when Aurangzeb's expeditions in the Deccan had strained the Mughal treasury, he ordered the defaulting rulers of the Shivalik hills to pay their annual tribute, and Alif Khan was sent to collect it from Kangra and its neighbours. The king of Kangra and Raja Dayal submitted, but Bhim Chand of Kahlur (Bilaspur) refused and formed an alliance of chieftains, supported by the 10th Sikh guru, Guru Gobind Singh. Alif Khan's army was defeated at Nadaun; authors date the battle variously, from 1687 to 4 April 1691. Guru Gobind Singh stayed at Nadaun for eight days before returning to Anandpur.

The poet Bulleh Shah called Nadaun the City of Innocent and is said to have coined the saying Aaye Nadaun, Jaaye Kaun: who comes to Nadaun would never want to go back. The Amtar-Nadaun Fort served as the summer court of Maharaja Sansar Chand of Kangra. Later Maharaja Ranjit Singh built a gurdwara where the Guru had pitched his tent, and granted Nadaun, previously part of the princely state of Kangra, as a jagir to Jodhbir Chand.

Nadaun is a Nagar Parishad in the Hamirpur district and a wholesale market town on the national highways NH 3 and NH 303, with 4,440 inhabitants at the 2011 census. The gurdwara on the Beas, affiliated to the Shiromani Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee in 1935, is a major site of Sikh pilgrimage. Its oldest school, GSSS Nadaun (Boys), Lala Lajpat Rai Samark, was established in 1863.
nader-shah: Nader was born in the fortress of Dastgerd in the northern valleys of Khorasan. He belonged to the semi-nomadic Qirqlu clan of the Turkoman Afshars, one of the seven Qizilbash tribes that had helped the Safavid dynasty establish its power. His father, Emam Qoli, was a herdsman who may also have been a coatmaker. When Nader was about 13 his father died, and he supported his mother by gathering firewood for the market. At 15 he enlisted as a musketeer for a governor and rose to be his right-hand man.

The Safavid state was in decline when the Ghilzai Afghans under Mahmud Hotaki defeated a force at the Battle of Gulnabad in 1722 and starved Isfahan into surrender. The Ottomans and Russians seized territory. In Khorasan Nader built up a small army, and he joined the cause of Tahmasp II, the son of the deposed shah, who made him chief of his army. In late 1726 Nader recaptured Mashhad. In 1729 he defeated the Abdali Afghans near Herat and the Ghilzai shah Ashraf at Damghan and Murchakhort, and in December he entered Isfahan and handed it to Tahmasp.

In 1730 Nader attacked the Ottomans and regained most of the lost territory, but Tahmasp then lost these gains and ceded Georgia and Armenia. Nader denounced the treaty, and in 1732 forced Tahmasp to abdicate in favour of his baby son Abbas III, for whom Nader became regent.

In January 1736 a great assembly on the Moghan plain, modelled on the qoroltai of Genghis Khan and Timur, agreed that Nader should be king. He was crowned Shah of Iran on 8 March 1736. He tried to bring Iran nearer to the Sunni states by replacing the Safavid Shia state religion with what he called the Ja'fari school, hoping the Ottomans would accept it as a fifth school of Sunni law; they refused, but allowed Iranian pilgrims to make the hajj. He minted silver coins called Naderi and paid his troops on time.

In 1738 he destroyed the last Hotaki seat at Kandahar and then invaded the Mughal Empire, taking Ghazni, Kabul, Peshawar and Lahore. In June 1747, convinced that his personal guard meant to kill him, he ordered them arrested, but the plan leaked and conspirators assassinated him in his tent at Quchan. His empire quickly broke up and Iran fell into civil war. His grandson Shahrokh Shah was the last of his line to rule and was deposed in 1796 by Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar.
nader-shahs-invasion-of-india: By the end of 1736 Nader Shah had secured his rule over Iran, and he then turned on the Ghilji Afghans of Hussain Hotak, taking Kandahar after camping at his new city of Naderabad. The Mughal Empire had fragmented since Aurangzeb's death in 1707 into kingdoms whose rulers owed only nominal allegiance to Muhammad Shah, while the Marathas under Bajirao I were expanding. Historians differ on Nader's motives: Laurence Lockhart points to famine and near-bankruptcy in Persia after years of war, and Michael Axworthy argues that he needed respite and money to pay his army before renewing war with the Ottomans.

Nader told the Mughals he was only pursuing fugitive Afghans. Ghazni submitted, and Kabul's citadel capitulated on 19 June after a week's siege. When his envoy to the Mughal court was murdered, his army sacked Jalalabad on 7 September. In November it destroyed the 20,000 tribal levies of Nasir Khan, the Mughal governor of Kabul, at the Khyber Pass and took Peshawar. It bridged the Indus at Attock, crossed the Chenab on 8 January 1739 and defeated the Mughals at the Battle of Karnal on 24 February. Muhammad Shah surrendered, and Nader entered Delhi on 20 March.

After a quarrel over prices and a rumour that Nader had been assassinated, rioters killed 3,000 of his troops on the night of 21 March. Next morning he ordered a general massacre. In about six hours some 20,000 to 30,000 men, women and children were killed, according to estimates, and a representative of the Dutch East India Company reported some 10,000 women and children taken as slaves.

Delhi was fined 20 million rupees, and Nader took the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor and Darya-i-Noor diamonds. Before leaving on 16 May 1739 he gave back to Muhammad Shah the lands east of the Indus. On the way home Sikhs attacked his heavily laden army, seized booty and freed captives. Free in the east, he turned west against the Ottomans. Axworthy argues that the campaign showed the East India Company how weak the Mughal Empire was.
nadine-gordimer: Nadine Gordimer was born on 20 November 1923 near Springs, an East Rand mining town outside Johannesburg, the second daughter of Jewish parents. Her father, Isidore, was a Lithuanian Jewish watchmaker who had emigrated at 13, and her mother, Hannah, came from London. The household was secular. Her father's experience as a refugee from Tsarist Russia helped form her political identity, but he was not an activist, whereas her mother, concerned about the poverty and discrimination faced by black people, founded a crèche for black children. As a teenager Gordimer saw police raid the family home and confiscate letters and diaries from a servant's room.

She was largely kept at home as a child, because her mother feared that she had a weak heart. Isolated, she began to write early and published her first children's story in 1937, at the age of 13; her first adult fiction appeared when she was 16.

Gordimer studied for a year at the University of the Witwatersrand, where she mixed for the first time with fellow professionals across the colour bar, and moved to Johannesburg in 1948. Her first collection, Face to Face, appeared in 1949. The New Yorker accepted a story in 1951 and began a long relationship that brought her work to a larger public, and her first novel, The Lying Days, was published in 1953. She married the art dealer Reinhold Cassirer in 1954, and the marriage lasted until his death in 2001.

The arrest of her friend Bettie du Toit in 1960 and the Sharpeville massacre drew her into the anti-apartheid movement. She joined the African National Congress while it was banned, was close to the lawyers defending Nelson Mandela, and helped him edit his speech from the dock, I Am Prepared to Die. She won the Booker Prize for The Conservationist in 1974. Burger's Daughter was banned under apartheid. She was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1991, the first South African and the first African woman to receive it, and later worked for HIV/AIDS causes. She died in her sleep at her Johannesburg home on 13 July 2014, aged 90.

Almost all of Gordimer's work deals with love and politics, above all with race in South Africa. She questions power relations and truth and tells the stories of ordinary people, revealing moral ambiguities, and her characters are shown more through their choices than through their claimed beliefs. The Lying Days is a semi-autobiographical Bildungsroman set in her home town, and Occasion for Loving of 1963 sets a love between a white woman and a black man against South African law, which criminalised such relationships. In 1985 Joseph Lelyveld observed that her work won great acclaim overseas but that reactions in South Africa were mixed.
naditu: The word nadītu comes from the Akkadian verb nadû, to throw down or to leave a field fallow, and has been read as fallow in the sense of a barren woman. It could be written with the Sumerogram LUKUR, which once designated a kind of priestess, but nothing shows that the lukur of the third millennium BCE had a comparable role, and the class most likely arose from social and economic changes of the Old Babylonian period. Tonia Sharlach compares the nadītu to medieval nuns and Marten Stol calls them nuns, while Katrin De Graef argues that the Akkadian word is better kept.

At Sippar women usually entered the cloister at about fifteen, after their family guaranteed in writing to provide for them. At a ceremony for Shamash a rope sacred to the god was placed on the initiate's arm, and she took a new name such as Amat-Šamaš, servant of Shamash. They came from many cities and ranks, among them daughters of Sumu-la-El, Sin-Muballit and Zimri-Lim and a sister of Hammurabi, though royal women held no higher rank. A nadītu brought a dowry that returned to her family at her death, which may have helped secure her brothers' inheritance. Adopted daughters, often freed slaves, cared for their mothers in return for becoming their heirs.

Many nadītu reached old age, perhaps because their seclusion spared them epidemics, and school texts in their houses suggest some could read. Some were left without enough food and appealed to the king.

Other cities had nadītu of their own: those of Ninurta at Nippur and of Zababa at Kish did not marry, while the nadītu of Marduk, found from Babylon to Larsa and Suhu, lived outside seclusion and could marry, under rules set out in the Code of Hammurabi. The cloister at Sippar, once thought abandoned under Samsuiluna, continued under Samsuditana. Its decline probably followed the economic troubles of Abi-Eshuh's reign and the impoverishment left by the wars fought between 1914 and 1727 BCE.
naemul-of-silla: Naemul, whose name can also be read Namul or Namil, was the 17th ruler of Silla. He was the son of Kim Mal-gu, a half-brother of King Michu, and of Queen Hyurye of the Kim clan, and the grandson of Kim Gudo Galmunwang. He married Michu's eldest daughter, Lady Boban. The Samguk sagi gives him the title isageum, borne by earlier rulers, while the Samguk yusa calls him maripgan, the title of later kings. Because the Chinese Book of Jin also uses the characters for maripgan when speaking of him, the title is usually thought to have begun with him.

Naemul is the first Silla king named in the Book of Jin. His reign appears to have seen a great influx of Chinese culture, and the widespread use of Chinese characters seems to date from his time. In 381 he sent a tribute mission under the envoy Widu to the king of Early Jin, travelling with Goguryeo's help; asked by its ruler Fu Jian, Widu explained that the name of his country had changed to Silla.

His later years were troubled by repeated invasions by the Wa of Japan and the northern Malgal tribes, beginning with a massive Japanese incursion in 364 that was repulsed with great loss of life. In 392 Silla allied with Goguryeo, sending Naemul's cousin Silseong there. The Japanese besieged the capital in 393; Silla won at Doksan, probably in present-day northern Pohang, in 394, but its army was destroyed in 395.

In 400 and 401 the alliance of Goguryeo and Silla fought the allied forces of Imna and Japan, and Silla held off Baekje only with the help of Gwanggaeto the Great. When Naemul died in 402 his sons were too young to rule, and the throne passed to Silseong, who returned from Goguryeo. One of those sons later reigned as King Nulji from 417 to 458.
nafpaktos: Nafpaktos lies on a bay on the north coast of the Gulf of Corinth, 3 km west of the mouth of the river Mornos. It is 9 km north-east of Antirrio and 18 km north-east of Patras. The ancient name Naupaktos means boatyard, from the Greek for ship and for to fix. Venetians called it Lepanto, and the Ottomans İnebahtı.

In Greek legend the Heraclidae built the fleet here with which they invaded the Peloponnese. In antiquity it was a town of the Locri Ozolae with the best harbour on the northern coast of the gulf. After the Greco-Persian Wars it fell to the Athenians, who settled there the Messenians forced out after the Third Messenian War in 464 BCE. It was the Athenian headquarters in western Greece during the Peloponnesian War and the scene of the Battle of Naupactus in 429 BCE. Philip II of Macedon gave it to the Aetolians, who defended it against the Romans for two months in 191 BCE. An earthquake destroyed it in 551/2.

From the late 9th century it was capital of the Byzantine thema of Nicopolis, and a harbour of the Byzantine navy. In 1165 Benjamin of Tudela found a Jewish community of about 100 there. After the Fourth Crusade it became part of the Despotate of Epirus, and in 1294 it was ceded to Philip I, Prince of Taranto, as part of the dowry of Thamar Angelina Komnene. It passed to the Catalans of the Duchy of Athens in 1361 and to the Albanian despot John Bua Spata in 1376 or 1377. Paul Spata sold it to the Republic of Venice in 1407.

After 1449 it was an isolated Venetian exclave in Ottoman territory, and Venice built strong fortifications. It fell to the Ottomans in 1499 during the Second Ottoman-Venetian War. In 1521 the town had 509 Christian, 84 Jewish and 28 Roma households. The Battle of Lepanto was fought at the mouth of the gulf on 7 October 1571, when Spanish, Papal and Venetian forces nearly destroyed Ottoman naval power; Miguel de Cervantes fought in it. Venice held the town again from 1687 to 1699, when the Treaty of Karlowitz returned it to the Ottomans. It became part of independent Greece in March 1829.

Nafpaktos had about 19,768 people at the 2011 census. Its main attraction is the port and the castle, both with Venetian remains, and the port has monuments to the Battle of Lepanto and a statue of Cervantes by the Mallorcan artist Jaume Mir. The Fethiye Mosque is the town's largest Ottoman-era mosque.
nafplio: Nafplio lies on the Argolic Gulf in the northeast Peloponnese, and most of its old town stands on a peninsula that forms a naturally protected bay. The city was originally almost isolated by marshes, and landfill projects, mostly since the 1970s, have nearly doubled its land area. The oldest reference to the town may be in the Aegean List of the mortuary temple of Amenhotep III, dated to the 14th century BCE, which records it as npry. In antiquity it was Nauplia, and under the Venetians it was called Napoli di Romania, to tell it from Naples.

In antiquity Nauplia was first independent of Argos and a member of the maritime confederacy that met on the island of Calaureia. About the time of the Second Messenian War it was conquered by the Argives, and from then on appears in history only as the seaport of Argos. By the time of Pausanias, in the 2nd century, the place was deserted.

In the Middle Ages it became a place of considerable importance, and in the time of the Crusades it first emerges from obscurity. It was taken in 1212 by French Crusaders of the Principality of Achaea and became part of the lordship of Argos and Nauplia, which was sold in 1388 to the Republic of Venice, who regarded it as one of their most important places in the Levant.

Under Venetian rule the city twice repelled Ottoman sieges, first by Mehmed the Conqueror during the war of 1463 to 1479, then by Suleiman. It surrendered to the Ottomans in 1540, who renamed it Mora Yenişehri and made it the seat of a sanjak. The Venetians retook it in 1685 and made it the capital of their Kingdom of the Morea, building the castle of Palamidi, but only 80 soldiers defended it and the Ottomans retook it in 1715. During the Greek War of Independence the town was a major Ottoman stronghold, besieged for over a year and finally surrendered by starvation. Forces under Staikopoulos and Kolokotronis captured Palamidi in November 1822.

Count Ioannis Kapodistrias, first head of state of liberated Greece, first set foot on the mainland at Nafplio on 7 January 1828. He was assassinated on 9 October 1831 by members of the Mavromichalis family on the steps of the church of Saint Spyridon. Nafplio remained the capital of the Kingdom of Greece under King Otto until 1834, when he moved the capital to Athens. The old town keeps its architecture influenced by the Venetians and the fortresses of Acronauplia, Palamidi and the Bourtzi in the harbour. Tourism developed after the Greek Civil War, and the city is capital of the regional unit of Argolis.
naftaly-frenkel: Accounts of Frenkel's background differ widely. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn called him a Turkish Jew born in Constantinople; others made him a Hungarian manufacturer, or a native of Odessa, Austria or the land of Israel, and the Finnish communist Arvo Tuominen, who met him in 1933, claimed he was related to the Swedish-speaking Finnish family of the Frenckells. In the Soviet Union he described himself as a merchant. His arrest in 1923 for illegally crossing borders covered smuggling, or perhaps being too successful a merchant, and he was sent to the camps of the Solovetsky Islands, known by the acronym SLON.

How he rose is unclear. One story has him posting a detailed critique of the camp's industries in the complaints box, which reached Genrikh Yagoda. By November 1924 the administration was asking for his early release, granted in 1927. Solzhenitsyn credits him with inventing the you-eat-as-you-work system, while many historians treat tales of his power as legend; Anne Applebaum wrote that he found a way to turn a prison camp into an apparently profitable economic institution. Under the scale those fit for heavy work received 800 grams of bread and 80 grams of meat, and invalids half that.

Frenkel dropped re-education, closed the camp journals and put criminal and political prisoners to work side by side on road building and tree felling. His Economic-Commercial Department outbid a civilian forestry undertaking in Karelia, angering the local authorities, though in 1929 the camp in fact ran a deficit of 1.6 million roubles. Fellow communists accused him of running a personal network of spies, and one commander admitted he had thought of murdering him. From November 1931 he managed the daily work on the White Sea–Baltic Canal, using many prisoners brought from Solovetsky.

While nearly all his former colleagues died in the purges, Frenkel was protected at the highest level, apparently by Stalin; when 48 Trotskyists were arrested at BAMlag in 1938 his case was delayed in Moscow. As a protégé of Lavrentiy Beria he headed railway construction, received the Order of Lenin three times and was discharged for ill health on 28 April 1947. He lived reclusively in Moscow in the 1950s and died in 1960.
nafud: The Nafud occupies a great oval depression in the northern part of the Arabian Peninsula. It is 290 kilometres long and 225 kilometres wide, covering about 65,000 square kilometres. It is an erg, a region of sand, noted for sudden violent winds that form large crescent-shaped dunes, and its sand is a brick-reddish colour. Rain falls once or twice a year. In some lowland areas near the Hejaz Mountains there are oases where dates, vegetables, barley and fruits are grown.

A corridor of gravel plains and sand dunes called the Dahna, about 1,287 kilometres long and 24 to 80 kilometres wide, joins the Nafud to the Rub' al Khali. One description places its beginning at the city of Tayma and extends it about 450 kilometres eastward.

In 2016 an 85,000-year-old fossilised human finger found in the Nafud by Mathieu Duval of Griffith University gave the earliest evidence of modern humans outside Africa and the Levant. The desert is thought to have been relatively inhabited between the Last Glacial Maximum and the end of the Pleistocene. Camel engravings at Jebel Misma and Jebel Arnaan in northern Saudi Arabia point to a seasonal human presence and to exchanges with Levantine groups between 12,800 and 11,400 years ago.

In 1917, during the Arab Revolt, forces led by Auda ibu Tayi attacked the Turkish-held port of Aqaba on its poorly defended eastern flank, by a long desert route that passed close to the edge of the Nafud. Colonel T. E. Lawrence asked Auda to let the group stray into the Nafud, but Auda refused because it was unnecessary. Their harsh journey therefore did not enter it, although the film Lawrence of Arabia shows otherwise.
nafusa-mountains: The Nafusa Mountains form the boundary between the Libyan coastal plain, the Jafara, to the north and the Tripolitanian Plateau to the south. The plateau's strata tilt upwards towards the north, so that its highest portion rises to over 750 m and ends abruptly in an escarpment with up to 350 m of topographic prominence. The range extends about 250 km, from just east of Gharyan, some 60 km south of Tripoli, to Wazzin at the Tunisian border, and is rarely more than 25 km deep. The mountain villages raise goats, olives and grain.

The mountains supported agriculture without significant interruption from the pre-Roman period onward. The inhabitants, originally entirely Berber and living in nucleated communities because water was scarce, built wadi walls that allowed olives and grain to be grown. In the Roman imperial period the range held agricultural settlements and fortified farms, and mausolea such as Henscir Suffit and Henscir al-Ausaf can still be seen. Evidence for Christian and Byzantine occupation is sparse.

After the great Berber Revolt of the 8th century, Ibadi missionaries who had fled the Umayyad Caliphate took refuge in the mountains and organised the Nafusa into a fighting force. Under Imam Abu al-Khattab al-Ma'afari they captured Tripoli in 757 and Kairouan in 758, but the Abbasid governor of Egypt defeated them at Tawergha in 761. The mountains themselves stayed unconquered, and through the 9th century the Ibadi kept an independent republic there, in close alliance with the Rustamid dynasty at Tiaret.

In 880 the Nafusa destroyed an invading Egyptian army of the Tulunids. In 896-97 the Aghlabid emir Ibrahim II defeated them at Manu, south of Gabès, and executed the prisoners as heretics, ending the imamate; Tahert fell shortly after, in 911. Ibadi Islam nevertheless remained strong, if clandestine, among the Berbers of the mountains for centuries afterwards.
nag-hammadi-library: Scholars first learned of the library in 1946. Jean Doresse, inquiring from 1947 to 1950, found that a local farmer, then a teenager, had dug the texts out of a graveyard in the desert near tombs of the Sixth Dynasty of Egypt. In the 1970s James Robinson sought out the farmer, who told a complex story involving a blood feud, digging for fresh soil and a sealed jar that he hesitated to break for fear of a jinn. Later scholars have suggested that the find began as grave robbing and that the fuller story was a cover.

Most of the tracts passed to Phokion J. Tanos, a Cypriot antiques dealer in Cairo, and then to the Department of Antiquities, which kept them from being sold abroad. After the revolution of 1952 they were handed to the Coptic Museum and declared national property. A single codex was sold to a Belgian dealer and acquired in 1951 by the Carl Gustav Jung Institute in Zurich as a birthday present for Jung. It is known as the Jung Codex, or Codex I, and reached Cairo only in 1975.

The codices are written in Coptic. Their 52 treatises are mostly Gnostic, with three works of the Corpus Hermeticum and a partial translation or alteration of Plato's Republic. The best known is the Gospel of Thomas, of which they hold the only complete text. Fragments of its sayings of Jesus had been found at Oxyrhynchus in 1898, and most interpreters date its composition to the second century, though some propose an earlier or later date. The buried manuscripts themselves belong to the third and fourth centuries.

The so-called Codex XIII is not a codex but eight leaves of the Trimorphic Protennoia, removed from a thirteenth book and tucked inside the front cover of the sixth. Not all scholars agree that the whole library is Gnostic: Paterson Brown has argued that the Gospels of Thomas, Philip and Truth cannot be so labelled.

James Robinson suggested that the codices belonged to a nearby Pachomian monastery and were buried after Athanasius condemned non-canonical books in his Festal Letter of 367. Lundhaug and Jenott expanded this view, and Linjamaa argued in 2024 that a small monastic elite used the books as part of a wider Christian library.

Publication was slow until the Messina Congress of 1966. A facsimile edition in twelve volumes appeared between 1972 and 1977, and Robinson's The Nag Hammadi Library in English followed in 1977, with a revised third edition in 1988.
nagabhata-i: The Gwalior inscription of his descendant Mihira Bhoja names Nagabhata as the founder of the imperial Pratihara line and traces the family to the hero Lakshmana. The date of his accession is unknown: his grand-nephew Vatsaraja ruled in Avanti in 783-784 CE, and allowing 25 years a generation, historians place Nagabhata's accession around 730. Historians such as R. C. Majumdar and Baij Nath Puri hold that Ujjain was the dynasty's original home. Dasharatha Sharma instead identified Nagabhata with Nāhada, whom a medieval Jain chronicle calls a soldier of fortune who made Jābālipura, identified with Jalor, his capital.

The Gwalior inscription credits Nagabhata with repelling an invasion of mlechchhas, identified with the Umayyad Arab Muslims. The 9th-century historian Al-Baladhuri lists the conquests of the Arab generals of Sindh, led by Junayd ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Murri or Al Hakam ibn Awana, but says only that Ujjain was invaded, apparently a tacit admission of failure. The historian R. V. Somani suggests that the Guhila ruler Bappa Rawal joined an anti-Arab confederacy formed by Nagabhata.

Nagabhata appears to have been defeated by the Rashtrakuta ruler Dantidurga. The Sanjan inscription of Amoghavarsha says that during a ceremony Dantidurga held at Ujjain, the Lord of Gurjara served him as pratihara, or door-keeper, a play on the dynasty's name. Several historians, among them D. R. Bhandarkar, identify him with Nagavaloka, the overlord named in the Hansot inscription of 756 CE; if so, he regained his power and ruled the area around Bharuch through a Chahamana vassal, perhaps taking it from the Chalukya feudatory Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin.

By the identification with Nagavaloka, Nagabhata ruled until around 760. The Gwalior inscription suggests that he was followed by Kakustha and Devaraja, sons of an unnamed brother, and the line passed to his grand-nephew Vatsaraja. An inscription of 795 by Gallaka, a subordinate of Vatsaraja, praises Nagabhata I for his victory over the invincible Gurjaras.
nagaland: Nagaland lies in the north-eastern region of India and is bordered by Arunachal Pradesh to the north, Assam to the west, Manipur to the south and the Naga Self-Administered Zone of the Sagaing Region of Myanmar to the east. It is a mountainous state of 16,579 square kilometres. It consists of 17 administrative districts and is inhabited by 17 major tribes, each distinct in customs, language and dress. The origin of the word Naga is unclear.

The early history of the Nagas is unclear. Ethnic groups migrated at different times and established their own mountain territories and village states. The first Europeans to enter the Naga Hills were Captain Francis Jenkins and Lieutenant Robert Pemberton in 1832. The British recorded ten military expeditions between 1839 and 1850 to stop raids on tea estates and trading posts. At the Battle of Kikrüma in February 1851 people died on both sides, after which the British adopted a policy of non-interference.

In 1944 the Japanese Army, with the Indian National Army, invaded from Burma and tried to take India through Kohima. The battle was fought from 4 April to 22 June 1944, coordinated with action at Imphal, and British and Indian troops repelled the attackers. After Indian independence the Naga National Council under Zapu Phizo demanded an independent Naga state and began an armed insurgency, and the Indian Army was sent in 1955. The State of Nagaland was formally inaugurated on 1 December 1963 as the 16th state of the Indian Union.

Nagaland had a population of 1,980,602 at the 2011 census. Kohima is the capital. The Naga people form over 90 percent of the population and speak mostly Sino-Tibetan languages. English is the official language and the medium of education, and Nagamese, a creole based on Assamese, is widely spoken. At the 2011 census 87.93 percent of residents were Christian, and Nagaland is known as the most Baptist state in the world.
nagao-clan: The Nagao traced their descent from the warrior lord Taira no Yoshifumi of the Kammu Heishi, the Taira line descended from Emperor Kammu, the 50th emperor of Japan. They counted among the Bando Hachi Heishi, the eight Taira clans of the Kanto region, with the Chiba, Miura, Kazusa, Doi, Chichibu, Oba and Kajiwara. The family name began when Kagehiro settled on the Nagao estate in Sagami Province and took its name.

The Nagao served the Uesugi clan as head retainers and held the office of shugodai, deputy governor, in Echigo, Kozuke and Musashi provinces. They divided into several branches. The Kamakura Nagao, named after the city where they lived, were lords of Kanno castle, and a junior member, Nagao Masanaga, settled in the Koshigeyama area and became lord of Tatebayashi castle.

The Shirai Nagao were deputy governors of Kozuke and Musashi and held the castles of Aomi, Hachigata and Shirai. The Echigo Nagao were deputy governors of Echigo, where they built and held Kasugayama Castle and its surrounding fief, in what is now Niigata Prefecture.

Nagao Tamekage, who died in 1536, was succeeded that year by his elder son Nagao Harukage. His younger son, Nagao Kagetora, became lord of Kasugayama in 1548. Adopted by Uesugi Norimasa, he took the name Uesugi Kenshin and in effect became head of the Uesugi clan. Kenshin's half-sister Aya-Gozen was the mother of Uesugi Kagekatsu, and her daughter Seien-in married Uesugi Kagetora. Nagao Fujikage fought under Kenshin at the fourth battle of Kawanakajima in 1561.
nagapattinam: Nagapattinam lies on the Bay of Bengal, on a plain of alluvial soil of sand, silt and clay, bounded on the south by the Uppanar river. It is about 300 kilometres from Chennai. The Vettar River and tributaries of the Kaveri are the main water bodies, and paddy is the chief crop of the region. The climate is tropical savanna, with a wet season from August to December brought by the northeast monsoon, and the town is in a cyclone-prone zone.

The name comes from Nagar, a reference to people from Sri Lanka who settled here, and pattinam, 'town'. Ptolemy mentions it as Nikam, one of the most important trade centres of the ancient Tamil country, and the poets Appar and Sambandar call it Nagai in the Tevaram.

Urn burials from the Sangam period show early habitation. The Tevaram poets of the 7th century describe a town with fortified walls and a busy port, and inscriptions suggest that the Kayarohanaswami Temple was begun under the Pallava king Narasimha Pallava II (691–729 CE). The town came to prominence under the Medieval Cholas and was their important port and a gateway for eastern naval expeditions; all those of Rajendra Chola I (1012–44) went through it. In the 11th century the Sailendra king of Srivijaya, Sri Mara Vijayattungavarman, built the Chudamani Vihara, a Buddhist monastery, with the patronage of Rajaraja Chola I.

The Portuguese made commercial contacts in the early 16th century and set up a commercial centre in 1554, and also carried on missionary work. Under an agreement with the Nayak king of Thanjavur the Dutch received ten villages from the Portuguese, built ten churches and a hospital, and issued pagoda coins with the town's name in Tamil. Nagapattinam became the capital of Dutch Coromandel.

After naval battles between British and French fleets off the coast, the East India Company took it from the Dutch in 1781, and a peace in 1784 formally ceded it. It was the headquarters of Tanjore district from 1799 to 1845 and became a municipality in 1866. The Great Southern of India Railway had its headquarters there from 1861 to 1875.

Nagapattinam is a city in Tamil Nadu and the headquarters of Nagapattinam district, created in 1991. It had 102,905 inhabitants in the census of 2011. Fishing in the Bay of Bengal is the main occupation, alongside trade and tourism. The Soundararajaperumal Temple, a Divya Desam of Vishnu, and the Kayarohanaswami Temple of Shiva are major pilgrimage sites, and the town is a base for visiting Nagore and Velankanni. The tsunami of 26 December 2004 struck the district severely.
nagara-river: The Nagara River rises in the city of Gujō in Gifu Prefecture and reaches the sea at Kuwana in Mie Prefecture. Together with the Kiso and Ibi rivers it is one of the Kiso Three Rivers of the Nōbi Plain. It was formerly called the Sunomata River. Over a length of 166 km it drains an area of 1,985 square kilometres in the Chūbu region before emptying into Ise Bay, and the government of Japan classifies it as a Class 1 river. It passes through or forms the boundary of communities including Gujō, Mino, Seki, Gifu, Ōgaki and Kuwana.

Downstream the Nagara converges with the Kiso and Ibi rivers and diverges from them several times. It belongs to the Kiso River system, but construction projects over the years have kept the rivers apart all the way to the mouth. Other works changed its flow too. Until the Shōwa period two minor rivers branched from it in the middle of Gifu, but construction in 1939 created the present course, and about 160 hectares of land were recovered. The Gifu Memorial Center, schools and other buildings now stand on it.

The river is known for clear water and is one of the Three Clear-Flowing Rivers in Japan, with the Kakita River in Shizuoka Prefecture and the Shimanto River in Kōchi Prefecture. Its middle section was included in 1985 in a national list of 100 waters. Nagaragawa Onsen, a group of hot springs mostly in Gifu with a high iron content, draws visitors.

Cormorant fishing, an ancient tradition in which cormorants catch fish, takes place on the river at Gifu, where it is called Cormorant Fishing on the Nagara River, and at Seki, where it is called Oze Cormorant Fishing. Eleven other places in Japan also host cormorant fishing, but only the fishing masters on the Nagara are Imperial Fishermen of the Household Agency.
nagarakretagama: The poem is a kakawin, written by a Buddhist cleric under the pen-name Prapañca and dated in its own closing lines to the month of Aśwayuja in Śaka 1287, 1365 CE. It belongs to the puja sastra, the Old Javanese literature of adoration, and often invokes a divine quality in the king and his family, yet Prapañca seems to have written it incognito after he had retired from the court. He named it Deśavarṇana, Description of Districts. The title Nagarakṛtāgama, Complete Doctrine of the State, appears only in a colophon of one manuscript line, copied in East Bali in 1740 by a scribe called Artha Pamasah.

Cantos 13 and 14 name the lands the king claimed, from Jambi, Palembang and Samudra on Sumatra to Barune (Brunei) and Solot (Sulu), Pahang, Kedah and Tumasik, where Singapore now stands, and east to Bali, Makassar, Banda, Ambon, the Onin peninsula and Timor. The poem describes the capital: a palace ringed by a thick, high wall of red brick, a north gate with doors of decorated iron, courtyards of religious buildings and servants' houses, and beyond them the compound of the chief minister Gajah Mada.

It tells of the royal walkabout, in which the family visited places of the realm and honoured the king's ancestors, and of Hayam Wuruk's worship at Candi Singhasari for his great-grandfather Kertanegara. A seven-day sraddha ceremony for the soul of the Queen Grandmother Gayatri Rajapatni, who had died twelve years before, ends with her deification as Prajnaparamita. Kertanegara is deified as a Shiva-Buddha, joining the gods of Hinduism and Buddhism into one Lord of the Mountains.

The text survived in palm-leaf manuscripts found in Bali and Lombok. In 1894 a Dutch East Indies military expedition destroyed the palace of Mataram-Cakranagara on Lombok and took a manuscript as part of the Lombok treasure. The Dutch philologist J.L.A. Brandes, who accompanied the expedition, is credited with saving the royal library from burning, and his edition of 1902 fixed the title Nagarakṛtāgama in scholarship.

Kept at Leiden University, the manuscript was given back to Indonesia during President Suharto's state visit to the Netherlands in 1970 and is held by the National Library of Indonesia. After its translation in the early 20th century the poem became an inspiration for the Indonesian independence movement, and UNESCO placed it on the Memory of the World register for Asia and the Pacific in 2008.
nagarjuna-sagar-dam: Survey work for a dam across the Krishna began in 1903, when the Nizam had British engineers start it. Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated construction on 10 December 1955, and work went on for twelve years under the engineering leadership of Kanuri Lakshmana Rao, entirely with local know-how. Raja Vasireddy Ramagopala Krishna Maheswara Prasad, known as the Muktyala Raja, lobbied for the project and donated land for it. The dam was the tallest masonry dam in the world at the time and the first of the major projects termed modern temples that were begun to achieve the Green Revolution in India.

The masonry dam is 124 metres tall from its deepest foundation and 1.6 kilometres long, with 26 flood gates, and is joined by an earth dam 3414 m long. Its reservoir has a gross storage capacity of 11.472 billion cubic metres. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi released water into the left and right bank canals on 4 August 1967. The right canal, the Jawahar canal, runs 203 km and the left, the Lalbahadur Shastri canal, 179 km, irrigating land in districts of present-day Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. The hydroelectric plant, its first unit commissioned on 7 March 1978 and its eighth on 24 December 1985, has a capacity of 815.6 MW.

The reservoir submerged 54 villages, 48 in Nalgonda and 6 in Guntur, and affected 24,000 people, whose relocation was completed by 2007. It also flooded Nagarjunakonda, the Buddhist settlement that had been the capital of the Ikshvaku dynasty in the 1st and 2nd centuries, where excavations yielded 30 Buddhist monasteries as well as artwork and inscriptions. The diversion of the river caused erosion of fluorine-rich volcanic rocks that contaminated groundwater in Nalgonda, shrank Kolleru Lake and brought salination to coastal land in Diviseema, and the Krishna ceased to be navigable. Between 1995 and 2004 a Krishna water project was built to carry water from the reservoir to Hyderabad.
nagarjunakonda: Coins of the later Satavahana kings and an inscription of Gautamiputra Vijaya Satakarni show that Buddhism had reached the region before the Ikshvaku kings. The site rose to importance in the first quarter of the 3rd century, when the Ikshvaku king Vashishthiputra Chamtamula made Vijayapuri his capital. The kings built temples to Shiva, Karttikeya and other gods, while their queens and lay women such as Bodhishri and Chandrashri paid for Buddhist monuments; Princess Chamtisiri funded the main stupa for ten years. The last Ikshvaku inscription dates from about 309 CE, and the Pallavas may have taken the territory by the 4th century.

In the 15th and 16th centuries a hill fortress, probably built by the Reddi rulers, made the place important again. A Gajapati inscription of 1491 records its commander, and in 1515 the Vijayanagara king Krishnadevaraya stormed it.

At its height the valley held more than thirty monasteries, the largest Buddhist centre in South India, with houses of several schools and of monks from Sri Lanka, Gandhara, Bengal, the Tamil kingdoms and China. The great stupa was 32.3 metres across and 18 metres high. Its reliefs belong to the Amaravati style. A palace area has rare secular reliefs, among them a figure of Dionysus, and Roman gold coins of Tiberius and Faustina the Elder point to trade with the Roman world. The inscriptions, in Prakrit and Sanskrit in the Brahmi script, are the earliest substantial Sanskrit inscriptions of South India.

A schoolteacher, Suraparaju Venkataramaih, reported an ancient pillar there in 1926. Excavations under A. H. Longhurst in 1927 to 1931 and T. N. Ramachandran in 1938 were followed in 1954 to 1960 by a rescue dig led by R. Subrahmanyam before the Nagarjuna Sagar Dam flooded the valley.

Monuments were moved to the top of the hill, now an island, where a museum was built in 1966, and others to the mainland east of the reservoir. The museum holds sculptures, coins, jewellery and stone tools, and many sculptures are in museums in Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata, Paris and New York. The island is reached by ferry.
nagarkurnool-district: Monuments and inscriptions found near the confluence of the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers show that the region has been inhabited since the Stone Age. The early Western Chalukya period lasted from about 535 to about 757 and the Rastrakuta period from 757 to 973; the Eruva Cholas also held it. The Krishna formed the southern boundary of the Kakatiya Empire, and the area later came under the Deccan sultanates. Local tradition holds that Gona Ganna Reddy, an agent of Rani Rudrama Devi, ruled from Nandi Vardhamana Puram, near Nagarkurnool.

The district covers 6,545 square kilometres of the central Deccan Plateau and the northern Nallamala Hills, a landscape of granite rocks and hills at an average elevation of 458 metres. Deccan thorn scrub and dry deciduous forests cover much of it, and the semi-arid climate leaves farming dependent on the monsoon. The Krishna runs along the southern border, and chains of linked lakes and ponds drain into the Dindubi river. The southern forests belong to the Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve, where the state has developed a jungle safari at Farahbad and river cottages near Somasila and Eegalapenta.

Agriculture is the mainstay of the economy, with paddy, maize and pulses, cotton and groundnut in places, and mango and citrus orchards, supported by the Kalwakurthy Lift Irrigation Scheme. Rice mills, seed processing and handloom weaving are the main small industries. The district has no railway, but national highways link Kalwakurthy with Hyderabad and Srisailam.

The town of Nagarkurnool is the headquarters of a district of four revenue divisions, Achampet, Nagarkurnool, Kalwakurthy and Kollapur, and 20 mandals. The 2011 census counted 861,766 people, about a fifth of them from Scheduled Castes and an eighth from Scheduled Tribes. Telugu is the mother tongue of most, followed by Lambadi and Urdu, and the great majority are Hindu.
nagasaki: The first recorded contact between Portuguese explorers and Japan came in 1543. In 1569 the daimyō Ōmura Sumitada granted a permit for a port for Portuguese ships at Nagasaki, set up in 1571 under the Jesuit missionary Gaspar Vilela. The harbour village grew into a diverse port city, and Portuguese imports such as tobacco and the sponge-cake castellas entered Japanese culture. In 1587 Toyotomi Hideyoshi placed it under his direct control and ordered the missionaries expelled, an order largely unenforced.

On Hideyoshi's order, twenty-six Catholics were crucified at Nagasaki in the following decade. Catholicism was officially banned in 1614, and a brutal persecution followed in which thousands of converts were killed, tortured or forced to renounce their faith. After the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637 the Portuguese were expelled, and the Dutch were moved from Hirado to Dejima, the artificial island in Nagasaki harbour that had been the Portuguese trading post. In 1720 the ban on Dutch books was lifted, and scholars flocked to Nagasaki to study European science and art, a movement called rangaku. Nagasaki became a treaty port in 1859 and later a centre of shipbuilding under Mitsubishi.

On 9 August 1945 the Boeing B-29 Bockscar, commanded by Major Charles Sweeney, carried a plutonium bomb called Fat Man from Tinian. Its primary target was Kokura, which was hidden by cloud and smoke, so it flew to the secondary target, Nagasaki, where cloud again obscured the city. A gap in the cloud let the crew see a racetrack, and they dropped the bomb on the Urakami Valley, between the Mitsubishi Steel and Arms Works and the Mitsubishi-Urakami Ordnance Works. It exploded at 11:02 a.m. at about 1,800 feet. The dead numbered 35,000, including 150 Japanese soldiers, 6,200 of the 7,500 employees of the Mitsubishi Munitions plant and 24,000 others, among them 2,000 Koreans.

Nagasaki is the capital and largest city of Nagasaki Prefecture, on Kyushu, and lies at the head of a long bay that forms the best natural harbour on the island. The city was rebuilt after the war, with new churches and temples, and a museum and memorials to the bombing; it remains primarily a port city with a shipbuilding industry. The Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
nagasena: According to Pali accounts, Nāgasena was born into a Brahmin family in the Himalayas and was well versed in the Vedas at an early age, before he turned to Buddhism. The Milindapañhā names his father as Soñuttara and his teachers as Rohana, Assagutta of Vattaniya and Āyupāla of Sankheyya near Sāgala. It says he learned the Tripiṭaka under the Greek Buddhist monk Dhammarakkhita near Pātaliputta, the modern Patna, and became an arhat under his guidance. He is described as a sage of the Sarvāstivāda school who lived around 150 BCE.

His exchanges with Menander I are recorded both in the Pali Milindapañhā and in the Sanskrit Nāgasenabhiksusūtra. Scholars agree almost universally that a core text was later expanded by many other authors, who followed the question and answer pattern of the early books. The version that survives is very long and shows signs of inconsistent authorship in its later volumes, and there is no agreed point at which Nāgasena's part ends and the work of other hands begins; monastic scholars have not regarded this as an important distinction.

Apart from the Milindapañhā, Nāgasena is known only from a Thai legend that credits him with the Emerald Buddha, said to have been made by him at Pātaliputta in 43 BCE and later brought to Thailand. In Mahayana Buddhism he is one of the Eighteen Arhats. Thangkas show him with a khakkhara, a monk's staff, in his right hand and a vase in his left, as on examples in the Cleveland Museum of Art and Singapore's Asian Civilisations Museum. Later statues often show a bald, elderly monk scratching his ear with a stick, a sign of the hearing kept pure for the truth.
nagorno-karabakh: Nagorno-Karabakh is a region of present-day Azerbaijan on the south-eastern stretch of the Lesser Caucasus. It forms part of the larger region of Karabakh, which lies between the rivers Kura and Araxes, and spans the area between Lower Karabakh and Syunik. Its terrain consists mostly of mountains and forest. The region is usually identified with the former Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast, which covered 4,400 square kilometres, although its historical extent is about 8,223 square kilometres. Urartian inscriptions of the 9th to 7th centuries BCE name it Urtekhini, and ancient Greek sources called it Orkhistene.

The region lies within the lands of the Kura-Araxes culture. Its ancient population was made up of local and migrant tribes, mostly non-Indo-European. According to the prevailing western theory they intermarried with Armenians who arrived after its inclusion in Armenia in the 2nd century BCE, or possibly the 4th; other scholars place Armenian settlement as early as the 7th century BCE. Arabs conquered the region in the mid 7th century. According to some sources the Armenian prince Sahl Smbatian revolted in 821 and founded the House of Khachen, which ruled Artsakh as a principality until the early 19th century. By 1000 the House of Khachen had proclaimed the Kingdom of Artsakh.

Karabakh became a Russian protectorate in 1805 by the Treaty of Kurekchay, and Persia ceded it to Russia by the Treaty of Gulistan in 1813. In 1823 the five districts corresponding roughly to the present region were 90.8% Armenian.
