After the October Revolution it passed into the Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic, which soon split into separate states, and from 1918 to 1920 Armenia and Azerbaijan fought a series of short wars over several regions, including this one.

On 13 February 1988 Karabakh Armenians began demonstrating in Stepanakert for unification with Armenia, and on 20 February the regional Soviet voted 110 to 17 to ask for the transfer. Moscow rejected the demand. Most of the region was governed by ethnic Armenians under the breakaway Republic of Artsakh from the end of the first Nagorno-Karabakh War in 1994, and talks mediated by the OSCE Minsk Group did not settle its status.

The region lies within the borders of Azerbaijan, on average about 1,100 metres above sea level, with steppe on the Kura lowland, forests of oak, hornbeam and beech on the lower slopes, and alpine meadows higher up. The Republic of Artsakh, which governed most of it from 1994, was formally dissolved on 1 January 2024.
nagorno-karabakh-autonomous-oblast: The area of Nagorno-Karabakh was disputed between the First Republic of Armenia and the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic during their short-lived independence from 1918 to 1920. After both became Soviet, the Kavbiuro of the Bolshevik Party decided to keep the area within the new Azerbaijan SSR while granting it broad regional autonomy.

At first the principal city of Karabakh, Shusha, and its surrounding villages were to be left out of the autonomy, since they were predominantly Azerbaijani, particularly after the massacre and expulsion of the majority Armenian population of Shusha. That decision was reversed in 1923, when Shusha was joined to the oblast despite protests from Muslim villages that favoured inclusion in the Kurdistan uezd instead. The oblast was formally established on 7 July 1923, and its capital was moved to Stepanakert, named after the revolutionary Stepan Shaumian.

At its formation the oblast covered 4,161 square kilometres. In the 1926 Soviet census its population was 125,200, of whom Armenians were 89.2 percent. By the 1989 census the Armenian share had fallen to 76.9 percent. The reasons given include a policy of Soviet Azerbaijani authorities to settle Azerbaijanis in the region, some out-migration of Karabakh Armenians, and a generally higher birth rate among Azerbaijanis than among Armenians.

The oblast had five districts: Mardakert, Martuni, Shusha, Askeran and Hadrut. Its highest executive power lay with the First Secretary of the oblast committee of the Communist Party of Azerbaijan, a post created in July 1923 and abolished on 27 August 1990.

The status of the oblast became a major public issue only in the late 1980s, but Karabakh Armenian activists, intellectuals and Soviet Armenian leaders had appealed to Moscow for its transfer to the Armenian SSR before. In November 1945 the Armenian First Secretary Grigory Arutinov appealed to Joseph Stalin, a proposal vetoed by Azerbaijan's Mir Jafar Baghirov. In 1966 an appeal signed by 1,906 Armenian intellectual and cultural figures was likewise vetoed by Baku.

Inspired by Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika, Karabakh Armenians began a mass movement to unite the region with Soviet Armenia. On 20 February 1988 the Supreme Soviet of the oblast voted to unify with Soviet Armenia. Open conflict followed between the local Armenian population and the government of the Azerbaijan SSR, and it escalated into the First Nagorno-Karabakh War by the end of 1991. On 26 November 1991 the Supreme Soviet of Azerbaijan abolished the oblast's autonomous status, and on 10 December the majority Armenian population declared independence as the Nagorno-Karabakh Republic, with the support of Armenia.
nagoya: Nagoya lies on the Pacific coast of central Honshu, north of Ise Bay on the Nōbi Plain, one of the most fertile areas of Japan. The city was built on low plateaus to keep off floodwaters. The Kiso River runs along its western border, and the Shōnai River comes from the northeast and turns south towards the bay. The orderly grid of its streets is ultimately credited to the shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu.

Oda Nobunaga and his protégés Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu were warlords based in the Nagoya area who gradually unified Japan. In 1610 Ieyasu moved the capital of Owari Province from Kiyosu, about seven kilometres away, to a more strategic site in what is now Nagoya. Nagoya Castle was built partly from materials taken from Kiyosu Castle, and the whole town around it, some 60,000 people, moved with it. Nearby Atsuta Shrine became a waystation called Miya on the Tōkaidō road between Kyoto and Edo, and a town grew up to serve travellers. The castle town and the shrine town together formed the city.

Nagoya was a major trading city and the seat of the Owari lords, the most important house of the Tokugawa clan. They encouraged trade and the arts, above all Tokugawa Muneharu, the seventh lord, who took a keen interest in drama and lived lavishly; actors began to visit the city, and wealthy merchants supported the arts further. Nō and Kyōgen theatre date back to the Owari lords, and the Misono-za, one of Japan's grand kabuki stages, developed in the Edo period.

In the early 1900s a convergence of economic factors brought rapid growth. The area's automobile, aviation and shipbuilding industries flourished, following older crafts such as bicycles, sewing machines and timepieces, and then ceramics, chemicals, oil, petrochemicals and steel. These industries made Nagoya a target of American air raids in the Pacific War, when the Mitsubishi A6M Zero fighter was built there, and many old buildings and artefacts were destroyed. The city had 153,370 households at the war's end in 1945, and it rebuilt as a leading centre of industry.

Nagoya is the capital of Aichi Prefecture and the largest city of the Chūbu region, with about 2.3 million people. It is the principal city of the Chūkyō metropolitan area, and its seaport is the largest in Japan. It is linked to Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto by the Tōkaidō Shinkansen. Atsuta Shrine and Nagoya Castle are its two best-known sights, and UNESCO recognises it as a Design City.
nagpur: Nagpur lies on the Deccan Plateau near the middle of the quadrilateral joining Chennai, Mumbai, New Delhi and Kolkata. The Zero Mile Stone marks the geographical centre of India and was used by the British to measure distances across the subcontinent. The city takes its name from the Nag River; pur means 'city' in many Indian languages. B. R. Ambedkar held that both were named after the Nags, opponents of the Indo-Aryans. An earlier name, Fanindrapura, comes from the Marathi word for a cobra's hood.

Human settlement around Nagpur goes back to the 8th century BCE. The first reference to the name Nagpur is in a 10th-century copper-plate inscription from Devali in Wardha District, which records a grant of a village under the Rastrakuta king Krsna III in the Saka year 862 (940 CE).

The Gond king Bakht Buland Shah of Deogarh founded the city in 1702 by joining twelve small villages. His successor Chand Sultan made Nagpur his capital and turned it into a walled town. After Chand Sultan died in 1739, Wali Shah, an illegitimate son of Bakht Buland, usurped the throne, and Chand Sultan's widow called in the Maratha leader Raghoji Bhosale of Berar. After 1743 a series of Maratha rulers began, starting with Raghoji Bhosale, who had conquered Deogarh, Chanda and Chhattisgarh by 1751.

The British East India Company took Nagpur in the 19th century and made it the capital of the Central Provinces and Berar. The reorganisation of states in 1956 moved Nagpur and Berar to Bombay State, and Nagpur became the second capital of Maharashtra under the Nagpur Pact, by which one session of the state legislature is held there. On 14 October 1956 B. R. Ambedkar and his supporters converted to Buddhism there, which started the Dalit Buddhist movement.

Nagpur is a major commercial centre of the Vidarbha region and is known for its oranges, which have earned it the name Orange City. It has its own bench of the Bombay High Court, established in 1936. Deekshabhoomi, where the 1956 conversion took place, is a Buddhist pilgrimage site with the largest hollow stupa in the world.
naha: Naha stands on the East China Sea coast of the southern part of Okinawa Island, the largest island of Okinawa Prefecture, the southernmost prefecture of Japan. The name is said, according to the Irosetsuden, to come from an older form, Naba, the word for a large mushroom-shaped stone that once stood in the city and gradually wore away and was buried.

Medieval Naha lay on a tiny island called Ukishima, joined to the mainland by a narrow causeway, the Chōkōtei, which led on to Shuri. The chief port for trade within the Ryūkyū Islands was Tomari, on the mainland to the north-east, where tribute ships from the Amami Islands also made port.

Pottery shows that the area traded with the Japanese archipelago and the Korean peninsula at least as early as the 11th century, and it was active as a port by the unification of the Ryūkyū Kingdom in the early 15th century. Its port area was split into East and West districts, with an open-air market before the royal trading office and the Tenshikan, the residence of visiting Chinese officials. Two forts, Mie gusuku and Yarazamori gusuku, guarded the harbour entrance.

Kumemura, a walled community, was the centre of classical Chinese learning. Tradition says it was founded by 36 Min families sent by the Ming court, but the historian Uezato Takashi points out that other Chinese, chiefly from Fujian, probably settled there too. A Confucian temple, a gift of the Kangxi Emperor, was built there in the 1670s and the Meirindō school was established in 1718. Wakasamachi was traditionally said to have been founded by Japanese settlers.

Commodore Matthew C. Perry's squadron stopped at Naha in 1853 on its way to Tokyo. The Ryūkyū Kingdom was replaced by the Ryūkyū Domain in 1872, with Naha as its capital, and in 1879 it was annexed by Japan as Okinawa Prefecture, Shuri and neighbouring municipalities being absorbed into the city. An Imperial decree of July 1899 made Naha an open port for trade with the United States and the United Kingdom. The modern city was officially founded on 20 May 1921.

Naha is the political, economic and educational centre of Okinawa Prefecture, with an estimated population of 317,405 in 2019. Its main street is Kokusai-dōri, and the Okinawa Urban Monorail is the only train system in the prefecture. The reconstructed Shuri Castle, with its main gate, the Shureimon, is registered with other gusuku and Okinawan sacred sites as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The martial art Naha-te was developed in the city, and Gōjū-ryū, Uechi-ryū, Ryūei-ryū and Tōon-ryū descend from it.
nahapana: Nahapana's name appears on his coins in Kharosthi, Brahmi and Greek forms, all derived from a Saka name meaning protector of the clan, and one of his coins names him as the son of Bhumaka. His dates are uncertain. A group of his inscriptions is dated to the years 41 to 46 of an unnamed era; scholars who take it to be the Shaka era, beginning in 78 CE, place his reign in 119-124 CE, while others propose 24-70 CE (Krishna Chandra Sagar) or about 66-71 CE (R. C. C. Fynes).

Modern scholars identify him with Nambanus, whom the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea names as ruler of the coast around Barygaza, a fertile country of wheat, rice, cotton and cattle with its metropolis at Minnagara. He established the Kshatrapa coinage in a style derived from Indo-Greek coins, with the ruler's profile and a Greek legend on one side and a thunderbolt and arrow with Brahmi and Kharosthi legends on the other.

His son-in-law Ushavadata, husband of his daughter Dakshamitra, built rest-houses, gardens and tanks at Bharukachchha, Dashapura, Govardhana and Shorparaga, campaigned north on his orders to rescue the Uttamabhadras from the Malavas, and gave a cave near Nasik to Buddhist monks. An inscription at Junnar names Ayama as his minister.

An inscription in Nasik Cave No. 3 says that the Khakharata race was rooted out, which may mean that his heirs were killed. James Burgess thought that as much as a century might separate Nahapana from Gautamiputra Satakarni, but most historians now hold that they were contemporaries. A Jain tradition, recorded in the Śrutavatāra of Bibudha Sridhara, says that he abdicated and became the monk Bhutabali, one of the two authors of the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama, the oldest Digambara sacred text.
nahdlatul-ulama: The name means Revival of the Ulama. The organisation was founded by religious scholars and merchants to defend traditionalist practice, following the Shafi'i school of law, and its members' economic interests. It set itself against the modernism of the Muhammadiyah and PERSIS and against the Salafi Al-Irshad, which rejected local customs shaped by Java's Hindu and Buddhist past. In theology NU follows the Ash'ari and Maturidi schools, in Sufism the path of al-Ghazali and al-Junayd. Its base remained East Java, and by 1928 it preached in Javanese as well as Arabic.

Under the Japanese occupation NU joined the Masyumi council, led in practice by Hasyim's son Wahid Hasyim. On 22 October 1945 it declared the fight against the returning Dutch a holy war binding on every Muslim, and NU led guerrilla groups such as Hizbullah. After independence it was part of the Masyumi party but left in 1952 and stood alone in 1955, coming third with 18.4 per cent of the vote, almost all of it from Java. In the 1950s it still sought an Islamic state, and it competed with the Communist Party for the support of the poor. In 1965 it sided with the army under General Suharto and was heavily involved in the mass killings of Indonesian communists.

Forced into the United Development Party in 1973, NU withdrew in 1984 under Abdurrahman Wahid, known as Gus Dur, who accepted the state ideology Pancasila as a noble compromise and later apologised for NU's part in the killings of 1965. After Suharto's fall he founded the National Awakening Party in 1998 and was elected president of Indonesia in 1999, but was deposed two years later. At its 2010 conference NU barred its officials from holding political posts.

NU describes its purpose as spreading Islamic teaching. It runs a network of 6,830 pesantren boarding schools and owns 44 universities, and it also funds hospitals and social services. Its highest body is the Syuriah, or Supreme Council, above the Tanfidziyah, the Executive Council, with regional boards reaching down to village branches. In 2014 it launched a campaign against extremism, and in 2019 it called for an end to the term kafir for non-Muslims, while its leaders have also issued a fatwa in favour of female genital mutilation.
nahj-al-balagha: Nahj al-Balagha, meaning Peak of Eloquence, is a collection of more than two hundred sermons, nearly eighty letters and almost five hundred sayings of Ali, the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad, the first Shia Imam and the fourth Rashidun caliph, who reigned from 656 to 661. It is credited to the Shia scholar Sharif al-Radi, who died in 1015, more than three hundred years after Ali. Al-Radi was a poet from a distinguished Shia family in Baghdad with connections to the Buyids, the Shia dynasty that ruled the area. His aims in compiling the book are described as literary, ethical and spiritual, and he gives no chains of transmission for his texts.

The sermons and letters offer a commentary on Ali's political career and have served as an ideological basis for Islamic governance. The best known is the letter of instructions to Malik al-Ashtar, Ali's newly appointed governor in Egypt, who was killed in 657 on the way to his post. It urges justice and compassion for all, regardless of class, creed and colour. Another letter admonishes Uthman ibn Hunayf, governor of Basra, for attending a lavish banquet, and a letter of life advice is addressed to Ali's eldest son Hasan.

The book also contains sharp criticism of Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman, and disapproval of Talha, Zubayr and Aisha, who opposed Ali at the Battle of the Camel in 656, along with passages on morality, the sovereignty of God and the Quran.

Nahj al-Balagha is regarded as an example of the most eloquent Arabic and has been the subject of many commentaries, translations and studies by Sunni and Shia authors. The Mu'tazilite scholar Ibn Abil-Hadid, who died in 1258, wrote a comprehensive commentary and called the work below the speech of the Creator but above the speech of creatures. It is commonly kept in Shia households, often beside the Quran.

Its authenticity has long been debated. The historian Ibn Khallikan, who died in 1282, first suggested that al-Radi or his brother Sharif al-Murtada wrote it rather than compiled it, and the Sunni theologians Ibn Taymiyyah and al-Dhahabi rejected most of it. The Shia regard it as authentic.

Scholars such as Husain M. Jafri, Laura Veccia Vaglieri and Muktar Djebli have traced much of its content to earlier works, among them those of al-Ya'qubi, al-Tabari and al-Jahiz. A stylometric study by Sarwar and Mohamed concluded that the book is internally consistent and not the work of al-Radi or his brother. The philosopher Muhammad Husayn Tabatabai answered that for Shia readers the author is Ali.
nahuas: The name Nahua comes from the Nahuatl word-root nāhua-, which means audible, intelligible, clear, and was used in contrast with popoloca, to speak unintelligibly. Archaeological, historical and linguistic evidence suggests that the Nahuas came from the deserts of northern Mexico and migrated into central Mexico in several waves. From about 600 CE the Nahuas rose quickly to power in central Mexico, expanding into areas earlier held by Oto-Manguean, Totonacan and Huastec peoples, and adopting maize agriculture, urbanism, a ritual calendar of 260 days and monumental architecture.

Around 1000 CE the Toltecs, usually thought to have been Nahua, held much of central Mexico from Tollan Xicocotitlan. After their fall, large population movements followed, and groups such as the Pipil and Nicarao reached north-western Costa Rica. In the Valley of Mexico city-states, or altepetl, contended for dominance: the Xochimilca south of Lake Texcoco, the Tepanecs to the west and the Acolhua to the east. One of the last Nahua groups to arrive, the Mexica, settled on an island in Lake Texcoco and ruled from Tenochtitlan. They formed the Aztec Empire after allying with the Tepanecs and the Acolhua of Texcoco.

In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed on the Gulf coast. The Tlaxcaltecs, a Nahua group who had never been subjugated by the Aztecs, fought the Spaniards, were defeated and then allied with them. Spanish and Tlaxcaltec forces took cities under Aztec rule and, after the Spaniards were driven from Tenochtitlan, besieged and took it. Nahua forces often formed the bulk of the Spanish expeditions against the Maya, Zapotecs and Mixtecs. The Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco, which the Franciscans opened in 1536 to educate young Nahua noblemen as priests, ceased to work to that end by the mid-16th century, and in 1555 Indians were barred from ordination.

Within twenty years of the Spanish arrival the Nahuas were writing their own language in the Latin alphabet. Their wills, town council records and petitions form a large body of sources, and from about 1650 they also wrote primordial titles, texts that assert a community's rights to its land. Classical Nahuatl was a lingua franca in central Mexico before the conquest, which is why the names of Guatemala and several Mexican states are Nahuatl.

About 1.5 million Nahuas speak Nahuatl and another million speak only Spanish. Fewer than 2,000 native speakers of Nawat remain in El Salvador and Nicaragua. The Nahuas are now the largest Indigenous group in Mexico, and the term Aztecs, once applied to them, has largely fallen out of favour in scholarship except for the Aztec Empire.
nahuatl: Nahuatl has been spoken in central Mexico since at least the seventh century CE. It belongs to the Nahuan branch of the Uto-Aztecan family, all of whose varieties descend from a single Proto-Nahuan language. Linguists in the 20th century largely held that Uto-Aztecan began in the southwestern United States and that early Nahuan speakers moved south into central Mexico in several waves. Jane H. Hill has proposed instead that the family began in central Mexico and spread north, a view that has met serious criticism.

The name comes from the Classical Nahuatl word nāhuatlahtōlli, 'clear language'. Many speakers call the language Mexicano, or use a term related to mācēhualli, 'commoner'. The Mexica of Tenochtitlan dominated central Mexico in the Late Postclassic period, and their influence made the variety spoken in their city a prestige language across Mesoamerica.

Nahuan languages are polysynthetic and agglutinative: roots take many prefixes and suffixes, and a single word can serve as a whole sentence. Classical Nahuatl had no case or gender, a base-20 number system, and stress on the penultimate syllable. Its speakers distinguished the language of commoners, macehuallahtolli, from that of the nobility, tecpillahtolli, whose formal oratory used parallel couplets and paired metaphors known as difrasismos.

Before the conquest, Aztec writing was pictographic. Codices served as aids to memory for genealogies, astronomical information and tribute lists, and were meant to be told rather than read. Nahuatl distinguished tlahtolli, speech, from cuicatl, song, much as prose differs from poetry. Varieties today differ considerably, and some are not mutually intelligible; the Mexican Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas recognises 30 of them.

After the Spanish arrived in 1519, Nahuatl lost its place as the leading regional language but stayed important in Nahua communities. Colonists and missionaries introduced the Latin script, and chronicles, grammars, poetry, administrative documents and codices were written in it in the 16th and 17th centuries. This Classical Nahuatl, based on the Tenochtitlan variety, is among the best-documented Indigenous languages of the Americas. In 1570 Philip II of Spain decreed that it should be the official language of the colonies of New Spain.

Nahuatl supplied Spanish, and through it many other languages, with words for things of central Mexico, among them chocolate, tomato, avocado, chili, coyote and axolotl. The names Mexico, Guatemala and Nicaragua derive from it. Its use has declined over time: in 1895 more than 5 per cent of Mexico's population spoke it, and by 2000 the figure was 1.49 per cent. About 1.7 million Nahuas speak it today, and Huasteca Nahuatl, with over a million speakers, is the commonest variety.
nair: The Nair, also called Nayar, are not one caste but, in the words of the anthropologist Kathleen Gough, a named category of castes, with many subdivisions whose customs differed between the north and the south of what is now Kerala. The origin of the name is disputed: some derive it from nayaka, an honorific meaning leader of the people, others from the community's link with the Naga cult of serpent worship. The anthropologist Christopher Fuller thinks the Nareae named by Pliny the Elder in his Natural History of 77 CE were probably the Nairs.

Copper-plate inscriptions of about the 7th to 9th centuries, recording grants of land and rights to Jewish and Christian traders, name Nair chiefs and soldiers of Eranad, Valluvanad, Venad and Palghat as witnesses, which suggests that by then they were vassal chieftains of the Perumals. Before British rule Kerala was divided into about ten states under rajahs, subdivided into nadus governed by hereditary Nair chiefs, the naduvazhi, who kept order and could call on the military service of all Nairs below them, usually a permanent force of 500 to 1,000 men.

Their dominance first weakened after Marthanda Varma became Raja of Venad in 1729. He curbed the Nair chiefs, brought Tamil Brahmins into his administration and reorganised the Nair army in the European style as a standing force, which fought the Dutch at the Battle of Colachel in 1741. After hostilities between the Nairs and the British in 1809 the British limited their place in the Indian Army, and after independence the Nair Brigade of the Travancore State Force became part of the 9th Battalion of the Madras Regiment.

Nairs lived in tharavads, joint families of the descendants of one ancestress, often of 50 to 80 members and sometimes as many as 200. Only the women lived in the main house, and authority lay with the karnavan, the eldest man, who controlled the common property and arranged marriages: the head of the family was the mother's brother, not the mother. Girls went through the pre-puberty rite of thalikettu kalyanam and later the sambandham, after which a woman might take one or more partners. None of these rituals survives in any significant way.

Most Nairs were literate in Malayalam, as many served as scribes and bailiffs of the royal courts, and from the 16th century they contributed increasingly to literature and drama. Their chief deity is Bhagavati, goddess of war and fertility, and serpent deities were kept in groves on the family land.
najaf: The area lies about 30 km south of ancient Babylon. Excavations point to settlement from the 1st century BCE, and the area holds a large Christian burial ground with remains of the Sassanid period. Wadi al-Salam is said to have been a holy cemetery for Jews called Baniqia. In Muslim tradition the city began with the burial of Ali ibn Abi Talib, whose grave was kept secret for fear of his enemies. The Abbasid Caliph Harun al-Rashid is said to have found it when a hunted deer took refuge at the spot, and he ordered a mausoleum, around which the town grew. The city's founding is dated to 791.

In the early 14th century Ibn Battuta visited the shrine, then called Meshhed Ali, and described a city of rich merchants and a treasury filled with votive offerings. The Ottomans took Najaf in the 16th century. The Safavid dynasty twice captured it during the Ottoman–Safavid War of 1623–1639 but lost it again in 1638. When the Portuguese traveller Pedro Texeira passed through in 1604 he found it in ruins with little more than 500 people, after the Euphrates shifted eastward towards Hilla, leaving Najaf and Kufa dry.

In the 18th century the city's scholarly life came to be dominated by Farsi-speaking scholars from Iran. Water returned in 1803, after the Hindiyya Canal of 1793 and a century of Ottoman efforts to shift the Euphrates, and the last city wall was rebuilt in 1811. The Hawza of Najaf has been a centre of Shia education since the 11th century CE and was possibly established in the 9th; Murtadha al-Ansari and Ali al-Sistani studied there, and Ayatollah Khomeini lectured in the city from 1965 to 1978.

The Ottomans were expelled in an uprising in 1915 and the British took over. In 1918 the sheikhs of Najaf rebelled and killed the British governor; the British besieged the city and cut off its water, and many Shia scholars were expelled to Persia, where they helped build up Qom. Najaf lost its religious primacy to Qom, which it did not regain until after 2003. From the 1950s many historic buildings near the shrine were demolished for new streets, and in 1958 the city wall was replaced by a ring road.

Najaf is the capital of Najaf Governorate, about 160 km south of Baghdad, with a population estimated at about 1.4 million. The Imam Ali Mosque, with its gilded dome, is regarded by Shia Muslims as the third holiest Islamic site, and the city is a major pilgrimage destination. The nearby Wadi al-Salam is described as the largest cemetery in the world; many of the devout hope to be buried there in order to rise with Ali on Judgement Day.
najaf-qoli-khan-bakhtiari: Najaf-Qoli Khan was born in 1846, the son of Hossein Gholi Khan Ilkhani and Bibi Mehrafrooz. He was the elder brother of Ali-Qoli Khan, better known as Sardar Assad, of Khosrou Khan, Sardar Zafar, and of Bibi Maryam Bakhtiari. After his father's death Mozaffar ad-Din Shah Qajar gave him the title Samsam al-Saltaneh, and on the death of his elder brother Esfandiar he became Ilkhani, the paramount chief of the Bakhtiari. In the Constitutional Revolution he sided with the opponents of Mohammad Ali Shah Qajar, and with Bakhtiari horsemen he took Isfahan in 1908 and governed it for a time.

On 26 July 1911 he became Minister of War in the cabinet of Mohammad Vali Khan Tonekaboni, and when that government fell he became prime minister. His first premiership was troubled. Mohammad Ali Shah re-entered Iran from Russia with Russian and Turkmen cavalry, and the deposed shah's brother Salar al-Doula led a rising in Kermanshah. A Russian ultimatum then gave the government 48 hours to expel the American financial adviser Morgan Shuster and his staff. His cabinet favoured accepting it, but the National Assembly rejected it by a large majority, and the government fell.

He returned as prime minister in May 1918, during the upheaval of the Bolshevik Revolution. After Vladimir Lenin renounced the privileges of the tsarist government, Samsam al-Saltaneh declared on 4 August 1918 the cancellation of the Treaty of Turkmenchay of 1828 and other Russian privileges, and on 8 August his cabinet voted to end all capitulations. Three days later Ahmad Shah Qajar reprimanded him at the Golestan Palace and ordered him to resign; he refused, and the shah named Vosugh od-Dowleh to form a new cabinet.

He later sat for Tehran in the fourth National Assembly and in 1921 declined the governorship of Khorasan. Reza Shah made him governor of the Bakhtiari region in 1929. He died in Isfahan in 1930 and was buried in the Bakhtiari family mausoleum at Takht-e Foulad.
najd: The name Najd means highland in Arabic. The region is a plateau between 762 and 1,525 m high, sloping from west to east. Its exact boundaries have varied: roughly the Hejaz lies to the west, the Nafud desert of al-Jawf to the north, the Ad-Dahna Desert to the east and the Empty Quarter to the south. Medieval geographers debated the line with the Hejaz and set the eastern edge at the strip of red dunes of the Ad-Dahna, some 100 km east of modern Riyadh.

The eastern sections, historically better known as Al-Yamama, have oasis settlements with farming and trade, while the rest was traditionally sparsely occupied by nomadic Bedouins. The Tuwaiq range runs through its centre, and most villages lie along wadis such as Wadi Hanifa near Riyadh.

Al-Magar, in south-western Najd, was an advanced Neolithic culture, possibly one of the first to practise widespread agriculture and to domesticate animals, particularly horses, before desertification. Radiocarbon dating of objects found there gives an age of about 9,000 years. In the 5th century the Ḥimyarites of Sheba sought a vassal state to control central and northern Arabia, and in 425 their king made Ḥujr 'Akīl al-Murār ibn 'Amr the first king of Kindah. The Kingdom of Kinda had its first capital at Qaryat Dhāt Kāhil, today Qaryat al-Fāw.

In the 16th century the Ottomans added the Red Sea coast to the empire and claimed suzerainty over the interior, to thwart the Portuguese. Their control varied over the next four centuries. The Al Saud emerged in Najd in 1744, when Muhammad bin Saud joined forces with the religious leader Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, founder of the Wahhabi movement. The first Saudi state, established around Riyadh in 1744, expanded rapidly and briefly controlled most of the present territory of Saudi Arabia, but was destroyed by 1818 by the Ottoman viceroy of Egypt, Mohammed Ali Pasha.

A much smaller second Saudi state, centred on Najd, was founded in 1824 by Turki bn Abdullah. Through the rest of the 19th century the Al Saud contested the interior with another ruling family, the Al Rashid, who won by 1891 and drove the Al Saud into exile in Kuwait.

Najd is divided into three main provinces: Riyadh Province, home to Riyadh, the Saudi capital since 1824; Qassim Province, known for its oases and date palm orchards along the Wadi Rummah, with Buraidah as its capital; and Ḥa'il Province in the north. About one third of the population of Saudi Arabia lives in the region, which is the home of the House of Saud.
najda-ibn-amir-al-hanafi: Najda was born around 655 into the Banu Hanifa, a branch of the Banu Bakr living in the Yamama, and was already influential among its Kharijites as a young man. In 680 he rose against the Umayyad Caliphate in the Yamama. During the Umayyad siege of Mecca in 683 he and his horsemen came to the aid of Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, but when Ibn al-Zubayr declared himself caliph, Najda and other Kharijite leaders went to Basra. There, under Nafi ibn al-Azraq, they fought their former ally's army before moving to Ahwaz.

Political differences with Nafi led Najda back to the Yamama, where the Kharijites under Abu Talut Salim ibn Matar held the estate of Jawn al-Khadarim and its 4,000 slaves. In 685 Najda seized a Mecca-bound caravan from Basra and shared the spoils among them, and the Kharijites of the Yamama, Abu Talut included, chose him as leader. He defeated the Banu Ka'b at the Battle of Dhu'l-Majaz, killed or captured many of the Abd al-Qays at Qatif, which became his headquarters, and in 686 ambushed and scattered a Zubayrid army of 14,000 sent from Basra. His lieutenant Atiyya ibn al-Aswad al-Hanafi took Oman, which its chieftains soon recovered.

By 687 Najda held northern Bahrayn and received allegiance and tribute from Sana'a and Hadramawt, and his power in Arabia exceeded Ibn al-Zubayr's. He refused the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik's offer of the governorship of the Yamama but stayed on friendly terms with him. In June 687 he led his followers on the Hajj at Mecca, then gave up a march on Medina for religious reasons and received the submission of Ta'if.

At the height of his power his partisans turned against him over his ties with Abd al-Malik, his unequal distribution of military pay and his favour to associates despite their religious offences. His former deputy Abu Fudayk killed him in Bahrayn. The historian Abd al-Ameer Dixon judged that Abd al-Malik's overtures had served their purpose by driving a wedge between Najda and his followers.
najera: Nájera is a small town in the Rioja Alta region of La Rioja, northern Spain, on the river Najerilla. It is a stopping point on the French Way, the most popular path of the Way of St. James. It is a former bishopric, now a Latin Catholic titular see, and the former capital of the Kingdom of Nájera–Pamplona. The Romans built the town of Tritium on land that now lies within Nájera and the neighbouring municipality of Tricio. The name Naxara, meaning town between the rocks, is of Arabic origin and dates from Muslim rule.

While still an Islamic possession, the town was the scene of a three-day struggle told in legend between Roland, one of Charlemagne's nobles, and the Islamic giant Ferragut. Ordoño II of León conquered it for Navarre in 923. It was the capital of the Kingdom of Nájera–Pamplona until Castile conquered it in 1054 after the battle of Atapuerca. The diocese of Nájera was established in 923 from territory of the suppressed Diocese of Calahorra, gained territory in 1077 and 1088, and was itself suppressed in 1170, its territory used to found the Diocese of Calahorra.

The town stayed multicultural. In 1142 the French abbot Peter the Venerable commissioned translations of important Islamic works in Spain, including the first translation of the Qur'an into a European language, and it has been suggested that he met his four translators at Nájera. A prosperous Jewish community lived there from the tenth century and received a relatively favourable legal status after the Christian conquest; its letters have been found in the Cairo Geniza. In 1367 Edward, the Black Prince fought the Battle of Nájera, intervening in a Castilian civil war on behalf of Pedro I of Castile.

The church of Santa María la Real was founded by García Sánchez III of Pamplona in 1052 and is the burial place of kings of Navarre; the monks left the adjoining monastery in the 19th century after anti-clerical reforms. A bridge over the Najerilla was rebuilt on Roman foundations in 1090 by San Juan de Ortega and remade in 1880. Excavations show the Alcázar, a Moorish fort abandoned in the 16th century, and the Monastery of Valvanera, begun in the 11th century, lies 33 kilometres away.
najran: The Najran oasis lies in the Wadi Najran, a fertile valley about 4,500 feet above sea level, about 15 miles long and 2 miles wide. A belt of sandstone over the granite has long made movement through it easier than across the surrounding mountains, which encouraged both trade and invasion. The oasis stands at the crossing of two caravan routes, one from Hadhramaut to the Hejaz and the eastern Mediterranean and another from Al-Yamama to Mesopotamia, and it is the obligatory passage into Yemen from the Hejaz. In antiquity it was a centre of agriculture, trade in incense, and the making of cloth and leather. The ancient city is now mostly in ruins at Al-Okhdood, south-east of the present city.

In the early seventh century BCE the Sabaean ruler Karib'il Watar conquered the federation that held Najran. Its trade is reflected in the Book of Ezekiel, which names Ra'mah among Sheba's trading partners. In 24 BCE the Roman prefect Aelius Gallus took the town, then had to retreat. In the second century Ptolemy called it a metropolis. In the second and third centuries it passed between Saba, Himyar and, briefly, the Kingdom of Aksum, before Himyar regained it.

Christianity may have reached Najran in the fifth century, probably along the trade routes, and the city became its centre in South Arabia. In 522 the Jewish Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas began campaigns against Christians in South Arabia. Inscriptions describe a siege of Najran lasting thirteen months under his commander Sharahil Yaqbul dhu-Yazan, a plunder of the area and the execution of 12,500 people. Syriac sources add that Dhu Nuwas broke an oath of safety sworn on a Torah scroll. The massacre of 523 aroused outrage among Christians, and a martyrium, the Kaaba of Najran, became a place of pilgrimage.

After the Islamic conquests the Christians of Najran agreed to pay tribute, and in 641 they were expelled to Mesopotamia near Kufa. The city then almost disappears from the record until the seventeenth century, when Ismaili Muslims established the Principality of Najran in 1633. After the First World War it was left in the new Kingdom of Yemen. Saudi Arabia launched a war over the disputed territory on 20 March 1934, which ended on 20 May with the Treaty of Taif.
naju: In the Later Three Kingdoms period of Korean history, the Naju area belonged to the kingdom of Later Baekje. Wang Geon, who later became Taejo of the Goryeo dynasty, occupied it, and it became a large base of his political support. He also married the daughter of the Magistrate of Naju, Lady Janghwa, who became the mother of Goryeo's second king, Hyejong.

The name of Jeolla Province comes from the first character of Jeonju and the first character of Naju. The capital of the former South Jeolla Province stood at Naju until it was moved to Gwangju in 1895.

One of the best-known events of its modern history is the Naju Tonghak Peasant Revolution of 1894, marked by fierce battles in Naju, resistance by the garrison of the Naju Eupseong fortress, and later suppression by Japanese and government troops.

In 1986 the official name of the city was changed from Geumseong to Naju, and in 1995 it was expanded to include Naju county. The Naju Plain, watered by the Yeongsan River, grows Naju rice, and the Naju pear, a large round fruit long cultivated along the river, appears on the district's logo. Naju pears and Oriental melons are popular gifts at Lunar New Year.

Naju was designated an Innovation City, and the opening ceremony for its construction was held on 8 November 2007, with President Roh taking part. Several public organisations moved there from Seoul, among them the Korea Electric Power Corporation, the Korea Internet and Security Agency and Arts Council Korea. The new city covers 7.327 square kilometres. Dongshin University, a private university, was founded in 1987, and the Korea Institute of Energy Technology opened in March 2022 in Naju Innovation City.

Local festivals include the Naju Pear Blossom Festival in April and the Naju Rapeseed Festival in May. Naju gomtang, a clear beef soup, and fermented skate from the old port of Yeongsanpo are local dishes.
nakba: The word nakba means misfortune or calamity in Arabic. Its first use for the defeat of 1948 is attributed to the Syrian historian Constantin Zureiq, a professor at the American University of Beirut, in his 1948 book Ma'na an-Nakba (The Meaning of the Disaster). Before 1948 the Arab phrase for a year of catastrophe referred to 1920, when European powers partitioned the Ottoman Empire.

The UN Partition Plan of 1947 assigned 56 per cent of Palestine to a Jewish state and 44 per cent to the Arab state, although Palestinians were the majority of the population. Small local clashes began on 30 November 1947 and escalated until March 1948. Some Palestinians had already begun to leave, expecting to return after the fighting.

Between December 1947 and March 1948, between 70,000 and 100,000 Palestinians, mostly from the urban middle and upper classes, were expelled or fled. Historians record massacres at Al-Khisas on 18 December 1947 and at Balad al-Shaykh on 31 December. Arab League armies entered Mandatory Palestine on 15 May 1948, after the Mandate ended, and expulsions and the destruction of villages then spread through rural areas. The Tantura massacre took place on 22 and 23 May.

Fighting and expulsions continued into the autumn, with the depopulation of Beersheba on 21 October and massacres at al-Dawayima and Safsaf on 29 October. On 11 December 1948 the UN passed Resolution 194, which declared that refugees wishing to return should be permitted to do so and that compensation should be paid for lost property. Armistices were signed between February and July 1949. By the end of the war most of the Palestinians living in the territory that became Israel had been expelled or had fled, and over 500 villages and eleven towns were destroyed or depopulated.

Israel prevented refugees outside its borders from returning, and Palestinians who remained were placed under martial law until 1966. A nationality law of 14 July 1952 ended their former Palestinian citizenship. Hebrew names replaced many Arabic place names. A second displacement followed in the Six-Day War of 1967, known as the Naksa, or setback. Today most Palestinians live outside the area of Mandatory Palestine.

The Palestinian national narrative treats the Nakba as a formative collective trauma, and Palestinians mark Nakba Day on 15 May. The Israeli national narrative places the same events within the War of Independence that established the state, and Israeli officials have often held that many Palestinians left willingly. Since the 1970s Israeli historians known as the New Historians have challenged that account. Some Israeli scholars in turn argue that Palestinian memory leaves out the attacks made by Arab irregular forces.
nakbe: Excavations suggest that people were living at Nakbe by the Early Formative period, about 1400 BCE. By the 8th century BCE it had monumental architecture, with some platforms 18 metres high, and earlier villages were levelled and filled to serve as foundations for the new buildings, so that the platforms and temples were planned together. The buildings fall into an East Group and a West Group of the formative periods. The largest is Structure 1, a pyramid flanked by two large stucco masks and crowned with three buildings in the triadic style.

Raised causeways paved with crushed white stone, the sacbeob or white ways, linked the parts of the city; the Kan Causeway stood 4 metres above the ground in places. Strombus shells, among the earliest major imports into the interior of northern Guatemala, exotic goods such as jade and obsidian, and human incisors inlaid with jadelike stone from about 2,800 years ago, point to growing differences of rank. Archaeologist Richard D. Hansen has argued that the demand for such imports may have required administrative and governmental organisations here earlier than elsewhere.

The site was first seen in aerial photographs in 1930, and Ian Graham began the first excavations in 1962. Large-scale work followed in the 1980s and 1990s under the RAINPEG Project, a joint effort of the Institute of Geophysics and Planetary Sciences of UCLA and Guatemala's Institute of Anthropology and History, directed by Hansen. A main aim was the limestone quarries: the team recovered 23 chert tools, among them bifacial picks and axes and hammerstones, and made replicas to learn how the Maya cut blocks from the bedrock and shaped them.

Nakbe Stela 1, smashed in antiquity into forty-five fragments, once stood 3.4 metres tall. Reassembled, it shows two figures face to face, one pointing to a disembodied head, a scene interpreted as the supernatural twins Hun-Apu and Ixbalanque of the Popol Vuh. After a thousand years of near abandonment, Late Classic Maya reoccupied the site, settling around the ruins and building the Codex Group. They raised no monuments, but left fine Classic ceramics, among them the Princeton Vase.
nakdong-river: The Nakdong River, or Nakdonggang, passes through the major cities of Daegu and Busan. It takes its name from its role as the eastern border of the Gaya confederacy in the Three Kingdoms era. It flows from the Taebaek Mountains to the South Sea, or Korea Strait, which separates Korea from Japan, and begins where the Cheoramcheon and Hwangjicheon streams meet at Gumunso in Taebaek, Gangwon Province.

Its width ranges from a few metres in the upper reaches to several hundred metres near the estuary. The Yeong, Geumho and Nam rivers are its major tributaries, and together they drain most of North and South Gyeongsang provinces, a watershed of 23,384 square kilometres.

The basin has been a favoured dwelling place for as long as people have lived on the Korean Peninsula, and numerous Neolithic remains have been found in the valley. Around the 1st century it is believed to have been inhabited by the tribes of the Byeonhan confederacy. During the Three Kingdoms period the Gaya confederacy controlled the valley until Silla overran it in 562. These states used the river for navigation and commerce, with a thriving trade in armour and weapons with neighbours including Japan of the Yamato period.

Through the Silla, Goryeo and Joseon periods the river stayed a major transport route in the Gyeongsang region. It carried inland fresh seafood such as mackerel, salted and dried against spoiling, and Andong was the farthest inland the fish could be brought before going bad, so that many people flocked there in the Joseon dynasty to eat fish.

In the Korean War the southern length of the river formed the western part of the Pusan Perimeter that UN forces fought to hold in the autumn of 1950. The bridge at Waegwan was blown up on 3 August 1950 to stop the North Korean advance on Daegu, killing a large number of South Korean refugees. Though some North Korean forces crossed the river, it mostly marked their furthest advance.

Apart from its southernmost reaches the river no longer serves as a major commercial waterway, but it feeds those who live near it through fishing and irrigation, and snails and catfish are used in local cooking. Dams near Andong have formed a chain of artificial lakes, the largest being Andong Lake. Floodplain wetlands such as Upo Wetland in Changnyeong County shelter rare birds, fish and plants, and the estuary, beside the Port of Busan, is important for waterbirds. The river and its tributaries are a major source of drinking water for the basin.
nakhchivan-autonomous-soviet-socialist-r: In the last years of the First World War Nakhichevan saw bloodshed between Armenians and Azerbaijanis, who both claimed the area. By 1914 the Armenian population had fallen slightly to 40 per cent, while the Azeri population had risen to roughly 60 per cent. After the dissolution of the Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic in May 1918, the region was contested between the Democratic Republic of Armenia and the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic. The Ottomans occupied it in June 1918 and massacred 10,000 Armenians. In December 1918 Jafargulu Khan Nakhichevanski declared a Republic of Aras, which led to the Aras War. By mid-June 1919 Armenia held the territory, but an Azerbaijani invasion followed and further violence left some 10,000 Armenians dead.

The Red Army occupied the region in July 1920 and on 28 July declared an autonomous Soviet republic with close ties to the Azerbaijan SSR. In November the Bolsheviks promised Nakhichevan to Armenia, but Lenin called for a referendum, which at the start of 1921 showed 90 per cent in favour of inclusion in the Azerbaijan SSR as an autonomous republic. The Treaty of Moscow between Bolshevik Russia and Turkey of 16 March 1921 settled the matter, adding the Sharur-Daralagez district so that Turkey shared a border with Azerbaijan, and the Treaty of Kars of 23 October reaffirmed it. On 9 February 1924 the Soviet Union placed the republic under the jurisdiction of the Azerbaijan SSR, and its constitution was adopted on 18 April 1926.

Under Soviet rule the republic became a centre of industry, notably the mining of salt, and a junction of the Moscow to Tehran and Baku to Yerevan railways. Public health improved: malaria, which had infected between 70 and 85 per cent of the population, was sharply reduced, and trachoma and typhus were eliminated. The Armenian share of the population fell from 15 per cent in 1926 to 1.4 per cent in 1979, while the Azeri share rose from 85 to 96 per cent.

In December 1989 Azeri inhabitants moved to dismantle the Soviet border with Iran. In January 1990 the Supreme Soviet of the republic declared an intention to secede from the USSR, in protest at the Soviet action in Black January, before Lithuania's declaration. Heydar Aliyev, born in Nakhichevan, returned there in autumn 1990 and was elected to the local Supreme Soviet. On 19 November 1990 the republic became the Nakhichevan Autonomous Republic within the Republic of Azerbaijan.
nakhon-pathom: Nakhon Pathom is a city in central Thailand and the capital of Nakhon Pathom province, about 50 kilometres west of Bangkok, in the middle of a wide plain crossed by watercourses such as the Tha Chin River. The city lay on the Gulf of Thailand 2,000 years ago, but the coast has been receding southward steadily as a result of sedimentation. Sugar cane has been grown in the area since the late 18th century, and old travel reports describe sugar factories on the Tha Chin every four to five kilometres, each surrounded by ten to fifteen houses and firmly in Chinese hands.

Nakhon Pathom is considered one of the oldest cities in Thailand, along with Ratchaburi and Sing Buri, and is said to have been founded as far back as 40 BCE. It was for a long time one of the important capitals of Dvaravati, a Mon kingdom reaching from Lop Buri to the area of Tun Sun. According to the archaeologist Charles Higham, two silver medallions from beneath a sanctuary at Nakhon Pathom, the largest of the moated sites, proclaim that it was the meritorious work of the King of Sri Dvaravati, Dvaravati being the Sanskrit term for that which has gates. The script is in south Indian characters of the seventh century. Nakhon Pathom was the largest Dvaravati centre.

Tradition holds that the Indian king Ashoka sent monks to Siam, that they arrived at Nakhon Pathom and toured the country from there, which gives the city its self-image as the place from which Buddhism spread through Siam. In April 1842 three groups of Chinese, organised in secret societies of about 1,000 men each under leaders named Khim, Ia and Phiao, caused trouble. Soldiers sent by the Siamese government arrested Khim and Phiao, but Ia escaped and robbed houses in the Samut Sakhon and Nakhon Pathom area until a large police operation overpowered his men.

The Phra Pathom Chedi, about 127 metres high, dominates the city. King Mongkut, as a wandering monk, rediscovered it in the jungle, and its restoration began in 1853. His son Chulalongkorn had it covered with fine Chinese tiles. A museum at the south entrance of the temple complex displays Dvaravati artefacts found during construction work on the chedi and in the surrounding excavations, along with Mon-style Buddha statues. The city also has Wat Song Thammakanlayani, Thailand's only bhikkhuni temple, and the Sanam Chandra Palace, King Vajiravudh's palace complex, which now houses a campus of Silpakorn University.
nakhon-ratchasima: Nakhon Ratchasima lies about 250 kilometres north-east of Bangkok, at the western edge of the Korat Plateau. It is the largest city of north-eastern Thailand and one of the four major cities of Isan. Historically it marked the boundary between Lao and Siamese territory. Its name joins Nakhon Raj, from the ancient town of Khorakapura, with Sema, another ancient town; both lay in Sung Noen District, 32 kilometres to the west. The short name Korat comes from the old Khmer name Angkor Raj.

Before the 14th century the area was under Khmer suzerainty, and Phimai to the north was probably more important. In the 17th century King Narai of Ayutthaya ordered a new city built on the site as a stronghold on the north-eastern frontier, and Siamese chronicles called it a second-class city ruled by a hereditary royal governor. After the Burmese destroyed Ayutthaya in 1767, a son of King Boromakot tried to rule from Phimai over Korat and other eastern provinces. King Taksin of Thonburi sent the brothers Thong Duang and Boonma, and the prince was executed in 1768. Thong Duang later became King Rama I.

In 1826 King Chao Anouvong of Vientiane, thinking Siam weakened, attacked Korat in a rebellion against Rama III that lasted two years. Lady Mo, wife of the deputy governor, is credited with freeing the city from his army, and a statue in the centre of the city honours her. The railway from Bangkok reached Korat in 1900 and was opened on 21 December 1900 by King Chulalongkorn. In October 1933 the city was the headquarters of the Boworadet Rebellion against the new government.

Nakhon Ratchasima is the capital of the province of the same name and the third-largest city in Thailand. Its economy has long rested on agriculture, as a processing centre for the rice, tapioca and sugar of Isan. From 1962 to 1976 Korat Royal Thai Air Force Base hosted Thai, United States and New Zealand air force units during the Vietnam War.
nakhon-si-thammarat: Nakhon Si Thammarat is a city municipality and the capital of Nakhon Si Thammarat province, about 610 km south of Bangkok on the east coast of the Malay Peninsula. The name comes from the Sanskrit Nagara Shrī Dharmarāja, and Dharmarāja means righteous ruler, an important Theravada concept. The city was originally coastal, but silting has moved the coastline away. Its long north-south shape dates to its original site on a flood-safe dune, and the modern centre lies north of the Old Town.

The earliest settlement nearby was Tha Rua, where Song dynasty ceramics of the twelfth century were found. The settlement then moved to Muang Phra Wieng, associated with Tambralinga, a polity under the Srivijaya sea power. An inscription at Wat Sema Muang records that by 775 the king of Srivijaya had established a foothold at Ligor and built a sanctuary to the Buddha.

The Chronicles of Nakorn Si Thammarat, composed in the seventeenth century, credit King Sri Thammasok in the thirteenth century with founding the present city, building Wat Phra Mahathat and introducing Singhalese Theravada Buddhism. An inscription at Chaiya says he ruled Tambralinga in 1231. The kingdom held authority over twelve cities from Chumphon to Pahang, and the Ramkamhaeng Stele of Sukhothai names the city in 1292. The kingdom ended in the fourteenth century, and the city was re-established by a son of the ruler of Phetchaburi, after which it came under Ayutthaya.

In the fifteenth century Ayutthaya appointed governors and the city became the main seat of Siamese authority in the south. Western sources called it Ligor, and the Japanese adventurer Yamada Nagamasa was made its governor in 1629. After the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767 the vice-governor Phra Palat Nu ruled the south until King Taksin subdued him in 1769. The Burmese sacked the city in 1786. Under Chao Phraya Nakhon Noi (1811–1838) it kept a relative autonomy. The governorship was abolished in 1896, and the city became a provincial capital in 1932.

Wat Phra Mahathat is the most important temple of southern Thailand and holds a tooth relic of the Buddha. Its chedi is 78 m high and surrounded by 173 smaller ones; it is in Sri Lankan style but is said to stand on an earlier chedi of the Srivijaya period. Of the city wall, which enclosed about one square kilometre, only the northern gate and a short stretch survive.
nakijin-castle: The castle's beginnings are uncertain. Local legend credits its building to Nakijin Seshu, long before the Shunten dynasty of tradition, and the Chūzan Seikan and Chūzan Seifu name a line of lords descended from Shunten's family and later from Prince Wakukawa, a son of King Eiso, until their descendant Hanishi destroyed the old lineage and so began the Hokuzan kingdom. Everything before Hanishi is known only from biographies and genealogies, and its dates belong to legend. The physical remains date to the 12th or 13th century, and the oldest surviving written mention is the record of Hokuzan's tribute in the Ming Taizu Annals.

The fortress stands on a rocky outcrop facing the East China Sea, with a steep drop into a gorge on the east and another down to the shore on the north, where a small inlet served it; Unten harbour, the kingdom's main port, lay some miles to the east.

The walls enclose an area 350 metres from north to south and 800 metres from east to west, and about 1,500 metres of their roughly fitted limestone remain. The royal residence, with a small garden and spring, occupied the highest enclosure, beside three shrines on the precipice, while lower enclosures held vassals' houses, offices, stables and garrisons. Several sacred utaki groves within the walls reflect a religious role older than the fortifications, and ceramics from China and Southeast Asia found there suggest its former prosperity.

After Hokuzan fell, lords of Hokuzan governing under the royal capital at Shuri lived in the castle for several centuries. In 1609 the Japanese Satsuma Domain invaded the Ryūkyū Kingdom and landed its forces at Unten harbour. They attacked the castle, with heavy casualties on both sides, took it and burned it, and it has lain in ruins since. It became a National Historic Site in 1972, a designation that also covers the 13th-century Shiina Castle ruins six kilometres away, which tradition holds to have been Hokuzan's earlier base.
nalanda: Nalanda lies in the ancient region of Magadha, in present-day Bihar, about 16 kilometres north of Rajgir and about 90 kilometres southeast of Patna. Bodh Gaya, another major Buddhist site, is about 80 kilometres to the southwest. The site lies between the artificial lakes of Gidhi, Panashokar and Indrapuskarani. Excavations at the nearby Juafardih site have yielded black ware carbon-dated to about 1200 BCE, so the region was settled long before the Buddha.

Its datable history begins in the 5th century. A seal names a king called Shakraditya as founder of a monastery there, and scholars identify him with the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I, whose coins found at the site support this. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who visited around 637, said that a long succession of kings had built up Nalanda. The Gupta patrons were Hindus, and later Harsha, the emperor of Kannauj, also supported it. Under the Buddhist Pala dynasty, which reigned from the mid-8th century, the Mahayana tradition of Nalanda gave way to Vajrayana, and the Palas built competing monasteries such as Vikramashila and Odantapura, only a few kilometres away, which probably drew monks from Nalanda.

Excavations in 1920 and 1921 found a thick layer of ash in the upper levels, which has been blamed on the troops of Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji, who plundered the region around 1200. The passage often cited, in the Tabaqat-i Nasiri, actually describes the destruction of Odantapura, though it is true that Nalanda was raided. The scholar Johan Elverskog argues that the end was not sudden: students were still there in the 13th century, and a monk ordained there travelled to the court of Khubilai Khan. After its decline the site was forgotten. Francis Buchanan-Hamilton surveyed it in 1811 and 1812, and Major Markham Kittoe identified it as Nalanda in 1847. Systematic excavation by the Archaeological Survey of India ran from 1915 to 1937.

The curriculum covered Madhyamaka, Yogachara and other Buddhist philosophies, and also the Vedas, logic, grammar, medicine and Samkhya. Pupils came from Korea, Japan, China, Tibet, Indonesia, Persia and Turkey. Yijing, who spent ten years there, took home many texts, which shows a well-equipped library; Tibetan sources name it Dharmaganja and describe three multi-storeyed buildings. Yijing also records that the monks decided matters in assembly, and that a single objection stopped a proposal. Shantarakshita and Padmasambhava, who helped found Buddhism in Tibet, came from Nalanda. Its ruins were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.
nallur-kandaswamy-kovil: The first Kandaswamy temple at Nallur was founded in 948 CE. According to the Yalpana Vaipava Malai, the temple was developed on the site in the 13th century by Puvenaya Vaku, a minister of the Jaffna king Kalinga Magha. A third temple is credited to Sapumal Kumaraya, an adopted son of Parakramabahu VI who ruled the Jaffna kingdom on behalf of the Kotte kingdom. Nallur was then the capital of the Jaffna kings, and the royal palace stood close to the temple, which also served as a fort with high walls.

Filipe de Oliveira, the Portuguese conqueror of the Jaffna Kingdom, destroyed the third temple in 1624. Its site is now occupied by St. James' Church, Nallur, in whose vicarage part of the original Shivalingam was kept until 1995, when it was destroyed during the recapture of Jaffna by the Sri Lankan armed forces. Cankilian Thoppu, the facade of the palace of King Cankili II, still stands in Nallur.

The fourth and present temple was built in 1734, under Dutch rule, by Don Juan Ragunatha Maapaana Mudaliyar, a shroff in the Dutch Katchery. It began as a building of brick and stone with a cadjan roof and two small halls, enshrining a vel, the divine spear of Murugan, and a Brahmin named Krishnaiyar was its first priest. The founder's descendants have kept the temple as its custodians ever since. The 7th custodian, Arumuga Maapaana Mudaliyar, built the first bell tower in 1899, paved the sanctum in granite in 1902 and raised the first enclosing wall in 1909.

Kumaradas Maapaana Mudaliyar, the 10th custodian from 1964 until his death in 2021, virtually rebuilt the whole complex, which became the largest Hindu temple complex in Sri Lanka. Its main entrance faces east under a five-storey gopuram in the Dravidian style. The nine-storey Shanmuha Raja Gopuram was unveiled on 21 August 2011, and the Gubera Raja Gopuram, which opened a northern entrance, on 4 September 2015.

The annual festival lasts twenty-five days and begins with the hoisting of the holy flag, the Kodiyetram; for centuries the cloth has been brought to the temple in a small chariot by a family of the Sengunthar Kaikola Mudaliyar. Its best-attended event is the Ther Thiruvila, the chariot festival, when Murugan and his consorts are carried out on a silver throne made in 1900. The temple is a central institution of Tamil identity in northern Sri Lanka, and the diaspora has built temples of the same name in Europe and North America.
nam-tien: In 1069, under Lý Thánh Tông, a Vietnamese army attacked the Cham capital Vijaya to punish raids on Vietnam; the Cham king Rudravarman III was captured and gave up Champa's three northern provinces, now Quảng Bình and the north of Quảng Trị. For the next centuries frontier lands changed hands in both directions, and in 1377 a Trần army besieged Vijaya without success during the Battle of Vijaya.

Under the Lê dynasty the wars turned decisive. A month-long siege of Vijaya in 1403 ended when the Vietnamese ran short of food, but after almost 70 years without a major clash the attack of early 1471 took the city, a move interpreted as a reaction to Champa seeking help from the Ming dynasty. The Nguyễn lords then seized Cham provinces and pressed into lands held by Cambodia, while Vietnamese settlers moved into the Mekong Delta, home of the Khmer; around a thousand settlers were killed in Cambodia in 1667 by a Chinese and Cambodian force.

Emperor Minh Mang annexed what remained of Champa in 1832, and Cham Muslims and Hindus were forced to eat foods their faiths forbade as punishment and to assimilate them. A revolt led by the Cham Muslim leader Katip Suma, educated in Kelantan, was quickly defeated. Minh Mang pursued a policy of acculturation aimed at the Khmer and the hill peoples, and Vietnamese of the period called themselves Hán nhân, Han people, to set themselves apart from their neighbours.

The term itself is modern. Vietnamese nationalists of the 20th century coined it for what they saw as a steady and inevitable expansion, perhaps taking the idea from Hung Giang's article La Formation du pays d'Annam of July 1928, and historians Nhung Tuyet Tran and Anthony Reid count it among the dominant themes of that nationalist narrative. In South Vietnam, Phan Khoang's history of Đàng Trong from 1558 to 1777 and Phạm Văn Sơn's Việt sử tân biên of 1959 praised it, while the Cham historians Dohamide and Dorohime described it in 1965 as invasion and occupation.

Scholars question the idea of a continuous movement. Michael Vickery argues that each push answered a particular event rather than a lasting policy, Keith W. Taylor rejects the concept, and Momorki Shirō calls it a Kinh-centric view. There is consensus that the expansion so described did not begin before the early 15th century, and some date it from 1471.
nama-people: The Nama, in older sources also called Namaqua, are the largest group of the Khoekhoe peoples. They live in Namibia, South Africa and Botswana, many of them in central Namibia and others in Namaqualand, which straddles the Namibian border with South Africa. They traditionally speak the Nama language of the Khoe-Kwadi family, though many also speak Afrikaans. They originally lived on the banks of the Orange River in southern Namibia and northern South Africa. The name Namaqua adds the Khoekhoe suffix -qua, meaning place of, to the people's name. Under pressure from the expanding Cape Colony some Khoekhoe, including Nama, crossed the Orange River into what became German South West Africa.

Jager Afrikaner led a Nama community from Little Namaqualand to found a permanent settlement north of the Garib, the Orange River, in 1795. In 1823-24 his son Jonker Afrikaner led part of the Oorlam Afrikaner community to the area of modern Windhoek, where they built a society centred on cattle, trade and Christianity. Hendrik Witbooi took over the leadership of the Witbooi Nama from his father Moses in 1884, led his people north in search of new land and clashed with the Herero under Chief Maharero, who had made a protection agreement with the new German colonial administration.

In April 1893 the German Landeshauptmann Curt von François attacked Witbooi's settlement at Hoornkrans with 214 soldiers, and German troops killed nearly one hundred Nama women and children in their sleep. After a year of skirmishing Theodor Leutwein, with enlarged forces, defeated the Nama, who had run out of ammunition, and forced Witbooi to sign a protection treaty. From 1904 to 1908 the German Empire waged war on the Nama and Herero, a war now called the Herero and Nama genocide: herds were confiscated, people were driven into the desert or interned in camps, as on Shark Island, and forced to work on railways and in the diamond fields. Witbooi was killed in battle on 29 October 1905.

The Nama practise communal land ownership. Music, poetry and storytelling are important, and they are known for leatherwork, skin karosses and mats, reed flutes, jewellery and clay pots. The traditional dwelling is the haru oms, or matjieshuis, a domed hut of reed mats on a frame of sticks, woven by women and easy to take down when grazing becomes scarce. Camps once held five to thirty huts with their doors facing the centre. Most Nama in Namibia today are Christian, and the women's formal dress, long and flowing, developed from the style of the missionaries of the 1800s. In December 2002 ancestral lands in the Richtersveld, including its national park, were returned to community ownership.
namara-inscription: The inscription is carved in five lines on a block of basalt that may have been the lintel of a tomb. Its subject, Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Amr, followed his father 'Amr ibn Adi in conquering much of Iraq and the Arabian Peninsula from al-Hirah as vassals of the Sassanids. When raids on Iran provoked a campaign by Shapur II, he retreated to Bahrain and then moved to Syria to seek help from the Roman emperor Constantine. Hisham Ibn Al-Kalbi, an early ninth-century scholar, says he became a Christian before his death, though Irfan Shahîd notes that the inscription has not a single Christian formula or symbol.

In James A. Bellamy's widely accepted translation, the text names the monument as that of Imru' al-Qays, son of 'Amr, king of the Arabs, and lists his deeds: he subdued the Asadis and their kings, put Madhhij to flight and drove them to the gates of Najran, the city of Shammar, subdued Ma'add, and made the nobles of the tribes viceroys, who became phylarchs for the Romans. It closes with the date of his death, the 7th day of Kaslul in the year 223 of the Nabatean era of Bostra, which corresponds to 7 December 328.

René Dussaud and Frédéric Macler found the stone on 4 April 1901 at al-Namara, about 100 kilometres south of Damascus, near the Roman frontier of the province of Arabia Petraea. Dussaud published the first tracing and reading, and later scholars, while differing in detail, kept his view that it was the king's burial monument. In 1985 Bellamy corrected the tracing of two contested words in the third line. The script has also been read as a late form of Nabataean in transition to Arabic. Irfan Shahid called it the most important Arabic inscription of pre-Islamic times; the Louvre holds it as AO 4083.
namdev: Little about Namdev's life is certain. The hagiographies, full of miracles, were written centuries after him and contradict one another; the story of his being found floating down a river first appears in Mahipati's Bhaktavijay of around 1762. His wife Rajai, his son Vitha and his mother Gonai are said to have written about him. Traditions differ on his birthplace, some naming Narsi Bahmani in Marathwada and others a place near Pandharpur on the Bhima. He was born into what is generally recognised as a Shudra caste, recorded as shimpi, tailor, in Marathi and as chhipa, calico-printer, in northern India.

A friendship with the yogi-saint Jñāneśvar was recorded by the hagiographer Nabhadas around 1600, though Jñāneśvar never mentions him and the matter is unsettled. Maharashtrian tradition has him die at eighty in 1350; Sikh tradition places his death at the Punjabi village of Ghuman, and there are shrines at the other claimed sites too.

Namdev's songs were bhajans, made to be sung: each used a particular raga, a refrain, and his signature Nama within the poem, and they were handed down orally within singing families. Of about 2,500 Marathi abhangs credited to him, perhaps 600 to 700 are authentic; Christian Novetzke calls the attribution of later songs to him anamnetic authorship, and some poems of the 15th-century Vishnudas Nama were joined to his. The state government of Maharashtra gathered his work into the Sri Namdev Gatha in 1970.

His songs combine devotion to a god with form and to the formless Brahman. He held rituals and pilgrimages to be futile beside loving devotion, and taught that devotion runs both ways, so that Vishnu is Namdev's slave as Namdev is Vishnu's.

With Jñāneśvar and Tukaram, Namdev's writings form the basis of Varkari belief, and his paduka, or footprints, are still carried in palanquin to the Vithoba temple at Pandharpur in the pilgrimages held twice a year. In the north the Dadupanth counts him among its five gurus with Dadu, Kabir, Ravidas and Hardas, and the Niranjani Sampraday reveres him too. Scholars debate whether the hymns in the Sikh scripture are by the Marathi saint or by another sant of the same name.
namdhari: Namdhari means bearers of the name; the other name, Kuka, comes from the Punjabi for a cry, after the ecstatic practices of the sect's devotional singing, and early British reports also called its members Jagiasi or Abhiasi. Namdharis differ from mainstream Sikhs in holding that the line of Gurus did not end with Guru Gobind Singh in 1708: they believe he lived on as a recluse under the name Ajapal Singh and passed the Guruship to Satguru Balak Singh, whom they recognise as the 11th Guru. Their 12th Guru, Satguru Ram Singh, moved the sect's centre to Sri Bhaini Sahib near Ludhiana.

Members receive Amrit at a young age and abstain from meat, alcohol, tobacco and drugs, following a strict lacto-vegetarian diet and supporting cow protection. They wear homespun white turbans and a white woollen cord of 108 knots that serves as a rosary. Their code of conduct, the Namdhari Rehatnama, prescribes bathing and meditation on the name of God early in the morning, the recitation of texts such as Jap Sahib and Rehraas, and the daily singing of hymns; it banned child marriage and gambling. Ram Singh administered Amrit to women and simplified the marriage ceremony, conducting the first such Anand Karaj weddings at Khote in 1863.

Ram Singh raised a white triangular flag at Sri Bhaini Sahib on 12 April 1857 and is regarded by Namdharis as the first Indian to use non-cooperation against British rule; the movement kept a covert postal service of trusted couriers. The partition of Punjab in 1947 forced thousands of Namdhari farmers and artisans, over 80 percent of them from Sialkot district, to leave West Punjab, and Satguru Partap Singh resettled many of them on land he acquired in Sirsa district. After the death of Satguru Jagjit Singh in 2012 the succession of Satguru Uday Singh was opposed by the followers of his elder brother, Thakur Dalip Singh, and the factions clashed violently on several occasions.
nameisis: Nameisis, also written Namejs, was a Semigallian duke who ruled the western part of Semigallia from his capital at Tērvete, in present-day Latvia. Very little is known of his life: he appears only in the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle and in some documents of the 14th century. He is first recorded in 1272, as one of the Semigallian nobles who signed a peace treaty with the Livonian Order and the Archbishop of Riga.

After the crusaders' defeat at the Battle of Aizkraukle in 1279, Nameisis allied with Traidenis, Grand Duke of Lithuania, and recognised him as his overlord. He overcame the Livonian garrison of Tērvete castle, and the Semigallians soon took other castles, so that the crusaders left Semigallia except for the hillfort of Mežotne. Crusader raids that summer pillaged the lands around Dobele and Tērvete but took no castle.

In autumn 1280 Nameisis attacked Riga, the crusaders' main stronghold. The attack failed once the crusaders had gathered a large force of their Latgalian allies before the city, but the Semigallians took prisoners, among them the Order's marshal, who was sent to Traidenis and later killed at Kernavė. In 1281 a Livonian attack on Dobele Castle was beaten off with Lithuanian help.

That autumn a united crusader army of about 14,000 men came against Tērvete with siege engines. Unable to resist, Nameisis signed a new treaty under which the Semigallians paid tribute and accepted German judges but kept their castles and lands.

Nameisis and many Semigallians later moved to Lithuania, and he is recorded fighting the crusaders at Christburg in East Prussia alongside Traidenis. He is not mentioned afterwards and is presumed to have been killed there. Four decades later, in the 1320s, Grand Duke Gediminas styled himself king of the Semigallians and invited to Vilnius priests who knew the Semigallian language.
namhansanseong: Namhansanseong stands on the mountain Namhansan in Gwangju, Gyeonggi Province, South Korea, and stretches 12 km along its crest. The location was highly defensible, and defensive works stood there before the present fortress. A 2005 excavation found a fortress called Jujangseong dating to the Silla period, and in the Goryeo period a fortification called Gwangju Fortress occupied the area.

The present fortress was motivated by Yi Gwal's Rebellion of 1624 and the Later Jin invasion of Joseon in 1627. King Injo ordered Yi Sŏ to build it, and Buddhist monk-soldiers were recruited from all eight provinces for the work. Features were added over time until it became the best equipped fortress in Korea.

The fortress proper has a circumference of 7.545 km and an interior area of 212.6637 hectares. It was built as an emergency capital in wartime and an administrative centre in peacetime, with an emergency palace for the king, military buildings and housing for ordinary people. It could hold about 4,000 people, and commoners and king were expected to live inside together, unlike in some European castles where commoners stayed outside.

Its design draws on fortress architecture of East Asia, combining aspects of the Joseon style of Korea, the Azuchi-Momoyama period of Japan, and Ming and Qing China. Its layout was shaped by the gunpowder weapons imported from Europe in a period of continuous warfare, and it shows how Buddhism played a part in protecting the state.

In the early twentieth century the fortress was a site of battles between the righteous armies and the Japanese, and in 1907 the Japanese destroyed much of it to reduce its use to Koreans. The removal of the Gwangju County Office in 1917 left it a remote mountain village, and it lost people and material in the Korean War of 1950–1953. Because colonial authorities moved its administrative functions away and demolished its military ones, the fortress kept its original layout, unlike most Korean fortress towns.

Since the 1970s it has been a provincial park, and walls were restored on a large scale. The emergency palace and the royal ancestral shrine have been restored since the 1990s. It was placed on the World Heritage tentative list in 2010 and inscribed by UNESCO in 2014.
namibia: Namibia covers 825,615 square kilometres and is the driest country in sub-Saharan Africa. It borders the Atlantic Ocean, Angola, Zambia through the Caprivi Strip, Botswana and South Africa. Its landscape falls into five areas: the Central Plateau, the Namib Desert, the Great Escarpment, the Bushveld and the Kalahari Desert.
