The Namib, a hyper-arid expanse of gravel plains and dunes, runs along the whole coast and gives the country its name; Namib is a Khoi word meaning vast place. The Central Plateau holds the highest point, Königstein, at 2,573 metres.

The Khoikhoi as pastoralists and the San as hunter-gatherers lived in the dry lands for thousands of years, and Damara and Nama peoples also inhabited them. Around the 14th century Bantu peoples began to arrive, and from 1600 the Owambo formed kingdoms such as Ondonga and Oukwanyama. The Portuguese navigators Diogo Cão in 1485 and Bartolomeu Dias in 1486 were the first Europeans to land, but did not claim the area. From the late 18th century the Oorlam people crossed the Orange River from the Dutch Cape Colony, and conflict with the Herero led to the Nama-Herero War of 1880.

In 1878 the Cape Colony annexed Walvis Bay and the Penguin Islands, and in 1884 the German Empire established rule over most of the territory as German South West Africa. Between 1904–08 German troops waged a punitive campaign against the Herero and Nama that escalated into what is often called the first genocide of the 20th century. South African forces defeated the Germans in 1915, and the League of Nations mandated the colony to South Africa in 1920.

South Africa applied apartheid to the territory after the National Party won power in 1948. The United Nations assumed direct responsibility in 1966, though South Africa kept de facto rule until 1973, when the UN recognised SWAPO as the official representative of the Namibian people. Namibia became independent in March 1990 after the South African Border War, and Walvis Bay and the Penguin Islands stayed under South African control until 1994. Namibia is a parliamentary democracy, and the 2023 census counted 3,022,401 people.
nana-asmau: Nana Asmaʾu was born in 1793 in the remote community of Degel and was named after Asmāʾ bint Abi Bakr, a Companion of Muhammad. In childhood she lived through the Fulani War (1804–08), the campaign of jihad that established the Sokoto Caliphate. Her father was Usman dan Fodio, the founder of the Caliphate, and her half-brother Muhammed Bello became its second Sultan.

Like her father she was educated in tafsir, or Qur'anic studies, and placed a high value on universal education. Dan Fodio and his followers were Qadiriyya Sufis who stressed the sharing of knowledge, and held that to learn without teaching was sterile and empty. She became a prolific author, and her scholarship ranged across law, theology, mysticism, history and politics. She was well versed in four languages: Arabic, Fula, Hausa and Tamacheq Tuareg.

More than sixty of her works survive, written over forty years, in Arabic, Fula and Hausa, all in the Arabic script. Many are historical narratives, and others are elegies, laments and admonitions. Her poems of guidance were used to teach the founding principles of the Caliphate. She witnessed many of the wars of the Fulani War and wrote of her experiences in the prose narrative Wakar Gewaye, The Song of Wandering.

Her writing in ʿAjamī, African languages written in Arabic script, allowed Islamic scholarship to reach beyond Arabic-literate elites, including rural women and newly Muslim communities. She became a counsellor to her brother Muhammed Bello when he took the Caliphate, and collaborated closely with him.

From about 1830 she created a cadre of women teachers called jajis, who travelled through the Caliphate teaching women in their homes. Each jaji used the writings of Nana Asmaʾu and other Sufi scholars, usually through recited mnemonics and poetry, to train learned women known as the ƴan-taru, the sisterhood. To each jaji she gave a malfa, a hat tied with a red turban, which was the ceremonial symbol of office of the Hausa priestesses in Gobir. In part the project began as a way to bring newly conquered captives into a Muslim ruling class, but it grew to include the poor and rural.

She died in 1864. In northern Nigeria, Islamic women's organisations, schools and meeting halls are commonly named for her. Her works were collected by Jean Boyd and Beverly B. Mack in The Collected Works of Nana Asma'u (1997), and Boyd's The Caliph's Sister appeared in 1989.
nanaimo: Nanaimo lies on the western shore of Nanaimo Harbour, about 111 kilometres north-west of Victoria and 55 kilometres west of Vancouver across the Strait of Georgia. It is called the Harbour City, and also the Hub City, because its streets originally radiated from the shoreline like the spokes of a wheel. It is the headquarters of the Regional District of Nanaimo and the main ferry terminal for the middle of Vancouver Island.

The Indigenous people of the area are the Snuneymuxw, and the city's name is an anglicised form of their word. The first Europeans known to reach the harbour belonged to a Spanish voyage of 1791 under Francisco de Eliza, who called it Bocas de Winthuysen. The Hudson's Bay Company settled there in 1852 as Colvile Town, after its governor Andrew Colvile, and in 1858 renamed it Nanaimo.

The company's attempt at a coal mine at Port Rupert had failed. In 1850 the Snuneymuxw chief Che-wich-i-kan, called Coal Tyee, brought coal samples to Victoria, and Governor James Douglas visited the site. The Snuneymuxw wished to keep exclusive control of mining, and Chief Wun-wun-shum offered coal in exchange for blankets, which the company agent Joseph William McKay thought impertinent. They kept their rights for a time but gradually lost them. The first shipment of coal left on the Cadboro in 1852, and the Nanaimo Bastion was built from 1853 to 1855. On 27 November 1854, 24 English miners and their families arrived and were greeted by McKay and 21 Scottish miners.

Chinese immigrants settled in the late nineteenth century. In 1884, after tension over the Dunsmuir company's use of Chinese strikebreakers, the company helped move Chinatown outside the city limits. In 1908 community members and 4,000 shareholders across Canada bought a site for a third Chinatown on Pine Street. From September 1914 to September 1915 a provincial jail in Nanaimo served as an internment camp for Ukrainian detainees. Lumber replaced coal as the main business in the 1940s, and the Harmac pulp mill opened in 1958.

Nanaimo is reached by ferries from Departure Bay, Duke Point and the harbour, by the Island Highway and by a regional airport. Its economy now rests on forestry, services, retail and tourism, and Buttertubs Marsh, a bird sanctuary of about 100 acres, lies in the middle of the city.
nanaya: Both the origin of Nanaya and the meaning of her name are unknown. Joan Goodnick Westenholz considers the name most likely Akkadian on the strength of its suffix, and points to a goddess written Na-na, without a divine determinative, in a few personal names from the Gasur and Diyala areas as her only possible forerunner. Others have proposed that she began as a minor Akkadian goddess or as a hypostasis of the Sumerian Inanna, but the evidence is inconclusive. Older theories of an Aramean or Elamite origin are now regarded as discredited.

Nanaya was above all a goddess of love, called bēlet ruʾāmi, lady of love. The physical side of love was strongly tied to her, and texts dedicated to her could be explicit. She was also a guardian of lovers, in some spells especially of the rejected or disillusioned. Many early Assyriologists treated her as a goddess of the planet Venus like Inanna, but in the 1990s Westenholz argued that the evidence for this is scarce and that she was more often linked with the moon, and most later studies have agreed.

God lists from the Ur III period onward place her in the circle of Inanna, usually third in her entourage after Dumuzi and Ninshubur. In some early sources her spouse was the god Muati, but from the Kassite period she was paired with Nabu instead. The oldest known depiction of her is on the kudurru of the Kassite king Meli-Shipak II, which shows her in a flounced robe and a feathered crown.

The first texts naming Nanaya date from the reign of Shulgi, when she was among the 12 deities who most often received offerings at Puzrish-Dagan. Her principal cult centre was Uruk, where her main temple was the Emeurur and she also had a sanctuary, the Ehilianna, within Inanna's Eanna temple. In Neo-Babylonian Uruk she was second only to Ishtar: Ishtar was the lady of Uruk and Nanaya the queen of Uruk.

Her worship reached Mari, the Hittite town of Malidaskuriya and Susa in Elam, where Greek authors regarded her as the city's main goddess. In the Hellenistic period her cult spread to Armenia, Sogdia and Bactria. The Kushan emperor Kanishka proclaimed in an inscription that he had received kingship from her, and she appears on Kushan coins, spelled Nana in Bactrian.
nanbu-clan: The Nanbu claimed descent from the Seiwa Genji of Kai Province and were thus related to the Takeda clan. Minamoto no Yoshimitsu received Kai after the Gosannen War, and his great-grandson Mitsuyuki took the name Nanbu from his estates there. Nanbu Mitsuyuki joined Minamoto no Yoritomo at the Battle of Ishibashiyama and in 1189 took part in the conquest of the Hiraizumi Fujiwara, for which he received wide lands in Nukanobu District in the far northeast of Honshū. The clan grew rich on warhorses, and its fortified horse ranches, numbered Ichinohe to Kunohe, went to Mitsuyuki's six sons, founding the clan's main branches.

After 1333 Nanbu Motoyuki went north with Kitabatake Akiie and founded Ne Castle, which moved the clan's seat from Kai to Mutsu. One branch served the Southern Court and another the Northern Court until they made peace in 1393. By the time of Nanbu Harumasa the clan held seven districts of northern Mutsu but was a loose group of rival branches. In 1572 Ōura Tamenobu, of a cadet branch, killed the Nanbu magistrate Ishikawa Takanobu and began taking the clan's castles, and the feud with his family, later called Tsugaru, lasted two centuries.

In 1590 Nanbu Nobunao led most branches to pledge loyalty to Toyotomi Hideyoshi at the Siege of Odawara and was recognised as chieftain. Kunohe Masazane rebelled, was quickly put down, and the Nanbu received Hienuki and Waga for the loss of Tsugaru. In 1592 Nobunao began Morioka Castle. The clan sided with Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara and held Morioka Domain, officially 100,000 koku, throughout the Edo period, adding branches at Hachinohe and Shichinohe.

In the Boshin War the Nanbu first tried to stay neutral, then joined the northern alliance under Nanbu Toshihisa and the elder Narayama Sado, took Ōdate from the Akita Domain on 7 October 1868 and surrendered on 29 October. Their lands were cut, part of them given to resettle samurai of Aizu, and in 1871 the branch heads lost their offices. The main line became counts in the new peerage, and the clan's former retainers included Hara Takashi, later Prime Minister of Japan.
nanchang: Nanchang lies in the north-central part of Jiangxi, in the hinterland of the Poyang Lake Plain, with the Jiuling Mountains to the west and Poyang Lake to the east. It stands on the right bank of the Gan River just below its confluence with the Jin River, some 40 kilometres south-west of the Gan's discharge into the lake. The name means southern flourishing, from a motto of developing the south that tradition attributes to Emperor Gaozu of Han.

The region was first incorporated into China under the Qin dynasty, which conquered it from the Baiyue peoples and organised it as Jiujiang Commandery. In 201 BCE, under the Han, the city received the name Nanchang and became the seat of Yuzhang Commandery, governed by Guan Ying, a general of Emperor Gaozu. In 589 the Sui made the commandery a prefecture named Hongzhou, and after 763 it was the provincial centre of Jiangxi. The Tengwang Pavilion was built in 653, and in 675 Wang Bo wrote his Tengwang Ge Xu in praise of it, which made the building and the city known to Chinese readers ever since.

In 959 the Southern Tang made Nanchang its southern capital, and it was the capital of Jiangxi Province under the Yuan. At the end of the Yuan period it became a battleground between Zhu Yuanzhang, founder of the Ming, and the rival warlord Chen Youliang. Early in the 16th century Zhu Chenhao, the Prince of Ning, launched a rebellion against the emperor from the city. Under the Wanli Emperor it housed exiled relatives of the emperor who were potential claimants to the throne, and members of the imperial family made up about a quarter of its population. Matteo Ricci came there while trying to gain entry to Beijing.

The city suffered considerably in the Taiping Rebellion of the 1850s, and its importance as a commercial centre declined as coastal steamships replaced the overland routes to Canton. On 1 August 1927 pro-communist Kuomintang officers under Soviet direction launched the Nanchang Uprising. They held the city for only a few days, but supplied a core of troops from which the People's Liberation Army later developed. In the Battle of Nanchang, which began on 17 March 1939, more than 80,000 Chinese soldiers were wounded or killed and the Japanese army had more than 20,000 casualties.

Nanchang is the capital of Jiangxi and an important railway hub of south-eastern China. In 1949 it was still an old-style administrative and commercial city of about 275,000 people with little industry, and it has since been extensively industrialised. The Tengwang Pavilion, destroyed in 1929, was rebuilt in the 1980s, and Bayi Square and Memorial commemorates the uprising of 1927.
nanda-bayin: Nanda was born at the Toungoo Palace on 9 November 1535 to Princess Thakin Gyi and General Kyawhtin Nawrahta, the future Bayinnaung, and was a grandson of King Mingyi Nyo and a nephew of King Tabinshwehti. He grew up mostly at the Pegu Palace and at 13 went with his father and uncle on their campaign in Siam, earning the title Minye Kyawswa for bravery at Ayutthaya. After Tabinshwehti's assassination in 1550 he fled with his mother and sister to his father, and when Bayinnaung took Toungoo on 11 January 1551 he made his 15-year-old son heir.

From 1557 Nanda took an ever larger part in his father's wars, becoming one of the king's four principal commanders with his uncles, and by the end of the reign he led whole campaigns himself. He also sat in the Pegu court, dominated by Mon ministers.

Nanda succeeded without incident when Bayinnaung died on 10 October 1581 and was crowned on 15 October. The empire rested on his father's personal ties with vassal rulers, and in the solar polity system each new high king had to win their loyalty again. A rebellion in the Shan states of Sanda and Thaungthut, now in Yunnan, was crushed in 1582–1583, but Ava and Siam rose in 1584. Ava was subdued; Siam was not.

Between 1584 and 1593 Nanda sent five invasions against Siam, all of which failed; his largest army, of 25,000 men in 1586, was about a third of Bayinnaung's in 1568. He replaced vassals with sons and loyalists where he could, but Mogaung revolted in 1590, and conscription drained Lower Burma, where many Mons fled to become monks, debt-slaves or refugees. Siamese forces besieged Pegu itself in 1594–1595, Prome revolted, and by 1597 every vassal had broken away.

Toungoo and Arakan agreed in late 1597 on a joint attack. The Arakanese navy, manned by Portuguese mercenaries, took Syriam in March 1599, and the allies besieged Pegu from April. After his heir Minye Kyawswa II defected and was executed by Natshinnaung, Nanda surrendered on 19 December 1599 and was taken to Toungoo, where Natshinnaung, whom Nanda had once refused a marriage, assassinated him on 30 November 1600. Historians judge him an energetic king undone by an overextended empire without the administration or vassals to hold it, and the Restored Toungoo reforms that lasted until 1885 grew out of his failures.
nandi-hinduism: Nandi, also called Nandikeshvara or Nandideva, is the bull vahana, or mount, of Shiva and the guardian deity of Kailash, the abode of Shiva. The Sanskrit word nandi means happy, joy and satisfaction. In the oldest Shaivite texts in Sanskrit, Tamil and other Indian languages the name was widely used for an anthropomorphic door-keeper of Kailash rather than for the mount, and Siddhanta texts distinguish between Nandi and the bull, Vṛṣabha. Applying the name to the bull is a development of recent syncretism of different regional beliefs within Shaivism.

Nandi is described as the son of the sage Shilada, who underwent severe penance for a child with immortality and the blessings of Shiva. According to the Shiva Purana, Nandi was born from a yajna performed by Shilada. He grew up as an ardent devotee and performed penance to become Shiva's gate-keeper as well as his mount.

Many Puranic legends are told of Nandi. In one, he cursed Ravana, the rakshasa king of Lanka, that a monkey would burn his kingdom, because Ravana behaved restlessly like a monkey while waiting to meet Shiva; Hanuman later burned Lanka when he searched for Sita.

According to Shaiva Siddhanta, Nandi is chief among the Siddhars. He passed on his learning to eight disciples, the Four Kumaras, Tirumular, Vyagrapada, Patanjali and Sivayoga Muni, who were sent out in eight directions. The Nandinatha Sampradaya, a line of gurus, claims descent from him.

The earliest detailed prescriptions for Nandi are in the Shaiva Agamas, composed and compiled between about the 5th and 12th centuries CE. They treat him as a permanent part of a Shaiva temple. The Kamikagama, dated c. 6th to 8th century CE, prescribes that Nandi be installed on the central axis facing the linga, and the Karanagama and Suprabhedagama, c. 8th to 10th centuries, give instructions for sculpting him as a recumbent bull with garlands, bells and necklaces. By the Chola period, from the 9th to the 13th century, large monolithic Nandi sculptures were prominent in temple architecture.

Almost all Shiva temples show a seated Nandi facing the main shrine, a form found as far as Cambodia. Devotees may whisper wishes into his right ear, in the belief that he carries them to Shiva. Nandi was the emblem of historical Tamil Shaiva monarchs such as the Pallava dynasty and the Jaffna Kingdom, and the seated bull appears on the modern Nandi flag of Shaivism, first hoisted in 1998.
nandivarman-ii: According to the Kasakkudi plates, Nandivarman II descended from Bhimavarman, younger brother of the Pallava king Simhavishnu, through a collateral line known as the Kadavas. His father, Hiranyavarman, belonged to the Kadavakula, and Nandivarman himself is described as one who was born to raise the prestige of the Kadava family. Hiranyavarman had four sons, Srimalla, Ranamalla, Samkramalla and Pallavamalla, and it was Pallavamalla who accepted the throne.

Accounts differ on where the family lived. Inscriptions beneath the panels of the Vaikuntha Perumal temple at Kanchipuram say that Hiranyavarman ruled in Kambujadesa, present-day Cambodia, with Bhimapura as his capital, while some historians place the branch at Simhapura in Champa, in what is now Vietnam.

Paramesvaravarman II left no heir, so the ministers, feudatories and advisers of the kingdom sent an expedition to neighbouring states and distant lands to find a suitable prince. They chose the twelve-year-old Pallavamalla, who was brought to Kanchipuram and crowned king of the Pallavas under the name Nandivarman.

The Rashtrakuta emperor Dantidurga helped him recover Kanchi by making war on the Chalukyas, and around 751 Nandivarman married Reva, Dantidurga's daughter. Besides the Vaikuntha Perumal temple he commissioned the Tiru Parameswara Vinnagaram. The Pallava kings bore the Tamil title Kaduvetti, destroyer or clearer of forests, after their reputed habit, like their ancestor Mukkanti Kaduvetti, of clearing forest land and settling communities on it.

Nandivarman died in 796, having come to the throne as a boy of twelve. He was succeeded by Dantivarman, his son by Reva, so that the Pallava throne passed to a grandson of the Rashtrakuta emperor who had helped him regain Kanchi.
naneghat: The pass lies about 120 km north of Pune and about 165 km east of Mumbai, reached from below by an ancient stone-laid trail. According to the Archaeological Survey of India it was the fastest route between the west-coast ports of Sopara, Kalyan and Thana and the inland centres of Nasik, Paithan and Ter. The name is read as coin pass, since tolls were collected there from traders; Charles Allen describes a carved stone container by the road that served as a toll box.

Near the top is a large man-made cave with stone seats along its walls, probably a shelter for travellers. Long inscriptions cover its left and right walls. The back wall held eight life-size relief figures, since hacked away, whose labels survive: among them Simuka Satavahana, Queen Nayanika with King Satakarni, the Maharathi Tranakayiro and the princes Hakusiri and Satavahana.

The inscriptions, in Brahmi script, open with praise of Dharma, Indra, Samkarshana and Vasudeva, the Moon and Sun and the four guardians of the world, and list the dakshina given at Vedic sacrifices, including two horse sacrifices, in thousands of cows, horses, elephants and karshapana coins. The queen, named Nayanika or Naganika, was probably queen mother when she sponsored the cave. Most scholars date the inscriptions to the early 1st century BCE, some to the 2nd century BCE.

William Sykes found the cave in 1828 and took it for a Buddhist shrine; he read a paper on it to the Bombay Literary Society in 1833. Bhagvanlal Indraji made a partial translation, and Georg Bühler published a complete one in 1883, calling the records among the oldest historical documents of western India. The numerals, used in at least 30 places, show that place value had not yet developed in India, and the mention of Samkarshana and Vasudeva is taken as evidence of the Bhagavata tradition under the Satavahanas.

The cave and the high point can be reached by road on Highways 60 and 61, and the nearest railway station is Kalyan on the Central Line. The site lies about 35 km from the Lenyadri group of Buddhist caves near Junnar.
nanjing: Nanjing lies in the Yangtze River Delta, in the lower Yangtze drainage area, in the southwestern corner of Jiangsu province. The Yangtze flows past the west side and then the north side of the city, and the Ningzheng Ridge surrounds it to the north, east and south. The Qinhuai River, called the mother river of Nanjing, runs through the main urban area to join the Yangtze, and Xuanwu Lake and Mochou Lake lie within the city. The climate is humid subtropical, shaped by the East Asian monsoon, with very hot summers.

Human habitation in the area dates to the Neolithic period. A settlement called Jinling existed around the 4th century BCE, and after Qin's unification it was renamed Moling. Throughout the Six Dynasties period the regimes of the southeast kept their administrative centre at Jiankang, originally Jianye, with brief exceptions in 221–229, 265–267 and 552–554. The city was the capital of Eastern Wu from 229 to 280, of the Eastern Jin and of each of the Southern dynasties, which ruled southern China from 317 to 589.

Emperor Wen of Sui ordered Jiankang demolished in 589, levelling its walls, palaces and residences and deporting the Chen ruler and officials to the Sui capital. For three centuries the settlement was demoted. It was the capital of the Southern Tang from 937 to 975. In 1356 Zhu Yuanzhang captured the area and reorganised it as Yingtian Prefecture; in 1368 he took the throne there as the Hongwu Emperor, founding the Ming dynasty, and named it Nanjing, Southern Capital. It was the Ming capital until 1421.

The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom held it from 1853 to 1864. After the Xinhai Revolution, delegates elected Sun Yat-sen provisional president there on 29 December 1911, and he was sworn in on 1 January 1912. Nanjing was the capital of the Republic of China from 1927 to 1937 and again from 1946 to 1949, and under Japanese occupation the seat of Wang Jingwei's collaborationist regime from 1940 to 1945. It suffered atrocities, most notably the Nanjing Massacre of 1937–1938. Communist forces captured it in April 1949, and it became capital of Jiangsu in 1952.

Nanjing is the capital of Jiangsu province and one of the Four Great Ancient Capitals of China. Its heritage sites include the Presidential Palace, the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum, the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum and the city wall. The first Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, a road and rail bridge begun in 1960 and opened to traffic in 1968, was designed and built by Chinese engineers.
nanjing-massacre: The Second Sino-Japanese War began on 7 July 1937, after the Marco Polo Bridge incident. After Japan captured Shanghai in November, its troops advanced on Nanjing, and along the 170 miles between the two cities they committed atrocities as part of a terror campaign, including a reported killing contest between two officers. General Iwane Matsui commanded the Central China Area Army, and Prince Yasuhiko Asaka was installed as temporary commander and issued an order to kill all captives. The Chinese garrison of some 81,500 soldiers, many of them untrained conscripts, was gathered under Tang Shengzhi. The government left the city in early December, leaving its administration to an International Committee led by the German John Rabe.

Japanese forces reached the city gates on 9 December, and the garrison collapsed on the night of 12 December. The massacre is dated from 13 December, when Japanese troops entered the city. They killed civilians, among them children, women and the elderly, and executed thousands of captured soldiers and men wrongly taken for soldiers. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East estimated about 20,000 rapes in the first month; other estimates range from 4,000 to 80,000. One third of the city was burned. The first three weeks were the most intense, and atrocities in the area continued until late March 1938.

A committee of foreigners had set up the Nanking Safety Zone in the western quarter of the city, which is credited with saving at least 200,000 lives. The Dane Bernhard Arp Sindberg and the German Karl Gunther turned a cement factory into a refuge for 6,000 to 10,000 people. Eyewitnesses included Rabe, the missionaries John Magee, who filmed and photographed events, and Lewis S. C. Smythe, and the journalist Frank Tillman Durdin.

Estimates of the dead differ widely, partly because the Japanese army destroyed records and disposed of corpses. The tribunal's figure was more than 200,000; newer estimates fall between 100,000 and 200,000; the range runs from 40,000 within the city to over 340,000 across the region, and China officially commemorates 300,000.

Matsui was convicted for failing to stop the crimes and, with Kōki Hirota and five others, hanged on 23 December 1948. Asaka was granted immunity as a member of the imperial family. Hisao Tani was tried in China and shot on 26 April 1947. The Memorial Hall for the victims opened in Nanjing in 1985. In Japan, some officials and a few historians deny or minimise the massacre, and it remains a point of contention in relations with China.
nannaya: Nannaya, also called Nannayya Bhattu, was born into a Telugu Brahmin family and lived at Rajamahendravaram under the patronage of the Eastern Chalukya king Rajaraja Narendra. The king admired the Mahabharata and wanted the message of the Sanskrit epic to reach Telugu speakers in their own language and idiom, so he commissioned Nannaya, a scholar versed in the Vedas, Puranas and Itihasas, to retell it. Nannaya began the work in about 1025 CE.

He wrote the Adi Parvam, the Sabaparvam and part of the Aranyaparvam in the Champu style. In the 13th century Tikkana wrote fifteen books, from the Virata Parvam to the Svargarohana Parvam, and in the 14th century Errana completed the Aranyaparvam, so that the three poets are known together as the Kavitrayam, the trinity of poets. The developed language of Nannaya's work suggests that Telugu literature other than royal grants and decrees existed before him, though no such works survive.

Legends also credit him with the Andhra-shabda-chintamani, said to be the first treatise on Telugu grammar, written in Sanskrit with the help of his friend Narayana Bhatta in five chapters of 82 verses in the Arya metre. Appa-kavi's Appakavīyamu of 1656 tells that the jealous Bhimana threw the work into the Godavari River, and that it survived only because Saranga-dhara, son of Rajaraja Narendra, had memorised it and later gave a copy to Yelakuchi Bala-sarasvati, who wrote a Telugu gloss on it. The grammar is held to be an imaginary work, probably fabricated by Bala-sarasvati himself.
nanny-of-the-maroons: Nanny is thought to have lived from about 1686 to about 1760. Much of what is known of her comes from oral history, since little written evidence survives, and the Maroons tell many versions of her early life. According to Maroon legend she was born an Asante, in what is now Ghana. In one story she escaped slavery, perhaps by jumping from a ship offshore, while her sister Sekesu was enslaved, so that Nanny became the mother of all Maroons and Sekesu of all the enslaved in Jamaica. Other versions make her a free woman of royal African blood.

By 1720 Nanny and Quao, sometimes called her brother, controlled an area of the Blue Mountains later named Nanny Town, which overlooked the Stony River from a 900-foot ridge. The Windward Maroons raided plantations for weapons and food and led freed slaves into their communities, and over 30 years Nanny was credited with freeing more than 1000 slaves. Between 1728 and 1734 British forces attacked Nanny Town repeatedly; they captured it more than once but could not hold it.

The Maroons signalled over long distances with the abeng, a cow horn, hid so well that British soldiers told of trees coming alive, and ambushed attackers forced to come single file along the one narrow path to their village. Maroons credited their success to Nanny's supernatural powers, linked to Obeah, while historians stress their mastery of guerrilla warfare and of the terrain. After the British treaty with Cudjoe in 1739, a separate grant of 1740 gave Nanny and her people 500 acres in the parish of Portland, where Moore Town now stands.

A 1733 entry in the Journal of the Assembly of Jamaica rewarded William Cuffee for killing Nanny, the rebels' old obeah woman, but the 1740 grant suggests she was still leading her people then. Some say she died of natural causes in the 1760s, and Maroon oral history places her remains at Bump Grave in Moore Town. Her portrait appears on the Jamaican $500 note, known as a Nanny, and she is honoured each October on National Heroes Day.
nanterre: Nanterre is the prefecture of the Hauts-de-Seine department in the western suburbs of Paris, about 11 km north-west of the centre of Paris. The eastern part of the commune, bordering Courbevoie and Puteaux, contains a small part of the La Défense business district, and the court of Nanterre hears many high-profile lawsuits because so many major corporations have their headquarters there. Saint Genevieve, patron saint of Paris, was born in Nanterre about 419 to 422. In January and February 1894 the police raided the anarchists living there, without much success.

Excavations between 1994 and 2005 uncovered a Gallic necropolis dated to the 3rd century BCE, together with the homes of working people from a later part of antiquity, near the bank of the Seine in the north-west of the commune. The work has suggested more than 15 hectares of pre-Roman or Roman-era construction, and it has led to debate about the exact location of the pre-Roman capital of the Parisii and the first site of Lutetia, the Roman-era Paris. The necropolis might be the sacred place to which the name refers. The finds may indicate that Nanterre was the pre-Roman settlement closest to the modern centre of Paris.

Julius Caesar mentions Lutetia in his account of an assembly held there with Gallic leaders in 53 BCE. It has often been taken for the Île de la Cité because he mentions an island, but the river at Nanterre also divides into two channels around an island. In 52 BCE the Parisii took up arms with Vercingetorix and were defeated by Titus Labienus, one of Caesar's legates. Caesar records that they destroyed the bridges and set fire to Lutetia before the Roman forces arrived.

The commune had a population of 97,783 in 2023. It is home to Paris West University Nanterre La Défense, one of the largest universities in the Paris region, and its town hall, in the shape of a truncated pyramid, was completed in 1973. Three stations of the RER A serve it, and the Paris La Défense Arena, opened in 2017, stands there. It is twinned with Craiova, Pesaro, Tlemcen, Veliky Novgorod, Watford and Žilina.
nantes: Nantes lies in north-western France on the Loire, 50 kilometres from the Atlantic coast and 340 kilometres south-west of Paris. With the seaport of Saint-Nazaire on the Loire estuary it forms one of the main north-western agglomerations of France, and it is the seat of the Loire-Atlantique department and of the Pays de la Loire region. The city belongs historically and culturally to Brittany, and its omission from the modern administrative region of Brittany is controversial.

The first inhabitants settled in the Bronze Age, apparently drawn by small iron and tin deposits, and the area exported tin as far as Ireland. Nantes remained allied with the Roman Empire until its collapse in the fifth century. Around 490 the Franks under Clovis I took it from the Visigoths after a sixty-day siege. It was the seat of a bishopric at the end of the Roman era and was captured by the Bretons in 851.

The marriage of Anne of Brittany to Charles VIII of France in 1491 began the union of the duchy with the French crown, ratified in 1532. Rennes then became the provincial capital, while Nantes kept a financial role through its Chamber of Accounts. In the 17th century it gradually became the largest port in France and was responsible for nearly half of the 18th-century French Atlantic slave trade.

On 18 July 1789 locals seized the Castle of the Dukes of Brittany in imitation of the storming of the Bastille. The slave trade, outlawed by the Revolution, re-established itself in the first decades of the 19th century, and Nantes was the last French port to conduct it, until about 1827. About 400,000 people may have been deported to the colonies.

Nantes has 327,734 inhabitants in the city proper and 1,050,815 in the metropolitan area, making it the sixth-largest city in France. It has 127 buildings listed as monuments historiques. Along the Loire, a memorial to slavery has a path of 2,000 glass inserts, 1,710 of them naming slave ships and their dates of departure from Nantes.
nantes-cathedral: Rebuilding began in the early to mid-fifteenth century, on the site of a Romanesque cathedral, when Nantes and Brittany were commercially prosperous. The foundation stone was laid on 14 April 1434 by Duke John V of Brittany and Jean de Malestroit, Bishop of Nantes. The first architect was Guillaume de Dammartin, later replaced by Mathurin Rodier, and work started with the west façade, the aisles of the nave and its side chapels. The building has been listed as a monument historique since 1862.

Scholars divide the construction into five phases. In the first, from about 1434 to about 1470, the west façade, the tower bay and the south aisle with its chapels were built. In the second, to about 1490, the nave and the north aisle were raised. In the third, from about 1500 to 1516, the great west window glass was installed in 1498 as a gift from Queen Anne, and the south transept was begun. The post-medieval phase, about 1626 to 1630, completed the high vaulting of the nave.

The rest of the north transept and the choir were finished between 1840 and 1891 under the city architect St. Felix Seheult. The wait was partly because the old Romanesque church stood beside the city's protective walls, which had to be taken down before the choir could be completed.

Two large towers, 63 m high, dominate the façade, which has an external pulpit for preaching to a crowd in the square and five richly decorated gates. The interior is 103 m long and the nave 37.5 m high. The elevation and regular plan are French, while most details are Late Gothic, such as the absence of capitals and the Flamboyant tracery. Inside are the tomb of Duke Francis II and Marguerite de Foix, parents of Anne of Brittany, made early in the sixteenth century by Michel Colombe and Jean Perréal, and the cenotaph of General de Lamoricière, set up in 1878.

Allied bombing damaged the cathedral on 15 June 1944. On 28 January 1972 a fire started on the roof, believed to have been caused by a workman's blow torch, and severely damaged the timber frame, leading to a complete restoration of the interior. On 18 July 2020 fires broke out in three parts of the cathedral and destroyed the main organ, built by Jacques Girardet in 1621. Police investigated arson, and about 100 firefighters fought the blaze.
nantucket: Nantucket lies about 30 miles south of the Cape Cod peninsula and forms, with the small islands of Tuckernuck and Muskeget, the Town and County of Nantucket, a combined county and town government. The name is probably adapted from a Wampanoag word whose meaning is uncertain; it may have meant far away island or sandy, sterile soil tempting no one. Its nickname, the Little Grey Lady of the Sea, refers to the island's look from the ocean when it is fog-bound. The island proper covers 47.8 square miles, and its highest points are Saul's Hill at 102 feet and Altar Rock at 100 feet.

The island had been home to Wampanoag people for thousands of years, and as many as three thousand lived there in groups governed by sachems. Thomas Mayhew secured Nantucket as part of a proprietary colony in 1641 and made treaties with the Wampanoag that helped keep the region out of King Philip's War. Settlement began in earnest in 1659, when Mayhew sold nine tenths of his interest to investors led by Tristram Coffin for thirty pounds and two beaver hats. Within two years two sachems gave up their rights to the island for 66 pounds, and in 1750 a judge upheld the deeds despite Wampanoag petitions that the sachems had lacked the authority to sell.

Wampanoag men often made up half or more of whaling crews, and by the start of the 18th century a system of debt bondage supplied settlers with Wampanoag labour. Settlers also brought enslaved African Americans, and slavery was not abolished on the island until 1773. Freed Black residents built a neighbourhood called New Guinea, and in the 19th century the Quaker island gave sanctuary to people escaping slavery on the mainland. Before 1795 the town was called Sherburne.

The National Park Service calls Nantucket, a National Historic Landmark District since 1966, the finest surviving architectural and environmental example of a late 18th and early 19th century New England seaport town. The district was extended to the whole island in 1975. The Jethro Coffin House and the Nantucket Whaling Museum are among its sites. The 2020 census counted 14,255 residents, and the number rises to around 80,000 in summer. Herman Melville's Moby-Dick takes its narrator from the island.
nanyang-henan: Nanyang is a prefecture-level city in the south-west of Henan province, the largest in Henan by administrative area, at about 26,600 square kilometres. It lies in the Nanyang Basin, in the gap between the eastern end of the Qin Mountains and the source of the Huai River, so that it is hard to class as northern or southern China. The name means south of the sun: yang is the south side of a mountain or the north side of a river. It comes from Nanyang Commandery, established in the region in the Warring States period. Before the name was tied to the city, the place was called Wan. North of the city stands Mount Du, known for the Dushan jade.

Remains of Homo erectus, the Nanzhao Man, were found near Xinghuashan, and a large Neolithic settlement flourished at Huangshan between 5,000 and 3,000 BCE, with jade workshops, high-level tombs and granaries. The Baliqiao site in Fangcheng County is a core settlement of the Erlitou culture. Nanyang was the capital of the state of Shen in the first millennium BCE.

After Qin unified the six states, unruly people were relocated to Nanyang, which brought wealthy and skilled merchants and artisans from the six states and made it one of the national centres of iron smelting. It became commercially important under the Han dynasty, with many iron foundries and a position where routes between major cities met, and it was a city of the Silk Road. Emperor Gengshi was enthroned on the banks of the Bai River at Nanyang. With the help of the 28 generals of the Cloud Terrace and financial support from Nanyang, Liu Xiu rose to power and founded the Eastern Han dynasty.

Nanyang became its southern capital, the second largest city after Luoyang, and was home to many influential families. It later declined somewhat but remained a political and cultural centre of south-western Henan.

Nanyang was the home of Zhang Heng, known as the sage of science, the physician Zhang Zhongjing, Fan Li, a merchant, and Zhuge Liang, who lived in the area. Its Han dynasty relics include portrait stones, portrait bricks and pottery dogs, the largest ancient iron-smelting workshop in China at the Wafangzhuang site, and the tomb of Zhang Heng. The Wuhou Temple recalls the Three Kingdoms period. Most locals speak the Henan dialect known as Nanyang Hua, and a local form of opera is called Wan bang.
napata: Napata was a city of ancient Kush at the fourth cataract of the Nile, about 1.5 kilometres from the east bank, at the site of modern Karima in Sudan. Its Egyptian name, npt, was given it by the Egyptian cult of Amun that founded it for Egyptian pilgrims. Thutmose III founded it in the 15th century BCE after conquering Kush. It was the southernmost permanent settlement of New Kingdom Egypt, and Jebel Barkal, a lone sandstone butte beside it, became the main Kushite cult centre of Amun, residence of the Egyptian state god Amun of Karnak.

From 1075 BCE the power of the High Priest of Amun at Thebes weakened Egyptian control, and the Kushites, increasingly estranged from the Theban clergy, regained autonomy and founded a kingdom centred at Napata. By about 750 BCE Napata was a developed city. Kashta attacked Upper Egypt, and Piye and Shabaka brought the whole Nile Valley under Kushite control. The Kushite kings ruled the whole of Egypt for about 57 years as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, believing that their power came through Amun of Jebel Barkal. Taharqa and others built or restored temples at Memphis, Karnak, Kawa and Jebel Barkal. Conflict with the Neo-Assyrian Empire ended their rule, and the kings withdrew to Napata, where they were buried under pyramids at El-Kurru and Nuri.

Napata remained the centre of Kush for two more generations, with an economy based on gold, and the Temples of Amun and Mut at the foot of Jebel Barkal were its most important. The Egyptians sacked it. The capital then moved to Meroë, an island area rich in iron, though Napata remained the primary religious centre.

In 23 BCE the Roman governor of Egypt Gaius Petronius invaded Kush with 10,000 men and reached Napata, and Augustus claims in the Res Gestae that a penetration was made as far as the town. King Natakamani rebuilt it, renovating the temple of Amun and building a palace, but the site was later abandoned and plundered. The American archaeologist George A. Reisner found ten complete or nearly complete statues of Taharqa and his successors in two caches, one in the Amun temple, together with ash that suggested to him that they had been deliberately destroyed. The earliest known standing structure at Jebel Barkal is the Enthronement Pavilion, dated to Thutmose IV.
napirisha: The name is usually written with the logogram dGAL, great god. In 1965 Hinz proposed the Elamite reading Napirisha, from napir, god, and risha, great, and later sources confirmed it; Achaemenid texts at Persepolis spell it in forms that show the compound was still understood. After deciphering Linear Elamite, Desset and his colleagues argued for the reading Napiresha.

Napirisha probably came from Anshan in the highlands, and entered Susa as a dynastic god with the Shimashki dynasty. He is seen as the main god of Anshan, as Inshushinak was of Susa, and his consort Kiririsha was the tutelary goddess of Liyan. His earliest sure mention is an oath sworn in his name on a tablet probably of the early Sukkalmah dynasty, though some Linear Elamite inscriptions may place him in the reign of Kindattu.

In the Surpu incantations Napirisha is identified with Ea, and scholars assume he shared Ea's link with subterranean waters; he is also sometimes thought to have been an underworld god. The god list Anshar=Anum equates him with Anu. In the Middle Elamite period he formed a triad with Kiririsha and Inshushinak and was always named first, which is taken to reflect the primacy of Anshan over Susa in royal ideology.

Scholars debate how far Napirisha and Inshushinak merged. Texts from Chogha Zanbil treat the pair as grammatically singular, which Grillot-Susini takes as a sign of syncretism, while De Graef and Vallat stress that they remained separate gods. Hinz's old view that Napirisha was a taboo name for Humban has been set aside since de Miroschedji showed the two were distinct.

A Middle Elamite temple to Napirisha, Kiririsha and the Bahahutep stood at Liyan, and shrines to him were found at Susa. Hutelutush-Inshushinak built him a temple at Anshan shared with Kiririsha, Inshushinak and Simut. His worship outlived the Elamite kingdoms: he appears 26 times in the Persepolis Fortification texts of the Achaemenid period.
naples: The city lies on the Gulf of Naples, on the western coast of southern Italy, and rises from sea level to an elevation of 450 metres. It stands between two volcanic regions, Mount Vesuvius and the Phlegraean Fields. The islands of Procida, Capri and Ischia can be reached from Naples by hydrofoil and ferry, and Sorrento and the Amalfi Coast lie to the south. Nearby are the Roman ruins of Pompeii, Herculaneum, Oplontis and Stabiae, destroyed in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, and to the west the port towns of Pozzuoli and Baia, part of the Roman naval facility of Portus Julius.

The site has been inhabited since the Neolithic period. In the second millennium BCE a Mycenaean settlement arose not far from the future city. Sailors from the Greek island of Rhodes probably established a small commercial port called Parthenope, named for a Siren of Greek mythology, on the island of Megaride in the ninth century BCE. By the eighth century BCE Cumaeans had expanded it to include Monte Echia, and in the sixth century BCE it was refounded as Neápolis, becoming one of the foremost cities of Magna Graecia.

The city grew rapidly under the influence of the Greek city-state of Syracuse and became an ally of the Roman Republic against Carthage. During the Samnite Wars it was captured by the Samnites, but the Romans soon took it from them and made it a Roman colony. In the Punic Wars its strong walls repelled the Carthaginian general Hannibal. Naples was later the capital of the Duchy of Naples (661–1139), of the Kingdom of Naples (1282–1816) and of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies until the unification of Italy in 1861.

Between 1925 and 1936 the Fascist regime expanded and upgraded the city. In the later years of the Second World War it suffered severe damage from the bombing of the Allied forces. The Four Days of Naples, an uprising against the German occupation forces, lasted from 27 to 30 September 1943, just before Allied forces arrived on 1 October. The city was extensively rebuilt after the war.

Naples is the capital of the region of Campania and the largest city of southern Italy, with 905,050 residents within its administrative boundaries. Its historic centre was listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1995. The University of Naples Federico II, founded by Frederick II in 1224, is thought to be the oldest state university in the world. Caravaggio's arrival in 1606 was a critical factor in the development of the Neapolitan school of painting, and the Teatro di San Carlo opera house dates from the 18th century.
napoleon: Napoleon Bonaparte was born Napoleone di Buonaparte on 15 August 1769 in Ajaccio, Corsica, a year after the Republic of Genoa ceded the island to France. His family was of Italian origin, the Buonapartes descending from a minor Tuscan noble family that had moved to Corsica in the 16th century. With the support of the French governor Charles Louis de Marbeuf, his father's patron, he obtained a royal bursary to a military academy on the mainland, and in September 1785 he was commissioned a second lieutenant in the artillery. He supported the French Revolution, but after a failed attempt to take Ajaccio in June 1793 the family fled to Toulon.

Napoleon rose rapidly after winning the siege of Toulon in 1793, and in 1796 a campaign against the Austrians and their Italian allies made him a national hero. In 1798 he led an invasion of Egypt and Syria. On 9 November 1799 (18 Brumaire) he and his fellow conspirators launched a coup against the Directory, and he became First Consul. He won the Battle of Marengo in 1800, sold Louisiana to the United States in 1803 and crowned himself Emperor of the French in December 1804.

He defeated the Third Coalition at Austerlitz, which led to the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, and beat Prussia in 1806 and Russia in 1807. In 1808 he installed his brother Joseph as King of Spain, provoking the Peninsular War. His invasion of Russia in 1812 ended in a catastrophic winter retreat from Moscow. After defeat at Leipzig in 1813 he abdicated in April 1814 and was exiled to Elba. He escaped ten months later, but the Seventh Coalition defeated him at Waterloo in June 1815.

The British sent him to Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, where he died on 5 May 1821 of stomach cancer, aged 51. His reforms included the Napoleonic Code, a system of public education, the Banque de France and the Concordat of 1801 with the Catholic Church, and he gave civil and religious equality to Protestants and Jews. Against this stand wars that historians say cost six million lives, the plunder of conquered territories, the abolition of the free press and of directly elected representative government, and the reinstatement of slavery in French colonies. Historians still debate whether he was an enlightened despot who laid the foundations of modern Europe or a man who brought great misery.
napoleon-iii: Charles-Louis Napoléon Bonaparte was born in Paris on the night of 19–20 April 1808, the son of Louis Bonaparte, King of Holland, and Hortense de Beauharnais. At fifteen he moved with his mother to Rome, where he and his brother Napoléon-Louis joined the Carbonari, secret societies opposed to Austrian domination of northern Italy.

When the Duke of Reichstadt, Napoleon I's son, died in 1832, Louis Napoleon became the de facto heir of the dynasty and leader of the Bonapartist cause. On 6 August 1840 he sailed from London to Boulogne with about sixty armed men in an attempt to overthrow King Louis-Philippe. It failed, and he was held in the fortress of Ham for six years, which damaged his health.

After the February Revolution of 1848 he returned to Paris and was elected president of the Second Republic on 10–11 December 1848. Barred from re-election, he carried out a coup d'état on 1–2 December 1851: soldiers occupied key points in Paris, the National Assembly was dissolved and a rising on 3 December was crushed, with an estimated 300 to 400 opponents killed.

The constitution of 1852 gave him unlimited ten-year terms and the authority to declare war, sign treaties and initiate laws, and he became Emperor. His government built railways, ports and canals, modernised banking, and had Georges-Eugène Haussmann rebuild central Paris. The Cobden–Chevalier Treaty with Britain of 23 January 1860 lowered tariffs, and workers gained the right to strike.

In foreign policy he allied with Britain in the Crimean War of 1854–1856 and fought for Sardinia against Austria, receiving Savoy and Nice in 1860. The attempt to create a Mexican empire under Archduke Maximilian ended in failure, and French troops withdrew in 1866 after the United States pressed for it.

In July 1870 Napoleon III reluctantly declared war on Prussia after pressure from the public. Despite failing health he took command of the army, which was rapidly defeated, and he was captured at Sedan. He was held at Schloss Wilhelmshöhe near Kassel from 5 September 1870 to 19 March 1871, while the Third Republic was proclaimed in Paris. He went into exile in the United Kingdom and died there on 9 January 1873.

His reputation has suffered from the failures in Mexico and against Prussia: Victor Hugo called him Napoleon the Small, and historians have often seen him as an authoritarian but ineffectual leader. His government also continued the preservation of medieval buildings under Prosper Mérimée and Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, among them Notre Dame Cathedral, Mont Saint-Michel and Carcassonne.
napoleon-louis-bonaparte: Napoléon Louis Bonaparte was born on 11 October 1804 and was a son of Louis Bonaparte, who ruled the Napoleonic Kingdom of Holland from 1806 to 1810 as King Louis I. His father was the younger brother of Napoleon I of France. His mother was Queen Hortense, daughter of Josephine de Beauharnais, Napoleon's first wife. His younger brother, Louis-Napoléon, became Emperor of the French in 1852 as Napoléon III.

His elder brother, Napoléon Charles, died in 1807 at the age of four, and Napoléon Louis became Prince Royal of Holland. As the second eldest nephew of Napoleon I, who then had no legitimate children, he was regarded as his uncle's likely eventual successor. He lost that presumptive status on 20 March 1811, when Napoleon's second wife, Marie Louise, gave birth to a son, Napoléon François Joseph Charles Bonaparte, styled the King of Rome and later Duke of Reichstadt.

In 1809 Napoleon I appointed him Grand Duke of Berg, a position he held until 1813. His title also included Cleves. On 1 July 1810 Louis I of Holland abdicated in his favour, and for the nine days between his father's abdication and the fall of Holland to the advancing French army he reigned as Lodewijk II, King of Holland.

When Napoleon I was deposed in 1815 after the Battle of Waterloo and the House of Bourbon was restored to the French throne, Napoléon Louis fled into exile, although the Bonaparte family never abandoned hopes of restoring the Napoleonic Empire. On 23 July 1826 he married his first cousin Charlotte, daughter of Joseph Bonaparte, the eldest brother of Napoleon I.

He and his brother Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte settled in Italy, where they embraced liberal politics and became involved with the Carbonari, who opposed Austrian domination of northern Italy. On 17 March 1831, while fleeing Italy during a crackdown on revolutionary activity by Papal and Austrian forces, Napoléon Louis died of measles at Forlì. He is buried at Saint-Leu-la-Forêt, Île-de-France. The French Empire was eventually restored by his younger brother, who became Napoléon III in 1852.
napoleonic-code: Before the Revolution France had no single body of law. Civil law consisted mainly of local customs, such as the Custom of Paris, together with exemptions, privileges and special charters granted by kings and lords. On 4 September 1791 the National Assembly resolved that there should be a code of civil laws common to the whole realm, and in 1793 the National Convention set up a commission under Jean-Jacques-Régis de Cambacérès. His drafts of 1793, 1794 and 1796 were all rejected, one as too technical, one as too brief and one never discussed. A fourth outline, partly by Jean-Ignace Jacqueminot, was also rejected.

After the Battle of Marengo, Napoleon appointed a new commission of jurists on 12 August 1800, among them Jacques de Maleville, François Denis Tronchet, Félix-Julien-Jean Bigot de Préameneu and Jean-Étienne-Marie Portalis. Napoleon did not draft the Code himself, but he and Cambacérès chaired many of the plenary sessions. The Legislative Body rejected the bill by 142 votes to 139 in December 1801. Napoleon then suspended all projects in January 1802 and pressed the legislature into submission, and the Code came into effect on 21 March 1804.

The Code borrowed its categories not from French law but from Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis. It was divided into persons, property, the acquisition of property, and civil procedure, which was moved into a separate code in 1806. Unlike Justinian's work it was a comprehensive rewrite, rationally arranged, written in the vernacular and without religious content. Its preliminary article required laws to be promulgated and published, forbade secret and retroactive laws, and barred judges from refusing justice because the law was insufficient while forbidding them to lay down general rules. On the family, it set the husband above his wife and children, and divorce by mutual consent was abolished in 1804.

Other Napoleonic codes followed: the code of civil procedure in 1806, the commercial code in 1807, the code of criminal procedure in 1808 and a criminal code in 1810. Article 294 of the code of criminal procedure allowed the defendant access to a lawyer before the Cour d'assises.

The Code was not the first civil code in Europe, since Bavaria, Prussia and Galicia had earlier ones, but it was the first modern code adopted with a pan-European scope. It strongly influenced the law of many countries formed during and after the Napoleonic Wars.

West of the Rhine and in Berg and Baden it applied until the German Civil Code of 1900, and Romania adopted a code with its influence in 1864. It is still in force in France, heavily amended, and is the main source of law in Mauritius. Louisiana's civil code also shows French influence.
napoleonic-wars: The wars grew out of the French Revolution and the French Revolutionary Wars. Alarmed by the Revolution and the execution of Louis XVI, several monarchies formed the First Coalition in 1793, but mass conscription and total war let France defeat it. There is no consensus on when the Revolutionary Wars ended and the Napoleonic Wars began: candidates are 9 November 1799, when Bonaparte seized power; 18 May 1803, when Britain declared war; and 2 December 1804, when he crowned himself Emperor. Britain was irritated by French actions after the Treaty of Amiens and angered by Napoleon's reordering of Switzerland, Germany, Italy and the Netherlands.

In 1805 Britain joined Austria, Russia and smaller powers in the Third Coalition. The Royal Navy overwhelmingly defeated a Franco-Spanish fleet at Trafalgar on 21 October 1805, and Napoleon never again threatened an invasion. On land he won at Ulm and Austerlitz, which led to the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, and defeated the Prussians at Jena-Auerstedt and the Russians at Friedland. His Berlin Decree of 21 November 1806 brought the Continental System into effect, closing French-controlled territory to British trade.

To enforce it Napoleon invaded Portugal and, in 1808, made his brother Joseph King of Spain, which started the Peninsular War. In June 1812 he invaded Russia, which had broken the Continental System, and the campaign ended in the near-destruction of the Grande Armée. A Sixth Coalition defeated him at Leipzig in October 1813, Paris fell in March 1814, and he abdicated in April and was exiled to Elba. He returned in February 1815 and ruled for about one hundred days until the Seventh Coalition defeated him at Waterloo in June 1815. He died on Saint Helena in 1821.

The wars introduced mass conscription and guerrilla warfare. The Napoleonic Code, largely retained where it was adopted, advanced civil law, and nationalism and liberalism spread. Independence movements in Spanish and Portuguese America emerged as a direct consequence. France's defeat made Britain the leading naval and economic power for the rest of the century. The Congress of Vienna redrew Europe's borders, and no major conflict between great powers followed until the Crimean War in 1853.
naqada: Naqada lies on the west bank of the Nile in Qena Governorate, about 20 km north of Luxor. The modern town includes the villages of Tukh, Khatara, Danfiq and Zawayda. Its Ancient Egyptian name was Nbyt, rendered as "City of Gold", and its Ancient Greek name was Pampanis. In the 1960 census it was one of the most sparsely populated areas, with only 3,000 inhabitants, mostly of the Christian faith, who preserved elements of the Coptic language until the 1930s.

The name of the place is said to reflect the wealth of the Eastern Desert in gold and the strategic position of Naqada and the facing town of Koptos for the commerce in that gold. The working of precious metals and a floodplain agriculture that produced surpluses created demand for a variety of crafts, and the region became more economically specialised and diversified than contemporary Lower Egypt. The town, called Ombos, was the centre of the cult of Set, and large tombs were built there about 3500 BCE.

Flinders Petrie first excavated the site in 1894 for the Egypt Exploration Fund. The cemetery held about 2,000 graves, with finds from the Amratian (Naqada I) and Gerzeh (Naqada II) phases. Petrie at first believed he had found a new people who had invaded Egypt in the First Intermediate Period. The excavations of Jacques de Morgan in the same region showed that the objects came from an earlier age, and Petrie revised his view. The graves differed from later Egyptian practice: bodies lay in covered pits near streams, and they lacked embalming.

The large quantity of remains made it possible to date the whole predynastic period across Egypt, and the Naqada culture takes its name from the town. Other sites of that culture include el Badari, the Gerzeh culture and Nekhen. The graves held amulets, hairpins and flint knives, and few held items of special value. This points to a developing upper class and an established middle group, and the wealth is thought to have come from a gold trade attested by seals in the cemeteries.

Fekri Hassan led a survey of the area with Washington State University between 1978 and 1981, which found more cemeteries and rediscovered the royal tomb found by de Morgan. The area of Nubt had been looted, and local farmers had used its deposits as fertiliser, called sebakh. In August 2018 the Egypt Exploration Society tested the area of Nubt for further research and protection.
naqsh-e-jahan-square: In 1598 Shah Abbas moved his capital from Qazvin in the north-west to Isfahan, an oasis on the Zāyande river in the middle of a dry landscape. The move put the capital further from the Ottomans and the Uzbeks and gave more control over the Persian Gulf, which had become an important trade route for the Dutch and British East India Companies. The chief architect of the remaking of the city was Shaykh Bahai, whose plan rested on two features, the Chaharbagh avenue and the Naqsh-e Jahan Square, built between 1598 and 1629. Abbas also wanted to centralise power, which earlier had been divided among the Qizilbash military and provincial governors.

The square measures 160 metres by 560 metres. The Shah Mosque stands on the south side, the Ali Qapu Palace on the west, the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque on the east and the Qeysarie Gate to the Grand Bazaar on the north. Lotfollah was the first of the four to be built and was a private mosque of the royal court, while the Shah Mosque, with the largest dome in the city, took over the Friday prayers from the older Jameh Mosque and was meant for the public. Its entrance portal is turned at an angle to the square, so that the dome and the portal are both in view from the square while the court inside faces Mecca.

Ali Qapu, meaning Exalted Porte, marked the entrance to the royal residential quarter, which stretched from the square to the Chahar Bagh Boulevard. The Safavid shahs watched polo, horse-racing and military exercises from its upper galleries.

The square was where the shah and the people met. By day tradesmen kept tents and stalls and paid a weekly rent to the government, and there were entertainers, cooked food and coffee-houses at the entrance to the Imperial Bazaar. At dusk the traders left and the square was taken by dervishes, jugglers, puppet-players and acrobats. It was cleared for public ceremonies such as Nowruz and for polo.

Under Abbas Isfahan became cosmopolitan, with Turks, Georgians, Armenians, Indians, Chinese and a growing number of Europeans, and he brought some 300 Chinese artisans to teach porcelain-making. The Italian traveller Pietro Della Valle, visiting in 1617, ranked the square above anything in Constantinople and, for its harmony, above Piazza Navona. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
naqsh-e-rostam: Naqsh-e Rostam, which means Mural of Rostam, lies about 13 km north-west of Persepolis in Fars province. Rock reliefs are cut into the face of the mountain, which holds the final resting place of four Achaemenid kings, among them Darius the Great and his son Xerxes. The carvings span more than a millennium, from the Elamites and Achaemenids to the Sasanians. A few hundred metres away is Naqsh-e Rajab, with four further Sasanian reliefs, three celebrating kings and one a high priest.

The oldest relief dates to the Elamite period but is almost completely erased. It was carved over in the Sasanian period to make the grandee relief of Bahram II, leaving only faint traces, including one figure, probably a Neo-Elamite king, that was kept in the new composition. The four Achaemenid tombs are cut high in the cliff and share one design. Each has a relief of the king holding a bow before a fire altar and a figure emerging from a winged disk, standing on a platform supported by two rows of 15 figures, each named in a short inscription as representing a province of the empire. Below is a false palace portico with bull's-head capitals.

The tomb of Darius alone carries an extensive inscription, DNa and DNb, which lists his conquests. It is assumed to be the oldest and the model for the others. The other three are believed to be those of Xerxes I, Artaxerxes I and Darius II, though that matching is somewhat speculative. The tombs were looted extensively after Alexander the Great's conquest of Persia.

Well below them are Sasanian reliefs. The best known shows Shapur I on horseback, with the Roman Emperor Valerian bowing to him and Philip the Arab holding Shapur's horse. It commemorates the Battle of Edessa in 260 CE, when Valerian became the only Roman emperor captured as a prisoner of war. Kirtir, the high priest, stands behind the king. Their placing suggests an intention to link the Sasanians with the earlier Achaemenid Empire.

Seven large Sasanian reliefs depict kings, including Ardashir I receiving the ring of kingship from Ohrmazd, Bahram II in combat with Roman and other enemies, Narseh and Hormizd II. The Ka'ba-ye Zartosht, a square tower of the 5th century BCE, copies a sister building at Pasargadae. In 1923 the archaeologist Ernst Herzfeld made casts of the inscriptions on the tomb of Darius, which are now in the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. A team from the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago led by Erich Schmidt excavated the site from 1936 to 1939.
narai: Prince Narai was a son of King Prasat Thong, who had usurped the throne in 1629 and founded the Prasat Thong dynasty, and of Princess Sirithida, a daughter of Songtham. The Royal Chronicle says the infant was seen to have four arms before having two, and that the king took this as a miracle and named him Narai, from Narayana, a name of the four-armed god Vishnu. After Prasat Thong's death in 1656 his son Prince Chai became King Sanphet VI, but Prince Si Suthammaracha plotted with Narai to bring him down, and Sanphet was executed after nine months.

Si Suthammaracha took the crown and made Narai viceroy of the Front Palace. The two soon fell out. Narai drew on Persian and Japanese mercenaries and on the Dutch East India Company, and on the Day of Ashura they stormed the palace. Si Suthammaracha was captured and executed on 26 October 1656.

Narai's reign was the most prosperous of the Ayutthaya period, with great commercial and diplomatic activity with the Middle East and the West. In the Burmese–Siamese War of 1662 to 1664 he brought Chiang Mai under direct control, led an army of 60,000 into Burma and besieged Pagan in 1664 before retreating. He built a new palace at Lopburi with the help of Jesuit architects and engineers. His destruction of the Sultanate of Singgora came in 1680.

The Greek adventurer Constantine Phaulkon, introduced at court in 1681, became Narai's closest counsellor and arranged the growth of French influence: French troops were stationed in Mergui and Bangkok. Embassies went to France in 1680, 1684 and 1686, and to Rome in 1688. Narai showed interest in both Catholicism and Islam, but there is no concrete evidence he wished to convert to either.

Narai fell gravely ill at Lopburi in March 1688. On 18 May Phra Phetracha, commander of the Royal Regiment of Elephants and the leading opponent of the French, seized the palace. Phra Pi, whom Narai had adopted as successor, was executed on 20 May and Phaulkon on 5 June. Narai died on 10 or 11 July, and Phetracha proclaimed himself king. He besieged the French troops at Bangkok, and after four months and a negotiated settlement they were allowed to return to France.

Narai is counted among eight Thai monarchs given the title the Great. The accounts of French, Persian and other visitors give a rare view of the Ayutthayan court, since most original records were destroyed with the city in 1767, and Thai literature flourished in his reign.
narakasura: Naraka and his kingdom first appear in the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, in passages written down no earlier than the 1st century, where he is not yet the son of the earth goddess and of Vishnu's boar incarnation, Varaha. That parentage is first told in Book II of the Harivamsa, assigned to the 5th century, and is expanded in the Vishnu Purana and the Bhagavata Purana. The fullest version is in the Kalika Purana of the 10th century, composed in Kamarupa itself, which says he came from Mithila and founded Pragjyotisha after overthrowing Ghatakasura, the last of the Kirata kings.

In the later texts the pious Naraka turned evil through his friendship with the asura Banasura of Śoṇitapura. He conquered the kingdoms of the earth, drove Indra from heaven, stole the earrings of the mother goddess Aditi and carried off 16,100 women. Krishna attacked his fortress riding Garuda with his wife Satyabhama, killed his general Mura and countered each of his divine weapons; when Krishna feigned a swoon, Satyabhama attacked and Krishna cut Naraka in two with his discus.

In Assamese tradition Naraka wished to marry the goddess Kamakhya, who set him the task of building a staircase up the Nilachal Hill to her temple in one night. As he neared the end, she made a cock crow before dawn, and he left the work unfinished and killed the cock, at a place identified with the village of Kukurakata.

The 7th-century Nidhanpur copperplate inscription names Naraka as the originator of the Varman dynasty, living three thousand years earlier, and he is cited as the forebear of all three dynasties that ruled Kamarupa in historical times. A hill south of Guwahati bears his name. Some traditions hold that before he died he asked that his death be marked with lights, and believers mark the victory over him as the release of his prisoners.
naranjo: Naranjo stands on a raised karst plateau between the Mopan and Holmul rivers. The city covers at least 8 square kilometres, its urban centre about 2.25, with 389 recorded buildings in the central area and over 900 around it. The epicentre has six triadic complexes, two ballcourts, two palace compounds and an E-group; the largest pyramid, Structure C-9, crowns a natural hill with a cave inside. Lacking a river at its core, the city relied on modified seasonal wetlands, reservoirs and plastered cisterns to store rainy-season water. Its emblem glyph Sa'aal means the place where maize gruel abounds.

Little is known before Ah Wosaaj Chan Kʼinich, whom the Calakmul ruler Tuun Kab Hix installed in 546 to draw allies away from Tikal; according to Altar 2 he paved a road in July 559. Caracol attacked Naranjo twice in 626, a hieroglyphic stairway believed to come from Caracol was added to Structure B-18 in the 7th century, and Calakmul retook the city in 631. Under K'ahk' Xiiw Chan Chaahk Naranjo defeated Caracol, but by 680 Caracol had recovered and done away with him.

Lady Six Sky's arrival in 682 is recorded on Stela 24. Her son Kʼakʼ Tiliw Chan Chaak acceded in 693 at the age of five, and between 693 and 698 the city made at least eight attacks, defeating Ucanal in 698 as well as Tikal; from 706 he led new campaigns, defeating Yaxha in 710. Lady Six Sky died in 741. After Tikal's victory of 744 the captured ruler Yax Mayuy Chan Chaak was probably sacrificed, but later kings followed, among them Itzamnaaj K'awiil, who repaved Ah Wosaaj's road in 790.

The site is part of Yaxha-Nakum-Naranjo National Park. Teoberto Maler mapped it in 1905 for Harvard's Peabody Museum, and parts of the stairway he removed in 1908 are in the British Museum. Looters smashed many sculptures in the 1960s and controlled the site from 1997 to 2001; a survey led by Vilma Fialko from 2002 found about 270 looters' tunnels and trenches. A conservation project began in 2002, and in 2006 Naranjo was placed on the World Monuments Watch.
narapatisithu: Narapatisithu was born in Pagan on 8 October 1150 to Prince Narathu and his wife, later known as Myauk Pyinthe, Queen of the Northern Palace; the chronicles disagree on his dates of birth and reign. When his elder brother Naratheinkha became king in 1171 and faced revolts by the Kudus of the Tagaung region and the Mons of the Tenasserim coast, he made Narapatisithu heir apparent and commander-in-chief.

In 1174 Naratheinkha seized his brother's wife Weluwaddy while Narapatisithu was away on a mission. Narapatisithu sent a band of 80 men led by Aungzwa to kill the king, and then took the throne as Sithu II, in honour of his grandfather Alaungsithu, with the regnal name Śrī Tribhuvanāditya Pavaradhammarāja.

After the unrest that had followed Alaungsithu's death in 1167, he persuaded a great-grandson of the Mon king Manuha not to rebel, and the rest of the reign saw no revolts. He built the Kyaukse weir and began the Mu canals in the present-day Shwebo District, though repeated attempts to carry irrigation into Minbu District failed. Besides the Sulamani he built the Gawdawpalin, Minmalaung, Dhammayazika and Chaukpala temples at Pagan.

His chief justice was Nadaungmya and his chief minister Ananda Thuriya. The first Burmese customary law, based on Alaungsithu's judgments, was compiled and applied across the kingdom, and the term Mranma for the Burmans was used openly in Burmese inscriptions. Through the primate Shin Uttarajiva most monks aligned with the Mahavihara school of Sri Lanka. The Pali Culavamsa tells of a Sinhalese raid on the coast in 1180; the Burmese chronicles do not mention it, and Htin Aung and Wilhelm Geiger judged the account conjectural or much exaggerated.

Sithu II died on 18 August 1211. On his deathbed, it is told, he placed the hands of his five sons on his chest and urged them to rule with mercy and justice and to live in brotherly love. He is remembered as the last important king of Pagan, and he is venerated as a nat, a spirit of Burmese folk religion, at the Kuni Shrine in Pakhan.
narasimhadeva-i: Langula Narasingha Deva I was the son of Anangabhima Deva III, who had already defended the Eastern Ganga kingdom of Kalinga against the Muslim rulers of Bengal. The epithet Langula has been explained in several ways; the eighteenth-century Gangavashanucharitam of Vasudeva Somayaji says that the king's long robe trailed behind him like a tail when he walked fast. The Kendupatana plates of his grandson Narasingha Deva II name his queen Sitadevi as a daughter of the Paramara king of Malwa. He was the first king of Kalinga to take the title Gajapati, lord of the elephants, first used in an inscription of 1246 at the Kapilash temple.

In 1242-1243 Narasingha Deva marched into Bengal, aided by his Haihaya brother-in-law Paramardi Dev, against Tughril Tughan Khan, governor of Bengal for the Delhi Sultanate. According to the chronicler Minhaj-i-Siraj, who accompanied the Muslim army, Tughan pursued the Odia forces to the frontier fort of Katasin, where a hidden detachment attacked his camp during the midday meal and he barely escaped. In 1244 Odia forces surrounded Lakhnauti, and the governor of Awadh, Qamruddin Tamur Khan, came to relieve it and replaced Tughan. A new governor of Bengal, appointed in 1247, later fought back, and Paramardi Dev was killed at Umurdan. The Lingaraja temple inscription also claims that he humbled the Kakatiya king Ganapati.

Narasingha Deva commissioned the Konark Sun Temple and other temples, among them those at Kapilash, Srikurmam and Simhachalam, and the fort at Raibania in Balasore. His titles show him as a follower of the Shaiva, Shakti and Jagannath traditions, and Sanskrit and Odia were both court languages; the poet Vidyadhara wrote his Ekavali at the court. The Lingaraja inscription says he founded the Sadashiva Matha to shelter refugees from Radha and Gauda. A popular legend tells how the boy Dharmapada saved the masons of Konark from the king's anger, but it has no known source before the 19th century.
narasimhavarman-i: Narasimhavarman I was the son of the Pallava king Mahendravarman I, whose love of art he shared. The Chalukya emperor Pulakeshin II had raided the northern Pallava provinces and forts in his father's time without taking the capital, Kanchipuram, and the long conflict between the two dynasties passed to the son. The Sri Lankan chronicle, the Culavamsa, calls him Kanduvethi, an epithet that historians link to the name Kadavan, later borne by the Kadava chiefs.

When Pulakeshin II attacked again, Narasimhavarman defeated him in several battles, among them one at Manimangalam, 20 miles east of Kanchipuram, where the Pallava king boasted that he saw the back of his enemy as he tore his army apart. He then advanced on Vatapi, where Pulakeshin II was defeated and killed, and the city was never again a capital. Many grants compare the destruction of Vatapi to the sage Agastya's killing of a demon of that name. His general Paranjothi, honoured as one of the 63 Nayanar saints, is said to have destroyed the city himself.

The Sinhalese prince Manavarman lived at his court and helped him against Pulakeshin. In return Narasimhavarman twice sent an army to Sri Lanka for him, and the second expedition succeeded; the Kasakudi copper plates refer to the conquest of Sri Lanka. In 640 the Chinese traveller Hiuen Tsang visited Kanchipuram, and the Nayanar poet-saints Appar and Sambandar lived in his reign.
