Narasimhavarman completed the works his father had begun at Mamallapuram, and the Pancha Rathas, a complex of monolithic rock-cut temples, were made in his reign; most of the monuments of Mahabalipuram, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, were finished under him. His son Mahendravarman II succeeded him in 668. In modern Tamil literature Kalki Krishnamurthy based Sivagamiyin Sabadham on his early years and Parthiban Kanavu on the later years of his rule.
narathihapate: Narathihapate was born on 23 April 1238 to Crown Prince Uzana and a commoner concubine from Myittha. Known at the palace as Min Khwe-Chi, he was not in line for the throne even after his father became king in 1251; that place belonged to his half-brother Thihathu, eldest son of the chief queen. When Uzana died in a hunting accident in May 1256 and Thihathu claimed the throne, the court under the chief minister Yazathingyan, preferring a prince they believed they could control, raised Khwe-Chi instead on 6 May 1256 and had Thihathu executed.

The young king proved quick-tempered and ruthless. He exiled Yazathingyan, then had to recall him to put down revolts in Martaban and Arakan; the minister died on the way home. The treasury, drained for years by the growth of tax-free religious lands, was never restored, and the king built the Mingalazedi Pagoda with forced labour.

The Mongols, who had conquered the Dali Kingdom in 1253–57, demanded tribute in 1271–72, and Kublai Khan sent a mission of his own in 1273; both were refused. After Mongol forces occupied a Burmese vassal state on the border, the Burmese army sent to recover it was beaten at Ngasaunggyan in April 1277. A fresh invasion took the forts of Ngasaunggyan and Kaungsin in December 1283 and Tagaung in February 1284, and by February 1285 the Mongols had reached Hanlin. Although they had no orders to attack Pagan, the king fled south to Lower Burma.

There he settled at Hlegya, west of Prome, unable to win the support of his three sons, who held the ports of Bassein, Dala and Prome, while Pegu and Martaban revolted. In June 1286 he accepted Mongol terms, and in January 1287 his embassy under the chief primate Shin Ditha Pamauk acknowledged Mongol suzerainty in Beijing in return for a withdrawal of troops.

About a month after the embassy returned in May 1287, the king set out for Pagan but was captured by his son Thihathu, Viceroy of Prome, and forced to take poison on 1 July 1287. The kingdom broke apart: the Mon Hanthawaddy kingdom rose in Lower Burma, Arakan became independent, and the Mongols occupied the north to Tagaung until 1303. The chronicles portray him as a cowardly glutton, but scholars hold that he was an ineffective ruler blamed unfairly for a decline that had begun before his reign.
narathu: Narathu was a middle son of King Sithu I and Queen Yadanabon, whose father, Dhamma Kyin, had been a minister at the court of King Kyansittha; the four main Burmese chronicles disagree on the dates of his life. His elder brother Min Shin Saw was heir apparent, but after a falling out with their father he was sent into exile at Aung Pinle Lake, near present-day Mandalay. Narathu then impressed the king with his handling of the kingdom's daily affairs and became heir apparent in all but name.

When the king fell violently ill in 1167, Narathu had him moved to the Shwegugyi Temple, which Sithu had built in 1131. The chronicles say that the king woke, was furious to find himself out of the palace, and that Narathu then put a blanket over his head. Min Shin Saw came with an army to claim the throne; Narathu submitted and led his coronation, and the new king was poisoned at his first meal. Deeply unpopular, Narathu shut himself in his palace and built the Dhammayangyi, the largest temple of Pagan, to atone for his sins. In a fit of rage he killed with his bare hands a queen who was a daughter of the chief of Pateikkaya, a tributary kingdom to the west.

In 1171 the chief of Pateikkaya sent eight assassins disguised as Brahmin astrologers, who hid swords under their robes, gained an audience and killed the king, then took their own lives when the guards rushed in. Narathu is therefore remembered as Kalaja Min, the king who fell by the kalars. The historian Gordon Luce proposed that assassins from the Kingdom of Polonnaruwa killed him instead, a theory Htin Aung rejected as conjecture.
narayanhiti-palace: The palace stands in Kathmandu, east of the Kaiser Mahal and next to Thamel. Its name joins Narayana, an epithet of the god Vishnu, whose temple faces the palace, and hiti, the Newar word for a water spout, after a stone drinking fountain east of the main entrance that features in local legends. The building has a floor space of 3,794 square metres in three parts, the guest, state and private wings, with interiors in a late Victorian style and rooms named after the districts of Nepal.

The site was first home to Chautariya families, among them Prime Minister Fateh Jung Shah, who was killed in the Kot massacre of 19 September 1846. Colonel Ranodip Singh Kunwar, brother of Jung Bahadur Rana, then took it over and, after becoming prime minister in 1877, enlarged it into a lavish palace; he was assassinated in its southern wing during the coup of 22 November 1885. His successor Bir Shumsher had the old palace pulled down in 1886 and a new one built by the architect Jogbir Sthapit for his son-in-law, King Prithvi Bir Bikram Shah, which moved the royal residence here from Hanuman Dhoka.

The 1934 Nepal–Bihar earthquake damaged that palace and killed two infant daughters of King Tribhuvan. King Mahendra had it replaced from 1963 with a building in Nepalese styles meant as a national symbol; its housewarming was held on 27 February 1970 for the wedding of Crown Prince Birendra. Among those killed in the royal massacre of 1 June 2001 were King Birendra and Queen Aishwarya. After the 2006 revolution the last king, Gyanendra, left the palace on 11 June 2008.

The former palace is now the Narayanhiti Palace Museum, where the royal crown jewels have been shown since October 2018. Visitors see Kaski Sadan, the reception hall where kings gave audience and prime ministers took their oath, and the throne room, Gorkha Baithak, whose pagoda-style ceiling rises 60 feet above the place of the throne. A Garuda outside the palace's Narayan temple is thought to date from the Licchavi period.
narbonne: Narbonne lies about 15 kilometres from the Mediterranean and was historically a prosperous port. In Roman times the river Aude, then called the Atax, divided into two branches, and the southern one followed the course of today's Canal de la Robine past the colony. The colony was founded near an older settlement on the hill of Montlaurès, about 4 kilometres to the north, where an oppidum dates back to the 6th century BCE. Hecataeus of Miletus, in the 5th century BCE, called the place a Celtic harbour and marketplace. The Via Domitia, the first Roman road in Gaul, joined Italy to Spain here and met the Via Aquitania, which ran towards the Atlantic through Tolosa and Burdigala.

Narbonne rose as a competitor to Massilia. Julius Caesar settled veterans of his 10th Legion there and tried to develop its port while Massilia supported Pompey. The province it headed, Gallia Transalpina, was later renamed Gallia Narbonensis after the city. It had an estimated 30,000 to 50,000 inhabitants.

According to Hydatius, a local military leader handed the city to the Visigoths in 462 in exchange for support, ending Roman rule there. It became the capital of Septimania, which held out against the Franks after the Battle of Vouillé in 507. Muslim forces took the region from 719 and called it Arbūnah, and Pepin the Short conquered Narbonne in 759.

French kings took effective control of the region only in the early 13th century, after the Albigensian Crusade. Narbonne became a major centre of Jewish learning, with an important exegetical school in the 11th and 12th centuries and a Jewish community of about 2,000 people in the 12th. Ermengarde of Narbonne, who ruled from 1134 to 1192, presided over a court where the spirit of courtly love developed.

The city declined from the 14th century. A change in the course of the Aude silted up its access to the sea, and a flood in 1320 swept away the dam the Romans had built. The plague and a raid by Edward, the Black Prince, did further harm. Its cathedral was never finished, partly because completing it would have meant demolishing the city wall. From the sixteenth century the townspeople worked to keep the old river channel navigable, and the resulting Canal de la Robine was linked to the Canal du Midi in 1776.

Narbonne is a commune and subprefecture in the Aude department of Occitania, the largest commune of the department though not its capital, which is Carcassonne. Its sights include the Cathedral of Saints Justus and Pastor, the Palace of the Archbishops, the Roman Horreum, a cryptoporticus once used as a grain warehouse, and remains of the Via Domitia in the city centre.
narendranagar: Narendranagar lies in the Shivalik foothills at an average elevation of 1,020 metres. The site was chosen for its scenery and for its nearness to the plains below: on a clear day Rishikesh, Haridwar and the Ganga can be seen from the town, where the river leaves the mountains for the plains of Haridwar. Before the move of the capital the place was the small town of Odathali.

Odathali was held to be a seat of spirituality and meditation since ancient times. According to legend the sage Uddhava performed severe penance there, and tradition says that Purasara, held to be the founder of astrology, studied the movements of planets and stars at the spot; the building known as his observatory now houses the local polytechnic.

The present town came into existence in 1919, when Maharaja Narendra Shah of Tehri Garhwal moved his capital from Tehri. In doing so he followed his predecessors Pratap Shah and Kirti Shah, who had founded Pratapnagar and Kirtinagar. The palace received an annexe to house the British Viceroy and his entourage, who visited fairly often, and its later guests included the Prime Ministers Lal Bahadur Shastri and Indira Gandhi, the spiritual leaders Anandmayi Ma and Swami Sivanand, and the last Viceroy, Lord Mountbatten of Burma.

In 1946 Narendra Shah abdicated in favour of his son Manabendra Shah, the last Maharaja. Shortly after India gained independence the state was merged with Uttar Pradesh. Several buildings of the princely capital, among them the hospital and the secretariat, are still in use, and the bazaar buildings are a century old.

Narendranagar is a town and municipal board of the Tehri Garhwal district in Uttarakhand; at the 2001 census it had 4,796 inhabitants. The palace, whose walls keep their original relief work and whose gateway is flanked by two World War I cannons, now houses the spa Ananda in the Himalayas.
naresuan: Prince Naret was born in Phitsanulok in 1555–56, the son of King Mahathammarachathirat of Phitsanulok and his queen consort Wisutkasat. His mother was a daughter of Maha Chakkraphat and Queen Suriyothai. When King Bayinnaung of the Toungoo dynasty took Phitsanulok and Ayutthaya during the Burmese–Siamese War, he required Maha Thammarachathirat to send his son to Bago as a royal hostage.

After six years in Pegu he returned to Ayutthaya about 1570, having followed Burmese military training alongside the sons of princes and nobles. That year his father appointed him Phra Maha Uparaja, or viceroy, at the age of 15, and sent him to rule Phitsanulok under the name Naresuan. In 1580 he led 3,000 men against a Khmer force of 5,000 that had set out to raid cities near Ayutthaya, and destroyed it.

After Bayinnaung died in 1581, Naresuan was called to Bago in 1584 to help his son Nanda Bayin against a rebellion. According to Prince Damrong, he learned at the border that Burmese forces meant to attack him, and he poured water from a gold goblet to declare that Siam had severed friendship with Hongsawadi. Nanda Bayin's armies later failed to take Ayutthaya, including in a five-month siege in 1586. Naresuan was crowned King of Ayutthaya as Sanphet II in July 1590, after the death of his father.

His best-known fight came in January 1593 at Nong Sarai, where the Burmese crown prince Mingyi Swa was killed. Thai tradition tells of a formal elephant duel in which Naresuan cut down Mingyi Swa with his ngao, or glaive. Burmese chronicles do not mention a duel, and the historian Terwiel concluded that no formal duel probably took place and that Swa was mortally wounded by a gun fired by Naresuan or a man with him. Naresuan afterwards captured Dawei and Tanintharyi, took Longvek in Cambodia, and became overlord of Lan Na.

In 1605 Naresuan raised an army of 200,000 men against a threat from the King of Ava. He reached the Fang District of Chiang Mai Province, fell ill, and died three days later on 25 April 1605, probably of smallpox. His brother Ekathotsarot succeeded him. Soon after his death Lan Na and Cambodia broke free of Siamese suzerainty.

His standing as a national hero was largely cemented in later centuries, especially after the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767. Prince Damrong Rajanubhab championed it. Royal Thai Armed Forces Day, 18 January, commemorates his victory in 1593, and Naresuan University in Phitsanulok bears his name.
narmada-river: The Narmada rises in a small reservoir called the Narmada Kund on the Amarkantak Plateau in eastern Madhya Pradesh and flows westward for about 1,312 km, entering the Arabian Sea through the Gulf of Khambhat 30 km west of Bharuch. Of that length 1,077 km lie in Madhya Pradesh and 161 km in Gujarat. It is the longest west-flowing river of India and, with the Tapti, one of only two major peninsular rivers that run east to west. It flows in a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges and therefore forms an estuary and not a delta. Near Jabalpur it falls about 9 metres at the Dhuandhara and runs through the Marble Rocks.

Its basin covers 98,796 square kilometres, 82 per cent of it in Madhya Pradesh, and has 41 tributaries, 22 of them from the Satpura range. About 60 per cent of the basin is arable land and 35 per cent forest.

The Periplus Maris Erythraei called the river the Namnadius and Ptolemy the Namadus. Narmada is a Sanskrit word meaning giver of pleasure. The valley is a graben bounded by two parallel faults, and its sediments hold fossils. William Sleeman found the first dinosaur fossil in India at Jabalpur in 1828, and in 1982 the Narmada Human, an extinct hominin, was found near Hathnora village, one of the earliest hominin bones in the region.

In Hinduism the Narmada is a goddess, like the Ganges. The Matsya Purana holds all its banks sacred. According to the Rewa Khand she was created from the sweat of Shiva as he performed penance, which makes her Shiva's daughter. The white quartz pebbles called banalinga found on its bed are believed to be Shiva in personified form. Pilgrims perform the Narmada Parikrama, a circumambulation of the river regarded as meritorious. Adi Shankara is said to have met his guru Govinda Bhagavatpada at Omkareshwar on its banks.

The valley carries dry deciduous forest dominated by teak and includes Kanha, Bandhavgarh and Panna National Parks. Thirty dams were planned on the river, and the largest, Sardar Sarovar, was built to a final height of 163 metres from its foundation. Its reservoirs have inundated archaeological and architectural sites, and the state's archaeology department made rescue excavations and moved a number of temples.
narmadapuram-district: The district has an area of 5408.23 square kilometres and lies in the valley of the Narmada River, which forms its northern boundary. It is bounded by the districts of Raisen to the north, Narsinghpur to the east, Chhindwara to the southeast, Betul to the south, Harda to the west and Sehore to the northwest. The western part of the district was split off in 1998 to become Harda District.

The Tawa River, the longest tributary of the Narmada, rises in the Satpura Range to the south and flows north to meet the Narmada at the village of Bandra Bhan. The Tawa Reservoir lies in the south-central part of the district. The district belongs to Narmadapuram Division.

The district was part of the Nerbudda (Narmada) Division of the Central Provinces and Berar. After India's independence in 1947 the area became part of the state of Madhya Bharat, later Madhya Pradesh.

The headquarters town was previously named after the Narmada river and was called Narmadapuram. It was later renamed after Sultan Hoshang Shah of Malwa, and the district took the name Hoshangabad. In the hills of the south, Pachmarhi served as the summer capital of the Central Provinces and Berar under the British Raj.

At the 2011 census the district had a population of 1,241,350, with 31.42 per cent living in urban areas. About 96 per cent of the people gave Hindi as their first language, and smaller numbers spoke Gondi and Korku. The land is fertile and canal irrigation from the Tawa Dam supports crops such as wheat, soya bean, mung bean, sugarcane, gram and paddy.

Itarsi is the main economic centre and rail hub, with a railway junction through which about 350 trains pass, and industrial units that include the Security Paper Mill and the Ordnance Factory. Pachmarhi, at an altitude of 3,555 feet in the Satpura hills, draws visitors to its waterfalls, among them Bee Falls and Duchess Falls, and to Dupgrah, the highest peak of the Satpuras. The Pachmarhi Sanctuary covers 461.37 square kilometres and is part of the larger Pachmarhi Biosphere Preserve.
narmer: Narmer is believed to have succeeded the king Ka. His name is written with the hieroglyphs for a catfish and a chisel and is often translated as raging catfish, though there is no consensus on the reading. The date commonly given for the start of his reign is about 3100 BCE, give or take 150 years, derived from several sources including the Turin Canon. A radiocarbon study of 2013 placed the reign of his successor Aha most likely between 3111 and 3045 BCE.

A majority of Egyptologists identify Narmer with Menes, the first king in the later king lists, which give only throne names, while Narmer is a Horus name. Sealings found at Abydos in the tombs of Den and Qa'a list Narmer as the first king, followed by Hor-Aha, and are taken as strong evidence for the identification. A vigorous minority argues that Menes was Hor-Aha.

The Narmer Palette, found at Hierakonpolis in 1897 and 1898, shows him wearing the crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the crown of Lower Egypt on the other. Whether it records a real event or is purely symbolic has been debated. In 1993 Günter Dreyer found at Abydos a year label of Narmer depicting the same scene, which most Egyptologists take to show a real event. Evidence suggests that unification had begun under Ka and Iry-Hor and that Narmer completed it by conquering a polity in the north-west Delta.

Egyptian presence in Canaan peaked in his time: 20 serekhs found there may belong to Narmer, though seven are uncertain. Tell es-Sakan was a walled city built in Egyptian style, probably an administrative centre. Scholars have argued over invasion against trade and colonisation, and the latter now predominates. Narmer's name appears in 98 inscriptions at 26 sites in Egypt, Canaan and Sinai.

Narmer's tomb lies at Umm el-Qa'ab near Abydos, two joined mud-brick chambers next to the tombs of Ka and Hor-Aha. It was pillaged repeatedly over thousands of years, so objects of other kings were found in it and his own in other graves. Excavations by Flinders Petrie in 1899 to 1903 and later by the German Archaeological Institute recovered inscriptions on wood and bone, seal impressions, flint arrowheads and knives, and part of an ebony chair leg. Kaiser identified the chambers as Narmer's in 1964. To the later Egyptians history began with Narmer and the unification, and everything before him belonged to myth.
narmer-palette: The palette was found by the British archaeologists James Quibell and Frederick W. Green during the 1897–98 season, in what they called the Main Deposit in the Temple of Horus at Nekhen. The Narmer Macehead and the Scorpion Macehead came from the same dig. Quibell and Green did not record the exact place and circumstances of the finds clearly, and Green's report put the palette in a different layer, one or two metres from the deposit, which is considered more accurate on the basis of the original excavation notes. Nekhen was one of four power centres in Upper Egypt that preceded its consolidation at the end of the Naqada III period.

The palette is 63 centimetres tall and 42 wide, shield-shaped and carved in low relief from a single piece of dark grey-green siltstone from the quarry at Wadi Hammamat, which was used from predynastic times. Older writing wrongly called the stone slate or schist. At the top of both sides an identical serekh, with a catfish (nꜥr) and a chisel (mr) spelling Narmer's name, is flanked by two bovine heads thought to represent the cow goddess Bat.

On one side the king raises a mace and pulls a kneeling captive up by the hair, while a sandal-bearer stands behind him and a falcon, representing Horus, holds a rope attached to the nose of a man's head. On the other side Narmer, drawn far larger than anyone else, leads a procession towards ten decapitated corpses. Below, two men hold ropes tied to the intertwined necks of two serpopards, whose circle forms the hollow where cosmetics would have been ground, and at the bottom a bull knocks down the walls of a city.

Palettes were typically used for grinding cosmetics, but this one is too large, heavy and elaborate for personal use. It was probably a ritual or votive object made for donation to a temple, and one theory holds that it ground cosmetics to adorn the statues of the gods. The Egyptologists Bob Brier and A. Hoyt Hobbs have called it the oldest Egyptian historical record.

Its meaning is debated. Some scholars treat it as a record of an important event, such as a conquest of Lower Egypt or a victory over the Libyans. Nicholas Millet argues that it shows the events of the year of its dedication, and Whitney Davis reads the king as a conquering hunter. John Baines suggests that the scenes are tokens of royal achievement, meant to assert that the king dominates the ordered world in the name of the gods. It stands in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
narni: Narni stands on a rock 240 metres above sea level on the left bank of the Nera, about 12 kilometres from the river's confluence with the Tiber. The town overlooks a narrow gorge of the Nera and the Terni valley, near the historical boundary between Sabina and Umbria, 14 kilometres from Terni and 82 from Rome. It lies very close to the geographical centre of Italy, marked by a stone with a sign in several languages. Its ancient name Narnia comes from the river, called the Nera or Nar, and before the Roman conquest the town appears to have been called Nequinum.

Narni was an important Umbrian city. In 300 BCE the consul Appuleius besieged it, and the inhabitants resisted so vigorously that the siege continued into the next year, when the consul Marcus Fulvius took the city and held a triumph over the Samnites and the people of Nequinum. The Roman Senate secured the conquest by establishing a colony. Its position above the Via Flaminia gave it importance in the wars of Belisarius and Narses against the Goths, and in the late 6th century the Exarchate of Ravenna and the Lombard Duchy of Spoleto contested it, since it controlled the southern part of the road between Rome and Ravenna.

A turning point came in 1527, when Landsknechts returning from the Sack of Rome besieged and looted it, with Terni assisting; about 1530 it was found largely deserted. Popes Paul III and Pius IV confirmed tax breaks to rebuild the walls and aqueducts, but a plague in 1591 weakened it again. The town came under the Roman Republic and then the Napoleonic Empire, and Pope Pius VII visited in 1800 and in May 1804.

Among the surviving Roman works is the Ponte d'Augusto, one of the largest Roman bridges ever built, by which the Via Flaminia crossed the Nera; one arch still stands. The Roman aqueduct of the Formina, about 13 kilometres long, was built in the 1st century CE under Tiberius and supplied the town until 1924. The Rocca Albornoziana is a square fortress with four corner towers, part of the papal system of fortresses set up after Avignon. The cathedral is dedicated to Saint Juvenal of Narni, the first bishop. C. S. Lewis named the land of Narnia after the town, having come across its name in an atlas as a child.
narona: Narona was founded as a Greek emporium, probably in the 3rd or 2nd century BCE, and is first mentioned in chapter 24 of the Periplus of Pseudo-Scylax. In the 1st century BCE it became the main Roman stronghold of the region, within the province of Dalmatia. A diocese was established there in 530, apparently subject to the Archdiocese of Salona; its only recorded bishop, Marcello, attended councils of bishops at Salona in 530 and 533. In 533 the diocese lost territory to the new dioceses of Makarska and Sarsenterum.

Narona came under Byzantine rule in the 6th century. The diocese was suppressed in 600, the city being in ruins, and its territory was merged into the Diocese of Ragusa. The settlement came to an end in the 7th century after Slavic tribes, among them the Narentines, arrived in the region. The bishopric was revived in name in 1933 as a titular see of the Catholic Church.

In 1995 excavators at Vid found a Roman temple dedicated by the governor Dolabella, which held statues of the emperors Claudius and Vespasian and of Augustus and his wife Livia. The statues had been vandalised in the 4th century and lay on the floor with their heads broken off. Arthur Evans had acquired the heads of Vespasian and of one Livia in the surrounding area in 1878, and these were reunited with their bodies. The statues have since toured major European museums. A cathedral and at least two other churches have also been dug up at the site, and Vid has an archaeological museum of Narona.
narseh: Narseh, also spelled Narses, was the youngest son of Shapur I and was born between 228 and 233 during the reign of his grandfather Ardashir I. Under his father he governed the eastern provinces of Hind, Sakastan and Turan. After Shapur died in 270, his son Hormizd I ruled for a year, and Narseh's older brother Bahram I took the throne with the aid of the Zoroastrian priest Kartir. Bahram settled with Narseh by giving him the governorship of Armenia, a frontier province that was constantly a cause of war between the Roman and Sasanian empires, and Narseh held the title Great King of Armenia, used by the heir to the throne. He was passed over again when Bahram II succeeded in 274.

After the death of Bahram II in 293, a group of nobles led by Wahnam proclaimed his son Bahram III shah in Pars. The other nobles thought him weak and pledged allegiance to Narseh, who met them at Paikuli in the province of Garmekan. To avoid bloodshed he offered peace; Bahram abdicated, and Wahnam was executed when Narseh entered Ctesiphon. He was the first Sasanian ruler not to ascend the throne as crown prince.

War with Rome broke out in 296. Galerius, Caesar under Diocletian, invaded Mesopotamia and after two indecisive battles was defeated at Callinicum. After a winter of preparation he invaded Armenia with 25,000 men and surprised Narseh at the Battle of Satala. Narseh's wife, sisters and a number of his children were captured, along with his military chest. Narseh sought peace. By the resulting treaty, five provinces beyond the Tigris passed to Rome, Armenia was extended to the fortress of Zintha in Media, Iran gave up its rights over Iberia, and formal dealings were to be held at Nisibis.

Narseh appears to have returned to the religious tolerance of his father, and he put an end to the persecution of Manichaeans, though probably not at once. In his inscriptions he emphasised Ahura Mazda, and the goddess Anahita features prominently in the Paikuli inscription. Kartir, who held elaborate titles under his predecessors, is called there simply the Mowbed of Ohrmazd.

The Paikuli inscription, in present-day Iraqi Kurdistan, is the only source for the reign of Bahram III and Narseh's rise. Narseh also had an investiture relief carved at Naqsh-e Rostam, between the tombs of Darius the Great and Xerxes I, showing him receiving the ring of kingship from a female figure often taken to be Anahita.
narses: Narses was born in Persarmenia, the part of Armenia ceded to the Sasanian Empire under the Peace of Acilisene. Details of his family, early life and castration are obscure. Some sources conflated him with Narses of the Kamsarakan family, but scholarly consensus holds that he had no verifiable tie to that house. Procopius first mentions him around 530, when he was Emperor Justinian I's steward, and he also dealt with the imperial finances. The historian Agathias described him as small and lean but stronger and more high-spirited than expected, clever at adapting to the times.

He became commander of the emperor's eunuch bodyguard around 532 and Grand Chamberlain around 537 or 538, and a patrician in the 550s. He is reported to have been pious, with a devotion to the Virgin Mary, generous to the poor and zealous in restoring churches.

In the Nika riots of 532 Narses was entrusted with gold and went among the Blue faction in the Hippodrome, distributing bribes and persuading senators and Blue leaders not to support Hypatius, whom the rebels had declared emperor. Many then abandoned the revolt, and Belisarius, John the Armenian and Mund stormed the Hippodrome while Narses and his detachment surrounded it. Contemporary sources report around 35,000 killed.

In 538 he led about 7,000 men to Italy to help Belisarius, but the two fell into suspicion of each other and he was recalled. In 551 he was sent back with supreme command and the emperor's treasury, raising 20,000 to 30,000 troops. After a naval victory at Sena Gallica, he defeated the Ostrogothic king Totila at Taginae in 552, using dismounted infantry in the centre with archers on the flanks. Totila was killed. At Mons Lactarius in 553 the Goths under Teias fought on foot for two days, and then surrendered on condition of leaving the country.

The Franks, led by the brothers Leutharis and Buccillinus, then invaded. At Casilinum in 554 Narses placed heavy infantry in the centre and had cavalry shoot arrows into the Franks; Agathias claims only five escaped.

For about twelve years Narses may have stayed in Italy, reorganising its government under Justinian's pragmatic sanctions, repairing bridges and rebuilding the walls of Rome. Some historians place his death in 567, others in 574. A legend says he was recalled by Justin II and the Empress Sophia, who sent him a golden distaff, and that he invited the Lombards into Italy; the historian Dunlap questions this, and Paul the Deacon wrote that his body was returned to Constantinople.
narshakhi: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Jafar Narshakhi was a Sogdian from the village of Narshak in the Bukhara oasis, and he is the first known historian of Central Asia. Nothing is known of him beyond his authorship of this one book. In his day Persian had largely replaced Sogdian in the populous parts of Sogdia, but he probably still spoke Sogdian well.

He wrote the History of Bukhara (Tarikh-i Bukhara) in a time of upheaval for the Samanids. Nasr II had converted to Isma'ili Shi'ism, which had spread through the work of missionaries and was regarded by the Sunni as a threat. His son Nuh faced turmoil in which his vizier and other members of the court were killed, and he purged the missionaries and killed Isma'ili converts, though the court remained tense. The book was composed for a patron who supported Sunni Islam against Isma'ilism, and the Samanids took the role of guardians of Sunni law.

The book preserves information about Bukhara found in no other contemporary source. Abu Nasr Ahmad al-Qubavi's Persian translation, made in the 12th century, both shortened the text and added material extending the history to 975. This Persian version was in turn abridged by Muhammad ibn Zufar ibn 'Umar later in the 12th century. Charles-Henri-Auguste Schefer published an abridged French translation in 1892, and in 1954 the historian Richard N. Frye translated the Persian abridgment into English.
nart-sagas: The Nart sagas form much of the basic mythology of the Abazin, Abkhaz, Circassian, Ossetian and Karachay-Balkar peoples and, to some extent, Chechen-Ingush folklore. The term nart comes from the Ossetian Nartæ, the plural of nar, a root of Iranian origin from Proto-Iranian *nar, 'hero, man'. In Ingush and Chechen the word nart means 'giant'. The stories exist as prose tales and as epic songs.

Some of the corpora have an ancient Iranian core inherited from the Scythians, Sarmatians and Alans, the last being the ancestors of the Ossetians. They also contain abundant local North Caucasian accretions of great antiquity, which sometimes reflect an even more archaic past.

Prominent characters include Sosruko or Soslan, a hero who sometimes also appears as a trickster; Batraz, the leader and foremost warrior of the Narts; Satanaya, their mother, a fertility figure and matriarch; Tlepsh, a blacksmith deity; and Syrdon, a trickster whom Georges Dumézil compared to the Norse god Loki. In the Vainakh epos the blacksmith Pkharmat steals fire from the gods for mortals. Uryzmaeg and Haemyts are twin brothers, and Haemyts is the father of Batraz.

The versions differ. The Ossetian ones divide the Narts into three clans, the brave Æxsærtægkatæ, the rich Borætæ and the wise Alægatæ, a division the Circassian versions lack. The Abkhaz describe the Narts as a single family of Satanaya's hundred sons. Some Chechen-Ingush legends depict the Narts as warlike bandits who fight against local heroes.

The first Westerner to note the stories was the German scholar Julius von Klaproth, who travelled in the Caucasus in the first decade of the 19th century. The earliest written account is attributed to the Kabardian author Shora Nogmov, who wrote in Russian in 1835-1843; it was published posthumously in 1861. Adolf Berge published a German translation in 1866.

The Ossetes regard the epic as central to their national identity, and scholars have valued it as a window on the Iranian-speaking cultures of antiquity. Dumézil used the Ossetian division into three clans to support his hypothesis that the Proto-Indo-Europeans were divided into three castes. Some motifs are shared with Greek mythology, such as Prometheus chained to Mount Kazbek or Mount Elbrus. C. Scott Littleton and Linda A. Malcor speculate that many aspects of the Arthurian legends derive from the sagas through the Alans.
narva: Narva lies at the eastern extreme point of Estonia, on the west bank of the Narva river, which forms the border with Russia. Its position at the crossing of trade routes and the river led to the founding of its castle and the town around it. The fortified settlement at Narva Joaoru, dated to around 1000 BCE, is the oldest known in Estonia. The name Narva first appears in the First Novgorod Chronicle in 1172.

The castle was founded in the second half of the 13th century, and its earliest written record dates from 1277. The town beside it received Lübeck city rights from the Danish king Valdemar IV in 1345. Trade, especially Hanseatic long-distance trade, remained its purpose, but because of opposition from Tallinn it never joined the Hanseatic League. In 1492 Ivan III of Moscow established the fortress of Ivangorod across the river.

Muscovy held Narva from 1558 to 1581, during the Livonian War. Under Swedish rule after 1581 the baroque Old Town was built, and from the 1680s a system of bastions was added that was among the strongest in Northern Europe. In November 1700 Narva was the setting for the first great battle between Charles XII of Sweden and Peter I of Russia, and Peter took the city in 1704. In 1857 Ludwig Knoop founded the Krenholm Manufacturing Company, which used the power of the Narva waterfalls and by the end of the century employed about 10,000 workers. Narva became part of the independent Republic of Estonia in 1918.

Soviet air raids on 6 and 7 March 1944 destroyed the baroque Old Town, and by the end of July 98 per cent of the city lay in ruins. The Soviet authorities demolished the ruins in the early 1950s and brought in workers from elsewhere in the USSR; the city, 65 per cent Estonian in 1934, became overwhelmingly non-Estonian. In January 1945 Ivangorod was separated from Narva and transferred to the Russian republic.

Narva is the third-largest city in Estonia, in Ida-Viru County, at the eastern extreme point of the country. Only three buildings of the old town survived the destruction of 1944, among them the baroque Town Hall.
narwar: Narwar lies at an average elevation of 452 metres, 42 km from Shivpuri. Its fort stands just east of the Sindh River and is surrounded by the Kali Sindh. Three dams lie near the town: the Harsi Dam, Mohini Sagar and the Madikheda dam. Many medieval Sanskrit inscriptions name the place Nalpura, the town of Nala.

Narwar is identified with Nalapura, the town of the Nishad Charita written by Shriharsha, capital of Nala, whose love for Damayanti is told at length in the Mahabharata. In the legend Nala left Damayanti asleep in the forests of Narwar, and she made her way through the dense forest to Chanderi, protecting herself from wild animals.

On 12 August 1602 Abu'l-Fazl ibn Mubarak, the courtier of Akbar who wrote the Akbarnama, was killed near Narwar on his way back from the Deccan. The attack, made by Vir Singh Bundela between Sarai Vir and Antri, was a plot contrived by Akbar's eldest son, Prince Salim, the later Emperor Jahangir, whose accession Abu'l-Fazl was known to oppose. His severed head was sent to Salim at Allahabad, and he was buried at Antri. In 1707 the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah I made Maharaja Gopal Singh of the Bhadawar state the imperial governor of Narwar.

In January 1859 the Maratha general Tatya Tope, who had escaped alone into the jungles of Paron after his defeat by the British, found refuge with Man Singh Kachwaha, Raja of Narwar, then in dispute with the Maharaja of Gwalior. The British promised Man Singh his safety and protection from the Maharaja's reprisals, and he led a detachment of General Richard John Meade's troops to Tatya Tope's camp, where he was captured asleep on 7 April 1859 and taken to Shivpuri for trial by a military court.
Narwar is a nagar parishad of the Shivpuri district of Madhya Pradesh; in the Gwalior State it had been the seat of Narwar District. At the 2001 census it had 15,748 inhabitants.
naryn-kala: Derbent lies at the most vulnerable point of the Caspian Pass, where the Greater Caucasus comes closest to the sea and leaves a single narrow strip of plain about 3 km wide. Naryn-Kala crowns the hill nearest the sea. Two parallel walls, 350–450 metres apart, run from the citadel to the shore and out into the water, so that the fortress could not be bypassed in the shallows, and they form a harbour; the medieval city lay between them. West of the citadel the Mountain Wall, Dagh-Bary, stretched for 40 km to close the valleys and passes.

The irregular citadel covers 4.5 hectares, about 180 metres wide and 255 metres long, with small towers every 20–30 metres and a gun tower in the south-west, and steep slopes guard it on three sides. Its walls are 2.5 to 3.5 metres thick and in places 20–25 metres high. Inside are baths, a water supply of ceramic pipes, the ruins of the Shah's palace and a large entrance portal. A cross-domed structure is held by some to be an early Christian church of the 4th and 5th centuries and by others to be a reservoir.

The fortress known today was built on the Dzhalgan ridge on the orders of the Sasanian ruler Khosrov I Anushirvan (531–579). The name has been translated from Middle Persian as Sunny Fortress, while other sources say it honours a daughter of the Persian Shah. From 735 Derbent and Naryn-Kala were the military and administrative centre of the Arab Caliphate in Dagestan, its largest trading port and the centre from which Islam spread there. Each new owner rebuilt and updated the walls, so that the history of the city can be traced in their layers.

Legend called the fortress the wall of Alexander the Great, though Alexander never came to the Derbent gates. After the Caspian campaign of Peter the Great, Derbent became part of the Russian Empire, and its beys presented the city keys to the emperor on a silver platter now kept in the Kunstkamera of Saint Petersburg. During the Persian expedition of 1796 Russian troops under Valerian Zubov retook the fortress and set their headquarters in the citadel. Excavations inside Naryn-Kala are still going on.
naser-al-din-shah-qajar: Naser al-Din Mirza was born on 17 July 1831 at Kahnamu, a village near Tabriz, the eldest son of Mohammad Mirza and the Qajar princess Malek Jahan Khanom. In 1835 the four-year-old Naser al-Din was named crown prince and given the governorship of Azerbaijan, with regents appointed to act for him. When Mohammad Shah died on 4 September 1848, he was in Tabriz, and he reached the throne with the help of Amir Kabir. His mother, called Mahd-e Olya, became the most powerful figure at court.

The state he inherited had little power. It lacked a standing army, and at his accession the army numbered barely 3,000 men, fewer than those of various tribal leaders. Local groups kept their own militias, and many people followed the fatwas of the ulama rather than state law. In August 1852 followers of the Bab tried to assassinate the shah, and thousands of Babis were killed afterwards. Amir Kabir was demoted and then executed on the shah's order after a court coalition formed against him.

In 1856 Naser al-Din launched the Second Herat War, and his uncle Hesam o-Saltaneh captured Herat in October after a nine-month siege. Britain declared war, landed at Bushehr in December, and under the Treaty of Paris of 4 March 1857 Iran withdrew from Herat and renounced its claims.

He visited Europe in 1873, 1878 and 1889, the first modern Iranian monarch to do so, and Queen Victoria made him a Knight of the Garter. He allowed newspapers, the telegraph and postal services, and patronised photography. A school of higher education, the Dar al-Fonun, opened in his reign, though enrolment was small. He also raised money by tax farming, and abuses by tax collectors fed resentment of a government seen as corrupt. In later years he granted concessions to Europeans for large payments. A concession of 1890 on all tobacco brought a national boycott and was withdrawn; many authorities see this as the origin of modern Iranian nationalism.

Mirza Reza Kermani, a follower of Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, shot the shah on 1 May 1896 while he was praying at the Shah Abdol-Azim Shrine near Tehran. The revolver is said to have been old and rusty. The shah was buried at the shrine and the funeral held six months later. His assassination and Kermani's execution marked a turning point in Iranian political thought that led to the Constitutional Revolution under his successor, Mozaffar ad-Din Shah. His own diary of the 1873 journey was published in several languages.
nashik: Nashik lies on the banks of the Godavari in the northern part of Maharashtra, about 165 km north-east of Mumbai and 584 m above sea level, on the western edge of the Deccan Plateau, an ancient volcanic formation. The Godavari rises on Brahmagiri Mountain at Trimbakeshwar, about 24 km away, and flows through the old residential settlement, now the central part of the city. The city is the administrative headquarters of Nashik district.

Hindu tradition gives the place a succession of names through the ages: Padmanagar, Trikantak, Janasthana and finally Navashikh, or Nashik. According to the Ramayana it is where Lakshmana cut off the nose of the demoness Surpanakha on the Godavari during the 14-year exile of Rama, Sita and Lakshmana, and the area around Panchavati is held sacred. In the Mughal period it was known as Gulshanabad. The Kumbh Mela is held here, as at Prayagraj, Haridwar and Ujjain, and according to the Puranas the sites are those where nectar fell from an immortal pot fought over by gods and demons.

In the early 20th century Nashik was a centre of political activity. Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and his brother founded a secret society, Abhinav Bharat, there in the 1900s, and on 21 December 1909 a member, Anant Kanhere, assassinated the district's governor A. M. T. Jackson in a theatre. Savarkar and others were arrested in what became known as the Nasik Conspiracy Case of 1910. In 1930 B. R. Ambedkar led the Nashik Satyagraha for Dalits to enter the Kalaram temple, and in 1932 he organised a movement there to abolish untouchability.

A tram ran from the Old Municipal Building to Nashik Road railway station from about 1889 for almost 44 years. The Sarvajanik Vachanalaya library was established around 1840 by the British. In 1925 Raosaheb Jairam Krishna Gaikwad began the table grape trade at Ozar, near the city.

The census of 2011 recorded 1,486,053 people, making Nashik the fourth largest city in Maharashtra after Mumbai, Pune and Nagpur; Marathi was the first language of most. The Trirashmi, or Pandavleni, Caves are a group of 24 Hinayana Buddhist caves cut from the 1st century BCE. Nashik is also known for its vineyards, and the Currency Note Press and India Security Press stand at Nashik Road.
nasir-ad-din-qabacha: Qabacha was a Kipchak Turk, one of the Turkic slaves whom Muhammad of Ghor, who had no children, trained as soldiers and administrators and treated as his sons; Muhammad is reported to have said that his thousands of Turkic slaves would be the heirs of his dominions. He appointed Qabacha governor of Multan in 1203. After Muhammad's assassination his empire was divided among these men: Qutb ud-Din Aibak took Lahore, Taj al-Din Yildiz Ghazni and Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji Bengal, while Qabacha held Multan.

Qabacha declared himself independent in 1210 and twice repulsed attacks by Taj al-Din Yildiz of Ghazni. Lahore was contested between him, Yildiz and Shams-ud-Din Iltutmish of Delhi. Yildiz, driven from Ghazni by Muhammad II of Khwarezm in 1214, was defeated and captured by Iltutmish at Taraori on 25 January 1216, after which Qabacha again occupied Lahore. In 1217 Iltutmish marched against him with a large army and defeated him at Mansura as he retreated towards Multan, but the presence of the Mongols on the north-west frontier kept Iltutmish from pressing him further until 1227.

When Iltutmish advanced on Uch, his lieutenant Nasiruddin Aiyitim besieged Multan, and Qabacha fled by boat to the island fortress of Bhakkar in the Indus. Iltutmish opened the siege of Uch on 9 February 1228 and sent his minister Kamaluddin Muhammad Junaidi, Nizam al-Mulk, in pursuit. Qabacha sent his son Alauddin Bahram Shah to make terms, and Uch surrendered on 4 May, but Junaidi kept up the siege of Bhakkar, and Qabacha drowned in the Indus. His troops passed into the service of Iltutmish, who left Junaidi to complete the conquest of lower Sindh.
nasir-al-dawla: Born al-Hasan ibn Abdallah, he was the eldest son of Abu'l-Hayja Abdallah ibn Hamdan, whom the historian Marius Canard regards as the real founder of the Hamdanid emirate of Mosul. The Hamdanids were a branch of the Banu Taghlib, an Arab tribe of the Jazira, and were allied and intermarried with the Kurds of the mountains north of Mosul. His father left him in charge of Mosul in his last years. After his father was killed in 929, his uncles, with the caliph's backing, contested the family's lands, and Hasan fought them for years, had his uncle Sa'id murdered, and in late 935 Caliph al-Radi recognised him as governor of Mosul and the whole Jazira for a yearly tribute of 70,000 gold dinars.

In early 942 Caliph al-Muttaqi fled to Mosul from the Baridis of Basra. Hasan had Muhammad ibn Ra'iq assassinated, took his place as amir al-umara with the title Nasir al-Dawla, and entered Baghdad with the caliph on 4 June 942. His brother Ali, victorious over the Baridis at al-Mada'in, became Sayf al-Dawla. Short of money and allies, the brothers left Baghdad after their troops mutinied under the Turkish general Tuzun in late 943.

From January 946 the Buyid Mu'izz al-Dawla ruled Baghdad, and Nasir al-Dawla fought him repeatedly. He briefly held Baghdad during a Daylamite revolt in 956-958, and twice lost Mosul, in 958 and 964, but each time the Buyids could not hold it: the Hamdanids withdrew to their mountain fortresses with the treasury and the tax registers, and local people harassed the occupiers. After 958 Sayf al-Dawla took over his tribute, and the Syrian branch of the family became the stronger.

From 964 his eldest son Abu Taghlib ruled in his place. In 967 Abu Taghlib, with his Kurdish mother Fatima bint Ahmad, deposed him and imprisoned him in the fortress of Ardumusht, where he died. Contemporaries criticised his rule harshly: the traveller Ibn Hawqal reported that he seized private land on flimsy pretexts until he was the biggest landowner of his province, and his cereal monoculture and heavy taxes made the two brothers, it was said, the wealthiest princes in the Muslim world.
nasir-jung: Mir Ahmad Ali Khan Siddiqi Bayafandi was born on 26 February 1712, the son of Asaf Jah I and his wife Saeed-un-nisa Begum. The Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah gave him the title Nasir Jung, and his successor Ahmad Shah Bahadur appointed him Subedar of the Deccan with the title Nasir-ud-Daula. He acted as his father's deputy while Asaf Jah was in Delhi from 1737 to 1741. In 1741 he tried to seize power for himself but was defeated by his father at the Eid Gah Maidan in Aurangabad on 23 July 1741. He later served as Subedar of Aurangabad in 1745 and 1746.

After his father's death Nasir Jung took the throne at Burhanpur on 2 June 1748 as the second Nizam of Hyderabad. His nephew Muzaffar Jung, the old Nizam's grandson through a daughter, disputed the succession, and Hussain Dost Khan, known as Chanda Sahib, joined Muzaffar Jung's cause in the hope of becoming Nawab of the Carnatic in place of Anwar-ud-din Muhammad Khan of Arcot.

The quarrel drew in the rival British and French trading companies. Joseph François Dupleix, governor-general of French India, saw a chance to extend French influence; since the two nations were at peace in Europe, both sides worked through alliances and local fighting, which became the Second Carnatic War. The French backed Chanda Sahib and Muzaffar Jung, while the British East India Company supported Nasir Jung and Muhammad Ali Khan Walajah, whose father Anwar-ud-din had been killed at the Battle of Ambur in 1749. By 1750 the French and their allies had won a series of successes in both the Deccan and the Carnatic.

During one of those French successes, on 16 December 1750, Nasir Jung was killed at Sarasangupettai, also called Dupleix-Fathabad, near Gingee, by the Pathan Himmat Khan. Muzaffar Jung then took the throne of Hyderabad. Nasir Jung was buried beside his father at Khuldabad, in the shrine of Burhan ud-Din Gharib. The war went on: Robert Clive's capture of Arcot in 1751 began a run of British victories, and the Treaty of Pondicherry of 1754-55 recognised Muhammad Ali Khan Walajah as Nawab of the Carnatic, while Dupleix was recalled to France.
nasir-khusraw: Nasir Khusraw was born in 1004 in Qubadiyan, a neighbourhood of Balkh in the Khurasan region, then controlled by the Ghaznavids. He came from a family of government bureaucrats and landowners and most likely followed Twelver Shi'ism before becoming an Isma'ili. He is said to have begun as a scribe and then worked as a financial administrator at Marw. When the Seljuks conquered Khurasan in 1040 he kept his office under them.

Around the age of 41 he underwent a sudden change in his spirituality, which he described as having the character of a dream. He resigned his office and converted to Isma'ilism. Many tales are told of him, including a forged autobiography that circulated for centuries, and much of his surviving writing seems to have been censored by hostile Sunni scribes, who removed references to Isma'ilism.

In December 1045 he decided to make a long journey ending in pilgrimage to Mecca. He set out in March 1046 with his brother Abu Sa'id and an Indian attendant, travelling through northern and western Iran, Armenia and Asia Minor, then to Syria, Palestine and Arabia. In August 1047 he reached Cairo, the capital of the Isma'ili Fatimid Caliphate. There he was taught Isma'ili teaching, law and administration, and he met the chief Fatimid missionary, al-Mu'ayyad fi'l-Din al-Shirazi, who instructed him in Isma'ili philosophy.

He was made a missionary and appointed Hujjat of Khorasan. After he returned to Greater Khorasan in 1052, the hostility his preaching met compelled him to flee. About 1060 he found refuge at Yamgan in the mountains of Badakhshan, where he spent his last decades and gathered a body of devoted followers. He was buried in a small mausoleum in the village of Hadrat-i Sayyid, which an inscription says was renovated in 1697.

His Safarnama, the Book of Travels, describes dozens of cities visited between 6 March 1046 and 23 October 1052, with details of colleges, caravanserais, mosques, rulers and populations. His Diwan holds poems mostly written in retirement, praising Ali, his descendants and the Fatimid imam al-Mustansir, and bitterly criticising the rulers of Khorasan. His other writings include Gushayish va Rahayish, translated as Knowledge and Liberation, the poems Rawshana-i-nama and Sa'datnama, Zaad-al-Musafirin and Wajh-i Din. A mathematics book is lost.

All his philosophical Isma'ili works are in Persian, unusual among the Fatimids, who mostly wrote in Arabic. He defended Persian as a language of art and science, and he taught that revelation must be read through esoteric interpretation (ta'wil), which points to the Imam of the Time. The Isma'ilis of Badakhshan and northern Pakistan revere him as Pir and regard him as their founder.
nasiriyah: Nasiriyah lies on the lower Euphrates, about 360 kilometres south-south-east of Baghdad, near the ruins of the ancient city of Ur. It is the centre of a date-growing area, and its cottage industries include boat-building, carpentry and silver working. Larsa is also nearby, and the Euphrates joins the Tigris for the last time about 10 kilometres from the city. The city museum holds a large collection of Sumerian, Assyrian, Babylonian and Abbasid objects.

Nasir al-Sadoon Pasha, of the Al Sa'dun family and chief of the Muntafiq confederation, founded the city in 1872 and gave it his name. In the same year it became the administrative centre of the Muntafiq sanjak. The Belgian architect Jules Tilly drew up a Western-style grid of long, straight, parallel streets with central squares and public gardens, unprecedented in Iraq at the time. The Sa'dun clan was Sunni, while most Muntafiq tribesmen were Shia. Nasir Pasha was appointed by the Ottomans as head of the province, and by 1908 his son Saadun Pasha virtually governed southern Iraq on their behalf.

Nasiriyah was a trading centre, exchanging goods with Baghdad and Basra and producing leather, grain and ghee. It had about 600 stone houses, most other buildings being mud brick, about 350 shops and five khans, and it had no wall. British forces took it in July 1915, when about 400 British and Indian and up to 2,000 Turkish soldiers died in the battle on 24 July. In 1920 it had 6,523 inhabitants, of whom Arab Muslims were 72.7 per cent, Mandaeans 9.7 per cent and Jews 8 per cent. The Iraqi Communist Party's first cell was founded there in the 1930s.

Nasiriyah is the capital of Dhi Qar Governorate, with a population of about 700,000, mostly Shia Muslims. A Mandaean community, which lived in the Subba Quarter on the north bank of the Euphrates, was among the largest in Iraq until 2003. The city is a major transport hub, and the ruins of Ur lie nearby.
nasjonal-samling: Nasjonal Samling was a Norwegian far-right party founded by the former Minister of Defence Vidkun Quisling and a group of supporters. It marked its founding on 17 May, Norway's national holiday, but was founded on 13 May 1933. Johan Bernhard Hjort led its paramilitary wing, the Hird, for a short time before leaving in 1937.

The 30-point programme that Quisling signed on 15 February 1934 called for a national government acting independently of party politics, for the protection of the Christian religion and for the interests of the nation to precede those of individuals, parties and countries. Romantic nationalism and authoritarianism dominated its ideology, and its propaganda relied on Nordic symbolism, including a golden sun cross on a red background that it said had been the symbol of St. Olaf.

Before the war the party never gained more than 2.5 per cent of the vote and elected no candidate to the Storting, yet it polarised the political scene. The established parties viewed it as a Norwegian version of the German Nazis and refused to cooperate with it. Antisemitism, anti-Masonry and differing views on religion divided it, and it had about 2,000 members when the Second World War began.

When Germany invaded Norway on 9 April 1940, Quisling broadcast from the studios of the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation in Oslo, proclaimed himself Prime Minister and ordered resistance to the Germans to end. King Haakon VII and the government of Johan Nygaardsvold refused to accept him, and the German forces quickly thrust him aside. Membership rose to 22,000 in December 1940 and peaked at about 44,000 in November 1943.

Reichskommissar Josef Terboven took control and appointed a government responsible to himself, with most ministers drawn from the party. Quisling became minister president only on 1 February 1942, and the administration remained controlled by Terboven, who was subordinate only to Adolf Hitler. Nasjonal Samling was the only legal party from 1942 to 1945.

The party was banned and disbanded at the end of the war in Europe, on 8 May 1945. The post-war authorities prosecuted its members as collaborators: nearly 50,000 were brought to trial, and about half received prison sentences. Quisling was executed for treason, together with a few other prominent members of the party. The lawfulness of the sentences has been questioned, since Norway had no capital punishment in peacetime.
nasr-i-samanid: Nasr was the son and successor of Ahmad ibn Asad, who ruled a large part of Transoxiana under the suzerainty of the Abbasid Caliphate. On his father's death Nasr received most of Transoxiana, including Samarqand, while his brother Ya'qub received Shash. The weakening of the Tahirid governors of Khurasan at the hands of the Saffarid ruler Ya'qub ibn Layth let Nasr rule virtually as an independent monarch, and the distance of his lands kept him out of the sudden power struggles in Iran. The Samanid branch at Herat, however, ended when the Saffarid ruler captured Ibrahim ibn Ilyas in 867.

About 870 Nasr sheltered the Banijurid ruler Da'ud ibn Abbas, who had fled Balkh. In 874 the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tamid sent Nasr an investiture for the governorships of Transoxania and Balkh, to counter the claims of Ya'qub ibn Layth, and the next ruler of Balkh, Abu Da'ud Muhammad ibn Ahmad, presumably became his vassal. The same year Hanafi clerics of Bukhara asked for his help: after the collapse of the Tahirids the city had fallen into a power vacuum and suffered raids by the Afrighid shahs of Khwarazm. Nasr sent his younger brother Isma'il, whom the city welcomed and who became its governor, although the Bukhar-Khudah formally remained in charge.

In 885 the brothers fell out over where the tax revenue should go, and a three-year struggle followed in which Isma'il won. He took effective control of the state but did not depose Nasr, because the caliph had invested Nasr with Transoxiana and regarded him as its only legitimate ruler. Isma'il stayed in Bukhara and continued to recognise his brother, who was left without power, until Nasr died in August 892 and Isma'il formally took over.
nasrid-dynasty: The Nasrids, also called the Banu Nasr or Banu al-Ahmar, descended from the Arab Banu Khazraj tribe and claimed direct male-line descent from Sa'd ibn Ubadah, a chief of that tribe and a companion of the Prophet Muhammad. Their founder was Muhammad I, and twenty-three sultans ruled Granada from 1232 until 1492. The territory they held included Granada, Jaén, Almería and Málaga.

As Christian campaigns of the Reconquista took Valencia, Játiva and Jaén, the Nasrids were for the most part made tribute-paying vassals from 1243. They allied with the Marinids of Fez, who both protected them and sought to dominate Granada, and they relied on the Zianids of Tlemcen as their main allies against Marinid influence. Granada remained a centre of Islamic culture. Its palace architecture of the 14th century, the Alhambra, was the work of Ismail I and Muhammad V.

In 1469 Ferdinand II of Aragon married Isabella I of Castile, uniting two Christian kingdoms with the common aim of conquering the last Muslim kingdom in the peninsula. While the Christian campaign began, the Nasrids fell into civil war: Sultan Abu l-Hasan Ali was ousted by his son and withdrew to Málaga. The son was captured at Lucena in 1483 and freed after swearing allegiance to Ferdinand and Isabella. Abu l-Hasan Ali later abdicated in favour of his brother, known as Al-Zaghal, who prevailed in the family struggle but was forced to surrender to the Christians.

The last Nasrid sultan surrendered Granada to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492. He was offered a lordship in the Alpujarras mountains but took financial compensation from the Spanish crown to leave the peninsula, and the remaining Muslim population was given the status of mudéjar.

The most visible evidence of the dynasty today is the Alhambra palace complex. Nasrid craftsmen made lustreware, first in Málaga, Murcia and Almería and by the 15th century in Manises, using ceramic overglaze techniques from 9th-century Baghdad. This pottery influenced the colourful glazed Italian ceramics known as maiolica.
nasrullah-khan-emir-of-bukhara: Nasrullah was a son of Emir Haydar bin Shohmurod, though the sources disagree whether he was the second or third son, a point that bore on his right to succeed. As hakim of Qarshi he made his name in putting down the Khitoy-Qipchoq rebellion, provoked by Bukhara's oppressive taxes and conscription. After Haydar's death his brother Mir Husayn reigned two months and was followed by Umar. Nasrullah won over Samarqand and the tribes of the Zarafshan Valley, took the throne on 24 April 1827, and freed the population from taxes for several years to secure support.

He reigned while the Russian Empire pressed from the north and British India from the south. In 1839 he declared war on Khoqand over the Pishaghar fort, took Khojand in 1839 and 1841, and made the khan recognise him as overlord. In 1842 he invaded Khoqand, where the poet Nodirabegim and other members of the royal family were executed, though Ming rule was soon restored. He took the allegiance of Balkh in 1832 and succeeded in Marv but failed in Balkh, and he made peace with Khiva in 1842.

He centralised power. In 1837–8 he executed the powerful qushbegi Muhammad Hakim on a charge of treason, abolished the post and employed viziers without tribal ties. He formed a standing army, the sarbaz, of Russian and Persian slaves trained by the Iranian fugitive Abdulsamad, moving 13,000 Uzbek cavalry to the irregular reserve. He enforced sharia through an appointed rais and built his religious standing on shrine veneration, visiting the shrine of Bahauddin Naqshbandi before his campaigns. Trade with Russia helped Bukhara's economy recover.

In the West he is best known for imprisoning and in 1842 executing the British envoys Charles Stoddart and Arthur Conolly, and for holding, then releasing, Joseph Wolff, who came seeking news of them in 1843. Tsarist and Soviet historians called him the butcher emir for executing his brothers and warring on his neighbours. He died on 20 October 1860 and was succeeded by his son Muzaffar.
nassau-castle: The castle stands on a rock outcrop about 120 metres above the Lahn and is associated with Dudo of Laurenburg, founder of the House of Nassau. His sons, Counts Rupert I and Arnold I, established themselves there with its tower and extended the complex in 1124. Because the site lay on land of the Bishopric of Worms, a bitter feud followed, and Worms disputed the title Count of Nassau that Rupert I took from the castle.

The dispute was settled in 1159 under Rupert's son Walram I through Hillin of Falmagne, Archbishop of Trier: the family gave up its claim to allodial title and received the castle and town of Nassau as a fief from the archbishop, and from then on its members were the Counts of Nassau. Henry II the Rich built the late-Romanesque palas between 1220 and 1230. When his sons Walram II and Otto I divided the county in 1255, the castle stayed their common possession.

The five-sided bergfried, 33 metres high, was built in the first half of the 14th century, and the housing of the castle keepers was destroyed in a family feud in 1372. The counts gave up the castle as a residence at the end of the Middle Ages. A 17th-century etching by Matthäus Merian shows the palas, the bergfried and a gate building still standing, but the remaining ruins were destroyed in the final phase of World War II.

The State Castle Administration of Rhineland-Palatinate took over the castle in 1965. The bergfried was restored from 1976, its roof and side towers rebuilt after Merian's etching, and the palas with its knights' hall was reconstructed in 1979 and 1980, when late-Gothic window arcades were rediscovered.
nataraja: Nataraja, also called Adalvallan in Tamil, is a depiction of Shiva as the divine cosmic dancer, and his dance is called the tandava. The Sanskrit name combines nata, meaning act, drama or dance, with raja, meaning king or lord. The pose is described in Tamil texts such as the Tevaram and Thiruvasagam and in Sanskrit texts such as the Amshumadagama and Uttarakamika agama.

Stone reliefs at the Ellora Caves, the Elephanta Caves and the Badami Caves, by around the sixth century, are among the oldest. Literary evidence suggests that the bronze form first appeared in the Pallava period, between the seventh century and the middle of the ninth, and Sharada Srinivasan argues that such bronzes were a Pallava innovation. Around the tenth century the image reached its mature expression in Chola bronzes, typically under four feet high. Reliefs are also found in South East Asia, including Angkor Wat and Bali.

The figure usually shows Shiva dancing in one of the Natya Shastra poses, standing on a lotus pedestal within a ring of flames, with his left leg lifted. He balances on a dwarf, Apasmara or Muyalaka, who stands for spiritual ignorance. Four-armed forms are most typical. The upper right hand holds an hourglass drum, the ḍamaru, for the rhythm of creation, and the upper left holds fire, signifying destruction. The lower right hand makes the abhaya mudra, a sign to fear not. His hair streams out in thin strands, and the headdress often carries a skull, a crescent moon and the river Ganges as a goddess.

The two chief forms of the dance are the lasya, gentle and linked with creation, and the ananda tandava, the dance of bliss, linked with destruction, so that Shiva destroys in order to create. Interpretations in Shaiva Siddhanta texts date from the twelfth century and later.

The Nataraja became a symbol of royalty in Tamil Nadu, and the dancing Shiva was part of Chola processions and festivals. Padma Kaimal suggests the figure meant different things in different contexts, such as lord of the cremation ground or an emblem of the Chola dynasty. At the Nataraja temple in Chidambaram the 108 poses of Bharatanatyam are shown with Sanskrit inscriptions from the Natya Shastra. Ananda Coomaraswamy read the dance as the source of all movement in the universe and a release of souls from illusion. In 2004 a two-metre statue of the dancing Shiva was unveiled at CERN in Geneva.
natchitoches-louisiana: Natchitoches is the parish seat of Natchitoches Parish and takes its name from the Natchitoches people, near whose village the post was set up. It was founded as a French outpost on the Red River for trade with Spanish-controlled Mexico, and French traders had settled there as early as 1699. Cane River Lake was formed from a part of the Red River when it changed course.

Early settlers were French Catholic immigrants and creoles, originally meaning ethnic French born in the colony. French creoles acquired lands that were developed in the antebellum years as the cotton-producing Magnolia and Oakland plantations. After the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, migration from the United States increased. The newcomers, primarily of English and Scots-Irish ancestry and Protestant faith, developed further cotton plantations along the Red River. Enslaved African Americans brought through the domestic slave trade did the work and supplied all other skills on these plantations, generating the revenues of the wealthy planters before the Civil War.

The United States government established a federal fur trade factory in 1805, moved to Sulphur Fork, Arkansas, in 1818. The city was incorporated on 5 February 1819. When the river shifted its course it bypassed the town and cut off its link to the Mississippi. During the Civil War Union soldiers retreating from a failed attempt to capture Shreveport set the town on fire, and Confederate cavalry arrived in time to help put out the flames. Union and Confederate troops both damaged the plantations along the river, including Magnolia and Oakland.

The town declined with the fall in the agricultural population through the mid-20th century. In the mid-1970s Mayor Bobby DeBlieux and other preservationists worked to attract tourists to its historic assets, and by the end of the 20th century the mile-long French colonial downtown along Cane Lake was designated a National Historic District.

Magnolia and Oakland plantations are National Historic Landmarks and part of the Cane River Creole National Historical Park, authorized in 1994. Their tours cover the history of slavery and its aftermath and the contributions of Black people and Creoles of color. Natchitoches is home to Northwestern State University of Louisiana, and it had a population of 18,039 at the 2020 census.
nathan-prophet: Nathan is a prophet of the Hebrew Bible whose name means given in Hebrew, and he is dated to about 1000 BCE. His actions are told in the Books of Samuel, Kings and Chronicles, chiefly in 2 Samuel 7 and 12. He appears as a court prophet and adviser in the time of King David. Chronicles records that he wrote histories of the reigns of both David and Solomon and was involved in the music of the temple. A lost Book of Nathan the Prophet is mentioned in 1 and 2 Chronicles.

In 2 Samuel 7, David reflects with Nathan on the contrast between his own comfortable house and the tent in which the Ark of the Covenant is kept. Nathan announces the covenant that God makes with David, a passage known as Nathan's Oracle, which contrasts David's plan to build a house, a building, for the Ark with God's plan to build a house, a dynasty, for David.

Later Nathan comes to David to rebuke him for adultery with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, whose death the king had also arranged to hide his wrongdoing. According to the Bible, he did so with a parable of a rich man with many flocks and a poor man with one lamb, an echo of which is found in Christian and Islamic tradition. He is also named in the heading of a psalm and, in 2 Samuel 12, gives Solomon the name Jedidiah.

In 1 Kings 1, Nathan tells the dying David of Adonijah's plot to become king. He advises Bathsheba to appeal to the king, and with Zadok the priest he proclaims and anoints Solomon as successor. The Midrash teaches that two seats flanked Solomon's throne, one for Nathan and one for Gad the Seer. Two sons of Nathan, Azariah and Zabud, are named as officers under Solomon.

Some speculate that parts of the lost Book of Nathan were incorporated into the books of Samuel or Kings, and the 15th-century scholar Isaac Abarbanel proposed that Samuel began his book and Nathan completed it. A grave at Halhul near Hebron is pointed out as his, though this is doubtful. The Eastern Orthodox Church commemorates him as a saint on the Sunday of the Holy Fathers before the Nativity.
nathdwara: Nathdwara lies in the Aravalli hills on the banks of the Banas River, in the Rajsamand district of Rajasthan. Its name means Gateway to Shrinathji. Shrinathji is a form of Krishna resembling his incarnation as a child of seven. According to the temple's account, the deity was first worshipped at Jatpura near Mathura and was moved in 1672 from the Govardhan hill, then kept at Agra for almost six months.

The shrine was built in the 17th century on the spot that Shrinathji himself chose, according to tradition. The image was being carried to protect it from the Mughal ruler Aurangzeb, and at the village of Sihad the wheels of the bullock cart sank axle-deep in mud and could not be moved. The accompanying priests took this as the Lord's chosen place, and a temple was built there under the rule and protection of Maharana Raj Singh of Mewar. It is also called the Haveli of Shrinathji.

Nathdwara is a major shrine of the Pushti Marg, also called the Vallabha Sampradaya or Shuddha Advaita, founded by Vallabhacharya. His son Vitthal Nathji organised the worship of Shrinathji there, and the royal family of Nathdwara, called Tilkayat, belongs to the lineage of Vallabhacharya. The image of Naveet Priya came with Shrinathji, and Madan Mohan was given to Shrinathji by the wife of Maharana Fateh Singh of Udaipur and Mewar. Both temples share the administration of the Shrinathji Temple. The image of Vithal Nath, the second of the seven svarups of the Pushti Marg, has a separate administration.

The 2011 census gave Nathdwara a population of 42,016. Artists working near the temple are known for pichwai paintings of the Mewar school, which centre on Shrinathji, shown as a black-faced figure of Krishna holding up Mount Govardhan, and they also paint small works on paper, mostly on themes from the legend of Krishna. A statue of Shiva called the Statue of Belief, 369 feet tall, opened at Nathdwara on 29 October 2022. Other temples in the town honour Khera Mata, Mahadeva and Hanuman, and Islam and Jainism have a small presence.
nathuram-godse: Nathuram Vinayak Godse was born on 19 May 1910 into a Maharashtrian Chitpavan Brahmin family. His father, Vinayak Vamanrao Godse, worked for the postal service. He was named Ramachandra at birth, but because his parents feared a curse on their sons after the loss of three earlier boys, he was brought up as a girl for his first years and made to wear a nose-ring, nath in Marathi. This gave him the nickname Nathuram, and he was treated as a boy after a younger brother was born. He attended school at Baramati through the fifth standard, then went to an aunt in Pune to study at an English-language school, but dropped out of high school.

Godse became an activist with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and the Hindu Mahasabha, although the exact dates of his membership are uncertain. He joined the RSS at Sangli in 1932 as a boudhik karyawah, a ground worker, while remaining in the Hindu Mahasabha. He wrote newspaper articles and worked with M. S. Golwalkar on an English translation of Babarao Savarkar's Rashtra Mimansa, until they fell out over credit. On the day of Vijayadashami in 1942 he formed his own body, the Hindu Rashtra Dal. In 1946 he claimed to have left the RSS over the partition of India, but sources do not bear this out, and his family says he never left.

He made two unsuccessful attempts on the life of Mahatma Gandhi in 1944. In May he led a group at a prayer meeting at Panchgani, and in September he was arrested with a dagger at Sevagram; both times he was released because Gandhi declined to press charges. At 05:05 pm on 30 January 1948 he stepped from the crowd at Birla House in New Delhi and fired three bullets into Gandhi's chest. Herbert Reiner Jr., a vice-consul at the American embassy, seized him until soldiers and police took him away. Godse had planned the killing with Narayan Apte and six others, and said that Gandhi had favoured Muslim demands during partition.

Godse was tried at the Punjab High Court at Peterhoff, Shimla, and sentenced to death on 8 November 1949. Gandhi's sons Manilal and Ramdas asked for the sentence to be commuted, but Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Chakravarti Rajagopalachari refused, and he was hanged at Ambala Central Jail on 15 November 1949.

Millions of Indians mourned Gandhi. The Hindu Mahasabha was vilified and the RSS was temporarily banned. The RSS has denied any connection with Godse, saying he left in the mid-1930s, while his brother Gopal Godse stated that all the brothers were members at the time of the killing. Some writers describe the assassination as the first act of Hindutva terrorism in independent India.
national-academy-of-sciences-of-ukraine: The Ukrainian Scientific Society in Kyiv and the Shevchenko Scientific Society in Lemberg, modern Lviv, were the predecessors of the academy. The Ukrainian Scientific Society took the initiative in April 1917. Under the first Ukrainian State, Mykola Vasylenko, the Minister of Education and Arts, proposed a commission, which was led by Volodymyr Vernadsky and drafted a bill for an academy, a national library and a national museum.

The Ukrainian Academy of Sciences was established in law on 14 November 1918, with the first twelve full members named at once. Its statute provided for three departments, history and philology, physics and mathematics, and social studies, and for all publications to be in Ukrainian. At its first General Assembly on 27 November 1918 Vernadsky was elected president and Ahathanhel Krymsky permanent secretary.

In its early years the academy worked through the Ukrainian–Soviet War, the Russian Civil War and the Polish–Soviet War, seeking recognition from each new power and stressing that it was not political. Despite hardship, famine, arrests and the emigration of some members, it survived and developed.

After the Bolsheviks took Kyiv, it received the mansion of Countess Levashova on 11 February 1919, and Soviet historians later counted 12 February 1919 as its founding day rather than 14 November 1918. Vernadsky resigned, and in 1921 it was renamed the All-Ukrainian Academy of Sciences and placed under the Narkom of Education. Between 1927 and 1930 the Soviet authorities took it over completely.

Repressions peaked in 1933–1934, and according to Natalia Polonska-Vasylenko over 250 members were persecuted in the 1930s. Humanities suffered most, and technical sciences became the main focus. In 1936 it lost its national status and became the Academy of Sciences of the Ukrainian SSR. It was evacuated from Kyiv in 1941 and returned in 1944.
