In 1963 it was subordinated to the Academy of Sciences of the Soviet Union, and in the 1970s most of its publications appeared in Russian.

Its official status is that of a self-governing higher scientific organisation. Its highest body is the General Assembly of full and corresponding members, and a Presidium, elected for five years, directs it in between. The Presidium meets in the former Levashova building on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv. It has three sections: physical-technical and mathematical sciences, chemical and biological sciences, and social sciences and humanities. Research institutes, observatories, botanical gardens, libraries and museums form its base, with regional centres in cities including Lviv, Odesa, Kharkiv and Dnipro. It sponsors awards such as the Bogoliubov Prize, founded in 1992.
national-and-kapodistrian-university-of-: The university was founded on 3 May 1837 by King Otto of Greece and was named the Othonian University in his honour. It was the first university in the liberated Greek state and in south-eastern Europe, and the second academic institution in the Greek lands after the Ionian Academy. It began with four faculties: Theology, Law, Medicine, and Arts, which included applied sciences and mathematics. In its first year it had 33 professors, 52 students and 75 non-matriculated auditors.

At first it was housed in the home of the architects Stamatios Kleanthis and Eduard Schaubert on the north slope of the Acropolis, a building that now houses the Athens University History Museum. In November 1841 it moved into its Main Building, designed by the Danish architect Christian Hansen in a neoclassical style. The front wing, the Propylaea, was finished in 1842 to 1843 and the rest in 1864. The painter Carl Rahl decorated it. With the National Library of Greece and the Athens Academy it forms the Athenian Neoclassical Trilogy.

After events that forced King Otto to leave the country the university was renamed the National University in 1862. In 1904 the faculty of Arts was divided into Arts and Sciences, and a department of chemistry followed in 1919. Between 1895 and 1911 about 1,000 new students matriculated each year, and the number reached 2,000 at the end of the First World War, so that entrance examinations were introduced for all faculties from the academic year 1927–28.

From 1911 to 1932 the university was split into two bodies: the Kapodistrian University for the humanities, named after Ioannis Kapodistrias, the first head of state of independent modern Greece, and the National University for the sciences. In 1932 they were merged as the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens. In the 1960s work began on a campus in the suburb of Ilissia.

The university's central administration still works from the Main Building. Many prominent figures studied there, among them the prime ministers Charilaos Trikoupis, Eleftherios Venizelos and Andreas Papandreou, and Constantine II, the last monarch of Greece. Two Nobel laureates in Literature studied or taught at the university.
national-assembly-of-bulgaria: The National Assembly was established in 1879 with the Tarnovo Constitution, which provided for a single chamber. Historical liberals favoured it, while conservatives disliked it and proposed replacing it with a bicameral parliament. From 1881 to 1883, under the Regime of Full Powers of Prince Alexander I, it was replaced by an appointed State Council of Bulgaria.

The same constitution introduced the Grand National Assembly, an organ called for matters of special jurisdiction. The First and the Third Grand National Assemblies elected the first two monarchs after liberation from Ottoman rule, Prince Alexander Battenberg and Prince Ferdinand Saxe Coburg-Gotha.

Before the Second World War the Grand National Assembly was also competent to elect a regency if the tsar had not come of age. It was abolished in 1947 and reintroduced by the 1991 constitution, which was adopted by the Seventh Grand National Assembly. That body had 200 members elected by proportional representation and 200 under a first-past-the-post system. Seven Grand National Assemblies have sat in all, the last from 10 July 1990 to 12 July 1991.

Between 1946 and 1989 the National Assembly was characterised as a rubber stamp for the Bulgarian Communist Party, which controlled nominations and elections at every level. A legacy of that period is that ministers are formally appointed and dismissed by the Assembly on the prime minister's advice, rather than by the President.

Under the constitution the Assembly has 240 members, elected for four years by proportional representation in multi-seat constituencies. A party needs at least 4 per cent of the national vote to enter. It enacts laws, approves the state budget, schedules presidential elections, selects and dismisses the Prime Minister and other ministers, declares war, concludes peace and ratifies international treaties. More than 121 members must be present for a session to begin. Constitutional changes of 2023 provide that a dissolved parliament continues to function until a new one is constituted.

A Grand National Assembly has 400 deputies and needs a two-thirds majority in three votes on separate dates. The main parliament building in central Sofia, designed in the Neo-Renaissance style by Konstantin Jovanović, is a monument of culture. The former headquarters of the Bulgarian Communist Party at the Largo, the Party House, has also served as a meeting place, and sessions returned there in 2023.
national-assembly-of-france: The name National Assembly has been attached to different bodies in French constitutional history. The first National Assembly of the French Revolution began the custom of seating left-wing parties to the left and right-wing parties to the right as seen from the president's seat, a practice the present chamber still follows. Under the Bourbon Restoration and the July Monarchy the term was not used, and the lower house was the Chamber of Deputies. Under the Second Empire it was the Corps législatif.

The National Assembly of the Third Republic was at first a unicameral constituent assembly. After the Constitutional Laws of 1875 the term referred to a joint sitting of the two houses of the bicameral legislature, whose lower house was the Chamber of Deputies and whose upper house was the Senate. After the Fall of France in 1940 the Vichy regime forced the Assembly to approve the French Constitutional Law of 1940, which left it effectively powerless. In 1943 Free France set up a Provisional Consultative Assembly in Algiers, representing the resistance movements, the political parties and the territories fighting the Axis.

After the May 1958 crisis, the constitution of the Fifth Republic greatly increased the power of the executive at the expense of Parliament, compared with the constitutions of the Third and Fourth Republics. The Assembly can dismiss the government by a motion of no confidence, called a motion de censure, and the president of the Republic can dissolve it and call new elections. In the Fifth Republic's first decades, the only successful motion of censure came on 5 October 1962, when the Assembly voted against President Charles de Gaulle's proposal to elect the president by direct universal suffrage. De Gaulle answered by dissolving it within days.

In 1997 President Jacques Chirac dissolved it, but the plan backfired because the new majority opposed him. A constitutional change of 23 July 2008 shared control of the agenda more evenly between the Government and the Assembly.

The Assembly is the lower house of the French Parliament under the Fifth Republic, with the Senate as the upper house. It has 577 deputies, each elected from a single-member constituency by a two-round system, so 289 seats form a majority. Their term is five years, subject to dissolution, and the president of the Assembly presides over the body. Its seat is the Palais Bourbon on the left bank of the Seine in the 7th arrondissement of Paris. The mandate of deputy cannot be held together with a ministerial office, and a deputy who joins the Government is replaced by a substitute.
national-assembly-of-hungary: The Diet of Hungary, called the Országgyűlés, was a legislative institution of the medieval kingdom of Hungary from the 1290s, and continued in its successor states, Royal Hungary and the Habsburg kingdom of Hungary. Its name in the Middle Ages was Parlamentum, and the word Diet came into use mostly in the early modern period. It met at regular intervals with interruptions between 1527 and 1918, and again until 1946.

In 1608 a two-part legislature was enacted as the Royal Hungarian Diet. The upper board held high nobles and high priests, the archbishops and bishops. The lower board, or board of envoys, held representatives of the common nobility, the clergy and the free royal cities. About 10 per cent of the voting-age population could vote for its delegates, 5 per cent of them county nobility and 5 per cent residents of free royal cities. The whole body numbered about 500 people in the 17th and 18th centuries.

The articles of the 1790 diet provided that it meet at least every three years, but since the Habsburg monarchy summoned it, the promise was often broken. It was reconstituted in 1867 after the Austro-Hungarian Compromise. The term Natio Hungarica, the Hungarian nation, designated the political elite who took part in the diet, consisting of the nobility, the Catholic clergy and a few enfranchised burghers, regardless of language or ethnicity.

Under communist rule the Assembly was defined as the supreme body of state power and, under the Constitution of 1949, was the sole branch of government on paper. In practice it ratified decisions already taken by the Hungarian Socialist Workers' Party and its Politburo and sat only twice a year. Between sessions the Presidential Council exercised most of its powers and could issue edicts in place of laws.

The liberal democratic character of parliament was restored with the fall of the Iron Curtain and the end of communist rule in 1989. The present body is unicameral, with 199 members elected to four-year terms, and it has met in the Hungarian Parliament Building in Budapest since 1902. It keeps the old name Országgyűlés but is called the National Assembly to distance it from the royal diet.
national-assembly-of-kuwait: The assembly had a predecessor, the National Assembly of 1938. Its merchant members tried to obtain a share of the oil revenue from the ruler, Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah, who refused and moved against them, and members of the assembly were arrested in 1939. It was formally dissolved that year, after one member, Sulaiman al-Adasani, was found with a letter signed by other members and addressed to King Ghazi of Iraq, asking for Kuwait's immediate incorporation into Iraq.

The assembly is a single chamber of 50 deputies, elected by single non-transferable vote for four-year terms, who sit together with the cabinet ministers appointed by the Emir; the constitution limits the cabinet to 16. Ministers have the same rights as elected members, except that they do not serve on committees and cannot vote when an interpellation leads to a vote of no confidence in a minister. Under Article 107 of the constitution the Emir may dissolve the assembly by a decree that gives its reasons, but not twice on the same grounds, and new elections must follow within two months.

Political parties are illegal in Kuwait, but members have grouped themselves in factions, among them a liberal bloc, an Islamist bloc and the Shaabi or populist bloc, whose main organisation is the Popular Action Bloc. The parliament building was designed by the Danish architect Jørn Utzon, who also designed the Sydney Opera House.

The assembly was suspended from 1976 to 1981 and again from 1986 to 1991. Kuwaiti women gained the right to vote in 2005, and in the 2009 election four women, Aseel al-Awadhi, Rola Dashti, Massouma al-Mubarak and Salwa al-Jassar, became the first to win seats. Between 2006 and 2024 the Emir dissolved the assembly 13 times. On 10 May 2024 it was suspended for a four-year re-evaluation of the constitution, the grounds given being inaction, corruption, bribery, vote buying and political deadlock.
national-autonomist-party: The party was created on 15 March 1874 by the union of the Autonomist Party of Adolfo Alsina and the National Party of Nicolás Avellaneda, who was its first president of the republic, from 1874 to 1880. The political scientist Luis L. Schenoni places its emergence within a wider convergence of autonomistas and nacionalistas after Argentina's victory in the Paraguayan War, and argues that the party helped to consolidate the state-building coalition that came out of it. Julio Argentino Roca took the presidency in 1880 under the motto "peace and administration".

In economic matters the party promoted a model of agricultural exports that favoured the cattle and cereal producers of the Pampas and was central to the building of the Argentine railways. It has been described as an "organ of the elite, an oligarchy of wealth and power." All the presidents from 1874 to 1916 came from its ranks: after Avellaneda and Roca came Miguel Juárez Celman, Carlos Pellegrini, Luis Sáenz Peña, José Evaristo Uriburu, Roca again from 1898 to 1904, Manuel Quintana, José Figueroa Alcorta, Roque Sáenz Peña and Victorino de la Plaza.

After the Revolución del Parque of 1890 a current formed within the party against the policies of Roca, known as its modernist line. Its leading figures, among them Roque Sáenz Peña, Carlos Pellegrini and Ramón J. Cárcano, sought to modernise the country's institutions and to open a true democratic system without the electoral fraud that kept the party in power. Its main opponent was the Radical Civic Union, founded after the 1890 revolution. Under Roque Sáenz Peña a law of secret universal suffrage was written, which made the free elections of 1916 possible.

After the electoral reform of 1912 and the Radical victory of 1916 the party broke apart. Much of it reorganised as the Conservative Party, and another faction gave rise to the Democratic Progressive Party, which still exists. In 1931, after the military coup of the previous year, the conservatives returned to power as the National Democratic Party, which led the Concordancia coalition. These traditional conservative forces were pushed to the margins after World War II and the rise of Peronism, and the National Democratic Party fell apart after 1955.
national-coalition-party: The party was founded on 9 December 1918, after the Finnish Civil War, by the majority of the Finnish Party and a minority of the Young Finnish Party. Both groups supported Prince Frederick Charles of Hesse as king of Finland in a new monarchy. The republicans of the two parties had founded the National Progressive Party the previous day. The founding meeting, with over 600 representatives, called for a national coalition across old party lines and for lawful order without compromise with revolutionary aspirations.

The party advocated a constitutional monarchy and, failing that, strong government powers within a republic. The monarchist aim failed and Finland became a parliamentary republic, in which the party argued for strong presidential powers. In the late 1920s and early 1930s fear of the Soviet Union moved it towards a very conservative position. In the 1933 election it formed a coalition with the Patriotic People's Movement and lost 24 of its 42 seats. Under its new chair, Juho Kusti Paasikivi, it broke with that movement in 1934.

During the Winter War and the Continuation War the party joined the wartime national unity governments. Paasikivi was prime minister from 1944 to 1946 and president from 1946 to 1956, and is remembered as the formulator of Finland's foreign policy after the Second World War. In 1951 the party changed its name from Kansallinen Kokoomuspuolue to Kansallinen Kokoomus, and in the 1950s it placed more emphasis on individual liberty and free-market reform. A minor split in 1958 produced the Christian Democrats.

From 1966 to 1987 the party was in opposition. By criticising the Finnish communists and President Urho Kekkonen of the Centre Party it lost the president's trust, and governments of the Centre Party and left-wing parties followed one another. In 1987 it had its best election result so far, and Harri Holkeri became its first prime minister since Paasikivi. It remained in government as a minor partner until 2003. Under Jyrki Katainen, chair from 2004 to 2014, liberalism became its main attribute, and in 2011 it was the largest party in parliament for the first time, with 44 of 200 seats.

The party is built from municipal and local chapters grouped into districts, together with women's, student and youth wings. A party conference, which meets every two years, elects the chair and a party council of 61 members. Its voters have come predominantly from urban areas, while rural areas tend to favour the Centre Party. Membership stood at 81,000 in 1970 and at 34,000 in 2016. The party is a member of the European People's Party.
national-congress-belgium: The National Congress was a temporary assembly convened in the aftermath of the Belgian Revolution, when a self-declared Provisional Government had taken charge of the country. Its task was to draw up a constitution for the new state. About 30,000 voters elected its 200 members on 3 November 1830, and Baron Erasme Louis Surlet de Chokier became its president.

The Congress chose a constitutional popular monarchy as the form of government and first offered the throne to Louis, Duke of Nemours, son of the French king Louis-Philippe. Other candidates were Auguste de Beauharnais and Archduke Charles of Austria. The choice of Nemours was unacceptable to the government of the United Kingdom, and while a new candidate was sought Surlet de Chokier was made Regent, with Etienne Constantin, Baron de Gerlache, taking his place as president.

The constitution, very progressive for its time, was accepted on 7 February 1831, and the Provisional Government was then dissolved. The Congress named Leopold of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha king on 4 June, and six weeks later, on 21 July, he swore allegiance to the constitution in front of the Church of St. James on Coudenberg in Brussels. The Congress sat until the election of the first Parliament on 29 August 1831.

The day of Leopold's oath, 21 July, has been Belgian National Day ever since. The Congress Column in Brussels was raised in the assembly's honour; at its base four bronze female figures stand for the liberties the constitution guaranteed, freedom of the press, of worship, of association and of education. The same four liberties name the streets that lead to the Place de la Liberté in the city's Freedom Quarter.
national-convention: The National Convention was created after the insurrection of 10 August 1792. The Legislative Assembly decreed the provisional suspension of King Louis XVI and called a convention to draw up a constitution with no monarchy. Its deputies were to be elected by all Frenchmen aged 21 or older, domiciled for a year and living by the product of their labour, so that it was the first French assembly elected by a suffrage without distinctions of class. The indirect election took place from 2 to 10 September 1792, with a turnout of 11.9 per cent. The Convention had 749 deputies, not counting 33 from the colonies, and lawyers were the most numerous. It first sat on 20 September 1792.

Three factions divided the Convention: the Montagnards or Mountain, the Marais or Plain, and the Girondins, also called Brissotins. Historians are divided on the makeup, but the Mountain was the largest, with around 302 to 309 deputies, against 178 to 227 Girondins and 153 to 250 in the Plain. On the fate of the king, most Montagnards favoured judgment and execution, while the Girondins were divided. Opinion turned against Louis on 20 November 1792 after the discovery of a cache of 726 documents. Military setbacks and the war in the Vendée, which began in March 1793, were used to portray the Girondins as soft, and the insurrection of 31 May to 2 June 1793 brought their fall.

From April 1793 power was delegated to the small Committee of Public Safety. After armed sections again surrounded the Convention on 5 September 1793, it put the Terror on the agenda and created a revolutionary army. The Committee then eliminated the Hébertists and the Dantonists, among them Georges Danton and Camille Desmoulins. Many deputies who had backed the Committee no longer supported it by mid-1794. After Robespierre's fall the Convention sat for another year, until a new constitution was written and the Directory began on 26 October 1795.

By a decree of 4 February 1794, after speeches by deputies from Saint-Domingue, the Convention extended to the whole French colonial empire the abolition of slavery that the commissioners Léger-Félicité Sonthonax and Étienne Polverel had proclaimed in Saint-Domingue in 1793. It did not affect Martinique or Guadeloupe, and the law of 20 May 1802 abolished the decree. The historian Anchel concluded in 1911 that the Convention had saved France from civil war and invasion and founded a system of public education, including the École Polytechnique and the École Normale Supérieure, and that it created the Grand Livre de la Dette publique.
national-fascist-party: Italy felt cheated by the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye of 1919 after the war of 1914 to 1918, despite having been a full partner of the Allies. The party exploited this perceived slight to Italian nationalism and presented fascism as best suited to govern, claiming that democracy, socialism and liberalism were failed systems. It was rooted in Italian nationalism and in the revolutionary syndicalism of Georges Sorel, and it sought to restore and expand Italian territory, claiming that modern Italy was the heir of ancient Rome and needed living space, spazio vitale, for settlers and control of the Mediterranean.

On 28 October 1922 Mussolini attempted a coup d'état that Fascist propaganda called the March on Rome, in which almost 30,000 fascists took part. After the Acerbo Law changed the electoral rules, the party clearly won the controversial elections of April 1924. In early 1925 Mussolini dropped all pretence of democracy and set up a dictatorship, and a law of 1928 formalised the party's status as the only legal one. Giacomo Matteotti, leader of the Socialist Party, strongly criticised the new laws in Parliament, and a few days later fascist blackshirts kidnapped and killed him.

On 25 July 1943, at the request of Dino Grandi, the Grand Council of Fascism asked the king to resume full authority, and he removed Mussolini as prime minister. Pietro Badoglio's government banned the party on 27 July. After German forces freed Mussolini in September, the party was revived as the Republican Fascist Party, the single party of the Italian Social Republic, with Alessandro Pavolini as secretary. It did not outlast Mussolini's execution and the end of that state in April 1945.

The party's action squads, the Blackshirts, violently suppressed socialist organisations in the early 1920s and in January 1923 became the Milizia Volontaria per la Sicurezza Nazionale by royal decree. Youth was central to its aims: the Opera Nazionale Balilla, set up in 1926, became compulsory for boys aged 6 to 18 and girls aged 8 to 14, and in 1937 the Gioventù Italiana del Littorio replaced it, directed against the influence of the Catholic Church on the young. The Fasci Femminili had 750,000 members by 1939. The party also ran Fasci Italiani all'Estero among emigrants, and its economic ideal was a corporatist system linking employer and employee syndicates.
national-front-colombia: Power-sharing had precedents in Colombia: President Rafael Reyes's Concordia Nacional gave half his cabinet to Liberals, and in 1946 the Conservative Mariano Ospina Pérez divided ministries and governorships equally under the Union Nacional. The Liberals under Jorge Eliécer Gaitán left that government in February 1948, and Gaitán's assassination on 9 April 1948 set off the riots of El Bogotazo and violence across the country. Laureano Gómez, elected after Ospina, was overthrown by General Gustavo Rojas Pinilla.

Rojas Pinilla at first had wide support, brought amnesties, an agrarian reform, roads, airports, television and the vote for women, but his offensive against rearmed peasants at Villarrica in 1955 and his attempt to stay in power provoked a general strike. On 10 May 1957 a five-man military junta replaced him.

The agreement took shape in exile and at home: the Accord of Benidorm of 24 July 1956 between Alberto Lleras Camargo and Laureano Gómez, the Pact of March 1957 against Rojas Pinilla's re-election, the Declaration of Sitges of 20 July 1957 and the Pact of San Carlos that November. A referendum approved the system on 1 December 1957. When the Conservatives could not agree on a first candidate, both parties accepted a Liberal, and Lleras Camargo was elected on 4 May 1958. Guillermo León Valencia, Carlos Lleras Restrepo and Misael Pastrana Borrero followed.

Third parties were barred, but their members ran on the two parties' lists. The Liberal Revolutionary Movement of Alfonso López Michelsen and Rojas Pinilla's National Popular Alliance (ANAPO), founded in 1961, gained seats, and in the election of 19 April 1970 ANAPO accused the government of fraud when Pastrana Borrero was declared the winner over Rojas Pinilla. Abstention was high, reaching 60.1 per cent in the presidential election of 1966.

The system gradually calmed the violence between the two parties, and by 1970 far fewer people identified with either one. Yet new guerrilla movements arose from discontent and new political ideas: the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) in 1964, the National Liberation Army (ELN) in 1965, the Popular Liberation Army in 1967 and, after the disputed 1970 election, the 19th of April Movement (M-19). A sharing of offices continued after 1974 until President Virgilio Barco ended it in 1986.
national-front-czechoslovakia: During World War II the Czech lands became the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia under Nazi rule, while Slovakia was nominally independent. The post-war order was worked out by the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia (KSČ), whose leaders were in exile in Moscow, and by Edvard Beneš for the government-in-exile in London, and it included a broad anti-Nazi coalition. Talks began in Moscow in December 1943, with the Communists and the other parties holding very different ideas of it.

The coalition was founded as the National Front in April 1945, when a Czechoslovak government was formed in Košice, newly liberated by Soviet troops, on the model of French tripartisme. The Slovak People's Party was banned for collaborating with the Nazis, and other pre-war parties, among them the Republican Party of Farmers and Peasants, were not allowed back.

From 1945 to 1948 the Front was dominated by the socialist parties, the KSČ holding key ministries. The Communists saw it as permanent, the other parties as a temporary coalition until normal conditions returned, and the two sides quarrelled often. After the KSČ seized power on 25 February 1948, the other parties were purged and gave up their original ideologies, and every member party had to accept the leading role of the KSČ as a condition of existing. The ČSSD was absorbed into the KSČ in June 1948.

Voters were offered a single list of candidates approved by the Front, usually endorsed by well over 99 percent. Non-Communist candidates sat in parliament, but seats followed a quota that guaranteed a large Communist majority. When the country became a federation of Czech and Slovak socialist republics in 1969, each part received its own National Front organisation.

After 1948 the Front became a broad patriotic organisation controlling nearly all organised activity in the country except religion. Besides the parties it took in mass organisations such as the Revolutionary Trade Union Movement, to which all unions belonged, the Czechoslovak Socialist Youth Union with 1.5 million members, the Czechoslovak Union of Women and even the Union of Philatelists. Party members held every controlling post in them, so that no secular body could stand wholly apart from the KSČ. The small allied parties kept sizeable memberships; in 1984 the People's Party had about 66,000 members.
national-hero-of-indonesia: The legal framework for the title was set by Presidential Decree No. 241 of 1958, under which it was first styled National Independence Hero (Pahlawan Kemerdekaan Nasional). It was first awarded on 30 August 1959 to the politician turned writer Abdul Muis, who had died the month before. The title kept that name for the rest of Sukarno's rule and was given its present name when Suharto rose to power in the mid-1960s. Special titles of the same rank have also been given: Hero of the Revolution to ten victims of the 30 September Movement in 1965, and Proclamator Hero to Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta in 1986 for reading the Proclamation of Indonesian Independence.

The title is given for deeds judged heroic, defined as actual deeds which can be remembered and exemplified for all time by other citizens, or extraordinary service furthering the interests of the state and people. The Ministry of Social Affairs sets seven criteria. The person must have been an Indonesian citizen who led an armed struggle or produced a concept or product useful to the state, kept up the struggle throughout life, had a wide-reaching impact and shown a high degree of nationalism. They must also have been of good moral standing, never surrendered to their enemies and never committed an act that taints their legacy.

A nomination passes through four steps and must be approved at each. The people of a city or regency propose a name to the mayor or regent, who passes the request to the provincial governor. The governor recommends it to the Ministry of Social Affairs, which forwards it to the president, represented by the Board of Titles (Dewan Gelar) of two academics, two people of military background and three earlier holders of an award or title. The title is conferred at a ceremony in Jakarta, held since 2000 in early November to coincide with Heroes' Day (Hari Pahlawan).

The heroes come from every part of the archipelago, from Aceh in the west to Papua in the east, and from many ethnic groups, among them native Indonesians, ethnic Chinese, Arabs and Eurasians. They include prime ministers, guerrillas, government ministers, soldiers, royalty, journalists and a bishop.
national-league-for-democracy: The National League for Democracy was founded on 27 September 1988, in the aftermath of the 8888 Uprising, a series of pro-democracy protests that ended when the military again took control of the country. It formed under the leadership of Aung San Suu Kyi, daughter of Aung San, a leader of the Burmese independence movement of the 1940s, whom concerned democracy advocates had recruited.

Its first chair was Brigadier General Aung Gyi, and Aung San Suu Kyi was general secretary. The party advocated a non-violent movement towards multi-party democracy and said it supported human rights, the rule of law and national reconciliation. Its flag bore the peacock, and its emblem was a traditional bamboo hat.

In the 1990 elections the party took 59 per cent of the vote and won 392 of 492 contested seats, but the ruling military junta did not let it form a government. The party was repressed, and Suu Kyi was under house arrest for 16 of the 21 years after 1996. In May 2003 dozens of NLD members were shot and killed in a military-sponsored massacre at Depayin.

The NLD boycotted the 2010 election because many prominent members were barred from standing, and was declared illegal on 6 May 2010. It re-registered in December 2011, won 43 of 45 seats in the 2012 by-elections and won a supermajority in the 2015 general election, paving the way for the country's first non-military president in 54 years. Critics faulted it for its response to military violence against the Rohingya from 2016.

The NLD won the 2020 election by a larger margin. The military claimed 8.6 million irregularities in voter lists, which the Union Election Commission rejected on 28 January 2021, and on 1 February the military seized power and detained Suu Kyi, President Win Myint and other leaders. Hundreds of NLD members were arrested. In January 2023 the junta enacted an electoral law designed to favour the military's proxy, the Union Solidarity and Development Party; the NLD refused to re-register, and the commission dissolved it on 28 March 2023, a decision the party rejected as illegitimate.

The party was described as liberal, social-liberal and, historically, social-democratic, and also as having no rigid ideology. It had a Women's Committee, which provided legal and social assistance to women in need, with committees at region, state, ward and village level. Suu Kyi called the 2008 constitution, drafted with the input of the armed forces and reserving 25 per cent of parliamentary seats for military appointees, undemocratic.
national-liberation-army-algeria: The ALN was the armed wing of the National Liberation Front (FLN), which the Revolutionary Committee of Unity and Action organised in March 1954. About two years later the FLN had absorbed most, though not all, of the Algerian nationalist organisations, reorganised itself and set up a provisional government. That government had five members in its executive and legislative bodies, all of them district heads. During the war of independence Colonel Houari Boumedienne, later President of Algeria, led the ALN against the French.

The army grew to nearly 40,000 men by 1957, while France, from 1956, deployed 400,000 soldiers against it in response. The ALN set up camps across the borders in Tunisia and Morocco to supply its fighters inside Algeria with arms and logistical support. The fighting went on until 18 March 1962, when the two sides signed a ceasefire at Évian-les-Bains. A referendum held in Algeria on 1 July under the Évian Agreement gave the separatists an overwhelming victory, and they declared independence two days later.

On the morning of 5 July 1962 seven companies of ALN soldiers entering Oran were fired on by some pieds-noirs, the white Europeans born in colonial Algeria. An enraged Arab crowd then swept into the pied-noir districts, already largely emptied, and attacked the estimated 40,000 pieds-noirs who remained there. The violence lasted several hours until the French Gendarmerie was deployed.

Once Algeria had won its independence from France, the ALN was converted into the regular armed forces of the new state, the Algerian People's National Armed Forces, and Boumedienne, its wartime commander, would later go on to become President of Algeria.
national-liberation-front-algeria: The Front grew out of Algerian nationalist sentiment that rose with the outbreak of WWII. When the Movement for the Triumph of Democratic Liberties, led by Messali Hadj, was limited by a double electoral college that gave French settlers and the larger Muslim community equal representation of 60 seats each, some members turned towards a military approach through its paramilitary Special Organisation, whose figures included Ahmed Ben Bella, Hocine Aït Ahmed and Mohammed Boudiaf.

After the capture of Ben Bella in 1951 and the dismantling of that body, its militants formed the Revolutionary Committee of Unity and Action. It was succeeded by the Front, established on 10 October 1954. The Declaration of 1 November 1954, written by the journalist Mohamed Aïchaoui, opened the war.

By 1956 nearly all nationalist organisations in Algeria had joined the Front, which had established itself as the main nationalist group by co-opting and coercing smaller ones. Messali Hadj's Algerian National Movement remained outside. The Front organised itself like a provisional government and divided the country into six wilayas, following Ottoman-era boundaries. Its National Liberation Army fought partly as guerrilla units inside Algeria and partly as a stronger, more conventional force based in Morocco and Tunisia, later led by Colonel Houari Boumédiène. The war killed between 300,000 and 1.5 million people. The Front is held responsible for over 16,000 civilian deaths, and is thought to have massacred thousands of harkis after the ceasefire of 19 March 1962.

After the Évian Accords, a power struggle split the leadership. Boumédiène's army put down resistance and installed Ben Bella as president, who outlawed opposition parties and purged dissidents such as Ferhat Abbas. In 1965 Boumédiène overthrew him, ruling by decree and marginalising the party. After his death in 1978, Colonel Chadli Bendjedid succeeded him, and riots in 1988 led to an amended constitution that allowed several parties.

The Front drew its legitimacy from three sources: nationalism and the war against France, a loosely interpreted socialism, and Islam as the foundation of national identity. Frantz Fanon was a member and influenced its ideology during the struggle. The Constitution of October 1963 declared Islam the state religion and Arabic the sole national language, with Arabization as a priority.

Its stress on a single Arab and Muslim identity led it to refuse the separate Berber identity of the roughly 20% of Algerians who are Berbers. Hocine Aït Ahmed founded the Socialist Forces Front and began a rebellion in Kabylia that the government defeated in 1965. Between 1961 and 1962 about 130,000 of Algeria's 140,000 Jews left, mostly for France. Its role as liberator of the country has remained the core of its self-image.
national-liberation-front-greece: Under the Metaxas regime the Communist Party of Greece (KKE) was outlawed, and more than 2,000 Communists were imprisoned or sent into internal exile. After the German invasion of April and May 1941 several hundred members escaped to the underground and began to rebuild the party. After the German attack on the Soviet Union on 22 June, it committed itself to a Popular Front line but largely failed to win over established pre-war politicians.

EAM was founded on 27 September 1941 by representatives of four left-wing parties: Lefteris Apostolou for the KKE, Christos Chomenidis for the Socialist Party of Greece, Ilias Tsirimokos for the Union of People's Democracy and Apostolos Vogiatzis for the Agricultural Party of Greece. Its charter called for the liberation of the nation from the foreign yoke and for the Greek people's sovereign right to decide their form of government. The KKE dominated it, and Georgios Siantos served as acting leader because Nikolaos Zachariadis was interned in Dachau.

The Great Famine, in which about 300,000 Greeks starved, radicalised opinion and brought support to EAM as the best organised resistance group. In March 1943 strikes and a demonstration in Athens forced the collaborationist government to drop plans for forced labour in Germany. Its army, ELAS, fought German, Italian and Bulgarian forces and, by late 1943, the rival resistance groups EDES and EKKA. In March 1944 EAM set up a government in the liberated mountain areas, the Political Committee of National Liberation, and held elections in April in which women voted for the first time in Greek history.

After liberation in October 1944 EAM joined the government of national unity under Georgios Papandreou, but disagreement over disarming ELAS led its ministers to resign on 1 December. On 3 December Greek gendarmes fired on an EAM demonstration in Athens, killing 25 protesters, and a month of fighting between ELAS and British and Greek government forces followed, known as the Dekemvriana, which the government won.

The Varkiza agreement led to the disbanding of ELAS, and in April the Socialist Party and the Union of People's Democracy left EAM, which became in effect an expression of the KKE. A conservative terror campaign, the White Terror, was launched against its supporters in 1945 and 1946, and the Greek Civil War broke out in March 1946 and lasted until 1949. The government later labelled EAM members symmorites, a word for criminals, and branded the movement anti-national. When PASOK came to power in 1981 the Greek state officially recognised EAM-ELAS as part of the National Resistance and gave state pensions to surviving fighters.
national-liberation-front-of-angola: The movement began in 1954 as the United People of Northern Angola, a separatist movement of the Bakongo that wished to re-establish their 16th-century feudal kingdom and also protested against forced labour. Holden Roberto was to be its king. It later took the name União das Populações de Angola under Roberto. In March 1961 it began an uprising in the north that killed thousands of white settlers and their servants, as well as assimilados and members of other peoples. The Portuguese sent soldiers, more than 50,000 people died in the violence by the end of 1961, and more than a million refugees were said to have fled to Zaire.

It then merged with the Partido Democratico de Angola to form the National Front for the Liberation of Angola. By February 1962 it had joined a government in exile in Kinshasa, with Roberto as president and Jonas Savimbi as foreign minister, which the Organisation of African Unity recognised as Angola's only freedom movement until 1971. Savimbi left in 1964 to form UNITA, citing Roberto's dictatorial leadership.

The United States began aiding the FNLA in 1961, and Algeria, Tunisia, West Germany, Israel, France, Romania, China and others supported it over the years. After the coup in Portugal in April 1974 the FNLA, the MPLA and UNITA competed for control of Angola. They signed the Alvor Agreement on 15 January 1975, which set independence for 11 November and a coalition government. Within 24 hours fighting broke out in Luanda, and the FNLA was expelled from the city.

From late January 1975 the CIA funded the FNLA, and the aid rose to $32 million for the FNLA and UNITA by September. South African forces entered Angola in Operation Savannah. On 10 November 1975 Roberto ordered an assault on Luanda through Quifangondo, unaware that the Cubans had reinforced the position, and it failed disastrously. The MPLA kept Luanda, and Agostinho Neto declared the People's Republic of Angola on 11 November. The Clark Amendment ended covert US aid on 19 December 1975, and São Salvador, the FNLA headquarters, fell on 15 February 1976.

After a pact of June 1978 between Angola and Zaire, Roberto was exiled to Gabon in November 1979. Remnants fought on as the FNLA-COMIRA until 1983. Before the first multiparty elections of 1992 the FNLA reorganised as a political party, winning 2.4 per cent of the vote and five seats.
national-liberation-front-south-yemen: In the late 1950s the pan-Arabism of the Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser threatened both British control and the rule of the region's sultans, and the British persuaded the feuding emirs to merge into the Federation of South Arabia. The Colony of Aden joined it in 1962. The next day the Yemeni ruler Muhammad al-Badr was overthrown, and the civil war in North Yemen between republicans backed by Nasser and royalists backed by Saudi Arabia and Britain spread into the south as the Aden Emergency.

In 1964 the NLF announced the start of its revolution in the Federation, and in 1965 the British suspended the Federation's government and imposed direct colonial rule. As parts of the NLF became more radical Marxist and split from the Egyptians, Abdullah al-Asnag formed the rival Front for the Liberation of Occupied South Yemen, FLOSY, and the two fought each other as well as the British. Riots in the old Arab quarter of Aden ran from January to mid-February 1967, and on 20 June a mutiny broke out in the Federation's army and police.

Britain announced in February 1967 that it would leave. Officially both fronts refused to talk to the British, but the NLF held secret talks with them aimed at defeating FLOSY, which Nasser backed. After the Six-Day War Egypt withdrew its troops from Yemen, and the NLF won over the federal army; on 7 November 1967 the army, with the NLF's help, beat a FLOSY attack and inflicted heavy losses. The British left by the end of November without an agreement on who would govern, and the last governor, Sir Humphrey Trevelyan, had Government House repainted for whoever emerged victorious.

The Federation ceased to exist on 30 November 1967, when the new republic was proclaimed, and the NLF ruled as the National Front. Qahtan Muhammad al-Shaabi was president until 22 June 1969, when a hard-line Marxist group within the front replaced him with Salim Rubai Ali. On 1 December 1970 the state was renamed the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen. In 1978 the front became the Yemeni Socialist Party, into which all other parties were merged, making it the only legal party.
national-museum-of-indonesia: On 24 April 1778 a group of Dutch intellectuals founded the Bataviaasch Genootschap van Kunsten en Wetenschappen, the Batavian Society of Arts and Sciences. This private body aimed to promote research in history, archaeology, ethnography and physics. One founder, J. C. M. Radermacher, gave a building in Old Batavia together with a collection of objects and books, which started the society's museum and library.

In 1862 the colonial government decided to build a museum to house and display the collections, and it opened in 1868. It is popularly called Gedung Gajah, the Elephant Building, after a bronze elephant given to Batavia by King Chulalongkorn of Siam in 1871. In 1931 a fire at the World Colonial Exposition in Paris destroyed most of the objects sent there.

After independence the institution was renamed the Indonesian Cultural Institute in February 1950. It was handed to the Indonesian government on 17 September 1962 as the Museum Pusat, the Central Museum, and became the Museum Nasional in 1979. A 1977 agreement between Indonesia and the Netherlands returned some treasures, among them the treasures of Lombok, the Nagarakretagama lontar manuscript and a Prajnaparamita statue of Java.

A new wing opened in 2007. Four gold objects of the 10th-century Eastern Mataram period were stolen on 11 September 2013. In March 2020 King Willem-Alexander of the Netherlands returned the kris of Prince Diponegoro, leader of the rebellion against Dutch rule that ended with the Java War in 1830. A fire on 16 September 2023 collapsed part of the old building and destroyed at least four rooms of precolonial artifacts. The museum reopened on 15 October 2024.

The museum holds about 141,000 objects, from prehistoric artifacts to ceramics, coins, ethnography, history and geography. It acquired them by expeditions, excavations, private collections, gifts and treasures taken in Dutch military campaigns against kingdoms in Java, Aceh, Lombok and Bali. Its collection of Hindu-Buddhist stone sculpture dates from the Tarumanagara period in the 5th century to the Majapahit period in the 15th, and includes a statue of Adityavarman as Bhairava over four metres tall. Its Chinese ceramics run from the Han to the Qing, in the largest ceramic collection in Southeast Asia. The treasure rooms hold gold objects such as the 9th-century Wonoboyo hoard found near Prambanan.
national-museum-of-iraq: After the First World War archaeologists from Europe and the United States began excavations throughout Iraq. To keep the finds in the country, Gertrude Bell began collecting artefacts in a government building in Baghdad in 1922. On 14 June 1926 the Iraqi government moved the collection to a new building and established the Baghdad Antiquities Museum, with Bell as director. She died later that year and Sidney Smith succeeded her.

In 1966 the collection moved to a two-storey building in the Al-Ṣāliḥiyyah neighbourhood on the east side of the Tigris, and the name changed to the Iraq Museum. Bahija Khalil, its first woman director, held the post from 1983 to 1989.

The collections cover more than 5,000 years of Mesopotamian history in 28 galleries and vaults, with art and artefacts of the Sumerian, Assyrian and Babylonian civilisations, as well as galleries of pre-Islamic and Islamic Arabian art. Among its best-known holdings are the Nimrud gold jewellery of the ninth century BCE and the stone carvings and cuneiform tablets from Uruk, which date to between 3500 and 3000 BCE. Because of the British connection, exhibits have always been labelled in English and Arabic.

On 9 April 2003 the museum's staff left the building during fighting nearby. Thefts took place between 10 and 12 April, and the staff, returning on 12 April, drove off further looters; US forces were deployed around the museum on 16 April. Investigators later counted three separate thefts. Forty pieces were taken from the galleries, among them the Warka Vase, the Mask of Warka and the Bassetki Statue, and about 15,000 items in all went missing, including thousands of cylinder seals. Early reports of 170,000 catalogued lots were later corrected. Critics, among them Irving Finkel of the British Museum, said the looting could have been prevented, and three American advisers resigned in protest. Officials of the US military replied that other priorities came first.

Recovery began at once. The Warka Vase was returned, and the statue of Entemena of Lagash was recovered in the United States in 2006. In 2012 Germany returned 45 relics, and in 2021 the United States returned 17,000 artefacts. After years of sporadic opening the museum was officially reopened on 28 February 2015.
national-pact: Under the French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon of 1922, France controlled the government, foreign relations and much of the infrastructure of both countries, and Lebanese politics centred on winning independence. As independence neared, the country's religious diversity made it hard to agree on how it should be governed. The pact came out of negotiations between the Shia, Sunni, Maronite and Druze leaderships in the summer of 1943, with the Maronite elite speaking for the Christian population and the Sunni elite for the Muslim, and it also established Lebanon's independence from France.

Christians accepted that Lebanon had Arab features, and Muslims gave up the aim of union with Syria and the Arab world. The president and the commander of the armed forces were to be Maronite Catholic, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim, the speaker of parliament a Shia Muslim, the deputy speaker and the deputy prime minister Greek Orthodox, and the chief of the General Staff a Druze. Parliament was to hold Christians and Muslims in a ratio of 6:5, resting on the census of 1932, which had found a Christian majority of 51%.

Riad Al Solh presented the pact to the public in his ministerial declaration of 7 October 1943 as the basis of a Lebanese identity separate from both the Western and the Eastern worlds. Dissent continued, but the system was generally tolerated until 1958, when Lebanon's acceptance of aid under the Eisenhower Doctrine and pressure from the Egyptian-Syrian United Arab Republic to unite with other Arab countries strained it.

No new census was taken while the generally poorer Muslim population grew faster than the Christian and many Christians emigrated, so Christians came to hold a disproportionate share of power. Critics argue that the pact produced immobilism and cemented sectarian divisions by institutionalising them, and the dissatisfaction and rifts that followed helped spark the Lebanese Civil War. The Taif Agreement of 1989 changed the parliamentary ratio to 1:1 and reduced the powers of the Maronite president.
national-party-of-honduras: The party traces its ideas to the national hero José Trinidad Cabañas, who held that the national interest stood above every other. In the late 19th century Ponciano Leiva and Luis Bogran worked to build an institution reflecting that outlook. On 27 February 1902, in Tegucigalpa, Leiva's Progressive Party and the movement led by General Manuel Bonilla Chirinos united in a National Convention backed by 40,000 signatures, which marked the founding of the National Party. Bonilla was the first of its members to become president of Honduras, serving from 1903 to 1907.

The party is conservative, and its platform rests on Christian humanist doctrine, with five main principles: common wealth, the dignity of the human person, equality, solidarity and subsidiarity. Its seal shows clasped arms for fraternity among Honduran citizens, a scale for equality between men and women and a burning torch for the defence of those in need, with the motto Social Justice with Liberty and Democracy. Its highest body is the National Convention of municipal, state, regional and national authorities, with a Permanent Commission, a National Committee, a committee in each of the 18 departments and local committees.

Honduras has had 14 presidents from the party, and it led the National Congress from 2009 to 2022. It has also faced corruption charges. In 2015 it was found to have financed the campaign of President Juan Orlando Hernández with money diverted from the Honduran Social Security through a scheme of companies, and the president said the party should return it. In March 2017 the New York district attorney's office accused the former president Porfirio Lobo of helping protect drug organisations. Hernández was extradited to the United States in April 2022, convicted of drug trafficking charges in March 2024 and sentenced to 45 years, and was pardoned by President Donald Trump in November 2025.
national-party-south-africa: The National Party was founded in Bloemfontein in 1914 by Afrikaner nationalists soon after the Union of South Africa was established. Its founding was rooted in disagreements between Prime Minister Louis Botha and his first Minister of Justice, J. B. M. Hertzog, whom Botha removed from the cabinet after Hertzog spoke publicly against the government's "one-stream" policy in 1912. Hertzog and his followers in the Orange Free State advocated a "two-stream" policy of equal rights for the English and Afrikaner communities. Nationalists in the Transvaal and Cape soon followed, and three provincial organisations existed in time for the 1915 general elections.

The party first governed South Africa in 1924. During the Great Depression it merged with the South African Party, and a splinter faction, the Purified National Party, became the official opposition. The Reunited National Party, formed after the fragmentation of the war years, came to power in 1948 and revived the name National Party, forming the first all-Afrikaner cabinet since 1910. After the Commonwealth condemned apartheid, its government made South Africa a republic outside the Commonwealth. The United Nations General Assembly labelled apartheid a crime against humanity on 16 December 1966.

In 1958 the party took 55% of the vote and its first clear majority, and in 1977 it had its best result, 64.8% of white voters and 134 of 165 seats. From the 1960s it divided between verkramptes, who opposed any departure from rigid apartheid, and verligtes, who were more moderate. Under P. W. Botha in the 1980s it created separate chambers for Coloureds and Indians but refused meaningful political rights to Black South Africans. F. W. de Klerk succeeded Botha in 1989 and persuaded the party to negotiate an end to apartheid. In 1994 it won 20.39% of the vote and 82 seats, and in 1997 it became the New National Party.

The party was a loose federation of four provincial parties, Cape, Transvaal, Natal and the Orange Free State, each with its own leader, press and constitution, linked by a Federal Council. The leader, who was also prime minister and later State President, was elected by the parliamentary caucus. A political culture rooted in Calvinist tradition, with an Afrikaner habit of obedience towards leaders, meant that under Botha decisions moved from the bottom up to the top down. A new party called National Party South Africa was registered on 5 August 2008, with no formal connection to the earlier one.
national-party-uruguay: The National Party, also called the White Party or Partido Blanco, is one of the oldest active parties in Uruguay, alongside the Colorado Party, and its origins go back to the establishment of Uruguay as an independent state. Its identity dates from 10 August 1836, when President Manuel Oribe decreed the use of a white banner inscribed Defenders of the Laws. At the battle of Carpintería, Oribe faced the revolutionary army of Fructuoso Rivera, and coloured badges were used to tell the sides apart, which is why the party is called the White Party. Oribe is recognised as its founder, while Aparicio Saravia is considered its idealist and chief historical caudillo.

During the Uruguayan Civil War the party's leader Oribe headed the interim co-government known as the Gobierno del Cerrito, while a Defense Government in Montevideo was led by the Colorado Joaquín Suárez. On 7 July 1872 the party approved its first Program of Principles, which called for respect for freedoms, peace, the representation of minorities, decentralisation, a stronger system of justice and the promotion of education.

The party was in opposition for much of the 19th and 20th centuries, against its traditional adversary the Colorado Party. Except for the administration of Luis Lacalle Pou, it has governed Uruguay for 35 years in all, counting the Gobierno del Cerrito. Lacalle Pou was sworn in as president in March 2020. Between 1942 and 1994 each party could run up to three presidential candidates, and the combined vote decided which party won; a referendum of 1996 limited each party to one candidate from 1999.

The party describes itself as liberal, nationalist, pan-Americanist and humanist, and it has traditionally defended decentralisation, in contrast to the centralist policy of the Colorado Party. Its voters are concentrated in rural areas and the interior of the country. It is made up of sectors ranging from centre-right to right. Three main factions are the centrist and Christian democratic National Alliance, the economic liberal and conservative Herrerism, and the social-liberal Wilsonist Current. Herrerism, dating from Luis Alberto de Herrera in the early 20th century, has been led by a family line that continued with the former president Luis Alberto Lacalle and his son Luis Lacalle Pou.
national-peoples-congress: The Congress traces its origins to the First National Congress of the Chinese Soviets of Workers', Peasants' and Soldiers' Deputies, held on 7 November 1931 in Ruijin, Jiangxi, on the anniversary of the Russian October Revolution. A second Soviet Congress followed in Fujian on 18 March 1932, and the official Second National Congress met from 22 January to 1 February 1934, when only 693 deputies were elected, 117 of them seats taken by the Chinese Red Army.

At the end of the Second Sino-Japanese War the Chinese Communist Party and the Kuomintang held a Political Consultative Conference, the first Political Consultative Assembly meeting in Chongqing from 10 to 31 January 1946. A second conference in September 1949 approved the Common Program, which served as the de facto constitution for the next five years, and chose the national anthem, flag, capital and state name of the People's Republic. Renamed the People's Political Consultative Conference, it acted as a de facto legislature until the Constitution of 1954 transferred that function to the National People's Congress.

The full Congress meets once a year, usually in the spring, for 10 to 14 days in the Great Hall of the People on the west side of Tiananmen Square in Beijing. Its sessions coincide with those of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, and together they are called the Two Sessions. The deputies, elected by provincial-level people's congresses, which are themselves indirectly elected, serve five-year terms; the work is part-time and unpaid. Before each session a Presidium is elected to run the daily business.

Between sessions the Standing Committee, of roughly 170 members, meets every two months and passes most of China's laws. It cannot amend the constitution or appoint or remove national-level personnel. Ten special committees draft and discuss legislation in specific fields. Under the constitution the Congress elects the president, the vice president, the chairperson of the Central Military Commission, and the heads of the Supreme People's Court, the Supreme People's Procuratorate and the National Supervisory Commission. It alone may amend the constitution, by a two-thirds vote of all deputies. Its organic law requires it to uphold the leadership of the Communist Party, and scholars have often called it a rubber stamp, though laws have occasionally failed to pass there.
national-peoples-power: The National People's Power, in Sinhala the Jathika Jana Balawegaya, was founded in 2019 by members of the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna and over 20 other groups: political parties, trade unions, women's rights groups and youth organisations, including members of ethnic minority communities. It was meant as a coalition of left-wing and progressive parties offering an alternative to the established political parties of Sri Lanka, and it contests elections under the symbol of a compass.

In the parliamentary elections of 2020, won in a landslide by the SLPP, the alliance took only 3 seats and remained a third party; it protested against the 20th Amendment to the Constitution of Sri Lanka when it was announced. Its support grew during the protests of 2022, amid discontent with the political establishment and the economic crisis.

In the presidential election of 2024 Anura Kumara Dissanayake led the first count with 42.31 percent of the vote and was elected after the second count with 55.89 percent. He formed an interim government of three ministers from the alliance, dissolved parliament as he had promised, and called early elections. On 14 November 2024 the alliance won 159 of the 225 seats, with 61.56 percent of the vote. It carried every electoral district except Batticaloa, and in Jaffna District became the first party that was not a Tamil party to win the most seats. A record 21 women were elected to parliament, 19 of them for the alliance.

The alliance is made up of 21 groups, among them the National Bhikkhu Front, the National Trade Union Centre, Doctors for Social Justice, University Teachers for Social Justice, the Progressive Women's Collective and the All Ceylon Estate Workers' Union. It is described as left-wing populist and centred on the working class. It holds both neoliberalism and classical socialism to have failed, and calls for a Sri Lankan economic model on socialist principles, with the state keeping a role in energy, financial markets and national security while limiting its part in profit-driven business.
national-redoubt-switzerland: The idea of a fortified Alpine refuge was older than the war. Fortification of the Swiss Alps began in the 1880s, soon after the Gotthard railway opened, with forts in the style of the Belgian engineer Henri Alexis Brialmont at Airolo and the Oberalp, Furka and Grimsel passes, and works cut into the mountainsides around Saint-Maurice. Interest waned after the First World War, but in the 1930s, as France built the Maginot Line and Czechoslovakia its border fortifications, Switzerland re-examined its defences, helped by the wish for public works during the Great Depression. Design began in 1935 and construction in 1937.

The plan of General Henri Guisan called for delaying actions in the broken border country so that the army could withdraw in good order to the Alps, where the government could hold out for a long time. Sargans needed new works, because the draining of the Rhine wetlands had opened an easy approach. After the fall of France the border zones lost priority on 23 June 1940, and the final plan of 12 July provided for a retreat to the Alps with supplies for indefinite resistance.

The plan was made known at the Rütli Report, a meeting of the army staff and the whole officer corps at the founding site of the Swiss Confederation. The lowlands, with most of the people and industry, were in effect to be given up, and the gold of the Swiss National Bank was moved from Zürich towards the Gotthard and Bern. After the Germans swiftly overran the Balkan countries in April 1941 the whole army was mobilised.

The strategy was one of deterrence, backed by economic concessions to Germany. Germany's invasion plan, Operation Tannenbaum, foresaw the division of Switzerland with Italy. Field Marshal Montgomery judged the redoubt an impractical absurdity, since it could not shield civilians from reprisals.

During the Cold War the redoubt lost priority: from 1953 Swiss policy stressed defence of the borders and cities and extended defence in depth to the whole country. The forts, holding guns, dormitories, kitchens and hospitals for 100 to 600 soldiers, were mostly closed in the 1990s and early 2000s as weapons changed. Several, such as Sasso da Pigna and Faulensee, became museums, and others now serve as data centres, a hotel or stores for cheese and valuables.
national-resistance-army: The army was formed in 1981 by the merger of Yoweri Museveni's Popular Resistance Army with the Uganda Freedom Fighters, the group of the former president Yusuf Lule. Museveni, then leader of the Uganda Patriotic Movement party, alleged electoral fraud after the Uganda Peoples Congress won the bitterly disputed general election of 1980, and declared an armed rebellion. He had gained guerrilla experience with the Mozambican Liberation Front, FRELIMO, in Mozambique, and had formed his own Front for National Salvation, FRONASA, in Tanzania to fight Idi Amin. The army was supported by Muammar Gaddafi.

In the Ugandan Bush War the army fought the government troops of the Uganda National Liberation Army, the UNLA, and defeated them in 1986. When it entered Kampala it had about 16,000 combatants, about a quarter of them Banyarwanda, and its deputy commander was Fred Rwigema. It then became the national army of Uganda.

From 1986 to 1990 Museveni's government tried to end a number of insurgencies and to establish its control over the army. It repeatedly claimed that the National Resistance Army had defeated the UNLA and other rebel groups, but insurgent activity went on, above all in the northern, eastern and western regions. In April 1988, 3,000 former fighters of the Uganda People's Army and of several smaller rebel groups accepted a government amnesty, surrendered and declared their support for Museveni.

In June 1988 Museveni concluded a peace agreement with Lieutenant Colonel John Angelo Okello, commander of the Uganda People's Democratic Army. The National Resistance Army took many fighters of both groups into its ranks, but thousands of others rejected the accord and went on fighting against it. After the Ugandan constitution of 1995 was enacted, the army was renamed the Uganda People's Defence Force.
national-salvation-front-romania: In March 1989 six prominent members of the Romanian Communist Party wrote an open letter to President Nicolae Ceaușescu criticising his abuses of power and his economic policies; it was read on Radio Free Europe. Later in 1989, before the party's 14th Congress, two leaflets signed National Salvation Front circulated, one questioning his management of the economy and his human rights record, the other asking the Congress not to re-elect him. Silviu Brucan said they were written by Alexandru Melian, a Bucharest professor with no link to the Front's leaders; Nicolae Militaru claimed that he and Ion Iliescu led a clandestine Front that asked Melian to write the appeal.

Ion Iliescu announced the creation of the Front in radio and television addresses on 22 December 1989, after Ceaușescu's overthrow, and the Front proclaimed itself the supreme power in Romania. Within four days it formed an interim government with Iliescu as president and Petre Roman as interim prime minister. On 27 December it abolished the one-party system and called for free elections, and on 6 February 1990 it became a political party.

Anti-Front demonstrations organised by the National Peasants' Party and the National Liberal Party in January and February 1990 degenerated into violence, and Iliescu called on the working class to support the Front against what he called fascist forces; these events became known as the first and second Mineriads. A larger demonstration, the Golaniad, began in April 1990 and lasted 52 days, until the third Mineriad violently dispersed it on 13-15 June. In the elections of 20 May 1990 the Front won 66% of the national vote and Iliescu was elected president with 85%.

Tension grew between Iliescu and Roman. After the fourth Mineriad in September 1991 Roman was forced to resign on 1 October 1991. On 7 April 1992 Iliescu and many others left the Front and created the Democratic National Salvation Front, later the Social Democratic Party. Roman kept the Front, which became the Democratic Party.

The Social Democratic Party and the Democratic Party, which later became the Democratic Liberal Party and merged into the National Liberal Party in 2014, both descend from the Front. Traian Băsescu entered politics as a Front member and served as Minister of Transportation in several of its governments.
national-union-portugal: The party was founded in July 1930, during the Ditadura Nacional. Officially it was not a party but an organisation of unity of all the Portuguese, open to all citizens regardless of their political or religious beliefs who adhered to the principles of Salazar's speech of 30 June 1930. It took in the republicans, monarchists and Catholics who supported the dictatorship. Its first leader was the Interior Minister, Colonel Lopes Mateus; Salazar became president, with Albino dos Reis as vice-president. Its ideology was corporatism, drawn from the encyclicals Rerum novarum and Quadragesimo anno and from Mussolini's corporate state.

Its members were mostly local notables: landowners, professionals, businessmen, Catholics, monarchists and conservative republicans. Young people were scarce; at its first congress 68% of the delegates were over 40. The party played no part in government and served to select deputies for the National Assembly and to lend legitimacy to non-competitive elections. Ministers, diplomats and civil servants were never required to join, and the regime's propaganda, youth and labour bodies were not tied to it. The historian António Costa Pinto calls it a moribund party created by decree, and Lawrence S. Graham and Harry M. Makler wrote that it scarcely existed outside election periods.

All other parties were banned. In 1934 Salazar arrested and exiled Francisco Rolão Preto in a purge of the National Syndicalists, most of whom then joined the National Union. The party had no internal activity until 1933 and from 1934 fell into a lethargy that lasted until 1944; in 1938 Salazar admitted its activities had almost been extinguished. It revived after World War II, when the opposition Movement of Democratic Unity was legal from 1945 to 1948, though the system gave it no realistic chance. The party won every seat in the National Assembly from 1934 to 1973.

In 1970, two years after Marcelo Caetano succeeded Salazar, it was renamed Acção Nacional Popular. Under Caetano the regime softened, censorship eased and the state syndicates were allowed to elect their own leaders, but his reforms stalled amid the colonial wars. Lacking any ideology beyond support for the regime, the party disappeared soon after the revolution of 1974 and has never been revived.
national-university-of-cordoba: In 1610 the Society of Jesus founded the Collegium Maximum in Córdoba, attended by students of the order, which was the precursor of the university. Under the administration of the Bishop of Tucumán, Juan Fernando de Trejo y Sanabria, advanced studies began at what became known as the Colegio Maximo de Córdoba, but it could not confer degrees. Pope Gregory XV granted that authority on 8 August 1621, and the document reached the city in April 1622. With that authorisation, and the approval of the Jesuit provincial Pedro de Oñate, the university began its official existence. It was the third oldest university of the Americas, after San Marcos in Peru (1551) and Saint Thomas Aquinas University in Colombia (1580).

The Jesuits controlled the university until King Carlos III expelled them in 1767, after which the Franciscans took over. For its first 150 years it studied only philosophy and theology. At the end of the 18th century law was added, and a conflict between the Franciscans and the secular clergy led to a royal decree renaming it the Royal University of Saint Charles and Our Lady of Monserrat, with secular clergy in charge under Monsignor Gregorio Funes. Funes introduced profound reforms and new subjects. The new regime of the May Revolution of 1810 took control of the university, and he stayed in his post.

The university was nationalised in 1856. Theological studies were eliminated in 1864, and under President Faustino Sarmiento foreign lecturers helped open the School of Exact, Physical, and Natural Sciences, with an Academy of Exact Sciences and an Astronomical Observatory. The School of Medicine opened in 1877, and the Law of Avellaneda of 1885, the first law on universities, set the framework for national universities.

In 1918 the university was the scene of the University Reform. Students inspired by the ideas of autonomy, co-governance and democratisation of education led a movement that spread throughout Latin America and had a lasting impact on higher education. Córdoba has been nicknamed La Docta, the Wise. The College of Monserrat, the original buildings of the university and the Jesuit church form the Jesuit Block, declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 2000.

The university is public and autonomous, with its own budget, administration and regulations, and since the early 20th century it has been the second largest in Argentina. Alumni include the presidents Carlos Menem, Fernando de la Rúa and Héctor Cámpora. In 1952 a campus, the University City, was established in the south of the city.
national-university-of-san-marcos: The university began in the general studies offered in the convent of the Rosario of the Order of Santo Domingo, now the Basilica and Convent of Santo Domingo, on 1 July 1548. The cabildo of Lima sent Fray Tomás de San Martín and Captain Juan Jerónimo de Aliaga to Spain, where they obtained the founding order from Charles I of Spain, who was Charles V of the Holy Roman Empire, and Queen Juana I of Castile. The official foundation is dated 12 May 1551, and the university began to function officially on 2 January 1553. In 1571 it received the pontifical degree from Pope Pius V and became the Royal and Pontifical University of the City of the Kings of Lima.

The university was first governed by clerics of monastic orders, and the Bourbon Reforms of the Age of Enlightenment turned it into a secular institution. Between 1792 and 1811 the amphitheatre and the medicine chairs developed in the Royal Hospital of San Andrés. San Marcos, the College of Law and Letters of San Carlos and the College of Medicine of San Fernando were watched by the viceroy, since professors and students were suspected of subversion.

At the start of the 20th century student activists pressed for reform, and in 1909 students joined protests against Peruvian dictatorial governments. In 1916 the Federation of Students of Peru was founded, led mainly by students from San Marcos, and it demanded updated curricula, the removal of untrained faculty and an end to government interference. The university system was later reorganised and autonomy was granted. Its first coat of arms, approved by Charles I in 1551, showed the Virgen del Rosario; after Pius V's bull of 1570 it gave way to the apostle Saint Mark and the lion.

San Marcos has been in several places. The first was the Dominican convent, the second near San Marcelo, and from 1575 the Plaza del Estanque, where the Congress of Peru now stands. Since 1966 its main campus has been the University City, which holds 17 of its 20 faculties and the archaeological complex of Huaca San Marcos. The Casona de San Marcos, its main cultural centre, is one of the buildings of the historic centre of Lima declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1988. In 2019 its colonial fund and founding documents, 1551 to 1852, entered UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

The Faculty of Medicine San Fernando derives from the Royal College of Medicine and Surgery of San Fernando, created in 1811. Students of San Marcos founded the University Sports Federation of Peru on 7 August 1924. Its graduates and professors have included twenty-one presidents of Peru, and members of the university are called sanmarquinos.
national-womens-monument: The idea of the monument came from Martinus Steyn, former president of the Orange Free State, while he was being treated in Europe after the Boer War. His wife, Rachel Isabella Steyn, known as Tibbie, had relatives and friends who died in the camps and close ties with the British anti-war campaigner Emily Hobhouse. On his return Steyn set up a committee; a school or hospital was rejected as lacking inspiration, and £10,000 was raised from the Afrikaner community between 1907 and 1911.

English-speaking members of the Bloemfontein Town Council delayed the start of building, feeling the memorial would reflect badly on Britain and on the local people who had supported the war. Prime Minister Louis Botha, who was pursuing reconciliation after the war, also disapproved.

The monument, designed by the Pretoria architect Frans Soff, stands about 3 km south of central Bloemfontein. It consists of an obelisk about 35 m high and low semicircular walls on two sides. The bronze group shows a bareheaded woman holding her emaciated, dying child, while a second woman looks into the distance calling on the Lord. It was drawn from a scene Hobhouse witnessed at the Springfontein camp on 15 May 1901. Hobhouse thought little of Van Wouw as a sculptor and felt the child looked asleep rather than dying. About 20,000 people attended the unveiling.

The burial of Steyn at its foot in 1916 began a new kind of commemoration. Christiaan de Wet was buried there in 1922, Hobhouse's ashes were placed there in 1926, and Tibbie Steyn, who had worried that soldiers' graves would dilute the focus on women and children, was herself buried beside her husband in 1955 by D. F. Malan. Since 1960 other memorials of the war have joined it, and the Anglo-Boer War Museum stands on the same grounds. The monument was later overshadowed as a national symbol by the Voortrekker Monument in Pretoria, opened on 16 December 1949. It is a Provincial Heritage Site of the Free State.
national-workshops: The workshops answered a crisis of unemployment in Paris. Agricultural and commercial distress had prevailed throughout 1847, and the political crisis that ended with the abdication of Louis Philippe added an industrial crisis to it. On 25 February 1848 a group of armed workers interrupted a session of the provisional government to demand the organisation of labour and the right to work.
