Under the influence of one of its members, Louis Blanc, the government passed a decree the same day guaranteeing government-funded work: it undertook "to guarantee the existence of the workmen by work" and "to guarantee work for every citizen". Blanc wanted a ministry of labour to carry it out, but his colleagues set it aside and instead appointed a labour commission under his presidency, with powers of inquiry and consultation only.

The decree was put into effect by the minister of public works, Marie, and various public works were begun at once. A workman first obtained a certificate from the landlord of his house or lodgings showing his address in Paris or the department of the Seine, which the police commissary of the district stamped. He took it to the office of the maire of his ward and received in exchange a note of admission to the national works, giving his name, residence and trade, with which a director of works with vacancies could take him on.

The system worked while the unemployed numbered fewer than 6,000. Once that number was passed, the men of each arrondissement went from one open work to the next without finding a place and came back to their mayors' offices tired, hungry and discontented.
nationalism: Scholars frequently place the beginning of nationalism in the late 18th or early 19th century, with the American Declaration of Independence or the French Revolution, though there is ongoing debate about forms of it in the Middle Ages and even antiquity. The French Revolution of 1789 is seen as an important starting point, above all for its impact on Germans, Italians and European intellectuals. The template of mobilising public opinion around a new state based on popular sovereignty went back further, to earlier constitutionalist movements such as the Corsican Republic and the American Revolution.

Primordialism, which arose in the Romantic era, held that there have always been nations, and most scholars have rejected it. Modernist accounts argue that nationalism arises in societies with a self-sustaining industrial economy, a central authority and a shared language. Benedict Anderson tied it to print capitalism and printed media in vernacular languages, and described nations as socially constructed communities imagined by those who belong to them.

Nationalism holds that the nation should be congruent with the state, that it should govern itself free from outside interference, and that it is the only rightful source of political power. It aims to build a single national identity from shared characteristics such as culture, ethnicity, homeland, language, religion or a belief in a shared history.

The most common classification is civic or ethnic, a distinction popularised in the 1950s by Hans Kohn and criticised since the 1980s as too rigid. Civic nationalism defines the nation as an association of people with equal political rights; Ernest Renan in 1882 called the nation a daily referendum. Ethnic nationalism defines it by shared heritage, language, faith and ancestry. Creole nationalism arose among the descendants of colonisers in Latin America after Napoleon seized control of Spain and Portugal, and independence was won in civil wars between 1808 and 1826.

In the 19th century nationalism became one of the most significant political and social forces in history, and it is typically listed among the top causes of the First World War. Napoleon's conquests of the German and Italian states around 1800 to 1806 stimulated demands for national unity. Japan's defeat of Russia in 1905 spurred new interest in nationalism in China, Turkey and Persia, and in China Sun Yat-sen founded the Kuomintang in defiance of the declining empire. Nationalism has been a feature of movements for freedom and justice, and has also been used to legitimise racial, ethnic and religious divisions and to start wars.
nationalist-faction-spanish-civil-war: The name Nationals (nacionales) was coined by Joseph Goebbels after a clandestine Spanish delegation led by Francisco Arranz asked Germany for materiel on 24 July 1936, to give German help to the rebels a cloak of legitimacy. The rebels, whom the Bishop of Salamanca, Enrique Pla y Deniel, had already called Crusaders, took to it at once; their opponents called them fascistas or facciosos. Their support came mainly from the conservative upper class, liberal professionals, religious organisations and landowning farmers, above all in rural areas such as Old Castile, Navarre and most of Galicia.

The Falange Española, founded by José Antonio Primo de Rivera, merged in 1934 with the Juntas de Ofensiva Nacional-Sindicalista of Ramiro Ledesma Ramos, and by September 1936 its 35,000 volunteers made up 55 percent of the faction's civilian forces. The CEDA of José María Gil-Robles gave its electoral funds to General Emilio Mola, the Carlists under Manuel Fal Condé raised the Requetés, at their peak 42,000 strong, and the assassination of the Alfonsist leader José Calvo Sotelo on 13 July 1936 helped legitimise the coup on the right.

In 1937 Franco's Unification Decree merged these movements into the Falange Española Tradicionalista y de las JONS under his own leadership, to the fury of many Falangists and Carlists. He then distanced the party from fascism, and it took up neotraditionalist National Catholicism. The historians Paul Preston and Julián Casanova nonetheless see the faction as a form of Spanish fascism built on the unity of the right and the military rebels.

The Army of Africa, garrisoned in Spanish Morocco under Franco, combined the Spanish Foreign Legion with the Regulares, troops recruited in Spanish Morocco under Spanish officers. More than 13,000 Moroccan troops were airlifted to the mainland on 20 Junkers Ju 52 planes supplied by Hitler between July and October 1936, and an estimated one in five members of the army was killed in the war. About 47% of the Civil Guard joined the rebels.

Fascist Italy had 35,000 men of the Corpo Truppe Volontarie in Spain by January 1937 under General Mario Roatta, and Germany sent the Condor Legion, tanks and aircraft. Portugal under António de Oliveira Salazar supplied ammunition and logistics and signed the Iberian Pact with Franco in 1939, while the Holy See was among the first states to recognise his government, by 1938.
nationalist-liberal-party: The Liberals had been one of Nicaragua's two main parties, with the Conservatives, since the 19th century. When Anastasio Somoza García took power in 1936 the Nationalist Liberal Party aligned itself with the United States and with other caudillos in Latin America, such as Rafael Trujillo, Oswaldo López Arellano and Fulgencio Batista. From 1936 to 1979 every President of Nicaragua was a member. The party at first kept a liberal programme, but it developed into little more than a political vehicle for the kleptocracy of the Somoza family.

Its members included Anastasio Somoza García, Luis Somoza Debayle and Anastasio Somoza Debayle, as well as other presidents of the period, among them Leonardo Argüello Barreto, Víctor Manuel Román y Reyes, René Schick, Lorenzo Guerrero and Francisco Urcuyo.

The party split twice over the Somoza family's wish to keep the presidency. In 1944 dissidents opposed to Somoza García running again for the presidency, among them Manuel Cordero Reyes, Roberto González Dubón, Carlos Morales, Gerónimo Ramírez Brown and Carlos Pasos, founded the Independent Liberal Party. It served for decades as a legal, centrist opposition and briefly sided with the Sandinistas in the overthrow of Somoza Debayle.

In 1968 a group led by the former labour minister Ramiro Sacasa Guerrero left in protest at Anastasio Somoza Debayle's plan to run again and formed the Constitutionalist Liberal Movement, which later became the Constitutionalist Liberal Party. After the FSLN won the first phase of the Nicaraguan Revolution in 1979, the new government banned and dissolved the party, and many Somoza loyalists later supported or joined the Contra rebel groups.
native-hawaiians: Native Hawaiians, or Kānaka Maoli, are the Indigenous Polynesian people of the Hawaiian Islands. Polynesians sailed to the islands in two voyages, one from the Marquesas and the next from Tahiti, known in Hawaiian as Kahiki. The settlers gradually became detached from their homeland and developed a distinct culture and identity, while keeping ties with other Polynesian peoples across the Pacific.

One theory holds that the first settlers from the Marquesas were followed by Tahitians who conquered them, citing the legends of Hawaiʻiloa and of the navigator-priest Paʻao. Early historians such as Abraham Fornander and Martha Beckwith accepted this view, while later historians such as Patrick Kirch do not mention it. King Kalākaua claimed that Paʻao came from Sāmoa. Another view is that a single, extended period of settlement populated the islands.

Native Hawaiian religion grew from Polynesian roots and centres on land (ʻāina) and family (ʻohana). It is polytheistic and focuses mostly on Wākea and Papahānaumoku, the father and mother of the islands, whose second child Hāloa is the god from whom all Hawaiians originate. Hula was traditionally a ritual dance honouring the gods. Each island was divided into moku, given to people of high standing. A moku was split into ahupuaʻa, each running from the sea to the top of the nearest mountain so that it supplied all necessary resources. Managers collected tribute for the island chief. Unlike peasants under European feudalism, Hawaiian peasants were never bound to the land.

The Hawaiian Kingdom was formed in 1795, when Kamehameha the Great conquered Oʻahu, Maui, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi. Kauaʻi and Niʻihau joined in 1810. When Captain Cook arrived in 1778 the population is estimated at between 250,000 and 800,000, its peak. In the first century after contact, diseases such as smallpox, measles and whooping cough, to which Kānaka Maoli had no resistance, nearly wiped them out.

In 1893 Sanford Dole's Committee of Safety overthrew the monarchy of Queen Liliʻuokalani, who had rejected the 1887 Constitution that severely limited her authority. Grover Cleveland challenged the overthrow, but President William McKinley eventually supported it. An 1896 law made English the only medium of instruction in schools. On 23 November 1993 President Bill Clinton signed the Apology Resolution, which apologised for the overthrow. A cultural revival began in the 1970s, helped by the 1978 State Constitutional Convention.
natives-land-act-1913: The Act, No. 27 of 1913 and later renamed the Bantu Land Act and the Black Land Act, was the first major segregation law passed by the Union Parliament. It followed earlier measures in the Cape: the colour-blind franchise of 1853 was narrowed by Cecil Rhodes's Franchise and Ballot Act of 1892, which tripled the wealth required to vote, and the Glen Grey Act of 1894 began the legal separation of races. Economic interests, political influence and racial prejudice all drove the new law.

Its first section declared that outside the scheduled native areas no Black African could buy, hire or acquire land except from another Black African, and that no one else could acquire land from a Black African; exceptions needed the Governor-General's approval and were laid before both houses of Parliament. Other sections set up a commission of at least five members to define the areas and report within two years, allowed the Governor-General to acquire land with funds voted by Parliament, and set fines or imprisonment for breaches.

Land in the reserves was held under communal tenure vested in chiefs and could not be bought, sold or pledged. Outside them the Act forbade sharecropping and labour tenancy by Black farmers on white-owned land. Its full enforcement was not immediate, but it pushed many people living in the white areas into wage labour, while it strengthened the chiefs as part of the state administration.

Protest meetings followed the bill's first reading on 25 February 1913, the first major one held by the South African Native National Congress (SANNC) at the Masonic Hall in Cape Town on 9 May. A deputation asked the Minister J. W. Sauer to drop the bill, and John Dube and Sol Plaatje went to Britain to seek its repeal, without success. John X. Merriman called it a stringent, Draconian and violent law, while John Tengo Jabavu welcomed it.

The Act is remembered as a step towards the institutional discrimination of the apartheid era. It was repealed by the Abolition of Racially Based Land Measures Act of 1991, and the Restitution of Land Act of 1994 allowed claims for lost land. In 2013 the South African government held a centenary ceremony to remember it.
nato: NATO has its roots in the Atlantic Charter, a 1941 agreement between the United States and the United Kingdom. On 4 March 1947 France and the United Kingdom signed the Treaty of Dunkirk, an alliance against a possible attack by Germany, and in March 1948 the Treaty of Brussels extended it to the Benelux countries as the Brussels Treaty Organization, commonly called the Western Union.

Talks on a wider alliance including North America began that month, shaped by the Truman Doctrine of 1947 and the February 1948 coup d'état in Czechoslovakia, and led to the North Atlantic Treaty, signed at Washington on 4 April 1949 by twelve founding members: Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, Iceland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, the United Kingdom and the United States.

The treaty was largely dormant until the Korean War led to an integrated military structure. Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe was formed in 1951, the post of Secretary General was created in 1952, and Greece and Turkey joined that year. West Germany joined in May 1955, a major factor in the creation of the Soviet-dominated Warsaw Pact. Doubts about the credibility of NATO's defence led France to leave the military structure in 1966; it returned to the integrated command in 2009.

NATO conducted no military operations during the Cold War. In the Bosnian War it began enforcing a United Nations no-fly zone on 12 April 1993. After the Srebrenica genocide, a two-week bombing campaign, Operation Deliberate Force, began in August 1995 against the Army of the Republika Srpska, and the Dayton Agreement followed in November 1995. NATO then deployed a peacekeeping force, IFOR, of almost 60,000 troops.

The treaty's central provision is that an armed attack on one member is an attack on all. Under Article 6 the area within which an attack permits that response includes member territory in Europe and North America, Turkey, and the islands of the North Atlantic north of the Tropic of Cancer. The main headquarters are in Brussels. Twelve of the present 32 members joined in 1949; the other twenty joined in ten rounds of enlargement.
natron: The English and German word natron is a French cognate derived through the Spanish natrón from Latin natrium and Greek nitron, which in turn derives from the Ancient Egyptian word nṯrj. It refers to Wadi El Natrun, or the Natron Valley, in Egypt, from which the ancient Egyptians mined natron for use in burial rites. The chemical symbol for sodium, Na, abbreviates the element's Neo-Latin name natrium, derived from natron. Nitrogen is also a cognate, through the Greek nitron. Niter is an obsolete name for natron, because in earlier times the two minerals were confused with each other.

Natron is a mixture of sodium carbonate decahydrate, a kind of soda ash, and around 17% sodium bicarbonate, with small quantities of sodium chloride and sodium sulfate. It is white to colourless when pure and gray or yellow with impurities. In modern mineralogy the term means only the sodium carbonate decahydrate that makes up most of the historical salt.

Natron forms as saline lakes dry up in arid environments. Pure deposits are rare because the decahydrate is stable only over a limited temperature range: it recrystallises at 32 °C to the heptahydrate and above 37 to 38 °C to the monohydrate. The mineral forms only if the brine stays at about 20 °C or below during evaporation, or up to about 30 °C where the lake is very alkaline. Sources include Wadi El Natrun, the shores of Lake Chad, Bilma in Niger, Lake Natron in Tanzania and Kenya, and the Great Hungarian Plain.

In ancient Egypt natron was harvested directly from dry lake beds and used for thousands of years as a cleaning product for home and body. Blended with oil, it was an early soap. Undiluted, it cleaned the teeth and served as a mouthwash. It went into early antiseptics for wounds and was used to dry and preserve fish and meat, to kill household insects, to make leather and to bleach clothing. Added to castor oil, it made a smokeless fuel that let artisans paint inside tombs without staining them with soot.

In mummification natron acted as a drying agent because it absorbs water, and its carbonate raises alkalinity, which creates a hostile environment for bacteria. The Pyramid Texts describe pellets of natron as funerary offerings, drawn from both Lower and Upper Egypt. Natron was an ingredient of Egyptian blue and the flux in Egyptian faience. The Romans and others used it with sand and lime in ceramics and glass until at least 640 CE. Most of its uses were later taken over by soda ash and baking soda.
nau-nihal-singh: Nau Nihal Singh was born on 11 February 1821, the only son of Kharak Singh and his first wife, Chand Kaur, and grew up close to his grandparents, Maharaja Ranjit Singh and Maharani Datar Kaur. In April 1837, at sixteen, he married Nanaki Kaur, daughter of Sham Singh Attariwala, in a wedding of great splendour planned by his grandmother; he later took three more wives.

At thirteen he took part in the Peshawar campaign of 1834 and was given the administration of the Attock region, and Peshawar province was farmed out to him for Rs 12,00,000 a year. He put down a revolt in the Derajat in 1835 and in April 1839 led a Sikh army to Peshawar in support of Colonel Wade's march across the Khyber Pass.

When his father succeeded Ranjit Singh he became crown prince, and with Kharak Singh incapable he returned to Lahore at eighteen to govern in his name under the vizier Dhian Singh Dogra; his reign began with his father's dethronement. Courtiers and the public saw him as a worthy successor. After performing his father's last rites beside the Ravi in Lahore, he was walking back through the Hazuri Bagh when a block of stone from a gate fell on him and two companions, killing Udham Singh, Dhian Singh's nephew, on the spot.

Alexander Gardner, a few steps behind, said the prince could walk after the fall, yet the physician Johann Martin Honigberger found his skull crushed in the tent where he was taken, and of the five men who carried him two died mysteriously and one vanished. Dhian Singh kept the death secret for three days. L. H. Griffin held that this was to await Sher Singh, and Honigberger suspected partisans of Kharak Singh and Chet Singh. Two of his wives reputedly committed sati on his pyre. His mother Chand Kaur claimed the throne, but Sher Singh was crowned on 18 January 1841. His samadhi stands in Lahore near those of his father and grandfather.
naucratis: Naucratis stood on the Canopic, westernmost, branch of the Nile in the western Delta, about 16 kilometres from Sais. It was an Egyptian town before the Greeks came, and later a military settlement occupied by mercenaries. The Canopic branch was one of the main waterways linking the Nile valley with the Mediterranean, and the most accessible in the Saite period. The early settlement grew into a busy trading port in which Greek traders settled and a large Greek community developed.

Herodotus wrote that Amasis, who was partial to the Greeks, gave the city of Naucratis to those who wished to settle in Egypt. Amasis, who defeated the pharaoh Apries in 570 BCE, closed the military camps of Greek mercenaries and moved the soldiers to Memphis. Archaeologists have proposed an earlier date of about 625 BCE for the first settlement on the site. Amasis turned it into a treaty port, probably to keep Greek activity in one place under his control; it was not the colony of any one city but an open emporion, like Al Mina in north Syria.

According to Herodotus, the walled shrine called the Hellenion was a joint undertaking of nine Greek cities: Chios, Klazomenai, Teos and Phocaea from Ionia, Rhodes, Halicarnassus, Knidos and Phaselis from the Dorian cities, and Mytilene from Aeolia. Miletus, Samos and Aegina had sanctuaries of their own. Egyptians mostly supplied grain, linen and papyrus, and the Greeks mostly paid in silver but also in timber, olive oil and wine. The Saite pharaohs drew mercenaries from the Greek settlements in the Delta.

Naucratis was Egypt's most important harbour in antiquity until the rise of Alexandria and the shifting of the Nile led to its decline, though Heracleion, also called Thonis, rivalled it as a port from the 6th to the 4th century BCE. Under the Roman Empire it remained a centre of Greek culture, and it produced several orators of the Second Sophistic in the second and early third centuries CE. The writer Athenaeus came from Naucratis.

Flinders Petrie rediscovered the site and dug there in 1884-1885, followed by Ernest Arthur Gardner in 1899 and David George Hogarth in 1903. They found temple ruins, including the Temples of Hera and Apollo and the Dioscuri, and possibly the Hellenion, and a Greek Temple of Aphrodite. Pottery from the site carries some of the earliest known Greek inscriptions, among them early Ionic writing. American archaeologists began the Naucratis Project in 1977; the northern sanctuary area lay under a lake formed by the risen water table, and farmers digging earth for fertiliser had destroyed much of the eastern site. The British Museum ran a project from 2012 to 2023 that produced an accurate topographic map of the site.
naum-of-ohrid: Information about Naum's early life is scarce. According to the Second Life of Saint Naum he grew up in Moesia, the Byzantine name for Bulgaria. According to the hagiography of Clement of Ohrid by Theophylact of Ohrid and other sources, he took part in the mission to Great Moravia in 863 with Cyril and Methodius, their disciples Gorazd, Clement of Ohrid, Angelar and Sava, and other Slavic missionaries.

For the next 22 years he worked with Cyril and Methodius and the other missionaries, translating the Bible into Old Church Slavonic. In 867 or 868 he was ordained a priest in Rome, with Gorazd and Clement, by the bishops Formosus and Gauderic. The missionaries devised the Glagolitic alphabet, whose descendant, Cyrillic, is still used by many languages. German clergy opposed their Slavic liturgy. By 885 their patrons and Cyril and Methodius themselves had died, and after a brief imprisonment Naum went to Bulgaria with Clement and Angelar.

In 886 the governor of Belgrade, then in Bulgaria, welcomed the disciples. Knyaz Boris, who had converted to Christianity in 864, feared Byzantine influence, since services were conducted in Greek, and saw Old Church Slavonic as a way to preserve Bulgaria's independence. He arranged two literary schools, one in the capital and one at Ohrid. Naum worked in the first from 886 to 893. In 893 the new ruler Simeon the Great called a council at Preslav, where Clement was made bishop of Drembica and Velika, and sent Naum to replace him at Ohrid.

In 905 Naum founded a monastery on the shore of Lake Ohrid, which later took his name. He died there on 23 December 910, and Clement began the process of canonisation, which made him the first native saint of Bulgaria. His cult is strongest around Ohrid and spread in the first half of the 18th century with the rise of Moscopole as a centre of Orthodox culture, reaching Mount Athos and even Vienna. Members of the Bektashi order made pilgrimages to the monastery, believing that their saint Sarı Saltık is buried there. His feast day was changed in 1727 from 23 December to 20 June.
naumburg: Naumburg lies in the south of Saxony-Anhalt at the confluence of the Unstrut and the Saale, near the border with Thuringia, about 60 kilometres south-west of Leipzig. It was founded at the crossing of two trade routes, the Via Regia and the Regensburg Road, and lies in a wine-growing region.

The first written record dates from 1012, when Naumburg is mentioned as the new castle of the Ekkehardinger, the margraves of Meissen. About 1028 the family seat was moved there from Kleinjena, and in 1030 the sources call it a civitas. A privilege of Conrad II in 1033 brought the merchants of Kleinjena to the town with guaranteed free trade. Ekkehard II and Hermann founded a Benedictine monastery of St George and a house of Augustinian canons at St Moritz. When the Ekkehardine line died out by 1046, the bishops became the rulers of the town.

In the Middle Ages it was a major trading centre on the Via Regia, and its trade fairs are first recorded in 1278. Leipzig's rise as a fair town from 1500 and the Thirty Years' War damaged its economy. In 1561 the Naumburg Diet recognised the unaltered Augsburg Confession. The church lands passed to the Dukes of Saxony in the mid-16th century, and in 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave Naumburg to Prussia. Under the German Democratic Republic it was a centre of mechanical engineering and a garrison town of the Soviet Air Force.

Naumburg has about 33,000 inhabitants. Its cathedral, a Romanesque structure with two Gothic choirs, replaced an earlier cathedral consecrated about 1042, and the new building began in 1242. In the west choir twelve life-sized statues of founders, from the workshop of the Naumburg Master, show the Thuringian-Saxon nobility in dress of the mid-13th century, among them Ekkehard II and his wife Uta. The cathedral became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018. The philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche spent his childhood in a house in Naumburg that is now a museum.
naumburg-cathedral: The town of Naumburg began about the turn of the ninth and tenth centuries, probably founded by Margrave Ekkehard I of Meissen, who built a residence on a rock about 25 metres high above the Saale, near the mouth of the Unstrut. His sons Hermann and Ekkehard II founded a small parish church there, first mentioned in 1021. In 1028 they won the approval of King Conrad II and Pope John XIX to move the episcopal see from Zeitz to Naumburg, because the castle offered more protection.
An early Romanesque cathedral was begun in spring 1029 east of the parish church and consecrated in 1044. A crypt added about 1160/70 is the only part of it to survive more or less unaltered.

The present building was begun about 1210 under Bishop Engelhard. The early Gothic west choir, which replaced the old parish church, was probably finished by 1260, and the high Gothic polygonal east choir followed about 1330. It is a double-choir, three-aisled basilica with a pair of towers at each end, so that visitors enter from the sides, and two rood screens divide the choirs from the nave.

The best-known works are by the Naumburg Master, working about the middle of the thirteenth century. The west choir holds twelve life-size donor figures, eight men and four women, thought to represent founders such as Margravine Uta von Ballenstedt with Margrave Ekkehard II, and Margravine Regelinda with Margrave Herman I. Carved in Grillenburg sandstone, they are unusually realistic for early Gothic sculpture, and the placing of lay people so prominently is unique in thirteenth-century Europe. The Master also made the western rood screen, with scenes of the Passion. The Elisabethkapelle holds the oldest known stone sculpture of Saint Elisabeth, probably made soon after her canonisation in 1235.

A fire in 1532 destroyed the roofs, after which the eastern towers were raised. In 1542 the cathedral became the see of Nicolaus von Amsdorf, the first German Protestant bishop. The Catholic diocese was administered by the Electors of Saxony after the death of Julius von Pflug in 1564 and dissolved in 1615. The interior became Baroque in the mid-eighteenth century, and a purification of 1874/8 restored a medieval look. The cathedral remains a Protestant parish church and part of the Romanesque Road tourist route. It was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 1 July 2018.
naumburg-master: The Naumburg Master, Naumburger Meister in German, is a notname: the sculptor's own name is unknown, and the works attributed to the master span a career of more than thirty years. The master very likely learned the craft in northern France at the height of the High Gothic style and was active in Noyon, Amiens and Reims around 1225, later perhaps coming to Metz in the Holy Roman Empire. Around 1230 the master worked on Mainz Cathedral, making its rood screen, now fragmentary, which includes a sandstone relief of Saint Martin known as the Bassenheim Horseman.

From Mainz the master travelled east along the Via Regia to the episcopal see of Naumburg, where the rebuilding of the cathedral had begun around 1210 and a Gothic west choir was added from about 1245-1250. Work there was probably finished by 1257, including twelve monumental donor portraits in Grillenburg sandstone, the works from which the notname comes. Some of the figures are identified by name and others cannot be assigned with certainty. On either side of the choir entrance stand the main benefactors, Margrave Eckard II of Meissen with his consort Uta von Ballenstedt and Margrave Herman I with his wife Regelinda.

By their style the master is also credited with the founder figures of Meissen Cathedral and with the tomb slab of a knight, Hermann von Hagen, a relative of a Naumburg canon, in Merseburg Cathedral. The master's art shaped the work of many masons across Central Germany and carried the new forms of architecture and sculpture of the late Hohenstaufen period into the region. The Naumburg works are counted among the most important artworks of the European Middle Ages.
navajo: The Navajo speak a Southern Athabaskan language of the Na-Dené family, which they call Diné bizaad, the People's language, and it is closely related to the languages of the Apache. The Navajo and Apache are believed to have migrated from north-western Canada and eastern Alaska, where most Athabaskan speakers live. The name Navajo comes from Spanish, from a Tewa word for farm fields adjoining a valley. Before 1600 the Spanish seem to have called them Apaches or Quechos, and by the 1640s they used the term Navajo for the Diné.

The Navajo met the United States Army in 1846 during the Mexican-American War, and on 21 November 1846 Narbona and other leaders made a treaty of peace with Colonel Alexander Doniphan at Bear Springs. Some Navajo and some New Mexicans did not honour it: Navajos raided New Mexican livestock, and New Mexicans took Navajo women, children and livestock. In the spring of 1864 the Army forced around 9,000 Navajo men, women and children to walk more than 300 miles to Fort Sumner for internment at Bosque Redondo, the Long Walk.

The government failed to supply enough water, wood, provisions and livestock for the 4,000 to 5,000 people held there, and crop failure, disease and raids followed. The Navajo call the period the Fearing Time. The first Bureau of Indian Affairs school opened at Fort Defiance in 1870, and children were sent to boarding schools to assimilate them. From 1933 the federal government imposed a livestock reduction that lasted into the 1950s. Many Navajo men volunteered for military service in the Second World War, among them the code talkers.

The Navajo were semi-nomadic from the 16th century through the 20th, with seasonal dwelling areas for livestock, farming and gathering. A system of clans, k'é, defines relations between families; it is exogamous, and clan members may live hundreds of miles apart yet remain bound. Navajo belief centres on restoring balance and harmony, and holds that the Diné passed through three worlds before reaching the Fourth, or Glittering, World.

Weaving and silversmithing are important arts. The Navajo learned to weave cotton on vertical looms from the Pueblo peoples, and Atsidi Sani learned silversmithing around 1878 and taught others. The Navajo Nation, enrolling more than 427,414 citizens, has the largest reservation in the United States, covering more than 27,325 square miles in Arizona, Utah and New Mexico.
naval-blockade: A blockade is the use of military force to prevent food, supplies, weapons or communications, and sometimes people, from entering or leaving a country or region. Unlike sanctions or an embargo, which are legal barriers to trade, it is physical. It differs from a siege in being usually directed at a whole country or region rather than a fortress or city, and its aim is not necessarily to conquer the area. Neutral parties must submit to inspection for contraband, which the blockading power may define narrowly or broadly, sometimes including food and medicine. Patrolling hostile ports to keep naval forces from putting to sea is also called a blockade.

Primitive naval blockades have been used for millennia, but early attempts were limited by how long ships could stay at sea without a break. The first successful full naval blockade was made by the British Royal Navy against France in the Seven Years' War. After the British victory at Quiberon Bay in 1759, Admiral Edward Hawke took command of the fleet off Brest and extended the blockade over the French Atlantic coast from Dunkirk to Bordeaux and to Marseille.

A distant blockade, in which ships stay well away from the coast, was almost impossible before the 16th century because of the nature of the ships. Its strategic importance became clear in the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, and the Union blockade of southern ports was a major factor in the American Civil War.

A close blockade places warships within sight of the coast. It is the most effective form and the hardest to keep up, because the ships stay at sea, exposed to storms and sudden attack. A loose blockade withdraws them beyond the horizon to lure the enemy out; Nelson used one at Cádiz in 1805, and the Franco-Spanish fleet under Villeneuve came out and fought at Trafalgar. Until 1827 blockades were always part of a war; the blockade of the Turkish-occupied Greek coast by France, Russia and Britain, which led to the battle of Navarino, is considered the first pacific blockade.

Blockades often starved civilians, as in Germany during the First World War and Biafra in the Nigerian Civil War. Since 1945 the United Nations Security Council determines their legal status, and modern law treats a blockade used to starve a civilian population as illegal and a war crime. Blockade runners, typically the fastest ships available, carried cargo through such lines.
naval-defence-act-1889: The act was passed under the government of Lord Salisbury and received royal assent on 31 May 1889. Parliament had at first opposed higher naval spending, but expert opinions laid before it in December 1888 and February 1889 were critical of the state of the navy, and the growth of the French and Russian fleets seemed to point to British weakness. Public support for expansion grew and pressed Parliament to act.

The two-power standard was not new: it had been used informally for some seventy years, and Britain had briefly met it in the 1850s. Britain already held naval superiority, and the act's formal adoption of the standard signalled an ambition to raise that lead still further.

The battleships were the centrepiece. Eight first-class ships were ordered, seven of the Royal Sovereign class and a half-sister, HMS Hood, together with two second-class battleships, HMS Centurion and HMS Barfleur. The Royal Sovereign class was larger and faster than any Russian or French battleship. Cruisers of the Edgar, Apollo, Astraea and Pearl classes were to protect British supply lines, and torpedo gunboats to guard the battle fleet.

The First Lord of the Admiralty, Lord George Hamilton, argued that so large a programme would deter other powers and so lower spending later. Because the money was guaranteed over five years, balances could be carried from one year to the next, so that building went on without the halts that an insufficient annual allowance had caused before.

The financing worked: the ships were built with low cost overruns and few delays. As a deterrent the act failed. France and Russia soon matched British building, together beginning 12 battleships, and Britain answered in 1894 with the Spencer Programme at a cost of over £31 million. The act probably contributed to a naval arms race, as Germany and the United States also enlarged their fleets. It was repealed by the Finance Act 1894, in force from 31 July 1894.
naveta-des-tudons: Navetas, of which Menorca and Majorca hold several dozen dwelling and funerary complexes, belong to the pre-Talaiotic age, before the island's Talaiotic culture. The name, a diminutive of nau, a ship, was given by Dr Juan Ramis in his book Celtic antiques on the island of Menorca of 1818, after their likeness to upturned boats. The Naveta d'Es Tudons, named after its site, the woodpigeons, served as a collective ossuary between 1200 and 750 BCE. Radiocarbon dates from bones in Menorca's funerary navetas point to use between about 1130 and 820 BCE, though navetas of this kind are probably older.

The tomb stands about 3 miles from Ciutadella, beside the road to Mahón, on slightly rising ground in a sloping valley. It is 14.5 m long, 6.5 m wide and 4.55 m high, and was once about 6 m high; its front is a trapezoidal façade and its rear a rounded apse. The walls are horizontal corbelled courses of large limestone blocks, dressed with a hammer and laid on a foundation of still larger blocks set on edge.

A low doorway of 0.57 by 0.75 m, rebated for a closing slab, leads through a short passage and an antechamber to the lower chamber, 7.45 m long, roofed with great slabs. Above it lies a narrower upper chamber with a ceiling only 0.85 m high, pierced by holes, probably for ventilation. The disarticulated bones of the dead were stored in the lower chamber once the flesh was gone, while the upper one was probably used to dry fresh corpses.

Navetas were described early in the 19th century but excavated only in the 20th. This one, entered in the Spanish heritage register on 3 June 1931, was excavated and restored by the archaeologist Lluís Pericot García in 1959–1960, when one trepanned skull was found and the missing top courses were put back. Bronze bracelets and buttons of bone and pottery from it are shown in the Museu de Menorca in Mahón. A local tale tells of two giants who competed for a girl, one building the naveta while the other dug a well. Menorcans avoided the navetas until well into the 19th century.
navigation-acts: Some principles of English mercantile law were older than the acts. An act of 1381 under Richard II required that goods be exported or imported only in ships belonging to the king's subjects, and Henry VIII required that a vessel be English-built with a mainly English-born crew.

The immediate cause of the first Navigation Act was the damage to English trade after the Eighty Years' War, when the lifting of Spanish embargoes in 1647 released the full power of the Amsterdam entrepôt. Within a few years Dutch merchants had overwhelmed English trade in the Baltic, with Iberia, the Mediterranean and the Levant, and had taken over much of the trade with the English colonies. In 1650 the Council of State prepared a policy to stop Mediterranean and colonial goods reaching England through Holland and Zeeland.

The Navigation Act of 9 October 1651, passed by the Rump Parliament, banned foreign ships from carrying goods from Asia, Africa or America to England or its colonies. Only ships with an English owner, master and mainly English crew were accepted, and breaking the rules meant forfeiting ship and cargo. The rules were aimed at the Dutch. After the Restoration the act of 1651 was declared void, but the Navigation Act of 1660, regarded as the basis of the system that lasted nearly two centuries, required crews to be 75% English and listed enumerated commodities, among them sugar, tobacco and cotton wool, that colonies could ship only to England or other English colonies.

The Staple Act of 1663 required European goods bound for the colonies to be trans-shipped through England, which raised their cost to the colonists. The Plantation Trade Act of 1696 consolidated earlier laws with stronger enforcement.

The acts were generally obeyed after 1696, except the Molasses Act of 1733, which was widely flouted because no effective enforcement existed until the 1760s. Stricter enforcement under the Sugar Act of 1764 became a source of resentment among colonial merchants, and in 1772 Rhode Island colonists burned the Royal Navy schooner Gaspee. The historian Robert Thomas argued in 1965 that the acts cost the colonies about £4 per £1,000 of income a year, while Ransom held in 1968 that their effect on the shape of the economy was larger.

The acts shielded English shipping from Dutch competition and supported the growth of the Royal Navy. In Ireland they were resented, and the Wool Act of 1699 forbade Irish wool exports. They were repealed in 1849 under the influence of free trade.
naxalites: Naxalism takes its name from Naxalbari in West Bengal, where peasants rose in 1967. Inspired by Maoism, Charu Majumdar wrote the Historic Eight Documents, which became the basis of the movement. In 1967 he, Kanu Sanyal and Jangal Santhal led a faction of the Communist Party of India (Marxist), the Siliguri group, that wanted a protracted people's war like the Chinese Communist Revolution. The party was then part of a coalition government in West Bengal, and its land minister Hare Krishna Konar had said that militant confiscation of land was integral to its programme. The Naxalbari uprising began the first wave of the Naxalite–Maoist insurgency. Historian Sumanta Banerjee called it a watershed in the recent history of India.

The movement rests on the claim that a class conflict divides agricultural workers from landowners, and that the Constitution of India lacks protections for tribal workers. Its supporters hold that the state failed to carry out land ceiling laws and tribal autonomy over natural resources.

The All India Coordination Committee of Communist Revolutionaries was organised in November 1967, and Sanyal announced the Communist Party of India (Marxist–Leninist) at a mass meeting in Calcutta in April 1969. Similar movements arose in Orissa, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala. Students in Calcutta left school to join, and Majumdar declared that revolutionary warfare should take place everywhere, announcing an annihilation line that called for the assassination of individual class enemies such as landlords, businessmen, police officers and politicians.

With government support, Operation Steeplechase killed and imprisoned suspected Naxalites, including senior leaders. Majumdar was arrested in July 1972 and died in police custody. Through repression and failures of unity the movement split into more than 40 small groups, and by 1973 its main leaders were eliminated or arrested. It spread to other states in the late 1970s, and by 1980 an estimated 30 groups with 30,000 members were active. Kondapalli Seetharamaiah founded the People's War group in 1980, and the People's Liberation Guerrilla Army was founded in 2000.
nayanars: The Tamil name Nāyaṉmār literally means hounds. Together with the Alvars, the Vaishnava saints of the same age, the Nayanars shaped the Bhakti movement of early medieval South India. They came from many backgrounds, among them Nadar, Vanniyar, Vellalar, Idayar, Kurumbar and Thevar families, oil-sellers, Brahmins, Vannar and Paraiyars. The first list of their names was made by Sundarar, who in eleven verses of his poem Tiruthonda Thogai sang the saints up to Karaikkal Ammaiyar and called himself the servant of servants. His list followed no order of date or importance and gave no account of the saints' lives.

The dates of Appar and Sambandar rest on Pallava and Pandya inscriptions. Mahendravarman I, son of Simhavishnu, ruled in the early seventh century and appears in inscriptions as Gunabhara; according to the Periya Puranam, Appar converted him to Shaivism. In the 10th century King Raja Raja Chola I gathered the volumes of the Tevaram after hearing hymns from them at his court, and his priest Nambiyandar Nambi arranged the Tirumurai. The hymns of Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar formed its first seven books, and the works of Manikkavacakar, the Tirumandiram of Tirumular and hymns of other poets the next three.

In the eleventh book Nambi added the Tirutontanar Tiruvanthathi, 89 verses with one for each saint; with Sundarar and his parents included, this became the canonical list of 63. In the 12th century Sekkizhar added the Periya Puranam as a twelfth book. The four foremost poets, Appar, Sundarar, Sambandar and the 9th-century Manikkavacakar, are known as the Nalvar, The Four, although Manikkavacakar is not counted among the 63.

With the twelve Alvars, the Nayanars are regarded as the principal Hindu saints of South India. Their lives passed into Kannada literature through the poet Harihara, whose works include the Nambiyannana Ragale and Tiru Nilakanta Devara Ragale; Sundarar is known in Kannada as Nambiyanna. Some groups arrange the saints' images in their temples in orders drawn from Sundarar's poem and the works of Nambi and Sekkizhar. At Tiruchuli the poet-philosopher Valluvar is worshipped as the 64th Nayanar, and since about 1905 he has joined the annual Mylapore procession of the 63.
nayarit: Nayarit is divided into 20 municipalities. It borders Sinaloa to the northwest, Durango to the north, Zacatecas to the northeast and Jalisco to the south, with a long Pacific coastline that includes the Marías and Marietas islands. The western ends of the Sierra Madre Occidental break up its terrain, and it has two volcanoes, Ceboruco and Sangangüey. The Río Grande de Santiago is its largest river and is of major importance for irrigation. Coastal lowlands and river valleys were historically covered with tropical dry forest, and a network of lagoons and mangroves extends along the northern coast.

Radiocarbon dating suggests that the Aztatlán culture settled the western Mexican coast, including parts of Sinaloa, Nayarit and Jalisco, as early as 900 CE, with some evidence for as early as 520 CE. The Huichol and Cora, Uto-Aztecan peoples, lived in the region when Hernán Cortés became the first known European to enter it and claimed it for Spain as part of Nueva Galicia. Under Nuño de Guzmán the Spaniards took the region with considerable brutality, and the people revolted in what was later called the Mixtón War. Spanish rule was also hindered by the terrain of the Sierra del Nayar, and the last independent Cora communities were incorporated by force in 1722. Intense Jesuit missionary efforts followed.

In the colonial period the port of San Blas was one of the most important trade ports on the American Pacific coast, and galleons from Manila arrived there before Acapulco rose. The priest José María Mercado began the struggle for independence in Nayarit, taking Tepic and San Blas before royalists defeated and executed him. The first constitution of the Mexican Republic, in 1824, placed Nayarit in Jalisco. In the second half of the 19th century it was among the most turbulent territories of Mexico, with a population in open revolt and demanding land. It was one of the last territories admitted as a state of the federation, on 1 May 1917.

Nayarit is home to four Indigenous groups: the Wixaritari (Huichol), the Naayeri (Cora), the Odam (Tepehuan) and the Nahuatl-speaking Mexicaneros. The state is predominantly agricultural, producing beans, sugar cane, maize, tobacco, mangoes and other crops, and fishing is also important. The beaches of San Blas and the Riviera Nayarit draw visitors, and the Islas Marías were designated a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2010.
naypyidaw: Naypyidaw lies between the Bago Yoma and Shan Yoma mountain ranges, near the town of Pyinmana, about 320 kilometres north of Yangon. The name is Burmese for abode of the king, generally translated as royal capital, seat of the king or abode of kings. It was traditionally used as a suffix to the names of royal capitals; Mandalay, for example, was called Yadanabon Naypyidaw. Pyinmana is a long-standing settlement and had been a pre-colonial governorship dating to the Pagan kingdom era.

The city was founded on a greenfield site, and construction began in 2002 and was completed by 2012. Military projects were overseen by the Quartermaster General Tin Aung Myint Oo and civilian ones by an army colonel, Thein Nyunt. Three main groups built the city: the military's engineering corps, contractors with family ties to high-ranking military officials, and the military conglomerate Myanma Economic Holdings Limited. One estimate puts the cost at between 3 and 4 billion US dollars, only part of it in cash.

Naypyidaw officially replaced Yangon as the administrative capital on 6 November 2005. On 27 March 2006, Armed Forces Day, more than 12,000 troops marched in the new capital in its first public event, a military parade held on a concrete parade ground with large sculptures of Kings Anawrahta, Bayinnaung and Alaungpaya. The official name was announced during these ceremonies.

Several reasons have been suggested for the move. Naypyidaw is more central than Yangon and a transport hub next to the Shan, Kayah and Kayin states, where a stronger government and military presence was thought to bring stability. The official explanation was that Yangon had become too congested to allow government offices to expand. The historian Michael Aung-Thwin suggests that the move was a return to the Dry Zone, where Burmese royal capitals had traditionally been placed over a millennium.

Naypyidaw is the capital and third-largest city of Myanmar. It is unusual among the country's cities in being an entirely planned city and not part of any state or region. It is the seat of the Assembly of the Union, the Supreme Court and the Presidential Palace, and has separate zones for ministries, residences, the military, diplomats and hotels. It combines a large area with very low population density, and its roads are largely empty. The Uppatasanti Pagoda, completed in 2009, is only 30 centimetres shorter than the Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon.
nazareth: Nazareth lies in Lower Galilee, in a natural bowl that rises from about 320 metres above sea level to the crest of the surrounding hills at about 488 metres. The town is about 25 kilometres from the Sea of Galilee and about 9 kilometres west of Mount Tabor. Finds in the neighbouring Qafzeh Cave show that the area was populated in prehistoric times, and archaeological evidence shows that Nazareth itself was occupied from the late Hellenistic period through the Roman and into the Byzantine period.

According to the Gospel of Luke, Nazareth was the home village of Mary and the site of the Annunciation, and in the Gospel of Matthew Joseph and Mary settled there after the flight to Egypt. Craig S. Keener notes that it is rarely disputed that Jesus came from Nazareth, an obscure small village not worthy of invention. The earliest non-scriptural reference dates from about 221, and the town was Jewish until the 7th century. Bishop Arculf saw two churches there around 670.

Tancred established the city as the capital of the Principality of Galilee during the Crusades, when it became important. It declined under Mamluk rule, and after the Ottoman conquest its Christian residents were expelled, returning once the Druze emir Fakhr ad-Dīn II permitted it. In 1620 he allowed the Franciscans to build a small church at the Grotto of the Annunciation. In the 18th century Daher al-Umar made Nazareth a large town by encouraging immigration, and in the late 19th and early 20th centuries European powers invested in churches, monasteries and schools.

Nazareth is the largest city in the Northern District of Israel, with a population of 75,704 in 2024, mostly Arabs, of whom 69 per cent are Muslim and 31 per cent Christian. It has been a centre of Christian pilgrimage since late antiquity. The Church of the Annunciation contains the Grotto of the Annunciation, where Catholic tradition holds that the angel Gabriel appeared to Mary; Greek Orthodox belief places that event at the Church of St Gabriel. The White Mosque is the oldest mosque in Nazareth.
nazca-lines: The lines were made by removing the reddish-brown, iron-oxide-coated pebbles that cover the desert and exposing the light yellow-grey, lime-rich subsoil beneath. The trenches are 10 to 15 cm deep, and the exposed layer hardens with morning mist into a crust that shields the lines from wind. Wooden stakes found at the ends of some lines support the view that simple tools and surveying equipment were enough, and one stake was carbon-dated to establish the age of the complex. Scholars distinguish two phases, a Paracas phase from 400 to 200 BCE and a Nazca phase from 200 BCE to 500 CE.

The plateau stretches more than 80 km between the towns of Nazca and Palpa, about 400 km south of Lima, and the main concentration of designs lies in a rectangle of 10 by 4 km. The lines total more than 1,300 km in length. Most run straight across the landscape. The largest figures reach about 370 m, and the hummingbird is 93 m long, the condor 134 m and the spider 47 m. Most are made from one continuous line. Other figures include a fish, a heron, a lizard, a dog and a human, as well as trees and flowers. Drones and machine-learning methods have added many geoglyphs in recent years, bringing the known figures to 358 in 2022.

Pedro Cieza de León mentioned the lines in 1553, describing them as trail markers. Toribio Mejía Xesspe saw them in 1927, and Paul Kosok, who flew over them in 1940 while studying irrigation in Peru, is credited with the first in-depth study. With Maria Reiche he proposed that the lines marked where the sun and other bodies rose on significant dates, but Gerald Hawkins and Anthony Aveni concluded in 1990 that the evidence was insufficient.

Johan Reinhard argued in 1985 that the lines were sacred paths linked to the worship of deities who gave water, and David Johnson linked some to the courses of aquifers. Nicola Masini and Giuseppe Orefici connect geoglyphs to the temples of Cahuachi and to pilgrimage. The lines were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994.
nazi-party: The party grew out of small nationalist groups formed in the last years of the First World War, in the culture of the Freikorps paramilitaries that fought communist uprisings in postwar Germany. On 7 March 1918 Anton Drexler, a Munich locksmith, formed a branch of a league called the Free Workers' Committee for a good Peace. He opposed the armistice and the Treaty of Versailles, held antisemitic, anti-monarchist and anti-Marxist views, and called for a union of völkisch nationalism with economic socialism that could draw workers from communism. The renaming of the German Workers' Party added Socialist and Workers' to appeal to the left, and National and German to the right.

Hitler was pardoned and released from prison on 20 December 1924. The ban on the party was lifted and it was formally refounded on 26 February 1925, with Hitler as undisputed leader. It disavowed any intention of taking power by force and followed what he called the path of legality. After Hitler became chancellor on 30 January 1933, the Nazis carried out Gleichschaltung, the coordination of German government and society. In June and July 1933 competing parties were outlawed or dissolved themselves, and the Law Against the Formation of Parties of 14 July 1933 made the Nazi Party's monopoly legal.

Central to Nazism was the idea of a people's community, Volksgemeinschaft, uniting Germans deemed racially desirable and excluding political dissidents and people deemed inferior or foreign. The party sought to disenfranchise, segregate and eventually exterminate Jews, Slavs, Romani, disabled people, homosexuals, Jehovah's Witnesses and political opponents. The Final Solution, a system of genocide, killed around 6 million Jews and millions of other victims in the Holocaust.

The Instrument of Surrender was signed on 8 May 1945, and the Allied Control Council formally abolished the party on 10 October 1945. Denazification followed alongside the Nuremberg trials, where several top leaders were found guilty of crimes against humanity. The use of its symbols remains outlawed in many European countries, including Germany and Austria.
nazism: Historians trace the roots of Nazism to European political culture before 1914. Almost all its essential elements, Martin Broszat points out, were present in the radical protest movements of pre-1914 Germany: a virulent antisemitism, a blood-and-soil ideology, the notion of a master race and the idea of territorial settlement in the East. Its ultranationalism came from pan-Germanism and the Völkisch movement, and the Freikorps paramilitary groups formed after Germany's defeat in the First World War were the source of its cult of violence. The idea of an Aryan race rested on 19th-century racial theories, among them those of Arthur de Gobineau.

Nazism, formally National Socialism, is the ideology of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party. The German Workers' Party, founded in 1919, was renamed the National Socialist German Workers' Party in 1920, partly to use both left-wing and right-wing terms. Most scholars classify the ideology as far-right. It opposed liberal democracy and rejected Marxist class conflict, and advocated dictatorship under the Führerprinzip, the leader principle, set out in Hitler's Mein Kampf.

Its core was a belief in a racial hierarchy with an Aryan master race at the top. The Nazis treated Jews as a mixed race responsible for the exploitation of the Aryans and classed Slavs as subhuman. They sought a homogeneous community of the people, the Volksgemeinschaft, and aimed to unite all Germans and to gain land in Eastern Europe under the doctrine of Lebensraum.

The Nazi Party became the largest party in the German parliament in 1932, without a majority. In January 1933 President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor, with the support of conservative nationalists who believed they could control him. Through the Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act the Nazis built a one-party state. Jews, Romani, political opponents and others were marginalised, imprisoned or murdered, and in the Second World War millions, among them two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population, were killed in the Holocaust.

After Germany's defeat Nazism came to be widely regarded as evil. Only a few fringe racist groups, usually called neo-Nazis, describe themselves as its followers, and the use of Nazi symbols is illegal in many European countries.
ndjamena: N'Djamena lies on the Chari River in the south-west of Chad, near Lake Chad, in a flat and semi-arid landscape with a short wet season from June to September and a long dry season. It is a port at the confluence of the Logone and Chari rivers and forms a transborder agglomeration with Kousséri in Cameroon, on the west bank of both rivers, to which it is linked by a road bridge. The name comes from the Arabic Niǧāmīnā, place of rest, the name of a nearby village.

The French commander Émile Gentil founded Fort-Lamy on 29 May 1900, naming it after Amédée-François Lamy, an army officer killed in the Battle of Kousséri about a month earlier. It was at first a colonial outpost, and until the 1920s it was under French military rule. During the Second World War the French relied on its airport to move troops and supplies, and on 21 January 1942 a lone German Heinkel He 111 bombed the airfield, destroying oil supplies and ten aircraft. The city held its first municipal elections on 18 November 1956, when the European district had four seats on a thirty-three-seat council.

Chad became independent in 1960. On 6 April 1973 President François Tombalbaye renamed the city N'Djamena, as part of his authenticité programme of Africanization. It was partly destroyed in the Chadian Civil War in 1979 and 1980, when almost all of its population fled across the Chari to Kousséri and did not return until 1981–82. Rivalry between Goukouni Oueddei and Hissène Habré led to fighting that divided the city into sectors held by different warlords, until Libyan tanks entered at Goukouni's request. Libyan troops left in 1981, and Habré took the city with little resistance in 1982. In 1990 he was dislodged in a similar way by his former general Idriss Déby.

The city had 9,976 inhabitants in 1937, 18,435 in 1947, 126,483 in 1968 and 529,555 in 1993, and its population passed a million by the early 2010s. Much of the growth came from refugees seeking safety.

N'Djamena is the capital and largest city of Chad and a special status province divided into 10 districts. It is the seat of the National Assembly, the Supreme Court and every national ministry. Meat, fish and cotton processing are its chief industries, and it is a regional market for livestock, salt, dates and grains. The Chad National Museum holds the partial skull of Sahelanthropus, called Toumaï, found in the north of the country.
ndwandwe: The Ndwandwe, also known as the Nxumalo, take their name from one of their early chiefs. Their chieftaincies were part of the Northern Nguni migration and settled during the eighteenth century between the Pongola River and the Black Umfolozi River, where they subjugated and absorbed the surrounding groups. By the later eighteenth century, under their king Yaka, they had become dominant there; the Ngwane, later known as the Swazi, lived to their north, and the Mthethwa, the Zulu and other groups to their south.

Zwide kaLanga, king from about 1805, had several royal settlements, with his main capital on Magudu Mountain south of present-day Pongola. In 1817 or 1818 his armies destroyed the Mthethwa under Dingiswayo at Mbuzi Hill, south of Magudu, which left him the most powerful leader in the region. Shaka, a lieutenant of Dingiswayo, gathered the remnants of the Mthethwa and other neighbouring peoples against him, and in the first encounter of the Zulu Civil War, also called the Zulu-Ndwandwe War, Shaka's forces survived the Battle of Gqokli Hill in 1818.

In 1819 Zwide launched a second expedition against the Zulu. Shaka let the Ndwandwe army into his territory and fought it with guerrilla tactics until a shortage of supplies forced it to turn for home. On the retreat, as it crossed the Mhlatuze River, it was divided and decisively defeated in the Battle of Mhlatuze River. Zulu campaigns of retaliation destroyed every settlement and killed anyone they met, and over the next five years the Ndwandwe nation broke apart.

Accounts of Zwide's end differ. Oral traditions of Ndwandwe descendants in the Pongola Valley hold that Shaka's soldiers killed him soon after the battle on the mountain that now bears his name, and that he was buried in a forest held sacred by the AmaNdwandwe on the southern slopes of Magudu Mountain, where other Ndwandwe leaders also lie. Another version has him flee north with some followers to the upper Komati River and die there in 1825.

Zwide's generals and sons led groups of the Ndwandwe north. One, under Soshangane, founded the Gaza Empire in present-day central Mozambique, and another, under Zwangendaba, settled in present-day Malawi as the waNgoni; others became chiefs of note in present-day Eswatini and Zambia. Most of the Ndwandwe were absorbed into the Zulu Kingdom. Their descendants live today in South Africa, Mozambique, Eswatini and Zimbabwe, and speak Nguni dialects.
ne-win: Ne Win was born Shu Maung into an ethnic Burman family in a small village near Paungdale, about 320 kilometres north of Rangoon. He spent two years at Rangoon University from 1929, studying biology in the hope of becoming a doctor, and was expelled in 1931 after failing an exam. He joined the nationalist Dobama Asiayone as Thakin Shu Maung, alongside Aung San and U Nu. In 1941 he was one of thirty young men chosen for military training by the Japanese operative Colonel Suzuki Keiji, formed the Burma Independence Army under Aung San and took the name Bo Ne Win, Commander Radiant Sun.

Toward the end of the Second World War the Burma National Army turned against the Japanese on 27 March 1945. After independence on 4 January 1948 uprisings broke out in the army and among ethnic minorities, and on 31 January 1949 Ne Win became Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces, replacing the Karen General Smith Dun. At U Nu's request he served as interim prime minister from 28 October 1958 and handed power back to U Nu on 4 April 1960 after elections.

On 2 March 1962 Ne Win seized power in a coup, declaring that parliamentary democracy was not suitable for Burma, and suspended the constitution. After riots at Rangoon University in July 1962 troops fired on protesters and destroyed the student union building. His government founded the Burma Socialist Programme Party, declared the only legal party in 1964, and pursued the Burmese Way to Socialism, which mixed nationalism, Marxism and Buddhism. It nationalised the economy, expelled many foreigners and restricted visits to three days and later one week. Burmanisation policies nationalised ethnic schools and hospitals, and the expulsion of many Chinese and Indians followed, with anti-Chinese riots in 1967.

In 1974 Ne Win proclaimed the Socialist Republic of the Union of Burma. His decrees withdrawing banknotes in 1985 and 1987, the second reportedly on an astrologer's advice that nine was auspicious, wiped out people's savings. Soldiers shot about 100 workers and students in June 1974, and in 1988 students began the 8888 Uprising on 8 August. Ne Win resigned as party chairman on 23 July 1988, warning that if the army shot it would shoot straight to hit.

The uprising ended on 18 September 1988 in a coup by the State Law and Order Restoration Council under Saw Maung; it is widely believed that Ne Win orchestrated it from behind the scenes. For about ten years he kept a low profile but kept some influence, which waned after 1998. He died under house arrest on 5 December 2002 at his lakeside house in Yangon. His death was not announced, and he was given no state funeral; only thirty people attended.
nea-paphos: Nicocles founded the city as a deep-water port to replace the unusable harbour at Palaepaphos, in modern Kouklia, the old centre of the city-kingdom of Paphos. Cyprus came under the Ptolemaic Kingdom between 323 and 272 BCE, a time of complete Hellenization, and Nicocles peopled the new town partly with residents of Marion, forcibly removed by Ptolemy I Soter. Nea Paphos flourished as a Ptolemaic shipbuilding centre and in the 2nd century BCE replaced Salamis as the island's administrative capital. Rome acquired Cyprus in 58 BCE and made it a province in 22 BCE, and the city remained the capital.

In the 4th century CE a series of destructive earthquakes led to the capital moving back to Salamis. Nea Paphos was rebuilt as an Early Christian bishopric and survived into the Byzantine era; the Basilica of Panagia Limeniotissa dates from the early 5th century.

The city was laid out on a rectangular street grid in the Hellenistic manner. Its agora, below the acropolis, took its formal layout in the 2nd century BCE and at one point covered 2.5 hectares, one of the largest Hellenistic agoras of the eastern Mediterranean, with an odeon, a probable asclepeion and metalworking shops. Imported pottery, amphorae and coins show trade with Egypt, the Levant, the Aegean, Asia Minor and the western Mediterranean. The theatre, from the end of the 4th century BCE, stood on Fabrika Hill overlooking the harbour.

The great Roman houses are named after their mosaics: the House of Dionysos, of the 3rd century CE, nearly 2,000 square metres with hunting scenes and myths; the House of Orpheus; the House of Aion, whose five-scene mosaic was found in 1983; and the Villa of Theseus, an elite residence and administrative building begun in the early 3rd century CE.

Excavations began in June 1965 under Kazimierz Michałowski of the Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology and continue with Cypriot and other teams. The site covers much of Kato Pafos in the modern city and is managed as the Paphos Archaeological Park, part of the Paphos World Heritage Site with the Tombs of the Kings and Palaepaphos.
neapolitan-war: After defeat at the Battle of Austerlitz, the Bourbon king Ferdinand IV was forced to cede Naples to the French in early 1806. Joseph Bonaparte ruled it until 1808, when Napoleon made him King of Spain and gave Naples to his brother-in-law Joachim Murat. After the Battle of Leipzig Murat moved away from Napoleon and in January 1814 signed a treaty with Austria. At the Congress of Vienna, however, support grew for restoring Ferdinand, above all from the United Kingdom, which had never recognised Murat and had guarded Ferdinand in Sicily. When Napoleon escaped from Elba, Murat sided with him again.

Murat declared war on 15 March 1815. He claimed 82,000 men, though the real number was nearer 50,000. His two Guard Divisions marched through the Papal States, forcing the Pope to flee to Genoa, while the main army advanced from Ancona. At Rimini on 30 March he issued the Rimini Proclamation calling Italian nationalists to war, but no general rising followed. He beat General Frederick Bianchi near Cesena and on the Panaro, took Bologna on 3 April and besieged Ferrara, while his Guard Divisions occupied Florence.

The turning point came at Occhiobello, where after two days of fighting Murat failed to cross the Po and lost over 2,000 men; the United Kingdom then declared war on him. Driven from his lines at Casaglia on 12 April, he lifted the siege of Ferrara and fell back to Ancona. At Tolentino, from 2 May, he attacked Bianchi but retreated after learning that Adam Albert von Neipperg had beaten Carrascosa at Scapezzano. His army fell apart as the Austrians advanced on Naples.

Murat fled to Corsica disguised as a sailor. On 20 May Generals Guglielmo Pepe and Michele Carrascosa concluded the Treaty of Casalanza, and on 23 May the Austrians entered Naples and restored Ferdinand. Murat landed at Pizzo in Calabria with 28 men on 8 October 1815, was captured and executed five days later. In 1816 Naples and Sicily were united as the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, while Austria formed the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia. Some see the Rimini Proclamation as the start of the Risorgimento, and Austria's intervention marked the Habsburgs as the chief opponent of unification.
near-east: The Near East is a transcontinental region around the Eastern Mediterranean. It takes in the historical Fertile Crescent, that is the Levant and Mesopotamia, together with Anatolia and Egypt, and occasionally the Balkan and Arabian peninsulas. Its limits vary between academic circles. The National Geographic Society treats Near East and Middle East as the same territories, generally accepted as comprising the countries of the Arabian Peninsula, Cyprus, Egypt, Iraq, Iran, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, the Palestinian territories, Syria and Turkey. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations defined the region similarly in 1997 but added Afghanistan.

The term was coined in the nineteenth century by Western geographers and was first applied to the Ottoman Empire. By 1914 that empire had lost all its European territories except Constantinople and Eastern Thrace, and the press called it the sick man of Europe. The position of its minorities and the fate of its former lands became known as the Eastern question. Near East came into use around the middle of the century for the part of the East nearest Europe, at the same time as Far East, and it replaced older names such as the Levant.

Until about 1855 neither term meant a particular region. During the Crimean War the British administration began to give them fixed meanings. A letter by the interpreter Thomas Taylor Meadows, reprinted in 1855, set the Near East beside the Far East as places to be watched. Scholars preferred Nearer East for the biblical lands and the cuneiform texts found there, as in D. G. Hogarth's book The Nearer East of 1902. Middle East entered diplomacy around the same years, in Thomas Edward Gordon's article of 1900 on Persia and Afghanistan.

The ancient Near East is a twentieth-century term meant to give the region a fixed sense for ancient history: the nations, peoples and languages of an enlarged Fertile Crescent, from the Nile Valley through Anatolia to the limits of Mesopotamia. Its languages include Sumerian and Akkadian. The wider term Near East has no single meaning. Governments and agencies define it each in their own way, and many university departments that bear the name teach the modern Middle East.
nearchus: Nearchus was a native of Lato in Crete and the son of Androtimus. His family settled at Amphipolis in Macedonia during the reign of Philip II, when Nearchus was probably a young boy. He was almost certainly older than Alexander, like Ptolemy, Erigyius and the other boyhood friends. With Ptolemy, Erigyius, Laomedon and Harpalus he was one of Alexander's mentors, and Philip exiled him over the Pixodarus affair. The exiles were recalled on Alexander's accession.

Nearchus was appointed satrap of Lycia and Pamphylia in 334/3 BCE, one of Alexander's earliest satrapal appointments. His naval blockade of Persian fleets threatening the Aegean helped Alexander's conquest of Phoenicia, Egypt and Babylonia. In 328 BCE he rejoined Alexander in Bactria with reinforcements, and after the siege of Aornos he led a reconnaissance mission, especially to learn about elephants.

In 326 BCE he was made admiral of the fleet built on the Hydaspes. His trierarchy was a financial responsibility: he put up the money for the boats. At Pattala he prepared to lead 17–20,000 men into the Persian Gulf while Alexander crossed the Gedrosian desert. Monsoon rains delayed the fleet for 24 days near the mouth of the Indus. It then passed Morontobara and the coast of the Fish-Eaters of Makran, and reached Carmania in southern Iran, where it met Alexander. It came to the mouth of the Tigris in 324 BCE.

At the Susa weddings Nearchus married the daughter of Barsine and Mentor. He was to command the fleet for Alexander's planned conquest of Arabia, but the king's death ended the plan. He then supported Heracles, Alexander's son by Barsine, and later joined Antigonus. His last mention is as an adviser to Demetrius in 313/2 BCE.

Nearchus wrote a history of his voyage together with a description of India, the Indike. It is lost, but its contents are known from Strabo and other later authors and from Arrian's Indica of the 2nd century CE. It likely had two parts: one on India's frontiers, population, castes, fauna, flora, cultures and armies, and one on the voyage towards Babylon. According to Arrian, he described how rice, sugarcane and cotton fabrics were grown, made and traded in the Indus Valley. He reputedly was the first Greek commander to visit Bahrain, which the Greeks called Tylos.
nearer-my-god-to-thee: The hymn was first set to music by Sarah Flower Adams's sister, the composer Eliza Flower, for William Johnson Fox's collection Hymns and Anthems. Many later composers made their own settings, among them Stephen Glover, Henry Tucker, Frederic N. Löhr and, jointly, William Sterndale Bennett and Otto Goldschmidt. In 1955 the English composer Sir Jack Westrup wrote an anthem setting for four soloists with organ.

Two tunes dominate. In the United Kingdom the hymn is usually sung to Horbury, written in 1861 by John Bacchus Dykes and named after a village near Wakefield where Dykes had found peace and comfort. In the rest of the world it is usually sung to Bethany, written in 1856 by Lowell Mason. British Methodists prefer Propior Deo, written by Arthur Sullivan in 1872.

The hymn has five verses, each ending with the refrain 'nearer, my God, to Thee'. The first accepts that the way upward may be a cross. The second recalls the wanderer after sunset, whose rest is a stone, and the verses that follow turn the way into steps to heaven, with angels beckoning, and the stony griefs into a Bethel to be raised. The last of the five imagines flight beyond sun, moon and stars. A sixth verse, set in the Father's home and the Saviour's love, was later added by Edward Henry Bickersteth Jr.

The hymn is associated with the sinking of RMS Titanic in 1912, because some survivors reported that the ship's string ensemble played it. Violet Jessop said in her 1934 account that she had heard it, but Archibald Gracie IV emphatically denied this, and the wireless operator Harold Bride said he heard a piece called Autumn, perhaps Archibald Joyce's waltz Songe d'Automne. The band's leader, Wallace Hartley, a British Methodist, liked the hymn and had wished to have it performed at his funeral. The hymn was also sung by the crew and passengers of the SS Valencia as it sank off the Canadian coast in 1906, which may be the source of the Titanic legend.

Tradition holds that the first lines were the dying words of President William McKinley in September 1901, and bands across the United States played the hymn, his favourite, in his memory on 14 September 1901. It was played at the burial of President James Garfield and at the funerals of Warren G. Harding and Gerald Ford. Carl Nielsen paraphrased the tune for wind band, Sigfrid Karg-Elert wrote six works on Bethany after the Titanic disaster, and Charles Ives quoted it in his Symphony No. 4.
nebiryraw-i: Nebiryraw I bore the throne name Sewadjenre, and his personal name is also rendered Nebiriau or Nebiryerawet. He belonged to the line of kings based at Thebes in the Second Intermediate Period. The Juridical Stela, the chief document of his reign, preserves both his names and gives his Year 1, the highest regnal year known for him. It also names an earlier king, Merhotepre, who may be Merhotepre Sobekhotep, and writes the king's own name as Neb-iri-er-au.

Other objects carry his name. A copper dagger with his throne name came from a cemetery at Hu, where Flinders Petrie found it in the late 1890s, and a small stela in the Egyptian collection at Bonn shows him with the goddess Maat. All his seals were made of clay or frit rather than the usual steatite, which suggests that no mining expeditions went to the Eastern Desert in his time. Two of them were found at Lisht, then part of the Hyksos realm; they may point to diplomatic contact between the Theban kings and the Hyksos, though this is uncertain.

Later king lists kept his name. The Karnak King List of the 18th Dynasty places Sewadjenre between Sankhibra and a king whose name ends in -khaure. The Turin King List of the 19th Dynasty calls him Nebiriawra, a variant of the form on the Juridical Stela, credits him with a reign of 26 years and names as his successor Nebiryraw II, who may have been his son. The archaeological finds are hardly enough to support so long a reign.

His throne name, with the epithets good god and deceased, also appears on the base of a bronze statuette of the god Harpocrates now in Cairo. It stands beside other royal names, among them Ahmose and Binpu, apparently princes of the 17th Dynasty, and a good god Neferkare, generally taken to be Nebiryraw II.
