The statuette is not contemporary: the cult of Harpocrates was introduced in the Ptolemaic period, about 1500 years after the people it names had lived.
nebuchadnezzar-i: Nebuchadnezzar I, in Babylonian Nabû-kudurrī-uṣur, meaning "Nabû, protect my eldest son" or "Nabû, protect the border", was the fourth king of the Second Dynasty of Isin. He ruled for 22 years according to the Babylonian King List C and was the most prominent monarch of the dynasty. He succeeded his father, Ninurta-nādin-šumi, and was followed in turn by his son Enlil-nādin-apli, his brother Marduk-nādin-aḫḫē and then his nephew Marduk-šāpik-zēri. He is unrelated to the later Nabû-kudurrī-uṣur II, known by the Hebrew form of the name, and does not appear in the Bible. Applying the name Nebuchadnezzar to the earlier king is therefore anachronistic but not inappropriate.

The length of his war with Elam and the number of his campaigns are not known. A later literary tradition says an invasion was thwarted when plague struck his army. A kudurru of his reign records a successful raid, made with the Kassite chieftain Šitti-Marduk and launched from Dēr in the hottest summer month, in which he routed the Elamite king Ḫulteludiš-Inšušinak on the banks of the river Ulaya. No source records a sack of Susa, but another kudurru says he retrieved the statue of Marduk, called Bēl, and that of the goddess Il-āliya. The victory was marked in hymns and poetry, including a poem on the recovery of Marduk's statue.

The Synchronistic History relates an agreement with the Assyrian king Aššur-rēša-iši I and two campaigns against the border fortresses of Zanqi and Idi, undertaken in breach of it. The first ended when Aššur-rēša-iši's main force arrived and Nebuchadnezzar burned his siege engines and fled; in the second the Assyrians apparently won and captured the Babylonian field marshal Karaštu. A kudurru also calls him conqueror of the Amorite lands.

Building inscriptions record his work on the temple of Adad in Babylon, and bricks from the temple of Enlil at Nippur carry his name. Only three economic texts, three kudurrus and a stone memorial tablet survive as contemporary records; one kudurru records a land grant at Nippur. Several literary texts are thought to come from his age, in Sumerian and Akkadian, and the sage Šaggil-kīnam-ubbib is said to have served under him.

Lambert has suggested that Marduk was raised to the head of the pantheon in his reign and that the Enûma Eliš was possibly composed then, though some historians claim an origin in the earlier Kassite dynasty. It has also been suggested that the return of Marduk's statue was a literary tradition of the first millennium BCE rather than a historical record.
nebuchadnezzar-ii: His Akkadian name was Nabû-kudurri-uṣur, meaning Nabu, watch over my heir. He was the eldest son of Nabopolassar, who ruled from 626 to 605 BCE and founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire in a rebellion against Assyria. Nabopolassar's inscriptions call him his eldest son, and his own inscriptions call him Nabopolassar's true or legitimate heir. He appears to have taken part in the campaign against Harran in 610 BCE, and the Babylonian Chronicles record that he commanded an army in a mountainous region in 607 BCE. Nabopolassar died a few weeks after the victory at Carchemish, and Nebuchadnezzar, who was still in Syria, hurried back and was proclaimed king in Babylon in mid-August.

His early reign saw few achievements and a failed invasion of Egypt, which led some vassals to doubt Babylon's power. In 604 BCE he took the city of Ascalon, whose king was carried off to Babylon and which was plundered and levelled; excavations confirm its destruction. King Zedekiah of Judah later revolted. In 587 BCE Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem and destroyed it and the Kingdom of Judah, deporting much of its population in what became known as the Babylonian captivity. No cuneiform sources survive for this episode, and the only known account of Judah's fall is the biblical one.
Tyre had also rebelled, and the Book of Ezekiel describes it in 571 BCE as recently captured. A stele from Tahpanhes records an attempted invasion of Egypt in 582 BCE, which Pharaoh Apries repelled.

Nebuchadnezzar greatly expanded and rebuilt Babylon, a task made possible by an economy sustained by his conquests. His inscriptions record work on many temples, including the restoration of the Esagila, the temple of Marduk, and the completion of the Etemenanki ziggurat. He restored the South Palace, built a new North Palace outside the walls facing the Ishtar Gate, rebuilt the Processional Street and the gate itself, and built a Summer Palace north of the inner city walls.

He died at Babylon in 562 BCE after 43 years on the throne, the longest reign of his dynasty, and the Babylonians remembered him favourably. His son Amel-Marduk succeeded him, though their relationship may have been poor. Because only one of his fifty or so known inscriptions deals with military action, historians such as Wolfram von Soden long saw him chiefly as a builder. The publication of the Babylonian Chronicle by Donald Wiseman in 1956 shifted attention to his wars. The Book of Jeremiah calls him a lion and a destroyer of nations. According to tradition he built the Hanging Gardens of Babylon for his wife Amytis, but no archaeological evidence for them has been found.
neches-river: The Neches rises in Van Zandt County west of Rhine Lake and runs for 416 miles (669 km) to its mouth on Sabine Lake near the Rainbow Bridge, forming the boundaries of 14 counties on the way. Two large reservoirs lie on it, Lake Palestine and the B. A. Steinhagen Reservoir. The Angelina River, which holds the Sam Rayburn Reservoir, joins it at the north end of Lake B. A. Steinhagen, and Village Creek and Pine Island Bayou, which drain much of the Big Thicket, join a few miles north of Beaumont. Tyler, Lufkin and Silsbee stand along its course.

The name is believed to come from the Caddo word Nachawi, wood of the bow, which Spanish settlers took up as Río Neches. The Sabine-Neches Navigation District, formed in 1909, manages the part of the river that belongs to the Sabine-Neches Waterway. From 2006 the United States Fish and Wildlife Service bought land along the upper river for the Neches River National Wildlife Refuge, including land where the city of Dallas had proposed a reservoir, Lake Fastrill. Dallas and the Texas Water Development Board sued in 2007, but in February 2010 the case was decided in the service's favour, and the refuge opened to the public in 2019.

Apart from its dams and lakes, much of the river is in a natural state. It forms the eastern border of Davy Crockett National Forest and much of the southern border of Angelina National Forest, and from Town Bluff Dam a 56-mile corridor down to Beaumont belongs to the Big Thicket National Preserve, which UNESCO recognises as a biosphere reserve. The lower forty miles, from the Interstate 10 bridge at Beaumont to Sabine Lake, are a deep-water ship channel lined with petrochemical plants, serving the Port of Beaumont and towns including Port Neches, Nederland and Port Arthur.
necho-i: Menkheperre Necho I, called Nekau in Egyptian and Nikuu in Akkadian, became ruler of Sais in 672 BCE and took the pharaonic titulary. A year later the Assyrians under Esarhaddon invaded Egypt, and Necho became one of his vassals. Esarhaddon confirmed his office and possessions and gave him new territories, possibly including Memphis. He is the first securely attested local Saite king of the 26th Dynasty, and according to Manetho he reigned for eight years, from 672 to 664 BCE.

In 669 BCE King Taharqa of the 25th Dynasty advanced from the south against the Delta principalities that were formally under Assyrian control. Esarhaddon died suddenly while preparing to return, and the counter-offensive was carried out by his son Ashurbanipal in 667 to 666 BCE. Taharqa was driven back to Thebes, but Ashurbanipal found that he and some rulers of Lower Egypt, among them Necho, were plotting against him. He captured them, killed part of the population of their cities and deported the prisoners to Nineveh.

Unexpectedly, Ashurbanipal pardoned Necho and restored him at Sais with his former possessions and many new territories, and made his son Psamtik mayor of Athribis. It has been suggested that he hoped to gain an Egyptian ally against a new offensive by the 25th Dynasty. According to historical records Necho was killed in 664 BCE near Memphis while defending his realm against a Kushite offensive led by Taharqa's successor Tantamani, and Psamtik fled to Nineveh. The Assyrians repelled the invasion and sacked Thebes. Psamtik I then received his father's offices and in time reunited Egypt under his sole rule.

Necho is known chiefly from Assyrian documents. Egyptian objects include a glazed pottery statuette of Horus with his cartouches and a dedication to Neith of Sais in the Petrie Museum, and a donation stela dated to his second year. Kim Ryholt, studying a papyrus from Tebtunis, concluded that he was a son of a king named Tefnakht, presumably Tefnakht II. Christian Settipani believes he married Istemabet, mother of Psamtik I.
necho-ii: Necho II, sometimes written Nekau, was the son of Psammetichus I and his Great Royal Wife Mehtenweskhet. His royal name, Wahem-Ib-Re, means carrying out the heart, that is the wish, of Re. When he came to the throne the Cimmerians and Scythians had ravaged Asia west of the Euphrates and helped the Babylonians shatter the Assyrian Empire, which was reduced to a remnant at Harran under a general who took the throne name Ashur-uballit II. Necho sent a force to help it on his coronation, but it was too small and the combined armies retreated west across the Euphrates.

In the spring of 609 BCE Necho led a large army, mainly mercenaries, along the coast route into Syria with his fleet beside it. At Megiddo, according to 2 Kings 23, he engaged the Judean king Josiah, who was killed. Necho took Kadesh on the Orontes and, with Ashur-uballit, crossed the Euphrates and besieged Harran, becoming the first pharaoh to cross it since Thutmose III, but failed to take it. He then deposed Josiah's chosen successor, Jehoahaz, and made Jehoiakim king, taking Jehoahaz to Egypt as a prisoner.

Nebuchadnezzar II defeated the Egyptians at Carchemish in 605 BCE and conquered Egyptian territory from the Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt. Necho could not recover it, and he turned to alliances with the Carians and the Greeks.

He began a canal from the Pelusiac branch of the Nile to the Red Sea, the earliest precursor of the Suez Canal, but never finished it, and he founded the city Per-Temu Tjeku at Tell el-Maskhuta. He formed an Egyptian navy by recruiting displaced Ionian Greeks. According to Herodotus, he sent Phoenicians who in three years sailed from the Red Sea round Africa and back to Egypt; scholars differ on whether the account is credible.

Necho died in 595 BCE and was succeeded by his son Psamtik II, who apparently removed Necho's name from almost all his father's monuments for unknown reasons, though Roberto Gozzoli doubts this, calling the evidence fragmentary and contradictory. Egyptologist Donald B. Redford observed that Necho was a man of action from the start, with an imagination beyond that of his contemporaries, who had the misfortune to foster the impression of being a failure.
nechtan-mac-der-ilei: Nechtan, also called Naiton son of Dargart, succeeded his brother Bridei IV in 706. It has been argued that he is the Nechtan son of Dargart named in the Annals of Ulster in 710, whose father would be Dargart mac Finguine of the Cenél Comgaill kindred of Dál Riata, who died in 686; on that basis, and because Bede notes that the Picts allowed matrilineal succession in exceptional cases, Der-Ilei is thought to have been his mother. His kin may have included Ciniod, killed in 713, and Talorcan son of Drestan, king of Atholl, whom Nechtan held captive in the same year.

Around 710 Abbot Ceolfrid of Monkwearmouth and Jarrow wrote to Nechtan on the dating of Easter, in a letter preserved in Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People. It treats its reader as an educated man, which led the historian Thomas Owen Clancy to call Nechtan a philosopher king. Ceolfrid also sent masons and craftsmen to help build stone churches, and Bede's claim that Nechtan dedicated his kingdom to Saint Peter has linked him with the Peterkirks at Rosemarkie, Duffus and Restenneth. In 711 the Annals of Ulster report a Pictish defeat at Northumbrian hands in Mag Manonn.

In 724, according to the Annals of Tigernach, Nechtan entered a monastery and left the throne to Drest, probably his half-brother's son. Drest had him imprisoned in 726, perhaps by moving him to a monastery controlled by his own partisans. By 728 Nechtan had returned to the struggle against Drest and Alpín, and after Óengus son of Fergus defeated Alpín a second time Nechtan was restored to the kingship; Óengus's army then beat Nechtan's enemies at Monith Carno, perhaps Cairn o' Mount.

Nechtan died in 732. It has been suggested that the St Andrews Sarcophagus was made for his remains, though it is more generally thought to have been made for Óengus himself. His reforms are seen as having brought Pictland closer to Northumbria, with notable results in art, and his expulsion of the Iona clergy as marking the coming of age of an independent Pictish church that nonetheless remained close to Iona and to Ireland.
neckar: The Neckar is a major right tributary of the Rhine, 362 kilometres long, flowing mainly through Baden-Württemberg with a short section through Hesse. It rises in the Schwenninger Moos conservation area near Schwenningen at 706 metres above sea level and reaches the Rhine at Mannheim, at 95 metres. Its largest tributaries are the Enz, the Kocher and the Jagst. Between Stuttgart and Lauffen it cuts a meandering, often steep-sided valley into Triassic limestones. The Romans knew it as Nicarus, Nicer or Nicerus, from an Indo-European root meaning to rise.

The primal Neckar began as a small escarpment river as the Black Forest slowly rose. At Horb the rift structure of the Swabian Lineament turned it to the north-east. Wide valley meadows built up through the backfilling of clay since settlement began in the Neolithic, with its deforestation and soil erosion.

Harbour installations and finds suggest that the river was navigated in the first century of the Roman period, chiefly on the lower Neckar, probably to carry building material for the Limes and provisions. The Franks probably revived navigation later. From about 1100 line boats and rafts are attested on the river, and weirs blocked it near several cities in the High Middle Ages. Heilbronn had a harbour in 1146, and in 1333 Emperor Louis IV granted the free imperial city a privilege to build a weir, which obstructed traffic for centuries. Agreements in 1342 and 1476 secured the passage of rafts, and the last raft went through Tübingen on 26 October 1899.

Because of flood risk the valley plains stayed unsettled for a long time, though their fertile soil was farmed intensively, and the steep valley sides became vineyards. Paths mostly kept to the heights and crossed the valleys only at fords. Mills used the river's power, and in the early 20th century power stations replaced them.

Since 1968 the Neckar has been navigable for cargo ships through 27 locks over about 200 kilometres, from Mannheim upstream to the port of Plochingen. Along the lower river a Castle Road passes many castles, among them Heidelberg Castle and Hornberg Castle, the home of Götz von Berlichingen. The Innere Brücke in Esslingen, with eleven stone arches, was built in the 13th century and is the oldest Neckar bridge still standing. Mark Twain, in A Tramp Abroad, wrote of voyaging down the river on a raft, and Friedrich Hölderlin wrote a poem entitled Der Neckar.
nectanebo-i: Nectanebo's Egyptian personal name was Nakhtnebef, meaning the strong one of his lord. Greek sources rendered it Nectanebis. He was an army general from Sebennytos, the son of an important military officer named Djedhor and of a lady whose name is only partly recorded. A stele found at Hermopolis provides some evidence that he came to power by overthrowing, and possibly killing, Nepherites II, the last pharaoh of the 29th Dynasty. It has been suggested that the Athenian general Chabrias helped him in the coup. He held his coronation at Sais and Memphis and moved the capital from Mendes to Sebennytos. He called Nepherites II inept and Achoris a usurper, but seems to have thought better of Nepherites I.

Nectanebo was a great builder and restorer, to an extent not seen in Egypt for centuries. On the island of Philae he began the temple of Isis by erecting its vestibule, and at Karnak he began the First Pylon in the precinct of Amun-Re. The earliest known mammisi, at Dendera, is believed to be his. He supported the cult of sacred animals, as archaeological finds at Hermopolis, Saft el-Hinna and Mendes show, and he was generous to the priesthood. A decree of his first year, found at Naucratis, assigned 10 per cent of the taxes on imports and local production there to the temple of Neith at Sais.

The Achaemenid king Artaxerxes II, who still counted Egypt a rebel satrapy, prepared for six years and sent a great army under the Athenian general Iphicrates and the Persian Pharnabazus. Nectanebo fortified the Pelusiac branch of the Nile, which forced the enemy fleet up the less defended Mendesian branch. Mutual distrust between Iphicrates and Pharnabazus kept them from reaching Memphis, and the annual Nile flood and the resolve of the defenders turned apparent defeat into complete victory. From 368 BCE many western satrapies rebelled against Artaxerxes, and Nectanebo gave financial support to the rebels and renewed ties with Sparta and Athens.

Nectanebo died in the 19th year of his rule. His tomb, sarcophagus and mummy have never been found. Late in his reign, probably to remedy the dynastic problems of his predecessors, he restored the old practice of co-regency and associated his son Teos with the throne. Soon after Teos came to power, however, his brother Tjahapimu betrayed him and put his own son Nakhthorheb, Nectanebo II, on the throne. Nectanebo I had founded the last native dynasty of Egypt, and his building programme gave later temples at Philae and Karnak their beginnings.
nectanebo-ii: Nectanebo II was the third and last pharaoh of the Thirtieth Dynasty. Persia had conquered Egypt in 525 BCE, and Egypt regained independence in 404 BCE. Persian attempts to reclaim it failed in 385, 383 and 373 BCE. In 360 BCE his uncle Teos set out on a campaign, and Nectanebo accompanied him and commanded the machimoi, the native warrior class. To raise money Teos taxed the Egyptians and seized temple property, which the priests resented, and they supported Nectanebo. Teos fled to the Persian court, where he died of natural causes.
A pretender from Mendes, probably a descendant of Nepherites I, then proclaimed himself pharaoh. The Spartan Agesilaus stayed loyal to Nectanebo, and the revolt was put down in the autumn of 360 BCE.

He began his reign by officiating at the funeral of an Apis bull at Memphis. His name appears at more than a hundred sites. He built a temple of Khnum at Abu and a temple of Amun at Sekhtam, and built most extensively at Sebennytos. Because he was a usurper, his religious building may have been meant partly to legitimise his rule. The reliefs of Sebennytos left a mark on the art of the Ptolemaic Kingdom.

Nectanebo used the years of peace to build a new army with Greek mercenaries. About 351 BCE the Persians tried again, and after a year of fighting he and his Greek generals Diophantus of Athens and Lamius of Sparta defeated them. His people acclaimed him as the divine falcon. In 345 or 344 BCE he sent 4,000 Greek mercenaries under Mentor of Rhodes to help a Phoenician revolt, but Mentor came to terms with the Persians.

In the winter of 343 BCE Artaxerxes III marched against Egypt with a force strengthened by Mentor, who knew the eastern frontier well. Nectanebo, who had flat-bottomed boats and fortified camps, lost, and Artaxerxes entered Memphis and installed a satrap. Nectanebo fled to Upper Egypt and then to Nubia, where its king Akhraten granted him asylum. His later fate is unknown.

A sarcophagus covered in hieroglyphs, taken to the British Museum after Napoleon's forces surrendered at Alexandria in 1801, bears his cartouche. It was once thought to be Alexander the Great's, and some argue that it later held his remains. Later legend in the Alexander Romance made Nectanebo the father of Alexander, who came to Olympias in the guise of Amun.
neferhotep-i: Neferhotep I seems to have come from a non-royal family of Thebes with a military background. His grandfather Nehy held the title officer of a town regiment, and his father Haankhef always appears as God's father and royal sealer, with his mother Kemi as king's mother. The Turin canon names Haankhef as his father, which is extremely rare, since it normally lists only pharaohs.

Neferhotep, his predecessor Sobekhotep III and his successor Sobekhotep IV proclaimed their non-royal origins on stelae and scarab seals, although Egyptian kingship normally rested on descent. Egyptologists such as Kim Ryholt and Darrell Baker believe he usurped the throne, and his relation to Sobekhotep III is unclear.

The Turin king list credits him with a reign of 11 years and 1 to 4 months. He is known from over 60 scarab seals, a statue from Elephantine and rock inscriptions at Sehel Island and Philae, with finds from Byblos to the fortresses of Buhen and Mirgissa in Lower Nubia. His most important monument is a heavily eroded stela of his second regnal year from Abydos, which tells how he ordered an image of Osiris made of silver, gold and copper for the god's yearly festival, after consulting the primeval writings of Atum in a temple library. A second Abydos stela, usurped from King Wegaf, forbids the building of tombs on the processional way of Wepwawet.

Scholars disagree over how much of Egypt he ruled. Ryholt holds that the Canaanite 14th Dynasty already controlled the eastern Nile Delta, while Manfred Bietak and others contend that he reigned over the whole country. A stela showing Yantinu, Governor of Byblos, before Neferhotep's cartouches helps link Egyptian and Near Eastern chronology, since a King of Byblos named Yantin-'Ammu is known from the archives of Mari in the time of Zimri-Lim and Hammurabi.

Near the end of his reign he shared the throne for a few months with his brother Sihathor, who died shortly before him. He probably then named another brother, Sobekhotep IV, as coregent, and Sobekhotep IV succeeded him. The circumstances of his death are unknown. The reigns of the two brothers mark the apex of the 13th Dynasty.

His tomb has not been formally identified. Josef W. Wegner, excavating a royal necropolis at Abydos since 2013, has suggested that tomb S9 could be his, beside S10, which is thought to belong to Sobekhotep IV.
neferhotep-iii: His full name was Sekhemre Sankhtawy Neferhotep III Iykhernofret. The Egyptologists Kim Ryholt and Darrell Baker place him third or fourth among the Theban kings of the dynasty, after Sobekhotep VIII. On his stela he repeatedly calls Thebes "my city" and praises himself as "the guide of victorious Thebes", which Ryholt reads as a sign that he ruled the Theban region alone. Baker notes that, apart from Bebiankh and Nebiryraw I, the dynasty's kings are attested only along some 200 km of the Nile valley from Hu to Edfu.

The stela presents him as one who nourishes his city, saving it from famine, and his throne name, the might of Ra who nourishes the Two Lands, points the same way: Upper Egypt appears to have suffered famines late in the dynasty, and another king of the period, Senusret IV, took a similar name. He also fought a defensive war against the Hyksos 15th Dynasty, which in the end overran the Theban state, and he calls himself the one who raised his city after it had sunk through strife with foreigners. After a short reign he was followed by another short-lived king, Seankhenre Mentuhotepi, whose own stela says "I am the king within Thebes, this is my city".

He is known chiefly from a single, heavily damaged stela from Thebes, now Cairo JE 59635 (CG 20799). It is thought to hold the earliest known mention of the Khepresh crown, for it calls him "adorned with the Khepresh, the living image of Re, lord of terror", and for reasons that remain unclear it writes his epithet Iykhernofret inside a cartouche. The Turin King List, at 11:3, names a Dual King Sekhemra S... with a reign of 1 year, usually identified with him, between kings of 16 years and of 1 year. In an older study Jürgen von Beckerath dated him instead to the end of the 13th Dynasty.
neferkauhor: Neferkauhor Khuwihapi was the sixteenth and penultimate king of the Eighth Dynasty, which would have ruled the Memphite region during the early First Intermediate Period, when Egypt was possibly divided between several polities. He reigned for little over two years and is one of the best attested kings of the period, with eight of his decrees surviving in fragmentary condition.

The Abydos King List, drawn up in the reign of Seti I some 900 years later, lists him as entry 55. He is believed to appear on the Turin Canon too, where his name is lost in a gap but the length of his reign is preserved as 2 years, 1 month and 1 day, following Kim Ryholt's reconstruction.

Two inscriptions on a wall in Shemay's tomb, dated to the first year of the reign, report the bringing of stone from the Wadi Hammamat, for which Coptos was the starting point. They seem to say that the work took 19 days. Three rock inscriptions in the Wadi Hammamat report the bringing of stone, one dated to year one of an unnamed king, and two mention an Idy who may be the same man.

The eight decrees come from the temple of Min at Coptos. In 1914 the philanthropist Edward Harkness gave four of them, inscribed on limestone slabs, to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Seven were issued on a single day in the first year of the reign, perhaps the day of his accession, in a year named the Year of Uniting the Two Lands. In the first he bestows titles on his eldest daughter Nebyet, wife of the vizier Shemay, assigns her a bodyguard and orders a sacred barque for a god called Two-Powers, perhaps Horus-Min.

The second and best preserved appoints Shemay's son Idy as count, overseer of priests and governor of Upper Egypt, over the seven southernmost nomes from Elephantine to Diospolis Parva, in place of his father. The third and fourth record a post in the temple of Min for Idy's brother, and the last orders the decree to be posted at the gateway of the temple, which explains where the decrees were found. The rest concern mortuary priests for the chapels of Nebyet and Shemay and inventories at the temple of Min.
nefertari: The name Nefertari is often translated as beautiful companion, and Meritmut as beloved of the goddess Mut, but a study of similar personal names argues that Nefertari is better rendered as the most beautiful one. Her family background is unknown, and there is no conclusive evidence linking her to the royal family of the 18th Dynasty. She married Ramesses II before he became king. Her sons included Meryatum, High Priest of Re in Heliopolis, and Pareherwenemef, who served in the army. Meritamen and Henuttawy are thought to be her daughters.

Nefertari appears beside Ramesses II in official scenes from the first year of his reign. In the tomb of Nebwenenef she stands behind him as he appoints Nebwenenef High Priest of Amun at Abydos, and at Luxor she leads the royal children. Under Ramesses the title Hereditary Princess was conferred on no queen who was not a king's daughter except Nefertari and the Queen Mother Tuya. Stamp seals bearing her name found at Qantir make her the only person besides pharaohs to whom such seals are attributed.

At Abu Simbel the small temple was dedicated to Nefertari and Hathor of Ibshek, and its dedication text says it was made for the Great Royal Wife for whose sake the sun shines. Two colossal standing statues of her in front of it equal those of Ramesses in size, and the temple was in use before the twentieth year of his reign. The small temple of the Ramesseum was dedicated to her and to Tuya.

Nefertari died before the twenty-fourth year of Ramesses II, since a stela of Heqanakht, the Viceroy of Kush, whose tenure ended that year, shows her already venerated as a goddess. Her tomb, QV66, covers 520 square metres and is covered with pictures of her. Ramesses is not shown in it, though she is the only queen depicted in his own tomb. The tomb was robbed in antiquity and was rediscovered and excavated by Ernesto Schiaparelli in 1904. Items the robbers overlooked are now in the Boston Museum of Fine Arts and the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. A pair of mummified legs found there, now in the Museo Egizio in Turin, are most probably her knees.
negev: The Hebrew name Negev, meaning arid land, appears to have been borrowed from Aramaic and to go back to the Akkadian nagbu, groundwater. In Arabic the region is an-Naqab. It covers at least 55 percent of Israel in an inverted triangle, with the Sinai desert on its western side and the Arabah valley on its eastern. It holds three huge craterlike makhteshim, Makhtesh Ramon, HaMakhtesh HaGadol and HaMakhtesh HaKatan. Rainfall falls from about 300 mm a year in the north to barely 50 mm in the Arabah.

Nomadic life in the Negev dates back at least 4,000 years and perhaps 7,000. The first urbanised settlements date from about 2000 BCE, and Pharaonic Egypt is credited with introducing copper mining and smelting here between 1400 and 1300 BCE. In the Hebrew Bible the Negev means only the northern, semi-arid part of the modern desert. Genesis has Abraham living there, and in Numbers Moses sends twelve scouts into it. Later it formed part of the Kingdom of Judah.

The Nabataeans arrived in the 4th century BCE and controlled the spice trade between Petra and the seaports of Gaza. Their rule ended when the Roman Empire annexed their lands in 106 CE. Under Byzantine rule from the 4th century Christianity spread and farming towns grew, using runoff water collected from wide areas and directed onto small plots, techniques studied by Michael Evenari. Wine from the northwestern Negev was exported in Gaza jars until a sharp decline in the mid-6th century, probably after the Late Antique Little Ice Age and the Justinianic Plague. A large 7th-century earthquake led to the abandonment of Avdat and Rehovot-in-the-Negev.

From the 8th to the 10th or 11th century the southern Negev flourished, with six Islamic settlements near Eilat, mines and the port of Ayla. Bedouin tribes then ruled the region largely independently for about a thousand years. In 1900 the Ottomans set up an administrative centre at Beersheba. British forces took the Negev in 1917, and it became part of Mandatory Palestine. The 1947 United Nations Partition Plan earmarked most of it for a Jewish state, and in the war of 1947–49 Israel secured it.

Beersheba, in the north, is the largest city and the administrative capital of Israel's Southern District, and Eilat, a port and resort, lies at the southern end on the Gulf of Aqaba. The region holds development towns such as Dimona, Arad and Mitzpe Ramon, kibbutzim, Bedouin towns, and Ben-Gurion University of the Negev.
negritude: Négritude takes its name from the French nègre, a word that had been used mainly as an insult, with the suffix -itude. Aimé Césaire deliberately took the word as a positive term and first used it in its present sense in the third issue, of May–June 1935, of L'Étudiant noir, a magazine he started in Paris with Léopold Sédar Senghor, Léon Damas and other students. His first published work, Conscience Raciale et Révolution Sociale, rejected assimilation, since to assimilate was to accept a culture that held African culture to be barbaric.

Earlier influences included the Haitian anthropologist Anténor Firmin, who in 1885 rebutted Arthur de Gobineau's theory of racial inequality, and the Harlem Renaissance of Langston Hughes, Claude McKay and others. Paulette and Jane Nardal introduced these writers to the Paris students at their Clamart Salon, and Paulette Nardal helped begin La Revue du Monde Noir in 1931. Paulette later complained that she and her sister were not acknowledged. Césaire called Haiti the place where négritude first stood up.

Its founders were dissatisfied with the Afro-French experience in France and shared a revolt against racism and colonial injustice. The writers opposed colonialism and Eurocentrism, asserted that Black people had a history and culture equal to others, and took pride in being Black. They drew on Marxist ideas and Surrealist style and showed Heideggerian influence. Each had his own aims. Césaire stressed accepting blackness as the way to decolonise the mind and blamed imperialism for the inferiority complex of Black people. Senghor wanted Black people in French lands to have a seat at the French table as equals, and later used négritude to seek a universal valuation of African people. Damas defended black qualities and addressed the colonised in general.

Neither Césaire nor Senghor at first envisaged independence from France, and Césaire called for the departmentalisation of Martinique. Two anthologies were central: Damas's Poètes d'expression française 1900–1945 of 1946 and Senghor's Anthologie de la nouvelle poésie nègre et malgache de langue française of 1948. A visual movement followed, and the Dakar School in Senegal, active from 1960 to 1974, was directly influenced by the philosophy.

Jean-Paul Sartre's essay Orphée Noir, the preface to Senghor's anthology, called négritude an anti-racist racism and carried it to French intellectual debate. Some Black writers of the 1960s thought it not militant enough, and Keorapetse Kgositsile held that it was too tied to a European view of blackness. Chinua Achebe and Wole Soyinka opposed it, Soyinka writing that a tiger does not proclaim its tigerness but jumps on its prey. Négritude inspired Afro-Surrealism, Créolité and Antillanité, and Frantz Fanon often referred to it. Scholars including Souleymane Bachir Diagne have since revived the study of it as a philosophy.
negros: Negros covers 13,309 square kilometres in the Visayas and is the fourth largest island of the Philippines. Its inhabitants are called Negrenses, or Negrosanons locally. The island was originally called Buglas, an old Hiligaynon word thought to mean cut off, because it was believed to have been separated from a larger landmass. Among its earliest inhabitants were the Ata, one of the Negrito Indigenous Peoples of Southeast Asia. The westernmost parts fell under the nominal rule of the Kedatuan of Madja-as, based on Panay and Guimaras, while the eastern coasts were influenced by the Rajahnate of Cebu.

The Spanish arrived in April 1565 and named the island Negros after the dark-skinned people they saw. Binalbagan and Ilog became towns in 1573 and 1584. In 1734 the island became a military district with Ilog as its first capital; the seat later moved to Himamaylan, and Bacolod became the capital in 1849. In 1890 Negros was divided into the provinces of Negros Occidental and Negros Oriental. Sugar shaped its later history: from 1914 to 1927 towns grew along railways serving sugar mills, haciendas covered the countryside, and many Basque settlers from Spain became plantation owners while workers came from Panay.

From 3 to 6 November 1898 the people of Negros rose against the Spanish government under the revolutionaries Juan Araneta and Aniceto Lacson. The Spaniards surrendered when armed columns approached Bacolod; the revolutionaries' weapons included rifles carved from palm fronds and cannon made of painted bamboo. Colonel Isidro de Castro signed the Act of Capitulation on 6 November. The Cantonal Republic of Negros proclaimed independence on 27 November 1898, became a protectorate of the United States on 30 April 1899, was renamed the Republic of Negros on 22 July 1899, and was annexed by the American military government on 30 April 1901. Silliman University was founded at Dumaguete that year.

Negros has the most component cities of any Philippine island. Sugar remained central to its economy, and in 1984 the collapse of sugar prices and a state trading monopoly left over 190,000 sugar workers without livelihoods in what became known as the Negros Famine. On 20 September 1985 paramilitary forces killed an estimated 20 to 30 farmers at Escalante. The island's two provinces are grouped with Siquijor in the Negros Island Region, reconstituted in 2024.
nehemiah: Nehemiah is the central figure of the Book of Nehemiah, which describes his work in rebuilding Jerusalem during the Second Temple period. According to that book, in the twentieth year of the Achaemenid emperor Artaxerxes I he was the king's cup-bearer. Learning that the remnant population in Judea was in distress and that the walls of Jerusalem were broken down, he asked the king for permission to return and rebuild the city. The book places this about thirteen years after the arrival of his contemporary Ezra in Jerusalem.

Artaxerxes sent him to Judah as provincial governor, gave him letters explaining his support and provided timber from the king's forest. Nehemiah defied the opposition of Judah's enemies on all sides, the Samarians under Sanballat the Horonite, the Ammonites and the Arabs, and rebuilt the walls within 52 days.

He took measures to repopulate the city and purify the community, enforced the cancellation of debt, helped Ezra publicize the law of Moses and enforced the divorce of Jewish men from their non-Jewish wives. After twelve years as governor he returned to the king at Susa. When he came back to Jerusalem he found that non-Jews were permitted to conduct business in the city on Shabbat and to keep rooms in the Temple. He purified the Temple and the priests and Levites and enforced observance of the law.

The historicity of Nehemiah, his mission and the Nehemiah Memoir has recently become controversial in academic scholarship. Maximalists view the book as a historical account, while minimalists doubt that he existed. The Second Book of Maccabees says that he brought the holy fire for the altar back from the diaspora and founded a library of the Holy Scriptures. The scene of the reading and explaining of the Torah in Nehemiah 8 became the model of synagogue worship. The Book of Sirach praises him for his building activities, mentioning him but not Ezra after Zerubbabel and Joshua. One rabbinic text identifies him with Zerubbabel. He is considered a saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church, which commemorates him on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers.
nehesy: Nehesy bore the throne name Aasehre, and most scholars place him early in the 14th Dynasty, as either its second or its sixth king. The Egyptologist Kim Ryholt proposed that he was the son and direct successor of the pharaoh Sheshi and a Nubian queen named Tati, a view Darrell Baker shares; Baker holds that Tati's origin explains her son's name. Because Sheshi is believed to have been of Canaanite origin, Nehesy too is thought to have had Canaanite descent.

Four scarabs, one of them from Semna in Nubia, suggest a brief coregency with his father; one scarab calls him King's son and 22 more Eldest king's son. Ryholt and Baker therefore think he became heir after the death of an elder brother, Prince Ipqu. Manfred Bietak and Jürgen von Beckerath make him the second king of the dynasty, and Bietak suggests that his father was an Egyptian military officer or administrator who founded an independent kingdom centred on Avaris.

Bietak dates the rise of this kingdom to around or just after 1710 BCE, as the 13th Dynasty slowly disintegrated; from then until Ahmose I captured Avaris no single ruler controlled the whole of Egypt. Ryholt instead dates the start of the 14th Dynasty a century earlier, to the reign of Sobekneferu. The Turin King List gives Nehesy a reign of 0 years, some months and 3 days. His authority may have reached across the eastern Delta from Tell el-Muqdam to Tell Habuwa, but his kingdom may have been much smaller.

Despite so short a reign he is the best-attested king of his dynasty, above all through scarab seals. A fragmentary obelisk from the Temple of Seth at Raahu, relief fragments found at Tell el-Dab'a in the mid-1980s and stelae from Tell Habuwa, ancient Tjaru, carry his name; the stelae first linked the name Nehesy to a throne name once ascribed to a Hyksos king. Places in the eastern Delta were long afterwards called The mansion of Pinehsy, a late Egyptian form of his name.

A stela found at Tjaru in 2005 shows a king's son Nehesy offering oil to the god Banebdjedet and names a king's sister Tany, a woman known from the time of the Hyksos king Apophis around 1580 BCE. Daphna Ben-Tor, who studied the scarabs, found that those naming the king's son differ in style from those naming the king, and asks whether some of the objects belong to a later Hyksos prince of the same name.
nekhen: Nekhen lies in Upper Egypt about 100 kilometres south of the modern city of Luxor. Its Egyptian Arabic name is el-Kōm el-Aḥmar, the Red Mound, and the Greek name Hierakonpolis means City of Hawks or City of Falcons, a reference to Horus. It was the religious and political capital of Upper Egypt at the end of prehistoric Egypt, c. 3200 to 3100 BCE, and probably also during the Early Dynastic Period. Horus is said to have had his origins there as its tutelary deity.

The first settlement dates from the Amratian culture, c. 4400 BCE, or the late Badarian culture, c. 5000 BCE. At its height, from c. 3400 BCE, Nekhen had at least 5,000 and possibly as many as 10,000 inhabitants. During the Naqada III period most of Upper Egypt was unified under rulers from Abydos at the expense of rival cities, especially Nekhen. The conflicts may be the ones shown on reliefs of the Naqada II period, such as the Gebel el-Arak Knife and the frieze of Tomb 100.

The temple of Horus of Nekhen was one of the most ancient in Egypt, and the body of Horus was supposedly entombed there. Because Horus was vital to the legitimacy of kings, Nekhen kept its importance long after the site had otherwise declined. There are later tombs of the Middle Kingdom, the Second Intermediate Period and the New Kingdom, and the temple was used as late as the Ptolemaic Kingdom.

The English archaeologists James Quibell and Frederick W. Green excavated the ruins at the end of the nineteenth century and found the Main Deposit, a foundation deposit beneath the temple, in 1894. Their excavation was poorly documented, and their reports sometimes contradict each other. John Garstang worked there in 1905 and 1906 and excavated a Predynastic cemetery of 188 graves.

The finds include the Narmer Palette, which shows the first king to wear both the crowns of Upper and Lower Egypt, and the Scorpion Macehead, which shows a king known only by the sign of a scorpion at what seems to be a ritual irrigation ceremony. Tomb 100, the Painted Tomb, of the Naqada II period, is the only known Predynastic tomb with a mural on its plaster walls. Excavations have also yielded some of the earliest physical evidence of beer production in Egypt, from residues dated to about 3500 to 3400 BCE, and a menagerie of c. 3500 BCE regarded as the oldest known zoological collection.
nellore: Nellore, also spelt Nelluru, stands on the banks of the Penna river in Andhra Pradesh, about 24 kilometres from the Bay of Bengal, and is the headquarters of Nellore district. It lies about 170 kilometres north of Chennai and 279 kilometres from Vijayawada. The name has several explanations. A story from the Sthala Purana connects it with a sacred lingam found beneath a nelli tree, the emblic myrobalan, while another derives it from the Tamil word nellu, meaning paddy or rice, in a region known for rice cultivation. In the medieval period the area was called Vikrama Simhapuri.

Nellore was ruled by Ashoka of the Mauryan dynasty in the 3rd century BCE. Other powers that held it include the Satavahanas, Kharavela of the Chedi dynasty, the Pallavas, the Pandyas and the Eastern Gangas of Kalinga. The Pallavas held it until the 6th century CE, after which the Cholas ruled it for a long period; Tamil inscriptions show it formed part of their kingdom until their decline in the 13th century. It then passed to the Kakatiyas, the Vijayanagara Empire, the Sultanate of Golconda, the Mughal Empire and the Arcot Nawabs.

In 1758 the Marathas under Balwant Rao captured Nellore from Nazibulla. In the 18th century the British took it from the Arcot Nawabs, and it became part of the Madras Presidency. John Boswell produced the first British account in 1873 as collector, covering climate, agriculture, taxation and the leading families, among them zamindars and poligars responsible for villages and lands under the British Raj. The British valued Nellore's cultivation and the port of Krishnapatam. Potti Sriramulu, who fasted until death for the formation of Andhra Pradesh, came from Nellore, and in 2008 the district was renamed in his honour.

The 2011 census recorded 505,258 people in the city. Its municipality was constituted on 1 November 1866 and became a corporation on 18 October 2004. Vikrama Simhapuri University is in the city. The Rottela Panduga, or Roti festival, is held every year at the Bara Shaheed Dargah on the banks of Swarnala Cheruvu and draws visitors of all faiths. The poet Tikkana, one of the Trinity of Poets, is among those associated with the city.
nelson-mandela: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was born on 18 July 1918 in the village of Mvezo, then part of South Africa's Cape Province. His forename Rolihlahla is a Xhosa term colloquially meaning troublemaker, and he later became known by his clan name, Madiba. His great-grandfather Ngubengcuka ruled the Thembu Kingdom, but Mandela's branch descended from a wife of the Ixhiba clan and so could not inherit the throne, though it was recognised as hereditary royal councillors. He studied law at the University of Fort Hare and the University of the Witwatersrand, joined the African National Congress (ANC) in 1943 and helped found its Youth League in 1944.

After the National Party government established apartheid, Mandela became President of the ANC's Transvaal branch and rose to prominence in the 1952 Defiance Campaign and the 1955 Congress of the People. He was prosecuted without success in the 1956 Treason Trial. Though at first committed to non-violent protest, he co-founded the militant Umkhonto we Sizwe in 1961 and led a sabotage campaign. Police captured him on 5 August 1962, and he was later sentenced to life imprisonment in the Rivonia Trial.

Mandela served 27 years in prison, on Robben Island and then at Pollsmoor and Victor Verster prisons. President F. W. de Klerk released him in 1990. In July 1991 Mandela was elected ANC President, and in the election of 27 April 1994 he led the ANC to victory and became President of South Africa, the first black head of state. His government promulgated a new constitution and created the Truth and Reconciliation Commission to investigate past human rights abuses.

Mandela declined a second term and retired in June 1999, succeeded by Thabo Mbeki. He founded the Nelson Mandela Foundation, which worked on rural development, school building and combating HIV/AIDS. He died on 5 December 2013. He received more than 250 honours, including the Nobel Peace Prize, and in South Africa he is often called Madiba and described as the Father of the Nation. Critics on the right denounced him as a communist terrorist, while some on the radical left thought him too ready to reconcile with apartheid's supporters.
nelsons-dockyard: After the English colonised Antigua in 1632, the Royal Navy began to use English Harbour on the island's south side as a refuge, well placed for watching neighbouring islands and sheltered from hurricanes. Fort Berkeley, on a peninsula at the harbour's mouth, is first recorded in 1704, and by 1707 naval ships used the harbour as a station, though there were no repair facilities. Its reputation was made in September 1723, when a hurricane drove 35 ships ashore in other ports of Antigua while HMS Hector and HMS Winchelsea, moored in English Harbour, were unharmed.

The first dockyard, St. Helena, was built on the eastern side in 1725: a capstan house for careening ships, a stone storehouse and three wooden sheds, with no quarters, so that the seamen did all the work themselves. From 1743 plans were made for the western side, and construction of the present dockyard began in the mid-1740s, with enslaved Africans from nearby plantations sent to work on it. Wooden storehouses stood by 1745, and land was reclaimed for wharves. Between 1755 and 1765 came quarters for the commander-in-chief, Thomas Shirley, more storerooms, a kitchen, the first part of the Saw Pit Shed and a stone wall around the yard.

The Engineer's Workshop, Guard House, Porter's Lodge, Mast Houses and Capstan House followed between 1773 and 1778. Many of today's buildings date from a programme of 1785 to 1794, among them the Engineer's House, the Pitch and Tar Store and the Copper and Lumber Store, completed in 1789. The Sail Loft followed in 1797, the Officers' Quarters in 1821, and in 1855 the Naval Officer's and Clerk's House, which now holds the Dockyard Museum. After the navy left in 1889 the yard fell into decay.

The Society of the Friends of English Harbour began restoring the dockyard in 1951 and reopened it to the public in 1961. Its original buildings now house two hotels, the museum, shops and restaurants beside a large marina, and it is part of Nelson's Dockyard National Park. It hosts Antigua Sailing Week and the Antigua Classic Yacht Regatta.
neman: The Neman, called Nemunas in Lithuanian and Niemen in Polish, is the largest river in Lithuania and the third largest in Belarus, and is navigable for most of its length. It begins as two small headwaters that merge about 15 km south-west of Uzda, some 55 km south-west of Minsk. Of its course, 436 km lie in Belarus and 359 km in Lithuania, and 116 km form the border between Lithuania and Russia's Kaliningrad oblast. It has some 105 first-class tributaries, the largest being the Neris, the Shchara and the Šešupė, and a basin of 98,200 km2.

In Lithuania the river makes loops that follow an underlying tectonic fault, not conventional meanders; near Prienai one loop, 17 km long, comes within 1.2 km of closing. Their castles served as the first line of defence against the Teutonic knights. At its delta the river splits into branches and canals, of which the main ones are the Atmata, Pakalnė, Skirvytė and Gilija, and it provides the main water inflow of the Curonian Lagoon, keeping the water almost fresh.

Ptolemy called the river Chronos, though some think that name was the Pregolya. It gave its name to the Neman Culture, a Neolithic archaeological subculture. In German the part flowing through historic Prussia has been called the Memel at least since about 1250, when the Teutonic Knights built Memelburg castle and the town of Memel at the mouth of the Curonian Lagoon, naming it after the river's indigenous name. The border between the State of the Teutonic Order and Lithuania, fixed in 1422 by the Treaty of Lake Melno, remained stable for centuries.

Napoleon and Tsar Alexander I signed the Treaty of Tilsit on a raft in the river in 1807, and Napoleon's crossing at the start of the 1812 invasion of Russia is described in War and Peace and mentioned in Pan Tadeusz. In 1919 the Treaty of Versailles made the river the border separating the Memel Territory from German East Prussia. The first stanza of the Deutschlandlied, written in 1841, names it as Germany's eastern boundary. Lithuanians call the Nemunas the father of rivers.

The river is used for fishing, hydropower, water supply, industry, agriculture, recreation and water transport. Its largest cities are Grodno in Belarus, Alytus and Kaunas in Lithuania, and Sovetsk in the Kaliningrad Oblast. A dam above Kaunas, built in 1959, formed the Kaunas Reservoir, the largest lake of its kind in Lithuania, and the Augustów Canal, built in the 19th century, connects the Neman with the Vistula. Nemunas Loops Regional Park and Nemunas Delta Regional Park were both founded in 1992.
nemanjic-dynasty: The House of Nemanjić was the most prominent native Serbian dynasty of the Middle Ages and produced twelve Serbian monarchs. Its progenitor, Stefan Nemanja, came from a cadet branch of the Vukanović dynasty, which had established the Serbian Grand Principality in the 1090s. Earlier, the Vlastimirović dynasty had founded the Serbian Principality in the eighth century, but the state broke up after the death of Časlav of Serbia around the 940s or 960s and the Byzantines annexed the region, holding it for a century until the Vojislavljević dynasty revolted in 1040.

By the mid-twelfth century Stari Ras was undisputedly under Serbian control and became the centre of defence and residence. In 1166 Stefan Nemanja took the throne. After him every monarch used Stefan as a personal or ruler's name, a tradition adopted for royal pretensions.

The rulers began as Grand Princes. With the crowning of Stefan Nemanjić in 1217 the realm became a kingdom, and the Serbian Orthodox Church was established in 1219, the year in which Saint Sava published St. Sava's Nomocanon, described as the first constitution in Serbia. Serbia reached its height of power under the dynasty.

In 1346 Stefan Dušan was crowned Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks, and the Archbishopric of Serbia was raised to a Patriarchate. Under Dušan Serbia reached its territorial, political and economic peak, proclaimed itself the successor of the Byzantine Empire and was the most powerful Balkan state of its time. He enacted an extensive constitution, known as Dušan's Code, and opened new trade routes, but the integration of society remained unfinished.

Dušan tried to organise a crusade with the pope against the Turks but died suddenly in December 1355. His son Uroš, called the Weak, succeeded him, and the empire slowly slid into feudal fragmentation as the Ottoman Turk sultanate spread into the Balkans.

The dynasty's rule ended in 1371 with the death of the childless Stefan Uroš V, which led to the fall of the Serbian Empire. Provincial lords took control of their provinces. The last remaining members were John Uroš, ruler of Thessaly and titular emperor, who died c. 1422-23, and his younger brother Stefan Uroš, ruler of Pharsalos.

The Nemanjići were key patrons of the Serbian Orthodox Church and built or endowed many monasteries. Several are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them Studenica, Gračanica, Hilandar, Đurđevi Stupovi, Sopoćani, Visoki Dečani, the Patriarchate of Peć and Our Lady of Ljeviš. Others include Žiča, Banjska, Mileševa, Gradac and Morača. Serbian medieval political identity was profoundly shaped by the dynasty's rule, which the Serbian Orthodox Church supported and cultivated. Nemanjić descent survived only through maternal lines in several Serbian houses.
nemesis-1839: Nemesis was the largest of six similar vessels ordered by the Secret Committee of the East India Company; her sister ships Phlegethon, Pluto, Proserpine, Ariadne and Medusa came from John Laird's yard at Birkenhead and from William Fairbairn & Sons at Millwall. Built in three months, she was 184 feet long, with a beam of 29 feet, a draught of 6 feet when full of coal and a burthen of 660 tons. Driven by sail and by two sixty-horsepower Forrester engines, she carried two pivot-mounted 32-pounder and four 6-pounder guns.

Her watertight bulkheads, the first used in a warship, let her survive damage to her hull on her sea trials and on the voyage out. She did not appear in the Company's list of ships, and The Times suggested that she carried a letter of marque, adding that "for the purpose of smuggling opium she is admirably adapted." To keep the voyage secret it was given out that she was bound for Odessa. In July 1840 she became the first iron ship to round the Cape of Good Hope, using compass corrections devised by Sir George Airy, the Astronomer Royal, though her compass performed poorly throughout her career.

Commanded by Captain William Hutcheon Hall, she first saw action in the Second Battle of Chuenpi on 7 January 1841, against the Chinese fleet at the Bocca Tigris forts. At the Battle of First Bar on 27 February she sank the Cambridge, an old East Indiaman that the Chinese had bought and rearmed. Her shallow draught took her through shallow water in the Broadway expedition of 13 to 15 March, and she helped capture Canton on 18 March. The Chinese called her the "devil ship". In 1842, under Captain Richard Collinson and based at Chusan, she fought at Taisam during the repulse of a much larger Chinese attack on Ningbo.

After the war she was sent against pirates near Indonesia and the Philippines, and then operated from Bombay, chiefly to Karachi. At the end of 1846, after rioting in Canton, Sir John Davis posted her to cover the Company's factory there, until she was withdrawn before February 1847. In May 1847 she attacked a flotilla of Sooloo pirate prows in the Brunei river, and early in 1853 she helped the Company's steamer Zenobia drive Burmese troops out of Bassein province. She sailed from Shanghai for Belfast on 1 February 1854.
nemocon: Nemocón is a municipality of the Central Savanna Province in the northern part of the Bogotá savanna, on the Altiplano Cundiboyacense. Its urban centre lies at 2,585 metres, 65 kilometres from Bogotá, and it is the northeasternmost municipality of the Metropolitan Area of Bogotá; the Bogotá River rises close by. The name is said to come from Enemocón, the cry or sadness of the warrior in the Chibcha language, though another account derives it from the zipa Nemequene.

Excavations by Gonzalo Correal Urrego in 1979 and Ana María Groot in 1992 showed that the area was settled early: scraper tools, bone tools and the food remains of hunter-gatherers who lived under rock shelters have been dated to 7640 BP. The site of Checua, 7 kilometres north of the town, has evidence from around 6500 BCE, and rock art has been found at several places in the municipality. Ceramics of the 4th century BCE show that salt was already being extracted.

In the Muisca period, which typically began in 800 CE, Nemocón was a market town where salt was traded, and its ceramics and those of Zipaquirá found elsewhere on the savanna are linked to that trade. Muisca women drew the salt from brine in large pots, and according to the chronicler Juan de Santa Gertrudis it was used to dry and preserve fish and meat. Under Spanish rule the salt was worked by the hand labour of the surviving Muisca. The modern town was founded on 26 July 1600 by Luis Henríquez, and by 1614 wheat was being grown there.

Salt is still extracted, and the town also lives from growing flowers and extracting kaolin. Its salt mine, with a museum, is the second largest in Colombia after the Salt Cathedral of Zipaquirá, and the town is linked to Bogotá by a tourist train. The remains of a mastodon have been found in the municipality.
neo-assyrian-empire: The Neo-Assyrian Empire began with the accession of Adad-nirari II in 911 BCE. Its early kings set out to reverse a long decline and retake lands lost in the late 11th century BCE. They presented the reconquest as a war to liberate Assyrians cut off from Assyrian territory. Under Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883 to 859 BCE) Assyria again dominated the Near East, his campaigns reached the Mediterranean, and he moved the capital from Assur to Kalhu, later called Calah in the Hebrew Bible and Nimrud by the Arabs. The empire grew further under Shalmaneser III (r. 859 to 824 BCE).

After Shalmaneser's death the empire stagnated in what is called the age of the magnates, when generals and officials held political power and central control was weak. Tiglath-Pileser III (r. 745 to 727 BCE) reasserted royal power, reorganised the army and more than doubled the empire, notably by conquering Babylonia and much of the Levant. Sargon II (r. 722 to 705 BCE), probably a usurper, founded the Sargonid dynasty. Under Sennacherib (r. 705 to 681 BCE) the capital moved to Nineveh, and under Esarhaddon the empire reached its largest extent with the conquest of Egypt.

After Ashurbanipal died in 631 BCE his son Aššur-etil-ilāni inherited the throne against considerable opposition, helped by the chief eunuch Sîn-šumu-līšir. The fall in the late 7th century was swift and violent, brought about by a Babylonian uprising and an invasion by the Medes, and scholars still debate its causes.

The empire's success rested on incorporating conquered lands into its administration, which was divided into provinces. Its army made large-scale use of cavalry and new siege techniques, and messages from high officials, stamped with their seals, travelled by relay stations and well-kept roads at a speed not surpassed in the Middle East until the 19th century. A resettlement policy moved part of the population of conquered lands to the heartland and underdeveloped provinces, which diluted local identities and helped Aramaic become the regional common language until the 14th century. The highest offices in the administration and army usually went to eunuchs of obscure origins, which ensured their loyalty to the king.
neo-destour: The party's formal name was the New Constitutional Liberal Party. Before the split, a younger group within the Destour had alarmed the party's elders by appealing directly to the people through its more radical newspaper, L'Action Tunisienne. Many of the young members came from the provinces and seemed closer to the wider Tunisian population, while the elders represented an established constituency in Tunis, though both sides sought change, whether autonomy or independence.

The break came at the Ksar Hellal Congress of 2 March 1934, and the new party was founded in Dar Ayed, the house of the activist Ahmed Ayed. Its prominent early leaders were Habib Bourguiba, Mahmoud El Materi, who led it until 1938, Tahar Sfar, Bahri Guiga and Salah ben Yusuf.

When war broke out in 1939 the leaders were deported to France. After the German occupation of Vichy France they were released in 1942 and handed over to Mussolini's government in Rome, which treated them with deference in the hope of winning support for the Axis. Bourguiba steadily refused to cooperate, but Hussein Triki worked with the Nazis and later served The Mahgreb, a North African organisation working for the German war effort.

In April 1955, in the last year of the struggle for independence, Salah ben Yusuf openly challenged Bourguiba over the gradual tactics of his autonomy negotiations with France, setting a pan-Arab line against Bourguiba's liberal, secular and pro-Western approach. The labour leader Ahmad Ben Salah kept the Tunisian General Labor Union on Bourguiba's side. The party expelled Ben Yusuf in October, and after a large street demonstration in November 1955 came to nothing he left for Egypt. Independence, negotiated largely by Bourguiba, took effect on 20 March 1956.

The Republic of Tunisia, constituted the next year, replaced the rule of the beys, and the Neo-Destour became the ruling party under Bourguiba, first as prime minister and then as president. In 1963 it was proclaimed the only legal party, though the country had in practice been a one-party state since independence. Its renaming in 1964 signalled a socialist phase of development, which ended in 1969 when Bourguiba dismissed Ahmad Ben Salah as economics minister. In 1988, under President Ben Ali, the party became the Rassemblement Constitutionel Démocratique, which was abolished with his regime in the Tunisian Revolution of 2011.
neo-hittite-states: The collapse of the Hittite New Kingdom is usually associated with the decline of Eastern Mediterranean trade networks and the fall of major Late Bronze Age cities in the Levant, Anatolia and the Aegean. In the 12th century BCE Wilusa (Troy) was destroyed and the Hittite New Kingdom suffered a devastating attack from the Kaskas, who occupied the Black Sea coasts. Hattusa was completely destroyed. The Early Iron Age in northern Mesopotamia then saw a dispersal of settlements and ruralization, and regional states with new political structures arose.

David Hawkins traced a dynastic link between the Hittite imperial dynasty and the Great Kings and Country-lords of Melid and Karkamish, showing continuity between the Late Bronze Age and the Early Iron Age. Work at the Temple of the Storm God at Aleppo and at Ain Dara, where the Late Bronze Age temples continue into the Iron Age without a break, points the same way.

The states fall into a northern group, where Hittite rulers remained in power, and a southern group, where Arameans came to rule from about 1000 BCE. The northern group includes the Tabalian region, Kammanu with Melid, Hilakku, Gurgum, Kummuh and Carchemish. The southern group includes Bit Gabbari with Sam'al, Bit-Adini with Til Barsip, Bit Agusi with Arpad and later Aleppo, and Hamath. They were highly decentralised, and some appear to have been loose confederations of sub-kingdoms. The Assyrian Empire subdued them in the 8th century BCE.

Luwian monumental inscriptions in Anatolian hieroglyphs continue almost without a break from the 13th-century imperial monuments to the Early Iron Age inscriptions of Karkemish, Melid and Aleppo. Many kingdoms chose them for monuments, often in bilingual or trilingual inscriptions with Aramaic, Phoenician or Akkadian versions. Mirko Novák notes that the rulers expressed in their titles and iconography an identity tied to the Hittite Empire, and holds that Neo-Hittite suits this cultural claim while Luwo-Aramean suits the languages, both naming one region and culture.
neoclassicism: Neoclassicism emerged as a Western cultural movement in the decorative and visual arts, literature, theatre, music and architecture, drawing on the art and culture of classical antiquity. It was born in Rome, largely through the writings of Johann Joachim Winckelmann during the rediscovery of Pompeii and Herculaneum. Its forerunner was the Italian archaeologist and art theorist Giovanni Pietro Bellori, whose lecture on the Ideal in art at the Accademia di San Luca in 1664 became a statement of idealist art theory and later the theoretical basis of Winckelmann's teaching.

The movement spread through Europe as art students finished the Grand Tour and returned from Italy with Greco-Roman ideals. In the visual arts it began about 1760 in opposition to the Rococo, whose grace, ornament and asymmetry it set against simplicity and symmetry.

Each neoclassical movement chooses some models from antiquity and ignores others. Between 1765 and 1830 its followers admired the generation of Phidias, but the sculpture they actually embraced was more often Roman copies of Hellenistic works. Because Greece lay in the Ottoman Empire and was considered dangerous, appreciation of Greek architecture came largely through engravings that were smoothed and regularised.

Painting lacked ancient models for history subjects, so artists such as John Flaxman, whose outline drawings illustrated the Odyssey, used Greek vases, and Raphael was often used as a substitute, as Winckelmann advised. Sculpture had too many models. Jean-Antoine Houdon made portrait busts of figures of the Enlightenment and travelled to America to make a statue of George Washington. In France the first phase of neoclassical design is called the Louis XVI style, 1774 to 1789, with straight lines and symmetry, and the second the Directoire and Empire styles.

Neoclassicism reached its peak in the early to mid 19th century and competed with Romanticism, though describing the two as opposites is an over-simplification, as the case of Ingres shows. In Prussia Karl Friedrich Schinkel built the Altes Museum in Berlin.

After the middle of the 19th century the style gave way to an eclecticism of classical styles, as at the Palais Garnier in Paris. In architecture it persisted into the 20th century, in the American Renaissance movement and in Beaux-Arts buildings such as the Lincoln Memorial, and in the 1920s and 1930s several totalitarian regimes chose it for state buildings. In music, Neoclassicism is a separate 20th-century movement that revived Baroque and Classical styles. A form of classical architecture continues in the 21st century under the name New Classical Architecture.
neolithic: The term Neolithic, from the Greek for new and stone, was coined by John Lubbock in 1865 as a refinement of the three-age system. The wide-ranging developments of the period, which appear to have arisen independently in several parts of the world, were later called the Neolithic Revolution, a term coined in the 1920s by the archaeologist Vere Gordon Childe. In West Asia farming appeared about 12,000 years ago, and there the period lasted until the Chalcolithic, marked by metallurgy, from about 4500 BCE.

In the Levant the Neolithic arose from the Natufian culture, whose people had come to depend on wild cereals and had begun to live in one place. Climatic changes associated with the Younger Dryas are thought to have pushed them toward farming. The founder crops of the Fertile Crescent were wheat, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax.

The identifying feature of Neolithic technology is the use of polished or ground stone tools, in contrast to the flaked tools of the Paleolithic. The polished stone axe above all allowed forest to be cleared on a large scale. Farmers made sickle blades and grinding stones, and also pottery, beads and statuettes. Mud-brick houses coated with plaster began to appear, so that some have called the period the Age of Clay.

Most Neolithic societies were relatively simple and egalitarian, though more hierarchical than the Upper Paleolithic cultures before them. In Eurasia states generally arose only with metallurgy. Outside Eurasia, states formed during the local Neolithic in three areas: the Preceramic Andes with the Caral-Supe civilisation, Formative Mesoamerica and ancient Hawaiʻi.

The Neolithic spread unevenly. Farming appeared in south-east Europe in the 7th millennium BCE, and archaeogenetics has shown that its spread to Europe was strongly tied to the migration of early farmers from Anatolia about 9,000 years ago. In north-west Europe the Neolithic began much later, from about 4500 BCE to 1700 BCE. In Egypt it lasted until about 3150 BCE, and in China until about 2000 BCE.

In Africa south of the Sahara the first food production was mobile herding, and archaeologists speak of a Pastoral Neolithic. In the Americas different terms are used, such as the Formative stage. Australia is generally held not to have had a Neolithic period. The temple of Ġgantija on Gozo is described as the oldest known freestanding structure.
neoplatonism: Neoplatonism is a modern term. It marks off the doctrines of Plotinus and his successors from those of Plato, and assumes that Plotinus's reading of Plato was new. Some scholars doubt that the label is useful, arguing that only marginal differences separate Plotinus from his immediate predecessors. In the nearly six centuries between Plato and Plotinus there had been an uninterrupted tradition of interpreting Plato, including the period now called Middle Platonism. Among the forerunners were Plutarch, the Neopythagorean Numenius of Apamea and the Hellenized Jew Philo. Plotinus was the pupil of Ammonius Saccas, whom Christians and pagans each claimed as an adherent of their own faith.

Its central idea is monism: all reality derives from a single first principle, the One. For Plotinus the One is simple, ineffable and beyond being, both the source and the end of all things, and the most adequate names for it are the One or the Good. From it emanate two further hypostases: Nous, or intellect, which contains the Platonic Forms, and Soul, whose actualizing of what it receives from Nous is the creation of the sensible world. Evil has no independent existence but is an absence of good. Human happiness can be reached in this world through philosophical contemplation, and all souls return to the One.

After Plotinus came three phases: Porphyry, who edited the Enneads and wrote a biography of his teacher; Iamblichus, who filled the space between the One and humanity with gods, angels and demons and made salvation a matter of theurgy, or rites; and the 5th and 6th centuries, when the academies of Athens and Alexandria flourished. Proclus placed individual henads, identified with the Greek gods, between the One and the divine Intellect. A revived academy at Athens, founded around 410, was closed by Justinian I in 529 because of the active paganism of its professors.

Augustine of Hippo passed through Neoplatonism on his way from Manichaeism to Christianity, and it led him to hold that evil is a privation of good and that God is not material. Islamic philosophers such as al-Farabi and Avicenna adapted it to Islamic monotheism, aided by Arabic translations, and Jewish thinkers such as Solomon ibn Gabirol and the Kabbalists used it too. In the West the works of Pseudo-Dionysius shaped medieval mysticism, including Meister Eckhart, and Thomas Aquinas drew on Proclus. Pletho carried its revival to Italy after the Council of Florence, which led to the Neoplatonism of Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. In the 17th century the Cambridge Platonists, among them Henry More, were called more truly Plotinists by Coleridge.
neoptolemus: In Greek mythology Neoptolemus was the son of the warrior Achilles and the princess Deidamia of Skyros. He was called Pyrrhus at birth, meaning red, and received the name Neoptolemus, young warrior, for his exploits at Troy. In the Cypria Achilles sails to Skyros, marries Deidamia and fathers him before being called to arms again. In the version of Hyginus, Achilles' mother Thetis hides him disguised as a woman at the court of King Lycomedes of Skyros to keep him from the war. Some accounts make Iphigenia his mother.

The Trojan seer Helenus, once captured, told the Greeks that Troy would fall only if they acquired the poisoned arrows of Heracles, held by Philoctetes, stole the Palladium and brought Achilles' son into the war. Odysseus fetched the young Neoptolemus from Skyros, and they went to Lemnos for Philoctetes, the subject of Sophocles' Philoctetes. In the sack of Troy he killed Priam and, in some accounts, Polites and Astyanax, the infant son of Hector and Andromache. The ghost of Achilles demanded the sacrifice of the princess Polyxena, and Neoptolemus carried it out.

He took Andromache as his concubine and, with her, Helenus and Phoenix, sailed to the islands off Epirus and became king there. By Andromache he fathered Molossos, ancestor of the Molossian kings, and, according to the myth, of Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great. Plutarch also names him as ancestor of Pyrrhus of Epirus. There are different accounts of his death. In one tradition Orestes killed him over Hermione, with Pylades sometimes aiding. In another a Delphian named Machaereus killed him at Delphi, where he had come to seek redress from Apollo for Achilles' death.

Neoptolemus was honoured as a hero at Delphi. Strabo and Pausanias say his tomb lay within the sacred precinct, and sacrifices were made to him yearly. The Greek phrase the punishment of Neoptolemus describes retribution in kind, from the tradition that he killed Priam at an altar and later died at an altar.

Ancient writers differ on his character. Sophocles shows him as kinder and honouring his promises, and the Heroicus of Philostratus calls him a man of noble character, though inferior to his father. Others portray him as brutal, and John Tzetzes says that the title Skyrian dragon refers to his violent nature. He appears in the work of Virgil, Seneca and Racine, and in a speech in Shakespeare's Hamlet.
nepal: Nepal is a landlocked, roughly trapezoidal country about 800 kilometres long and 200 kilometres wide, with an area of 147,516 square kilometres. It lies mainly in the Himalayas but includes a small strip of the Indo-Gangetic Plain in the south. Eight of the world's ten highest mountains stand there, among them Mount Everest. The Himalayas rose from the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates, which began about 75 million years ago, and lakes held back by the rising ranges broke through as late as 100,000 years ago, leaving fertile valleys such as the Kathmandu Valley. Kathmandu is the capital and largest city.

The oldest archaeological evidence of human settlement in Nepal dates to about 30,000 years ago. Around 600 BCE small kingdoms and confederations of clans arose in the south, and from one of them, the Shakya polity, came the prince who became Gautama Buddha, traditionally dated 563 to 483 BCE. By 250 BCE the southern regions were under Maurya influence. The emperor Ashoka made a pilgrimage to Lumbini, the Buddha's birthplace according to Buddhist tradition, and the inscription on the pillar he raised marks the starting point of properly recorded Nepalese history. By the 4th century CE much of Nepal was under the Gupta Empire.

The Kathmandu Valley was the seat of the Newar confederacy known as Nepal Mandala, and its traders dominated the Himalayan branch of the Silk Road. By the 18th century the Gorkha Kingdom had unified Nepal under the Shah dynasty. The country was never colonised, but after the treaty of Sugauli it served as a buffer state between Imperial China and British India, and the Rana dynasty of premiers allied with the British Empire.

Parliamentary democracy was introduced in 1951 after the Nepali Congress overthrew the Rana regime. King Mahendra started the partyless Panchayat system in 1962, and monarchs suspended parliamentary democracy in 1960 and 2005. The Nepalese Civil War ended with a secular republic in 2008, ending the world's last Hindu monarchy, and the Constitution of 2015 made Nepal a federal parliamentary republic of seven provinces.

The 2021 census counted 29.5 million people in 125 ethnic groups speaking 123 mother tongues. The Nepali are descended from four major migrations, and among the earliest inhabitants were the Kirat of the east, the Newars of the Kathmandu Valley and the Tharus of the Terai. Nepal declared untouchability illegal in 1963.
nepal-sambat: The era began on 20 October 879, in the reign of Rāghavadeva, and its historical origin remains unknown. A 14th-century chronicle says a new era was dedicated to Pashupati in his reign, which led the historian Petech to link it to a sacred event; Baburam Acharya held that it marked the end of the Licchavi dynasty and the founding of the Thakuri. The orientalist Sylvain Lévi derived it from the Shaka era, and Gautama V. Vajracharya argued that it began when the Shaka era reached its year 801.

Folklore tells that the merchant Sankhadhar Sakhwa obtained sand that turned to gold and used it to clear the valley's debts. Manuscripts of 1645 and 1743 name the era after him, but his historicity is debated.
