Nepal Sambat was the official calendar of Nepal until the end of the Malla dynasty in 1769, and appeared on coins, stone and copper-plate inscriptions, royal decrees, chronicles, Hindu and Buddhist manuscripts and legal documents. The name was first used in Nepal Sambat 148 (1028 CE). A letter from the Ming emperor to Shaktisimha of Nepal is dated in it, as are gold coins of Pran Narayan of Koch Bihar, and Newar merchants in Lhasa used it in their documents and inscriptions. An intercalary month is added every three years, and traders traditionally opened new account books on its first day.

The Shahs replaced it with the Shaka era, though a treaty with Tibet was dated Nepal Sambat 895 (1775 CE), and Bikram Sambat superseded the Shaka era in 1903. A campaign to restore it began in the 1920s under Dharmaditya Dharmacharya, an activist based in Kolkata, and grew after 1951; the Panchayat regime arrested its activists, and in 1987 police broke up a New Year run in Kathmandu. Sankhadhar Sakhwa was declared a national hero on 18 November 1999, and from 11 November 2023 the government included Nepal Sambat in official documents beside Vikram Sambat. Newars mark its New Year with the Mha Puja.
nepalese-civil-war: In January 1990 the United Left Front was formed and, together with the Nepali Congress, became the backbone of the movement for democratic change. Communist groups uneasy about that alliance formed a parallel front, the United National People's Movement, which called for elections to a constituent assembly.

In November 1990 the Communist Party of Nepal (Unity Centre) was formed, and in January 1991 it set up the United People's Front of Nepal under Baburam Bhattarai to contest elections. In 1991 the front became the third-largest party in parliament, but it split over tactics: one group under Pushpa Kamal Dahal, known as Prachanda, argued for immediate armed revolution, while Nirmal Lama's group held that Nepal was not yet ripe for it.

On 13 February 1996 the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) began what it called the people's war, with the stated aim of overthrowing the monarchy and founding a people's republic, making wide use of guerrilla warfare. In June 2001 King Birendra and most of the royal family were killed in the royal massacre, and Gyanendra was crowned king. Peace talks begun in August 2001 collapsed on 23 November, when the Maoists attacked police and army posts in 42 districts. On 26 November the government declared a state of emergency and deployed the Nepal Army.

On 4 October 2002 King Gyanendra dismissed Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba and took executive power. A ceasefire from 29 January 2003 ended on 27 August 2003, when the Maoists withdrew from it. On 1 February 2005 the king dissolved the government and banned news reports; the army arrested political leaders, journalists and activists, and telephone and internet connections were cut. In November 2005 the Maoists agreed to work with opposition parties against the king.

After weeks of pro-democracy protests in April 2006 the Maoists announced a truce, and the Comprehensive Peace Accord was signed on 21 November 2006 by Prime Minister Girija Prasad Koirala and Prachanda. It let the Maoists take part in government and placed their weapons under United Nations monitoring.

More than 17,000 people were killed, over 4,000 by Maoists and over 8,200 by government forces between 1996 and 2005, and an estimated 100,000 to 150,000 were displaced. Parliament set up a Truth and Reconciliation Commission and a commission on disappearances, both established in 2013. The Nepalese Army took control of the Maoist People's Liberation Army on 10 April 2012.
nepali-congress: The party grew out of two organisations founded in Calcutta. The Nepali National Congress was founded by Bishweshwar Prasad Koirala on 25 January 1947, and the Nepal Democratic Congress by Subarna Shamsher Rana on 4 August 1948. They merged on 10 April 1950, with Matrika Prasad Koirala as first president. On 27 September 1950, at Bairgania in Bihar, the party announced an armed revolution against the Rana regime.

After King Tribhuvan took refuge in the Indian Embassy on 6 November 1950, the party's Congress Liberation Army attacked Birgunj, which fell by 12 November, and a first People's Government was declared. Matrika Prasad Koirala became prime minister in November 1951, the first commoner to hold the post. In 1956 the party adopted democratic socialism, and in February 1959 it won 74 of the 109 seats in the House of Representatives.

King Mahendra's coup of 1960 sent many leaders to prison or exile. Parties were prohibited from 1960 to 1989, yet the party persisted from India and backed the multiparty side in the 1980 referendum. It won 110 of 205 seats in 1991 and 111 in 1999. A feud between Girija Prasad Koirala and Sher Bahadur Deuba split it in 2002, and the factions reunified on 24 September 2007. In the 2013 Constituent Assembly election it won 196 of 575 elected seats, and the new constitution was promulgated on 20 September 2015 under Sushil Koirala.

The party has led the government fourteen times and produced seven prime ministers. It is the only party in Nepal elected with a majority, in 1959, 1991 and 1999. In September 2025 protests left 19 protesters dead; the home minister Ramesh Lekhak, of the party, resigned, protesters vandalised party offices, and Deuba was assaulted at his home.
nepherites-i: Nepherites I, known in Egyptian as Nefaarud I, is believed to have been a general from the Delta city of Mendes. In the autumn of 399 BCE he rose against the pharaoh Amyrtaeus, defeated him in open battle and executed him at Memphis. He then crowned himself at Memphis, possibly also at Sais, and moved the capital from Sais to Mendes. His choice of the Horus name of Psamtik I and the Golden Horus name of Amasis II, both of the 26th Dynasty, is thought to show that he wished to recall an earlier golden age.

Evidence of his building work has been found across the country: at Thmuis, Buto, Memphis, Saqqara and Mendes in Lower Egypt, a chapel at Akoris, and a statue worshipped at Akhmim. At Karnak he added a storeroom and a shrine for a sacred bark. A basalt sphinx bearing his name, now in the Louvre, was in Europe by the 16th century and once adorned a fountain in the gardens of the Villa Borghese in Rome.

In foreign affairs Nepherites resumed Egyptian intervention in the Near East. According to Diodorus Siculus, in 396 BCE he supported the Spartan king Agesilaus in his war against the Persians, sending 500,000 measures of grain and material for 100 triremes. The cargo reached Rhodes just after the Persians had retaken the island, and it was seized by the philo-Persian admiral Conon of Athens.

Nepherites died in the winter of 394/393 BCE after a reign that Manetho gives as six years; his highest securely attested date is his fourth regnal year. The Demotic Chronicle says only that his son was allowed to succeed him. This son is generally thought to have been Hakor, who ruled for a year before being overthrown by an apparently unrelated claimant, Psammuthes, and retook the throne the following year. A tomb thought to be his was found at Mendes in 1992–93 by a joint team from the University of Toronto and the University of Washington, identified by a shabti bearing his name, though definitive proof has not been found. Fish-filled vessels at the site may point to an earlier temple of the goddess Hatmehyt.
neptune: Neptune was probably associated with freshwater springs before the sea. His close identification with the Greek Poseidon limits what is known of his own theology. The lectisternium of 399 BCE shows that Poseidon, Artemis and Heracles had been introduced in Rome and worshipped as Neptune, Diana and Hercules. Servius names Neptune explicitly as the god of rivers, springs and waters, and it has been speculated that he continues an Indo-European freshwater deity. His name is of unclear origin. Varro derived it from nuptus, covering, while Georges Dumézil linked it with the Indian and Iranian Apam Napat and the Irish Nechtan, all meaning descendant of the waters. The Etruscans called him Nethuns, though the view that Neptune derives from the Etruscan name has been disputed.

In the Greek-inspired tradition Neptune is a brother of Jupiter and Pluto, and Salacia is his wife. Roman writers also named Venilia beside him, and ancient and modern authors differ on what these companions represent. Varro connected Salacia with salum, the sea, and Venilia with ventus, the wind. By the first century BCE Neptune had supplanted Portunus as the god of naval victories, and Sextus Pompeius called himself the son of Neptune. The Falisci, who called themselves Neptunia proles, regarded him as their divine ancestor. He was one of only four Roman gods to whom a bull was properly sacrificed, the others being Apollo, Mars and Jupiter.

The Neptunalia fell on 23 July, at the height of summer when fresh water was scarcest, between the festivals of the Lucaria and the Furrinalia, which were also tied to water. People built shelters of branches in a wood between the Tiber and the Via Salaria and drank spring water and wine to escape the heat. It was a time of merrymaking when men and women could mix without the usual constraints.

Neptune had one temple in Rome, near the Circus Flaminius, dating back to at least 206 BCE. Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus restored it about 40 BCE, and it held a marine group by Scopas Minor. Agrippa later dedicated the Basilica Neptuni on the Campus Martius in honour of the naval victory at Actium. Like Poseidon, Neptune was also worshipped as a god of horses, Neptunus equestris, and a patron of horse-racing.
nereid-monument: Xanthos was a chief city state of the Lycians, ruled by a dynasty under the Achaemenid Persian Empire, and its rulers' line is marked by a tradition of pillar tombs. Arbinas was the son of the dynast Kheriga, but had to take Xanthos and other Lycian cities by force of arms in around 390 BCE to reclaim his birthright. He then ruled western Lycia from Xanthos, built the monument as his tomb, and died in around 370 BCE. The design follows the Ionic temples of the Athenian Acropolis, and the monument was the main inspiration for the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus.

The temple had four columns on its east and west faces and six on the north and south. Its podium carried two friezes of 22 blocks each. The lower shows battle scenes of soldiers in Greek armour, with no clear overall story; the upper shows on each side the siege of a city with Lycian merlons, thought to represent Arbinas's conquest of the Lycian cities. There Arbinas sits in Persian style under a parasol, his feet on a footstool, while hoplites and archers scale walls with ladders and lead prisoners away.

On the cella frieze Arbinas dines on a couch of his own, larger than the other banqueters, with hair and beard like the kings of Persia or Assyria and a Persian drinking horn. The east pediment shows him seated with his wife, which Ian Jenkins suggests was inspired by Zeus and Hera on the Parthenon frieze. Eleven of the life-size female figures in wind-blown drapery survive, some with dolphins, a cuttlefish or a bird at their feet. Thurstan Robinson argues that they are better seen as eliyãna, Lycian water-nymphs, than as Greek Nereids.

The tomb is thought to have stood until the Byzantine era and then to have been destroyed by local Christians for its stones and metals. An expedition led by the British archaeologist Charles Fellows, which included George Scharf, found the ruins in the early 1840s, and Fellows at first took the monument for that of Harpagus, the 6th-century BCE conqueror of Lycia. Its style soon showed it to be at least a century later, but only in the late 20th century did scholars agree on its date and its probable owner.

Lacking records of where each piece was found, the British Museum relied on drawings, marks on the stones and style to place the blocks; its reconstruction of the east façade dates from 1969 and stands in room 17.
neretva: The Neretva, also called the Narenta, is the largest karst river of the Dinaric Alps. Of its 225 kilometres, 208 are in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the last 22 in Dubrovnik-Neretva County in Croatia. The upper course rises at the foot of Zelengora and Lebršnik and cuts gorges 600 to 800 metres deep. Below Jablanica it enters a third canyon, 800 to 1,200 metres deep, between the mountains of Prenj, Čvrsnica and Čabulja. Mostar is the largest town on its banks. Below the confluence of the Trebižat and Bregava the valley spreads into an alluvial fan of 20,000 hectares, and the river splits into several branches to form a delta.

In antiquity the river was known as Narenta, Narona and Naro, and finds of Illyrian culture, among them ancient shipwrecks at Hutovo Blato, show daily and religious life along it. At Mogorjelo near Čapljina stood a suburban villa of the 4th century with mills, bakeries, an olive oil refinery and forges, destroyed in the middle of that century during an invasion of western Goths; a church dedicated to Hermagor was built on its ruins at the end of the 5th.

In 1557 the Ottoman sultan Suleiman commissioned the Old Bridge at Mostar to replace a wooden suspension bridge, designed by Mimar Hayruddin, a student of Sinan. Its inscription dates its completion to 974 AH, between 19 July 1566 and 7 July 1567. Artillery fire destroyed it on 9 November 1993, and it was rebuilt under UNESCO from 1,088 stones and opened on 23 July 2004. In early 1943 some 20,000 Partisans under Josip Broz Tito were caught with their backs to the river near Jablanica while they struggled to save some 4,500 wounded and typhus patients from some 150,000 Axis troops.

Four large dams on the main stream supply electricity, flood protection and water storage, and the lake at Jablanica, made in 1953, flooded a fertile valley known simply as Neretva since the Middle Ages. In Croatia land reclamation has reduced the delta's twelve branches to three. The delta has been a Ramsar site since 1992 and Hutovo Blato, now a nature park, since 2001. The basin shelters many endemic fish, including three species of trout.
neriglissar: Neriglissar, in Akkadian Nergal-šar-uṣur, meaning Nergal, protect the king, was the fourth king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. He was unrelated to earlier Babylonian kings and may have been of Aramean ancestry. His own inscriptions call him the son of Bel-shum-ishkun, who was probably a man of the Aramean clan of the Puqudu. Under Nebuchadnezzar II he was an active businessman and landowner, with estates at Sippar and Uruk, one of the king's leading officials with the title Simmagir, and an army officer of the rank rab māg.

He married one of Nebuchadnezzar's daughters, possibly Kashshaya, a proposal made by David B. Weisberg in 1974 that later historians have accepted. She may have been older than any of the king's sons, so Neriglissar may have stood for a wealthier and better established branch of the family, set against the younger and more legitimate branch of Amel-Marduk.

The last document dated to Amel-Marduk is a contract of 7 August 560 BCE; four days later documents are dated to Neriglissar. The Babylonian writer Berossus says Neriglissar plotted against Amel-Marduk, who had ruled capriciously, and had him killed. To secure his position Neriglissar married his daughter Gigitum to Nabu-shuma-ukin, administrator of the Ezida temple in Borsippa. He continued work on the Esagila, the main temple of Babylon, and repaired the royal palace and the bank of the Euphrates.

In his third year, 557 BCE, he marched into Anatolia after rumours that Appuwashu, king of Pirindu, planned to raid Syria. Neriglissar defeated Appuwashu's ambush, pursued him through mountainous country to his capital Ura and sacked it, then destroyed the city of Kirshu. The contemporary chronicle says he took the island of Pitusu by boat and set fires along the passes towards Lydia. Appuwashu escaped, but Pirindu became a buffer state between the Babylonian, Lydian and Median realms.

Neriglissar turned for home in February 556 BCE. The last documents of his reign date from 12 and 16 April 556 BCE, and the Uruk King List gives him three years and eight months. His son Labashi-Marduk succeeded him but was deposed and killed after two or three months in a coup, and Nabonidus took the throne. The reasons are unclear; perhaps the family was seen as commoners without noble blood. Neriglissar was nonetheless remembered favourably, and Nabonidus names him with Nebuchadnezzar as a good king.
nerik: Nerik lay to the north of the Hittite capitals Hattusa and Sapinuwa, probably in the Pontic region. Excavations from 2005 to 2009 led to its identification with Oymaağaç Höyük, on the eastern side of the Kızılırmak River, 7 km northwest of Vezirköprü. The site was occupied in the Middle and Late Bronze Age. Its storm god, held to be the son of Wurušemu, the Sun-goddess of Arinna, was associated with Mount Zaliyanu near the city, which was believed to bring it rain.

Nerik was founded by speakers of the Hattic language under the name Narak, and a tablet of the Hattusa archive, CTH 737, records a Hattic incantation for a festival there. The Hittites took the city under Hattusili I and kept up a spring festival there, the Puruli, in honour of the Storm-god of Nerik, at which the myth of the slaying of the serpent Illuyanka was recited. The Hittites blamed the Kaska for the city's ruin, and the Puruli festival had to be moved to Hattusa; by the reign of Tudhaliya I the Kaska occupied the site.

In the reign of Muwatalli II his brother and governor Hattusili III recaptured Nerik and rebuilt it as its High Priest, naming his firstborn son Nerikkaili after it, although he later passed him over for the succession. Seven years after Muwatalli's son Mursili III became king, Mursili gave Nerik to another governor, and Hattusili rebelled and took the throne himself. Nerik disappears from the record with the fall of the Hittite kingdom, around 1200 BCE.

Rainer Maria Czichon and Jörg Klinger of the Free University of Berlin began excavating Oymaağaç Höyük in 2005. It is the northernmost place in Anatolia with remains of the Hittite Empire: fragments of tablets, a bulla with the stamps of the scribe Sarini, traces suggesting monumental architecture and mining tools for the copper of nearby Tavşan Mountain. Cuneiform tablets found there point to the site as Nerik, and an inventory lists silver trays and golden bullae kept in a shrine.
nerio-i-acciaioli: Nerio, in full Rainerio, was the second son of Jacobo Acciaioli and Bartolomea Riccasoli, of a Florentine banking family that lent to the Angevin kings of Naples and managed their finances in Frankish Greece. In 1360 his kinsman Niccolò Acciaioli sent him to the Peloponnese, and in 1362 adopted him as his son. Nerio bought the Achaean baronies of Vostitza and Nivelet for 6,000 ducats, and after Niccolò's death in 1365 took Corinth on mortgage from Niccolò's son Angelo, who never redeemed it. In 1372 Pope Gregory XI called him lord of the town of Corinth.

With the help of its burghers Nerio took Megara, which controlled the road to Thebes and Athens, in late 1374 or early 1375. He encouraged the Navarrese Company to invade the Duchy of Athens in 1379 and later gained Thebes and Livadeia from them. To resist the Navarrese he allied with Theodore I Palaiologos, Despot of the Morea, who married his elder daughter Bartolomea. In 1385 his forces occupied much of Attica and Boeotia, but the Acropolis held out until 2 May 1388. Nerio then appointed Italian and Greek officials, made Greek the language of government and let the Orthodox archbishop live in the lower town.

His seizure of Nauplia brought conflict with Venice, which bought Argos and Nauplia from Maria of Enghien in December 1388. On 10 September 1389 the Navarrese commander Pedro de San Superano seized Nerio at Vostitza. To win his release in late 1390 he ceded Megara to Venice, sent his daughter Francesca as a hostage and promised to make Theodore give up Argos, which he could not do. His forces took Neopatras from the Catalans before the end of 1390.

After Sultan Bayezid I invaded Thessaly in late 1393 and took Neopatras and Livadeia, Nerio agreed to pay him an annual tribute. On 11 January 1394 Ladislaus of Naples conferred the duchy on Nerio and his legitimate male heirs. In a will of 17 September, which the historian Peter Topping called eccentric, he left Athens to the Church of Saint Mary, the Parthenon, named Francesca his main heiress and gave Thebes and Livadeia to his illegitimate son Antonio. He died on 25 September 1394 and was buried in the Parthenon. His brother Donato soon had to cede Athens to Venice, and Antonio seized the duchy in 1403.
neris: The Neris, called the Viliya in Belarus and the Wilia in Polish, rises in northern Belarus and flows westward. It passes through Vilnius and joins the Nemunas, or Neman, from the right bank at Kaunas, as its main tributary. Its length is 510 km, of which 276 km lie in Belarus and 235 km in Lithuania. The river drains a basin of 25,100 square kilometres, 10,920 of them in Belarus and 13,849 in Lithuania. Its main tributaries in Belarus include the Narač, Servač, Ilija and Ašmianka, and in Lithuania the Vilnia, Verkė, Šventoji and Dūkšta. Belarus's largest reservoir, the Vileyka Reservoir, lies on the Viliya.

The Neris connects successive Lithuanian capitals, Kernavė and Vilnius, and along its banks lie burial places of the pagan Lithuanians, among them the Karmazinai hillfort and burial mound 25 km from Vilnius. The upper river before the 12th century was inhabited by the Balts of the archaeological East Lithuanian Barrow Culture.

The river's two names have a complicated origin. Neris is of Baltic origin, related to the Lithuanian nerti, to dive or swim downstream, and probably once meant a swift, swirling flow. Viliya was formerly Velja, a Slavic word meaning big or great. Place names in Vilnius and Kaunas preserve both, for example Paneriai and Valakampiai in Vilnius and Vilijampolė in Kaunas. One explanation is that the Balts and the Slavs each named the river from the confluence of the Neris, now called the Narač, and the Velja, in the borderland between them. Some linguists instead link Viliya with the Lithuanian words velnias and vėlė.
nero: Nero was born Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus on 15 December 37 at Antium, the only child of Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Agrippina the Younger. His uncle was the reigning emperor Caligula, and through his mother he was a descendant of Augustus. His father died when he was three. By the time he was eleven, his mother had married the emperor Claudius, who adopted him as his heir. When Claudius died in 54, Nero came to the throne at the age of sixteen with the backing of the Praetorian Guard and the Senate.

In his early years Nero was guided by his mother, his tutor Seneca the Younger and the praetorian prefect Sextus Afranius Burrus. His first speech to the Senate, prepared by Seneca, promised to end secret trials and to respect the privileges of senators. Agrippina meant to rule through her son, and the struggle between them ended with her murder in 59. Roman sources also implicate him in the deaths of his stepbrother Britannicus and his wife Claudia Octavia. Modern scholars think the reign went well before Agrippina's death, and a successful expedition explored the sources of the Nile.

The general Corbulo fought the Roman–Parthian War of 58 to 63 and made peace with Parthia. Suetonius Paulinus defeated a major revolt in Britain led by Queen Boudica, who had burned Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium. The Great Fire of Rome began on the night of 18 to 19 July 64 and destroyed three of the city's fourteen districts and severely damaged seven more. Suetonius records a belief that Nero started it to clear land for his Golden House, and Tacitus says he seized Christians as scapegoats and had them burned alive. In 65 a conspiracy led by Gaius Calpurnius Piso failed, and Seneca and the poet Lucan were among those who died. The First Jewish–Roman War began in 66.

In March 68 Gaius Julius Vindex, governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, rebelled against Nero's tax policies and called on Servius Sulpicius Galba to declare himself emperor. Verginius Rufus defeated Vindex at Vesontio in May, but support for Galba grew, the Praetorian prefect Nymphidius Sabinus deserted Nero, and he was declared a public enemy. Nero fled Rome and killed himself in 68, which began the civil wars of the Year of the Four Emperors.

Most surviving sources, chiefly Tacitus, Suetonius and Cassius Dio, are hostile, but none was written during his reign, and some modern historians question their reliability, noting his popularity among ordinary Romans. In the eastern provinces a legend arose that he had not died, and at least three leaders of short-lived rebellions presented themselves as Nero reborn.
nero-claudius-drusus: Drusus was the younger son of Livia Drusilla and her first husband, Tiberius Claudius Nero, who was legally declared his father before the couple divorced. He was born between mid-March and mid-April 38 BCE, three months after Livia married Augustus. Rumours that Augustus was the real father arose, though Livia was already pregnant when she met him. Drusus was raised in his legal father's house with his brother Tiberius, and the two remained close. He married Antonia Minor, the daughter of Mark Antony and Augustus' sister Octavia, and they had Germanicus, Claudius, a daughter named Livilla and at least two children who did not survive childhood.

In 19 BCE Drusus was allowed to hold public offices five years before the minimum age. As quaestor he fought Raetian raiders in the Alps, and in late 15 BCE he became governor of the three Gaulish provinces, with his base at Lugdunum. There he founded the council of the Gaulish provinces, and in 10 BCE he inaugurated the altar of Rome and Augustus at Condate.

From 14 BCE he built military bases along the Rhine and allied with the Batavi. In 12 BCE he sailed from near Nijmegen along canals built for the purpose to the mouth of the Ems, where the Chauci accepted Roman supremacy. In 11 BCE he ascended the Lippe, defeated the Tencteri and Usipetes and survived a Cheruscan ambush at Arbalo, after which his men acclaimed him imperator. In 10 BCE he drove back the Chatti and Sicambri. As consul in 9 BCE he led the army through the lands of the Marsi and Cherusci and crossed the Elbe, where he set up a trophy. The sources suggest he may have won the spolia opima, but he died before any ceremony.

On the return from the Elbe Drusus fell from his horse. He survived the fall, but infection set in and he died about a month later, with Tiberius at his side. His ashes were placed in the Mausoleum of Augustus. The Senate granted him the hereditary title Germanicus, which passed to his sons and was later borne by Caligula and Nero. His soldiers raised the Drususstein at Mogontiacum, now Mainz, and parts of it still stand.

Historian Michael McNally considers him the ablest of the Roman commanders who tried to conquer Germania. His death slowed Roman expansion, and after the loss of Publius Quinctilius Varus's army in the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest the Rhine became the de facto border of the empire. When his son Claudius became emperor in 41 CE, new honours were voted to Drusus, including annual games on 14 January.
nervion: The Nervión, called Nerbioi in Basque, runs 72 kilometres from its source at the provincial limits of Burgos and Álava to the sea, flowing from south to north. Soon after its source it forms the Nervión Waterfall in the Delika canyon in Álava, and it then enters the province of Biscay through the city of Orduña. It re-enters Álava through the towns of Amurrio and Llodio before running back into Biscay and entering the Bilbao metropolitan area at Ugao-Miraballes.

Its main tributaries are the Cadagua and Galindo from the west and the Arratia, Ibaizabal and Asua from the east. The basin covers 1,900 square kilometres. The tide reaches 15 kilometres inland, to Bilbao's old town. Some regard the Ibaizabal as an equally important river, so the whole system is often called Nervión-Ibaizabal, and the final stretch is just the Estuary of Bilbao.

The traditional name of the stretch between the estuary and Basauri, where the Ibaizabal and Nervión merge, is Ibaizabal, meaning wide river in Basque, according to evidence from the eleventh century to the twentieth. Miguel de Unamuno and the Bilbao mayor Javier Ybarra also called it the Ibaizabal.

The Orduña pass, which links Spain's inner plateau with the Nervión valley, has had a great economic effect since ancient times. In the Middle Ages it served as a natural border between the Biscay lordship and the counties of Castile, and tolls were collected there. The valley was a vital corridor for Biscay, and the main rail line from Bilbao to the rest of Spain was built along the river in 1870.

Bilbao's seaport, the most important on the north coast of Spain, depended on the navigability of the final 15 kilometres of the river. The engineer Evaristo Churruca drew up a large project to solve the river's traditional navigation problems. The estuary divided Greater Bilbao: the Left Bank held steel, smelting and shipbuilding factories and their workers, and the Right Bank was a residential area for the factory owners.

After a century of intense industrial activity the lower river, especially the final 25 kilometres, was ecologically dead. In 1990 the local authorities began a plan of sanitation, and over about fifteen years the river became clean and full of aquatic life as the most polluting industries disappeared. As heavy industry withdrew, the navigable part of the river was given up in favour of the sea port, which freed the banks for urban development.
nestor-kirchner: Néstor Kirchner was born on 25 February 1950 in Río Gallegos, then a federal territory. His mother, María Juana Ostoich Dragnic, was Chilean and of Croatian descent. He studied law at the National University of La Plata, where he met Cristina Fernández, and the couple returned to Río Gallegos to open a law firm. He ran for mayor of Río Gallegos in 1987 and for governor of Santa Cruz in 1991. Although he received only 30 percent of the vote, below the 36 percent of the UCR, the Ley de Lemas added the votes of another Peronist faction to his own and he was elected. He was reelected in 1995 and 1999 after an amendment to the provincial constitution.

Eduardo Duhalde, appointed president by Congress after the December 2001 riots, urged Kirchner to run in 2003 to prevent Carlos Menem's return. Menem won a plurality in the first round but resigned, fearing defeat in the runoff, and Kirchner took office on 25 May 2003. He kept Roberto Lavagna as minister of economy. Argentina negotiated a swap of its defaulted debt and repaid the International Monetary Fund. Several Supreme Court judges, among them its president Julio Nazareno, resigned while facing impeachment, and new judges were appointed.

Kirchner regarded the Dirty War as an unresolved issue. Congress annulled the full stop and due obedience laws in August 2003, and in 2005 the Supreme Court declared them and Menem's presidential pardons unconstitutional, so that many cases against the military were reopened. In foreign policy he opposed the proposed Free Trade Area of the Americas and sent forces to Haiti. In the 2005 midterm elections his wife Cristina Fernández de Kirchner defeated Hilda González de Duhalde in the election for senator for Buenos Aires Province.

Kirchner did not seek reelection in 2007, and his wife ran and was elected. He stayed influential, leading the PJ, and in December 2007 took part in Operation Emmanuel in Colombia, which sought the release of FARC hostages. He was narrowly defeated in the 2009 midterm election for deputy of Buenos Aires Province and was appointed Secretary General of UNASUR in 2010.

Kirchner died of cardiac arrest on 27 October 2010 at the age of 60, at home in El Calafate. He had undergone surgery on a carotid artery in February and an angioplasty in September. His body was flown to the Casa Rosada for a state funeral, and three national days of mourning were declared.
nestor-lakoba: Lakoba was born on 1 May 1893 in the village of Lykhny to a peasant family. His father died three months before his birth. He entered the Tiflis Seminary in 1905 but was expelled in 1911 for revolutionary activity, and in Batumi he began working with the Bolsheviks, joining them officially in September 1912. He was nearly deaf and wore hearing aids all his life, and Stalin jokingly called him Adagua, the Deaf One. In 1918 he and Efrem Eshba overthrew the Abkhaz People's Council twice, but Georgian forces defeated the Bolshevik rebels and both men fled to Russia.

Lakoba headed the government of Soviet Abkhazia as chairman of the Council of People's Commissars until 17 April 1930, and afterwards as chairman of the Central Executive Committee of the Abkhaz Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic. A commission of 1925 reported that his administration pursued Abkhazification, favouring ethnic Abkhaz, who were only 25 to 30 percent of the population. He promoted coal mining, roads, railways, malaria drainage and schools, and by the 1930s Abkhazia supplied up to 52 percent of the Soviet Union's tobacco exports.

His friendship with Stalin, who holidayed in Abkhazia, let him delay collectivisation, and a report of 1929 calling for his removal was stopped by Stalin. By January 1931 the party forced collectivisation through, provoking large protests, and Lakoba could only soften its harshest measures and stop mass deportations. He had supported the rise of Lavrentiy Beria, who then worked against him, and in December 1935 he refused Stalin's offer of the leadership of the NKVD.

On 26 December 1936 Beria summoned Lakoba to Tbilisi. After a dinner the next day, at which he was served a glass of poisoned wine according to the account, Lakoba showed signs of poisoning at the opera and died early on 28 December. The official cause was a heart attack, and his internal organs were removed before his body returned to Sukhumi. He was then accused of nationalist deviationism. Nine of thirteen relatives tried in 1937 were shot, including his two brothers, and his wife Sariya died in prison in 1939 and his son Rauf was shot in 1941. Lakoba was rehabilitated in 1953, and in Abkhazia he is revered as a hero.
nestor-makhno: Makhno was born in Huliaipole, then in the Katerynoslav Governorate, on 7 November 1888, the youngest of five children of former serfs. His father died when he was ten months old. In the 1905 revolution, at sixteen, he joined the revolutionary movement and became a member of the Union of Poor Peasants, an anarchist communist group in his home town. On 26 March 1910 a court-martial sentenced him to hang, but because of his youth the sentence was commuted to life at hard labour. In Butyrka prison in Moscow he read Peter Kropotkin's Mutual Aid and contracted tuberculosis.

Makhno returned to Huliaipole in March 1917 and was elected chairman of a Peasants' Union, which soon represented most of the peasantry of the district. In 1918 the German and Austro-Hungarian occupation forces took Huliaipole. Makhno returned secretly in July and launched an insurgency. At the Dibrivka forest he and Fedir Shchus broke an Austrian encirclement with a surprise counterattack, and the insurgents gave him the title Bat'ko, Father.

He allied with the Red Army against the Whites, but his movement and the Bolsheviks quarrelled over its autonomy. In 1919 he denounced the otaman Nykyfor Hryhoriv for pogroms. After the Battle of Perehonivka he routed the White Army and his forces held most of southern and eastern Ukraine, where they again tried to establish anarchist communism. A short-lived alliance with the Bolsheviks drove Wrangel's forces out of Crimea. In late November 1920 the Red Army attacked the Makhnovists by surprise and besieged Huliaipole, and Makhno escaped with his Black Guards and retook the town a week later.

In July 1921 Mikhail Frunze demanded the definitive liquidation of the Makhnovist movement. Wounded, Makhno crossed into Romania in August 1921 with his wife Halyna and about 100 followers and was interned. He reached Paris in April 1925, worked briefly in a foundry and a Renault factory, and wrote memoirs and articles for radical newspapers. Illness and depression marked his last years, and he quarrelled with Ida Mett and Volin over his memoirs. He died of tuberculosis on 25 July 1934, aged 45.

Makhnovist groups worked clandestinely through the 1920s, and some fought as partisans in World War II. Anarchists cite him as an inspiration, and in Huliaipole a statue of him stands in the main square and a museum has an exhibition devoted to him.
netherlands-trading-society: The Nederlandsche Handel-Maatschappij, or NHM, was established by royal decree in The Hague in 1824 to promote trade, shipping and agriculture, above all between the Netherlands and the Dutch East Indies. It was a private company with publicly traded shares. Its founding was an attempt to bring new life to that trade after the depression of the years of French domination, 1795-1814, and the collapse of the Dutch East India Company two decades earlier, so that it is sometimes called the VOC's successor. With a playful nod to the older company's greatness it was known as Kompenie Ketjil, the little company.

In 1826 the NHM opened an office in Batavia, now Jakarta, known as De Factorij. Financing trade and shipping led it into banking: it moved overseas into banking in the 1870s and began banking in the Netherlands in 1902. Branches followed in Singapore in 1858, Penang in 1888, Hong Kong in 1906, and Bombay and Calcutta in 1920, these chiefly for the diamond trade. Its branch in Jeddah, opened in 1926 to serve Indonesian Muslims making the Hajj, was the first commercial bank in the kingdom and until 1948 the only one.

In 1934 a financial restructuring cut its capital by 75 percent. It opened an agency in New York in 1941, became in 1948 the first foreign bank licensed by the new government of Pakistan, and in 1951 and 1954 opened branches in Mombasa, Dar-es-Salaam, Kampala and Beirut. The Indonesian government nationalised its plantations in 1959 and its banking operations in 1960, forming Bank Ekspor Impor Indonesia, later Bank Mandiri.

In 1964 the NHM merged with De Twentsche Bank to form Algemene Bank Nederland, a predecessor of ABN AMRO. Its former headquarters at Vijzelstraat 32 in Amsterdam, built in 1919-1926 and named De Bazel after its architect Karel de Bazel, is decorated with details recalling Indonesia, and its brickwork earned it the nickname spekkoek. The building now houses the Amsterdam Archives.
neubrandenburg: Neubrandenburg stands on the shore of the lake Tollensesee in the south-east of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and forms the urban centre of the Mecklenburg Lakeland. It is part of the European Route of Brick Gothic, which leads through seven countries along the Baltic Sea coast, and is nicknamed the City of Four Gates, Stadt der Vier Tore, for its medieval gates. Its Low German name is Niegenbramborg, meaning New Brandenburg.

The region was left largely empty during the Migration Period and was resettled by Slavs, who formed the Veleti, from the 7th century. After the Saxons subdued the area in the mid-12th century, German colonisation intensified after 1200. Premonstratensian monks founded Broda Abbey on the lakeshore about 1240. The city was founded in 1248, when the Margrave of Brandenburg decided to build a settlement in the northern part of his fief and named it after the older city of Brandenburg to the south. The city later became part of Mecklenburg.

It flourished as a trade centre until the Thirty Years' War. Swedish troops garrisoned it during the advance of Gustavus Adolphus, but forces of the Imperial Catholic League retook it in 1631 and were widely reported to have killed many Swedish and Scottish soldiers as they surrendered. From 1701 to 1934 Neubrandenburg belonged to Mecklenburg-Strelitz. The writer Fritz Reuter lived there from 1856 to 1863, and a railway joined it to Berlin in 1864.

In the Second World War two prisoner-of-war camps, Stalag II-A and Oflag II-E/67, stood at Fünfeichen within the city limits. A few days before the war ended in 1945, the Red Army burned down about 80 per cent of the old town, including the City Hall, the Grand Ducal Palace and St Mary's Church. In East Germany the centre was rebuilt in the 1950s and 1960s, and in 1952 the city became the centre of a Bezirk. Its population rose from about 20,000 at the war's end to about 90,000 in the late 1980s.

Neubrandenburg has kept its medieval city wall entire: it is 7 metres high with a perimeter of 2.3 kilometres and four Brick Gothic gates from the 14th and 15th centuries, among them the Stargarder Tor. St Mary's Church, completed in 1298, was restored in 1975 and houses a concert hall opened in 2001. The city has been the capital of the Mecklenburgische Seenplatte district since 2011 and has a University of Applied Sciences, founded in 1991. Its population is about 65,000.
neuburg-an-der-donau: Neuburg an der Donau is the capital of the Neuburg-Schrobenhausen district in Bavaria and is more than 1,200 years old. People have lived on the hill where the palace now stands since the Bronze Age. A Roman settlement on the high hill above the Danube formed part of the Limes, the frontier between the Empire and its Germanic enemies. The municipality has 16 divisions, among them Bergen, Bittenbrunn, Joshofen and Zell. Munich Airport is 82 km away.

The Aiglolfings built a massive castle in the early Middle Ages on the site of the old Roman fortress. Neuburg was part of an episcopal see, and in the 10th century it passed to the counts of Scheyern and through them to Bavaria. It was ceded to the Rhenish Palatinate at the close of a war. For a time it was the capital of a small principality, Palatinate-Neuburg, ruled by a cadet branch of the family of the elector palatine of the Rhine, with an area of about 2,600 square kilometres and about 100,000 inhabitants. During the Thirty Years' War Swedish troops conquered and occupied the town several times between 1632 and 1634 while crossing the Danube.

In 1742 the principality was united again with the Rhenish Palatinate, with which it passed to Bavaria in 1777. In 1800, during the War of the Second Coalition, the French army defeated Austrian troops at the Battle of Neuburg. The town was bombed by the Allies in April 1943 and liberated by the US Army in late April 1945. On 30 June 1972 it became a Grosse Kreisstadt, similar to a county seat.

A defensive wall surrounds the old town. The Renaissance ducal palace, Neuburg Castle, was built in 1530-45 under Otto Henry, Elector Palatine, and took its present form under Philip William, Elector Palatine. It houses several museums, including a Baroque gallery of the Bavarian State Picture Collection and an archaeology museum. Other sights are the late Renaissance court church, built in 1607/08 by Josef Heintz, the Town Hall of 1603/09, the rococo Provincial Library of 1731/32, and the baroque churches of St Peter and St Ursula. Grünau, a Renaissance hunting lodge of Otto Henry, stands 7 km further east.
neuchatel: The French and German names, Neuchâtel and Neuenburg, both mean new castle, from the Old French neu and châtel. The castle after which the city is named was built by Rudolph III of Burgundy, who presented it to his wife Ermengarde in 1011, as the Latin Novum castellum. Human traces in the area are much older. The oldest is a Magdalenian hunting camp dated to 13,000 BCE, found at Monruz in 1990. Three tiny lignite earrings found there are thought to be the oldest known art in Switzerland. Gallo-Roman baths of the 2nd and 3rd centuries were found at the mouth of the Serrière in 1908, and a Merovingian cemetery at Serrières held 38 graves of the 7th century.

Neuchâtel was originally part of the Kingdom of Burgundy and was absorbed into the Holy Roman Empire in 1033. At the time of Rudolph's gift it was probably the centre of a newly created royal court. The domain of the counts of Neuchâtel was first called a city in 1214. For three centuries the county flourished. In 1530 its people accepted the Reformation, and the city and territory were proclaimed indivisible, so that future rulers had to seek investiture from the citizens.

The city came under Prussian control in 1707. In the Treaty of Paris of 15 February 1806 Prussia ceded the principality to Napoleon, as part of a bargain over Hanover in which Napoleon forced Prussia to give up more than it had hoped. Napoleon's marshal Berthier became Prince of Neuchâtel and built roads and restored infrastructure, but never set foot in his domain. After Napoleon's fall Frederick William III of Prussia reasserted his rights, and the city remained Prussian until 1848, when Neuchâtel became a republic.

Neuchâtel is the capital of its canton, with about 45,000 inhabitants since the merger of 2021 with Corcelles-Cormondrèche, Peseux and Valangin. It is a centre of the Swiss watch industry and is home to the French-speaking University of Neuchâtel. The entire old city is listed in the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites. Its Hôtel de Ville dates from 1790, and the Laténium museum is devoted to regional prehistory, particularly the La Tène culture.
neukamerun: Theodor Seitz, governor of Kamerun from 1907, had argued for taking territory from the French Congo. The occasion came with the Agadir Crisis of 1911 over French influence in Morocco. France and Germany agreed to negotiate on 9 July 1911 and signed an agreement on 4 November. In return for recognising France's rights in Morocco and handing over a strip of north-eastern Kamerun near Fort Lamy, between the Logone and Chari rivers, Germany received part of the French Congo. The Congo River was Germany's only major river outlet from Central Africa, and the new lands were meant to improve its access to it.

The cession gave Kamerun one corridor to the Congo along the Sangha River and another to the Ubangi at the town of Zinga, with a small strip of French territory enclosed between the two. A strip of northern Gabon was also included, which left the Spanish colony of Rio Muni surrounded. The colony grew from 465,000 km2 to 760,000 km2 and became known as Grand Kamerun, with Otto Gleim as governor. The handover took two years and was completed when the Ouham Region of Ubangi-Shari was transferred on 1 June 1913.

The exchange was debated in Germany, where opponents argued that the new lands offered little chance of commercial profit, and the colonial secretary eventually resigned over the matter. During World War I, France, eager to recover the territories, seized them in 1916 after the German forces in the region fell. After the war France governed Cameroun as a League of Nations mandate separate from French Equatorial Africa, and the boundary returned to its line before 1911, except that the strip between the Logone and Chari stayed with French Equatorial Africa. The lands of Neukamerun now lie in Chad, the Central African Republic, the Republic of the Congo and Gabon.
neum: Neum is the only town on the 20-kilometre coastline of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and so the country's only access to the Adriatic Sea. It is enclosed by the Klek Peninsula, lies 47 km north-west of Dubrovnik, 50 km south of Mostar and 122 km south-west of Sarajevo, and cuts off the southernmost Croatian exclave from the rest of Croatia.

The Neum corridor dates to the Treaty of Karlowitz of 1699, which separated the Republic of Ragusa from the Dalmatian possessions of Venice by two buffer zones ceded to the Ottoman Empire: Neum and the bay of Klek to the north, and Sutorina with Herceg Novi to the south. The borders were reaffirmed in 1718 by the Treaty of Passarowitz. After the fall of Venice in 1797 and the Congress of Vienna in 1815, the Austrian Empire tried in vain to buy the enclaves back from the Ottomans, and stationed a warship to block access to the port of Neum until the Treaty of Berlin gave Bosnia and Herzegovina to Austria-Hungary in 1878.

The Austro-Hungarian Navy considered a naval base at Neum-Klek, with coastal batteries proposed by General Franz Conrad von Hötzendorf, but the project never passed the planning stage before 1914. In 1918 Neum joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, renamed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929. Josip Broz Tito's federal Yugoslavia founded its republics on their borders of 1878, declared at the 1943 AVNOJ session in Jajce, which is why the enclave belongs to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since 1991 its border with Croatia has been an international border.

The municipality had 4,653 inhabitants in 2013, 3,013 of them in the town. Croats form most of the population, followed by Bosniaks and Serbs. Tourism is the leading contributor to the local economy, with about 7,000 beds for visitors and several large hotels. Since Croatia joined the European Union in 2013 the two crossings on the Adriatic Highway have been external borders of the Union. The Pelješac Bridge, opened in 2022, bypasses Neum.
neumark: The Neumark, also called East Brandenburg, was bounded by the Oder to the west and south, by Pomerania to the north and by Greater Poland to the east. The Warta and Noteć rivers and their marshes dominated its landscape. Its towns included Landsberg, Soldin, Küstrin, Arnswalde, Friedeberg and Königsberg in the New March, and it long remained a land of agriculture and forestry, its middling towns mostly farmer-citizen towns.

In the 10th century the area came under the first Polish state of Mieszko I and Bolesław I and became the Lubusz Land. From the 1230s Low German colonists settled along the Warta and Noteć at the invitation of Pomeranian and Polish lords. The Ascanian margraves of Brandenburg had a foothold east of the Oder by 1242, bought the Lubusz Land with the Archbishopric of Magdeburg in 1252, and extended their hold through purchases and marriages; Margrave John I founded Landsberg an der Warthe in 1257. The land across the Oder came to be called the New March after the middle of the 15th century.

After the Ascanians died out in 1320 the region was neglected under the Wittelsbach and Luxembourg margraves, as it later was under the Teutonic Knights. From 1535 to 1571 it was the separate margraviate of Brandenburg-Küstrin under John, a younger son of Elector Joachim I Nestor, who made it Lutheran and moved his seat to Küstrin in 1548. In the Thirty Years' War Swedish and imperial troops ravaged it, and plague struck in 1626 and 1631. Under the Kingdom of Prussia Huguenot settlers and textile industry came, Frederick II drained the Warta and Noteć lowlands, and after 1815 most of it joined the Frankfurt region of the Province of Brandenburg.

In 1939 the Neumark had 645,000 inhabitants. The Red Army reached it at the end of January 1945, and civilians who had not fled in time suffered greatly. Under the Potsdam terms the region was placed under Polish administration and its Germans were expelled; by 1950 over 95 per cent of the people were newcomers, most of them Poles expelled from the eastern lands annexed by the Soviet Union. Since 1999 almost all of the former Neumark lies in the Lubusz Voivodeship, while villages west of the regulated Oder remained in Germany.
neumarkt-in-der-oberpfalz: Neumarkt is the capital of the Neumarkt district in the Upper Palatinate and has about 40,000 inhabitants. It lies in a valley on the western edge of the Franconian Jura. The valley floor is mostly sandy, which gave the earlier name Neumarkt auf dem Sand. The Ludwig Canal runs north to south through the area and crosses the European water divide. Traces of settlement go back to the Neolithic period, and the surroundings hold burial mounds and Celtic embankments.

The town is assumed to have been first founded by the Bavarii in the 6th or 7th century, and its founding as a new market on the trade route between Nuremberg and Regensburg is assumed to date from the early 12th century. It was first mentioned in a document in 1135. The city fell to the Wittelsbachs in 1329 through the Treaty of Pavia. In the 15th century Count Johann von Pfalz-Neumarkt made it the seat of his government and built the church of St Johannes, the Court Chapel and a castle. His successors were Otto I, his son Otto II and Frederick II, who later became Elector and moved to Heidelberg. After they left, the town lost much of its importance.

Swedish troops occupied it from 1633 to 1635 and from 1646 to 1649 and plundered it twice. The Ludwig Canal, built from 1830 to 1846, made Neumarkt a port, and the Express-Werke, established in 1884, were continental Europe's first bicycle factory. In 1934 the town took the added name Dietrich-Eckart-city, in memory of Dietrich Eckart, a founder of the Nazi Party born there. Air raids on 23 February and 11 April 1945 largely destroyed the town; a direct hit on the station bunker killed 400 people. American troops captured it on 22 April 1945 after a house-to-house battle with SS troops. On 1 June 1972 it became the district seat.

The Lammsbräu Brewery is in the town. Neumarkt's natives include Christopher of Bavaria, King of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, who was probably born there, and Otto II, Count Palatine of Mosbach-Neumarkt, a bridesman at the Landshut Wedding, astronomer and mathematician. The monument to Eckart in the city park has since been rededicated to Christopher.
neuschwanstein-castle: Neuschwanstein stands in Schwangau in the Swabia region of Bavaria, above the village of Hohenschwangau. Ludwig's father, King Maximilian II, bought the ruined castle of Schwanstein in 1832 and replaced it with the neo-Gothic Hohenschwangau Castle, finished in 1837, where Ludwig, born in 1845, spent much of his childhood. Above it stood the ruins of two medieval castles, which Ludwig sketched in his diary in 1859. When he became king in 1864 a new palace there became the first of his building projects; it was named New Hohenschwangau Castle and renamed Neuschwanstein only after his death.

The design drew on castle Romanticism and on Ludwig's enthusiasm for the operas of Richard Wagner. Two journeys in 1867 gave detailed inspiration: one in May to the reconstructed Wartburg near Eisenach, the setting of Wagner's Tannhäuser, and one in July to the Château de Pierrefonds, which Eugène Viollet-le-Duc was turning into a historicist palace for Napoleon III.

The medieval ruins were demolished in 1868 and the foundation stone was laid on 5 September 1869. Eduard Riedel drew the plans in the Neo-Romanesque style; Georg von Dollmann took over the civil works in 1874 and Julius Hofmann the project in 1884. The king moved into the Palas in 1884. Ludwig paid for the palace from his private means and by borrowing, not from public funds. Its cost in his lifetime was 6.2 million gold marks, almost twice the first estimate.

The palace was fitted with the latest technology of its time, among it a battery-powered bell system for servants, telephone lines, running warm water and toilets with automatic flushing. Murals pay homage to the legend of Lohengrin, the Swan Knight. If completed it would have had more than 200 rooms, but no more than about 15 rooms and halls were finished.

Ludwig II died in 1886 with the castle unfinished. The keep of 90 metres planned for the upper courtyard was never built, and work on other parts continued afterwards in simplified form. The palace was opened to the public shortly after his death. Because of its secluded position it survived both world wars. Until 1944 it served as a depot for art looted from France by the Nazi organisation known as the Einsatzstab Reichsleiter Rosenberg, and in April 1945 the SS considered blowing it up, a plan that was not carried out. Since 2025 it has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site covering the palaces of King Ludwig II. Neuschwanstein is a symbol of the Romantic era and inspired Disneyland's Sleeping Beauty Castle.
neuse-river: The Neuse is formed by the confluence of the Flat and Eno rivers near Durham, in the Piedmont, and enters the Falls Lake reservoir in northern Wake County, where its fall-line shoals, the Falls of the Neuse, now lie submerged. About 275 miles (443 km) long, it is the longest river entirely within North Carolina, and its basin of 5,630 square miles also lies wholly inside the state. It flows past Raleigh, Smithfield, Goldsboro and Kinston to New Bern, where the Trent River joins it, and enters Pamlico Sound near Hobucken.

Like other rivers of the coastal plain, the lower Neuse runs through bottomland swamp, but near Goldsboro it cuts a narrow gorge of 30 metres through limestone and sandstone at the Cliffs of the Neuse. Its flow swings between floods that spill over its banks and droughts that leave a trickle that can be forded on foot.

Indigenous peoples lived along the river for thousands of years, and archaeological studies have found waves of settlement. Explorers named the river after the Neusiok people, and the name is among the three oldest surviving English-applied place names in the U.S., in use since the first Raleigh expeditions. Arthur Barlowe and Phillip Amadas, sent by Sir Walter Raleigh, landed on the North Carolina coast on 2 July 1584, and in their report to Raleigh wrote of the country Neusiok, situated upon a goodly river called Neuse.

In 1865, during the American Civil War, the Confederates burned the ironclad Ram Neuse, one of the last they had built, when low water kept it from passing downriver. Its remains were found nearly a century later in another dry spell, raised in 1963 and set beside the river at the Governor Caswell Memorial in Kinston.

The Quaker Neck Dam, built in 1952 to hold cooling water for a power plant, was removed in May 1998, opening 127 kilometres of the main river to migrating fish. The Neuse River Trail, a greenway of 34.5 miles, runs from Falls Lake Dam in Raleigh to Clayton. Wastewater, stormwater runoff and nutrient pollution have caused water-quality problems in the estuary.
neustrelitz: Neustrelitz lies on the shore of the Zierker See in the Mecklenburg Lake District, in the Mecklenburgische Seenplatte district of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Its name, New Strelitz, refers to the older town of Strelitz, whose own name comes from the Polabian word Strelci, meaning archers or shooters. From 1994 until 2011 Neustrelitz was the capital of the district of Mecklenburg-Strelitz.

The village of Strelitz was first mentioned in 1278 and grew into a small town. In the 17th century it belonged to the duchy of Mecklenburg-Güstrow, which ceased to exist after the last duke died in 1695. The Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz was then established in 1701, with a territory that included an exclave around Ratzeburg, now in Schleswig-Holstein. In 1712 the castle and the town of Strelitz burnt down. The duke and his family afterwards lived at their hunting lodge on the Zierker See, and the new town of Neustrelitz was built around it.

Neustrelitz remained the ducal seat until 1918 and was then the capital of the Free State of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. In 1934 that state was merged with Mecklenburg-Schwerin to form the Gau of Mecklenburg. The old town of Strelitz survived the fire as a small village and was absorbed into Neustrelitz in 1931. When Red Army troops of the 2nd Belorussian Front entered the town on 30 April 1945, 681 people committed suicide. During the Nazi period the town's asylum for the mentally ill took part in the mass murder of disabled people and served as a transit station for those judged unfit.

The centre is characterised by Baroque architecture and centres on the Marktplatz, where the Stadtkirche, built from 1768 to 1778, faces the Rathaus of 1841 by Friedrich W. Buttel, a disciple of Karl Friedrich Schinkel. The Baroque palace was destroyed in 1945, but the palace gardens remain, with an 18th-century Orangerie, the neo-Gothic Schloßkirche of 1855 to 1859 and a temple of Hebe. The Louise Temple, built in 1891 in the form of a Greek temple, was meant to house the tomb of Queen Louise of Prussia, born a princess of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. The town has a station on the Berlin Northern Railway with direct connections to Berlin and Rostock.
neutral-confederacy: No name the people used for themselves is known with certainty. Samuel de Champlain called them la Nation neutre in 1615, and his map of 1612 placed the word Chonnonton in their country; some scholars read it as their own name, the people who tend or manage deer, while Conrad E. Heidenreich concluded in 1976 that it almost certainly referred to the Seneca. The Wendat called them Attawandaron, often read as people whose speech is awry, and the Haudenosaunee called them Atirhagenrat. Their nations included the Aondironon, the Wenrehronon and the Ongniaahraronon.

Their villages lay in what is now southwestern Ontario, with concentrations on the Niagara Peninsula and around present-day Hamilton and Milton and one cluster across the Niagara River near Buffalo. A village was used for about 20 years and then left once game and soil were exhausted. They hunted deer, elk, moose, beaver and black bear and caught catfish, whitefish, salmon and trout. The Jesuit Relations of 1652 report that hardly anyone among them was without tattoos.

Their language, extinct for more than three centuries, was Iroquoian and close to Wendat. Jean de Brébeuf and Pierre Joseph Marie Chaumonot judged it different enough to write a separate grammar and dictionary, now lost. Archaeology adds much: the Lawson site in London, Ontario, a fortified village of the 1500s with 19 longhouses, lies beside the Museum of Ontario Archaeology, and the Southwold Earthworks near St. Thomas are a National Historic Site of Canada.

Étienne Brûlé passed through their country around 1615 and spent the winter of 1625–1626 among them. The Recollect priest Joseph de La Roche Daillon lived for five months in 1626–1627 with the chief Souharissen, visited 28 villages and estimated the population at 40,000. Souharissen, whom a report of 1627 called chief of the whole nation, led raids against the Mascouten and died around 1646. An alliance with the Wenrohronon against the Haudenosaunee ended in 1639.

Smallpox and measles had already reduced the Neutrals when the Haudenosaunee, having destroyed the Wendat, declared war on them around 1650. Some survivors were taken into Seneca villages in upstate New York; the Kenjockety family, one of the last to trace its descent to the Neutrals, still lives among the Senecas. The archaeologist Mary Jackes, who studied a burial ground found at Grimsby in 1976, linked the collapse to famine, disease, severe weather and intensifying war.
neuwied: Neuwied lies on the east bank of the Rhine, 12 km north-west of Koblenz, in the north of Rhineland-Palatinate. The railway from Frankfurt am Main to Cologne runs through it. One of the largest Roman castra on the Rhine has been excavated nearby, and Caesar's Rhine bridges are believed to have been built in the area. The inner town stands on a former bed of the Rhine and is at great risk of flooding, so it is one of the very few towns in the region protected by flood-prevention levees.

Count Frederick III of Wied founded Neuwied in 1653 as a fortress on the site of the village of Langendorf, destroyed in the Thirty Years' War. It was meant to be the new residence of the lower county, to secure its only access to the Rhine and to let the impoverished state share in Rhine trade. Because the flood-prone site attracted few settlers, the counts of Wied, especially Frederick III, Frederick William and John Frederick Alexander, granted self-administration and extensive religious tolerance there. Religious refugees came from other German territories, France and Switzerland, and from the middle of the 18th century Calvinists, Lutherans, Catholics, Mennonites, Inspirationalists, Moravian Brethren and Jews all lived in the town.

The newcomers helped the economy to rise in the 18th and 19th centuries. The cabinetmakers Abraham and David Roentgen, who belonged to the Moravian Brethren, and the Mennonite clockmaker Peter Kinzing sent work to courts between Versailles and Saint Petersburg, and John Frederick Alexander's Rasselstein iron rolling mill made Neuwied one of the first industrial locations in Germany. On 18 April 1797 French forces under General Louis Lazare Hoche defeated the Austrians under General Franz von Werneck at the Battle of Neuwied.

The town is the capital of the district of Neuwied and has 13 suburban districts, the largest being Heimbach-Weis. Its population grew from 5,600 in 1831 to 18,000 in 1905 with industrialisation, and reached 63,000 after several communities were incorporated. Neuwied is the native town of the paternal ancestors of John D. Rockefeller, whose family name is traced to the abandoned village of Rockenfeld, now within the municipal territory, and the birthplace of William of Wied, who briefly held the title of King of Albania in 1914. It is twinned with the London Borough of Bromley, Drom HaSharon, Güstrow and Suqian.
neva-river: The Neva is the only river flowing out of Lake Ladoga. It leaves the lake near Shlisselburg and crosses the Neva lowlands to reach Neva Bay in the Gulf of Finland, a course of 74 kilometres, though the shortest distance from source to mouth is 45. Its name is widespread in Finnic languages, where it means poor fen in Finnish, watercourse in Karelian and waterway in Estonian. The river is young. Recent research dates the breakthrough that created it, and the Ivanovo rapids, to 1410–1250 BCE, whereas older books gave about 2000 BCE.

From the 8th to the 13th century the Neva formed a waterway from Scandinavia to the Byzantine Empire, and from the 9th century the area belonged to Veliky Novgorod, which was almost constantly at war with Sweden. On 15 July 1240, at the confluence of the Izhora and the Neva, an army led by the 20-year-old Prince Alexander Yaroslavich defeated a Swedish force that planned an invasion, and he received the name Nevsky. After the Ingrian War of 1610–17 and the Treaty of Stolbovo the river became part of Swedish Ingria, and from 1642 its capital was Nyen, near the Nyenschantz fortress. Financial and religious oppression drove out much of the Orthodox population, and 60 percent of the villages stood empty by 1620.

The Great Northern War of 1700–21 brought the valley into the Russian Empire. Saint Petersburg was founded at the river's mouth on 16 May 1703 and became the capital of Russia in 1712. The river was cleaned, cut with canals and enclosed with embankments, the first of them wooden, begun in 1715 and faced with granite from the early 1760s. The first permanent bridge, the Blagoveshchensky Bridge, opened in 1850.

More than 300 floods have been recorded since 1703, three of them catastrophic: on 10 September 1777, 7 November 1824 and 23 September 1924. Electric tramways ran on the ice each winter from 1895 to 1910. During the Siege of Leningrad, from 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944, German forces captured Shlisselburg and cut the city's land and water communications.

The river flows through Saint Petersburg and the towns of Shlisselburg, Kirovsk and Otradnoye. It is navigable throughout and forms part of the Volga–Baltic Waterway and the White Sea–Baltic Canal. It freezes from early December to early April, and it is the main source of water for Saint Petersburg.
nevada: Nevada is a landlocked state in the Western United States. It borders Idaho to the northeast, Oregon to the northwest, California to the west, Arizona to the southeast and Utah to the east. Almost the whole state lies within the Basin and Range Province, broken up by many north-south mountain ranges with endorheic valleys between them. Nevada comprises most of the Great Basin as well as a large part of the Mojave Desert.

The Sierra Nevada lies in the rain shadow to the west, and Nevada is the driest state in the country. The Humboldt River crosses the north from east to west and ends in the Humboldt Sink near Lovelock. The Walker, Truckee and Carson rivers run eastward from the Sierra Nevada and end in Walker Lake, Pyramid Lake and the Carson Sink. The Colorado River forms much of the boundary with Arizona and drains much of the south.

The earliest inhabitants included the Goshute, Southern Paiute, Mohave and Washoe peoples. Francisco Garcés was the first European in the area, which was claimed as part of the Spanish Empire and belonged to the Viceroyalty of New Spain. It became part of the province of Alta California in 1804, when the Californias were split. After the Mexican War of Independence was won in 1821, Alta California became a territory of Mexico with a small population.

The United States annexed the area in 1848 after its victory in the Mexican-American War, and in 1850 it was incorporated into the New Mexico and Utah territories. The discovery of silver at the Comstock Lode in 1859 caused a population boom and became an impetus for the creation of Nevada Territory out of western Utah Territory in 1861. Nevada became the 36th state on 31 October 1864, the second of two states added to the Union during the Civil War after West Virginia. For that reason it is called the Battle Born State.

In 1940, with just over 110,000 people, Nevada was by far the least populated state. Legalized gambling and lenient marriage and divorce laws then made it a major tourist destination. Las Vegas grew from a gulch of 100 people in 1900 to 10,000 by 1950 and 100,000 by 1970.

The capital is Carson City and the largest city is Las Vegas. The state's name is Spanish for snowy, and its official nickname is the Silver State because of silver's historical importance to its economy. The 2020 census counted 3,104,614 people, nearly three-quarters of them in Clark County, which contains the Las Vegas-Paradise metropolitan area. Tourism is the largest employer, and mining remains a substantial sector, with gold the most valuable mineral. About 80 per cent of the land is managed by the United States federal government.
neville-family: In the male line the family was of native English origin and may have belonged to the pre-Conquest aristocracy of Northumbria. Dolfin, son of Uhtred, is first recorded in 1129 holding the manor of Staindrop in County Durham from the Prior of Durham, and Raby, in that parish, remained the principal seat until 1569. The name came through a marriage: Isabel de Neville, heiress of the Anglo-Norman Geoffrey de Neville, married Robert FitzMaldred, and their son Geoffrey (died c. 1242) took his mother's more prestigious surname while keeping his father's arms, a silver saltire on red.

The family rose through royal office in the north, as sheriffs, castellans and justices. Ralph Neville was summoned to the House of Lords at its establishment in 1295, and from 1334 the Nevilles were regularly wardens of the marches against Scotland. In 1346 a later Ralph Neville commanded the army that defeated the Scots at the Battle of Neville's Cross and captured King David II. In 1397 Richard II created Ralph Neville Earl of Westmorland, and by then only the Percy Earls of Northumberland matched the family's power in the north, which bred a bitter rivalry between the two houses.

Earl Ralph's second marriage, to Joan Beaufort, half-sister of Henry IV, split the family: the sons of this marriage received most of the lands, and the Nevilles of Middleham fell out with the Nevilles of Raby, who kept the earldom. Joan's son Richard Neville became Earl of Salisbury by marriage, and his son Richard became Earl of Warwick the same way. Salisbury and Warwick were the chief supporters of Richard, Duke of York, who had married Salisbury's sister Cecily, and after Edward IV took the throne in 1461 John Neville received the earldom of Northumberland in 1465. Warwick later broke with Edward over the king's marriage to Elizabeth Woodville and rebelled in 1469 and 1470.

After the deaths of Warwick and his brother John, Marquess of Montagu, in 1471, their lands were divided between the king's brothers George Plantagenet, Duke of Clarence, and Richard, Duke of Gloucester, who made Middleham Castle his main residence. The Raby line, Lancastrian throughout the wars, survived much diminished. In 1569 Charles Neville, Earl of Westmorland, joined the Percys in the Revolt of the Northern Earls against Elizabeth I; he fled abroad, was attainted and died in 1601 without a male heir. The Bergavenny branch endured, later as Earls and then Marquesses of Abergavenny, at Eridge Park in East Sussex, held by the family since 1448.
new-amsterdam: New Amsterdam stood at the southern tip of Manhattan Island, around Fort Amsterdam, which was meant to defend the Dutch West India Company's fur trade on the North River, now the Hudson. The Munsee name for the tip of the island was Manhattoe. The town's limits did not extend north of the wall of Wall Street, and Broadway was its main road north. The fort held a barracks, a church, the house of the company director and a warehouse.

Henry Hudson explored the area in 1609 in the Halve Maen in Dutch service. Beaver pelts were prized in Europe for making waterproof felt hats, and merchants sent trading voyages in the following years. The first settlers of New Netherland landed on Noten Eylandt, now Governors Island, on 20 May 1624, and the colony was made a province of the Dutch Republic, with New Amsterdam its capital from 1625. Slavery was introduced in 1626. In that year Peter Minuit is said to have bought Manhattan from the Canarse for 60 guilders' worth of trade goods, but the deed has not survived, so its terms are unknown.

The town received municipal rights from Governor Peter Stuyvesant on 2 February 1653. In 1654 the first Jews arrived, among them refugees from Recife, and the company's directors overruled Stuyvesant's attempt to turn them away. In the Peach War of September 1655 several hundred Munsee occupied the town, and attacks on Pavonia and Staten Island followed, with 40 deaths reported. Population in New Amsterdam reached about 2,500 by 1664.

On 27 August 1664, in a time of peace, four English frigates entered the harbour and demanded surrender. The Dutch did not resist, and the Articles of Surrender were signed on 6 September. In June 1665 the town was reincorporated as New York City, named after the Duke of York, later James II. The Dutch retook it briefly in August 1673 and renamed it New Orange, but under the Treaty of Westminster they gave it up, and control passed to the English on 10 November 1674. By the Treaty of Breda of 1667 the Dutch had received Surinam and Run.

No 17th-century building survives, but the street plan of the Financial District largely does, and Broad Street follows a canal filled in 1676. The Castello Plan of 1660 shows nearly every structure. Writers such as Russell Shorto argue that the Dutch town left a lasting mark on New York's culture, in its diversity and tolerance.
new-athos: New Athos lies on the shore of the Black Sea in the Gudauta Municipality of Abkhazia, about 22 km from Sokhumi and 17 km from Gudauta, between the sea and the Iverian Mountain. It was previously known under Greek names, among them Nikopol, Anakopia, Nikopsis and Absara, and later as Psyrtskha.

Excavations at the Anakopia Fortress, at the edge of the town, show that it was in use from the 5th to the 12th century, though some archaeologists date its defences to the 7th century. Anakopia is associated with the fortress of Tracheia mentioned by Prokopius. It was the capital of the Abkhazian princedom in the orbit of the Byzantine Empire, and then of the Abkhazian Kingdom after the archon Leon II declared himself king in the late 8th century. The capital later moved to Kutaisi. Demetre ceded Anakopia to the Byzantine Empire in 1033, and the Georgians retook it in 1072. According to tradition Simon the Zealot died in Abkhazia and was buried in Nicopsis.

In 1874 Russian monks from the overcrowded Rossikon Monastery on Mount Athos came to the Caucasus to find a place for resettlement, fearing that the Ottoman Empire would oust Russians from Athos if the Russo-Turkish War broke out. They chose Psyrtskha, and the Neo-Byzantine New Athos Monastery, dedicated to St. Simon the Canaanite, was built there in the 1880s with funds from Tsar Alexander III. Russian monks were later allowed to stay on the old Athos, so the new monastery was less occupied than expected. It was closed in 1924, during the Soviet persecution of religion, and later used as a storage facility, tourist base, hospital and museum. Its return to the Orthodox Church began in 1994.

The monastery by the sea is a popular destination for Russian tourists. An older church of St. Simon the Canaanite, dated to the 9th or 10th century and reconstructed in the 1880s, stands near the town on the Psyrtskha stream. The monks built a small hydroelectric power station and artificial lake on the river between 1892 and 1903. The New Athos Cave, a karst cave in the Iverian Mountain a few kilometres from the town, has been served by a railway since 1975.
new-bern: New Bern lies at the confluence of the Neuse and Trent rivers, two tidal waterways, near the headwaters of Pamlico Sound in North Carolina's Inner Banks region. It is the county seat of Craven County and lies 112 miles east of Raleigh. Settlers named it after Bern, the Swiss region from which many of them and their patron had come. Christoph von Graffenried had the original plan of the town laid out in the shape of a cross.

The Palatines and Swiss under von Graffenried founded New Bern in October 1710, making it the second-oldest European-settled colonial town in North Carolina after Bath. The governor's palace, now Tryon Palace, served as the capitol of North Carolina from 1770 until the government moved to Raleigh in 1792, after a fire had destroyed much of the capitol. No printer worked in the colony until 1749, when the Assembly commissioned James Davis. He settled in New Bern, became its first postmaster and founded the North-Carolina Gazette, the colony's first newspaper.

In the early 19th century it grew into the largest city in North Carolina on the trade in goods and slaves tied to plantation agriculture, and after losing the capital it traded by sea with the Caribbean and New England. Union forces took the town in the Battle of New Bern in 1862 and held it to the end of the war. Nearly 10,000 enslaved people escaped to the Union camps in the region, and the army set up the Trent River contraband camp, where missionaries taught literacy. The population rose from 5,432 in 1860 to more than 20,000.

From the 1870s the lumber industry became the chief part of the economy, and by 1890 New Bern was the largest lumber centre in North Carolina, with as many as 16 mills. The boom lasted until the 1920s and left some of the finest homes in the South. The city has four historic districts on the National Register of Historic Places, with buildings dating back to the early 18th century, and two local historic districts. In the 19th century it was called the Athens of the South. It had a population of 31,291 at the 2020 census.
