new-book-of-tang: Chinese dynasties customarily compiled the history of their immediate predecessor as a way of strengthening their own legitimacy, and under the Later Jin dynasty of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period the Old Book of Tang had already been written. In 1044 Emperor Renzong of Song ordered a new compilation, believing that the older work lacked organisation and clarity. A team of Song scholars led by Ouyang Xiu and Song Qi took 17 years over it. The result, in ten volumes and 225 chapters, was simply called the Tangshu, or Book of Tang, until the 18th century.

The new history differed greatly from the old in arrangement and content. The annals of the emperors, in volumes 1 to 10, are much shorter: Ouyang Xiu tested accounts by reason and removed whatever contained myth or superstition, which cut many biographies of emperors and leading figures. The treatises, in volumes 11 to 60, are much expanded. Rites and Music is the largest, filling twelve volumes, and there are treatises on the horse trade with Tibet and on military affairs.

It was the first of the standard histories with a treatise on selecting and appointing officials, which describes the examination system that became increasingly important after 780. Volumes 61 to 75 revive the use of tables, listing not only emperors but chancellors and jiedushi, and a table of the Tang bureaucracy that the older work lacked.

The biographies include four women absent from the Old Book of Tang, who maim or kill themselves; Woman Lu gouges out an eye to assure her dying husband that she will never take another. They were meant to deter readers from such extremes, and biographies of 35 overly filial and fraternal men stand beside them.

Ouyang Xiu and Song Qi admired the plain ancient prose of Tang writers such as Han Yu rather than the ornate style of Tang official documents, and they reworded the documents they quoted. In doing so the direct wording of the Tang court records was lost, some shortened passages became unclear, and many errors entered in the search for more ancient words.
new-braunfels: The settlement was founded in 1845 by Prince Carl of Solms-Braunfels, Commissioner General of the Mainzer Adelsverein, or Noblemen's Society, which organized hundreds of Germans to settle in Texas. Immigrants began arriving at Galveston in July 1844 and travelled by ship to Indianola, then set out overland for the Fisher-Miller land grant. At the urging of John Coffee Hays, they stopped near the Comal Springs, and Prince Carl bought two leagues of land from Rafael Garza and Maria Antonio Veramendi Garza for $1,111. The first settlers forded the Guadalupe River on Good Friday, 21 March 1845. They built a fort, the Zinkenburg, named for the engineer Nicolaus Zink, divided the land and began to plant crops.

Prince Carl had little business experience and kept no financial records, and the Adelsverein was an organization of noblemen with no practical background in running a colony. When John O. Meusebach arrived as his successor, the finances were in disarray and Prince Carl was detained in Galveston for unpaid bills. According to Nicolaus Zink, Prince Carl had planned a German feudal state, bringing immigrants secretly to military fortresses. Meusebach, who had renounced his own title of nobility, invited Americans to settle in the society's territory. He put a financial structure in place and arranged food and shelter, and Hermann Friedrich Seele became the first teacher of the German-English school on 11 August 1845.

In May 1846 Meusebach learned that 4,304 emigrants were on their way, while no funds or new settlements existed. On 31 December 1846 a crowd of about 120 men pushed into his house demanding his resignation, and the next day other colonists passed resolutions condemning them. He stabilised the colony's finances and encouraged neighbouring settlements, the largest of which was Fredericksburg. By 1850 New Braunfels, with 1,723 people, was the fourth-largest city in Texas. In 1852 the Zeitung newspaper was founded under the botanist Ferdinand Lindheimer.

New Braunfels is the county seat of Comal County, on the Balcones Fault, where the Texas Hill Country meets rolling prairie. A string of artesian springs, the Comal Springs, gives rise to the Comal River, which winds about 3 miles (5 km) through the city to the Guadalupe. The city is known for its German Texan heritage, shown in the sausage festival Wurstfest held each November, and in the Sophienburg Museum. Its newspaper, now the Herald-Zeitung, was published in separate English and German editions until 1967.
new-castle-delaware: New Castle lies on the Delaware River, six miles (10 km) south of Wilmington. The Dutch West India Company settled it under Peter Stuyvesant on the site of an indigenous village called Tomakonck, "Place of the Beaver", to assert a claim based on a prior agreement with the people of the area. Dutch authorities laid out a grid of streets and a common green in the centre of the town, which continues to this day.

The colony of New Sweden seized the fort on Trinity Sunday in 1654 and renamed it Fort Trinity. The Dutch conquered New Sweden the following year, and the settlement became Nieuw-Amstel, named after the Amstel. That ended the Swedish colony as an official entity, but Swedish influence stayed strong. The English seized New Netherland in 1664 and the Dutch regained the town in 1673, but it was returned to Great Britain the next year under the Treaty of Westminster.

In 1680 the Duke of York conveyed New Castle to William Penn, who first set foot on American soil there on 27 October 1682. Lord Baltimore contested the transfer, and the boundary dispute was not resolved until the survey of 1763 to 1767 by Mason and Dixon. Delaware's residents, uneasy with Quaker influence, petitioned for a separate legislature, granted in 1702, and Delaware broke from Pennsylvania in 1704. During the Revolution, with the town besieged by William Howe, the government moved to Dover in May 1777.

A portage of 16 miles (26 km) between the Delaware River and Chesapeake Bay brought business to the port. New Castle became the eastern terminus of the New Castle and Frenchtown Railroad, the second-oldest rail line in the country, launched in 1828 with horse-drawn cars and converted to steam in 1832. By 1840 rail lines connected Philadelphia and Baltimore through Wilmington, and traffic declined sharply.

The 2020 census counted 5,551 residents. The decline left most homes unaltered, so the historic district, about four blocks square, holds roughly 500 buildings dating from 1700 to 1940 and is a National Historic Landmark. The city is home to Broad Dyke, the first dyke built in the United States, and the cupola of its court house is the centre of the Twelve-Mile Circle that defines much of the border between Delaware and Pennsylvania.
new-christians: More than a hundred thousand Iberian Jews converted to Catholicism in Spain after the pogroms of 1391. After the Alhambra Decree of 1492, issued by Ferdinand and Isabella, and a similar Portuguese decree of 1497, the Jews who remained became officially Christian by default: over 200,000 converted and between 40,000 and 100,000 were expelled. Converts of Jewish origin were generally called Conversos, or in a more derogatory way Marranos, and those of Muslim origin Moriscos. After the Reconquista, 200,000 of the 500,000 Muslims had been converted.

The category had no meaning in Christian theology. It was introduced by Old Christians who claimed that pure Christian bloodlines, limpieza de sangre or cleanliness of blood, set them apart, and it worked in practice as a mechanism of racial antisemitism and, for Moriscos, of anti-Berber or anti-Arab prejudice. By law it covered converts and their baptised descendants to the third generation, the fourth being exempt; later it came to include anyone with New Christian blood from time immemorial.

New Christians were barred from universities, many professions, the clergy and emigration to the Americas, and faced limits on whom they could marry and where they could live. Since many conversions had been coerced, they were suspected of being judaizantes, secret practisers of Judaism, and the Spanish Inquisition of 1478 and the Portuguese Inquisition, including the Goa Inquisition, prosecuted them, at times to execution. Some of Converso descent were still accepted as sincerely Catholic and rose to prominence, among them Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross and Luis de Santángel. In Portugal the Marquess of Pombal ended the legal distinction between New and Old Christians in 1772.

Some New Christians reached the Iberian colonies of the New World by forging or buying certificates of clean blood; their descendants, unable to return to Judaism, became the Christian-professing Sephardic Bnei Anusim of Latin America. Others left the peninsula in a continuous flow from the 1600s to the 1800s for Amsterdam and London, where they returned to Judaism and whose descendants became the Spanish and Portuguese Jews. Waves of Moriscos settled across North Africa and in the provinces of the Ottoman Empire.
new-deal: From 1929 to 1933 manufacturing output fell by a third, prices fell by 20 per cent and unemployment rose from 4 to 25 per cent. Roosevelt introduced the phrase in accepting the Democratic nomination in 1932, pledging a new deal for the American people, and beat the incumbent Herbert Hoover in a landslide. He attributed the Depression to the instability of markets and to inadequate demand, and held that stabilising the economy required large government intervention. His Secretary of Labor, Frances Perkins, brought a list of priorities that included a forty-hour week, a minimum wage and Social Security.

In the first hundred days of 1933 Congress granted every request Roosevelt made. Historians call the measures up to 1935 the First New Deal and sum them up as relief, recovery and reform. The Emergency Banking Act and the Banking Act of 1933 created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. Other laws created the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Agricultural Adjustment Administration, the Tennessee Valley Authority and the Civilian Conservation Corps, whose camps were run by army officers.

The Second New Deal, from 1935, was more progressive and more controversial. The Works Progress Administration employed more than 8.5 million workers, who built 650,000 miles of roads and 125,000 public buildings, and also supported artists and writers. The National Labor Relations Act of 1935 guaranteed collective bargaining, the Social Security Act introduced pensions and benefits, and the Fair Labor Standards Act prohibited child labour and set a 40-hour week and a minimum wage.

When the Supreme Court struck down New Deal programmes, Roosevelt proposed in 1937 to add five justices, but the plan failed. A new downturn in the autumn of 1937 raised unemployment from 14.3 per cent in May 1937 to 19.0 per cent in June 1938, and in 1938 the Republican Party and conservative Democrats joined to block further legislation. Most historians accept that full employment came only when the United States entered the Second World War in December 1941.

The New Deal created a coalition of labour unions, blue-collar workers, city machines, racial minorities, white Southerners and intellectuals that dominated presidential elections into the 1960s, and it enlarged the power of the federal government. Historians divide over its effects: progressives support it, conservatives oppose it, and New Left historians say it did too little for minorities.
new-delhi: New Delhi lies on the Indo-Gangetic Plain, on the floodplain of the Yamuna River, and there is little difference in elevation across the city. The area was once part of the Aravali Range, of which the Delhi Ridge, sometimes called the Lungs of Delhi, is all that remains. The municipality covers 42.7 square kilometres and forms a small part of the larger metropolitan area of Delhi. In everyday speech Delhi and New Delhi are often used interchangeably, although they are distinct administrative entities.

Under British rule Calcutta was the capital of India until December 1911. It had become a centre of nationalist movements from the late nineteenth century, and Viceroy Curzon's partition of Bengal produced a large upsurge in political activity, including assassinations of British officials, and a boycott of British goods. The colonial government reunited Bengal and moved the capital. Old Delhi had been the political centre of several empires, among them the Delhi Sultanate and, from 1649 to 1857, the Mughal Empire. The British government of India also judged that Delhi, in the centre of northern India, would be logistically easier to govern from.

George V laid the foundation stone of New Delhi, south of the old city, during the Delhi Durbar of 1911. The land was acquired under the Land Acquisition Act of 1894. The city was designed by the British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker and took about twenty years to build. Viceroy Irwin inaugurated it on 13 February 1931.

The plan was chosen above all to be a symbol of British power and supremacy. Its architecture follows a British Classical and Palladian tradition, with some Hindu and Islamic features that were included through the persistence of Viceroy Hardinge and historians such as E. B. Havell. The city is structured around two promenades, the Rajpath, or King's Way, which runs from the Rashtrapati Bhavan, formerly the Viceroy's House, on Raisina Hill to India Gate, and the Janpath, which crosses it at right angles.

New Delhi is the capital of India and the seat of all three branches of its government, with the Rashtrapati Bhavan, Parliament House and the Supreme Court. It is part of the National Capital Territory of Delhi and is administered by the New Delhi Municipal Council. Hindi is the most widely spoken language and English is the main formal language of business and government. The city has about 145 foreign embassies and high commissions, and many regional offices of United Nations bodies. The National Museum, formally inaugurated on 15 August 1949, holds about 200,000 works of art covering over 5,000 years.
new-england: New England consists of six states in the north-eastern United States: Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont. The southeast is covered by a narrow coastal plain, while the west and north are dominated by the rolling hills and worn-down peaks of the northern end of the Appalachian Mountains. The Atlantic fall line lies close to the coast, which let many towns use water power from rivers such as the Connecticut. Its hills and jagged coastline are glacial landforms left by the retreat of the ice sheets about 18,000 years ago.

Humans reached the region at least 10,500 years ago. At the time of European colonisation its communities spoke Eastern Algonquian languages, and the prominent peoples included the Abenakis, Mi'kmaq, Penobscot, Pequots, Mohegans, Narragansetts, Nipmucs, Pocumtucks and Wampanoags. In 1620 the Pilgrims arrived on the Mayflower and established Plymouth Colony, beginning permanent European colonisation; ten years later Puritans founded Massachusetts Bay Colony. Most of the earliest Puritan settlers came from eastern England.

Relations alternated between peace and skirmishes. The bloodiest early conflict was the Pequot War of 1637, which ended in the Mystic massacre. In 1643 Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth, New Haven and Connecticut formed the New England Confederation for mutual defence. King Philip's War, from June 1675 to April 1678, set the colonists and their Indian allies against a widespread uprising, with killings and massacres on both sides, and hundreds of captive Indians were sold into slavery. In 1686 King James II, concerned at the colonies' independent ways, established the Dominion of New England, an administrative union that was highly unpopular. Over the following 126 years of the region's history, its people fought four French and Indian Wars.

Colonists from New England led resistance to British taxes in the late 18th century, and the first battles of the American Revolutionary War were fought in 1775. In 1787 the first cotton mill in America was founded at Beverly, Massachusetts, and the Blackstone Valley has been called the birthplace of America's industrial revolution. Immediate abolitionists such as William Lloyd Garrison, John Greenleaf Whittier and Wendell Phillips were based in the region.

Boston is the largest city of New England and the capital of Massachusetts. The region has the Connecticut River running through it from north to south, and its states are divided into small municipalities called towns, many governed by town meetings. It has some of the oldest institutions of higher learning in the United States, among them Harvard College, founded in 1636 at Cambridge, and Yale University, founded in 1701.
new-france: New France was the territory France colonised in mainland North America, beginning with Jacques Cartier's exploration of the Gulf of Saint Lawrence in 1534. Around 1523 the navigator Giovanni da Verrazzano, commissioned by King Francis I to find a western route to Cathay, had anchored in the Narrows of New York Bay and named the place Nouvelle-Angoulême. In the 16th century the lands served mainly to extract resources such as furs through trade with indigenous peoples, and successful settlements began in Acadia and Quebec in the seventeenth. In 1627 Richelieu signed the act founding the Company of One Hundred Associates, which required the colony to be peopled by natural-born French Catholics. In 1650 New France had only seven hundred colonists.

At its peak in 1712 New France had five colonies, each with its own administration: Canada, Hudson Bay, Acadia, Terre-Neuve and Louisiana. It reached from Newfoundland to the Canadian Prairies and from Hudson Bay to the Gulf of Mexico. The economy shifted from Atlantic fisheries to the fur trade, carried by coureurs des bois from Montreal. Samuel de Champlain fought the Iroquois in 1609, and the French and Iroquois were at war until the Great Peace of Montréal in 1701. The census of 1666, organised by the intendant Jean Talon, counted 3,215 people, and the crown sent about 800 unmarried women, the Filles du Roi, to even out the numbers of men and women. In 1754 the population was 69,000.

The Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 gave Hudson Bay, Newfoundland and mainland Acadia to Britain; France founded Île Royale, where it built the Fortress of Louisbourg. The British expelled the Acadians in the Great Upheaval from 1755 to 1764. In the Seven Years' War they took Louisbourg in 1758, and in September 1759 General James Wolfe defeated General Louis-Joseph de Montcalm at the Battle of the Plains of Abraham. The governor-general, the Marquis de Vaudreuil-Cavagnal, surrendered to Jeffery Amherst on 8 September 1760. By the Treaty of Paris, signed on 10 February 1763, France ceded Canada, Acadia and Louisiana east of the Mississippi to Britain and the rest to Spain.

Spain returned its part of Louisiana to France in 1800 by the secret Treaty of San Ildefonso, and Napoleon Bonaparte sold it to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, which ended French colonial efforts on the North American mainland. The only remnant of French rule is the islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon, while Quebec remains predominantly French-speaking. The dispersed Acadians settled in Quebec, Louisiana, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and in Louisiana their descendants are called Cajuns. Historians have long debated the Conquest, which some see as a disaster for French Canada and others as a protection for its language and religion.
new-guinea: New Guinea, also known as Papua, has an area of 785,753 km2. It lies in Melanesia, in the southwestern Pacific, separated from Australia by the 150-kilometre-wide Torres Strait. Both landmasses lie on the same continental shelf and were joined in the Pleistocene, when sea levels were low, as the landmass of Sahul. The island has the third-largest remaining rainforest in the world and the highest plant biodiversity of any island. Its shape is often compared to that of a bird-of-paradise, giving the names Bird's Head Peninsula in the northwest and Bird's Tail Peninsula in the southeast. The Spanish explorer Íñigo Ortiz de Retes gave the island its name in 1545, because its peoples seemed to him to resemble those of Guinea in Africa.

Humans arrived on New Guinea perhaps 60,000 years ago, probably by sea from Southeast Asia during the last glacial period, although the date is debated. Their descendants developed one of the earliest known agricultures: the highlands were an early and independent centre of agriculture, with evidence of irrigation going back at least 10,000 years, and sugarcane was cultivated around 6000 BCE. Today almost a thousand tribal groups live on the island, with a near-equivalent number of languages, making it the most linguistically diverse area in the world.

The western part of the island had contact with kingdoms elsewhere in the Indonesian region; the Negarakertagama mentions Wanin and Sran as part of Majapahit's tributary. The sultans of Tidore claimed sovereignty over various coastal areas, whose exports included resins, spices, slaves and the highly prized feathers of the bird-of-paradise. In the 1780s Sultan Nuku of Tidore, who rebelled against Dutch colonisation, called himself Sultan of Tidore and Papua. After Tidore became a Dutch tributary, much of its claimed territory came under Dutch rule as part of the Dutch East Indies.

Portuguese and Spanish sailors made the first known European contact in the 16th century. Jorge de Menezes saw the western tip in 1526-27 and named it ilhas dos Papuas, and in 1606 Luís Vaz de Torres explored the southern coast. In 1942 the Japanese invaded the Dutch territory and the Australian territories in the eastern half. The highlands, northern and eastern parts became key battlefields, including those for Port Moresby, Milne Bay and the Kokoda track. Papuans often gave vital help to the Allies, and about 216,000 Japanese, Australian and U.S. servicemen died in the New Guinea campaign.

The island is divided politically into roughly equal halves along a north-south line. The eastern half is the mainland of Papua New Guinea, independent since 1975 and formerly administered by Australia. The western half, formerly Dutch, is divided into six Indonesian provinces. The two major cities on the island are Port Moresby and Jayapura.
new-hampshire: New Hampshire is part of the six-state New England region. It is bounded by Quebec to the north and north-west, Maine and the Gulf of Maine to the east, Massachusetts to the south and Vermont to the west. Its main regions include the Great North Woods, the White Mountains, the Lakes Region, the Seacoast and the Merrimack Valley. It has the shortest ocean coastline of any coastal state in the United States, 18 miles (29 km).

The White Mountains span the north-central part of the state and include Mount Washington, at 6,288 feet (1,917 m) the tallest peak in the north-eastern United States. The Old Man of the Mountain, a face-like rock profile in Franconia Notch, disintegrated in May 2003 but remains a symbol of the state.

Algonquian-speaking Abenaki peoples, largely divided between the Androscoggin, Cowasuck and Pennacook nations, inhabited the area before European colonisation. English and French explorers visited in 1600–1605, and David Thompson settled at Odiorne's Point in present-day Rye in 1623. The first permanent European settlement was at Hilton's Point, present-day Dover. After several years of petitions from Robert Tufton Mason, the colony became a Royal Province in 1679, the first in New England. Dover and Durham were burned in 1689 and 1692 during King William's War.

New Hampshire was one of the Thirteen Colonies that rebelled against British rule. In 1774 its people seized Fort William and Mary from the British, and in 1776 it became the first of the colonies to establish an independent government and state constitution. In 1788 it was the ninth state to ratify the United States Constitution, bringing it into effect. It was an active centre of abolitionism and fielded close to 32,000 Union soldiers in the Civil War. Rapid industrialisation followed, and the Amoskeag Manufacturing Company in Manchester was the largest cotton textile plant in the world.

Concord is the state capital and Manchester the most populous city, and the state has 1,377,529 residents. Its motto, Live Free or Die, reflects its role in the Revolutionary War, and its nickname, the Granite State, refers to its granite formations and quarries. French Canadians formed the most significant influx of immigrants, and a quarter of residents have French American ancestry. The state constitution of 1783 is its supreme law.
new-jersey: New Jersey lies between the Hudson and Delaware rivers. It is bordered to the north and northeast by New York, to the east and southeast by the Atlantic Ocean, to the west by the Delaware River and Pennsylvania, and to the southwest by Delaware Bay and Delaware. At 7,354 square miles (19,050 km2) it is the fifth-smallest state by land area. It is broadly divided into North, Central and South Jersey, with the Jersey Shore along the Atlantic coast.

Pressure from the collision of North America and Africa gave rise to the Appalachian Mountains. Around 18,000 years ago glaciers reached New Jersey, and as they retreated they left behind Lake Passaic along with rivers, meadows, swamps and gorges.

People have lived in New Jersey since the 6th millennium BCE, beginning with the Lenape, whose name for the land is Scheyichbi. The Lenape were several autonomous groups who practised maize agriculture to supplement hunting and gathering around the Delaware River, the lower Hudson River and western Long Island Sound. They were divided into matrilineal clans grouped in three phratries identified by the animal signs Turtle, Turkey and Wolf. They first met the Dutch in the early 17th century, and their main dealings with the Dutch and later settlers were through the fur trade.

Dutch and Swedish colonists founded the first European settlements. The British later seized control and established the Province of New Jersey, named after the Channel Island of Jersey. The colony's fertile lands and relative religious tolerance drew a large and diverse population. New Jersey was among the Thirteen Colonies that supported the American Revolution and hosted several pivotal battles and military commands in the American Revolutionary War, which earned it the title Crossroads of the American Revolution. It remained in the Union during the American Civil War.

The state capital is Trenton and the most populous city is Newark. The 2020 census counted 9,288,994 residents, and New Jersey has the highest population density of any state. It lies at the centre of the Northeast megalopolis, and its central position helped fuel rapid growth and suburbanization in the second half of the 20th century. It is home to Princeton University and to Rutgers University, headquartered in New Brunswick. Among inventions credited to the state are FM radio, the motion picture camera, the light bulb, the phonograph and the transistor.
new-julfa: New Julfa lies along the south bank of the Zayanderud in Isfahan. Its Armenian name is Nor Jugha, and it takes its name from the older city of Julfa, also called Jugha or Old Julfa, which is now divided between Jolfa in Iran and Julfa in Azerbaijan. Its people developed a distinct form of Eastern Armenian, the New Julfa dialect, spoken largely in Iran and Southern California, which members of the community call Persian Armenian or Iranian Armenian. Early on the quarter also housed Catholic missionary priests and a few foreigners, among them the Geneva clockmaker Jacques Rousseau, uncle of the philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau.

Over 150,000 Armenians were forcibly moved from Julfa by the mandate of Abbas the Great. Iranian sources state that the Armenians came to Iran fleeing persecution by the Ottoman Empire, while historical records indicate that Shah Abbas treated the people of Julfa well, hoping that their knowledge of the silk trade would benefit Iran. From its foundation the quarter was administered by the Armenian noble house of Lazaryan, which moved to Imperial Russia after the death of Nader Shah in 1747. One of its members, Ivan Lazarevich Lazarev, became a court banker to Catherine the Great and an Imperial Count in 1788.

The historian Fernand Braudel wrote in 1947 that the Armenians had a trade network stretching from Amsterdam to Manila. New Julfa became its hub, with merchants reaching as far west as Cádiz and London and a few crossing the oceans to Acapulco or Mexico City. Families from the quarter settled in Bengal, though some scholars argue that Surat, Bengal and Hooghly were independent nodes. New Julfan Armenians later settled in Manila, Hong Kong, Australia and Singapore, where the Sarkies Brothers founded the Raffles Hotel in 1887. Levon Khachikyan and Sushanik Khachikyan edited and published several New Julfan account books.

New Julfa remains an Armenian quarter with an Armenian school and sixteen churches. The best known is the Holy Savior Cathedral, called the Vank, of 1655, seat of the Armenian Apostolic Diocese of Persia and India; the Saint Jacob Church dates from 1607. The Museum of Khachatur Kesaratsi stands in the cathedral's compound. David Petrosyan of the Central Asia-Caucasus Institute counted 10,000 to 12,000 Armenian inhabitants in 1998.
new-kingdom-of-egypt: The New Kingdom followed the Second Intermediate Period and was succeeded by the Third Intermediate Period. The concept was coined in 1845 by the German scholar Christian Charles Josias von Bunsen, as one of three golden ages. Possibly as a result of the Hyksos rule, Egypt expanded into the Levant, reaching its largest territorial extent. In response to Kushite raids during the Second Intermediate Period, its rulers also pushed far into Nubia and held wider territories in the Near East.

Ahmose I, viewed as the founder of the Eighteenth Dynasty, continued the campaigns of Seqenenre Tao and Kamose against the Hyksos until Egypt was reunified. Thutmose I reached the Euphrates, the first pharaoh to cross it. After the reign of Hatshepsut, who restored the trade networks and sent a mission to the Land of Punt, Thutmose III conducted at least 16 campaigns in 20 years and is recorded as capturing 350 cities, crossing the Euphrates against Mitanni. Amenhotep III was the wealthiest of the dynasty's kings. Akhenaten, who changed his name in honour of the Aten, showed little interest in international affairs, and the Hittites extended their influence into the Levant.

The Nineteenth Dynasty began with the vizier Ramesses I, whom Horemheb had named heir. Seti I took Kadesh from the Hittites, though it soon reverted to them. Ramesses II fought the Hittite king Muwatalli II at the Battle of Kadesh, where he was caught in an ambush but rallied his troops; the outcome was undecided and led to a peace treaty. He built the Ramesseum and Abu Simbel and founded the capital Pi-Ramesses in the Delta. Later in the Nineteenth Dynasty a troubled court put the usurper Amenmesse on the throne, and a period of anarchy ended with Setnakhte, who founded the Twentieth Dynasty.

In the eighth year of Ramesses III, inscriptions record campaigns against the Sea Peoples, and he also fought Libyan invaders. The cost of these wars drained the treasury, and in his twenty-ninth year the tomb-builders of Deir el Medina, unpaid in rations, staged the first known labour strike in recorded history. A plot by one of his secondary wives to place her son on the throne led to a trial of the conspirators. Under his successors Egypt suffered droughts, famine and unrest. By the reign of Ramesses XI the High Priests of Amun ruled Upper Egypt, and Smendes, who founded the Twenty-first Dynasty at Tanis, controlled the north.

The later part of the period, from the Nineteenth Dynasty, is called the Ramesside period after the eleven pharaohs named Ramesses. Egyptian presence in the Levant is still attested at Byblos under Ramesses III, and the presence of the Sea Peoples in Canaan may have contributed to new states there, such as the Philistian pentapolis.
new-laws: The New Laws were issued on 20 November 1542 by Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor and King Charles I of Spain. They answered a reform movement that judged the Laws of Burgos, issued by Ferdinand II of Aragon on 27 December 1512 to regulate relations with the conquered peoples, to be ineffective. Missionaries such as Bartolomé de las Casas and Francisco de Vitoria pressed for stricter rules against forced labour and expropriation, and some of their arguments questioned the legitimacy of the conquest itself.

The laws forbade enslaving indigenous people for any reason, even war or rebellion, and ordered those already enslaved freed unless the owner could prove in Spain that the enslavement was lawful. Labour as carriers against their will or without fair pay was to end, as was sending people to fish for pearls. Indigenous people were to owe the encomenderos only tribute, to be paid wages for any work, and to be kept out of the mines unless absolutely necessary.

Only the viceroy could grant encomiendas, and officials, clergy and religious orders holding them were to return them to the Crown. Grants were no longer to pass by inheritance but would lapse at the holder's death, which was meant to end the system gradually. The laws also reorganised colonial government, creating general captaincies such as the Kingdom of Guatemala.

In Peru the first viceroy, Blasco Núñez Vela, tried to enforce the laws and was overthrown by a revolt of encomenderos under Gonzalo Pizarro, whose forces killed him in 1546. Charles sent the bishop and diplomat Pedro de la Gasca, who provisionally suspended the laws; Pizarro, who had declared Peru independent, was later captured and executed. In New Spain the viceroy Antonio de Mendoza did not enforce the most disputed parts, and the encomenderos there did not rebel.

In the Province of Paraguay a cleric reported in 1558 that the laws had still not been published, and Guaraní women were sold as slaves to the Portuguese port of São Vicente. The Crown revoked the inheritance restriction in 1545, issued a weaker version of the laws in 1552, and later took most of the ordinances into the Laws of the Indies. Even so, the New Laws freed thousands of indigenous workers from forced servitude.
new-left: The origins of the New Left have been traced to several factors. Prominent among them was the confused response of the Communist Party of the USA and the Communist Party of Great Britain to the Hungarian Revolution of 1956, which led some Marxist intellectuals to seek a more democratic approach to politics, opposed to what they saw as the centralised and authoritarian politics of the pre-war leftist parties. The term nouvelle gauche was already current in France in the 1950s, and the British movement borrowed it.

In Britain, Nikita Khrushchev's Secret Speech denouncing Joseph Stalin led many to leave the Communist Party of Great Britain. The Marxist historians E. P. Thompson and John Saville, suspended from the party for refusing to stop their journal Reasoner, relaunched it in 1957 as The New Reasoner. Thompson brought the concept of a New Left to Britain in a lead essay of 1959.

In the United States the name was loosely given to radical political movements of the 1960s that arose mainly among college students, associated with anti-war campus protests, among them the Free Speech Movement. At its core stood Students for a Democratic Society, which by 1962 had become the most important of the new campus radical groups. Tom Hayden wrote its founding document, the Port Huron Statement, which called for participatory democracy based on non-violent civil disobedience. The organisation marshalled antiwar, civil rights and free speech concerns and brought together liberals and more revolutionary leftists. Its community-organising Economic Research and Action Project lasted barely two years, as the escalating U.S. commitment in Vietnam drew organisers back to the campuses.

In Europe the New Left appeared first in West Germany and West Berlin, where Subversive Action, an early grouping conceived as the German branch of the Situationist International, became a leading faction within the German Socialist Students' Union. It was associated with Rudi Dutschke.

Some who called themselves New Left rejected the labour movement and Marxism's theory of class struggle, while others developed their own versions of Marxism, such as the New Communist movement in the United States, drawn from Maoism, and the K-Gruppen in the German-speaking world. In Japan the movement grew out of the 1960 Anpo protests against the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty and climaxed in 1968 and 1969, when the Zenkyōtō movement barricaded dozens of universities; in the 1970s it became known for violent internal splits and terrorism, and its influence waned. In Latin America the term covers the left between the Cuban Revolution of 1959 and 1990.
new-mexico: New Mexico is a landlocked state in the south-west, sharing the Four Corners region with Utah, Colorado and Arizona. The Rio Grande and its valley run north to south through the centre. The Sangre de Cristo Mountains lie east of the river in the north, the Great Plains reach into the eastern third, the Colorado Plateau dominates the north-west, and the Chihuahuan Desert extends through the south. The landscape is more varied than its popular image as arid desert.

The name was given long before present-day Mexico took it in 1821. After the Spanish conquered the Aztecs in the early 16th century, they called the region they began to explore Nuevo México, after the Kingdom of Mexico. In 1581 the Chamuscado and Rodríguez Expedition named the area north of the Rio Grande San Felipe del Nuevo México. The Spaniards had hoped to find wealthy cultures like the Mexica, but the cultures proved unrelated and lacking in riches.

The first known inhabitants were the Clovis culture of Paleo-Indians. Later came the Mogollon and the Ancestral Pueblo cultures, known for sophisticated pottery and urban development, with pueblos or remains at Acoma, Taos and Chaco Culture National Historical Park. The Navajo and Apache arrived in the late 1400s.

Esteban de Dorantes was the first person from the Old World to reach New Mexico, in 1539, and was killed by Pueblo peoples. Juan de Oñate y Salazar began Spanish colonisation in 1598. In the Ácoma Massacre of 1599 his army set fire to Acoma Pueblo and approximately 800 to 1,000 Ácoma were killed, and Oñate then ordered that the right foot of every man over 25 be cut off. Santa Fe was founded in 1610 as the government seat of Nuevo México in New Spain.

The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 was the first successful revolution against colonial rule in the Americas. Spanish rule returned in 1692. After Mexican independence in 1821 the province became an autonomous territory, and the United States annexed it after the Mexican–American War in 1848. New Mexico was a territory for 64 years and became the 47th state on 6 January 1912. It hosted key facilities of the Manhattan Project and was the site of the first nuclear test, Trinity, in 1945.

Santa Fe is the capital, the oldest state capital in the United States, and Albuquerque is the largest city. The state is home to one-third of the Navajo Nation, 19 federally recognised Pueblo communities and three federally recognised Apache tribes.
new-orleans: New Orleans lies in the Mississippi River Delta, south of Lake Pontchartrain, on the banks of the Mississippi about 105 miles upriver from the Gulf of Mexico. It was originally settled on the river's natural levees, the high ground, and after the Flood Control Act of 1965 the Army Corps of Engineers built levees around a much larger area that included former marshland. Half of the city is now at or below local mean sea level. Before European colonists arrived, the Choctaw called the area Bulbancha, meaning land of many tongues.

French colonists founded the city in 1718, and it was the territorial capital of French Louisiana. The Third Treaty of San Ildefonso in 1800 restored French control of New Orleans and Louisiana, and Napoleon sold both to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. The city then grew rapidly with Americans, French, Creoles and Africans, and later with Irish, Germans, Poles and Italians. Sugar and cotton were cultivated with slave labour on large plantations nearby.

In the last campaign of the War of 1812 a British force of 11,000 tried to capture the city, and Andrew Jackson, leading militia, regulars and local privateers under Jean Lafitte, defeated it in the Battle of New Orleans on 8 January 1815. The Treaty of Ghent had been signed already, but neither army had learned of it.

In April 1862 the Union Navy occupied the city, and General Benjamin F. Butler became military governor. After the war a legislative amendment of 1889 with a grandfather clause effectively disfranchised freedmen, and public schools remained segregated until 1960. The city was the fifth-largest in the country in 1860, but after the mid-19th century growth shifted elsewhere as railways and highways reduced river traffic.

On 29 August 2005 the federal levee system failed during Hurricane Katrina, and about 80 percent of the city flooded. More than 1,300 people died, thousands of residents were displaced, and the population fell by over 50 percent.

New Orleans is a consolidated city and parish, coextensive with Orleans Parish, and the most populous city in Louisiana, with 383,997 inhabitants at the 2020 census. It remains a major port and commercial hub for the Gulf Coast, with a maritime industry and petrochemical production nearby. The French Quarter, its historic heart, is known for French and Spanish Creole architecture. The city is known for its music, Creole cuisine and the Mardi Gras celebrations, and its strong Roman Catholic tradition goes back to its French and Spanish settlement.
new-providence: New Providence is the most populous island of the Bahamas, and nearly three quarters of the country's people live on it. The Indigenous Lucayan people called it Nema, meaning middle-water. The name New Providence is said to come from a 16th-century governor who thanked Divine Providence for surviving a shipwreck, and the word New was added later to tell it from Providencia in the western Caribbean, used by pirates. The island was nominally under Spanish control after Columbus, but the Spanish government showed little interest in developing it or the rest of the Bahamas.

The first lasting European settlement in the Bahamas was on Eleuthera in 1648, followed by New Providence in 1666. By 1670 more than 900 people lived at Charles-Town. Weak governors left it open to French and Spanish attack, and it became a pirate base before the Spanish destroyed it in 1684. Colonists from Jamaica resettled in 1686, and in 1695 Governor Nicholas Trott rebuilt the town and a fort, naming both Nassau after the Prince of Orange-Nassau, later William III of England. After attacks in 1700 and 1703 the fort was abandoned.

Without cannon or soldiers, the island became a pirate base. By 1713 more than 1,000 pirates outnumbered the 400 to 500 law-abiding inhabitants. In 1718 Governor Woodes Rogers, sent by George I, offered a pardon to any pirate who gave up the trade, and by combining it with the threat of execution he eventually cleared Nassau of pirates. In March 1776 Esek Hopkins's American squadron raided the island in the Battle of Nassau, the first amphibious assault by American forces. A Spanish force under Bernardo de Gálvez took it in May 1782.

After the American Revolution several thousand Loyalists and their slaves came, hoping to restart plantation farming, but the shallow soils and sparse rain defeated them. The island prospered chiefly through its large British military establishment, whose forts were abandoned by 1850. It had two booms: as a port for Confederate blockade-runners during the American Civil War and as a smuggling centre for spirits during Prohibition.

Nassau, on the island's east side, is the national capital, and all three branches of the Bahamian government sit on New Providence. It had 292,522 people at the 2022 census. It is the commercial centre of the Bahamas, and most of the country's tourists use its hotels and port. Tourism began in the late 19th century, when the island billed itself as the sanitarium of the western hemisphere for its mild climate, and by the late 1920s it was well established as an American vacation destination.
new-ross: New Ross lies in south-west County Wexford on the River Barrow, on the border with County Kilkenny, 20 kilometres north-east of Waterford. Its Irish name is Ros Mhic Thriúin, and it was formerly known as Rosspontum or Rosspont. It is Ireland's only inland port, 32 km from the sea; the port brought in steel, coal, grain, fertiliser and wood, and still takes small to medium bulk cargo vessels.

The earliest settlement dates to the 6th century, when St Abban of Magheranoidhe founded a monastery in what is now Irishtown. The area lay in the territory of Dermot McMurrough and came to prominence when the Anglo-Normans conquered it. William Marshal and his bride Isabella de Clare arrived early in the 13th century, and a motte was built at Old Ross to hold the territory, with a medieval borough of English and Welsh settlers around it. The town grew around the bridge William Marshal built, and received a royal charter around 1279.

The town was fought over in the Irish Confederate Wars of the 1640s. In 1643 it resisted a siege by James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormond, who fought the Battle of New Ross with an Irish army under Thomas Preston, 1st Viscount Tara. Oliver Cromwell reconquered it in 1649, discharging three cannon shots at the Aldgate, now called the Three Bullet Gate.

The battle of New Ross on 6 June 1798 was one of the bloodiest of the rebellion. The United Irishmen attacked from their camps on Carrigbyrne Hill and Lacken Hill and defeated the garrison, but British reinforcements returned later in the day, took the rebels by surprise and recaptured the town. It was the first major defeat the rebels faced.

New Ross had a population of 8,610 in 2022, making it the fourth-largest town in the county. It is home to the Dunbrody replica famine ship and the Ros Tapestry Project, a series of 15 embroidered panels made by about 150 volunteers, which depict among other subjects William Marshal's founding of the town. The Kennedy family homestead, the ancestral home of US President John F Kennedy, lies 8 km to the south.
new-testament: The New Testament was written in Koine Greek by various authors, although the historical Jesus is generally agreed to have spoken primarily Aramaic. Its books are thought to have been written by Jewish Christians living in the Roman Empire under Roman occupation. The author of the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles is frequently regarded as an exception, and scholars are divided on whether he was a Gentile or a Hellenistic Jew.

Literary analysis suggests that many of its texts were written in the mid-to-late first century, and there is no scholarly consensus on the date of the latest text. Some scholars date many or all of the books before 70 CE, while others date some texts much later. Richard Pervo dated Luke–Acts to about 115 CE, and David Trobisch places Acts in the mid-to-late second century.

The collection has 27 texts: four gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, epistles attributed to Paul and other authors, and the Book of Revelation. Each gospel narrates the life, death and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth. The word gospel derives from the Old English gōd-spell, meaning good news, and the Greek equivalent is euangélion. Beginning in the late second century the four accounts were called the Gospel according to a named author. The first author to name the canonical gospels explicitly was Irenaeus of Lyon, in his book Against Heresies, written around 180.

The order of the books differs between traditions. In the Latin West, before the Vulgate, the Gospels stood in the order Matthew, John, Luke and Mark. An early edition of Paul's letters was arranged from longest to shortest, and Hebrews was placed in different positions within it. The 16th-century Luther Bible places Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation last, which reflects Martin Luther's views on their canonicity.

The canon developed gradually. In the first centuries many books were widely considered inspired, but no single canon was formally recognised. About 140 CE Marcion accepted only a version of Luke and ten of Paul's letters, and rejected the Old Testament entirely. Most other Christians rejected his canon, and scholars such as Adolf von Harnack and David Trobisch have argued that the church formed its own canon partly in response to him. The 27-book canon was formalised by the late fourth century.

The text was transmitted in manuscripts, now numbering in the thousands, which contain variants. The earliest date from the late second to early third centuries, with Papyrus 52 a possible exception. Textual criticism uses them to reconstruct the earliest recoverable text. Catholics, Orthodox, evangelicals and many other Protestants regard it as inspired scripture. Catholics and Orthodox receive it together with sacred tradition, whereas Protestants hold that doctrine is to be derived from scripture alone.
new-westminster: New Westminster, colloquially New West, lies in the Lower Mainland region of British Columbia and is a member municipality of the Metro Vancouver Regional District. It stands on the Burrard Peninsula, mainly on the north bank of the Fraser River as the river turns southwest towards its estuary, 19 kilometres southeast of the City of Vancouver proper. It adjoins Burnaby and Coquitlam and faces Surrey and Delta across the river. Queensborough, a part of the city, lies on the eastern tip of Lulu Island, next to Richmond.

The area was originally inhabited by the Kwantlen First Nation. The discovery of gold in British Columbia and the arrival of gold seekers from the south prompted fear among the settlers that Americans might invade and take over the area. Richard Clement Moody founded the city as the capital of the Colony of British Columbia, and it served as capital until the mainland and Vancouver Island colonies were merged. It was the largest city of the British Columbia mainland from its foundation until the first decade of the 20th century, when Vancouver surpassed it in population.

Much of the street network still follows the original grid laid out by the Royal Engineers at the time of settlement. The grid is oriented to the riverfront, so streets run northwest to southeast and avenues southwest to northeast. The British Columbian, later The Columbian, the province's second newspaper, was founded in New Westminster by John Robson, later premier, and ran for 123 years until its last issue on 15 November 1983.

The New Westminster Museum and Archives is built around the 1865 Irving House, said to be the oldest intact house in the Lower Mainland. Other heritage items include the 1937 paddlewheeler Samson V and dozens of heritage homes, many from the 19th century.

The city's May Day celebration began in 1870 and gives it the longest-running May Day celebration of its type in the British Commonwealth. Held on the Victoria Day weekend as the Hyack Festival, it is known for the Hyack Anvil Battery Salute, begun by the New Westminster Fire Department in colonial times as a substitute for a 21-gun salute. With no cannons in the early colony, the firemen put gunpowder between two anvils and ignited it from a safe distance, hurling the upper anvil into the air.
new-zealand: New Zealand comprises two main islands, the North Island (Te Ika-a-Māui) and the South Island (Te Waipounamu), and more than 700 smaller islands. They are separated by Cook Strait, 22 kilometres wide at its narrowest point. The country is long and narrow, with about 15,000 kilometres of coastline and a land area of 268,000 square kilometres, and its exclusive economic zone covers more than 15 times its land area.

The Southern Alps divide the South Island along its length; Aoraki / Mount Cook, at 3,724 metres, is the highest of 18 peaks over 3,000 metres. The North Island is marked by volcanism, and the Taupō Volcanic Zone has formed a large plateau, with Mount Ruapehu its highest mountain and Lake Taupō, the largest lake, in the caldera of one of the world's most active supervolcanoes. New Zealand is prone to earthquakes.

The first people to reach the islands were Polynesians in oceangoing waka, believed to have arrived in several waves between about 1280 and 1350. According to most Māori oral traditions, the explorer Kupe first discovered the islands, followed by a great fleet from Hawaiki. The belief in a single great fleet has since been superseded by the view that settlement was a planned event spread over several decades. No remains, artefacts or structures can be reliably dated earlier than the Kaharoa eruption of Mount Tarawera around 1314.

Abel Tasman's crew met a hostile reception from Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri in 1642, and four of his crew were killed. Europeans did not return until James Cook mapped almost the entire coastline in 1769. The potato and the musket transformed Māori agriculture and warfare, and the intertribal Musket Wars covered over 600 battles between 1801 and 1840, killing 30,000 to 40,000 Māori. The Māori population fell to around 40% of its pre-contact level during the 19th century, with introduced diseases the major factor.

New Zealand is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary democracy, though its constitution is not codified. The upper house, the Legislative Council, was abolished in 1950. The 2023 census enumerated a resident population of 4,993,923, and 84.5% of the population lives in urban areas. Around 80% of New Zealanders are of European descent and 15% Māori.

From the early 20th century until the late 1960s Māori culture was suppressed by the attempted assimilation of Māori into British New Zealanders. Since the mid-1980s the economy has moved from a protectionist and highly regulated model to a liberalised free-trade economy. Aotearoa, often translated as land of the long white cloud, is the present Māori name for the country.
new-zealand-first: Winston Peters, a former Minister of Māori Affairs in Jim Bolger's National government, had been dismissed from the Cabinet in 1991 after publicly criticising the economic policy of the Minister of Finance, Ruth Richardson, which cut benefits in the Mother of All Budgets of 1991. In June 1992 he was told he could not stand again for National in Tauranga. Tauranga's voters re-elected him as an independent at a by-election in April 1993, and at the general election six months later New Zealand First won 8.4% of the vote and two seats, Tauranga and Northern Māori, won by Tau Henare.

In 1996, the first election under mixed-member proportional representation, the party won 13% of the vote and 17 seats, among them all five Māori electorates, whose MPs became known as the Tight Five. Its coalition with National ended on 14 August 1998, when Shipley, at the head of the government, sacked Peters from Cabinet in a dispute over selling the government's stake in Wellington International Airport. Henare led four MPs into a new party, Mauri Pacific, and the eight who left kept National in power until 1999, when New Zealand First fell to 4% and Peters held Tauranga by 63 votes.

The party recovered to 10.38% in 2002. In 2005 Peters lost Tauranga by 730 votes to Bob Clarkson, and the party gave Labour confidence and supply until 2008, when a dispute over donations, including from Owen Glenn, ended with the Privileges Committee censuring Peters and the party out of parliament. It returned with 6.59% in 2011, won 11 seats in 2014 and nine in 2017, and on 19 October 2017 agreed a coalition with Labour in which Peters became Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs.

In 2020 its vote fell to 2.6% and all its MPs lost their seats, while the Serious Fraud Office charged two people after investigating the NZ First Foundation. With 6.08% of the party vote in 2023 it entered a coalition with National and ACT. Its support has come mostly from middle-aged and elderly, rural and Māori voters, and it has campaigned for binding referendums, for pensioners' interests and for an annual cap of 7,000 to 15,000 migrants.
new-zealand-national-party: The party was formed in May 1936 by a merger of the United Party and the Reform Party. The United Party, called the Liberal Party until 1927, drew support from the cities, businesses and middle-class voters. The Reform Party had a rural base and strong support from farmers, then a large share of the population. Like other New Zealand parties, National consists of two bodies: the membership organisation outside parliament and the Parliamentary National Party of elected members.

Sidney Holland became the first National prime minister after the 1949 general election and held office until 1957. His government kept compulsory unionism and the welfare state set up by Labour. During the 151-day Waterfront Dispute of 1951 it acted against the maritime unions, and in the snap election that followed it won 54 of 80 seats. Keith Holyoake succeeded him, lost in 1957 to Labour under Walter Nash, and returned in 1960, winning again in 1963, 1966 and 1969 before retiring in 1972.

Robert Muldoon led the party back to power in 1975 with interventionist economic policies, including Bill Birch's Think Big investments in energy. Jim Bolger won a landslide in 1990 and continued the free-market reforms known as Rogernomics. Jenny Shipley became the first woman prime minister in 1997, and a Labour-led coalition defeated her in 1999. In 2002 National took only 27 of 120 seats, its worst result. It returned under John Key on 8 November 2008, winning 58 seats, and governed until 2017. Christopher Luxon led it to victory on 14 October 2023, with 38.08% of the party vote and 48 seats.

National has been described as a broad church of conservative, liberal, populist and libertarian tendencies, united in its early years by opposition to socialism. Its principles include recognition of the Treaty of Waitangi as the founding document of New Zealand, limited government and competitive enterprise. It has spent more time in government than any other New Zealand party.
newar-buddhism: A lively regional Buddhism flourished in the Kathmandu Valley in the first millennium, but its change into a distinct cultural and linguistic form appears to have come in the fifteenth century, at about the time when other regional forms of Indic Buddhism, such as those of Kashmir and Indonesia, were fading. After Indian monasteries were destroyed in the Muslim conquests of the 12th century, the valley became a centre of Buddhist learning, and Tibetan scholars came there to obtain texts.

Newar Buddhism is a non-monastic society organised by caste and descent in the male line. Its clergy, who do not take vows of celibacy, belong to two castes: the vajracharya, who perform rituals for others, and the shakya, who perform them mostly within their own families. Other Buddhist castes such as the Urāy act as patrons, and they also support Tibetan, Theravada and even Japanese clerics.

The tradition uses Sanskrit for all ritual and study and is the only living Buddhist Sanskrit tradition. It has kept the Sanskrit originals of many Mahayana and Vajrayana scriptures otherwise lost in India and survived elsewhere only in translations made in regions such as Tibet and China, and Newar Buddhists still copy manuscripts. Its nine principal sutras, the Navagrantha, include the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, the Saddharma Puṇḍarīka and the Laṅkāvatāra; the lost Tathāgataguhya was replaced by the Guhyasamāja Tantra. From the 19th century Brian H. Hodgson and others sent manuscripts from Nepal to scholars in Calcutta and Europe.

The tradition is known for elaborate rituals and for its art: chaityas, the courtyard monasteries called baha and bahi, statues, paubha scroll paintings and mandalas of sand, as well as the Chachā ritual song and dance and Gunlā Bājan music. Its great street festivals in the valley's three cities include Samyak, with almsgiving and a display of Buddha images, the holy month of Gunla, the chariot processions of Jana Baha Dyah Jatra in Kathmandu and Bunga Dyah Jatra in Lalitpur, and the Bajrayogini Jatra of Sankhu and Pharping.
newar-people: The Newars, who call themselves Newa, are primarily inhabitants of the Kathmandu Valley and its surroundings, and the creators of its historic civilisation. The valley and nearby territories formed the Newar kingdom of the Nepal Mandala. The Newars are regarded as a nation community with a relict identity, derived from an ethnically diverse, previously existing polity. They descend from the varied peoples who have lived there since prehistoric times, together with Indo-Aryan tribes such as the Licchavis, Kosala and Mallas, who arrived at different periods and merged with the local population by marriage and by adopting its language and customs.

A Sanskrit inscription of 512 at Tistung, west of Kathmandu, contains the phrase greetings to the Nepals, showing that Nepal named both country and people. Newar rule in the Nepal Mandala ended with its conquest by the Gorkha Kingdom in 1768.

For over two millennia the Newa civilisation preserved a microcosm of classical North Indian culture in which Brahmanic and Buddhist elements had equal standing. The Malla dynasty patronised the Maithili language, giving it equal status with Sanskrit at court, and invited Maithil Brahmin priests, many of whom settled in the valley. People arriving from Tibet in the north and Tirhut in the south added to the diversity and shaped the dominant culture.

The economy rested on trade, industry and agriculture, with social groups tied to hereditary professions providing ritual and economic services. Towns and villages specialised in particular goods, and rich farming produced a surplus for export. The caste system was first introduced under the Licchavis but took its present shape in the medieval Malla period.

Nepal Bhasa, a Tibeto-Burman language, binds the Newars together. Its literature began as prose in the fourteenth century with a law book of 1380 and a chronicle of 1389. Mahendra Malla, who reigned from 1560 to 1574, is known as the first poet of the language, and its dramas were written mostly in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. It was written in scripts descended from Brahmi, including Ranjana and Bhujimol. According to the 2021 census, 89.1 percent of Newars were Hindu, 9.0 percent Buddhist and 1.9 percent Christian, and both traditions share festivals and worship deities of both.

Newar art is primarily religious. Its paubha painting, sculpture and metalwork in lost-wax casting are well known, and the earliest dated paubha, the Vasudhara Mandala, was painted in 1365. Brick buildings with carved windows and doors characterise the architecture, and the Kathmandu Valley holds seven UNESCO World Heritage Sites and 2,500 temples and shrines. The windows reached their peak in the mid-eighteenth century. Festivals include jatras, processions of a car or portable shrine, and masked dances.
newcastle-upon-tyne: Newcastle upon Tyne stands on the northern bank of the River Tyne, opposite Gateshead, about 74 kilometres south of the border with Scotland. It is England's northernmost city and the most populous settlement of the Tyneside conurbation. It was historically part of the county of Northumberland, and since 1974 it has belonged to the metropolitan county of Tyne and Wear. Fragments of Hadrian's Wall are still visible in parts of the city, especially along the West Road, and the line of the wall can be traced east to the Roman fort of Segedunum at Wallsend.

The first recorded settlement was Pons Aelius, a Roman fort and bridge across the Tyne, named after the family name of the emperor Hadrian, who founded it in the second century. After the Roman departure it became part of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Northumbria and was known as Munucceaster, or Monkchester. Conflicts with the Danes in 876 left the settlements along the Tyne in ruins, and after the rebellion against the Normans in 1088 Monkchester was nearly destroyed by Odo of Bayeux. The settlement took its later name from a castle built in 1080 by Robert Curthose, the eldest son of William the Conqueror.

Throughout the Middle Ages Newcastle was England's northern fortress. A stone wall 7.6 metres high was built round the town in the thirteenth century to defend it in the border war against Scotland. The Scottish king William the Lion was imprisoned there in 1174, and the town was successfully defended against the Scots three times in the fourteenth century. In 1400 Henry IV separated it from Northumberland and made it a county in itself. A royal act of 1530 restricted all shipments of coal from Tyneside to Newcastle Quayside, giving a monopoly to a cartel of burgesses known as the Hostmen, and this helped the town prosper. Elizabeth I granted a new charter in 1589.

During the Industrial Revolution it became one of the world's largest shipbuilding and repair centres. Electric trams were introduced in 1901 and gradually replaced by trolley buses from 1935, with the tram service ending in 1950. The Tyne and Wear Metro, opened in five phases between 1980 and 1984, was Britain's first urban light rail system.

Newcastle is a metropolitan borough with city status, governed by Newcastle City Council, and the largest settlement of North East England. The Anglican St Nicholas' Cathedral has a lantern tower dating from 1474, and the city has two other cathedrals, St Mary's, designed by Augustus Welby Pugin, and the Coptic Orthodox Cathedral. Its landmarks include the Tyne Bridge, the Swing Bridge and the castle. The Great North Run starts here, and Newcastle United has played at St James' Park since 1892.
newcastle-west: The town, An Caisleán Nua Thiar in Irish, stands on the River Arra, a tributary of the Deel, in the middle of a broad bowl-shaped valley of West Limerick once known as the valley of the Wild Boar, apparently because the animal was plentiful when the area was thickly wooded; a boar appears on the town's crest. Its coat of arms carries the motto As Dúchas Dóchas, which may be translated as Our Hope springs from our Traditions. It lies on the N21 road from Limerick to Tralee, between Rathkeale and Abbeyfeale.

The FitzGerald family arrived some time after 1194 and had completed their castle in stone by 1298. The town was sacked in 1302 and destroyed in 1315. Two earls of Desmond died here: Gearóid Iarla in 1399 and James, the 8th earl, in 1462. Three battles were fought nearby in the reign of Elizabeth I. In the late 16th century the landlord, Sir William Courtenay, held 10,500 acres here; a Catholic, he was denounced in the House of Commons as a papist recusant in 1624.

The town held markets three days a week and fairs through the year, and its Thursday hiring fairs for farm workers drew large crowds. During the famine many hundreds of people who died in the workhouse were buried in unmarked graves behind what is now St. Ita's Hospital, and emigrants from across West Limerick took their leave at the Bridge of Tears before setting out for Cork and the voyage to North America. The Church of the Immaculate Conception was built in 1828 on a site given by the Earl of Devon. The railway reached the town on 1 January 1857 and closed in 1975.

Newcastle West is the county town and, apart from Limerick city, the largest town in County Limerick, with 7,209 people in 2022. The castle demesne holds about 99 acres of parkland, and the Desmond hall is open for guided tours from May to September. The old railway line is now the Great Southern Trail for walkers and cyclists. A monument unveiled by President Seán T. O'Kelly in 1955 commemorates 17 volunteers killed in the War of Independence and the Civil War.
newlands-resolution: Annexation had been disputed since 1893, when President Grover Cleveland, on taking office in March, withdrew an earlier annexation proposal and sent the former Georgia Representative James H. Blount to Hawaii to investigate; Blount called for the restoration of Queen Liliʻuokalani. In 1897 President William McKinley signed a treaty of annexation with the Republic of Hawaii, but it lacked two-thirds support in the Senate and never came into force. Between 11 September and 2 October 1897 the Hui Aloha 'Aina and Hui Kulai'aina groups gathered 21,269 signatures on a Petition Against Annexation, more than half of the 39,000 native Hawaiians.

When the United States went to war with Spain in April 1898, the Republic of Hawaii declared its neutrality, but according to the historian Ralph S. Kuykendall it then did all it could to aid the Americans, and Honolulu became a mid-ocean stopover for troops sent across the Pacific. The resolution, drafted by Representative Francis G. Newlands of Nevada, a member of the Silver Party, needed only a majority in each house. It passed the House of Representatives by 209 votes to 91, 182 of them Republican, and the Senate by 42 to 21. President McKinley signed it on 7 July 1898.

Queen Liliʻuokalani sent a letter of protest to the House of Representatives, stating that her throne had been taken illegally. On 12 August 1898 a ceremony on the steps of ʻIolani Palace marked the transfer of Hawaiian sovereignty to the United States. None of the former Hawaiian leadership attended, and there were no celebrations that night.

The United States assumed $4 million of Hawaiian debt. The resolution set up a five-member commission, among them Sanford B. Dole and Senators Shelby M. Cullom and John T. Morgan, to study the laws Hawaii needed. Its report led to a debate of over a year in Congress, where members objected that an elected territorial government could lead to the admission of a state with a non-white majority.

The annexation took place without a referendum of any kind and was opposed among the Polynesian population. The Hawaiian sovereignty movement has disputed its legality, while the US Supreme Court gave it tacit recognition in DeLima v. Bidwell in 1901 and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals recognised the resolution in Arakaki v. Lingle in 2007.
newport-rhode-island: Newport lies on Aquidneck Island in Narragansett Bay, about 33 miles south-east of Providence and 74 miles south of Boston. It is the most populous municipality on the island. The Newport Bridge, the longest suspension bridge in New England, joins it to Conanicut Island across the East Passage of the bay. The city has a total area of 11.4 square miles, of which about a third is water.

Eight founders, among them Nicholas Easton, William Coddington and John Clarke, began the settlement on the island's southern side in 1639. Many had belonged to the settlement at Portsmouth with Anne Hutchinson and her followers. Newport grew to be the largest of the four original settlements that formed the Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, and in 1640 the second Baptist congregation in Rhode Island was formed there under John Clarke.

Newport was a major centre of the slave trade in colonial and early America. Ships carried sugar and molasses produced by enslaved people in the Caribbean to Rhode Island, where it was distilled into rum and exchanged in West Africa for captives. In 1764 Rhode Island had about 30 rum distilleries, 22 of them in Newport. Captives continued to be brought in illegally after a state law of 1787 and federal acts of 1794, 1800 and 1807. On 8 December 1776 a British force occupied the city without opposition, which closed a haven for privateers on the route to New York.

From the middle of the 19th century wealthy families built summer houses, beginning with Kingscote in 1839 and Chateau-sur-Mer in 1852, and between 1870 and 1915 large mansions modelled on the royal palaces of Europe.

The Newport Historic District, one of three National Historic Landmark Districts in the city, has one of the highest concentrations of colonial houses in the United States. Mansions such as The Breakers, Marble House and Rosecliff are open as museums. The city has been linked to the Navy for generations: it held the Naval Academy during the Civil War, and it houses the Naval War College. It staged the first American national tennis championships in 1881, the first U.S. Open golf tournament in 1895 and the America's Cup races from 1930 to 1983. Its population was 25,163 at the 2020 census.
nez-perce-war: The Nez Perce Treaty of 1855 left the tribe a reservation of 7,500,000 acres in Idaho, Oregon and Washington territories, closed to white settlers without its permission. After gold was found near present-day Pierce, Idaho, in 1860, some 5,000 gold-seekers rushed onto the land and founded Lewiston illegally. In 1863 a group of mostly Christian Nez Perce was coerced into signing away 90 per cent of the reservation, and the bands that rejected that treaty, mostly followers of the traditional religion and including Chief Joseph's band in the Wallowa valley, stayed on their lands.

In May 1877 General Oliver Otis Howard gave the non-treaty bands 30 days to move and jailed the old leader Toohoolhoolzote for speaking against it. The bands agreed to go, but on 14 June three young men of White Bird's band, among them Wahlitits (Shore Crossing), whose father had been shot by a settler, killed four white men in the Salmon River settlements, and other raids followed.

In the first battle, at White Bird Canyon, after the civilian volunteer Arthur Chapman fired on a Nez Perce truce party, 34 cavalrymen were killed while three warriors were wounded. The bands fought skirmishes near Cottonwood from 3 to 5 July, escaped Howard's attack on the Clearwater River and crossed Lolo Pass into Montana Territory.

The two-day Battle of the Big Hole cost both sides heavily, including many Nez Perce women and children. Refused help by the Crow, the bands passed through Yellowstone National Park, fought a delaying action at Canyon Creek on 13 September, and were attacked by surprise at Snake Creek on 30 September by troops under Nelson A. Miles. Ollokot, Poker Joe and Looking Glass led the warriors in battle, while Joseph guarded the camp.

Howard and Miles had promised the 418 who surrendered a return to Idaho, but General William Tecumseh Sherman overruled them, and the prisoners were sent by train to Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, and held on swampy bottomland. Joseph pleaded in Washington in January 1879 without success. In 1885 he and 268 surviving Nez Perce were allowed back to the Pacific Northwest, though he had to settle on the Colville Indian Reservation in Washington, where he died in 1904. His surrender speech was transcribed by Lieutenant C. E. S. Wood, whom some critics suspect of embellishing it. Many sites of the war are preserved in Nez Perce National Historical Park.
ngai-tahu: Ngāi Tahu means People of Tahu, after the ancestor Tahupōtiki, younger brother of Porourangi and a descendant of Paikea. Tradition holds that he was born at Whāngārā around 1450 and took the Tākitimu canoe to the South Island. The iwi arose in the Gisborne District of the North Island, alongside Ngāti Porou and Ngāti Kahungunu, all intermarrying with the local Ngāti Ira. Its people moved down the coast to the Heretaunga and on towards Wellington before crossing to the South Island.

There they met iwi who had come earlier: Kāti Māmoe, who had arrived about a century before and conquered Waitaha, as well as Ngāi Tara, Rangitāne, Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri and Ngāti Wairangi. Ngāi Tahu absorbed several of these groups, and most families of Ngāi Tahu descent today also have Ngāti Māmoe ancestry.

In the 18th century, after establishing their dominance down to Kaikōura, Ngāi Tahu chiefs pushed further south. In the 1820s the Kaihuānga feud, sparked when a woman wore a dogskin cloak belonging to the paramount chief Tamaiharanui, showed the force of an ariki's tapu. After Europeans arrived, Ngāti Toa, allied with Ngāti Tama, and Ngāti Rārua invaded Ngāi Tahu territory with muskets, and in the 19th century European settlers, mostly British, came in their hundreds of thousands.

Over 270 people of Ngāi Tahu descent served in the First World War, some in the New Zealand (Māori) Pioneer Battalion. In 2021 the iwi began legal proceedings against the government, claiming that successive governments had failed to protect the waterways and asking the Crown to recognise its rangatiratanga over rivers across most of the South Island.

The tribal area, or takiwā, is the largest in New Zealand, running from the White Bluffs and Kahurangi Point in the north to Stewart Island / Rakiura, and comprises 18 rūnanga based on traditional settlements, each with its marae. The five primary hapū are Ngāti Kurī, Ngāti Irakehu, Kāti Huirapa, Ngāi Tūāhuriri and Ngāi Te Ruahikihiki. In the 2023 census 84,969 people affiliated with the iwi. Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu, its governance body, works under the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998. Many southern Ngāi Tahu once spoke a distinct dialect, sometimes called Southern Māori, and the iwi runs its own radio station, Tahu FM, founded in 1991.
ngaruawahia: The town lies 20 kilometres north-west of Hamilton, beside the Hakarimata Range. Its name means the opened food pits and comes from a feast of the 17th century. Te Ngaere, a Ngāti Tamainupō chief, and Heke-i-te-rangi, a Ngāti Maniapoto woman, had eloped and settled there, causing a rift between their tribes. When their first child was born, Ngāti Maniapoto were invited to the celebration, the boy was named Te Mana-o-te-rangi in their honour, and peace was made as Te Ngaere called for the food pits to be broken open.

Pōtatau Te Wherowhero settled beside the confluence after his crowning and died there two years later. During the invasion of the Waikato, after the fall of Rangiriri pā, General Cameron told Māori that Governor Grey would come to talk peace only if his forces could enter Ngāruawāhia unopposed. Cameron entered the deserted town on 8 December 1863, but Grey never came. Despite Māori protest, confiscated land was sold to European settlers from 1864, and the town was renamed Queenstown, then Newcastle in 1870, before taking back its own name in 1878.

A road-rail bridge over the Waikato River opened in 1876. Turangawaewae House was built between 1912 and 1919 as the Te Kauhanganui building, in a blend of Arts and Crafts and traditional Māori styles. An army camp was built at nearby Hopuhopu in the 1920s and returned in 1993 to Waikato-Tainui, who made it their headquarters. Queen Elizabeth II visited in 1953 and 1974, when the Māori Queen Te Ātairangikaahu welcomed her to the marae. The Great Ngaruawahia Music Festival of 1973 was the first large outdoor music festival in New Zealand.

The town had 7,992 people at the 2023 census, 54.0 per cent of whom identified as Māori. It has two marae of the Ngāti Mahuta and Ngāti Te Weehi hapū of Waikato Tainui, Tūrangawaewae and Waikeri-Tangirau, and a river regatta held every March since 1896.
