Its name was officially gazetted as Ngāruawāhia in 2019.
ngawang-namgyal: Ngawang Namgyal, known colloquially as the Bearded Lama, was born at Ralung Monastery in Tibet, the son of the Drukpa Kagyu lineage-holder Mipham Tenpa'i Nyima. Through his father he descended from Tsangpa Gyare, founder of the Drukpa lineage. In his youth he was enthroned as the eighteenth Gyalwang Drukpa and recognised as the reincarnation of the scholar Kunkhyen Pema Karpo.

His recognition was opposed by Lhatsewa Ngawang Zangpo, a disciple of Pema Karpo, who supported a rival claimant, Gyalwang Pagsam Wangpo, a son of the Chongje ruler. The ruler gained the support of Karma Phuntsok Namgyal, king of Tsang and a patron of the rival Karma Kagyu school, who by 1612 controlled Ü and Tsang.

After a misunderstanding with the Karma Kagyu lama Pawo Tsugla Gyatsho, the Tsang ruler demanded compensation and the surrender of Ralung's sacred relics, to be given to the rival incarnation. Faced with arrest, and following visions in which, it is said, the guardian deities of Bhutan offered him a home, Ngawang Namgyal left Tibet in 1616 for western Bhutan and founded Cheri Monastery at the head of the Thimphu valley. In 1629 he built Simtokha Dzong at the entrance to the valley, from which he could control traffic between Paro and Trongsa.

He subdued rivals in western Bhutan, including the Lhapa, and in the 1630s unified the warring fiefdoms for the first time, while letting the Nyingma and some Sakya communities continue in central and eastern Bhutan. Under the Tsa Yig legal code he established a dual system of government in which a spiritual leader, the Je Khenpo, presides over religious institutions and an administrative leader, the Druk Desi, heads secular affairs. A modified form of this system continues. He also sought a Bhutanese cultural identity separate from the Tibetan culture it derived from.

He died in 1651, and power passed to the penlops, the local governors, rather than to a successor. To prevent a dynastic struggle and a return to warlordism they kept his death secret for fifty-four years, issuing orders in his name and explaining that he was on a long silent retreat. His death is marked as a national holiday, Zhabdrung Kuchoe, on the tenth day of the third month of the Bhutanese calendar.
ngazargamu: Ngazargamu, also written Gazargamu, Gazargamo and Birni Gazargamo, stood in the fork of the Komadugu Gana and the Komadugu Yobe rivers, near present-day Geidam, about 150 km west of Lake Chad in Yobe State. It lay at the southern end of the trans-Saharan trade routes, closer to the rising markets of Hausaland than earlier royal seats, and in the middle of a salt-producing district of Bornu, salt being a profitable article of trade. At its height the city covered about 1,500 hectares; estimates of its population range from 60,000 to 250,000.

In the 14th century the Bilala took Njimi, and the Sayfawa dynasty lost its old heartland east of Lake Chad. For a time the empire had no fixed capital and suffered civil wars between branches of the dynasty, until Ali I Gaji gathered power in the later 15th century and made Ngazargamu his seat. By the 17th century caravans came from Tunis, Tripoli and Cairo, from Timbuktu, Agades and Gao, and from Kordofan and the Nile, bringing silk, carpets, weapons and books, paper and glass beads from Venice, and gold and kola nuts from Ashanti. A description by Mallam Salih ibn Ishaku, translated by H. R. Palmer in the 1920s, speaks of six hundred and sixty roads and four Friday mosques.

In 1808 the Fulani, fighting Kanem-Bornu in the Fula jihads, captured and destroyed the city, and Mai Ahmad Alimi fled and abdicated in favour of his son Dunama IX Lefiami. With the help of Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi, Dunama drove the Fulani back and settled in the ruins, but he left again in 1809 when Ibrahim Zaki approached. He never returned, and in the early 1810s his uncle Muhammad IX Ngileruma chose Kafela as the new capital.

The roughly circular earth rampart on which the city stood is still about 7 metres high, with traces of a ditch outside it and of a wall that once ran round a circuit some two kilometres across, entered by five gates. Inside are ruins of red brick buildings, rare in pre-modern Africa: a large central complex, very likely the palace of the mai, and smaller structures probably used by leading figures. In 2015 the government of Yobe State formed a committee to conserve the ruins and promote the site.
ngo-dinh-diem: Ngô Đình Diệm was born on 3 January 1901 in Huế, into a prominent Catholic family. His father, Ngô Đình Khả, was a high-ranking mandarin at the court of Emperor Thành Thái, and the family's ancestors were said to be among Vietnam's earliest Catholic converts. Diệm was educated in French-speaking schools and joined the civil service in 1921. He became governor of Bình Thuận Province in 1929 and interior minister in 1933 under Emperor Bảo Đại, but resigned after three months and denounced the emperor as a tool of France. He turned to Vietnamese nationalism, opposed to both communism and colonial rule, and in 1950 left for Japan, the United States and Europe.

Diệm returned to Saigon on 24 June 1954 and was appointed prime minister of the State of Vietnam two days later. The Geneva Accords of 21 July 1954 divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, and Diệm, helped by his brother Ngô Đình Nhu, consolidated his power in the south. In the referendum of 23 October 1955 he defeated Bảo Đại by an official 98.2 per cent, a result condemned as fraudulent because the votes far exceeded the number of registered voters. He then proclaimed the Republic of Vietnam with himself as president. His government was backed by anti-communist countries, above all the United States, and opened schools and universities, among them the University of Saigon and the University of Huế.

From 1957 Diệm faced assassination and coup attempts and an insurgency backed by North Vietnam, later organised as the Viet Cong. His campaigns known as Denounce the Communists held tens of thousands of suspected communists in re-education centres, though estimates of the numbers imprisoned and killed differ widely. In 1962 he began the Strategic Hamlet Program. Historians regard his government as favouring Catholics in public service, military promotions and land allocation, which antagonised many Buddhists and led in 1963 to the Buddhist crisis.

As the crisis deepened, the army's leading generals, led by Dương Văn Minh, prepared a coup, and the United States ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. gave them assurances that Americans would not interfere. The coup began on 1 November 1963. Diệm and Nhu escaped but were recaptured the next day and assassinated on the orders of Minh. South Vietnam was then unable to form a stable government, and several coups followed. Historians remain divided: orthodox scholars call Diệm a corrupt tyrannical puppet, while revisionists see an independent leader who did what his young regime needed to survive. Some credit him with stabilising the south and with progress in education.
ngo-quyen: Ngô Quyền was born at Đường Lâm, in present-day Sơn Tây district of Hanoi, under the Tang dynasty. He was the son of Ngô Mân, an influential official in Phong, whose ancestor Wu Ridai had been a local chief. Vietnamese tradition holds that a strange light shone on him at birth and three black moles were seen on his back, and that his mother named him Quyền, meaning authority and power. From 905 the Tang lost control of the region to local rulers, and in 930 the Southern Han invaded and removed the Khúc clan from power.

In 931 Dương Đình Nghệ led a revolt that drove out the Chinese, and Ngô Quyền served under him, rising quickly through military and civil ranks. By 934 he was military governor of Ái Châu, Dương Đình Nghệ's home province and power base, and he married Dương's daughter, Lady Dương. When Dương Đình Nghệ was assassinated in 937 by the usurper Kiều Công Tiễn, Ngô Quyền took command of the army, defeated Kiều Công Tiễn and had him executed. The Southern Han used the turmoil as a pretext to intervene, and in 938 the emperor Liu Yan sent a fleet.

At the Bạch Đằng, Ngô Quyền used shallow-draught boats to lure it onto pikes hidden beneath the rising tide; thousands of Southern Han soldiers were killed, among them the admiral Liu Hongcao, a prince of the emperor. Hundreds of the trapped ships were burned. Lê Hoàn used similar tactics in 981, and Trần Hưng Đạo against the Mongols in 1288.

As king he moved the capital to Cổ Loa, the old capital of Âu Lạc, and revived ancient rituals and dances with sword and battle axe, while keeping an administration in the Chinese style, down to court etiquette. After his death in 944 his brother-in-law Dương Tam Kha seized the throne for a time, until his sons Ngô Xương Văn and Ngô Xương Ngập established a joint rule, which lasted until the royal family collapsed in 966. The 13th-century historian Lê Văn Hưu and later histories all recognised his importance. The historian K. W. Taylor writes that the battle led directly to the abandonment of political titles in the Tang manner, and a central district of Haiphong bears his name.
ngo-si-lien: The dates of Ngô Sĩ Liên's birth and death are not known. He was said to have been born in the village of Đan Sĩ in Hà Đông, Hanoi, and some sources say he lived to the age of 99, which would place his birth around 1400 and his death late in the reign of Lê Thánh Tông. In his youth he took part in the Lam Sơn uprising of Lê Lợi, which led to the retreat of the Ming dynasty and the foundation of the Lê dynasty.

In the imperial examination of 1442, under Lê Thái Tông, he gained the title of Doctorate (Tiến sĩ) and became an official at the court of three successive emperors, Lê Thái Tông, Lê Nhân Tông and Lê Thánh Tông. In 1473 he was appointed Director of the National Bureau for Historical Record (Viện Quốc sử). He served at a time when Confucianism was gradually prevailing over Buddhism at court, above all under Lê Thánh Tông.

An official chronicle of the dynasty commissioned in the Quang Thuận period (1460–1469) was later lost. Ngô Sĩ Liên, a member of the board of compilation, wrote his own version in 15 volumes, revising Lê Văn Hưu's Đại Việt sử ký and the Đại Việt sử ký tục biên. Some have explained this as a wish to express his own opinions, others as a wish to promote Confucian ideology. Following the method of Sima Guang, author of the Zizhi Tongjian, he drew on official documents and on collections of legends such as the Việt điện u linh tập and the Lĩnh Nam chích quái.

He divided the past into the Peripheral Records (Ngoại kỷ), for everything before the Đinh dynasty, and the Basic Records (Bản kỷ) from the Đinh in the 10th century, and added Records of the Three Reigns (Tam triều bản kỷ) for Lê Thái Tổ, Lê Thái Tông and Lê Nhân Tông. His 72 comments show a Neo-Confucian scholar who judged earlier rulers by Confucian standards and was harsh on the Lý dynasty, whose mistakes he wanted the Lê to avoid. Several historians have argued that he fabricated the Hồng Bàng dynasty of the Peripheral Records, whether for political ends or to stress Vietnam's independence from China.
ngungunhane: Ngungunhane was born around 1850 and named Mdungazwe; oral tradition places his birth in Gaza between the Zambezi and the Incomati, most probably on the Limpopo, where the main Nguni settlements then stood. His grandfather Soshangane had led a Nguni army north from Zululand during the Mfecane in the 1820s and 1830s, made about two hundred chiefs his vassals, and founded the Gaza Empire with its capital at Chaimite. The Nguni displaced, absorbed or killed many of the peoples they found, and their arrival broke the peace of the Portuguese traders on the coast.

After Soshangane's death in 1858 his sons Mzila, Ngungunhane's father, and Mawewe fought for the throne. Mawewe won and tried to destroy his brothers' families, and Mzila fled to the Transvaal, probably with his son. When Mawewe demanded tribute from Lourenço Marques, the Portuguese backed Mzila, who accepted Portuguese overlordship by treaty on 1 December 1861 and, with two thousand rifles from Portugal, became undisputed ruler by 1864, moving the capital north to Mossurize.

Mzila ruled with an iron hand but his warriors raided the Portuguese posts of Sofala and Inhambane, while European explorers, missionaries and traders pushed ever further into Gaza, and Portugal dreamed of a belt of colonies from Mozambique to Angola. Mzila died in late August 1884, as the powers met at the Berlin Conference. The rightful heir was his half-brother Mafemane, son of the principal wife, but Mdungazwe fought for the throne, killed him, and drove his other half-brothers Hanyani and Mafabazi into exile. Sworn in as ruler in 1884, he took the name Ngungunhane and was called the Lion of Gaza.

His reign ended on 28 December 1895, when General Joaquim Mouzinho de Albuquerque seized him in the fortified village of Chaimite, the old capital of his grandfather. Because he was already known to the European press, the Portuguese chose exile over the firing squad usual in such cases. He was taken to Lisbon with his son Godide and other dignitaries, held briefly at the Fort of Monsanto, and then sent to the island of Terceira in the Azores, where he died on 23 December 1906. Some of his sons fled Mozambique with their uncle Mpisane Nxumalo and settled at Bushbuckridge in Mpumalanga, South Africa.
nguyen-du: Nguyễn Du was born on 3 January 1766 in the Bích Câu area just outside the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, near the Temple of Literature. His father, Nguyễn Nghiễm, was a high-ranked minister, and the family came from the village of Tiên Điền in what is now Hà Tĩnh Province. Many of its members passed the civil service examinations and became poets. His father retired in 1771 and died in 1776, and his mother died in 1778, leaving him an orphan at twelve.

After the Tây Sơn rebels swept north and Emperor Lê Chiêu Thống fled to Qing China, Du took refuge in his wife's homeland of Quỳnh Côi. He later called the years that followed ten years of wind and dust. In 1796 he set out to join Nguyễn Ánh in the south but was arrested by a Tây Sơn general and held in Nghệ An for three months.

In 1802 Nguyễn Ánh defeated the Tây Sơn and became Emperor Gia Long. Du pledged his support when the emperor's procession passed Nghệ An and was made district magistrate of Phù Dung, then prefectural magistrate of Thường Tín. In late 1807 he presided over the provincial examinations in Hải Dương, and in 1809 he became Administrative Commissioner of Quảng Bình. Sources differ on his conduct: his family's genealogy calls him simple and loved, while the official biographies describe him as frequently humiliated by superiors and nervous before the emperor.

Gia Long died in February 1820 and his son Minh Mạng asked Du to lead a delegation to Qing China to announce the change of ruler. Du fell ill, probably with cholera, and died on 16 September 1820 at the age of 54. Minh Mạng gave him the posthumous name Trung Thanh.

Du wrote in Literary Chinese and in the Nôm script, in forms ranging from Vietnamese adaptations of Tang styles to the folk metres song thất lục bát and lục bát. His Truyện Kiều, originally titled Đoạn trường tân thanh, is a verse novel of 3,254 lines in lục bát. It prefers the vernacular to learned Sino-Vietnamese vocabulary and introduced idioms that remain in common use. Scholars disagree on when it was written. Popular belief places it after his trip to China in 1813, but other evidence suggests a date before 1809, or even before the Nguyễn dynasty began in 1802.

In the early twentieth century Du became a national figure. In 1924 the critic Phạm Quỳnh praised the poem as the guardian of the language, and a debate followed in which Ngô Đức Kế and Huỳnh Thúc Kháng objected to honouring a poem about sex work at a time of colonial rule. His ancestral house in Hà Tĩnh was designated a Special National Site in 2012.
nguyen-hoang: Nguyễn Hoàng was the second son of Nguyễn Kim. When his father was assassinated by a supporter of the Mạc, command of the Lê royalist army passed to his brother-in-law Trịnh Kiểm. His elder brother Nguyễn Uông died soon after, believed to have been poisoned by Trịnh Kiểm, and Nguyễn Hoàng asked to be sent to govern Thuận Hóa in the south. The reason Trịnh Kiểm agreed is unclear; one anecdote holds that he hoped the Mạc garrison troops there would rid him of his brother-in-law.

Thuận Hóa had once been Champa territory, ceded to Đại Việt by the Cham king Jaya Simhavarman III, and was then held by Mạc forces. Nguyễn Hoàng defeated their commander, the Duke of Lập, and took the province in 1558. In 1573 Emperor Lê Thế Tông gave him the title Grand Master (Thái phó), and he was later made Duke of Môn. He held court at Ái Tử from 1558 to 1570, at Trà Bát from 1570 to 1600 and at Dinh Cát, the present Huế, from 1600.

In 1592, when Trịnh Tùng besieged the Mạc capital, the present Hanoi, Nguyễn Hoàng sent troops and supplies, and his army helped destroy the remaining Mạc forces. For reasons that are not known, he refused to recognise the new emperor Lê Kinh Tông and in 1600 took the title Good Prince; his nephew Trịnh Tùng had received a similar title, Pacifying Prince, a year earlier.

Nguyễn Hoàng died on 20 July 1613 after ruling the south for 55 years. Of his ten sons most had died in battle or stayed in the north, and his sixth son Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên succeeded him. His descendant Nguyễn Ánh later became emperor of a united Vietnam. He is still remembered in central and southern Vietnam, above all in Huế, where his 400th death anniversary was marked in 2013.
nguyen-huu-tho: Nguyễn Hữu Thọ was born on 10 July 1910. He was a French-educated lawyer in Cochinchina and a member of the French Section of the Workers' International (SFIO). He took part in the Vietnamese struggle for independence, joined the Vietnamese National Popular League (Liên Việt) in 1948 and the Communist Party in 1949. His political career began in 1949, when he led protests against French colonial rule of Indochina and against the patrols of US naval warships off the coast of southern Vietnam. He was arrested and held from 1950 to 1952, and a long hunger strike in prison enhanced his reputation.

After the partition of Vietnam in 1954 Thọ remained in the south. He came to support the 1954 Geneva agreements and opposed the government of President Ngô Đình Diệm. In August 1954 he founded the Committee in Defense of Peace and the Geneva Agreements, which sought reunification through the elections proposed for 1956. The South Vietnamese government crushed and banned the committee in November of that year, and Thọ and other members were jailed after a police raid. He remained in detention until he escaped in 1961.

The National Front for the Liberation of South Vietnam had been co-founded by Thọ on 20 December 1960, and after his escape he became chairman of its Central Committee. The front launched an armed insurgency against the government of South Vietnam during the Vietnam War. In 1965 he gave a speech on the front's fifth anniversary that was later published as a booklet in English. In 1969 he became Chairman of the Consultative Council of the Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam, a post he kept until South Vietnam was merged with the north in 1976.

When the Socialist Republic of Vietnam was founded on 2 July 1976, Thọ became one of two vice-presidents under President Tôn Đức Thắng and the first mayor of Ho Chi Minh City. After Tôn Đức Thắng died in 1980 he served as acting president until Trường Chinh took the post in July 1981. He was then Chairman of the National Assembly until 1987, Vice-Chairman of the Council of State from 1981 to 1992, and from 1988 to 1994 chairman of the Vietnamese Fatherland Front. He was awarded the Lenin Peace Prize in 1983-84. He died in Ho Chi Minh City on 24 December 1996, aged 86.
nguyen-kim: Nguyễn Kim claimed descent from Nguyễn Trãi, one of the chief aides of Lê Lợi. His father, Nguyễn Hoang Du, was one of the leaders of the first revolt against Mạc Đăng Dung, a high-ranking officer of the weakened court; when that revolt was crushed his father was executed. In 1527 Mạc Đăng Dung deposed the reigning Lê monarch, Lê Cung Hoàng, and made himself ruler of Đại Việt, and a second revolt followed, led by Nguyễn Kim and his son-in-law Trịnh Kiểm.

In 1529 Nguyễn Kim went to Laos and submitted to King Photisarath, who gave him the territory of Xam Neua to administer. As Mạc Đăng Dung put down the Lê loyalists in Thanh Hóa, the remnants of the old court took refuge in Nguyễn Kim's domain. In 1533 he proclaimed Prince Lê Ninh, a son of Emperor Lê Chiêu Tông, king of Đại Việt, a claim Photisarath recognised and supported with resources. Envoys went to Ming China in 1536 and 1537 to denounce Mạc Đăng Dung as a usurper and ask for help, but the Ming called off their intervention.

The war against the Mạc went on through most of the sixteenth century, the Lê slowly regaining power with the help of two military clans of Thanh Hóa, the Nguyễn and the Trịnh. Although the families were allies and linked by marriage, a rivalry grew between Nguyễn Kim and Trịnh Kiểm, whose own ambitions the alliance did not restrain.

Nguyễn Kim was murdered in 1545 by a Mạc general who had come to surrender, and the Trịnh gained the upper hand. Trịnh Kiểm then had Nguyễn Kim's elder son killed. The youngest son, Nguyễn Hoàng, fearing the same fate, asked through his sister, Trịnh Kiểm's wife, to be made governor of the distant southern frontier lands of Thuận Hoá and Quảng Nam. Trịnh Kiểm agreed, and in 1558 Nguyễn Hoàng went south, the beginning of a political division of the country between the Trịnh and the Nguyễn lords that lasted 250 years.
nguyen-lords: The Nguyễn traced their descent from a clan of Thanh Hóa Province that had supported Lê Lợi in his war of independence against the Ming dynasty. After Mạc Đăng Dung overthrew the emperor Lê Cung Hoàng in 1527, Nguyễn Kim and his son-in-law Trịnh Kiểm led the resistance in the name of the Lê. Nguyễn Kim died on 20 May 1545, the same day he visited the camp of the Mạc commander Dương Chấp Nhất, and his eldest son Nguyễn Uông was then secretly killed by Trịnh Kiểm, who took control of the government.

Kim's second son Nguyễn Hoàng, fearing the same fate, had his sister ask Trịnh Kiểm to make him governor of the southern frontier province of Thuận Hóa, land that had once belonged to Champa. He moved there with his family and loyal generals in 1558 and was later made governor of Quảng Nam as well.

In 1600 Nguyễn Hoàng broke off relations with the northern court, arguing that the Trịnh, not the Lê emperor, ruled. He died in 1613 after 55 years in the south. When Trịnh Tùng had the emperor executed in 1620, his successor Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên refused to send taxes or to recognise the new emperor, and open war with Trịnh Tráng followed in 1627. Peace with Trịnh Tạc began a long era of relative calm between north and south.

The Nguyễn then turned south. They fought Champa in 1611, 1629, 1653 and 1692, ruling the Cham court through the Principality of Thuận Thành, and invaded Cambodia in 1658, 1690, 1691, 1697 and 1713. Vietnamese had been allowed to settle at Prey Nokor, later Saigon, in 1623, and after a campaign begun in 1755 the Nguyễn held the Mekong Delta and the port of Hà Tiên. In 1771 heavy taxes and defeats in Cambodia set off the Tây Sơn uprising; the Trịnh attacked from the north in 1774, and by 1777 Gia Định had fallen and nearly the whole family had been killed except the nephew Nguyễn Ánh, who fled to Siam.

The realm was called Đàng Trong, the Inner Realm, and by Europeans the Kingdom of Cochinchina. In 1744 Nguyễn Phúc Khoát took the title Nguyễn Vương to match the Trịnh lords. The Nguyễn were more open to Europeans than the Trịnh: the Portuguese set up a trading post at Hội An, and Portuguese engineers helped them cast bronze cannon. Alexandre de Rhodes reached the court at Huế in 1640, but Nguyễn Phúc Lan later sentenced him to death and allowed him to leave.
nguyen-nhac: Nguyễn Nhạc was born in Tây Sơn District of Quy Nhơn Province, modern Bình Định, the elder brother of Nguyễn Lữ and Nguyễn Huệ; the Vietnamese historian Trần Trọng Kim described him as courageous and clever. The brothers lived by trading betel and learned martial arts from Trương Văn Hiến. Nhạc became a tax collector for the Nguyễn lords, but gave the taxes he collected to poor farmers and fled with his brothers to live as an outlaw. Hiến urged him to revolt, citing a prophecy of revolt in the west and success in the north.

The revolt of 1771 aimed to overthrow Trương Phúc Loan, regent for the young lord Nguyễn Phúc Thuần, and to enthrone the prince Nguyễn Phúc Dương, and it drew the poor as well as Montagnards, Chams and Sino-Vietnamese. Nhạc took Quy Nhơn by having himself delivered to its prison and opening the city gate at night. When the Trịnh of the north invaded and took Phú Xuân, he was beaten at Cẩm Sa and made peace with them. He took the title king of Tây Sơn in 1776, with his capital at Đồ Bàn Citadel, and in 1778 crowned himself emperor with the era name Thái Đức.

When Huệ captured Thăng Long against his orders in 1786, Nhạc marched north with 2,500 men, promised to take no territory from Tonkin and withdrew, proclaiming himself the Central Emperor and giving Lữ Gia Định and Huệ the lands north of Hải Vân. War between Nhạc and Huệ soon followed. Huệ besieged Quy Nhơn for months until Nhạc appealed to him from the walls, and the brothers agreed a boundary at Bến Bản. After Huệ proclaimed himself Emperor Quang Trung in 1788, Nhạc gave up the imperial title and called himself King of Tây Sơn.

The quarrel between the brothers let Nguyễn Ánh return to Cochinchina, and in his last years Nhạc held only Quy Nhơn, Quảng Ngãi and Phú Yên. When the Nguyễn attacked Quy Nhơn in 1793 he had to ask for help from Huệ's successor Nguyễn Quang Toản, whose general Phạm Công Hưng relieved the city and then claimed it for the emperor of Phú Xuân; Nhạc died soon after, vomiting blood. After Nguyễn Ánh overthrew the dynasty in 1802, his tomb was razed, his remains were crushed to ashes and his skull was locked up in prison.
nguyen-phu-trong: Nguyễn Phú Trọng was born on 14 April 1944 in Đông Hội Commune, Đông Anh district of Hanoi. His official biography gives his family background only as average peasant. He took a bachelor's degree in philology at Vietnam National University, Hanoi, between 1963 and 1967, and joined the Communist Party of Vietnam on 19 December 1967.

He worked for the party's theoretical journal Tạp chí Cộng Sản in several periods between 1968 and 1996. In 1981 he went to the Soviet Union to study at the Academy of Sciences and received a Candidate of Sciences degree in history in 1983; he became an Associate Professor in 1992 and a Professor in 2002.

Trọng joined the party's Central Committee in January 1994, its Politburo in December 1997 and the National Assembly in May 2002. From January 2000 to June 2006 he was secretary of the party committee of Hanoi, the de facto head of the city authority, and on 26 June 2006 he was elected Chairman of the National Assembly, a post he held until 2011.

Trọng was elected General Secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam at the 11th National Congress in 2011 and re-elected in 2016 and again on 31 January 2021, when he became the first leader since Lê Duẩn to serve more than two terms. Soon after taking office he became head of the Central Steering Committee for Anti-Corruption, which in 2012 was placed directly under the Politburo. A large anti-corruption campaign followed, which he compared to a burning furnace; between 2017 and 2020 the Politburo took disciplinary action against 110 senior party members, and the president Nguyễn Xuân Phúc later resigned after scandals involving his subordinates.

In foreign policy he visited China in October 2011, and in July 2015 he became the first Vietnamese party chief to make a state visit to the United States. Following the death of President Trần Đại Quang, the National Assembly elected him president on 23 October 2018, making him the third person after Hồ Chí Minh and Trường Chinh to head both party and state. He held the presidency until 2 April 2021, when Nguyễn Xuân Phúc succeeded him.

On 18 July 2024 Trọng was replaced on a caretaker basis as General Secretary by President Tô Lâm because of ill health, and he died on 19 July 2024 at Central Military Hospital 108 in Hanoi, aged 80. A state funeral was held on 25 and 26 July, ending with his burial at Mai Dịch Cemetery.
nguyen-trai: Nguyễn Trãi, whose pen name was Ức Trai, came from a family of Hải Dương Province and was born in Thăng Long, present-day Hanoi, the capital of the declining Trần dynasty. Under the brief Hồ dynasty he passed the examinations and served for a time in the government. In 1406 Ming forces invaded and conquered Vietnam, and the occupiers tried to make the country a Chinese province, putting down every rebellion harshly.

In 1417 Nguyễn Trãi joined Lê Lợi, who was resisting the occupation from the mountains of Thanh Hóa Province. He served the movement as chief adviser, strategist and propagandist, and wrote Lê Lợi's political statements. Until 1423 the rebels waged a guerrilla campaign; after a truce they moved south to Nghệ An and won control of the land from Thanh Hóa southwards. When the Ming general Wang Tong reached the Red River Delta in 1426, the rebels cut his supply lines and held the countryside, while Nguyễn Trãi sent letters to the Ming commanders to weaken their resolve and seek a favourable peace.

In 1427 the Xuande Emperor sent two large relief armies, defeated on the frontier, above all at the Battle of Chi Lăng-Xương Giang. Wang Tong sued for peace, and the Chinese prisoners were given provisions and allowed to go home. Nguyễn Trãi rose high at the new court, but intrigue kept him from the regency after Lê Lợi died; it went to Lê Sát, who governed for the young Lê Thái Tông. Finding court life ever harder, Nguyễn Trãi retired to his country home in the mountains of Chí Linh, north of Hanoi, to write poetry and meditate.

The young emperor began an affair with Nguyễn Thị Lộ, a wife or concubine of Nguyễn Trãi, and fell ill and died soon after visiting the scholar's home. The nobles accused both of regicide and had them executed with most of their extended families. Twenty years later Emperor Lê Thánh Tông declared Nguyễn Trãi wholly innocent and gave him the posthumous title Count of Tán Trù.

Many of his writings on literature, history, geography and ceremony were lost after his execution. Most surviving poems were collected in Ức Trai Thi Tập by Dương Bá Cung, printed in 1868. Loren Baritz, in a 1985 history of American involvement in Vietnam, saw in his essay on strategy against the Chinese, which placed the political and moral struggle above military action, an anticipation of the Communists' strategy of insurgency. Most cities in Vietnam have major streets named after him.
nguyen-van-linh: Linh was born Nguyễn Văn Cúc on 1 July 1915 in Hanoi, into a civil servant's family from Hưng Yên province, and later took the name Nguyễn Văn Linh as a nom de guerre; he was also known as Mười Cúc. Arrested by the French on 1 May 1930 while handing out anti-imperialist leaflets, he was sentenced to life imprisonment on Côn Đảo. Released in 1936 after the victory of the Popular Front in France, he joined the Indochinese Communist Party, worked in Haiphong, Hanoi and Saigon, and was sent back to Côn Đảo after his arrest in Vinh in 1941.

After the August Revolution of 1945 Linh led the resistance in Saigon–Chợ Lớn and rose in the Nam Bộ Regional Committee, which directed the party in the south. He entered the Central Committee in 1960 and in January 1961 became secretary of the re-established Central Office for South Vietnam (COSVN), later serving as deputy to Phạm Hùng. According to his official biography he directed preparations in the Saigon area for the Tet Offensive of 1968.

After the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975 he was the city's party secretary and joined the Politburo in December 1976. He favoured a slow transformation of the formerly capitalist South, which set him against the party leader Lê Duẩn, and he was dropped from the Politburo in 1982. Back in Ho Chi Minh City as party secretary, he backed state enterprises that widened their autonomy and returned to the Politburo in June 1985.

As general secretary Linh signed a newspaper column in Nhân Dân, "Things to be done immediately", which attacked corruption; the political scientist Carlyle Thayer saw it as the start of a period of press liberalization. Linh nevertheless rejected multiparty politics, and in 1990 the Central Committee disciplined the Politburo member Trần Xuân Bách for promoting pluralism. In September 1990 he took part in secret talks with Jiang Zemin and Li Peng in Chengdu that reached agreement on Cambodia and on normalizing relations with China.

Citing poor health, Linh stepped down at the Seventh Congress in June 1991 and was succeeded by Đỗ Mười. In retirement he criticized some effects of the reforms, including the gap between rich and poor. He died of liver cancer in Ho Chi Minh City on 27 April 1998. The Western press often called him the "Vietnamese Gorbachev", while the scholar Martin Gainsborough wrote that he was as capable as anyone of tightening political control.
nguyen-van-thieu: Thieu was born in Phan Rang on the south central coast of Vietnam, the youngest of five children of a small, well-off landowner who farmed and fished. His elder brothers raised money for him to attend the elite schools run by France, including the École Pellerin in Huế. After the Second World War he joined the Viet Minh, rose to be a district chief, and left after a year, saying he had come to know that they were communists. He moved to Saigon and joined the forces of the French-associated State of Vietnam. Later, after his marriage, he converted to Catholicism.

In 1956 Thieu became head of the National Military Academy at Đà Lạt for four years and was sent to the United States for training in 1957 and 1960. In November 1960 he sent infantry of his 7th Division to help crush a coup attempt against President Ngô Đình Diệm. Yet he led the 5th Division in the coup of 1 November 1963: his troops assaulted Gia Long Palace, which fell at 06:37, and Diệm was captured and killed. Thieu joined the Military Revolutionary Council and was made a general. In 1965 he became figurehead chief of state with Air Marshal Nguyễn Cao Kỳ as prime minister, ending the series of short-lived juntas.

He was elected president in September 1967 with Kỳ as running mate, and he held office until 21 April 1975, sidelining Kỳ and concentrating power. When the communists attacked the cities at the Lunar New Year of 1968 he was away from Saigon at his wife's family home in Mỹ Tho, and Kỳ took command in the capital. Thieu was re-elected unopposed in October 1971, after he passed legislation limiting candidacy. He opposed the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973. In 1975, after the loss of Phước Long, he decided to hold only the most populous areas and ordered the Central Highlands abandoned. His contradictory orders in the northern I Corps led to panic and collapse.

Thieu resigned on 21 April 1975, saying, I resign, but I do not desert, and he left for Taiwan four days later. He afterwards lived in London and then in Massachusetts, where he kept a low profile and never wrote an autobiography. He died in 2001. Historians describe his regime as military-dominated, evolving towards authoritarianism, with a lively press and civil society; the press accused him of tolerating corruption.
ngwane-v: Bhunu was born on 11 May 1876, a son of King Mbandzeni and Labotsibeni Mdluli, whose father Matsafeni Mdluli had been a governor under Mswati II. His father named him Bhunu, meaning Boer, at a time of intense contact between the Swazi kingdom and Dutch settlers. He was also known as Mahlokohla and Hhili, and had a younger brother, Prince Malunge. On 3 June 1890, aged 14, he was shown to the nation before the year of mourning for his father had ended, and he was formally installed at the age of 19.

His royal capital was at Zombodze, while the Queen Mother lived at Lobamba. Under the Swaziland Convention, a partial Boer administration ran beside his own, the concessions granted by his father and by Mswati II were enforced, and he and Labotsibeni received a stipend from taxes, postal revenue and concession payments. The taxes drove many Swazis to work in the tin and gold mines of the kingdom or of the South African Republic, though Transvaal authority was never fully applied and Swazis went on being ruled by traditional methods.

In 1898 Ngwane allegedly ordered the killing of the royal governor Mbhabha Nsibandze and his collaborators. Prosecuted by the Transvaal authorities, he fled to Zululand, returned under guarantees of safety and was tried at Bremersdorp, present-day Manzini, arriving with a large Swazi army; he was charged only with public disturbance and fined. When war broke out between the British and the Boer republics in 1899, President Paul Kruger withdrew the white residents and advised him to rule his country in peace, and Swaziland declared its neutrality.

He died aged 23 while dancing the sacred incwala ceremony, and poisoning was suspected. His death was kept from the nation until the ceremony was over. The Swazi council chose his wife Lomawa Ndwandwe as Queen Mother and their four-month-old son Sobhuza II as king, under the regency of Labotsibeni and Prince Malunge until 1921. Sobhuza went on to rule for 82 years. Mahlokohla Street, one of the main streets of Mbabane, is named after him.
ngwenya-mine: The mine lies on Bomvu Ridge, north-west of Mbabane. Its name means crocodile in siSwati, after the crocodile shape of the mountains that held it, which heavy mining from the 1960s defaced. The deposit is of red and specular haematite, and its iron ore holds up to 60 per cent iron.

Stone Age artefacts found during archaeological work in the late 1960s and early 1970s were first dated by radiocarbon to more than 20,000 years ago; later radiocarbon dates put the oldest mining at 41,000 to 43,000 years ago. Red ochre from the site was extracted by the ancestors of the San and used in rock paintings, which are common in Eswatini. By about 400 CE pastoralist Bantu groups from north of the Lepelle river had settled there; they smelted iron ore and traded their iron widely.

The ore was prospected in the middle of the 19th century. The Swaziland Iron Ore Development Company, owned by the Anglo-American Corporation, began open-pit mining in 1964, and a ten-year contract made a Japanese company its largest customer. The works brought the Goba railway line, linking the mine with the Mozambique Railway System, and an electricity supply network. An estimated 20,000,000 tonnes of ore were extracted and about 32 million tons remained in the ground; the company reportedly stopped because the mine flooded.

The land was later donated to the Swaziland National Trust Commission. In 2008, as the government considered reopening the mine, the commission submitted the site for the UNESCO list of World Heritage Sites, but the submission was not accepted. The Indian group Salgaocar worked the modern mine from 2011 to 2014, after King Mswati III dismissed the commission's request to protect the area and replaced its board. Those operations heavily polluted the water sources of Mbabane and threatened Disa intermedia, a protected orchid that grows only in the region.

The inactive ancient mine is called the Lion Cavern, and the modern mine nearby is flooded. A visitor centre opened in 2005 in a building donated by the Republic of China in Taiwan, but it burnt down in September 2018, and all the ancient artefacts displayed there were lost.
niagara-escarpment: The escarpment is an arc-shaped, broken ridge about 1,050 kilometres long, generally facing north, that runs round the top of the Great Lakes Basin. In Rochester, New York, the Genesee River falls over it in three waterfalls; in Ontario it follows the Lake Ontario shore through St. Catharines and Hamilton, turns north at Milton towards Georgian Bay, and forms the spine of the Bruce Peninsula and Manitoulin Island, before crossing the Upper Peninsula of Michigan and the Door Peninsula to end in Dodge County, Wisconsin.

It is not a fault line but the product of unequal erosion. A cap of hard dolostone of the Silurian Lockport Formation, laid down on the floor of an Ordovician-Silurian tropical sea, overlies softer shale; as streams wear the shale away, the caprock is undercut and a cliff is left. The process is quickest at Niagara Falls, and in places, as north of Georgetown, Ontario, glacial deposits such as the Oak Ridges Moraine bury the ridge.

In High Cliff State Park in Wisconsin, animal and geometric effigy mounds of the escarpment's early inhabitants stand beside the remains of a limestone quarry and kiln of the early 20th century. The ridge was a major obstacle to the Erie Canal, which climbed it by a series of locks, and the town that grew there took the name Lockport, New York. The Welland Canal later carried ships across it between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario. Hamilton, Ontario, straddles the ridge, which residents call the Mountain, and from 1892 to 1936 the Hamilton Incline Railway carried people up and down it.

UNESCO designated the escarpment a World Biosphere Reserve in February 1990, and the Niagara Escarpment Commission, an agency of the Ontario government, regulates land use along it. Its cliffs hold the oldest forest ecosystem in eastern North America, including an eastern white cedar dating from 688, the oldest tree in Ontario. The Bruce Trail follows it from Queenston to Tobermory, and wine regions lie along it in New York, Ontario and Wisconsin.
niagara-on-the-lake: Niagara-on-the-Lake lies on the Niagara Peninsula at the point where the Niagara River meets Lake Ontario, across the river from New York. Before British settlers came, the point where Fort Mississauga stands was inhabited by at least three Native American peoples: the Neutral in the 15th century, the Seneca in the late 17th century and the Mississauga in the 18th. The town takes in the former villages of Queenston and St. Davids and the settlements of Virgil and Glendale.

The settlement was founded in 1781 as Butlersburg, after Colonel John Butler, commander of Butler's Rangers, and was a British military base and a haven for loyalists fleeing the United States after the American Revolution. John Graves Simcoe renamed it Newark in 1792, when it became the first capital of Upper Canada, and the legislature first met at Navy Hall on 17 September 1792. Simcoe later moved the capital to York because Newark was so close to the American border. It was renamed Niagara in 1798, and the Act Against Slavery of 1793 was signed by the first legislative session on the site of what became Parliament Oak Public School.

Fort George was built just south of the settlement between 1796 and 1799. In the War of 1812 American forces took the town in May 1813 after a two-day bombardment from Fort Niagara and their fleet, followed by a fierce battle. The British retook the fort in December 1813, and American soldiers burned the town to the ground as they withdrew. Laura Secord became known for walking 32 kilometres in 1813 to warn British forces of an impending American attack. The citizens rebuilt the town after the war. The name Niagara-on-the-Lake was adopted about 1880 as a postal address and became official in 1970.

Most of the former military sites, including Fort George, Navy Hall and Butler's Barracks, have been restored, Fort George in the 1930s as a Depression work project, and Parks Canada manages them with other sites as the Niagara National Historic Sites. The historic district was designated a National Historic Site of Canada in 2003. Niagara-on-the-Lake is the only municipality in Canada whose mayor is by law called the Lord Mayor, a title fixed by an act of 1969. Its population was 19,088 at the 2021 census.
niagara-river: The Niagara River flows north from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario and forms part of the border between Ontario to the west and New York to the east. It is sometimes described as a strait, is about 58 km long and drops 99 metres in all. Over the past 12,000 years Niagara Falls has moved roughly 11 kilometres upstream from the leading edge of the Niagara Escarpment, leaving a gorge below the falls, which also holds the Niagara Whirlpool and further rapids. Grand Island and Navy Island are the two largest of its islands, and Goat Island and Luna Island divide the falls into the Horseshoe, Bridal Veil and American sections.

The origin of the river's name is debated. The Iroquoian scholar Bruce Trigger derives it from a branch of the Neutral Confederacy, called the Niagagarega on several late 17th-century French maps, while George R. Stewart proposes the Iroquois town of Ongniaahra, meaning point of land cut in two.

The river and falls became known outside North America in the late 17th century, when the French explorer Louis Hennepin first saw them and wrote of them in A New Discovery of a Vast Country in America in 1698. In 1764 the British military engineer John Montresor built an inclined wooden tramway at what is now Lewiston, New York, called The Cradles, the earliest recorded railway in America. In 1781 the Niagara Purchase covered a strip of land 6.5 kilometres wide along the west bank.

Fort George and Fort Niagara at the river's mouth and Fort Erie at its head defended it and were important in the Seven Years' War and the American Revolutionary War. The Battle of Queenston Heights took place near the river in the War of 1812. Navy Island served as a French naval base in the 18th century and as a small Royal Navy shipyard from 1763 until about 1818, after the Rush-Bagot Treaty. Before the American Civil War many African Americans escaping slavery crossed the river on the Underground Railroad to Canada; a monument at Lewiston commemorates them and the local volunteers who helped. In the 1880s the river became the first waterway in the world harnessed for large-scale hydroelectric generation.

Power plants on the river include the Sir Adam Beck stations on the Canadian side, built in 1922 and 1954, and the Robert Moses plant on the American side, built in 1961. The International Control Dam of 1954 regulates the flow, and ships bypass the falls by the Welland Canal.
niall-glundub: Niall Glúndub, Niall Black-Knee, was a son of Áed Findliath and belonged to the Cenél nEógain, one of the kin groups of the Uí Néill, who traced their descent from Niall of the Nine Hostages. His mother was Máel Muire, a daughter of Kenneth MacAlpin, King of Scots. He is first recorded in 911, when he succeeded his brother Domnall mac Áeda as King of Ailech after Domnall withdrew into religious life.

Niall extended his power over neighbouring kingdoms, defeating the kings of Dál nAraidi and the Ulaid at the battles of Glarryford and Ballymena, in present-day County Antrim, before he was beaten by the High King Flann Sinna of the Clann Cholmáin at the Battle of Crossakiel in County Meath. He married Flann's daughter Gormflaith ingen Flann Sinna, and on Flann's death in 916 succeeded him, his claim backed by the clans of Leth Cuinn, the northern half of Ireland. As High King he revived the Óenach Tailteann, a traditional assembly of the Irish clans.

From 914 the Northmen of the Uí Ímair invaded the south, weakening the Eoghanacht of Munster and setting up a longphort at Waterford. Niall marched south to help Munster, and in the summer of 917 fought a large, indecisive battle in which many nobles and tributary kings of his following died. The army of the King of Leinster, called to reinforce him, was destroyed near St Mullins, leaving Leinster tributary to the Northmen.

The Northmen went on settling and re-established their stronghold at Dublin after a gap of 15 years. Niall advanced into Leinster with the Uí Néill clans, the Airgíalla and the Ulaid, but his army was routed by the Northmen under Sihtric Cáech, and he died on 14 September 919 with twelve other chieftains. Donnchad Donn mac Flainn, son of Flann Sinna, followed him as High King, and his own son Muirchertach mac Néill as King of Ailech.
niall-of-the-nine-hostages: The early Irish annals say little about Niall, and his dates rest on later reckoning: the Annals of Inisfallen place his death before 382 and the Chronicon Scotorum in 411, while the Annals of the Four Masters date his reign to 379–405 and Geoffrey Keating to 368–395. Because his sons are recorded between 429 and 516, Kathleen Hughes and Francis J. Byrne argue that events were pushed back to suit an early date for Saint Patrick; Byrne, following James Carney, dates his death to about 452. The High Kingship itself became a reality only in the 9th century.

The tale of the sons of Eochaid Mugmedón, possibly of the 11th century, makes Niall the son of the High King Eochaid by his second wife, Cairenn Chasdub, daughter of a king of the Saxons; Keating calls her a daughter of the king of Britain. Left on the ground at birth for fear of Eochaid's first wife Mongfind and raised by the poet Torna, Niall later returned to Tara and freed his mother from forced labour.

In the legend a druid, Sithchenn, tested Eochaid's five sons in a burning forge, from which Niall saved an anvil, and then sent them hunting; only Niall kissed the hag guarding a well, who became the Sovereignty of Ireland and promised the kingship to his descendants. Another story has Mongfind poison her brother Crimthann, leaving the high kingship to Niall. T. F. O'Rahilly held that Niall and his sons broke up the ancient kingdom of Ulster, and he and Byrne argue that the late sources preserve genuine traditions of raids on Britain.

All sources name Eochaid, son of Énnae Cennsalach of Leinster, as his killer and place his death outside Ireland: on the English Channel, in Brittany, among Pictish bards in Scotland or beside the Loire. Byrne suggests he died raiding Roman Britain. His body is said to lie at Faughan Hill near Navan in County Meath, and his nephew Nath Í succeeded him. His epithet is explained by hostages from the five provinces and from Scotland or other peoples, or, as O'Rahilly suggests, by the nine hostages owed by the Airgíalla. A 2006 genetic claim that millions of men descend from him is no longer thought plausible.
niamey: Niamey lies in the western part of Niger, surrounded by the Tillabéri Region, mostly on the plateau of the left bank of the Niger River, with a few developments on the alluvial plain of the right bank. At the core of the Sahel it has a hot semi-arid climate, with monthly highs from 32 °C in January to 41 °C in April, and an annual rainfall of 500 to 750 millimetres falling mostly between early June and early September. The Niger is the city's only permanent river.

The area was of little importance before the colonial era and served as a buffer zone between the Sahelian kingdoms. In the late sixteenth century its residents included Zarma and other Songhai refugees from the Moroccan invasion of the Songhai Empire, Hausa-speaking Maouri hunters and the Fula. French forces began their invasion of Niger in 1891. The first European mentions of Niamey come from the 1897 mission of Émile Auguste Léon Hourst and the 1899 Voulet–Chanoine Mission, which set fire to it. Captain Henri Salaman established a military post there in 1901.

Niamey replaced Zinder as the territorial capital from 1903 to 1911 and again in 1926, after which large-scale development followed. The first city plan, in 1930, relocated neighbourhoods and segregated European and indigenous districts, which remained separate until the 1950s. In 1956 Niamey held Niger's first municipal elections and elected Djibo Bakary as its first mayor. Its population had reached 33,816 by 1960, the year of independence. In the 1970s and 1980s growth was fuelled by the national uranium boom and by droughts that brought rural migrants.

Niamey is the capital and largest city of Niger and its main economic centre, with a large informal economy and extensive urban agriculture. The languages of its two largest peoples, Zarma and Hausa, serve as lingua francas. The city is divided into five communes, four on the left bank and one on the right, and is home to Abdou Moumouni University and the Niamey National Hospital. The 2022 estimate gave it 1,407,635 inhabitants.
nian-rebellion: Nian was a word of the Huaibei dialect for loosely affiliated gangs. The movement was formed in the late 1840s by Zhang Lexing and numbered about 2,000 by 1851. It had no clear goals beyond criticism of the government and the slogan "kill the rich and aid the poor". The Yellow River flood of 1851 and a second breach of its banks in 1855 brought great loss of life and famine, which a government drained by the First Opium War and the Taiping Rebellion could not relieve. The Nian borrowed sworn brotherhood, banners and trigram flags from the White Lotus, but most members were desperate peasants seeking survival, plunder and freedom from taxes.

In 1851 the Nian began raiding village grain stores and silver caches. In 1855 Zhang Lexing attacked government troops, and by summer the Nian cavalry, armed with modern firearms, had cut communications between Beijing and the Qing armies fighting the Taiping. The rebels fortified captured towns as bases for raids, while peasant support and fortified earthwall communities sustained them. In 1856 several bands formed a confederation of five banner armies, each drawn largely from one clan, but by 1858 it had effectively dissolved. Hong Xiuquan gave Nian leaders titles, but the two rebellions never fully coordinated.

The Mongol general Senggelinqin destroyed most of the Nian infantry and killed Zhang Lexing in an ambush in 1863, but from late 1864 the Taiping commanders Lai Wenguang and Fan Ruzeng took over the Nian, whose cavalry remained intact. In late 1865 Senggelinqin was killed in an ambush. Zeng Guofan then hemmed in the horsemen with canals and trenches, and after one of his lines was broken Li Hongzhang and Zuo Zongtang replaced him. In late 1866 the Nian split into an Eastern Army under Lai Wenguang and a Western Army, which was defeated south-west of Beijing; most Nian territory was retaken by late 1867, and the remnants were crushed early in 1868.

The Nian failed to topple the dynasty largely because they never joined forces with the Taiping, accepting the Taiping king's appointments but not his orders. Yet the floods, the fighting and the Qing forces' scorched-earth tactics ruined the countryside and caused countless deaths, depriving the dynasty of taxes and trade duties and leaving its economy precarious. In the long term the rebellion became one of the major factors in the collapse of Qing China.
nibelungenlied: The anonymous poet, likely from the region of Passau, drew on an oral tradition of Germanic heroic legend, the Nibelungen saga, which has part of its origin in historic events and individuals of the 5th and 6th centuries. Various historical figures and events had been melded into one plot, political motives had been personalised into feuds and preferences, and persons who never lived at the same time appear as contemporaries.

The poet suppressed the mythological parts of Siegfried's story. The slaying of the dragon is reduced to one stanza in a retrospective tale told by Hagen, while Siegfried himself is shown as receiving a courtly education in Xanten. The poem is conventionally dated to around 1200, since Wolfram von Eschenbach alludes to it in his Parzival, written about 1204 or 1205.

In the first part Siegfried, educated at court in the Netherlands, comes to Worms to ask for Kriemhild, sister of the Burgundian kings Gunther, Gernot and Giselher. He helps Gunther win the warrior-queen Brünhild, and marries Kriemhild, but the two women become rivals, and Hagen, a vassal of Gunther, kills Siegfried with Gunther's involvement. In the second part the widowed Kriemhild marries Etzel, king of the Huns,. After years she persuades Etzel to invite her brothers and Hagen to a feast. They come with an army, and her revenge ends in the death of all the Burgundians who went and in the destruction of Etzel's kingdom and of Kriemhild herself.

The poem is written in four-line stanzas, each with three long lines split by a caesura and a longer fourth line. It was meant to be sung, though no melody survives, and its formulaic language is taken as a sign of fictive orality.

There are 37 known manuscripts and fragments, which suggests the poem was among the most popular works of the German Middle Ages. Medieval readers were most interested in the destruction of the Burgundians, and the Nibelungenklage, a sequel written soon afterwards and found in all manuscripts, tried to make sense of the horror and to absolve Kriemhild. The poem was forgotten after around 1500 and rediscovered in 1755 by Jacob Hermann Obereit; Johann Jacob Bodmer called it the German Iliad.

It became the German national epic and was used for nationalist purposes, and in anti-democratic, reactionary and Nazi propaganda before and during the Second World War. In 2009 the three main manuscripts were inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.
nicaea: Nicaea lay in the northwestern Anatolian region of Bithynia, in a fertile basin at the eastern end of Lake Ascanius, between ranges of hills. Its west wall rose from the lake itself, which protected it from siege on that side and kept a source of supplies open. Strabo describes a Hellenistic city laid out as a square of about 700 metres on a side, with four gates and streets meeting at right angles. After an earthquake the Emperor Hadrian visited in 123 CE and began a rebuilding, and the city was enclosed by a wall some 5 kilometres long with more than a hundred towers.

Antigonus I Monophthalmus refounded the city about 315 BCE as Antigoneia, and after his defeat at Ipsus in 301 BCE Lysimachus renamed it Nicaea for his wife. Before 280 BCE it passed to the kings of Bithynia and became a royal seat, beginning a rivalry with Nicomedia that lasted for centuries. Rome took it in 72 BCE, and the Goths sacked it in 258 CE. In 325 CE the first Ecumenical Council met there and adopted the Nicene Creed. The council of 787, attended by Pope Hadrian I, dealt with the iconoclastic controversy and recognised the veneration of images as legitimate.

In 1081 the city fell to Turkish allies of the rebel Nikephoros Melissenos, and the Seljuk Turks made it their capital until 1097, when it returned to Byzantine control after a month's siege with the help of the First Crusade. After the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204, Nicaea escaped Latin occupation. Theodore Laskaris was crowned emperor there in 1208 and founded the Empire of Nicaea, and the exiled Patriarchate of Constantinople also resided there until 1261. It surrendered to Orhan and the Ottomans after a long siege on 2 March 1331, and the church of Hagia Sophia became a mosque.

The ancient city lies within the Turkish city of İznik, whose name comes from Nicaea. Much of the wall survives, though roads have pierced it in many places, and it is a tourist destination. Excavations are under way at the Ottoman kilns where the historic tiles were made, and the ruins of a fourth-century basilica of Saint Neophytos were found under the shallow water of Lake İznik. The Church of the Dormition, one of the most important Byzantine churches in Asia Minor, was destroyed in 1922.
nicard-dialect: Niçard was historically spoken in the city of Nice and a few surrounding communes, and is known in French as niçois and in Italian as nizzardo. Classifications of Occitan hesitate between treating it as a dialect of its own and placing it within Maritime Provençal. Some Italian irredentists have claimed it as a Ligurian dialect. Niçard shares some sound archaisms, among them words stressed on the third syllable from the end, with Occitan areas as distant as Aranese, and like Aranese it bears a heavy influence from a neighbouring language: Italian in the case of Niçard, Catalan in that of Aranese.

Niçard is written in two forms. The classical orthography, which keeps to the native traditions of the language, was developed by Robert Lafont in Phonétique et graphie du provençal (1951) and L'ortografia occitana, lo provençau (1972), and by Jean-Pierre Baquié in Empari lo niçard (1984); it is regulated by the Conselh de la Lenga Occitana. The Mistralian orthography, closer to written French, was invented by the Félibrige, and the city also has an Acadèmia Nissarda. An Italian orthography was abandoned after Nice passed to France, and was briefly brought back in 1942 and 1943, when Italy occupied and administered the city.

Most people of Nice and its region no longer speak Niçard, and the few who do are fully bilingual in French, the dialect having ceased to be an everyday language decades ago. A revival of its use has nonetheless begun: some local television news has been presented in Niçard with French subtitles, and street signs in the old town are written in it beside French. The linguist Domergue Sumien, treating Occitan as a pluricentric language, counted Niçard among its seven regional standards to be taught, and the French Ministry of National Education names it nissart-langue d'oc. The Niçard song Nissa La Bella is often regarded as the anthem of Nice.
niccolo-iii-deste: Niccolò was born in Ferrara on 9 November 1383, the son of Alberto d'Este and Isotta Albaresani. He inherited the city in 1393 at the age of ten and was guided by a regency council backed by the republics of Venice, Florence and Bologna. His uncle Azzo X d'Este, a descendant of Obizzo II d'Este, disputed his right to rule because of his illegitimate birth, although his father had legitimated him. In 1395 Azzo invaded Ferrara with a mercenary army but was defeated and captured by the regency's troops at the Battle of Portomaggiore.

Niccolò was also a condottiero. In 1397 he married Gigliola da Carrara, daughter of Francesco II da Carrara, lord of Padua, who died of plague in 1416. In 1403 he joined the league against Gian Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan, as Captain General of the papal army under Pope Boniface IX, and in 1405 he ceded the family's ancestral lands near Este to Venice. The fencing master Fiore dei Liberi dedicated his treatise Fior di Battaglia to him in 1410, and in 1413 he made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. In 1418 he married Parisina Malatesta, daughter of Andrea Malatesta, and two years later, fearing the ambitions of Filippo Maria Visconti, he ceded Parma to him.

After the executions of 1425 he decreed death for every woman in his lands found guilty of adultery, then had to withdraw the order when it became clear it would depopulate Ferrara. That year he again commanded the anti-Visconti league. In 1429 he married his third wife, Ricciarda of Saluzzo, daughter of Thomas III of Saluzzo, who bore him Ercole I d'Este in 1431 and Sigismondo d'Este in 1433.

The choice of Ferrara as the seat of the council of 1438 confirmed his standing among the princes of Italy. He died on 26 December 1441. He had children by at least eleven women, among them the illegitimate sons Leonello and Borso, and his daughters married into the houses of Malatesta, Gonzaga, Montefeltro and Sforza, Isotta wedding Oddantonio da Montefeltro, Duke of Urbino, and Beatrice marrying Tristano Sforza.
niccolo-machiavelli: Niccolò di Bernardo dei Machiavelli was born in Florence on 3 May 1469, the third child and first son of the attorney Bernardo di Niccolò Machiavelli and Bartolomea di Stefano Nelli. His father was born illegitimate and so could not become a full citizen of Florence or take part in its politics, which also affected Niccolò, who could not obtain full citizenship rights.

He grew up in a tumultuous era. At eight he saw the violence that followed the Pazzi conspiracy, which aimed to kill Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici in a church; only Giuliano died. As a young man he heard the sermons of Girolamo Savonarola but was not swayed. In 1494 Florence restored the republic and expelled the Medici, who had ruled for some sixty years.

Machiavelli's civil service began shortly after Savonarola was burned at the stake for heresy. For many years he served as a senior official in the Florentine Republic with responsibilities in diplomatic and military affairs, working as secretary to the second chancery from 1498 to 1512, while the Medici were out of power.

When the Medici retook power in 1512 he was expelled from his duties. Soon afterwards he was mistakenly suspected of treason and sent into exile. A year later he took up the life of a political writer. He died on 21 June 1527.

His best-known book, The Prince (Il Principe), was written around 1513 but not published until 1532, five years after his death. It addresses not only hereditary princes but also new princes who have founded their own dynasties, and holds that the virtues commonly recommended to rulers can hinder them. A ruler must be willing to act unscrupulously when necessary. He held that it was better for a ruler to be widely feared than greatly loved, and that violence may be needed to stabilise power. The saying that the ends justify the means is often wrongly attributed to him.

The Discourses on Livy, composed c. 1517, is said to have paved the way for modern republicanism, and his works influenced Enlightenment authors such as Jean-Jacques Rousseau and James Harrington. His name came to evoke unscrupulous acts, and commentators such as Leo Strauss have called him a teacher of evil. Scholars disagree on whether his works form a coherent system and whether he was a philosopher proper, and he is often called the father of modern political philosophy and political science.
niccolo-paganini: Niccolò Paganini was born in Genoa on 27 October 1782, the third of six children of Antonio and Teresa Paganini. His father was an unsuccessful ship chandler who supplemented his income as a musician and by selling mandolins. Paganini began on the mandolin at five and moved to the violin at seven. In Parma, Alessandro Rolla sent him to his own teacher Ferdinando Paer and later to Gasparo Ghiretti. He is thought to have developed his relationship with the guitar about 1796, and preferred to play it in intimate rather than public concerts.

In 1801 Paganini became first violin of the Republic of Lucca, though much of his income came from freelancing. In 1805 Lucca was annexed by France and given to Napoleon's sister Elisa Bonaparte, whose husband Felice Baciocchi he taught for ten years. He left the court late in 1809 to resume freelance work. A concert at La Scala in Milan in 1813 was his first break. In 1827 Pope Leo XII gave him the Order of the Golden Spur.

His continental tour began in Vienna in August 1828 and took in every major city in Germany, Poland and Bohemia until February 1831 in Strasbourg, followed by tours of Paris and Britain. Theme and variations were his most popular pieces, and he also played modified works by Rodolphe Kreutzer and Giovanni Battista Viotti. He owned 11 Stradivari at his death.

He was diagnosed with syphilis as early as 1822, and his treatment with mercury and opium had serious side effects. He ended his concert career in September 1834. In Genoa he published his compositions and violin methods rather than guarding their secrets, as was widely believed. In 1836 he set up a casino in Paris, whose immediate failure left him in financial ruin.

Paganini left Paris at Christmas 1838 and settled in Nice, where his condition worsened. He refused the last rites when a priest was sent in May 1840, thinking them premature, and died on 27 May 1840 of internal haemorrhaging before another could be summoned. Because of this and his rumoured association with the devil, the Church denied him a Catholic burial in Genoa. It took four years and an appeal to the Pope for his body to be moved to Genoa, but it was not buried there. It was finally buried in a cemetery in Parma in 1876 and reinterred in a new cemetery there in 1896.
niccolo-piccinino: Piccinino was born in Perugia, the son of a butcher, and was enrolled in the city's butchers' guild; Pope Pius II later called him scornfully the son of a butcher. His family in fact owned a house with a butchery nearby and belonged to the landed middle class, and according to tradition one of his uncles had been podestà of Milan. He began his career in the company of Braccio da Montone, and after the deaths of Braccio in 1424 and soon after of his son Oddo he became leader of the company.

After a short time with the Florentine Republic he entered the service of Filippo Maria Visconti in 1425 and fought, with Niccolò Fortebraccio, in the Wars in Lombardy against Pope Eugene IV, Venice and Florence. He beat the Venetians at the Battle of Delebio on 19 November 1432 and papal forces at Castel Bolognese in 1434. When Francesco Sforza defeated and killed Fortebraccio at Fiordimonte, Piccinino was left in sole command of the Visconti army and seized cities in Romagna by treachery. In 1438 Scaramuccia da Forlì forced him to give up his attempt on Brescia, and in 1439 he fought Sforza, now in Venetian service, in Lombardy.

Hoping, like many condottieri, to win a dominion of his own, he had the duke send him to Umbria, but was defeated at Anghiari in 1440, though his captured men were freed at once, as was usual in wars of soldiers of fortune. Back in Lombardy he surrounded Sforza at Martinengo and demanded the lordship of Piacenza as the price of his capture, but the duke made a truce with Sforza instead.

When Sforza's power in the Marche alarmed the pope, the king of Naples and the Visconti, Piccinino was given command of their joint forces. He drove Sforza from the Marche but was defeated at Montelauro, and while he was preparing a new effort he was suddenly recalled to Milan; his army was beaten in his absence, and he died of grief and of his wounds on 15 October 1444. He left two sons, Jacopo and Francesco, both condottieri.
niccolo-tommaseo: Niccolò Tommaseo was born on 9 October 1802 at Sebenico (Šibenik), which passed in quick succession under Venetian, Napoleonic and Habsburg rule. Culturally and ethnically Italian, he also had a genuine interest in Illyrian popular culture. He was educated at Spalato (Split) in a humanistic and Catholic tradition, and graduated in law at the University of Padua in 1822. He then worked as a journalist between Padua and Milan, where he met Alessandro Manzoni and Antonio Rosmini-Serbati.

In Florence from 1827 he wrote for the Antologia of Giovan Pietro Vieusseux and became a friend of Gino Capponi. His Nuovo Dizionario de' Sinonimi della lingua italiana of 1830 confirmed his reputation. After Austria protested against an article defending the Greek revolution and the journal closed, he went into voluntary exile in Paris, where he published the political work Dell'Italia (1835), the verses Confessioni (1836), a commentary on the Divine Comedy (1837) and Memorie Poetiche (1838).

In Corsica, with Salvatore Viale, he collected the island's oral traditions. In Venice he published the first parts of the novel Fede e bellezza, and the anthology Canti popolari italiani, corsi, illirici, greci (1841). The critic Jovan Skerlić counted him, as Nikola Tomazeo, part of Serbian literature as well as Italian.

In 1847 he returned to journalism and, as an outspoken defender of a free press, was arrested. He was freed in the liberal revolution led by Daniele Manin and took office in the revived Venetian Republic, and when Habsburg control returned he was exiled to Corfu, accused of Italian irredentism. Half blind, he wrote essays there, including Rome et le monde, arguing that the Church should give up temporal power.

He moved to Turin in 1854 and to Florence in 1859, where he lived at a villa in Settignano. His opposition to the House of Savoy led him to refuse all honours, including a seat in the Senate. His last years went to the Dizionario della Lingua Italiana, issued from 1861 and completed in 1874, after his death on 1 May of that year. He is considered a precursor of Italian irredentism.
nice: Nice lies on the French Riviera, at the foot of the French Alps, about 13 kilometres west of Monaco and 30 kilometres west of the French–Italian border. It consists of two large bays, and the city rises from the flat beach into gentle hills bounded by mountains that mark the southern and nearly the western edge of the Ligurian Alps. The Terra Amata archaeological site shows early use of fire and the construction of houses. The settlement of Nikaia was probably founded around 350 BCE and named for Nike, the Greek goddess of victory, in honour of a victory over the neighbouring Ligurians.

Nikaia became one of the busiest trading ports on the Ligurian coast, with a rival in the Roman town of Cemenelum, whose ruins are in the district of Cimiez. It repulsed the Saracens in 729, but they pillaged and burned it in 859 and again in 880 and held the surrounding country for most of the 10th century. In the Middle Ages the city, as an ally of Pisa, was the enemy of Genoa, and it kept its municipal liberties despite attempts by the King of France and the Holy Roman Emperor to subjugate it.

In 1388 the commune placed itself under the protection of the Counts of Savoy, becoming the County of Nice. In 1561 Emmanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy, replaced Latin with Italian as the language of government. The Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 gave the city back to the Duke of Savoy. The armies of the French First Republic conquered the county in 1792, and it reverted to the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia in 1814.

The Treaty of Turin of 1860, signed by the Sardinian king and Napoleon III, ceded the county to France as a reward for French help in the Second Italian War of Independence. A plebiscite was held on 15 and 16 April 1860, and the yes vote won 86 percent in Nice. Opponents of annexation called for abstention, and the result is described as partly due to pressure from the authorities.

Nice is the prefecture of the Alpes-Maritimes department in the region of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur. From the second half of the 18th century English aristocratic families began to spend their winters there, and the Promenade des Anglais, inaugurated in its refurbished form in 1931, takes its name from these visitors, who included Queen Victoria. Marc Chagall and Henri Matisse are commemorated in the city's museums. UNESCO proclaimed Nice a World Heritage Site in 2021 for its history as a winter resort.
nicene-christianity: Nicene Christianity takes its name from the Nicene Creed, formulated at the First Council of Nicaea in 325 and amended at the First Council of Constantinople in 381. The dispute that set it apart from Arianism, its main rival at the time of Nicaea, concerned Christology, the nature of the divinity of Jesus. Nicene Christianity regards Jesus as divine and co-eternal with God the Father, while Arianism treated him as the first among created beings and inferior to the Father.

Religious historians and scholars often define Nicene Christianity more narrowly, as the first form of the state church of the Roman Empire endorsed by the emperors. By that definition the Nicene Church ceased to exist after the Council of Chalcedon in 451, which was called to settle disagreements over the human and divine natures of Christ and concluded that he had two distinct but inseparable natures.

After Chalcedon the Roman Empire made Chalcedonian Christianity its official religion, and the churches that held that Christ had a single nature were excommunicated by the Empire and became the Oriental Orthodox Churches. Arianism, the faith of the Gothic kingdoms, was eclipsed during the 7th century as those kingdoms converted to Nicene Christianity.

In its broader sense the term covers every denomination that adheres to the teaching of the Nicene Creed, which includes the vast majority of Christian churches today. Those outside it include both Protestant and non-Protestant nontrinitarian groups: most of the Latter Day Saint movement, though not the Community of Christ, formerly the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, as well as Jehovah's Witnesses, the Unitarian Church of Transylvania and Oneness Pentecostals.
nichiren: Nichiren was born on 16 February 1222 by the lunar Chinese calendar, which is 6 April in the Gregorian calendar. At twelve he began Buddhist study at Seichō-ji, a temple of the Tendai school, and he took the name Zeshō-bō Renchō on becoming a monk at twenty. Between 1233 and 1253 he studied the major traditions of Japan, including Tendai, Pure Land Buddhism and Shingon, and became convinced of the pre-eminence of the Lotus Sutra. On 28 April 1253 he returned to Seichō-ji to lecture on its supremacy and, according to one of his letters, first declared Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō on Mount Kiyosumi that day.

Nichiren arrived in Kamakura in 1254. Between 1254 and 1260 half the population perished in a succession of calamities that included drought, earthquakes, epidemics, famine, fires and storms. He argued that these sufferings came from the weakened spiritual condition of the people, which led the kami to abandon the nation, and that the root cause was the mass adoption of the exclusive nembutsu teachings of Hōnen. When Mongol envoys again demanded submission in 1269, he felt that his predictions of 1260 were being fulfilled and sharpened his attacks on Zen, Shingon and Risshū in letters to prominent leaders.

The bakufu suppressed his community by exile, imprisonment, land confiscation and expulsion from clan membership. On Sado Island he was lodged in a dilapidated temple in a graveyard, where he and a few disciples endured bitter cold and hunger, and a majority of his followers apparently abandoned their faith. His conditions improved after the winter of 1271–1272. He was pardoned with effect from 14 February 1274 and returned to Kamakura on 26 March, then retired to Mount Minobu in Kai province, from where he directed his followers mainly through letters, including during the Atsuhara affair of 1279. He fell ill in 1282 and died on 13 October 1282 at a disciple's home in Ikegami.

Nichiren believed Japan had entered the Age of Dharma Decline, when only Lotus Sutra practice was effective. He taught that all beings, whatever their class or gender, can attain Buddhahood in this life through chanting the sutra's title, and held that the Three Great Secret Dharmas were the title, the object of worship and the place of ordination. His collected writings run to over 700 manuscripts, among them On Securing the Peace of the Land through the Propagation of True Buddhism, written between 1258 and 1260. Today more than forty registered organisations follow his teachings, including Nichiren-shū, Nichiren Shōshū and the lay movement Soka Gakkai, and the emperor Go-Kōgon bestowed the title Nichiren Dai-Bosatsu on him in 1358.
nicholas-i-mystikos: Nicholas was born in 852 on the Italian Peninsula and became a friend of the Patriarch Photius I. After Photius was dismissed in 886 Nicholas fell into disfavour and retired to a monastery.
