Emperor Leo VI the Wise brought him out of it and made him mystikos, a dignity that designated either the imperial secretary or a judicial official.

Nicholas was appointed patriarch on 1 March 901 but fell out with Leo VI over the emperor's fourth marriage, to his mistress Zoe Karbonopsina. He reluctantly baptised their son, the future Constantine VII, but forbade the emperor to enter the church and may have been involved in the revolt of Andronikos Doukas. He was deposed on 1 February 907 and replaced by Euthymius. Exiled to his own monastery, he held the deposition unjustified and involved Pope Sergius III in the dispute.

He was restored to the patriarchate around the accession of Leo's brother Alexander on 11 May 912. A long struggle with the supporters of Euthymius followed and ended only when Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos issued the Tomos of Union in 920. Alexander died in 913 after provoking a war with Bulgaria, and Nicholas became the leading member of a seven-man regency for the underage Constantine VII. He faced the advance of Simeon I of Bulgaria on Constantinople, negotiated a peaceful settlement, crowned Simeon emperor of the Bulgarians in a makeshift ceremony outside the city and arranged the marriage of Simeon's daughter to Constantine.

The concession was unpopular, and by March 914 Zoe Karbonopsina, with the support of the magistros John Eladas, had overthrown him and replaced him as foremost regent. She revoked the agreement and war with Bulgaria resumed. After the general Leo Phokas the Elder was heavily defeated at the battle of Achelous in 917, the admiral Romanos Lekapenos took over in 919, married his daughter Helena to Constantine and became emperor in 920. Nicholas then became one of his strongest supporters and handled renewed negotiations with the Bulgarians until his death on 15 May 925.

Nicholas wrote many letters to notables and foreign rulers, among them Simeon I of Bulgaria, and a homily on the sack of Thessalonica by the Arabs in 904. He was a critical thinker who went so far as to question the authority of quotations from the Old Testament and the notion that the emperor's command was unwritten law. His feast day in the Eastern Orthodox Church is 16 May.
nicholas-i-of-russia: Nicholas was born in 1796 at Gatchina Palace, the ninth child of Grand Duke Paul and Grand Duchess Maria Feodorovna, who was born Sophie Dorothea of Württemberg. He had two older brothers, the future Emperor Alexander I and Grand Duke Constantine Pavlovich. He trained as a military engineer. On 13 July 1817 he married Princess Charlotte of Prussia, who took the name Alexandra Feodorovna when she converted to Orthodoxy. All seven of their children survived childhood.

Nicholas began his reign on 14 December 1825 (old style). The accession was marred by a demonstration of some 3,000 young army officers and other liberal-minded citizens who wanted a constitution and representative government. He ordered the army to smash it, and the Decembrist revolt was quickly put down. Determined afterwards to restrain Russian society, he relied on the Third Section of the Imperial Chancellery, headed by Alexander Benckendorff, which ran a network of spies and informers.

In 1833 Sergey Uvarov devised the programme of Orthodoxy, Autocracy and Nationality as the regime's guiding principle. It brought repression of independent-minded intellectuals such as Pushkin and Lermontov and persecution of non-Russian languages and non-Orthodox religions. Taras Shevchenko was exiled to Siberia by the tsar's direct order after writing a poem that mocked him. Nicholas also removed local autonomies, Bessarabia's in 1828 and Poland's in 1830. An edict of 1827 required Jewish boys to serve 25 years in the army from the age of 18, and an estimated 70,000 Jews were conscripted between 1827 and 1854.

Nicholas was crowned King of Poland in Warsaw on 12 (24) May 1829. After the November Uprising of 1830–31 he replaced the kingdom's constitution with the Organic Statute, which declared Poland's eternal incorporation into Russia. In foreign policy he acted as protector of legitimism and guardian against revolution, which earned him the label gendarme of Europe. His army numbered one million men, but its equipment and tactics were outdated, and its commanders in the Crimean War were old and incompetent.

Nicholas died on 2 March 1855 at the Winter Palace in St. Petersburg, during the Crimean War. He caught a chill, refused medical treatment and died of pneumonia, and there were rumours that he was committing passive suicide. He was buried in the Peter and Paul Cathedral and succeeded by his son Alexander II. Lev Tolstoy popularised the nickname Nicholas the Stick in 1891. The empire spanned over 20 million square kilometres at his death, but needed reform.
nicholas-ii: Nicholas II was born on 18 May 1868 (6 May in the Old Style calendar) at the Alexander Palace in Tsarskoye Selo, the eldest child of the future Emperor Alexander III and Maria Feodorovna, born Princess Dagmar of Denmark. He was educated privately and trained for military service, though he was widely considered ill-prepared to rule. He became heir apparent on 1 March 1881, when his grandfather Alexander II was assassinated by the Narodnaya Volya. In April 1894 he proposed to Alix of Hesse at Coburg, and they were engaged on 20 April. He became emperor on 1 November 1894, when his father died.

Nicholas believed that his authority came from God and that his duty was to keep his absolute power intact. Early in his reign a deputation of zemstvo representatives presented the Tver Address, proposing constitutional reform, and he rejected it. He pursued an aggressive policy in Manchuria and Korea, which led to the Russo-Japanese War. Defeat, together with the demonstrations shot on Bloody Sunday in January 1905, fed the Revolution of 1905. On 5 August 1905 he issued a manifesto convening the State Duma, and in the October Manifesto he pledged civil liberties and a Duma with legislative powers. The 1906 constitution nevertheless described him as the supreme autocrat, and ministers answered only to him.

In 1904 his son Alexei was born, who had haemophilia, an illness that complicated the question of the succession. In 1907 the Anglo-Russian Convention settled central Asian disputes with Britain and led to the Triple Entente. The government condemned the Kishinev pogrom, though in private Nicholas reportedly admired the mobs. His Russification measures in Finland, begun with the February Manifesto of 1899, were deeply unpopular.

In the First World War Nicholas took command at the front in 1915, leaving the capital to intrigue and strikes, and the failure to supply the army and the population brought riots and mutinies. He abdicated in March 1917, ending 304 years of Romanov rule, and tried to pass the throne to his brother Michael.

Britain offered the family asylum on 19 March 1917 but withdrew the offer in April. The family was held first at Tsarskoye Selo, then in Bolshevik custody, and was executed at Yekaterinburg on 17 July 1918. Their remains were reburied in Saint Petersburg in 1998, and in 2000 the Russian Orthodox Church canonised them as passion bearers. The majority view among historians is that he was well-intentioned but a poor ruler.
nicholas-ii-of-opava: Nicholas II belonged to the Opava branch of the Přemyslovci family. His father, Duke Nicholas I of Opava, had held Opava since 1269, and his mother was Adelheid of Habsburg, a niece of King Rudolf I. He supported King John of Luxembourg of Bohemia, who in 1318 gave him Opava as a fief and at the same time raised it to an independent duchy. In the same year he married Anna, the only sister of Duke Leszek of Racibórz.

Nicholas moved the ducal residence from Hradec nad Moravicí to Opava. When Leszek died without children in 1336, Racibórz reverted to the Bohemian crown, and King John granted it in 1337 to his loyal vassal. Holding both Opava and Racibórz, Nicholas became one of the most powerful princes of the upper Oder, and through the personal union Opava turned more towards Silesia. The dukes of Opole also claimed Racibórz, and King John sold them the Moravian town of Prudnik instead. A document of 1350 names Nicholas Burgrave of Kłodzko, and he also served as chamberlain of the Kingdom of Bohemia. In 1355 he had to give up Koźle and Gliwice.

He married three times. After Anna's death he married Hedwig, a daughter of Duke Konrad I of Oleśnica, in May 1342, and in 1360 Jutta, a daughter of Duke Boleslaw II of Opole-Falkenberg. His daughters married into the houses of Mazovia and Moravia: Euphemia wed Duke Siemowit III of Mazovia in 1335, and Margaret Margrave John Henry of Moravia in 1349.

Nicholas died on 8 December 1365. His eldest son, John I, founded the Opava-Ratibór line of the family, while his younger sons divided the Opava lands: Nicholas III held Głubczyce, Wenceslaus I was Duke of Opava from 1377 to 1381, and Przemko I ruled Opava from 1365 to 1433.
nicholas-of-amsdorf: Nicolaus von Amsdorf was born on 3 December 1483 in Torgau, on the Elbe. He studied at Leipzig and then at Wittenberg, where in 1502 he was among the first to matriculate in the newly founded university, and he became professor of theology in 1511. Like Andreas Karlstadt, he began as a leading exponent of the older scholastic theology, but under Luther's influence he gave up his Aristotelian positions for a theology founded on the Augustinian doctrine of grace.

Amsdorf remained one of Luther's most determined supporters. He was with him at the Leipzig conference of 1519 and the Diet of Worms in 1521, and he was privy to the secret of Luther's seclusion at the Wartburg. He helped the first efforts of the Reformation at Magdeburg in 1524, Goslar in 1531 and Einbeck in 1534, took part in the debates at Schmalkalden in 1537, and in 1539 spoke out strongly against the bigamy of the Landgrave of Hesse.

After the death of Philip of the Palatinate, bishop of Naumburg-Zeitz, he was installed in the see on 20 January 1542, the first Lutheran bishop in the Holy Roman Empire. He found the position painful and longed to return to Magdeburg, but Luther persuaded him to stay. After he had to yield to his rival Julius von Pflug, he lived under the protection of the young duke of Weimar. There he took part in founding the University of Jena in 1558, opposed the Augsburg Interim of 1548 and oversaw the Jena edition of Luther's works.

In his later years Amsdorf argued that good works were not only useless but harmful to salvation, and a small sect that adopted this view was named after him. He urged the High Lutheran party to separate from Melanchthon in 1557 and persuaded the Saxon dukes to oppose the Frankfurt Recess in 1558. He died at Eisenach on 14 May 1565 and was buried in the church of St. Georg there, where his effigy survives. Many of his letters and shorter writings are kept in manuscript, among them five volumes of Amsdorfiana in the Weimar library, a valuable source for the knowledge of Luther.
nicholas-of-cusa: Nicholas was born in Kues, Latinized as Cusa, in south-western Germany, the second of four children of Johan Krebs, a prosperous boat owner and ferryman, and Katherina Roemer. He probably received early schooling from the Brethren of the Common Life at Deventer and entered the Faculty of Arts of Heidelberg University in 1416. He received a doctorate in canon law from the University of Padua in 1423, where he met the later cardinals Julian Cesarini and Domenico Capranica and became a friend of the mathematician Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli. He then taught and practised canon law at Cologne from 1425, and became secretary to Otto of Ziegenhain, Prince-Archbishop of Trier.

Skilled in the study of old manuscripts, Nicholas identified the Donation of Constantine as a fake in 1433, as Lorenzo Valla confirmed a few years later, and exposed the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals as forgeries. At the Council of Basel in 1432 he represented a claimant to the see of Trier and wrote De concordantia catholica, a synthesis of ideas on church and empire that balanced hierarchy with consent. Initially a conciliarist, he supported moving the council to Italy to meet the Greeks, who needed help against the Ottoman Turks. Between the summer of 1437 and early 1438 he was in the delegation to Constantinople to bring back the Byzantine emperor for the Council of Florence of 1439.

He became papal legate to Germany from 1446, was made a cardinal by Pope Nicholas V, and in 1450 was named Bishop of Brixen. His Great Legation of 1450 to 1452 involved almost 3,000 miles of travel and reform, though many of his reforms failed. As bishop he tried to reclaim lost diocesan revenues, which Duke Sigismund of Austria opposed; Sigismund imprisoned him in 1460, and Pope Pius II excommunicated the duke. Nicholas never returned to his bishopric and died at Todi in Umbria on 11 August 1464. His heart rests in the chapel altar of the Cusanusstift in Kues, the home for the aged he founded.

In De docta ignorantia, finished in February 1440, Nicholas argued that the finite human mind cannot fully know the divine, infinite mind, which he called the Maximum, but can become aware of its limits and so reach learned ignorance. The work shows the influence of Neoplatonism and negative theology. Shortly after the Fall of Constantinople in 1453 he wrote De pace fidei, imagining a meeting in Heaven of representatives of all nations and religions, which agrees on one faith in a variety of rites. In 1433 he proposed a method of electing Holy Roman Emperors that was essentially the Borda count.
nicias: Nicias came from a wealthy, slaveowning aristocratic family of conservative politics and inherited a fortune from his father, Niceratus. He rose to prominence while Pericles led Athens and became his frequent military and political colleague. Historians note that he was honest, impervious to bribes, respectable and admired for his devotion to religion. He won popularity by public generosity, especially in religious causes: Plutarch records a statue of Athena, a shrine to Dionysus and a bridge of boats for the festival on Delos.

Thucydides first mentions him in 428 BCE, when he captured the island of Minoa off Megara. Later campaigns took Cythera and Methone, but he avoided significant engagements and had a reputation for caution. After the Athenian success at Sphacteria in 425 BCE, Nicias offered Cleon his command, expecting him to refuse. Cleon accepted and succeeded, and it was Nicias who lost standing.

After Cleon and the Spartan general Brasidas were killed at Amphipolis, Nicias and the Spartan king Pleistoanax negotiated the Peace of Nicias, concluded in March 421 BCE for fifty years. Most wartime gains were to be returned and prisoners released, but Boeotia, Corinth, Elis and Megara refused to sign. Alcibiades defeated Nicias in the election for general in 420 BCE. In 417 BCE Nicias and Alcibiades combined to have Hyperbolos ostracised instead of either of them.

In 415 BCE Nicias opposed the Sicilian Expedition, but his argument about its cost led the assembly to vote for it and to appoint him alongside Alcibiades and Lamachus. After Alcibiades was recalled and Lamachus killed, Nicias neglected the northern wall at Syracuse, and the Spartan Gylippus entered the city. A lunar eclipse on 27 August 413 BCE led him to delay the withdrawal again. The fleet was defeated on 9 September, and on 18 September the Athenians were surrounded at the Assinaros river. Nicias surrendered to Gylippus but was executed by the Syracusans.

Thucydides judged that he, of all the Hellenes of his time, least deserved such a fate. J. B. Bury blamed both Nicias and the assembly that chose him, calling Nicias indecisive and fearful of the consequences of failure.
nicobar-islands: The Nicobar Islands are an archipelago in the eastern Indian Ocean, 150 kilometres north-west of Aceh on Sumatra and about 1,300 kilometres south-east of the Indian subcontinent. With the Andaman Islands to the north they mark the boundary between the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea. They cover 1,841 square kilometres in three groups, northern, central and southern. The largest island is Great Nicobar, at 922 square kilometres, whose southern point, Indira Point, is also the southernmost point of India. The islands belong to a great arc created by the collision of the Indo-Australian Plate with Eurasia, and the climate is warm and tropical, with heavy monsoon rain.

The islands are believed to have been inhabited for several thousand years. Six indigenous Nicobarese languages belong to the Austroasiatic family, and the Shompen of southern Great Nicobar may be of Mesolithic Southeast Asian origin. The earliest known reference to the name is in the Sri Lankan Pali chronicles, the Dipavamsa and the Mahavamsa, which describe an island of naked people. In the ninth century the Persian explorer Abū Zayd al-Sīrāfī called the islands Lanjabālūs. The modern name probably derives from the Chola name Nakkavaram, which appears on the Thanjavur inscription of 1050 CE.

Organised European colonisation began with the Danish East India Company in the 18th century, when the islands were administered from Tranquebar as Frederiksøerne. Moravian missionaries who tried to settle on Nancowry died in great numbers from disease, and outbreaks of malaria repeatedly forced the settlers out until the islands were gradually abandoned for good from 1848. Between 1778 and 1783 William Bolts tried to found an Austrian colony, mistakenly assuming Denmark–Norway had given up its claims. Denmark formally ended its presence on 16 October 1868, selling its rights to the United Kingdom, which in 1869 made them part of British India.

Japan occupied the islands between 1942 and 1945, and the British regained them after the Japanese surrender in 1945. Together with the Andaman Islands they became part of India in 1950 and a union territory in 1956.

The islands form the Nicobar district of the union territory of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The 2011 census of India recorded 36,844 people, among them the Nicobarese and the Shompen. They are recognised as a distinct terrestrial ecoregion with many endemic species, and the Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve was added to UNESCO's network of biosphere reserves in 2013. On 26 December 2004 a tsunami devastated the coast, killing at least 6,000 people in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
nicola-pisano: His birth date and origins are uncertain. The archives of the Cathedral of Siena record him as the son of Petrus de Apulia, which points to Apulia, and he was probably trained in the workshops of the emperor Frederick II, whose coronation he attended. His only surviving works from this period are two griffon heads. Around 1245 he moved to Tuscany to work at the castle of Prato, whose portal lions are probably by him, and he then worked on the façade of the Cathedral of Saint Martin in Lucca, where the Deposition from the Cross, the Nativity and the Adoration of the Magi are attributed to him. He moved to Pisa between 1245 and 1250, and his son Giovanni Pisano was born there.

Around 1255 he received the commission for the pulpit of the Pisa Baptistery, which he finished and signed Nicola Pisanus in 1260, helped by assistants including Arnolfo di Cambio and Lapo di Ricevuto. Its hexagonal parapet holds five Carrara marble reliefs from the life of Christ, and the figures wear Roman dress. He probably knew Roman sarcophagi in the Camposanto of Pisa, among them the Phaedra sarcophagus, and the nude Fortitude derives from a Roman Hercules. Between 1260 and 1264 he completed the work of the architect Diotisalvi on the dome of the baptistery. In 1264 he was asked to design the Shrine of Saint Dominic in Bologna, though his own part was probably small.

In September 1265 he was commissioned to make a marble pulpit for Siena Cathedral, carved between the end of 1265 and November 1268 with his son Giovanni and assistants including Arnolfo di Cambio. It resembles the Pisa pulpit but is larger and is considered his masterpiece; its subject is salvation and the Last Judgement. In July 1273 he was commissioned to make the altar of San Jacopo in Pistoia Cathedral, demolished in 1786. His last major commission was the reliefs of the Fontana Maggiore at Perugia in 1277–1278, designed by Fra Bevignate and Boninsegna, where most of the carving was done by Giovanni and assistants.

Pisano was no mere imitator of antiquity: his figures are original creations, formed by close study of ancient models. Surveys of Italian Renaissance art often begin in 1260, the year of the Pisa pulpit, and his works are counted among the most important precursors of Renaissance sculpture. He also remained attached to Gothic art, and the Siena pulpit shows this. Arnolfo di Cambio is seen as the true inheritor of his classical style, while Giovanni Pisano mixed French Gothic with classical elements. Giorgio Vasari included a life of Nicola Pisano in his Lives.
nicolae-ceausescu: Ceaușescu was born in the village of Scornicești, the third of nine children of a poor peasant family. His father owned about 3 hectares of land and a few sheep, and Nicolae helped the family income by tailoring. He left the village school at eleven for Bucharest. He joined the Romanian Communist Party in his teens and was repeatedly imprisoned under the pre-war and wartime regimes for his activism. After the Second World War he rose through the party under Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej. As a high official in the agricultural and defence ministries he had an important role in forced collectivisation, during which over 80,000 peasants were arrested between 1949 and 1952, according to the party's own data.

When Gheorghiu-Dej died on 19 March 1965, Ceaușescu was not the obvious successor, but the Politburo chose him as a compromise candidate and elected him general secretary on 22 March. He eased press censorship, and in a speech on 21 August 1968 he condemned the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia, which raised his popularity. In October 1966 he had issued Decree 770 restricting abortion and contraception, which led to child abandonment and swelled the orphanages. After visiting China, North Korea, Mongolia and North Vietnam in 1971 he began to emulate North Korea's system. He was head of state from 1967 and in 1974 made the presidency an executive office. The Securitate carried out mass surveillance and repression.

Western governments briefly saw him as an anti-Soviet maverick and lent to him, and he borrowed more than 13 billion dollars from the West. Plans to make Romania a major oil refiner failed, and he sought to repay the debts through austerity, with rationing of food, electricity and heating. In 1987 more than 20,000 workers marched in Brașov against these policies. A coup planned for October 1984 failed when the unit assigned to it was sent to harvest maize.

On 17 December 1989 Ceaușescu ordered the military to open fire on demonstrators in Timișoara, causing many deaths and injuries. The protests reached Bucharest, and he and his wife Elena fled by helicopter but were soon captured after the armed forces turned on them. A show trial convicted both of economic sabotage and genocide, and they were executed by firing squad on 25 December, ending 42 years of Communist rule. Opinion in Romania on his rule remains divided, and polling has found that many Romanians retain admiration for him.
nicolas-avellaneda: Nicolás Remigio Aurelio Avellaneda Silva was born on 3 October 1837 in San Miguel de Tucumán. After his father died during a revolt against Juan Manuel de Rosas, his mother took him to Bolivia. He studied law at Córdoba without graduating and in 1857 moved to Buenos Aires, where he directed El Nacional and met Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, who helped him become a teacher of economics. He sat in the house of representatives in 1859, and under Sarmiento's presidency served as minister of justice and education.

Elected in 1874 at 37, Avellaneda was the youngest president Argentina had elected and the first civilian. Bartolomé Mitre contested his legitimacy, but Julio Argentino Roca defeated Mitre's forces, and Avellaneda pardoned him. A customs law of 1875 raised duties on industrial goods by 40 per cent, and a crisis followed; he dismissed 6,000 public employees and cut salaries by 15 per cent, saying two million Argentines would economise on their hunger and thirst to honour debts abroad. His Immigration and Colonization Law guaranteed newcomers lodging and help finding work, railways grew by 89 per cent, and in 1876 the first refrigerated ship, Le Frigorifique, opened the way to frozen meat exports.

The government pursued the Conquest of the Desert against the Indigenous peoples of the south. Minister Adolfo Alsina built a 374-kilometre trench in 1876; after his death Roca took over and argued for the subjugation, expulsion or elimination of the Indigenous peoples. In 1879 the Minister of War's report counted 1,313 Indigenous men killed and 1,271 taken prisoner, with 10,513 women and children captured. In 1880 Buenos Aires province rose against Roca's election; after about 3,000 deaths an agreement ended the fighting, and Avellaneda's bill making Buenos Aires a federal district passed on 21 September.

Avellaneda returned to the Senate in 1883 and served until his death on 24 November 1885, aged 48, on a ship returning from medical treatment in France. He was the shortest-lived president of Argentina, and a prolific writer whose works fill twelve volumes.
nicolas-de-ovando: Ovando was born around 1460 in Extremadura, the second son of Captain Diego de Cáceres Ovando and Isabel de Flores Gutierrez. Some place his birth at Brozas, but the chronicler Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, who knew him well, called him a native of Cáceres. He entered the Order of Alcántara, a military order founded in 1156 that had fought the Moors in the Reconquista, and rose to the rank of Commander-Major. As Commander of Lares he became a favourite of the Catholic Monarchs, above all Queen Isabella I of Castile.

On 3 September 1501, after complaints from Christopher Columbus and others about Francisco de Bobadilla, Isabella named Ovando to replace him as Governor of the Indies. He sailed from Spain on 13 February 1502 with thirty ships, the largest fleet yet sent to the New World, carrying around 2,500 colonists chosen as a cross-section of Spanish society, among them Francisco Pizarro and Bartolomé de las Casas, with 13 Franciscans. The fleet reached Santo Domingo in April 1502.

Finding the natives in revolt, Ovando and his subordinates suppressed them in bloody campaigns, including the Jaragua and Higüey massacres, and sent disorderly colonists back to Spain in chains. According to las Casas, slaughter, enslavement and disease had cut the native population to 60 000 by the census of 1507, and the decline went on; some sources estimate that hundreds of thousands died forced to dig gold. After conquests by his lieutenants Juan Ponce de León and Juan de Esquivel he founded several towns, developed mining, introduced sugar cane from the Canary Islands and sent out expeditions across the Caribbean.

Keeping a deathbed promise to Isabella, King Ferdinand II of Aragon recalled Ovando in 1509 to answer for his treatment of the native people. Diego Columbus succeeded him, but the crown let Ovando keep the property he brought back. He probably spent his last years at Brozas, the seat of his order. In February 1511 Ferdinand ordered him to join a campaign against Oran that never took place. Ovando died in Seville on 29 May 1511 and was buried in the monastery of San Benito de Alcántara.
nicolas-de-pierola: Piérola was born on 5 January 1839 in Arequipa, in southern Peru, to an aristocratic but impoverished, ultra-Catholic family, and he was known as El Califa, the Caliph. He studied theology at the Seminario de Santo Toribio in Lima and later took a law degree. He married Jesusa de Iturbide, believed to be the illegitimate daughter of Agustín Jerónimo de Iturbide y Huarte, a son of Emperor Agustín de Iturbide of Mexico.

As finance minister under President José Balta from 1868 to 1871 he won broad powers from Congress to negotiate the guano contract with the Dreyfus house of Paris. Under Pardo's administration he was impeached for misappropriating funds and acquitted once Congress backed him. On 6 May 1877 his followers seized the ironclad Huáscar at Callao in a bid to overthrow President Mariano Ignacio Prado; after the inconclusive Battle of Pacocha against two British ships the vessel surrendered, and Piérola left for Valparaíso and Europe.

He returned in 1879, during the War of the Pacific with Chile. When Prado left for Europe to buy arms, Piérola seized power after heavy fighting and took full control on 23 December 1879. He censored the press, so that El Comercio did not appear for three years, and promoted officers for loyalty rather than experience. Expecting the Chilean attack on Lima from the north, he marched troops to Ancón; it came from the south, Peru lost the battles of San Juan and Miraflores, and Lima fell in January 1881. Chile never recognised his government, and he resigned on 28 November 1881.

He founded the Democratic Party in 1889 and, allied with the Civil Party of Peru, raised fighters who occupied Lima and ousted Andrés Avelino Cáceres; over a thousand people were killed during his entry into the city. Unopposed in the election of 1895, he received 4150 of 4310 valid votes. His term is generally held to have opened the Aristocratic Republic. He introduced the Libra Peruana, a gold coin of the same value as the British sovereign, and sponsored Japanese immigration. He lost the race for mayor of Lima in 1900, withdrew from the presidential election of 1904 and died in Lima on 23 June 1913.
nicolas-durand-de-villegaignon: Villegaignon was born in Provins, was educated in Paris and took a law degree at Orleans. In 1531 he joined the Knights of Malta, whose grand master was his uncle, Philippe Villiers de L'Isle-Adam. Although the Franco-Ottoman alliance kept France itself out of direct war with the Turks, he fought for the Order, which sided with Charles V. He served in the fleet gathered off Majorca in 1534 for the attack on Tunis and Hayreddin Barbarossa, and was wounded in the expedition against Algiers in 1541.

In 1548 he commanded the French galleys that carried the five-year-old Mary, Queen of Scots, promised to the Dauphin, to France, sailing round Scotland while the English fleet expected them from the other direction, and landing at Roscoff. Back in Scotland in February 1549 he helped take Ferniehirst Castle from the English and argued for a fortification at Roxburgh. Commanding the Knights in Mdina, he helped repel the Ottomans at Malta in 1551, was present at the Siege of Tripoli, wrote an account of it in 1553 and defended the defeated commander, Gaspard de Vallier, against the Grand Master d'Homedes.

The colony in Brazil began with two ships and 600 soldiers and colonists, mainly French Huguenots and Swiss Calvinists. Besides giving them a refuge, he hoped to exploit brazilwood, a valuable source of red dye and timber, and to search for precious metals and stones. A dispute over the Eucharist led him to expel those who held Calvin's view from his fortified island. He left the colony under his nephew Bois-le-Comte while seeking funds and ships, and after its fall gave up his claims for 30,000 écus from the Portuguese Crown.

In 1560 he challenged Calvin to a debate on the Eucharist, which Calvin declined, and he took part in the repression of the Amboise conspiracy. Pierre Richier attacked his conduct in Brazil in a pamphlet of 1561. From 1568 he represented the Order of Malta at the French court, and he died on 9 January 1571 as commander of the Order's commandery at Beauvais. The quarrel continued in print, with André Thévet's account of 1572 and Jean Léry's reply of 1578. Villegagnon Island in Rio de Janeiro and a street in Mdina bear his name.
nicolas-grunitzky: Nicolas Grunitzky was born in Atakpamé on 5 April 1913. His father was German and his mother Togolese, of Ghanaian royalty. He studied civil engineering at the ESTP in Paris and worked as a public administrator before leaving to form his own company. He became secretary-general of the Togolese Party of Progress and was elected to the Togolese Representative Assembly in 1951.

Grunitzky also served in the French National Assembly from 1951 to 1958, winning elections in 1951 and 1956. Supported by France, he became prime minister of the Republic of Togo, still under French administration, on 12 September 1956. This office existed under the loi cadre system, which created a limited national government in the French colonial possessions.

His Togolese Party of Progress and its northern ally, the Union of Chiefs and Peoples of the North, were defeated in elections held on 16 May 1958 by the Committee of Togolese Unity of Sylvanus Olympio and its nationalist allies Juvento. Grunitzky went into exile. The new government declared independence on 27 April 1960, and Olympio, his chief political rival and brother-in-law, was elected the first president.

A coup in 1963 ended with the assassination of Olympio. The Insurrection Committee, headed by Emmanuel Bodjollé, appointed Grunitzky president. This was the first military coup in West Africa after independence, and it was organised by soldiers under the direction of Sergeant Étienne Gnassingbé Eyadema. Grunitzky tried to unify the country by including several political parties in his government. He held office from 1963 to 1967, when a bloodless military coup led by Eyadema, by then a lieutenant colonel, toppled him and he went into exile in Paris. He was injured in a car accident in Côte d'Ivoire and died of complications in a hospital in Paris on 27 September 1969.
nicolas-jenson: Jenson reached Mainz in October 1458, when a number of established printers were working there under whom he could have served an apprenticeship. Some have supposed that he studied under Johann Gutenberg, but there is no verifiable evidence of it; Gutenberg's first press had by then been seized by Johann Fust, and his activities in these years are uncertain. Jenson left Mainz in 1461. In Venice his early training as a goldsmith gave him a feeling for the sculptural nature of type, and Andrea Torresano learned printing and typography while working for him.

Jenson's technical skill and business sense set him apart from his contemporaries. To lower prices and drive out less productive rivals he cut a cursive gothic type, which let him print a text and its gloss on the same page for the first time. He launched two book trading companies, in 1475 and in 1480, the second under the name Johannes de Colonia, Nicolaus Jenson et socii. His partner John of Cologne specialised in law books, and their combined firm, known as The Company, was responsible for 43% of Venetian editions in 1481.

His roman letters borrowed their shapes from the calligraphic hand called littera antica, itself based on Carolingian minuscule, with serifs taken from Imperial Roman capitals. A Greek typeface for quotations followed in 1471 and a black letter type in 1473, used for books on medicine and history. In later years he printed mainly liturgical, theological and legal texts in gothic types, keeping roman for the occasional commission.

Among his editions were the works of Julius Caesar in 1471, a Natural History of Pliny the Elder in 1476 in Cristoforo Landino's vernacular translation, financed by the Strozzi family and printed in 1,025 copies, 25 of them on vellum, and a Latin Bible in 1479. For that Bible Pope Sixtus IV gave him the honorary title of Count Palatine.

Jenson has been a central figure for students of early printing since the 19th century, when the artist William Morris praised the beauty of his roman type. He is remembered for perfecting roman type as a revival of Latin inscriptional letters, and later typefaces such as Golden Type and Cloister Old Style were inspired by his. His Caesar of 1471 has been praised for the clarity and simplicity of a roman type drawn from inscriptions on Roman monuments.
nicolas-perrenot-de-granvelle: Nicolas Perrenot de Granvelle was born at Ornans in 1486, into a family of modest standing in the Franche-Comté. In 1513 he married Nicole de Bonvalot, daughter of Jacques de Bonvalot, lord of Champagney; the couple had 15 children. He became a lawyer and was called to the Parlement of Dole before entering the service of Charles V, who was elected emperor in 1519 at the age of 19.

Granvelle quickly became one of the emperor's trusted advisers, and his sons and sons-in-law went on to hold prominent posts at the imperial court. In 1527 he bought the seigniory of Grandvelle in the Bailiwick of Amont, in what is now the Haute-Saône department, whose name, later spelt Granvelle, he carried. After the death of Mercurino Gattinara in 1530 he became one of the emperor's most trusted advisers on the affairs of the Holy Roman Empire, and he kept that role for the rest of his life. He was also made suzerain of the imperial city of Besançon and held an influential position in the Netherlands.

Granvelle died on 27 August 1550, aged 64, while attending the Imperial Diet at Augsburg. He had gathered a significant art collection and a library, which is now in the Bibliothèque municipale de Besançon. Four of his children played prominent political roles: Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle, Archbishop of Mechelen and cardinal; Thomas Perrenot de Granvelle, Spanish ambassador in London, Paris and Vienna; Jérôme de Perrenot, a diplomat for Ferdinand I and guardian of the young William the Silent; and Frédéric Perrenot de Champagney, a soldier and diplomat for the Habsburgs. Within two generations the family had become the most powerful and the richest in the Franche-Comté, a rise of which the Granvelle Palace in Besançon is the symbol.
nicolas-remy: Rémy, known in Latin as Remigius, studied law at the University of Toulouse and practised in Paris from 1563 to 1570. In 1570 his uncle retired as Lieutenant General of Vosges and Rémy was appointed to the post, and in 1575 he became secretary to Duke Charles III of Lorraine. He was a Catholic and wrote his Latin works with the blessing of the Church, but he was not a priest; he married at least once, possibly twice, and had several children.

His work as a witch-hunter is said to have begun with a personal loss. According to the story, a favoured son died in a street accident after an old beggar woman, refused money by Rémy, had cursed him. In 1582 Rémy prosecuted the woman for bewitching the boy and had her put to death. He appears to have believed fully in what he was doing, and he described himself as a soldier in a war against anti-Christian forces allied with the Devil.

In 1592 he retired to the country to escape the bubonic plague and there compiled the notes of his campaign into his book. He wrote that a number of people about equal to those burned had escaped punishment by flight or by a stubborn endurance of the torture. The historian William Monter has doubted his figures: the well-preserved records of Lorraine from the 1580s amount to barely a sixth of what Rémy claimed, and his book names only about 125 people tried for witchcraft. Monter called the claim a literary flourish, while adding that the documented reality is dreadful enough.

Besides poems and several books of history, Rémy wrote the Daemonolatreiae libri tres, or Demonolatry, published in Latin at Lyon. Showing much influence from Jean Bodin, it was reprinted several times and translated into German, and in parts of Europe it replaced the Malleus Maleficarum as the best-known handbook of witch-hunters. Rémy taught that the Devil could appear as a black cat or a man and delighted in Black Masses, and that demons had sexual relations with women. He dedicated the book to the Cardinal of Lorraine.
nicolas-rolin: Rolin was born into a bourgeois family of Autun, and the house of his birth is now the town museum, the Musée Rolin. His first marriage, in 1398, was part of a triple wedding: his widowed mother married Perrenet Le Mairet, a bourgeois of Beaune, and her two sons married two of his daughters. All three brides were dead within a few years. Rolin next married Marie des Landes, before 1407, a match that opened his way into the bourgeoisie of Paris. In 1421 he married Guigone de Salins.

Rolin was closely linked with Duke John the Fearless, who was godfather to his third son, and in 1422 Philip the Good made him chancellor. He held the post for more than forty years and was one of the principal architects of the duke's success. He took part in drafting the Treaty of Arras of 1435, by which Charles VII recognised the independence of Burgundy and so separated it from the English in the Hundred Years' War.

His sons rose with him. Jean Rolin became bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône in 1431 and of Autun in 1436, and was made a cardinal in 1448 by Pope Nicholas V as part of the diplomacy between Burgundy and the Papacy. Antoine held court offices, among them chamberlain to Charles the Bold, and Louis was killed at the Battle of Grandson in 1476.

Rolin owned the Château d'Oricourt and in 1435 commissioned the painting of himself before the Virgin and Child from Jan van Eyck, now in the Louvre. Having founded the Hospices de Beaune with Guigone de Salins, he established in 1452 a new religious order to serve it, Les sœurs hospitalières de Beaune, and ordered from the Flemish painter Rogier van der Weyden an altarpiece of the Last Judgement for the hospital. He died on 18 January 1462.
nicolas-salmeron: Nicolás Salmerón Alonso was born on 10 April 1838 at Alhama la Seca in the province of Almería, was educated at Granada and became assistant professor of literature and philosophy at Madrid. Discontent with Isabella II's government and the monarchy grew in her last years, and Salmerón joined a small party that advocated a republic. He directed the opposition paper La Discusión and worked with Emilio Castelar on La Democracia. In 1865 he became a member of the directing committee of the Republican Party, and in 1867 he was imprisoned with other suspects.

Elected to the Cortes in 1871, he defended the right of the Socialist Party to toleration, though he did not belong to it. After Amadeo of Savoy resigned the crown on 11 February 1873, Salmerón became a leader of those seeking a republic. As minister of justice in the Figueras cabinet he abolished the death penalty. He was elected president of the Cortes and then, on 18 July 1873, president of the Executive Power of the Republic, succeeding Francisco Pi y Margall, at a time when the Federalist Party had thrown all the south of Spain into anarchy.

Salmerón was compelled to use troops to restore order. When the generals insisted on executing rebels taken in arms, he resigned on 6 September, opposed to capital punishment, and was elected president of the Cortes again on 9 September. His successor Castelar restored order by drastic means. Salmerón took part in the attack on Castelar in the Cortes on 3 January 1874, which provoked the generals into closing the chamber and setting up a provisional military government.

Salmerón went into exile and stayed abroad until 1881, when Sagasta recalled him. In 1886 he was elected to the Cortes as Progressive deputy for Madrid and tried without success to combine the republican factions into a party of moderate views. On 18 April 1907 a member of the more extreme Republican Party shot at him in Barcelona without wounding him. He died at Pau on 21 September 1908, aged 70, the last living president of the First Spanish Republic.
nicolaus-copernicus: Nicolaus Copernicus was born on 19 February 1473 in Thorn (Toruń), in Royal Prussia, a semi-autonomous and multilingual region of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland. His parents were German-speaking. His father was a merchant from Kraków, and his mother was the daughter of a wealthy Thorn merchant. He was the youngest of four children. His brother Andreas became an Augustinian canon at Frauenburg (Frombork), and his sister Barbara became a Benedictine nun.

His mother tongue was German, and he wrote most of his surviving works in Latin, the principal language of European scholarship. Whether he spoke Polish is uncertain, since the evidence is indirect. While studying canon law at the University of Bologna in 1496 he signed into the German student organisation, the Natio Germanorum.

Copernicus obtained a doctorate in canon law and was also a mathematician, astronomer, physician, classics scholar, translator, governor, diplomat and economist. From 1497 he was a canon of the Warmian Cathedral chapter. In 1517 he derived a quantity theory of money, a key concept in economics, and in 1519 he formulated an economic principle that later came to be called Gresham's law. He never married. He died on 24 May 1543, just after the publication of his book De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres).

Copernicus formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its centre. Its publication in 1543 was a major event in the history of science, triggering the Copernican Revolution and contributing to the Scientific Revolution. A similar heliocentric model had been developed eighteen centuries earlier by Aristarchus of Samos, and Copernicus likely arrived at his model independently. In an early unpublished manuscript he mentioned the moving Earth theory of Philolaus, but he removed the reference from the published text.

The immediate result of publication was only mild controversy. The Council of Trent, which met from 1545 to 1563, did not discuss his theory. The Dominican Giovanni Maria Tolosani denounced Copernicanism in 1545, arguing that it was scientifically unproven because Copernicus assumed the motion of the Earth without offering a physical theory for it. The Catholic Church took no official action until about six decades after the book appeared.
nicomedes-i-of-bithynia: Nicomedes I, the eldest son of Zipoetes I, was the second king of Bithynia and succeeded his father in 278 BCE. He began his reign by killing two of his brothers, but the third, later called Zipoetes II, rebelled and kept independent sovereignty over a considerable part of Bithynia for some time. Meanwhile Antiochus I Soter, king of the Seleucid Empire, who had already made war on Zipoetes I, threatened invasion. Nicomedes formed alliances with Heraclea Pontica and with Antigonus II Gonatas, and Antiochus invaded but withdrew without risking battle.

Against his brother Nicomedes called in more powerful auxiliaries. The Celts, who had crossed the Bosphorus under Leonnorius and Lutarius and were besieging Byzantium, allied with him, and he provided them with the means to cross into Asia, where they founded Galatia. He then turned their weapons against Zipoetes II, defeated and killed him, and reunited the whole of Bithynia. The Celts probably later supported him against Antiochus, but no details of the war or of the peace are recorded. Bithynia seems to have been left undisturbed and rose to great power and prosperity during his long and peaceful reign.

Like his father and many other Greek rulers of Asia, Nicomedes founded a new capital to perpetuate his name. The site, near the Megarian colony of Astakos, was so well chosen that Nicomedia remained one of the richest and most prosperous cities in Anatolia for more than six centuries. Eusebius places its founding in 264 BCE. It was probably this Nicomedes who tried to buy the statue of Venus by Praxiteles from the city of Knidos, offering to cancel all the city's public debts.

The length of the reign after the founding of Nicomedia is unknown, but his death is dated to around 255 BCE. By his first wife, Ditizele, a Phrygian, he had two sons, Prusias and Ziaelas, and a daughter, Lysandra. His second wife, Etazeta, persuaded him to set these children aside and leave the crown to her own offspring, who were still infants at his death. He placed them in the care of two kings, Antigonus II Gonatas and Ptolemy II Philadelphus, and of the free cities of Heraclea Pontica, Byzantium and Cius. Despite these precautions his son Ziaelas quickly established himself on the throne.
nicomedes-iv: Nicomedes IV Philopator was the first son and successor of Nicomedes III of Bithynia. Sources differ on his mother. Memnon of Heraclea says she was Nysa, his father's wife, while Granius Licinianus says he was the son of a first wife called Aristonica, who died nine days after his birth. He had a half-sister, Nysa, and a half-brother, Socrates Chrestus, born to his father's concubine Hagne, and possibly another half-brother, Pylaemenes III. His reign began at his father's death, and the first few years were relatively peaceful.

Mithridates VI of Pontus, who was Nicomedes's maternal grand-uncle and one of Rome's main enemies in the late Republic, soon began to harass the borders of Bithynia. In 90 BCE Socrates Chrestus, helped by Mithridates, defeated Nicomedes's army and forced him to flee to Italy. Rome's influence brought his restoration through Manius Aquillius, but Aquillius encouraged him to raid Mithridates's territory, and Mithridates struck back in 88 BCE. Nicomedes fled to Rome again, and Mithridates conquered Bithynia and the Roman provinces of Asia, starting the First Mithridatic War.

Lucius Cornelius Sulla fought Mithridates for three years, and in 85 BCE Mithridates sued for peace and paid a heavy fine. Nicomedes was restored in 84 BCE, and in the peaceful years that followed Bithynia came increasingly under Roman control. In 80 BCE the young Gaius Julius Caesar was sent to his court to raise a fleet. He stayed so long that a rumour of a sexual relationship arose, which Caesar's enemies later used to call him the Queen of Bithynia. It is unknown whether the relationship existed, and Caesar denied it vigorously.

As one of his last acts, in 74 BCE, Nicomedes bequeathed the whole kingdom of Bithynia to Rome. The Roman Senate quickly voted to make it a province. Mithridates VI had other plans for Bithynia, and the death of Nicomedes and his bequest led directly to the Third Mithridatic War.
nicomedia: The site had earlier been a Megarian colony called Astacus, a name that meant lobster in Greek. After Lysimachus destroyed it, Nicomedes I of Bithynia rebuilt it in 264 BCE as Nicomedia, and it remained one of the most important cities of north-western Asia Minor. Under Rome it was the metropolis and capital of the province of Bithynia. The letters of Pliny the Younger to Trajan, written while he governed the province, mention its senate-house, forum, a temple of Cybele and an aqueduct on which the city had spent 3,318,000 sesterces without finishing it. The Goths sacked Nicomedia in 253 CE.

Diocletian made it the eastern capital of the Roman Empire when he introduced the Tetrarchy, and he built an enormous palace, an armoury, a mint and new shipyards. On 23 February 303 he ordered the city's new church razed and its scriptures burnt, and the next day issued the First Edict Against the Christians. Fires then damaged his palace, and Galerius blamed the Christians and had eight people executed by the end of April. Constantine the Great defeated Licinius at Chrysopolis in 324, lived mainly at Nicomedia for six years, and declared nearby Byzantium the new capital in 330. He died in a villa near the city in 337.

A great earthquake on 24 August 358, followed by a fire, devastated the city, which was rebuilt on a smaller scale. Justinian I added public buildings in the sixth century, and because it lay on the roads to Constantinople it stayed a major military centre in the Byzantine campaigns against the Caliphate. Its bishopric became a metropolitan see in 451. In the 1080s Alexios I Komnenos used it as his main base against the Seljuk Turks, and the First and Second Crusades both encamped there.

The Latin Empire held it briefly after 1204, until Henry of Flanders agreed in 1207 to evacuate it in exchange for prisoners held by Theodore I Laskaris of Nicaea. After the Byzantine defeat at the Battle of Bapheus in 1302 the Ottomans besieged it in 1304 and 1330, and it fell to them in 1337. The Byzantines retook it after the Battle of Ankara, and it passed definitively to the Ottomans in 1419.

The ruins lie beneath the densely populated city of İzmit, which has largely prevented full excavation. Surviving remains include sections of the Roman walls, the foundations of a 2nd-century marble nymphaeum, a large cistern and parts of the harbour wall. The 1999 earthquake led to the clearing of debris that uncovered statues of Hercules, Athena, Diocletian and Constantine, and excavation of the site identified as Diocletian's palace has since covered a large area.
nicopolis-lesser-armenia: Nicopolis, whose Greek name means city of victory, lay in a well-watered plain at the foot of a thickly wooded mountain. Pompey settled it with veterans of his army and with local peasants after his decisive victory over Mithridates VI of Pontus in the Third Mithridatic War. The Roman highways of the region, leading to Comana, Polemonium, Neocæsarea and Sebasteia, radiated from the city, which already had a large population in the time of Strabo.

Mark Antony gave Nicopolis to Polemon in 36 BCE; from 54 it was governed by Aristobulus of Chalcis, and in 64 Nero annexed it definitively to the Roman Empire. It became the metropolis of Lesser Armenia and the seat of the provincial diet that elected the Armeniarch, with an altar of the Augusti and temples to Zeus Nicephorus and to Victory. It later formed part of the province of Armenia Prima.

Christianity reached the city early. Under Licinius, about 319, forty-five of its inhabitants were martyred, and the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches venerate them on 10 July. About 472 John the Silent built a church there to the Virgin. In 499 an earthquake destroyed Nicopolis, and none but the bishop and his two secretaries escaped death. Justinian I rebuilt the walls and founded a monastery in memory of the Forty-Five Martyrs, but the city never regained its former splendour and was superseded by Koloneia.

Under Heraclius it was taken by the forces of Chosroes II, and from then on it was a minor town and a suffragan see of Sebasteia, at least until the 11th century; in the 9th to 11th centuries it belonged to the theme of Koloneia. Gregory of Nicopolis, one of its bishops, resigned his see in the 11th century and retired to Pithiviers in France.

Under the Ottomans the site was occupied by the Armenian village of Purkh, near Enderes, in the sanjak of Kara-Hissar and the vilayet of Sivas. The town of Koyulhisar in north-eastern Turkey now stands on it, and the Catholic Church lists Nicopolis in Armenia as a titular see.
nicosia: Nicosia stands on the fertile Mesaoria plain, in the rain shadow of the Troodos Mountains. Its climate is hot and semi-arid, with long, hot, dry summers and mild winters, and most of the rain falls in winter. The names Lefkosia in Greek and Lefkoşa in Turkish come from Leucosia, a form that became common in the Byzantine period and is usually interpreted as meaning the white estate. Earlier Greek sources in late antiquity gave several names built on the Greek words for white or poplar and for god, among them Leuteon, Leucon and Leucopolis.

Nicosia has been continuously inhabited since approximately 2500 BCE, near the onset of the Bronze Age, when the first settlers established themselves on the Mesaoria plain. The city-state of Ledra is associated with the area. Most Mycenaean-era ruins lie on the hill of Ayia Paraskevi, 6 km south-east of the centre, and Ledra is said to have been one of the twelve kingdoms of ancient Cyprus founded by the Achaeans after the Trojan War. The earliest written reference to the settlement is an Assyrian inscription of the reign of Esarhaddon (r. 681–669 BCE), on a clay prism of about 672 BCE, which records it as Lidir. Its ruler Onasagoras is recorded as having paid tribute to Esarhaddon.

By 330 BCE Ledra was a small town of little significance, economically and politically dependent on the nearby town of Chytri, with farming as the main occupation. It did not share the growth, driven by trade, of the Cypriot coastal towns. Some sources say Leucos, a son of Ptolemy I Soter of Egypt, restored it around 280 BCE, though one scholar dismissed this as an early modern fancy based only on speculation about the name. Nicosia has been the capital of Cyprus since the 10th century. In 1308 the Lusignan king Henry II of Jerusalem repaired the Benedictine Abbey of Our Lady of Tyre, one of the oldest Armenian churches, after an earthquake destroyed it.

Nicosia is the capital of Cyprus and its financial and main business centre, and the southeasternmost capital of any member state of the European Union. It is the last divided capital in Europe. After Cyprus became independent from British rule in 1960, the Bloody Christmas conflict of 1963 between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots set off intercommunal violence, and in 1964 the two communities separated into the south and north of the city. In 1974 Turkey invaded Cyprus days after a coup backed by the Greek junta, and the island was divided, with the dividing line running through Nicosia. The northern part is the de facto capital of Northern Cyprus. The city has the Cyprus Museum, the island's largest and oldest archaeological museum.
nidaros-cathedral: Nidaros Cathedral stands over the burial site of King Olav II, who was killed in 1030 at the Battle of Stiklestad and was canonised as Saint Olav a year later by Grimketel, Bishop of Nidaros; the pope later confirmed the canonisation. Around 1070 King Olav Kyrre, the saint's nephew, began a stone church on the site of a wooden one. It was dedicated to the Holy Trinity but was commonly called Kristkirken. When it was finished around 1090, Olav's shrine was placed over its altar. It was the largest church in Norway of its time, and almost all Norwegian royals of the 11th and 12th centuries were buried in it. Later walls were built on its foundations.

The cathedral was built over some 230 years, from 1070 to its substantial completion in 1300. It was the cathedral of the Catholic Archdiocese of Nidaros from 1152 until the Reformation, when in 1537 it became part of the Church of Norway. Fires damaged it badly in 1327 and 1531, and the nave was destroyed and not rebuilt until the restoration of the early 1900s. In 1708 the church burned down completely except for the stone walls, and lightning struck it in 1719. Major rebuilding began in 1869 under the architect Heinrich Ernst Schirmer and was nearly finished by Christian Christie; the work was officially completed in 2001.

The oldest parts are the octagon and its ambulatory, the site of the original high altar and Saint Olav's reliquary casket, perhaps inspired by the Corona of Canterbury Cathedral. The choir shows English influence and seems modelled on the Angel Choir of Lincoln Cathedral. The silver-gilt casket was melted down for coinage by Christian II and the saint's remains were buried in an unknown place beneath the cathedral.

The architecture is Romanesque and Gothic, and it is the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world. It has been an important destination for pilgrims from Northern Europe, who reach it by the Pilgrim's Route, and the consecration of new Norwegian monarchs takes place there. In 1814 it was one of the churches that served as polling stations for the first national elections, for the assembly that wrote the Constitution of Norway. It holds two organs, the Steinmeyer organ of 1930 and a Baroque organ by Joachim Wagner, built in 1738–40 and restored in 1993–94. The church seats about 1,850 people.
nidwalden: Nidwalden lies in the centre of Switzerland. Lake Lucerne bounds it on the north and mountain chains of the Urner Alps on the other sides, and it borders Obwalden, Lucerne, Schwyz, Uri and Bern. It is one of the smallest cantons, with an area of 276.1 square kilometres, of which about 40 per cent is inhabited or used for farming. Forests cover about a third of the canton, and about a quarter is mountain or glacier. Its eleven municipalities include Stans, Hergiswil and Buochs.

The earliest settlement dates to the Neolithic, with sites near Stansstad from 4000 to 3100 BCE, and a La Tène grave of a ten-year-old girl has been found in Stans. In Roman times the valleys were inhabited by a Gallo-Roman or Celtic population, whose names survive in many towns, rivers and mountains. By the 8th century the Alemanni entered the valleys and intermingled with them, and a church was built at Stans.

By the late 13th century the major powers in Nidwalden were the Habsburgs, Murbach Abbey and Engelberg Abbey. In 1291 Rudolph of Habsburg bought Obwalden from Murbach Abbey, and in response the people of Nidwalden, with Obwalden joining shortly before the document was signed, allied with Uri and Schwyz, an alliance regarded as the foundation of the Old Swiss Confederacy. Institutionalised assemblies and courts appeared towards the end of the 14th century. The two halves of Unterwalden met together in the 14th and 15th centuries, but were never really one: Obwalden, for example, took no part in the annexation of Bellinzona, Riviera and Blenio.

The ideas of the French Revolution were unpopular in Nidwalden, where many resented the limits placed on freedom of worship by the Helvetic Republic of 1798. French troops attacked the canton on 9 September 1798, badly damaged its infrastructure and killed at least 400 people. After Napoleonic rule ended in 1814 most of the changes were reversed. Nidwalden adopted a new constitution only in 1877, and abolished its open assembly, the Landsgemeinde, in 1997.

Nidwalden is a canton of the Swiss Confederation, traditionally counted as a half-canton, with its seat of government and parliament at Stans. About three quarters of its people were Catholic at the 2000 census and most speak German. Agriculture, centred on cattle and dairy farming, dominated the economy until the middle of the 20th century; tourism centres on the lake and on resorts such as Klewenalp, Stanserhorn and Bürgenstock.
niels-bohr: Niels Henrik David Bohr was born in Copenhagen on 7 October 1885, the second of three children of Christian Bohr, Professor of Physiology at the University of Copenhagen, and Ellen Adler, daughter of the Danish Jewish banker David Baruch Adler. His younger brother Harald became a mathematician and played football for Denmark at the 1908 Summer Olympics. Niels enrolled at the University of Copenhagen in 1903 and studied physics under Christian Christiansen. In September 1911, with a Carlsberg Foundation fellowship, he went to Cambridge, where he failed to impress J. J. Thomson, and then to Manchester at the invitation of Ernest Rutherford.

Bohr proposed that the energy levels of electrons are discrete and that electrons revolve in stable orbits around the nucleus but can jump from one level to another. Later models have replaced it, though its underlying principles remain valid. He also conceived the principle of complementarity, that items can be analysed in terms of contradictory properties, such as behaving as a wave or as a stream of particles. This notion dominated his thinking in both science and philosophy.

In April 1917 he began a campaign for an Institute of Theoretical Physics, backed by the Danish government, the Carlsberg Foundation, industry and private donors. Legislation establishing it passed in November 1918, and he became its director. Now the Niels Bohr Institute, it was a focal point for quantum mechanics in the 1920s and 1930s, when most of the best-known theoretical physicists spent time there.

In 1933 Bohr offered refugees from Nazism temporary posts and financial support, and helped them find places, among them James Franck, Lise Meitner and Edward Teller. In September 1943 word reached him that the Nazis regarded his family as Jewish and that he was in danger of arrest. The Danish resistance helped him reach Sweden by sea, and he persuaded King Gustaf V to make public Sweden's willingness to give asylum to Jewish refugees. Historians disagree on how far this led to the rescue of over 7,000 Danish Jews. He joined the British Tube Alloys project and was part of the British mission to the Manhattan Project.
After the war Bohr called for international cooperation on nuclear energy and helped to establish CERN. He died on 18 November 1962, and the element bohrium is named after him.
niels-juel: Juel was the son of Erik Juel and Sophie Sehested, both of Danish noble descent, who lived in Jutland, where his father was a local official and judge. He was born on 8 May 1629 in Christiania, where the family had taken refuge during the invasion of Jutland in the Thirty Years' War. From 1635 to 1642 he was brought up by his aunt Karen Sehested at the Stenalt estate near Randers, and in 1647 he entered the Sorø Academy. His brother Jens Juel became a diplomat.

In 1652 Juel entered Dutch service, learning his trade under the Dutch Admiral Maarten Tromp and Admiral Michiel de Ruyter in the First Anglo-Dutch War and sailing with de Ruyter to the Mediterranean against North African pirates. While ill at Amsterdam in 1655 and 1656 he gained a thorough knowledge of shipbuilding. He entered Danish service in 1656, was made admiral in 1657 and helped defend Copenhagen against King Charles X of Sweden in the Dano-Swedish War of 1658–60.

In the Scanian War he took the supreme command on the death of Cort Adeler in November 1675. His tactic was to cut off part of the enemy's force and concentrate his whole attack on it, first tried at the Battle of Jasmund on 25 May 1676. Superseded by the Dutch Admiral Cornelis Tromp, he took a leading part in the victory off Öland on 1 June 1676. On 1 June 1677 he defeated Erik Carlsson Sjöblad at the Battle of Møn, and on 30 June, with 25 ships of the line against Henrik Horn's 36, he won at Køge Bay, reading a shift of the wind correctly. He was made lieutenant admiral general and a privy councillor.

From 1678 Juel held the supreme command again, blockading Swedish ports. After the Treaty of Lund in 1679 he worked as an administrator and reformer, above all as chief of the admiralty from 1683, and the navy grew into a blue-water force. He married Margrethe Ulfeldt in 1661, and they had four children. Granted Valdemar's Castle on Tåsinge in 1678, he died on 8 April 1697 and was buried in the Holmen Church in Copenhagen.
nieuwe-waterweg: By the middle of the 19th century Rotterdam was already one of the largest port cities in the world, chiefly through the transshipment of goods from Germany to Great Britain. The growth of shipping brought a problem of capacity: the river delta had too many branches, the natural Meuse-Rhine branches were silting up, and the port was becoming hard to reach. A canal through the Hook of Holland had been designed as early as 1731 by Nicolaas Samuelsz Cruquius, and in 1863 a law provided for a new canal for large ocean-going ships from Rotterdam to the North Sea.

Construction began on 31 October 1863 with the expropriation of farmland from Rozenburg to Hook of Holland. Two parallel dikes then took two years to build, and the engineer Pieter Caland proposed extending them 2 km into the sea to break the coastal currents and reduce silt in the shipping lane. Digging of the waterway itself began on 31 October 1866 and was finished three years later, the spoil being used to strengthen other dams and dikes. Last, the dam separating the new channel from the sea and the river was removed.

The first waterway, a breach through the dunes, was only 4.3 kilometres long; in around 1877 the channel was made much larger and wider. It now runs about 20.5 kilometres from het Scheur, west of Maassluis, to the Maasmond, where it joins the dredged North Sea channel of the Maasgeul. It forms the artificial mouth of the Rhine, and no bridge or tunnel crosses it.

Currents and erosion have widened the shipping lane, and it is dredged to a depth of 14.5 to 16 metres below Amsterdam Ordnance Datum, which together with the Maasgeul and Eurogeul lets ships with a draught of 23 metres reach Europoort. The mouth is marked by two light towers called the Paddestoelen, the mushrooms. In 1997 the Maeslantkering, the last part of the Delta Works, was put into operation near the mouth to protect Rotterdam from storm surges. The Dutch agency Rijkswaterstaat maintains the channel.
nigde: Niğde lies in the Central Anatolia region of Turkey at an elevation of 1,276 metres, near ancient trade routes, particularly the road from Kayseri to the Cilician Gates and on to the Mediterranean coast. It stands between the volcanic Melandiz Mountains to the north and the Niğde Massif to the south-southeast, a metamorphic dome with abandoned antimony and iron mines and marble quarries that yield pure white crystalline marble. The climate is cold semi-arid, with hot, dry summers and cold, snowy winters.

The area has been settled by Hittites, Assyrians, Greeks, Armenians, Romans, Byzantines and Turks. In the early Middle Ages the town was known as Magida, and was settled by the remaining inhabitants of nearby Tyana after Tyana fell to the Arabs in 708 or 709. By the early 13th century it was one of the largest cities in Anatolia and one of the principal cities of the Sultanate of Rûm. After that sultanate fell, Niğde was taken by Anatolian beyliks such as the Karaman Beylik and the Eretna Beylik. When Ibn Battuta passed through in the 14th century he reported it ruinous. It did not pass into Ottoman hands until 1467.

According to the Ottoman population statistics of 1914, the sanjak of Niğde, then part of the Konya Vilayet, had 291,117 inhabitants, of whom 227,100 were Muslims, 58,312 Greeks and 4,935 Armenians. Most of the Christian population of the late 19th century lived in the Eski Saray quarter near the Sungur Bey Mosque, where the remains of two large stone churches survive. In the 1950s and 1960s the Turkish authorities settled immigrant Turks from Bulgaria and other Balkan countries there, and Niğde University was opened in 1992.

Medieval monuments are scattered around the centre, especially around the market place. They include the Sungur Bey Mosque of the early 14th century, which combines Selçuk and Gothic elements, among them quadripartite vaulting and a rose window; the Alaaddin Mosque of the 13th century, with a portal decorated with muqarnas; the Hudavend Hatun tomb; and the Ak Medrese of 1409, built under the Karamanoğlu dynasty. Niğde Castle dates in part to Selçuk times. Kemerhisar, the site of ancient Tyana, has a long surviving stretch of Roman aqueduct, and the rock-cut Eski Gümüşler Monastery, built by the Byzantines, was rediscovered in 1963.
niger-delta: The Niger Delta lies directly on the Gulf of Guinea and separates the Bight of Benin from the Bight of Bonny. As officially defined by the Nigerian government, it extends over 70,000 square kilometres and makes up 7.5 per cent of the country's land. Historically and on maps it consists of Bayelsa, Delta and Rivers States, but in 2000 the government of Obasanjo added Abia, Akwa Ibom, Cross River, Edo, Imo and Ondo States to the region.

It is densely populated, with about 31 million people from over 40 ethnic groups speaking around 250 dialects. The Ijaw are the largest group, present in six states, and the main language groups are the Ijaw languages, Ibibio-Efik and the Edoid languages. It was sometimes called the Oil Rivers because it was once a major producer of palm oil.

The area was the British Oil Rivers Protectorate from 1885 until 1893, when it was expanded as the Niger Coast Protectorate. In the west the British signed separate Treaties of Protection with kings of the four primary groups, the Urhobo, Isoko, Ijaw and Itsekiri. The core of the delta later became part of the eastern region of Nigeria, created in 1951. In 1953 the non-Igbo peoples of that region, among them the Ibibio, Annang, Efik, Ijaw and Ogoja, demanded a state of their own, the Calabar-Ogoja-Rivers state, which became a major issue in the status of minorities during the debates on independence.

Isaac Adaka Boro declared an Independent Niger Delta Republic before the Nigerian Civil War of 1967 to 1970, in which the people of the delta suffered heavily from loss of life, hunger and starvation, and schools closed. Rivers State, Cross River State, Akwa Ibom State and Bayelsa State were created from the old eastern region. After the war communities demanded social and environmental justice, and Ken Saro Wiwa and the Ogoni were the lead figures. The Ogoni Bill of Rights appeared in 1990, and Saro Wiwa and nine other activists were arrested and killed in 1995. In 1998 the Ijaw issued the Kaiama Declaration on control of resources.

Oil operations began in the region in the 1950s, run by multinational corporations. Since 1975 the region has accounted for more than 75 per cent of Nigeria's export earnings. The pollution and gas flaring that came with the industry, together with arguments over the sharing of oil revenue, have fed environmental movements and conflicts in the region. Revenue allocation was contested well before independence, and the derivation formula governs the share that oil-producing states keep.
niger-river: The Niger is the main river of West Africa, about 4,180 kilometres long, with a drainage basin of 2,117,700 square kilometres. It rises in the Guinea Highlands near the Sierra Leone border, only 240 km from the Atlantic, yet runs directly away from the sea into the Sahara. Near Timbuktu it turns sharply southeast and flows through Niger and Nigeria into the Gulf of Guinea. This boomerang course baffled geographers for two centuries; it apparently arose because two ancient rivers joined, the lower capturing the upper. Between Ségou and Timbuktu lies the Inner Niger Delta, braided streams, marshes and lakes whose seasonal floods make the land productive for fishing and agriculture.

When the African humid period ended some 5,500 years ago and the Sahara dried, people moved to the fertile Niger bend. Yams, African rice and pearl millet were domesticated in the region, and farming, fishing and herding led to settlements such as Djenné-Djenno, now a World Heritage Site. The bend became an origin and destination of trans-Saharan trade, which fuelled the Ghana, Mali and Songhai empires, and ports such as Timbuktu and Gao became centres of learning. Gold, salt, kola nuts, fish, livestock, textiles and slaves moved along the river. Trade brought Islam to the region in approximately the 14th century.

Pliny connected the river to the Nile, and the notion persisted into the 19th century, even through the accounts of Leo Africanus, who first used the name Niger for it in 1550, and Ibn Battuta. The African Association was formed in England in 1788 to find the river. In June 1796 the Scottish explorer Mungo Park became the first European to see its middle part, and he died in 1806 on a second expedition. In 1830 Richard Lander and his brother were the first Europeans to follow the river to the ocean. The modern states of Niger and Nigeria take their names from it.

The river flows through Guinea, Mali, Niger, Benin and Nigeria, and its basin covers ten countries. Its main tributary, the Benue, joins it at Lokoja. Dams serve hydropower and irrigation, among them the Sélingué, Markala, Kainji, Shiroro and Jebba dams. The Inner Niger Delta covers about 20,000 square kilometres in the wet season and 3,900 in the dry, and supports migratory birds, fishing, farming and herding.
nigeria: Nigeria lies in West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea, between the Sahel to the north and the Atlantic Ocean to the south. It borders Niger, Chad, Cameroon and Benin. The Niger and Benue rivers converge in a Y shape and empty into the Niger Delta, one of the world's largest river deltas. The highest point is Chappal Waddi, at 2,419 metres.

The far south has a tropical rainforest climate, with mangrove swamps along the coast. Between the far south and the far north lies savannah, which divides into Guinean forest-savanna mosaic, Sudan savannah and Sahel savannah.

The Nok civilisation thrived between 1500 BCE and 200 CE. It produced life-sized terracotta figures that are among the earliest known sculptures in Africa, and it independently invented iron smelting by about 550 BCE and possibly a few centuries earlier. The Kano Chronicle records the history of the Hausa city state of Kano from around 999 CE, and other Hausa cities such as Daura, Katsina and Gobir have recorded histories dating to the 10th century.

The Kingdom of Nri of the Igbo people consolidated in the 10th century and lasted until it lost sovereignty to the British in 1911, and the oldest bronzes in West Africa made by the lost-wax process come from Igbo-Ukwu, a city under Nri influence. The Yoruba had developed one of the earliest city-states in Africa at Ile Ife by the 8th century. The Kingdom of Benin, founded by the Edo people, had a densely populated capital that served as a hub for regional and transatlantic trade in cloth, ivory, pepper and salt.

The name Nigeria was coined on 8 January 1897 by the British journalist Flora Shaw, after the Niger River. The modern state took its present shape in 1914 with the merging of the Southern Nigeria Protectorate and the Northern Nigeria Protectorate. Independence as a federation came on 1 October 1960, followed by a civil war from 1967 to 1970, a series of military governments, and civilian rule from 1999.

Nigeria is a federal republic of 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, with a bicameral National Assembly. More than 250 ethnic groups live there, speaking about 500 languages, and the Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo together make up over 60% of the population.
night-of-the-long-knives: President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933, and within months rival parties had been eliminated and Germany was a one-party state. Hitler nevertheless did not command the army, which remained under Hindenburg's formal leadership and guarded its independence. Its officers, many drawn from the Prussian nobility, regarded the Sturmabteilung (SA) as a plebeian rabble.

Ernst Röhm, the SA's chief of staff, wanted the army and the SA merged under his leadership and lobbied to become Minister of Defence, a post held by General Werner von Blomberg. He also spoke for a continuation of the revolution, a second revolution that would redistribute wealth. Göring, Goebbels, Himmler and Hess all positioned themselves against him. On 21 June 1934 Blomberg told Hitler at Neudeck that Hindenburg was close to declaring martial law and handing government to the Reichswehr unless Hitler acted against Röhm.

At about 04:30 on 30 June 1934 Hitler flew to Munich, where he accused the city's SA police chief, August Schneidhuber, of treachery; Schneidhuber was executed that day. Hitler then went with SS and police to the Hanselbauer Hotel in Bad Wiessee, where he personally arrested Röhm and other SA leaders. The Breslau SA leader Edmund Heines was shot after being found in bed with a young SA man, a detail Goebbels later stressed in propaganda.

The killings went beyond the SA. In Berlin an SS unit stormed the Vice-Chancellery on Göring's orders, and Gestapo officers shot Franz von Papen's secretary Herbert von Bose.
