Papen's associates Edgar Jung and Erich Klausener were also murdered. Kurt von Schleicher and his wife were killed at their home, as were Gregor Strasser and Gustav Ritter von Kahr.
Röhm was held at Stadelheim Prison. On 1 July Theodor Eicke and Michael Lippert gave him a pistol and ten minutes; when he did not use it they shot him.

Hitler justified the purge to the Reichstag on 13 July 1934, claiming that as the supreme judge of the German people he had ordered the ringleaders shot. The army largely applauded, and a telegram of thanks attributed to Hindenburg was later admitted by Göring to have been written by the Nazis. At least 85 people died, and some estimates run from 700 to 1,000; more than 1,000 perceived opponents were arrested.

Viktor Lutze replaced Röhm, and the SA's membership fell from 2.9 million in August 1934 to 1.2 million in April 1938. The purge strengthened the military's support for Hitler and swept aside legal prohibitions on extrajudicial killing.
nihon-shoki: The compilation goes back to Emperor Tenmu, who ordered twelve people, including Prince Kawashima, to edit the old history of the realm. The Shoku Nihongi records that Prince Toneri completed the work on imperial orders and submitted it in May 720 as thirty volumes of history and one of genealogy, with the help of Ō no Yasumaro, to Empress Genshō. The Sinicized court wanted a written history comparable with the annals of the Chinese, and the compilers seem to have taken the thirty volumes of the Han ji and Hou Han ji as a model. The court nonetheless chose the title Nihon, origin of the sun, rather than the Chinese term Wa.

The work is a synthesis of older documents: records kept at the Yamato court since the sixth century and documents and folklore submitted by clans serving the court. The Tennōki and Kokki, compiled by Prince Shōtoku and Soga no Umako, had been burned in the Isshi Incident of July 645. Three Baekje documents are cited mainly for diplomatic affairs, and some sources appear anonymously as aru fumi, some document.

The Nihon Shoki opens with the creation myth and the first seven generations of divine beings, beginning with Kuninotokotachi, and carries its account to events of the 8th century. It is more elaborate and detailed than the Kojiki and is written in classical Chinese, with notes on how words were pronounced in Japanese. The first chapters hold myths such as Izanagi and Izanami and Amaterasu and Susanoo, and Chapter 3 begins the line of emperors with Jimmu. It is believed to record accurately the later reigns of Emperor Tenji, Emperor Tenmu and Empress Jitō.

Most scholars agree that its founding date of 660 BCE and its earliest emperors are mythical. Their reign lengths, and those of Ōjin and Nintoku, were probably exaggerated to make the imperial line sufficiently ancient. For the eight emperors of Chapter 4, the Kesshi Hachidai, only birth, reign, consorts and tomb are recorded.

The book has proved an important tool for historians and archaeologists, since it holds the most complete extant historical record of ancient Japan. With the Kojiki its stories are called the Kiki stories, and they give an origin for the gods, the islands and the imperial family, connecting the emperor to the sun goddess Amaterasu. The tale of Urashima Tarō grew from a brief entry for the 22nd year of Emperor Yūryaku. William George Aston completed the first English translation in 1896.
niigata-prefecture: Niigata Prefecture lies in the Chūbu region of Honshu and stretches about 240 kilometres along the Sea of Japan from south-west to north-east, with a coastal plain between the mountains and the sea. It also includes Sado Island, the sixth-largest island of Japan in area after the four main islands and Okinawa Island. It borders Toyama, Nagano, Gunma, Fukushima and Yamagata prefectures. The prefecture is generally divided into four areas: Jōetsu in the south, Chūetsu in the centre, Kaetsu in the north and Sado Island. The mouth of the Shinano River, the longest river in Japan, lies within it. Niigata is the capital and largest city, with Nagaoka, Jōetsu and Sanjō among the other major cities.

Until after the Meiji Restoration the area was divided into Echigo Province on the mainland and Sado Province. In the Sengoku period the Nagao clan, at times vassals of the Uesugi, ruled a fief in the west from Kasugayama Castle. Its most notable member, Nagao Kagetora, better known as Uesugi Kenshin, unified the leaders of Echigo Province and became its sole ruler. By taking the surname Uesugi he also became head of the Uesugi clan and brought its realm under his control.

The port of Niigata was the first Japanese port on the Sea of Japan to be opened to foreign trade after Matthew Perry opened Japan, and it has since played an important role in trade with Russia and Korea. In the 1960s and 1970s the Etsuzankai organisation, led by the politician Kakuei Tanaka, was highly influential in bringing infrastructure improvements to the prefecture, among them the Jōetsu Shinkansen high-speed rail line and the Kanetsu Expressway to Tokyo.

Agriculture is the major industry, and rice is its principal product. The area around Uonuma produces the Koshihikari variety, widely considered the highest-quality rice in Japan. The prefecture is known for sake, senbei, mochi and arare, and the ornamental carp known as koi originated there. Sanjō and Tsubame produce 90 per cent of all the silverware made in Japan. The Kinzan gold mine on Sado Island was active until it closed in 1989. Much of the tourism centres on skiing, in the alpine areas of Myōkō and Yuzawa, and on hot springs. Yasunari Kawabata's novel Snow Country, published in 1947, is set in Yuzawa.
nijmegen: Nijmegen lies on the Waal close to the German border, on hills that give a wide view over the Waal and Rhine valley. The Romans valued the position and built a military camp there in the first century BCE. The city is the largest in Gelderland and has been a university city since 1923, when a Catholic university, now Radboud University Nijmegen, opened there.

By 69 CE a village called Oppidum Batavorum had formed near the camp. It was destroyed when the Batavi, the original inhabitants of the Rhine and Meuse delta, revolted. The Romans then built a larger camp for Legio X Gemina. In 98 Nijmegen was the first of two settlements in what is now the Netherlands to receive Roman city rights, and in 104 Emperor Trajan renamed the town Ulpia Noviomagus Batavorum.

Charlemagne kept a palace there in 777. Henry VI, later Holy Roman Emperor, was born there in 1165, and in 1230 his son Frederick II granted the town city rights. In 1247 it was ceded to the count of Guelders as security for a loan that was never repaid, so it has remained part of Gelderland. The Limbourg brothers, painters, were born and educated in the city. It hosted the negotiations that produced the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1678, which did not bring a lasting peace. Its fortifications were dismantled in 1874.

On 22 February 1944 American aircraft bombed the centre, killing over 750 people; the NIOD later concluded that the raid was an accident caused by poor communications. In September 1944, during Operation Market Garden, the Allies fought to take the Waal bridges, and British Grenadier Guards and elements of the American 82nd Airborne Division liberated the city.

The Waal was first bridged by a rail bridge in 1878 and by a road bridge in 1936. The Smetius Collection, assembled by Johannes Smetius in the 17th century, preserves Roman finds from the town, and the city is known for the Vierdaagse, the International Four Days Marches.
nika-riots: By the sixth century the chariot-racing factions, the demes, had become a focus for social and political grievances, part street gang and part political party, and only the Blues and Greens still had influence. Justinian I at first favoured the Blues, then took a more neutral line as he tried to limit the factions' power, and the factions became more inclined to unite. His officials John the Cappadocian and Tribonian were unpopular for high taxes, alleged corruption and harsh treatment of debtors, and John's taxes hit the senatorial elite. The defeat at Callinicum in 531 against Sasanian Persia damaged the emperor's standing further.

In 531 the city prefect Eudaimon arrested members of both factions for murder. On 10 January 532 two of them, a Blue and a Green, survived their hanging when the scaffold broke, and monks took them to the church of St Laurence. Justinian commuted their sentences to imprisonment, and when the factions demanded a pardon he ignored them.

On 13 January 532 the crowd at the Hippodrome insulted Justinian, and by the twenty-second race the chants had changed to the single cry Nika. The riot lasted a week, and fires destroyed much of the city. The rioters demanded the dismissal of John the Cappadocian and Tribonian, and Justinian gave way. He then carried a Bible before the crowd and promised amnesty, but many refused his apology and called for Hypatius, a nephew of Anastasius I, to be emperor.

Justinian considered fleeing, but Procopius reports that Theodora dissuaded him, saying royalty is a fine burial shroud. Justinian sent the eunuch Narses with gold to the Blues' leaders, and in the middle of Hypatius's acclamation the Blues withdrew. Troops under Belisarius, Mundus and Constantiolus then stormed the Hippodrome. Belisarius captured Hypatius and Pompeius while Mundus killed those remaining, Blues and Greens alike.

According to Procopius around 30,000 people died, though many may have been trampled. Justinian had Hypatius and Pompeius executed and exiled the senators who had supported the riot, and he confiscated the property of some. Later he gave titles and land back to their children and reinstated John the Cappadocian. He rebuilt Constantinople and the Hagia Sophia. Factional violence did not end, and in 565 the city prefect Julian had to purge the factions.

Historians disagree about the causes. Geoffrey Greatrex stresses Justinian's miscommunication and inconsistency towards the factions, and J. A. S. Evans holds that reforms, senatorial discontent and faction grievances all contributed. Clemens Koehn argues that the rioters acted with unusual military organisation.
nikephoros-i: Nikephoros was born in about 750. Contemporary sources, including Theophanes the Confessor and Patriarch Nikephoros, call him a Greek from Seleucia in Isauria, and modern scholars agree. Writers outside the Byzantine world, among them Michael the Syrian, al-Tabari and Mas'udi, report a tradition that he descended from the last Ghassanid ruler, Jabala ibn al-Ayham, which is unlikely, since no reliable contemporary source says so. Under Empress Irene he served as general logothete, or finance minister, and was sometimes called the Logothete.

In 802 Charlemagne opened marriage negotiations to unite the Western and Eastern empires. Some officials, among them Niketas Triphyllios and Leon Sarantapechos, feared the proposal and began a conspiracy led by Nikephoros. While the Frankish ambassadors were still in Constantinople the guards were falsely told that the courtier Aetios was forcing Irene to yield the throne to his brother, and they sided with Nikephoros. Irene was removed, and Patriarch Tarasios crowned him in the Hagia Sophia on 31 October 802. He crowned his son Staurakios co-emperor on Christmas Day 803. He reorganised the empire, resettled poor soldiers and peasants from Asia Minor in Thrace, Macedonia, Epirus and Greece, and managed the finances with strict discipline, which earned him hostility.

The general Bardanes Tourkos rebelled in 803, possibly over army pay, and was blinded after he surrendered. Nikephoros appointed the iconodule layman Nikephoros as patriarch in 806 and convened a synod that declared Constantine VI's second marriage lawful, which angered the monks of Stoudios, including Theodore the Stoudite, who were banished in 809. Ecclesiastical historians such as Theophanes portrayed him unfavourably. In Italy he sent fleets to Venice after Charlemagne recognised it as a Frankish fief, and concluded the Pax Nicephori, though he refused to acknowledge Charlemagne's imperial status.

After he refused tribute to Harun al-Rashid, Nikephoros suffered a severe defeat at Krasos in Phrygia. In 806 Harun invaded with an army reported at 135,000 and took Heraclea Cybistra and Tyana, and Nikephoros agreed to an immediate payment of 50,000 nomismata and an annual tribute of 30,000. In 811 he invaded Bulgaria and sacked Pliska, but Khan Krum ambushed and destroyed his army in the Varbitsa Pass, and Nikephoros was killed. Krum is said to have made a drinking cup from his skull.

The defeat was disastrous for Byzantine morale and political stability. Later iconoclast writers pointed to the disasters under Nikephoros I and Michael I Rhangabe, who was married to Nikephoros's daughter Prokopia, as a vindication of iconoclasm.
nikephoros-ii-orsini: Nikephoros was the son of John Orsini of Epirus and Anna Palaiologina. When his mother allegedly poisoned his father in 1335, he succeeded as a child of seven, and Anna ruled as regent. She could not appease the Byzantine Emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos, who annexed the Epirote part of Thessaly in 1336 and advanced on Ioannina. Andronikos refused to accept the boy as a vassal, installed his own governors in Epirus and arranged his marriage to Maria Kantakouzene, daughter of his chief minister John Kantakouzenos.

The anti-Byzantine faction of the nobility smuggled Nikephoros to the court of Catherine II of Valois, titular Empress of Constantinople, at Taranto, hoping for Angevin help. In late 1338, at Catherine's instigation, the Epirotes rose in Arta in his name and seized the Byzantine governor Theodore Synadenos, but Andronikos and Kantakouzenos put down the revolt and besieged Nikephoros in Thomokastron, whose garrison surrendered on a promise of his safety. He was married to Maria, made panhypersebastos and kept in Kantakouzenos's household; when his father-in-law became Emperor John VI in 1347 he was raised to despotes, and from 1351 he governed Ainos and the cities along the Hellespont.

In late 1355, after the death of Stefan Uroš IV Dušan, who had conquered Epirus in the late 1340s, Nikephoros returned to Greece. In spring 1356 he took Thessaly and drove Dušan's brother Simeon Uroš, the husband of his sister Thomais, out of Arta.

The countryside had been overrun by Albanian clans and could not be controlled. To avert a Serbian reaction, Nikephoros set aside Maria and prepared to marry Theodora of Bulgaria, sister of Dušan's widow Helena, but the Epirote nobility, with whom Maria was popular, forced him to recall her. Soon afterwards he was killed fighting the Albanians at the Battle of Achelous in Aetolia. He may have had a son, Manuel, perhaps the Antony Kantakouzenos who was a monk at Meteora in 1404.
nikephoros-ii-phokas: Nikephoros Phokas was born around 912 into the Phokas family, which had produced several generals, among them his father Bardas Phokas, his brother Leo Phokas and his grandfather Nikephoros Phokas the Elder. He became military governor of the Anatolic Theme in 945 under Emperor Constantine VII, and in 954 or 955 he replaced his father as Domestic of the Schools, which put him in charge of the eastern army.

In 960 a fleet of 308 ships carrying 50,000 troops was assembled against the Muslim Emirate of Crete, and the minister Joseph Bringas entrusted the expedition to Nikephoros. After a nine-month siege of the fortress town of Chandax he entered it on 6 March 961 and soon took the whole island. He then marched into Cilicia, captured Anazarbos and later, with John I Tzimiskes, entered Aleppo on 24 December.

Emperor Romanos II died on 15 March 963. On 2 July the army proclaimed Nikephoros emperor at Caesarea, and once Bringas had been forced to flee Constantinople he was proclaimed there on 16 August and married the empress Theophano. In the east he completed the conquest of Cilicia in 964 and 965, taking Mopsuestia and Tarsus, while Niketas Chalkoutzes recovered Cyprus. In the west he was less successful: a fleet sent to Sicily was routed and Rometta fell, and his fighting with the German emperor Otto I in Apulia and Calabria brought no lasting gains.

His popularity rested on his conquests. To pay for the army he cut court spending, curtailed the immunities of the clergy and forbade new monasteries, and heavy taxes and a debased currency provoked riots. He also asked the church to honour soldiers killed fighting the Saracens as martyrs, a demand that proved unpopular. A devout man, he helped his friend, the monk Athanasios, found the Great Lavra on Mount Athos.

The plot against Nikephoros began when he dismissed Michael Bourtzes after the disobedience at Antioch. According to Joannes Zonaras and John Skylitzes, Theophano and Tzimiskes had become lovers and conspired against him. On 11 December 969 Tzimiskes and his entourage entered the bedchamber through a door Theophano had left unlocked and killed him. Tzimiskes took the throne, and a rising of the Phokas family under Nikephoros's nephew Bardas Phokas was quickly subdued. In legends told on Crete under Venetian rule he was a point of reference, and the Kallergis family, the most prominent of the island's nobility, claimed descent from him.
nikephoros-iii-botaneiates: Nikephoros was born in 1002 into the Botaneiates family, a prominent military family of the Anatolic Theme. According to the historian Michael Attaleiates, the only source for this, his grandfather and father served as commanders under Basil II. Attaleiates also says the family was related to Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas, a claim Nikephoros probably used to add legitimacy to his later rule. He married a woman named Vevdene, with whom he had one son, and later married Maria of Alania, the former wife of Michael VII.

Nikephoros served as a commander under Constantine IX Monomachos during the Pecheneg revolt of 1048–1053. After the Battle of Zygos Pass in 1053, Attaleiates records, he held his retreating cavalry together for eleven days under constant attack until they reached Adrianople, and he was made magistros. In 1057 he helped Isaac I Komnenos overthrow Michael VI Bringas, leading forces at the Battle of Petroe.

Under Constantine X Doukas he became doux of Thessalonica and then, around 1065, of Antioch, where he repelled raids from the Emirate of Aleppo. He was relieved of the command around 1067, probably through the efforts of civil officials who wished to weaken the military aristocracy. After a period of exile and retirement he was recalled by Michael VII as kouropalates and governor of the Anatolic Theme.

In 1077 Nikephoros wrote to Michael VII urging action against the Seljuk Turks in Anatolia. Michael was insulted by the directness of the appeal, and Nikephoros rebelled to protect himself, raising an army of native troops and Turkish mercenaries. The Senate proclaimed him emperor on 7 January 1078, Michael abdicated and became a monk, and Nikephoros entered Constantinople in April.

He faced the revolts of Nikephoros Bryennios and Nikephoros Basilakes, both put down by Alexios Komnenos and punished with blinding, and in 1079 a failed attempt on his life by the Varangian Guard. A rebellion by Konstantios Doukas ended his planned campaign in the east. He spent heavily on donatives and forgave debts in arrears, and he secured the submission of Theodore Gabras and Philaretos Brachamios, governors who had become de facto independent. In 1081 Alexios Komnenos, sent against a Norman invasion, instead seized Constantinople on 1 April. Nikephoros abdicated and became a monk at the Monastery of Peribleptus.
nikephoros-phokas-the-elder: Nikephoros was the son of a native of Cappadocia called Phokas, the founder of the Phokas family, who caught the attention of Emperor Basil I the Macedonian on a campaign in the 870s and was made a tourmarches. The young Nikephoros was taken into the imperial retinue and soon joined the guard corps of the manglabitai. Before 878 he was promoted to protostrator and given a palace near the Church of St. Thecla, and he later became military governor of the theme of Charsianon, where he won successes against the Arabs.

He replaced Stephen Maxentios, who had been defeated by the Arabs, as single commander in southern Italy, leading troops of several western themes reinforced from Asia Minor, among them a Paulician detachment. Byzantine sources credit him with recovering Taranto, Bari, Santa Severina, Rhegion, Tropai and Amantia; at Amantia he kept the news of Basil's death and his own recall secret until the Arab garrison had surrendered under a promise of safe passage. He settled many Armenians in the region, and John Skylitzes reports that he stopped soldiers from carrying off local Italians to be sold as slaves in the East.

Back in Constantinople he was made patrikios and Domestic of the Schools, in effect commander-in-chief of the army, after the death of Andrew the Scythian. In 895 he led a large army against Tsar Simeon of Bulgaria, though it is unclear whether he fought a battle: a Magyar invasion stirred up by Byzantium and the navy's operations on the Danube forced Simeon to seek a truce. Leo VI's Tactica also records a raid he led near Adana in Cilicia, returning by a different route to avoid the Arab army sent to cut him off.

His death reportedly encouraged Simeon to resume the war, with heavy losses for his successor, Leo Katakalon. Leo VI praised his military talents, he was credited with a sharpened stake driven into the ground against cavalry, and Skylitzes called him a brave and prudent man, pious towards God and just towards men. His sons Bardas Phokas the Elder and Leo Phokas the Elder both became Domestics of the Schools, as did his grandsons Nikephoros, later emperor, and Leo Phokas the Younger.
niketas-choniates: Niketas Choniates was born around 1155 in Chonae, near the present-day town of Honaz in Turkey, into a family of lesser nobility. The family lacked the wealth of the Constantinopolitan aristocracy, but his father could afford to send Niketas and his brother Michael to Constantinople in 1164 for an education. Niketas studied rhetoric, literature, theology, law and politics under John Mauropous. He admired Homer, Hesiod and Plato, whom he often blended with Christian theology.

He began as a junior tax official in the Province of Pontos around 1180, probably through connections made by his brother, and held several minor posts before becoming known as an orator. In 1189 Emperor Isaakios II made him Governor of Thrace at Philippolis. When Frederick Barbarossa marched through the Balkans on the Third Crusade, Isaakios first ordered him to rebuild the city's fortifications and then to tear down the new walls to keep the Germans from holding a fortified city. Niketas complied and fled just before the crusaders arrived. He later portrayed Isaakios as incompetent, passive and over-taxing.

In 1191 Isaakios made him Judge of the Velum, head of a tribunal for civil suits. In 1194, under Alexios III, he became logothete tou genikou, the highest post in the civil service and head of the senate. Alexios V dismissed him in early 1204 without a reason that Niketas accepted, and he stayed in the senate.

Crusaders' fires in August 1203 destroyed Niketas's main residence, and he moved to a smaller house near the Hagia Sophia. During the sack of Constantinople in April 1204 he hid with Venetian friends. On 17 April, once the plundering had eased, he left through the Golden Gate with his pregnant wife and the Patriarch John X Camaterus, carrying his infant son. He settled at Nicaea at the court of Theodore I Lascaris, devoted himself to writing and died in 1217.

His Chronike diegesis, often published in English as O City of Byzantium, is an eyewitness account of the sack. He also wrote the Thesaurus Orthodoxae Fidei, preserved complete in manuscripts but published only in part, a chief source for the heresies of the twelfth century. Hieronymus Wolf printed the History in 1557, Immanuel Bekker edited it in 1835, and Harry J. Magoulias translated it into English in 1984.
nikita-khrushchev: Nikita Sergeyevich Khrushchev was born on 15 April 1894 in the village of Kalinovka, in the Kursk Governorate of the Russian Empire, to poor peasant parents. His father worked in the Donbas, where wages were much higher, and left the family in Kalinovka between visits. Khrushchev worked as a metal worker in his youth and was a political commissar in the Russian Civil War. In 1921 he was made assistant director for political affairs at the Rutchenkovo mine in the Donbas, and he had only four years of formal schooling.

Under the patronage of Lazar Kaganovich, who became head of the Party in Ukraine in 1925, Khrushchev rose quickly through the Soviet hierarchy. He expressed vehement support for the Moscow Trials of the Great Purge, and in 1938 he was sent to govern the Ukrainian SSR, where he continued the purges. In the Second World War he served as a political commissar and as an intermediary between Stalin and his commanders, and he was present at the Battle of Stalingrad.

Recalled to Moscow, he headed the Party in Moscow city and province from December 1949. After Stalin's death on 6 March 1953 a power struggle followed, in which Khrushchev prevailed over rivals including Lavrentiy Beria and was elected First Secretary of the Central Committee. On 25 February 1956 he delivered the Secret Speech at the 20th Party Congress, which denounced Stalin's purges and brought a less repressive era. His domestic policies, particularly in agriculture, were often ineffective. His years in office saw the tensest period of the Cold War, culminating in the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.

Early in the 1960s his hold on power weakened because of his domestic failures and his handling of the Cuban Missile Crisis. Leonid Brezhnev began plotting his removal in March 1964, and he was ousted on 14 October 1964. He received a pension and a house, fell into deep depression, and was treated as a non-person. His memoirs were smuggled to the West and published in part in 1970.

Khrushchev died of a heart attack on 11 September 1971, aged 77. He was denied a state funeral and was buried in the Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow, with troops surrounding it. Many of his innovations were reversed after his fall. The historian Robert Service describes him as at once a Stalinist and an anti-Stalinist, a trouble-maker and a peacemaker.
niklot: Niklot, also written Nyklot, became chief of the Obotrite confederacy, which included the Kissini and the Circipani, between 1130 and 1131, and held that position until his death. He was at the same time Lord of Schwerin, Quetzin and Malchow. His open resistance began when the German King Lothar III, later emperor, granted the Obotrite realm to his Danish vassal Canute Lavard. Niklot fought Lothar and Canute together with Pribislav of Wagria, son of Budivoj.

After the murder of Canute in 1131, Niklot and Pribislav of Wagria divided the Obotrite territory, and Niklot received the eastern lands. To weaken Pribislav in the following years he allied with Saxon lords, above all Count Adolf II of Holstein, and allowed Slavic pirates to attack the Danes. His Saxon allies turned against him during the Wendish Crusade of 1147. He held out against the siege of his fortress at Dobin but was forced to pay tribute to the crusaders, and afterwards arranged peaceful terms with Adolf of Holstein, Henry the Lion and Henry of Ratzeburg.

His religion is uncertain. After the death of the Christian Obotrite prince Henry, Niklot is said to have returned to the traditional pagan beliefs. According to the Chronica Slavorum of Helmold, however, he promised to Christianize his lands as part of the peace, and in the late 1150s he wrote to Henry the Lion that the god in heaven should be the duke's God, while the duke would be the god of the Obotrites.

By 1158 King Valdemar the Great of Denmark had begun to pay Henry the Lion for help, and Niklot retaliated. The Danish king and the Saxon duke allied in 1160. While the Danes harried the coast and kept the Rani occupied, the Saxons killed Niklot at his stronghold of Burg Werle in August 1160, and the Christians partitioned most of the Obotrite territory. His death ended Slavic control of Mecklenburg as far as the Peene River. His son Pribislav recovered the inheritance as Prince of Mecklenburg in 1167 as a Saxon vassal, and another son, Wertislaw, was the father of Nicholas I, Lord of Mecklenburg.
nikola-altomanovic: Nikola was a župan of the House of Vojinović, the son of Altoman Vojinović, a notable voivode in Zeta. The killing of his uncle Vojislav Vojinović in 1363 allowed him to take over his uncle's domains. In the decade after the death of Stefan Dušan the authority of the Serbian emperor declined, while the Mrnjavčević family steadily increased its power and lands.

In 1365 Nikola allied himself with Emperor Uroš V and Lazar Hrebeljanović against King Vukašin Mrnjavčević and his allies, a conflict that culminated in the Battle of Zvečan. The Mrnjavčević were then the most powerful Serbian noble family, with a wide network of subjects and allies among Serbs, Bulgarians and Albanians and a large mercenary force. Uroš was captured early in the battle and Lazar withdrew with his heavy cavalry, leaving Nikola alone on the field. He stayed until he was badly maimed and was presumed dead for the next year, and his alliance with Lazar never recovered.

At its height his lordship ran from Rudnik over Polimlje and Podrinje into eastern Herzegovina with Trebinje, reaching as far as Konavle and Dračevica, on the border of the Republic of Dubrovnik. In the autumn of 1371, after the Serbian defeat by the Ottomans at the Battle of Maritsa, he divided some lands with Lazar.

In 1373 a military alliance formed against him: the Bosnian Ban Tvrtko I Kotromanić, Đurađ I Balšić, lord of Zeta, Nikola Gorjanski, prince of Mačva, and King Louis I of Hungary. In the same year their forces invaded his domain and besieged him in Užice, his capital fortress. After his defeat he was blinded by Stefan Musić, a voivode of Lazar, and his lands were divided between Moravian Serbia, Zeta and Bosnia. For the first time the Bosnian state reached roughly its modern border with Serbia.
nikola-i-of-montenegro: Nikola was born on 7 October 1841 in the village of Njeguši, the home of the reigning House of Petrović. His father, Mirko Petrović-Njegoš, was a Montenegrin warrior and elder brother of Danilo I. After 1696 the dignity of vladika, or prince-bishop, had been hereditary in the family and passed from uncle to nephew, but Danilo declined the episcopal office, married and made Montenegro a secular principality. Mirko renounced his own claim, and his son was named heir. Nikola spent part of his boyhood in Trieste and was sent to the Lycée Louis-le-Grand in Paris, where he showed little taste for the city and wished to return home.

Nikola succeeded his assassinated uncle on 13 August 1860, while still in Paris, and married Milena Vukotić in Cetinje that November. He carried out military, administrative and educational reforms, and Russia supplied military missions, money and arms. In 1876 he declared war on the Ottoman Empire. In the campaign of 1877–1878 he captured Nikšić, Bar and Ulcinj, and the war extended the frontier and gave Montenegro a coast on the Adriatic. The Congress of Berlin recognised its independence in 1878.

He gave the country its first constitution in 1905 under pressure from a population wanting more freedom, and introduced a currency, the perper, in 1906. On 28 August 1910, at his jubilee, he took the title of king at the petition of the Skupština. In the Balkan Wars of 1912 he was an enthusiastic ally and captured Scutari after a siege, defying the Concert of Europe. In 1914 he was the first to go to Serbia's aid against Austria-Hungary.

In January 1916 Montenegro was conquered by Austria-Hungary, and the king fled to Italy and then to France. After the end of the First World War a meeting at Podgorica voted to depose him and annex Montenegro to Serbia, which soon joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, renamed Yugoslavia in 1929. Nikola claimed the throne from exile until he died in Antibes in 1921. He was buried in Italy, and in 1989 his remains, with those of his queen and two of their twelve children, were reburied in Montenegro.

He was also a poet and dramatist, known for the patriotic song Onamo, 'namo! and the drama The Balkan Empress. Five of his six daughters married princes and kings, which earned him the nickname father-in-law of Europe.
nikola-karev: Nikola Yanakiev Karev was born in Kruševo on 23 November 1877 and went to the Bulgarian Exarchist school there. In 1893 he moved to Sofia, where he worked as a carpenter for the socialist Vasil Glavinov, met Dimitar Blagoev and joined the Bulgarian Workers' Social Democratic Party. Returning to Ottoman Macedonia in 1898, he graduated from the Exarchist gymnasium in Bitola and from 1900 taught in Exarchist schools in Gorno Divjaci and Kruševo. That year a conference of Macedonian socialists near Kruševo called for a multinational Macedonian republic within a Balkan socialist federation, and Karev joined the revolutionary organisation as leader of a regional band, or cheta.

In May 1903 he told Stamatis Stamatiou of the Greek daily Akropolis that the revolutionaries wanted a republic on the model of Switzerland, giving autonomy and democracy to its different peoples. When Kruševo fell to the rebels in August, he became president of the provisional government of the Kruševo Republic. He is said to have written the Kruševo Manifesto, which called on local Muslims to join the Christians. A council of 60 was elected, 20 each from the Bulgarian Exarchists, Aromanians and Greek Patriarchists, with a government of six. The insurgents killed several Patriarchists accused of spying and attacked local Muslims, while Karev tried to limit the attacks and the looting. On 12 August he withdrew into the hills.

He went back to Bulgaria and joined the Narrow Socialists, and his requests for an Ottoman amnesty went unanswered. On 16 March 1905 his cheta re-entered Ottoman territory, and soon after he was killed in fighting with Ottoman soldiers near the village of Rajčani.

After World War II, historians of Socialist Macedonia made the Kruševo Republic a forerunner of the new republic, with Karev as its socialist link. His remains were moved to Kruševo in 1953, kept in the museum's storage, and in April 1990 placed in the Ilinden memorial. He is considered a national hero in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, and an equestrian statue of him stands before the Parliament in Skopje.
nikola-pasic: Nikola Pašić was born in Zaječar in eastern Serbia on 18 December 1845. Accounts of his family origins differ: Serbian and Slovenian writers place his ancestors in the Tetovo region or at Veliki Izvor near Zaječar, while some Bulgarian writers claimed a Bulgarian origin, which Serbian authors refuted. He studied engineering in Switzerland and became politically active at the Polytechnical School in Zürich, among Serbian students who later formed the core of the socialist and radical movement, including Svetozar Marković.

Pašić became leader of the movement after Marković died in 1875 and was elected to the National Assembly in 1878. The People's Radical Party, the first systematically organised Serbian party, was formally established in January 1881 with Pašić as its first president. After the Timok Rebellion against King Milan I he was sentenced to death in absentia, fled, and spent six years in Bulgaria until a pardon in 1889. He was then president of the National Assembly and mayor of Belgrade, and became prime minister for the first time in 1891.

After the murder of King Alexander I in 1903 the Radicals won the elections of 4 October and stayed in almost uninterrupted power for fifteen years. Pašić led governments during the customs war with Austria-Hungary that began in 1906 and was a major player in forming the Balkan League. The Balkan Wars almost doubled Serbia's territory. After the Assassination in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, historians disagree about how much he knew beforehand. He led the government in exile on Corfu, where the Corfu Declaration paved the way for a South Slav state.

The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was proclaimed on 1 December 1918, and Pašić was regarded as its de facto prime minister, but Prince-regent Alexander asked Stojan Protić to form the government and Pašić stepped down on 20 December. He represented Serbia at the Paris Peace Conference and was prime minister again from 1921 to July 1924 and from November 1924 to 1926. Both he and Alexander wanted a unitary state, he because he feared a federal one would fall apart and that Serbs could be outvoted. During his last term the kingdom's first constitution was created. He died of a heart attack on 10 December 1926. A square in Belgrade bears his name and holds his statue.
nikola-petkov: Nikola Dimitrov Petkov was born on 8 July 1893, a son of the politician Dimitar Petkov; his brother Petko Petkov was shot dead by an unknown assassin in 1924. He graduated from the 1st Sofia Boys High School in 1910 and studied law and politics at the Sorbonne, returning to serve in a Guards regiment in the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913. He finished his studies in Paris in 1922 and worked at the Bulgarian legation there, but resigned after the coup of 9 June 1923 removed the agrarian government of Aleksandar Stamboliyski, and stayed in France as a journalist.

Back in Bulgaria from 1929, he edited the newspapers Zemya and Zemedelsko zname and published a book on Stamboliyski. After the coup of 19 May 1934 he worked with the democratic parties, among them the Labours' Party, the legal organisation of the banned Bulgarian Communist Party. Elected to the 24th National Assembly, he lost his seat in December 1938 for his anti-fascist activity and was interned at Ivailovgrad. In 1941, after G. M. Dimitrov emigrated, he took over the leadership of his wing of the BZNS, was sent to the Gonda Voda camp, and helped to found the Fatherland Front, work he continued while interned at Svishtov from 1943.

From 9 September 1944 to 26 August 1945 he was minister without portfolio in the first Fatherland Front government. From January 1945 he led the anti-communist United opposition, and from 26 November 1946 he sat in the 6th Great National Assembly. Mark Ethridge, sent by the State Department in 1945 to report on Bulgaria to President Truman, called him the bravest man he had ever known.

The communists treated his defence of parliamentary democracy as counter-revolutionary. His immunity was lifted on 5 June 1947 and he was arrested inside the parliament building, where colleagues who tried to stop it were beaten. At a staged trial with four co-defendants, in which the defence was denied legal representation and the right to present evidence, he was convicted of espionage and sentenced to death on 16 August. He was hanged on 23 September 1947, denied a Christian burial and buried in an unknown grave; a false confession printed afterwards was so plainly faked that it was soon dropped. He was rehabilitated on 15 January 1990.
nikolai-avksentiev: Avksentiev was born into the Russian nobility on 28 November 1878, went to school in Penza and studied law at Moscow University, from which he was expelled in 1899 for organising an uprising. He was one of the Heidelberg SRs, Russian students at the University of Heidelberg in the 1890s, among them Vladimir Zenzinov, who were influenced by neo-Kantian philosophy and Marxism. In the 1905 Revolution he was elected to the Saint Petersburg Soviet, was arrested with its other leaders, defended his party's position at an open trial in 1906 and was exiled to Obdorsk in Siberia, from where he escaped abroad in 1907.

In exile he wrote a doctoral thesis at Heidelberg on the concept of the Superman and edited the party newspaper The Banner of Labor. He led the right wing of the Socialist Revolutionaries, favouring legal forms of struggle and opposing the terrorist tactics of the Left SRs, and in the First World War he belonged to the party's Defencist wing. After the February Revolution he chaired the Executive Committee of Peasants' Deputies and in 1917 served as Minister of the Interior under Alexander Kerensky. He also chaired the Pre-Parliament and was elected to the Constituent Assembly from Penza. Leon Trotsky called him "the complete caricature of a statesman".

After the October Revolution he helped organise the Committee for the Salvation of the Homeland and Revolution and was imprisoned in the Peter and Paul Fortress; he was released, by the account of I. I. Manukhin, through the intervention of Isaac Steinberg, the Socialist Revolutionary People's Commissar of Justice. In March 1918 he became a leader of the Russian Revival Union, and at the end of May the party's Central Committee sent him to Siberia, seen as a base of resistance to the Bolshevik regime. After Alexander Kolchak's coup of 18 November 1918 he was briefly arrested.

He left Russia by way of Vladivostok and settled in Paris, where he was active in émigré circles and in Freemasonry, as he had been earlier in the irregular freemasonic lodge of the Grand Orient of Russia's Peoples. After the Nazi invasion of France he and his wife Berthe escaped to the United States on an emergency visa obtained through the Jewish Labor Committee and the American Federation of Labor. There he published the magazine For Freedom. He died in New York City in March 1943.
nikolai-bobrikov: Nikolay Ivanovich Bobrikov was born in the village of Strelna near Saint Petersburg. His father, Ivan Bobrikov, was a military physician and his mother, Alexandra Seeland, was a Baltic German. He attended the 1st Cadet Corps and became an officer in 1858, later taking a degree at the Nikolay general staff academy.

He served on the staff of the Kazan military district and from 1867 as chief of staff of the 22nd infantry division in Novgorod, and became a colonel in 1869. In 1876 he was sent to Bucharest as Russian military official, and in 1878 he became a major general during the Russo-Turkish War. He was promoted to lieutenant general in 1884, becoming chief of staff of the guard and of the Saint Petersburg military district, and to general of the infantry in 1897. He was an energetic and capable man whose views were strongly Russian nationalist.

Emperor Nicholas II appointed Bobrikov Governor-General of Finland and of the Finnish Military District on 29 August 1898. His Russification programme aimed, among other things, to unify the Finnish army, make Russian the language of the Senate, education and administration, bring the University of Helsinki under tighter control, let Russian citizens hold office in Finland, end the Finnish markka and remove the customs border with Russia.

He was involved in creating the February Manifesto of 1899, which began what Finns remember as the first Years of Oppression and allowed the Diet to be overruled when imperial interest required. Half a million Finns signed a petition asking Nicholas II to revoke it, but the Emperor did not even receive the delegation. In 1900 Bobrikov ordered that correspondence between government offices be conducted in Russian. The Finnish army was abolished in 1901, and conscripts could be made to serve with Russian troops anywhere in the empire; only 42% of the conscripts reported to the first call-up in 1902. In 1903 the Emperor gave him dictatorial powers to dismiss officials and close newspapers.

Bobrikov became very unpopular in Finland as an adamant supporter of curtailing the grand duchy's extensive autonomy. On 16 June 1904 Eugen Schauman, a Finnish nationalist born in Kharkov, shot him three times in Helsinki and then shot himself twice. Schauman died instantly, while Bobrikov, mortally wounded, died in hospital in the early hours of the following morning.
nikolai-bukharin: Nikolai Bukharin was born in Moscow on 27 September (9 October, new style) 1888, the second son of two schoolteachers. His political life began at sixteen, when he took part in student activities at Moscow University during the Russian Revolution of 1905. He joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1906 and became a Bolshevik. In 1910 he was arrested and exiled internally to Onega, but he escaped abroad the next year and met Lenin and Leon Trotsky. He returned to Moscow by way of Japan in May 1917, and on 10 October 1917 he was elected to the Central Committee.

After the October Revolution Bukharin became editor of Pravda. He led the Left Communist faction in 1918 and wrote The ABC of Communism with Yevgeni Preobrazhensky. Initially a supporter of war communism, he backed the New Economic Policy in 1921 and became its chief theorist. After Lenin's death in 1924 he became a full member of the Politburo and allied with Joseph Stalin against Trotsky, Grigory Zinoviev and Lev Kamenev.

It was Bukharin who formulated the thesis of 'socialism in one country' that Stalin put forward in 1924. His slogan to the peasants, 'Enrich yourselves!', and his proposal to reach socialism 'at snail's pace' left him open to attack.

When Stalin turned to rapid industrialisation and agricultural collectivisation, Bukharin was labelled the leader of the Right Opposition. He lost his place in the Comintern and the editorship of Pravda in April 1929 and was expelled from the Politburo on 17 November of that year. Reelected to the Central Committee in 1934, he edited Izvestia and was a principal architect of the 1936 Soviet Constitution.

Bukharin was arrested on 27 February 1937 and tried in the Trial of the Twenty One, from 2 to 13 March 1938, with Alexei Rykov, Genrikh Yagoda and others. The defendants were accused of belonging to a Bloc of Rightists and Trotskyites and of plotting to assassinate Lenin and Stalin, poison Maxim Gorky and partition the Soviet Union. The French author Romain Rolland wrote to Stalin asking for mercy. Bukharin was executed on 15 March 1938 at the Kommunarka shooting ground. His wife, Anna Larina, was sent to a labour camp but lived to see him officially rehabilitated in 1988 under Mikhail Gorbachev.

Lenin had called him a most valuable and major theorist of the party, though he doubted that Bukharin's views were fully Marxist. His works include The Economics of the Transition Period (1920) and, written in prison, Philosophical Arabesques.
nikolai-yezhov: Yezhov was born on 1 May 1895. For most of his life he reported that he was born in Saint Petersburg, but under interrogation he said he had lied to portray himself as a deeply rooted proletarian and that, according to his mother, he was born in Marijampolė, now in Lithuania. The reliability of these confessions has been questioned, as they may have been forced or fabricated. He completed only elementary education, served in the Imperial Russian Army from 1915 to 1917 and fought in the Red Army in the Civil War. From 1929 to 1930 he was Deputy People's Commissar for Agriculture.

In 1934 Yezhov was elected to the Central Committee, and in 1935 he became its secretary and chairman of the Central Commission for Party Control. Stalin used the murder of Sergei Kirov as a pretext for purges and personally chose Yezhov to carry them out; Yezhov oversaw the falsified accusations against Kamenev, Zinoviev and their supporters. He became People's Commissar for Internal Affairs on 26 September 1936, after the dismissal of Genrikh Yagoda, and was welcomed as a well-liked man who had not come from the security organs.

He investigated Yagoda himself and later admitted that he had fabricated a charge of mercury poisoning to raise his authority. In 1937 and 1938 at least 1.3 million people were arrested and 681,692 shot for crimes against the state, and the Gulag population grew by 685,201. Between 50 and 75 per cent of the members of the Supreme Soviet and of the officers of the military were stripped of their positions. Yezhov said that it was better for ten innocent people to suffer than for one spy to get away.

Yezhov was relieved of the NKVD post at his own request on 25 November 1938. His wife Yevgenia died by suicide on 19 November. He was arrested on 10 April 1939. At his closed trial on 2 February 1940 he said his confession had been obtained under torture and admitted that he had purged 14,000 fellow Chekists, but said he was surrounded by enemies of the people. He was shot on 4 February 1940 in a basement built to his own specification, and his ashes were placed in a common grave at the Donskoye Cemetery. The execution remained secret, and as late as 1948 rumours said he was still alive.
nikolai-yudenich: Nikolai Nikolayevich Yudenich was born in Moscow, where his father was a minor court official. He graduated from the Alexandrovsky Military College in 1881 and the General Staff Academy in 1887. From 1892 he served in the Turkestan Military District, took part in the Pamir Expedition in 1894 and became a colonel in 1896. He commanded the 18th Infantry Regiment during the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-1905, was wounded at the Battle of Sandepu and again at the Battle of Mukden, and was promoted to major general at the war's end. He became a lieutenant general in 1912 and in 1913 chief of staff of the Caucasus Military District.

At the start of the First World War Yudenich became chief of staff of the Russian Caucasus Army, which won the Battle of Sarikamish against Enver Pasha. In January 1915 he became General of Infantry and replaced Count Illarion Vorontsov-Dashkov as commander of the Caucasus Campaign. His forces captured Van in May 1915 but withdrew two months later, and the Ottoman 3rd Army reoccupied it in August. In 1916 he won the Battle of Erzurum and the Trebizond Campaign, then beat off a Turkish counterattack at the Battle of Erzincan, where Mustafa Kemal was present. He received the Order of St. George, second degree, the last time the decoration was awarded in the Russian Empire.

After the February Revolution he commanded the Caucasus Front, but in May 1917 the Provisional Government removed him for insubordination, and on Alexander Kerensky's orders he retired. He supported the Kornilov revolt. After the October Revolution he hid from the Bolsheviks and reached Finland in January 1919, where he was proclaimed leader of the White movement in northwestern Russia. Admiral Aleksandr Kolchak's government in Omsk named him commander-in-chief of the forces fighting the Bolsheviks in the Baltic region and northwestern Russia.

In September 1919 Yudenich had about 17,000 troops, 53 guns and six tanks supplied by Britain. In early October he attacked Petrograd, which was lightly defended, and on 19 October his troops reached its outskirts. He failed to secure the vital railway from Moscow, which let the Revolutionary Military Council send large reinforcements, and the Red Army drove his force back into Estonia in November. The Estonian High Command disarmed and interned what remained of the Northwestern Army. He was arrested on 28 January 1920 while trying to escape to Western Europe, and was later released.
He then went into exile in France, where for his remaining thirteen years he played no significant role among the White emigres. He died at Saint-Laurent-du-Var, near Nice, on 5 October 1933.
nikolaus-federmann: Nikolaus Federmann was born in Ulm around 1505. In 1529 the Welser family of Augsburg, who had agreed to explore the territory of Venezuela, sent him to Santo Domingo, and as their agent he brought settlers and miners from Seville to Coro in 1529 and 1530. The governor Ambrosius Ehinger made him his deputy and, on leaving for Hispaniola for his health, handed him charge of the colony on 30 July 1530.

In September 1530, without the authorisation of the Real Audiencia of Santo Domingo, Federmann led 110 foot soldiers, 16 horsemen and 100 natives into the northern basin of the Orinoco in search of the South Sea and a trade route to Asia. He returned to Coro on 17 March 1531 with 5,565 pesos of gold, and Ehinger banished him to Europe for four years. In Augsburg he wrote an account of the journey, the Indianische Historia, published in 1557. A later expedition to La Guajira, in search of pearls and to found a town he meant to call Ulma, failed, and he returned to Coro after reaching Cabo de la Vela in February 1536.

On his last expedition he travelled along the eastern edge of the Eastern Ranges of the Colombian Andes, through the Llanos, following the salt trade route to the Muisca Confederation, most of which Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada had already conquered. Federmann and Sebastián de Belalcázar re-founded Bogotá on 27 April 1539, Quesada's first founding of 1538 having failed the Crown's requirements; most of their soldiers stayed there to reinforce Quesada's troops. In mid May 1539, without having found El Dorado, he left for Cartagena to sail to Spain.

In Europe the Welser family accused Federmann of breaching his contract and keeping back funds, and demanded 100,000 ducats in emeralds and 15,000 in gold. Unable to pay, he spent weeks in prison in Antwerp, then defended himself in Ghent and before the Council of the Indies at Valladolid, accusing the Welser family in turn of evading taxes. By a settlement of 19 October 1541 he gave up his lands in New Granada. Suspected by the Inquisition of being a Lutheran, he died in prison in Valladolid in February 1542.
nikolaus-ludwig-von-zinzendorf: Born in Dresden on 26 May 1700 into the House of Zinzendorf, one of the most prominent noble families of the region, Nikolaus Ludwig was the only son of Count Georg Ludwig von Zinzendorf und Pottendorf by his second wife, Baroness Charlotte Justina von Gersdorff. He was called Ludwig or Brother Ludwig by his intimates. He went to school at the Franke Foundations at Halle, where Pietism was strong, and in 1716 entered the University of Wittenberg to study law.

In 1722 Zinzendorf offered asylum to persecuted wanderers from Moravia and Bohemia and let them build the village of Herrnhut on a corner of his estate of Berthelsdorf. Most of the first refugees were recruited by Christian David. The village drew other persecuted groups, and the mixture of beliefs produced intense conflict. The community signed the Brotherly Agreement and his Manorial Injunctions on 12 May 1727, and a communion service at Berthelsdorf on 13 August 1727, called the Moravian Pentecost, began a new period of spiritual growth. He was consecrated a bishop at Berlin on 20 May 1737.

The community began sending missionaries in 1732, to the enslaved in the Danish-governed West Indies and to the Inuit of Greenland, helped by Zinzendorf's connections at the Danish court. In 1736 accusations from neighbouring nobles and doubts about his orthodoxy led to his banishment from Saxony, and he spent years in exile and travel as the Pilgrim Count. In 1739 he left Europe to visit the mission on Saint Thomas, and in 1741 he visited Pennsylvania, where he met Benjamin Franklin and the leaders of the Iroquois. With the help of Conrad Weiser he reached agreements for the free movement of Moravian missionaries.

Zinzendorf saw the renewed community as a spark for the renewal of all denominations, not as a new church. He organised its people into communal families, called choirs, based on age, marital status and gender. He taught that decisions on interpreting Scripture were to be made communally and that the Gemeinde, not the ecclesiastical and political institution, was the true Church.

He wrote many hymns, of which the best known is Jesus, Thy blood and righteousness. His son Christian Renatus, whom he had hoped to make his successor, died in 1752 of tuberculosis, and Zinzendorf himself died on 9 May 1760. The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America commemorates him on that day as a hymnwriter and a renewer of the church.
nikolay-chkheidze: Nikoloz Chkheidze, commonly known as Karlo Chkheidze, was born on 21 March 1864 into the aristocratic House of Chkheidze at Puti in the Kutais Governorate, in what is now the Zestaponi Municipality of the Imereti province of Georgia. He married Alexandra Taganova, and they had four children, one of whom accompanied him in exile. In 1892 he became a founder, with Egnate Ninoshvili, Silibistro Jibladze, Noe Zhordania and his brother Kalenike Chkheidze, of the first Georgian Social-Democratic group, Mesame Dasi, the Third Group. In the 1890s he promoted the Social Democratic movement in Georgia and later became a leading Social Democrat in the Russian Empire.

From 1907 to 1917 Chkheidze sat in the Russian State Duma for the Tiflis Governorate and gained popularity as a spokesman for the Menshevik faction of the Russian Social Democratic Party. In the revolution of 1917 he became Menshevik president of the Executive Committee, and then chairman, of the Petrograd Soviet. He failed to prevent the rise of Bolshevism and refused a post in the Provisional Government, though he supported its policies, advocated revolutionary defencism and voted to continue the war against the German Empire.

He was in Georgia when the Bolsheviks seized power in October 1917, and he stayed there. On 23 February 1918 he became leader of the Transcaucasian Federation in Tiflis, which was dissolved some months later. After the Act of Independence of Georgia was adopted on 26 May 1918, he was elected chairman of the National Council. In February 1919 he was elected to the Constituent Assembly, and on 12 March its president. There he chaired the Georgian delegation to the Versailles Conference and unsuccessfully proposed to Georges Clemenceau and David Lloyd George a French or British protectorate over Georgia's foreign affairs and defence. He oversaw the writing of the Constitution by Razhden Arsenidze and fourteen other deputies.

When the Red Army invaded Georgia in March 1921, Chkheidze fled with his family to France by way of Constantinople. In 1923 and 1924, as part of the Social Democratic Labour Party of Georgia in exile, he opposed a national uprising, arguing with Irakli Tsereteli, Datiko Sharashidze and Kale Kavtaradze in a group called Oppozitsia that the Red Army and Cheka were too strong and the unarmed Georgian people too weak. After the August Uprising of 1924, 10,000 Georgians were executed and between 50,000 and 100,000 deported to Siberia or Central Asia. Chkheidze died by suicide on 13 June 1926 at his official residence in Leuville-sur-Orge and was buried at the Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris.
nikortsminda-cathedral: Nikortsminda Cathedral, a Georgian Orthodox church in the Racha region, was built in 1010-1014 during the reign of Bagrat III of Georgia. It was repaired in 1534 by King Bagrat III of Imereti, and a three-storied bell-tower beside it was built in the second half of the 19th century. The frescoes inside date from the 17th century. The cathedral was damaged in the 1991 Racha earthquake and restored afterwards.

Stylistically the cathedral reflects the Georgian cross-dome type of architecture, following a six-conch-within-rectangle plan, with a short-armed rectangular cross plan and a short segment to the west. The rectangular western apse has adjoining side chapels. Five interior apses support a massive dome, which rests upon half-pillar-shaped apse projections and is lit by the twelve windows of its drum, framed by unbroken arcatures and ornamented architraves. The altar apse bema and the western passage enlarge the interior space, and spherical pendentives carry the transition from the drum to the dome circle. The twelve windows light the interior abundantly.

The facades are covered with smoothly hewn stone and decorated with unbroken arcatures and rich ornament, including multiple-figured narrative reliefs. These show episodes such as the Transfiguration, the Judgment Day and the Ascension of the Cross, figures of Saint George and Saint Theodore, and real and mythic animals, forming one premeditated programme. The interior also has ornamental sculptural reliefs, which reflect the mastery of late-medieval Georgian ecclesiastical art. Its decoration is counted among the most beautiful of all Georgian churches, since several different styles can be seen. The cathedral is on the Tentative List for status as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
nikos-kazantzakis: Nikos Kazantzakis was born in Kandiye, now Heraklion, in Crete, on 18 February 1883 (Old Style), according to family records; the census of Heraklion listed his birth year as 1881, a discrepancy he settled himself in one of his letters. Crete was then still under Ottoman rule. From 1902 to 1906 he studied law at the University of Athens, writing a thesis on Friedrich Nietzsche and the philosophy of right and the state. In 1907 he went to the Sorbonne to study philosophy and fell under the spell of Henri Bergson. His first published work, in 1906, was the narrative Serpent and Lily, signed with the pen name Karma Nirvami.

In Berlin, where the political situation was explosive, Kazantzakis discovered communism and admired Lenin. He never became a committed communist, and after visiting the Soviet Union and witnessing the rise of Stalin he became disillusioned with Soviet-style communism. In 1926 he interviewed Miguel Primo de Rivera and Benito Mussolini as a journalist. During the Second World War he was in Athens, where he and Ioannis Kakridis translated the Iliad. In 1945 he led a small party on the non-communist left and entered the Greek government as Minister without Portfolio, resigning the next year. He headed the UNESCO Bureau of Translations in 1946 and 1947, then left to write, and produced most of his literary output in the last ten years of his life.

He began The Odyssey: A Modern Sequel in 1924 and completed it in 1938. Divided into 24 rhapsodies, it follows Odysseus on a final journey after Homer's poem. Critics were split: some praised it as an unprecedented epic, many viewed it as a hybristic act. His novels appeared mainly between 1940 and 1961: Zorba the Greek in 1946, Christ Recrucified in 1948, Captain Michalis, The Last Temptation of Christ in 1955 and Report to Greco in 1961. He wrote in Demotic Greek, to show that the spoken language could produce literature.

Many Orthodox clergy condemned his work, and a campaign was started to excommunicate him; the top leadership of the Church rejected it. He lost the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature to Albert Camus by a single vote, and was nominated in nine different years. Suffering from leukaemia, he set out late in 1957 on a last trip to China and Japan. He was taken ill, transported to Copenhagen and then to Freiburg, where he died on 26 October 1957, aged 74. He is buried on the Martinengo Bastion of the Walls of Heraklion; his epitaph reads "I hope for nothing. I fear nothing. I am free." He remains the most translated Greek author worldwide.
niksar: Niksar is the seat of Niksar District in Tokat Province, at an average altitude of 350 metres. It lies between the Canik Mountains to the north and Dönek Mountain to the south, in the Niksar Lowland, one of the most important lowlands of the Black Sea Region. Tributaries of the Kelkit River irrigate its land, about 32 per cent of which is farmed. The town is known for walnuts, tomato paste and grape leaves, the main ingredient of dolma. It has always counted as an important place in Anatolia because of its location, climate and productive farmland.

The town has been ruled by Hittite, Persian, Greek, Pontic, Roman, Byzantine, Danishmend, Seljuk and Ottoman empires. In the Hellenistic period it was called Cabira and was a favourite residence of Mithridates VI, who built a palace there, and later of King Polemon I and his successors.

The Battle of Cabira of the Third Mithridatic War was fought there in 72 or 71 BCE, and the city passed to the Romans. Pompey made it a city and named it Diopolis, and Pythodoris, widow of Polemon, made it her capital under the name Sebaste. It was called Neocaesarea in Roman times, perhaps from the reign of Tiberius, judging by its coins. An earthquake destroyed it in 344.

In the Middle Ages Muslims and Christians disputed it. After the Battle of Manzikert it changed hands several times: Seljuk commanders took it, the Byzantines retook it, and for a time it belonged to the Norman mercenary Roussel de Bailleul, who held it until 1075. Danishmend Gazi, founder of the Danishmend dynasty, then conquered it and made it his capital, and as Niksar it became a centre of science and culture.

His mausoleum stands in a large cemetery just outside the town. Bohemond I of Taranto was held prisoner in Niksar castle from 1100 to 1103. Later it was governed by the Seljuks of Rum, the Eretnids and the Beylik of Tacettin. After Kadı Burhanettin was killed, Süleyman Çelebi took it for the Ottomans under Bayezid I.

Neocaesarea was a bishopric of the late Roman province of Pontus Polemoniacus and the civil and religious metropolis of Pontus. About 240 Gregory Thaumaturgus became its bishop, and according to Gregory of Nyssa the city then had only seventeen Christians and at his death in 270 only seventeen pagans. A council met there around 315. Paul of Neocaesarea and Thomas, a martyr of the 9th century, were also bishops. The Annuario Pontificio lists it as a titular see, Neocaesarea in Ponto. Niksar was added to Turkey's World Heritage tentative list in 2018.
niksic: Nikšić lies at the centre of the Nikšić field, a karst plain of 48 square kilometres at an elevation of 640 metres, and at the foot of Trebjesa hill. The plain is ringed by rocky mountains, a typical landscape of western Montenegro. The Zeta river rises there and flowed over the plain in frequent floods until the Perućica hydroelectric power plant was built in 1960, which also created three artificial lakes near the city: Krupac, Slano and Vrtac.

In antiquity the area was settled by the Illyrian tribe of the Endirudini, who appear among the tribes that surrendered to Octavian in 33 BCE, and the Roman Empire built a military camp there. The Ostrogothic fortress that followed it was called Anagastum, which became the Slavic Onogošt, the name of a town and county in the Middle Ages. In 1373 Onogošt passed to the Kingdom of Bosnia and later came under the Kosača family. It then belonged to the Ottoman Empire for more than four hundred years as part of the province of Herzegovina, and in its last decades served as a significant fortified stronghold. In 1807 forces under Petar I Petrović-Njegoš with 1,000 Russian troops tried to take it, but the Ottomans prevailed.

On 18 July 1876 Montenegro defeated Ottoman forces at the Battle of Vučji Do, on the western edge of the municipality. On 27 August 1877 the Montenegrin army under Mašo Vrbica took the town after a siege of 47 days. The English archaeologist Arthur Evans, who witnessed the talks that followed, recorded that Prince Nikola promised the Muslim citizens who stayed freedom of religion and the keeping of their property. The Treaty of Berlin confirmed the town as part of the Principality of Montenegro, and in 1883 the prince commissioned the Croatian architect Josip Slade to draw its first urban plan.

Nikšić is the second-largest city of Montenegro, with an urban population of 66,700 in the 2023 census, and its municipality is the largest in area in the country. Its streets still follow Slade's plan, radiating from the central square in a half spider-web pattern; very little of the Ottoman architecture remains. After the Second World War the city became the heart of Montenegrin industry, with steel and iron works, bauxite mines, a brewery and wood processing, and its population grew tenfold. The Boris Kidrič metal works employed over 6,500 workers by 1985. The city has three faculties of the University of Montenegro and a cultural centre in King Nikola's former palace.
nile: The Nile is 7,088 km long and flows north through north-east Africa into the Mediterranean Sea. The White Nile, the longer tributary, begins near Lake Victoria; the Blue Nile begins near Lake Tana in Ethiopia and contributes over twice the water volume of the White Nile. They meet at Khartoum, and the river then flows through the Nubian Desert to Cairo and empties near Alexandria into a large delta. The Blue Nile floods between July and October because of summer monsoon rains. The Nile has followed its present course for about 15,000 years.

When the climate of the eastern Sahara became drier around 3,900 BCE, herding peoples had to migrate to the Nile valley to survive, which was the origin of the Nubian cultures and of Ancient Egyptian civilization. The annual flood deposited silt along the banks and supported crops in the desert, though droughts that caused crop failures also brought famine. Irrigation, flood prediction and taxation called for new mathematical and administrative skills. South of the second cataract lay Nubia, home of the Kerma culture and the Kushite Empire. European explorations around Lake Victoria in the late 19th century located the river's source.

After British rule of Egypt began in 1882, the Aswan Low Dam was completed in 1902. Egypt and Sudan divided the river's flow by agreements of 1929 and 1959, and Egypt completed the Aswan High Dam in 1970. The basin spans eleven countries.
nile-delta: The Nile Delta is formed in Lower Egypt where the Nile spreads out and drains into the Mediterranean Sea. It runs from Alexandria in the west to Port Said in the east, covering some 240 kilometres of coastline, and is about 160 kilometres long from north to south, beginning at Cairo. It is called an arcuate delta, since seen from above it resembles a triangle or a flower. Aristotle speculated that it had been built up for agriculture, as the region of Egypt dried.

Today the Nile divides into two main distributaries, the Damietta and the Rosetta, which reach the sea at port cities of the same names. Ptolemy and other ancient writers recorded seven branches, from the Pelusiac in the east to the Canopic in the west. Modern Egyptologists think that five main branches existed at one time in the Pharaonic era. Three of them have dried up over the centuries through flood control, silting and changing relief, and only the Damietta and the Rosetta survive.

People have lived in the delta for thousands of years, and it has been intensively farmed for at least the past five thousand. It was a major part of Lower Egypt, and many archaeological sites lie in and around it, among them Avaris, Bubastis, Mendes, Sais, Tanis and Pelusium. The Rosetta Stone was found in the delta in 1799 in the port city of Rosetta. The sunken city of Heracleion, off the coast, has yielded a small Greek temple, granite columns and bronze coins from the reign of Ptolemy II.

The Butic Canal was an ancient east-west watercourse of the delta, with a reconstructed length of about 185 to 200 kilometres, which would make it the longest canal in Egypt. The earliest, indirect, reference is in Flavius Josephus, in events around 70 CE. The geographer Ptolemy of the 2nd century CE described it as spanning the whole width of the delta. According to Schiestl, the eastern part is much better attested and probably much older, while the western part was completed only in Roman times.

The delta is a rich agricultural region, with topsoil as much as 21 metres deep. It once flooded each year, but this ended after the Aswan Dam was completed in 1970. The delta no longer receives nutrients and sediments from upstream, so its soils have become poorer and large amounts of fertiliser are used. About 70 million people live in the delta region, and Cairo is its largest city. Other large cities include Alexandria, Port Said, Mansura, Tanta and Zagazig. The outer edges of the delta are eroding, and its low-lying land is vulnerable to rising sea level and subsidence.
nimba-range: The Nimba Range forms the southern end of the Guinea Highlands, beside the Toura Mountains. It is a narrow ridge about 40 km long running from north-east to south-west, made mostly of Precambrian granite and quartzite holding deposits of iron ore. The name Mount Nimba may mean either Mount Richard-Molard, the highest peak, or the whole range; other peaks, all in Guinea, include Grand Rochers at 1,694 m and Mont Sempéré at 1,682 m. About fifty springs rise in it, among them the sources of the Cavally, Cestos and Sassandra rivers.

About 3,000 mm of rain falls on the highest ground and 700 to 1,200 mm lower down, most of it between May and October. Above 600 m lie Guinean montane forests: lower montane forest, cloud forest above 900 m dominated by the Guinea plum, and grassland and montane savanna on the summits. Below 600 m they give way to Western Guinean lowland forest, and the range is surrounded by forest-savanna mosaic and savanna.

The range is home to more than 2000 species of vascular plants, 317 of vertebrates, 107 of them mammals, and more than 2,500 of invertebrates. Its endemic animals include the Nimba viviparous toad, Lamotte's roundleaf bat, Myotis nimbaensis and the Nimba otter shrew, and its western chimpanzees use stones as tools. In 1943 the colonial government set up a Strict Nature Reserve in the Ivory Coast part of the range and extended it into Guinea the following year. The area stayed protected after Guinea and Ivory Coast became independent, and UNESCO declared Mount Nimba a biosphere reserve in 1980 and a World Heritage Site shortly afterwards.

The Mount Nimba Strict Nature Reserve of Guinea and Ivory Coast covers much of the range, which BirdLife International lists as an Important Bird Area. Because its rapids and waterfalls isolate streams and have favoured the rise of new species, the WWF counts it as a distinct freshwater ecoregion, with endemic fish, frogs and the Nimba stream crab. Mining of its high-grade iron ore is the main threat to its landforms and wildlife.
nimes: Nîmes lies where the alluvial plain of the Vistrenque meets the hills of Mont Duplan, Montaury and Mont Cavalier, between the Mediterranean and the Cévennes. A Neolithic site at Serre Paradis shows semi-nomadic cultivators there between 4000 and 3500 BCE, and the menhir of Courbessac, about 2500 BCE, is considered the oldest monument in the city. Mont Cavalier was the site of the early oppidum, whose wall of the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE had a dry-stone tower that was later incorporated into the Tour Magne. The god Nemausus, a water deity, gave his name to the city, which had a healing spring.

The Roman province of Gallia Transalpina was established in 121 BCE, and from 118 BCE the Via Domitia, linking Italy with Hispania, was built through the later site of the city. Nîmes became the Roman colony Colonia Nemausus sometime before 28 BCE, and veterans of Julius Caesar's legions received land on its plain. Augustus launched a building programme that included a ring of ramparts 6 kilometres long with 14 towers, of which the Porte d'Auguste and the Porte de France remain. The Maison Carrée dates from the late 1st century BCE and was dedicated to Roma and Augustus. The amphitheatre, from the end of the 2nd century, was one of the largest in the Empire. Emperor Constantine gave it baths.

The Visigoths took the city in 472. The Umayyads held it by 725, and in 736 and 737 Charles Martel largely destroyed it, including the amphitheatre. Pepin the Short captured it in 752. Local authorities then settled in the amphitheatre's ruins, and a Jewish community, which had grown in the 7th century, built the first documented synagogue in 1089. After Raymond VII of Toulouse's last effort, Saint Louis brought Nîmes under the crown. It became a Protestant stronghold and suffered repression and episodes such as the Michelade massacre until the middle of the 17th century. Then it prospered, and its population grew from 21,000 to 50,000.

Nîmes is the prefecture of the Gard department in Occitanie and has 148,561 inhabitants (2019). Its monuments include the Arena, the Maison Carrée, the Tour Magne and the Pont du Gard, which lies 20 kilometres to the north-east and carried the aqueduct across the river Gard. Its Roman heritage has earned it the name of the French Rome.
nimlot-of-hermopolis: Nimlot ruled Hermopolis during the 25th Dynasty. He may have been a son of King Osorkon III of the 23rd Dynasty, and it is likely that this king installed him as governor of Hermopolis around 754 BCE. Around 749 BCE he proclaimed himself king. His wife Nestanetmeh bore the title of queen.

When the Kushite king Piye campaigned to conquer Middle and Lower Egypt, around 729–728 BCE, Nimlot was at first his ally or vassal. He then changed sides and joined the coalition led by Tefnakht. Piye marched north at once and besieged Hermopolis until Nimlot capitulated. As compensation for his defection Nimlot had to hand over rich tribute, including a horse and a precious sistrum, and Piye, a great lover of horses, scolded him harshly for the poor state of his stables.

Nimlot's submission turned the campaign in Piye's favour, and the Kushite king went on to defeat Tefnakht's coalition. On Piye's Victory stele, Nimlot is one of four kings shown subdued, with Iuput II of Leontopolis, Osorkon IV of Tanis and Peftjauawybast of Herakleopolis. He alone stands rather than kneels, since Piye chose him as his interlocutor, while the others were held impure because they ate fish. Before returning south Piye confirmed Nimlot in his office.

Around 725 BCE Djehutyemhat succeeded him. He is distinct from a later ruler of Hermopolis known as Nimlot E, called Lamintu in Akkadian, who held the city when the Assyrians under Ashurbanipal invaded Egypt in 667/666 BCE.
nimrud: Nimrud lies in Iraq about 30 kilometres south of Mosul, in the Nineveh Plains of Upper Mesopotamia, some 10 kilometres north of the meeting of the Tigris and its tributary the Great Zab. The city covered about 360 hectares. Its Assyrian name was Kalhu, and its biblical name was Calah. The name Nimrud was recorded by Carsten Niebuhr in the mid-18th century, and it spread widely when 19th-century scholars linked the site with Nimrod of Genesis.

Calah stood on a commercial route between Ashur and Nineveh. It began as a trading settlement founded under Shalmaneser I, but the site had fallen into disrepair when Ashurnasirpal II chose it as his capital. He cleared the ruins and built an entirely new city, with walls 7.5 kilometres long, temples, royal offices, a palace meant to surpass all earlier ones, botanical gardens of foreign plants and a zoo. His inscriptions give no reason for the move; scholars suggest that Ashur had little room left, that Calah was more central, or that he sought independence from Ashur's great families. A stele describes a ten-day celebration in 864 BCE for 69,574 guests.

Shalmaneser III built a palace of more than 200 rooms and the Great Ziggurat. Tiglath-Pileser III carried out major building and introduced Eastern Aramaic as the empire's common language. Calah was the imperial capital from 879 to 706 BCE, when Sargon II moved the government to Dur-Sharrukin; Sennacherib later moved it to Nineveh. Assyrian kings were buried at Ashur, but their queens lay at Calah. The city remained a major centre and royal residence until it was largely destroyed during the Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire, between 626 and 609 BCE.

Austen Henry Layard began excavating Nimrud in 1845, and he shipped two colossal winged guardian figures to the British Museum in 1847.
