Max Mallowan's team resumed work in 1949 and found the 244 Nimrud Letters. In 1988 the Iraqi Department of Antiquities found four queens' tombs. The excavations revealed bas-reliefs, ivories, a well-preserved statue of Ashurnasirpal II and the palaces of Ashurnasirpal II, Shalmaneser III and Tiglath-Pileser III. Objects from the site are held in at least 76 museums worldwide. In 2015 much of the excavated remains were destroyed, and reconstruction work has followed.
nine-years-war: The Treaty of Nijmegen of 1678 ended the Franco-Dutch War at the high point of Louis XIV's expansion. Over the following years he used courts at Metz, Besançon and Breisach, which usually found in his favour, to claim territory under the vague wording of earlier treaties, and by 1682 he had secured the whole of Alsace except Strasbourg. The Truce of Ratisbon of 1684 guaranteed these borders for twenty years. After 1685 his revocation of the Edict of Nantes sent as many as 200,000 Huguenots into exile and helped William of Orange build his long-sought alliance against France.

In September 1688 Louis led an army across the Rhine to press the Holy Roman Empire into accepting his claims. Philippsburg fell on 30 October and Mannheim capitulated on 11 November. That month the Glorious Revolution brought England's resources to William. James II, sheltered by Louis, landed in Ireland on 12 March 1689 with 6,000 French troops, but his forces could not take Derry. On 12 May 1689 the Dutch and the Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I signed an offensive compact in Vienna, the core of the Grand Alliance.

The main fighting took place around France's borders: in the Spanish Netherlands, the Rhineland, Savoy and Catalonia. Marshal Luxembourg defeated the Prince of Waldeck at the Battle of Fleurus on 1 July 1690, but the victory brought little benefit. The war was dominated by sieges and the defence of fortresses, and by 1695 field armies had grown to nearly 100,000 men, which drove the Maritime Powers into a fiscal crisis while France struggled under a shattered economy. The conflict spread overseas as King William's War in North America, and in 1693 the Dutch took Pondichéry in India. Secret talks began in 1695, and by 1696 the main belligerents were financially exhausted.

The peace conference opened in May 1697 at William III's palace at Ryswick near The Hague, and the settlement was largely worked out through private talks between Marshal Boufflers and William Bentinck, the Earl of Portland. France kept the whole of Alsace but gave up Lorraine and its gains on the right bank of the Rhine, which were restored to their rulers. Louis XIV recognised William III as king of England. The Dutch gained barrier fortresses in the Spanish Netherlands and a favourable commercial treaty, and Spain regained Luxembourg and other territories.

Both sides saw the peace as a pause, since it did not settle who would succeed the childless Charles II of Spain, a question that had dominated European politics for over thirty years. It led to the War of the Spanish Succession in 1701.
nine-years-war-ireland: The Kingdom of Ireland was established as an English client state in 1542, and by the early 1590s the English state's control had spread from the Pale over much of the island. The execution of Gaelic lords, the pillaging of settlements by appointed sheriffs and the persecution of Catholics bred resentment among the Gaelic nobility. In 1591 the Lord Deputy Fitzwilliam had The MacMahon hanged and his lordship in Monaghan divided for resisting an English sheriff. Hugh O'Neill, granted the earldom of Tyrone in 1585, could arm and feed over 8,000 men with Spanish aid, and from 1591 Hugh Roe O'Donnell had been in contact with Philip II of Spain.

The war is generally dated from May 1593, when Hugh Maguire resisted the appointment of Humphrey Willis as sheriff of Fermanagh. O'Neill at first helped the English, hoping to be made Lord President of Ulster, but when the post was marked for his enemy Henry Bagenal he joined the rising openly in February 1595 with an attack on the Blackwater Fort. After a confederate victory at the Battle of Clontibret, up to 2,000 English troops were killed at the Battle of the Yellow Ford in 1598, among them Bagenal, the heaviest English defeat in Ireland to that time. Risings followed across the country, and in Munster as many as 9,000 men rebelled.

Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex, arrived in 1599 with over 17,000 troops but achieved little. His successor, Lord Mountjoy, landed forces at Derry and Carrickfergus, whose commanders devastated the countryside to bring famine and killed civilians at random. After the rout at Kinsale on 5/6 January 1602, Hugh Roe O'Donnell left for Spain to plead for another landing and died of a fever in 1602. O'Neill held out in the forests of Tír Eoghain until 30 March 1603, when he signed the Treaty of Mellifont; the last holdout, West Breifne, fell on 25 April 1603.

James I granted the Ulster chiefs pardons and their estates on condition that they give up their Irish titles and private armies, for England could no longer afford the war. Irish sources claimed that as many as 60,000 people died in the Ulster famine of 1602–03 alone, and at least 30,000 English soldiers died in Ireland, mainly of disease; the total was certainly at least 100,000. It was the largest and costliest conflict England fought in the Elizabethan era. After the lords left in 1607, their lands were confiscated in 1608.
nineteenth-amendment-to-the-united-state: The Constitution of 1789 left voter qualifications for the House of Representatives to the states. Women had voted in several colonies before 1776, but after independence every state except New Jersey adopted a constitution denying them the vote, and New Jersey withdrew it in 1807. In 1869 two rival organisations formed: the National Woman Suffrage Association under Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony, which lobbied Congress, and the American Woman Suffrage Association under Lucy Stone, which worked state by state.

From the 1890s Wyoming, Colorado and Idaho gave women the vote, and from 1910 seven more western states followed. Alice Paul and Lucy Burns revived the national campaign, organising a parade of more than 5,000 people in Washington on 3 March 1913, the day before Woodrow Wilson's inauguration, and then founded the Congressional Union. African-American suffragists such as Mary Church Terrell and Ida B. Wells-Barnett often linked the vote to civil rights.

The First World War changed the argument. Carrie Chapman Catt's National American Woman Suffrage Association supported the war effort and argued that women's service deserved the vote, while Paul's National Woman's Party picketed the White House from 1917 and pointed to the contradiction of fighting for democracy abroad while restricting it at home. Wilson declared his support in 1918 and appealed to the Senate in person, but on 30 September 1918 the proposal fell two votes short. The House passed the amendment on 21 May 1919 and the Senate on 4 June 1919.

Illinois, Wisconsin and Michigan ratified within days, on 10 June 1919. The thirty-sixth state ratification, which secured adoption, came on 18 August 1920, and the adoption was certified on 26 August 1920. The Supreme Court unanimously upheld the amendment in Leser v. Garnett.

The amendment enfranchised about 26 million women in time for the 1920 presidential election. The powerful women's voting bloc that politicians had feared did not appear for decades, but the fear helped pass the Sheppard-Towner Maternity and Infancy Protection Act of 1921. The amendment did not fully enfranchise African American, Asian American, Hispanic American and Native American women, since state laws and constitutions kept many from voting.
Catt and Emma Smith DeVoe helped found the League of Women Voters in 1920, and Paul's party began work on the Equal Rights Amendment, introduced in every session of Congress from 1921 to 1971.
ninety-five-theses: In the Catholic Church of Luther's day, indulgences lessened the temporal punishment due for sins, which would otherwise be satisfied in purgatory. Clergy profited from selling them, and the pope sanctioned the sales for a fee. In 1515 Pope Leo X granted a plenary indulgence to finance the building of St Peter's Basilica in Rome, and Johann Tetzel was commissioned to preach it in 1517.

Luther, professor of moral theology at Wittenberg, had preached against the abuse of indulgences as early as 1514. He grew especially concerned when parishioners returned from buying Tetzel's indulgences and said they no longer needed to repent. He wrote the Theses in the autumn of 1517.

The first thesis states that when Christ said Repent, he willed the whole life of believers to be one of repentance. Luther treats repentance as an inner struggle with sin and not merely sacramental confession. Theses 5 to 7 say that the pope can release people only from punishments he has himself imposed, not from the guilt of sin. Theses 41 to 47 argue that indulgences discourage works of mercy: giving to the poor is incomparably more important than buying one.

Theses 56 to 66 attack the doctrine of the treasury of merit on which indulgences rest, and Luther says the true treasure of the church is the gospel of Jesus Christ. In the final theses he sets out difficult questions that laypeople were asking, such as why the pope does not simply empty purgatory. The Theses are framed as propositions for debate, and Luther invited scholars from other cities to take part, though there is no evidence that such a debate was held.

On 31 October 1517 Luther sent the Theses with a letter to Archbishop Albert of Brandenburg, under whose authority the indulgences were sold. Philip Melanchthon later said that Luther posted them on the door of All Saints' Church in Wittenberg, but this conflicts with several of Luther's own statements, and he may not have posted them at all. They were soon copied and printed, and several hundred copies of the Latin text were printed in Germany in 1517.

Rome treated Luther as a threat. In 1518 Tetzel had Konrad Wimpina write 106 theses against him, and in October Thomas Cajetan examined him at Augsburg. Luther was excommunicated in 1521. The controversy was the beginning of the Reformation. From 1527 31 October was kept as its beginning, and in 1668 it became Reformation Day, a holiday in Electoral Saxony.
nineveh: The remains of Nineveh stand on a level part of the plain on the east bank of the Tigris, at its junction with the Khosr River. A fortification wall of about 12 km encloses an area of 750 hectares. The Khosr divides the site: to the north lies Tell Kuyunjiq, with the acropolis, and to the south Tell Nabī Yūnus, the mound of the Prophet Jonah, where a shrine and a palace of Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal lie. Roughly a third of the ruins is overlaid by the eastern suburbs of Mosul.

Nineveh was founded as early as 6000 BCE, in the late Neolithic. By the Ubaid period it was a proto-city, growing to 40 hectares between 4500 and 4000 BCE, and in the Uruk period it was a trade colony of Uruk at the highest navigable point on the Tigris. In the early 2nd millennium BCE it came under Shamshi-Adad I and became a centre of worship of Ishtar. The Assyrian king Ashur-uballit I reclaimed it in 1365 BCE from Mitanni.

Under the Neo-Assyrian kings, from Ashurnasirpal II onward, temples and palaces multiplied. Sennacherib made it a truly influential city around 700 BCE, laying out new streets and squares and building the South West Palace, about 503 by 242 metres with at least 80 rooms, many lined with sculpture. Nineveh was then the largest city in the world for about fifty years, until a coalition of Assyria's former subject peoples, including the Babylonians, Medes and Scythians, sacked it in 612 BCE after a bitter civil war.

The city never again served as a political or administrative centre. It was resettled under the Seleucid Empire, and by 554 it was a bishopric of the Church of the East. After the Arab conquest of 641, Mosul eclipsed it, and it was mostly abandoned by the 14th century after Timur's massacres and dispersal of Assyrian Christians.

Carsten Niebuhr recorded the site's location on the Danish expedition of 1761 to 1767, and Claudius Rich explored it in 1820. In 1842 Paul-Émile Botta, the French consul at Mosul, began digging the mounds; his workers came upon Sargon II's palace at Khorsabad, about 20 km away. Large numbers of Assyrian sculptures from Nineveh are now in museums around the world.
Nineveh also appears in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis, in the book of Nahum, which denounces it, and in the stories of Jonah and Tobit. The shrine of Jonah on Nabī Yūnus was destroyed in 2014.
ning-an: Ning'an is a county-level city in the south-east of Heilongjiang province, on the Mudanjiang River, about 20 km south-west of Mudanjiang and bordering Jilin province to the south. The terrain is largely hilly, and the Changbai Mountains run through it. Upstream lies Lake Jingpo, a natural reservoir formed by volcanic eruptions about 10,000 years ago. The Manchu name Ningguta means six, because the town was once guarded by six grandsons of Möngke Temür.

Shangjing Longquanfu, one of the capitals of the Balhae kingdom between 756 and 785 and between 793 and 926, lay within the modern city, near Dongjingcheng and Bohai. In the early Qing, Ningguta was one of the most important towns in Manchuria beyond the Willow Palisade. The Hurka River valley was the traditional homeland of the Jianzhou Jurchens, later called Manchus, and after the conquest of China in 1644 the Qing ruling family continued to regard the area as its place of origin.

In 1652 the Qing sent 2000 horsemen under Sarhuda to set up the first garrison beyond the palisade. In 1658 Sarhuda, with a fleet of several dozen ships and a Korean force under General Shin Ryu, sailed down the Hurka and the Sungari to defeat the smaller fleet of the Cossack Onufriy Stepanov. In 1662 the post became the Ningguta Military Governor, with Sarhuda's son Bahai the first holder. The early fortress stood about 50 km to the north-west, on the Hailang River, and in 1676 the military governor moved to Jilin City.

Ningguta remained important in the 18th and 19th centuries, when its deputy lieutenant-general was the top official for the region east to the Sea of Japan, home to Tungusic peoples such as the Nanais. Jesuits who visited in 1709 found a centre of trade in ginseng and sable pelts. Convicts were sent to the area from 1660, and anti-Qing rebels captured in southern China from 1661, so that villages around the town held exiled Han Chinese and Manchus.
The area became Ning'an Fu in May 1910 and Ning'an County in March 1913, and in 1993 the county was upgraded to a county-level city under Mudanjiang. In 2004 its reported population was 440,000.
ningbo: Ningbo is a sub-provincial city in the north-east of Zhejiang. Hangzhou Bay separates it from Shanghai to the north, Zhoushan and the East China Sea lie to the east, and Shaoxing and Taizhou border it on the west and south. Its administered area includes 531 islands and 1,562 kilometres of coastline. The name combines ning, meaning serene, with bo, meaning wave. Its abbreviation, Yong, comes from Yong Hill and the Yong River that flows through the city.

The earliest relics of human activity found in the city's area come from the Jingtou Mountain site in Yuyao, dating to 6300 BCE, and show early consumption of seafood and rice. Sites of the Hemudu culture have yielded cultivated rice, farming tools, remains of dry-fence buildings and domestic livestock. Ningbo was known as a trade city on the Silk Road at least two thousand years ago, and the Ayuwang Temple near it is one of the nineteen Ashokan stupa sites in China.

From the Tang dynasty Ningbo was an important commercial port. In the Song period, when it was called Mingzhou or Siming, Arab traders lived there in separate quarters, and a Jewish community was large enough that, after a flood destroyed Torah scrolls at Kaifeng in 1642, the Jews of Ningbo sent a replacement. European writers long knew the city as Liampó. The Portuguese began trading there around 1522 and had a sizable community by 1542, probably on nearby islands such as Shuangyu. They raided Chinese ports and enslaved people, and were driven out in 1548.

Ningbo was one of the five treaty ports opened by the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842. British forces took the walled city briefly in the First Opium War and repulsed a Chinese counter-attack on 10 March 1842. In 1861 the Taiping forces took the city almost unopposed and held it for six months. In 1940 Japanese aircraft dropped ceramic bombs filled with plague-bearing fleas on Ningbo, and the bacteriologist Huang Ketai reported at least 109 deaths from plague in November and December.

Ningbo had a population of 9.4 million at the 2020 census. The port of Ningbo-Zhoushan is among the largest in the world by cargo. Its dialect belongs to Wu Chinese, and the city is known for tangyuan, stuffed rice-flour dumplings, and for seafood. The Hemudu site and museum, Moon Lake Park, excavated in 636, and the Ningbo Museum are among its sights. In 2016 the governments of China, Japan and Korea named it a City of Culture in East Asia.
ningirsu: The earliest known mention of Ningirsu and his temple in Girsu comes from the Figure aux Plumes, a monument of the Early Dynastic II period (2700–2600 BCE), and he already appears in the early god lists from Fāra and Abu Salabikh. He was regarded as the son of Enlil and Ninhursag, though several scholars think an older tradition made him a son of Enki. His sister Nanshe was the second deity of the Lagash pantheon, his wife was Bau, and their children included the gods Igalim and Shulshaga.

Whether Ningirsu and Ninurta began as one god or two is debated. Michael P. Streck notes that they appear separately in the early god lists and suggests two deities merged in the second half of the third millennium BCE, while Thorkild Jacobsen read them as two names of the same god.

His name means Lord of Girsu. As owner of the land, he was believed to have the mortal ruler administer his domain on his behalf. His common epithet, warrior of Enlil, first appears in the inscriptions of the rulers of Lagash during their long border war with Umma, where he is said to appoint them to defend his territory and to intervene on the battlefield in their favour.

On the Stele of the Vultures he is a massive figure holding a mace and a battle net in which defeated enemies from Umma are imprisoned, and he stands on a war chariot pulled by lions. His emblem, the Anzû bird over two lions, is rarely seen outside Lagash. Ur-Nanshe built several of his temples, and Gudea rebuilt the E-ninnu with copper, wood, stone, silver, gold, carnelian and alabaster brought from outside Mesopotamia.

After the collapse of the Ur III state the region of Lagash declined and never recovered its political importance, and the cult of its gods faded. Hammurabi still provisioned the E-ninnu, and the god appears in Kish as late as the reign of Samsuditana and in curses on two Middle Babylonian kudurrus.

His identity was gradually absorbed by Ninurta. Ningirsu is the hero of the Old Babylonian versions of the myths Lugale and the Epic of Anzû, while the Standard Babylonian versions give the role to Ninurta. He also appears in the Lament for Sumer and Ur among the tutelary gods forced to leave their cities.
ninisina: The name Ninisina, Mistress or Queen of Isin, follows a common Sumerian pattern in which the sign NIN is joined to a place or an object; some forty percent of the earliest attested Sumerian deities were named this way. The oldest evidence of her worship comes from Isin in the Early Dynastic period: oath formulas, an entry in the god list from Fara and a passage of the Zame Hymns. Her temple at Isin, the Egalmaḫ, exalted palace, already existed in the third millennium BCE, and she appears in an inscription of Manishtushu on a macehead in the Sargonic period.

Believers held Ninisina to be skilled in the medical arts, a divine physician or midwife who could also drive out demons. Her parents were Anu and Urash. She was probably first thought of as unmarried, but by the Ur III period at the latest the warrior god Pabilsag was regarded as her husband, and her children Damu and Gunura were healing deities like her, while Šumaḫ served as her sukkal, a divine attendant. When the kings of Isin lost control of Uruk, she took on traits of Inanna, gaining a warlike side, while Inanna was at times linked with healing.

Her importance rose with Isin's. In the Isin-Larsa period she was the royal goddess of the dynasty of Isin, invoked in its kings' titles and shown handing them the rod-and-ring symbol, and her cult was brought to Larsa, Uruk and Ur. Isin was abandoned under Samsu-iluna and rebuilt by Kurigalzu I; she was still worshipped in the Neo-Babylonian period.

Many works of Mesopotamian literature mention her. Ninisina's Journey to Nippur, known in a Sumerian and a later bilingual version, gives the most detailed description of a divine procession in Sumerian literature. Hymns were written for her on behalf of Ishbi-Erra, Iddin-Dagan and Lipit-Ishtar, and one describes her teaching medicine to her son Damu. After those for Inanna, laments in which she mourns her city or Damu are the most common known. Scholars such as Irene Sibbing-Plantholt warn against treating her as simply interchangeable with Gula, Ninkarrak and other healing goddesses, who began as separate local deities.
ninja: Ninja is the on'yomi reading of the two characters 忍者, read in the native kun'yomi as shinobi, a shortened form of shinobi-no-mono. The word shinobi appears as early as the late 8th century in poems of the Man'yōshū, and means to steal away or hide.

Historical accounts of the ninja are scarce, despite many folktales. Later tradition gives the title retrospectively to Yamato Takeru, a prince of the 2nd century, and says that Prince Shōtoku employed a spy named Otomono Sahito, though evidence for him is thin. Only from the 15th century were spies specially trained, and in the Sengoku period documents began to call stealthy soldiers shinobi.

By the Sengoku period shinobi served as spies, scouts, surprise attackers and agitators. Ninja families were organised into guilds with their own territories and a system of rank. The jōnin, or upper person, was the highest, representing the group and hiring out mercenaries; below were the chūnin, his assistants, and the genin, field agents drawn from the lower class who carried out the missions.

The best-known ninja came from the province of Iga and the adjacent region of Kōka. Their families were jizamurai, peasant-warriors who in the unrest of the Sengoku period formed ikki, leagues for self-defence, and sold their services as mercenaries and spies. The remote mountains of Iga may have favoured their secretive development.

Daimyōs hired professional ninja between 1485 and 1581, and Iga ninja were sought for siege warfare, including night attacks and ambushes. Oda Nobunaga forced the Kōka ikki to become his vassal in 1574 and in 1581 invaded Iga and wiped out the organised clans. Survivors fled, some to the mountains of Kii and others to Tokugawa Ieyasu, who treated them well, and Hattori Hanzō and other former Iga members later served as his bodyguards. Tradition holds that Iga and Kōka ninja helped Ieyasu escape through Iga after Nobunaga's death, though researchers at Mie University suggest it was Kōka jizamurai militias rather than ninja, and the scholar Tatsuo Fujita doubts the account of Hanzō's ninja army.

Under the Tokugawa a ninja is said to have planted the besiegers' flag on the gate at the Siege of Hataya in 1600, and Iga warriors saw action at the siege of Osaka in 1614. The last detailed record of ninja in open warfare comes from the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637 to 1638, when Kōga ninja were recruited against the Christian rebels at Hara Castle. After the establishment of the Tokugawa shogunate in the 17th century the ninja faded into obscurity.
ninlil: Ninlil was a Mesopotamian goddess regarded as the wife of Enlil, and the meaning of her name is uncertain. A late explanatory text translates it as "lady of the breeze", which matches a theory that Enlil's name means "lord wind". At an early date she was identified with the goddess Sud of Shuruppak, who was also associated with Enlil, and eventually fully absorbed her. In the myth Enlil and Sud, Ninlil is the name Sud received after marrying Enlil, and Nisaba, the goddess of writing, and her husband Haya are her parents. Her Akkadian name was Mullilu, in Neo-Assyrian sources Mullissu, which Herodotus transcribed as Mylitta.

As Enlil's wife Ninlil shared many of his functions, above all the declaring of destinies, and stood at the top of the pantheon. A late hymn calls her ruler of earth and heaven and says that Enlil made no decision without her. Kings of the Third Dynasty of Ur considered both of them the source of royal authority. She was the mother of Nergal, Nanna and Ninurta. She was chiefly worshiped at Nippur and nearby Tummal, where the Ekur temple complex held her Kiur and the Eitimaku, described as her bedchamber.

In the myth Enlil and Ninlil, the inexperienced Ninlil is warned by her mother Nunbaršegunu to avoid Enlil. He seduces and impregnates her, and the fifty great gods and the seven gods of destinies judge him ritually impure and exile him from Nippur. Ninlil follows him and gives birth to Nanna, Nergal, Ninazu and Enbilulu. Scholars debate whether his crime was rape or premarital sex.

Ninlil was taken into Hurrian religion, where she and Enlil were among the primeval gods and could be invoked as witnesses of treaties. In Syrian cities such as Mari, Emar and Ugarit she was closely associated with Shalash, the spouse of Dagan, a god regarded as analogous to Enlil. From the reign of Tiglath-Pileser I onward she was viewed as the wife of the Assyrian head god Ashur, and in this role developed into Mullissu, who was conflated with Ishtar of Nineveh, also recast as Ashur's consort.
nino-visconti: Ugolino Visconti, known as Nino, was a son of Giovanni Visconti and a grandson of Ugolino della Gherardesca. He succeeded his father as giudice of Gallura in 1275 or 1276 and spent most of his life moving between Pisa and Gallura. He was the first husband of Beatrice d'Este, daughter of Obizzo II d'Este, and his emblem was a cock, a canting device on Gallura from the Latin gallus.

His chaplain, a friar named Gomita, was caught taking bribes to release prisoners, and Nino had him hanged, an act commended for its justice; Dante placed Gomita in the eighth circle of the Inferno. In 1288 Nino began to share power in Pisa with his grandfather, but the two quarrelled. When the elder Ugolino sought the help of Archbishop Ruggieri degli Ubaldini to expel him, the archbishop exiled them both and named his own podestà and capitano del popolo.

Nino never set foot in Gallura again. From exile he attacked Pisa together with Genoa, Lucca and the Florentine Guelfs until peace was made in 1293, and he later died in Sardinia. His daughter Joanna inherited the title of Gallura and married Rizzardo IV da Camino, Count of Ceneda and Lord of Treviso. Occitan poets knew him: two anonymous coblas are addressed to him, and Terramagnino da Pisa addressed his Doctrina de Cort to him.

Dante may have befriended him during the part of his exile Nino spent in Florence. In the eighth canto of the Purgatorio Dante meets him outside St Peter's gate and greets him as giudice Nin gentil. Nino asks him to remind his young daughter Giovanna to pray for him and complains that his widow Beatrice has remarried into the Milanese Visconti. Commentators have read his wife and daughter as figures of Eve and Mary, and many see misogyny in his words about Beatrice.
ninomiya-sontoku: Ninomiya Sontoku, also known as Ninomiya Kinjirō, was born on 4 September 1787 into a poor peasant family in Kayama, in Ashigarakami District of Sagami Province, with the name Kinjirō. His father died when he was 14 and his mother two years later, and he was placed in his uncle's household. While working his uncle's land he studied on his own, then took up abandoned land, turned it into farmland and restored his household by the age of 20. In his twenties he became a wealthy landlord.

He was then recruited to manage a small feudal district in financial difficulty and revived its economy, above all through agricultural development. Hearing of this, the daimyō entrusted him with the Odawara Domain. A story is told that when famine struck Odawara he proposed opening the public granaries, and when fellow officials objected that the shōgun's permission was needed, he replied that until it came no one, the officials included, could eat the public rice; they agreed that the people should be fed at once. He was later given charge of one of the shogunate's estates, a great honour for a man of his origins, and in all he is said to have rebuilt about 600 villages.

His methods became a standard of land development and economic management in feudal Japan. He stressed compound interest, little understood by samurai and peasants, and worked out its growth over 100 years on the soroban. He treated the village as a community whose surpluses were invested in new land or saved for bad years, rewarded migrants who established farms, and founded mutual funds called gojoukou, forerunners of credit unions, from which members borrowed without interest for 100 days while all shared the cost of a default.

Ninomiya died on 17 November 1856, and the emperor later gave him the Lower Fourth Rank. He left no written philosophy; his disciples Tomita Takayoshi, Fukuzumi Masae and Saitō Takayuki recorded his ideas, which joined Buddhism, Shinto and Confucianism into practical ethics and held farming to be the highest human work, the cultivation of what the kami give. His followers carried them on as the Hōtokusha movement. Statues of him as a boy carrying firewood and reading as he walks stand at many Japanese schools; the oldest surviving one, of concrete, was set up in 1924 at Maeshiba, now part of Toyohashi.
ninurta-kudurri-usur-i: His name means "Ninurta protect my offspring" or "my border", an ambiguity that may be intentional. He was the second king of the Bῑt-Bazi or 6th Dynasty of Babylon, and ruled in an era of economic and political retrenchment. King List A gives him three years, while the Dynastic Chronicle records that he ruled for just two. A fragment of the Assyrian Synchronistic King List names Ashur-nirari IV as his contemporary, rather than Ashur-rabi II, who better matches the chronology now favoured.

Two Luristan arrowheads are inscribed with his name and were probably votive offerings for temples, though there is a remote possibility that they belong to his later namesake, who ruled for less than a year. A legal document from his second year, issued at Kār-Marduk, which may have been his capital, is known because the Bīt-Abi-Rattaš kudurru, from the reign of Nabû-mukin-apli about 974 to 939 BCE, opens by recalling it.

It settled a case of manslaughter: Arad-Sibitti had killed the female slave of Buruša the bow-maker with an arrow. The king pronounced judgement and ordered him to give the plaintiff seven slaves in compensation. Seven high-ranking witnesses attended, three of them of Kassite origin and one, the officer Ammenna, a Hurrian.

He may be the eleventh king of the text known as Prophecy A, whose rule likewise lasts three years. It describes the apocalyptic events of that reign: cities destroyed, rebellion, hostility against Akkad, a break with the rites at the Ekur and Nippur, and fragmentary but ominous events involving the Amurru and weapons. He was succeeded by his brother, Širikti-Šuqamuna.
nioro-du-sahel: Nioro was founded around 1240 by Beydari Tamboura, a Diawambé slave. King Bodian Moriba, who reigned from 1818 to 1832, made it the capital of the Bambara kingdom of Kaarta in place of Yélimané, and the town became an important trading centre between Upper Senegal and the Sudan. After El Hadj Umar Tall took it, it became his capital, and in 1856 he had a great mosque built there, after which a large Muslim community settled in the town.

Umar Tall's son Ahmadu, his successor at the head of the Toucouleur Empire, made his brother Muntaga Tall faama of Nioro in 1874. Encouraged by French overtures, Muntaga rebelled in 1885; Ahmadu laid a long siege, and rather than surrender Muntaga killed himself by blowing up his powder magazine. Ahmadu then based himself in Nioro and tried to build a fully Islamic society there.

In late 1890 the French marched on the town. Ahmadu's army, led by the Wolof king in exile Alboury Ndiaye, failed to hold it against Lieutenant Colonel Louis Archinard in January 1891, and Ahmadu fled east to Bandiagara. Nioro became one of the first cercle seats of French Sudan. From 1910 it was the centre of Hamallism, a Sufi movement that grew out of the Tijaniyyah under Sheikh Hamallah; its followers were hostile to colonial rule and were violently repressed, above all in 1940–1941.

During the struggle that led to the Sudanese Republic in 1960, Nioro was a stronghold of the Sudanese Union – African Democratic Rally. It is a town and urban commune 241 km from Kayes and 443 km by road north-west of Bamako, served by an airstrip, and the commune counted 109,565 inhabitants in 2023.
nippur: Nippur, called Nibru in Sumerian and Nibbur in Akkadian, lay at the site now known as Nuffar, about 200 km south of modern Baghdad and roughly 100 km southeast of ancient Babylon. It stood on both sides of the old bed of the Shatt-en-Nil canal, an early course of the Euphrates, which divides the ruins into an East Mound and a West Mound. Occupation reached back to the Ubaid, Uruk and Jemdet Nasr periods, and the site reached a maximum of 130 hectares, in the Ur III period and again in the Kassite period.

Nippur never held political hegemony in its own right, yet control of it mattered, because it was thought able to confer the overall kingship on rulers from other city-states. Its importance came from the Ekur, the temple of Enlil, and from the temple of his son Ninurta. The Tummal Chronicle credits Enmebaragesi of Kish with first building up the sanctuary and lists later rulers, among them Gilgamesh of Uruk, who kept up its ceremonies. Early kings of Uruk and Ur left inscribed door-sockets and stone vases there.

Kings of the Ur, Isin and Larsa dynasties rebuilt the temple, and Rim-Sin I of Larsa styled himself shepherd of the land of Nippur. Under Hammurabi, who reigned from 1792 to 1750 BCE, the religious and political centre moved to Babylon, Marduk became lord of the pantheon, and the Ekur was to some extent neglected. The Kassite dynasty restored it, and Kurigalzu I built the Ekurigibarra within it around 1375 BCE. After a long period of neglect from the mid-12th century BCE, when the Euphrates changed course, building resumed under Sargon II, and Ashurbanipal restored the Ekur on a larger scale than before; the ziggurat of that period measured 58 by 39 m.

In the Seleucid period the temple was turned into a fortress, which was occupied until about 250 CE. Nippur remained inhabited in Islamic times, when geographers called it Niffar, and a Christian bishop of the Church of the East sat there until the late 900s. By the early 1200s, when Yaqut al-Hamawi wrote, it had been abandoned.

The ruins in Al-Qādisiyyah Governorate, Iraq, have yielded thousands of cuneiform tablets, including Kassite temple archives and the records of the house of Murashu, commercial agents of the Achaemenid period whose tablets date between 454 and 404 BCE. One house of the Old Babylonian period, a scribal school, produced 1,407 tablets. The ziggurat of Ur-Gur stood 25 m high, and excavators also identified temples of Gula and Inanna.
niqmaddu-ii: Niqmaddu II was the son of Ammittamru I, whom he succeeded, and had a brother named Nuriyãnu; a legal text suggests that his wife may have been Pisidqi. His name, written Níqmâdâd in Akkadian, took up that of an earlier Amorite ruler called Niqmaddu, a choice meant to strengthen the supposed Amorite origins of his dynasty. The exact date of his accession is unknown. He came to the throne while Suppiluliuma I of Hatti was taking the lands west of the Euphrates from Tushratta of Mitanni in six campaigns, and during this period his father died.

He kept good relations with Egypt and may have been a contemporary of Akhenaten and Tutankhamun. In the Amarna letter EA 49 he addressed the pharaoh as the Sun, his lord, and asked for two palace attendants from the land of Cush and a physician, since, he wrote, there was none in Ugarit. An alabaster vase shows him beside a woman in Egyptian court dress, whose name is not preserved. Early in his reign he gave way to the Amorites in a dispute over the Shiyannu region.

His place as a Hittite vassal is recorded in four documents from the time of Suppiluliuma: a letter to him, a treaty, a decree setting Ugarit's tribute, and an inventory of that tribute. The treaty's introduction tells how Itur-Addu of Mukiš, Addu-nirari of Nuhašši and Agi-Tešub of Niya turned against the Hittite king, captured cities of Ugarit and carried off its people. Niqmaddu stayed loyal and asked for help, and Suppiluliuma sent princes and noblemen with troops and chariots, who defeated the enemy and handed the captives to him. He rewarded them with silver, gold and copper and came before the Great King at Alalah. The treaty's last part lists the towns and mountains of Ugarit's territory.

He commissioned the Baal Cycle about the god Haddu, or Baal, in which he is named as King nqmd. He had a son, Niqmepa, and was briefly succeeded by Arhalba, who came to the throne under the Hittite king Mursili II.
nis: The ancient name Naissus is probably derived from an older form, *Nāviskos, from the Celtic name of the Nišava river, meaning trough valley. The first settlement may have been founded by Celts at the end of the 3rd century BCE, though little archaeological evidence survives from before the Roman period. The road running south down the Morava valley from Belgrade forks at Niš: one line leads to Thessalonica and Athens, the other eastward to Sofia and Istanbul.

During the Roman conquest of the Balkans, between 168 and 75 BCE, the city served as a base of operations. It is first mentioned in Roman documents near the beginning of the 2nd century CE and appears in the Geography of Ptolemy of Alexandria. Several Roman emperors were born in Naissus or used it as a residence, among them Constantius III, Constans, Vetranio, Julian, Valentinian I, Valens and Justin I. Emperor Claudius Gothicus decisively defeated the Goths at the Battle of Naissus. Its role in the Byzantine Empire earned it the nickname Imperial City.

In 805 Bulgarian Emperor Krum took the town and its surroundings, and in the 11th century Byzantium reclaimed them. The Ottoman Sultan Murad I took the city in 1385 after a siege of 25 days. It returned to Serbian rule in 1443 but fell to the Ottomans again in 1448 and stayed under them for 241 years, as a seat of military and civil administration. The Austrian army seized it in 1689 during the Great Turkish War and the Ottomans regained it in 1690. They retook it again in 1737 without resistance, after an Austrian occupation that year. The existing fortress was built in 1719–1723 on the site of Roman, Byzantine and medieval fortifications.

After liberation in 1878 the city became part of the Principality of Serbia. A library and the first hotel opened in 1879, a grammar school in 1878 and the City Hall was built in 1882–1887. From 1929 to 1941 Niš was the capital of the Morava Banovina of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. During the German occupation in the Second World War the Crveni Krst concentration camp operated here. About 30,000 people passed through it, and over 10,000 were shot on nearby Bubanj hill. On 12 February 1942, 147 prisoners staged a mass escape.

Niš is the third-largest city in Serbia and the administrative centre of the Nišava District, with a city proper of fewer than two hundred thousand people. It is the seat of the University of Niš and has an international airport named after Constantine the Great. Its industries include tobacco, electronics and mechanical engineering.
nishapur: Nishapur stands at an elevation of 1250 metres on a wide fertile plain at the south-western foot of the Binalud range, in Razavi Khorasan province. Its name is said to come from the Sasanian king Shapur I, who founded the city in the 3rd century, and from Middle Persian words meaning new or good. Nearby mines have supplied the world with high-quality turquoise for at least two millennia, and the city has sometimes been called the city of turquoise. The region lies at a rather high risk of earthquakes, and the historical earthquakes of the 12th and 13th centuries ruined the city.

Under the Sasanian Empire Nishapur was the capital of the satrapy of Abarshahr, whose governor bore the unique title of kanarang. It was a vital centre of administration and of communications between Bactria, India and Sagistan, and the region took part in the Indian and Chinese trade. The people of Nishapur chose not to fight the Rashidun Caliph Umar's army and surrendered on condition of paying tribute. Abdullah Tahir reformed the city in 830, when it was the capital of the Tahirid dynasty, and Tughril chose it as the capital of the Seljuk dynasty in 1037.

From the Abbasid era to the Mongol invasion, Nishapur grew into a significant cultural, commercial and intellectual centre of the Islamic world. With Merv, Herat and Balkh it was one of the four great cities of Khorasan, a seat of government in the eastern caliphates and a trading stop on routes from Transoxiana, China, Iraq and Egypt. It reached the height of its prosperity under the Samanids in the 10th century.

In the 9th and 10th centuries it was one of the great centres of pottery, with bold polychrome ware that shows advances in glaze technology, and it was a centre of Sufism and, in the 10th century, of Ismaili missionary activity. Omar Khayyam and Attar of Nishapur were born there. The Mongols destroyed it and slaughtered most of its population in 1221. Unlike its neighbour Merv, it recovered. In 1592 Abbas the Great took Nishapur back from the Shaybanids.

Nishapur is the capital of Nishapur County and the second most populous city of Razavi Khorasan. The ruins of the ancient city, a protected archaeological area, lie to its south and south-east, alongside the mausoleums of Omar Khayyam and Attar. The present mausoleum of Khayyam, designed by Hooshang Seyhoun, was completed in 1963. Finds from the excavations, including pottery from Tepe Madraseh, are held in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the British Museum and museums in Iran.
nissanka-malla: Nissanka Malla, also known as Kirti Nissanka and Kalinga Lokaswara, was born in 1157 or 1158. His rock inscription at Galpota names his parents as Queen Parvati and King Jayagopa, the reigning king of Sinhapura, and others at Dambulla and Ruwanwelisaya place him in the Kalinga dynasty and the line of Prince Vijaya. He was a son-in-law or nephew of Parākramabāhu I, and his two wives were Kalinga Subadradevi and Gangavamsa Kalyanamahadevi.

He came to Polonnaruwa at the invitation of Vijayabâhu II, the successor of Parākramabāhu I, who made him his Aepa, or sub-king. When Vijayabâhu was killed by Mahinda VI, who reigned for only five days, Nissanka Malla killed Mahinda and took the throne. He justified his right by his descent from Vijaya, the first king of Lanka, and declared in his Galpotha inscription that non-Buddhists should not be placed in power in the island.

He reduced much of the heavy taxation imposed by Parākramabāhu I and gave money, gold, cattle and land to the people, believing that oppression and taxes drove them to robbery. He restored good relations with Ramanna after the Polonnaru-Pagan war, kept ties with the Khmer Empire and sent missionaries to Cambodia. He invaded Rameswaram, where he renovated a temple and renamed it Nissankesvara, but his attacks on the Pandyan and Chola states failed, whatever his inscriptions claim.

Seeking to outdo Parākramabāhu I as a builder, he raised the Nissanka Latha Mandapaya, whose eight granite pillars are carved as lotus stems with opening buds, the Hatadage, built to hold the Relic of the tooth of the Buddha, and the Rankot Vihara, the fourth largest stupa in Sri Lanka. At the Dambulla cave temple he had the interior and 50 Buddha statues gilded, which later earned it the name Swarnagiri, golden rock; one inscription puts the cost at 7 lakhs and another at 1 lakh. His spending later left the kingdom almost bankrupt.
nithard: Nithard was the son of Charlemagne's daughter Bertha and of Angilbert, and was born around the time Charlemagne was crowned emperor in December 800. He was probably raised either at the imperial palace, where his mother lived until the emperor's death, or at the monastery of Saint-Riquier, where his father was lay abbot. He was most likely educated at the imperial schola, which offered the military and literary training he is known to have had.

Nithard served his cousin Charles the Bald in war and in peace. He fought at his side during the Carolingian civil war and at the battle of Fontenoy in June 841. In the winter of 842 he became lay abbot of Saint-Riquier in commendam. He probably died of wounds received while fighting for Charles against the Northmen near Angoulême. In the 11th century his body, with the fatal wound still visible, was found in the grave of his father Angilbert.

Nithard's Historiae, also called De dissensionibus filiorum Ludovici pii (On the Dissensions of the Sons of Louis the Pious), consists of four books on the Carolingian empire under the sons of Louis I, above all in the troubled years between 838 and 843. It throws light on the causes of the empire's break-up. The first three books were written before his appointment at Saint-Riquier, and the fourth in the spring of 843, after he took up office there. All were dedicated to Charles the Bald and written at his request. Nithard described the work as a lament for the age of Charlemagne, when peace and concord ruled because the people followed the way of the common welfare and so the way of God.

The books are rough in style, partisan and sometimes wrong in detail, but their author knew the events at first hand and was a man of action rather than a recluse. As a military writer he stands in a tradition with Xenophon, Julius Caesar and Ammianus Marcellinus, and his account of the cavalry exercises of Gaul is valuable for the study of Carolingian techniques. Only two manuscripts of the Historiae survive, one roughly contemporary and one an incomplete Renaissance copy. The standard critical edition is that of Philippe Lauer, published in Paris in 1926, and an English translation by Bernhard Walter Scholz and Barbara Rogers appeared in 1972.
nitocris-i: Nitocris was the daughter of Psamtik I by his queen Mehytenweskhet. Before her career the Assyrians had invaded Egypt in 671 BCE, sacked Thebes and robbed its temples. In the south the office of God's Wife of Amun was still held by women of the vanished 25th Dynasty: Shepenupet II, a daughter of Piye, with Amenirdis II, a daughter of Taharqa, already named as her heir. Between them they practically controlled Upper Egypt. Psamtik chose not to remove them by force, which would have been unpopular, but to have his daughter adopted into the succession.

In his regnal year 9, on a date identified with 2 March 656 BCE, Nitocris left Sais for Thebes with a royal flotilla led by Sematawytefnakht, admiral and nomarch of Herakleopolis Magna. After sixteen days it reached Thebes, whose people acclaimed the princess. Shepenupet II and Amenirdis II met her, adopted her formally and agreed to pass their properties to her, and so indirectly to Psamtik. The officials of Thebes, among them the mayor Mentuemhat and the High Priest of Amun Harkhebi, pledged daily donations, mainly of food. Beyond the adoption itself, the arrangement amounted to the reunification of Upper and Lower Egypt under Psamtik.

When she took up the office itself is not known, but she held it until Year 4 of Apries. Building works in her name are attested at Karnak, Luxor and Abydos. In her eighties she adopted her great-niece Ankhnesneferibre, daughter of Psamtik II, keeping the office in her family.

The Adoption Stela that records these events was unearthed at Karnak in 1897 by Georges Legrain and moved to the Cairo Museum. It is of red granite, about 1.8 m high and 1.4 m wide. Its opening is lost; the rest reports Psamtik telling his court of his plan to give his daughter to Amun, the journey south and the list of donations. Nitocris was buried at Medinet Habu in a tomb chapel she shared with her natural mother and her adoptive grandmother. Her sarcophagus was later reused in a Ptolemaic tomb at Deir el-Medina and is now in the Cairo Museum.
nitra: Nitra lies at 167 m in the valley of the Nitra River in the Danubian Lowland, with part of the city rising at the foot of Zobor hill, 587 m high, in the southernmost reaches of the Tribeč mountains. It is roughly halfway between Bratislava, 92 km away, and Banská Bystrica, 118 km away. The name derives from the Nitra River.

The oldest finds in Nitra are dated to 25,000 to 30,000 years ago, and the site has been inhabited in all periods of the last 5,000 to 7,000 years. The Madarovce culture built the first fortification on Castle Hill by about 1,600 BCE, and a large Iron Age hillfort stood on Zobor. In the Roman period the Germanic Quadi settled the area, and Nitra is mentioned as their possible capital in 396 CE.

The first Slavs reached what is now Slovakia at the end of the 5th and early 6th centuries, and the densest Slavic settlement is documented around Nitra. The first mention of the city dates to the 9th century. After Great Moravia broke up, Nitra, unlike other great Moravian centres such as Mikulčice-Valy and Pohansko, kept its status as a prestigious centre until the 13th century. Older accounts held that the Magyars destroyed it, but archaeology shows no destruction by fire.

In the early 14th century Matthew III Csák damaged the town and castle several times, while the bishop of Nitra stayed loyal to the king, who in 1313 confirmed the bishopric's privileges and extended them to the administration of the whole Nitra County. After the First World War the Hungarian National Council in Nitra turned to the Czechoslovak Army to restore order and formally protested on 10 December 1918 against the occupation, but the town became part of Czechoslovakia.

Nitra has a population of 75,301 and is the seat of the University of Constantinus the Philosopher and the Slovak University of Agriculture. Its sights include Nitra Castle with St. Emmeram's Cathedral, the old town and the Piarist church of St. Ladislaus, remodelled in the baroque style in 1742 to 1748. The oldest church of the city is that of Saint Stephen, built in the 11th and 12th centuries on a 9th-century foundation. The Yeshiva of Nitra, the last yeshiva surviving in occupied Europe during the Second World War, moved afterwards to Mount Kisco, New York.
nitta-yoshisada: Nitta Yoshisada, also known as Minamoto no Yoshisada, was born in 1301, the eldest son of Nitta Tomouji. In 1317 he succeeded his father as lord of Nitta Manor in Kōzuke Province and head of the Nitta clan. His rivalry with Ashikaga Takauji arose largely because the Ashikaga were ranked above the Nitta, although descended from a younger ancestor: the Nitta's forebears had not fought beside their Minamoto cousins in the Genpei War and so had never gained power or prestige at Kamakura.

Ordered in 1331 to join a shogunate army at the Chihaya fortress, Yoshisada instead answered the call of Prince Morinaga and Emperor Go-Daigo to strike at the Hōjō. He rallied kinsmen and vassals, among them his brother Yoshisuke, and marched on Kamakura through Musashi. Kamakura is ringed by steep hills, and strong Hōjō forces held the Gokurakuji and Kewaizaka passes, so he went round Inamuragasaki Cape at low tide. According to the Taiheiki he threw his sword into the surf and prayed to the sea god Ryūjin, who drew back the waters. A stele erected in 1917 at Sode no Ura dates the crossing to 21 May 1333.

After the city fell Go-Daigo made him governor of Echigo and vice-governor of Harima and Kōzuke. In 1335 he received an imperial commission to destroy Takauji and his brother Ashikaga Tadayoshi, and in a see-saw campaign in which the capital changed hands several times he was defeated and the brothers advanced on Kyoto. After his defeat at the Battle of Minatogawa he withdrew with the emperor to Hieizan. When Go-Daigo agreed to return to Kyoto on 13 November 1336, he entrusted Yoshisada with escorting Prince Takanaga and Prince Tsunenaga to Echizen Province.

At the siege of Kanegasaki in 1337 the two princes and Yoshisada's son Nitta Yoshiaki were killed, though Yoshisada escaped. At the siege of Kuromaru, fighting Hosokawa Akiuji, an ally of Takauji, his horse was brought down by arrows and he was pinned beneath it; according to the record he drew his short sword and cut off his own head, and several of his samurai took their own lives beside him. He died on 17 August 1338. In 1882 he was posthumously given the Senior First Rank.
niue: Niue lies in a triangle drawn between Tonga, Samoa and the Cook Islands, about 2,400 kilometres north-east of New Zealand and 604 kilometres north-east of Tonga. It has a land area of about 261.46 square kilometres and is nicknamed The Rock, from its traditional name, the Rock of Polynesia. The terrain has two levels: a limestone cliff along the coast with a central plateau about 60 metres above sea level, and a coastal terrace about 500 metres wide. A coral reef surrounds the island, with its only major break on the central west coast, near the capital, Alofi. The wet season runs from November to April and the dry season from May to October.

Archaeological evidence suggests that Polynesians from Samoa settled Niue around 900 CE. According to Niuean tradition, further settlers came from Tonga in the 16th century as a war party. Until the beginning of the 18th century the island seems to have had no national government or single leader, and chiefs and heads of families held authority over parts of the population. A succession of patu-iki, or kings, then ruled, beginning with Puni-mata. Tui-toga, who reigned from 1875 to 1887, was the first of them to adopt Christianity.

The next documented European visitors represented the London Missionary Society. After many years of trying to land a European missionary, they abducted a Niuean named Nukai Peniamina and trained him as a pastor at the Malua Theological College in Samoa. He returned in 1846 and, after attempts in other villages had failed, was allowed to land at Mutalau, whose chiefs protected him day and night at the fort in Fupiu.

In 1889 the chiefs of Niue wrote to Queen Victoria asking her to stretch out your mighty hand, that Niue may hide herself in it and be safe, and expressed anxiety that another nation might take the island; the British did not at first take up the offer. A petition by Cook Islanders in 1900 asking for annexation included Niue if possible. The New Zealand Parliament restored self-government in 1974 with the Niue Constitution Act, after a referendum in which Niueans chose among independence, self-government and continuation as a New Zealand territory; the majority chose self-government. Robert Rex was elected by the Niue Assembly as the first Premier in 1974 and held the post until his death 18 years later.

Niue is a self-governing island country in free association with New Zealand, and its people are citizens of New Zealand. It is a parliamentary democracy divided into 14 villages, each sending a member to the Niue Assembly. Niue is bilingual, with Niuean and English spoken, and a large majority of Niueans live in New Zealand.
nivelles: Farmers had been turning the region into agricultural land since about 4,000 BCE. In the 7th century it belonged to the Frankish kingdom of Austrasia, and Pippin of Landen, Mayor of the Palace, rebuilt a villa there. After his death in 640 the bishop of Maastricht, the future Saint Amand, urged his widow Itta to found an abbey on the estate. Her daughter Gertrude became its first abbess and was venerated as a saint after her death. Growing crowds of pilgrims required ever larger churches, ending in the Romanesque building dedicated in 1046 in the presence of Wazo, Prince-Bishop of Liège, and the emperor Henry III. This was the golden age of the monastery, whose lands reached Friesland, the Moselle and the Rhine.

In the 13th century the town that had grown around the church became part of the Duchy of Brabant. Its artisans and guild members fought the abbesses and the dukes for their rights, which Joanna, Duchess of Brabant, finally granted in the 14th century. A rising of the thread manufacturers in 1647 sent many entrepreneurs to France and began an economic decline that the 17th-century wars between France and the Spanish Netherlands deepened, with successive sieges and occupations. In 1830 Nivelles was among the first towns to send patriotic troops to Brussels in the Belgian Revolution, and heavy industry, including metallurgy and railway construction, grew in the following years.

Nivelles lies in the province of Walloon Brabant and is its main town. Almost the entire city centre was destroyed on 14 May 1940, leaving only the walls of the collegiate church of St Gertrude standing, and the rebuilding of the church was completed in 1984. The church dates from the 11th to the 13th century and is one of the best examples of Romanesque architecture in Belgium. Merovingian and Carolingian tombs have been found beneath it, and its crypt is one of the largest of its kind in Europe.

A bell-striking figure of about 1400 in one of the towers, called Jean de Nivelles, marks the hours. Processional giants include Goliath, which dates from 1365, and a religious procession in honour of Saint Gertrude, which began in the 13th century, is held every year. The town also has a 16th-century Recollets convent, an archaeological museum and a carnival with Gilles, dating from the 19th century.
nivkh-people: The Nivkh call themselves by a word meaning the people; Russian explorers of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries termed them Gilyak, a name linguists dispute and that Soviet officials replaced with the Nivkh endonym. They are believed to be the original inhabitants of the region and to descend from a proposed Neolithic people that migrated from the Transbaikal region during the Late Pleistocene. Their origins are hard to discern from current archaeological research. Their fishing and coastal sea-mammal hunting resemble those of the Koryak and Itelmen on the Kamchatka Peninsula, and their dog-sledge rigging is similar too.

Vassili Poyarkov was the first Russian to write of the Nivkh, in 1643. For many centuries they were tributaries of the Manchus. After the Treaty of Nerchinsk in 1689 they acted as intermediaries between Russians, Manchus and Japanese, and also the Ainu, who were vassals of the Japanese. Contact with the southern Sakhalin Ainu was generally hostile, though the two traded. The Russian Empire annexed the region after two treaties in 1858 and 1860.

After the October Revolution the Soviet government embraced the name Nivkh as a mark of native self-determination, created a brief autonomous okrug and granted extensive fishing rights, which lasted until the 1960s. Other policies proved devastating: the Nivkh were forced into kolkhoz collectives, and fishermen who held that ploughing the earth was a sin were hard to convert to agriculture. In the 1930s Nivkh people often disappeared under suspicion of pro-Japanese sentiment. When the collectives were abandoned after 1991, rapid economic hardship followed for a people that depended on them.

The Nivkh were traditionally fishermen, hunters and dog breeders, living near the coast in summer and wintering inland along streams to catch salmon. Villages held three or four households shared by several families, drawn from two to eight clans. A clan, khal, was united by marriage ties and a common derived deity, and arranged marriages and settled disputes. Winter dwellings were a round dugout called the ryv or a gabled one-room house heated by a kang.

Traditional religion was animist and worked through shamans, who diagnosed and cured disease. The Bear Festival, held in January or February, centred on a bear raised for several years in a corral by local women, who treated it like a child. The bear was held to be a sacred manifestation of ancestors and gods, and was dressed, offered a banquet and sacrificed. The Nivkh language is an isolate or small family. Most Nivkh now speak Russian, and under five percent speak Nivkh; the 2021 census counted 3,842.
nizam-al-mulk: Abu Ali Hasan was born in the village of Radkan, near Tus, to a dehqan family. He studied Shafi fiqh and the Ashari school of theology. His father, Ali ibn Ishak, served as a financial officer to the Ghaznavids and fled to Ghazni after the Seljuk Turks defeated the Ghaznavids at the Battle of Dandanaqan in 1040. The son later left the Ghaznavid court for Seljuk service, and by 1059 was chief administrator of the whole province of Khorasan. Alp Arslan, whom he helped defeat a rival claimant, made him his vizier and gave him the title Nizam al-Mulk, meaning order of the realm.

Alp Arslan's strength lay in the military sphere, and domestic affairs were handled by Nizam al-Mulk. He built the administrative organization that strengthened the sultanate under Alp Arslan and his son Malik-Shah I. Military iqta fiefs, governed by Seljuk princes, supported the soldiery and settled the nomadic Turks among the farming population, which let the sultan field a large standing army without relying on tribute from conquest. Nizam accompanied Alp Arslan on most campaigns and conquered the citadel of Estakhr in 1067. He missed the Battle of Manzikert on 26 August 1071, having been sent to Persia with a convoy.

After Alp Arslan was assassinated in 1072, Nizam stood behind Malik-Shah I against his uncle Kavurt, who was defeated and later poisoned, presumably on Nizam's orders. Under his guidance the Seljuk armies contained the Ghaznavids in Khorasan, rolled back the Fatimids in Syria, reduced Georgia to a tributary state and kept the Abbasid caliphs powerless. In his last years rivals worked against him. Terken Khatun, Malik-Shah's wife, wanted her son Mahmud as heir, while Nizam and most of the army favoured Berkyaruq. In 1091 the Isma'ilis under Hassan-i Sabbah seized the fortress of Alamut, and Nizam besieged it but had to withdraw.

Nizam is known for founding the Nizamiyya madrasas, named after him, in cities including Baghdad, Isfahan, Nishapur, Mosul, Basra and Herat. He is also traditionally credited with the Siyasatnama, a treatise on kingship written after Malik-Shah asked his ministers for books on government. His was the only one approved. It uses historical examples to discuss justice and effective rule and has been compared to Machiavelli's The Prince.
He was assassinated on the road from Isfahan to Baghdad on 14 October 1092. The usual account says an Assassin disguised as a Sufi stabbed him near Nahavand as he was carried in a litter.
nizam-ali-khan: Mir Nizam Ali Khan was born on 7 March 1734, the fourth son of Asaf Jah I and Umda Begum. His full style named him Asaf Jah II, Nizam ul-Mulk, Nizam ud-Daula, Fateh Jang, Sipah Salar and Nawab Subedar of the Deccan. In 1759 he was appointed leading commander and administrator of the Deccan, having earned a name as a capable commander through his methods of fighting the Marathas. In 1757 and 1760 the then Nizam, Salabat Jung, had been defeated by Sadashivrao Bhau at Sindhkhed and at Udgir.

After the Marathas were routed at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761, Nizam Ali advanced with an army of 60,000, drove them back as far as Puna and forced them to sue for peace. He then seized Bidar Fort and arrested Salabat Jung, who had the support of the French East India Company. The Mughal emperor Shah Alam II ratified the act with a firman removing Salabat Jung as Subedar of the Deccan and appointing Nizam Ali in his place.

In 1762 the Maratha leader Raghunathrao, at odds with Madhavrao Peshwa, allied with the Nizam, who marched on Poona unaware that he would be betrayed; in 1763 Madhavrao I and Raghunathrao together defeated him at the Battle of Rakshasbhuvan and imposed a treaty. In 1795 the Marathas of Madhavrao II defeated him again at the Battle of Kharda, and he had to cede Daulatabad, Aurangabad and Sholapur and pay an indemnity of Rs. 30 million. A French general, Monsieur Raymond, served as his military leader and adviser. Judging that the fall of Tipu Sultan of Mysore was near, he then entered the subsidiary alliance with the British East India Company.

Asaf Jah II died at Chowmahalla Palace in Hyderabad on 6 August 1803, aged 69. His favourite wife was Bakhshi Begum; another consort, Tinat-un-Nisa Begum, was the mother of his successor, Sikander Jah, Asaf Jah III. The Sawānih-i-Deccan, a Persian work compiled by Munim Khan, one of his military commanders, is a source for the administration of the Asaf Jahis.
nizam-of-hyderabad: Nizam is a shortened form of Niẓām ul-Mulk, Administrator of the Realm, the title given to Asaf Jah I when the Mughal emperor Farrukhsiyar appointed him viceroy of the Deccan. Asaf Jah I, born Mir Qamaruddin Khan, descended from two prominent Mughal families. His grandfather Abid Khan, a Persian from Samarkand, became a favourite of Aurangzeb, and his father Ghazi Uddin Khan helped conquer the Bijapur and Golconda sultanates in 1686. His mother was a daughter of the former grand vizier Sa'dullah Khan. The Nizams ruled Hyderabad State, now parts of Telangana, the Marathwada region of Maharashtra and the Kalyana-Karnataka region of Karnataka.

In 1724 Asaf Jah I defeated Mubariz Khan to establish autonomy over the Deccan and began the Asaf Jahi dynasty. He never formally declared independence: he flew the Mughal flag, was never crowned, and Friday sermons were given in the name of Aurangzeb, a practice that lasted until 1948. After his death in 1748 his sons, backed by neighbouring states and foreign forces, contended for the throne, and the accession of Asaf Jah II, who reigned from 1762 to 1803, ended the instability. In 1768 he signed the treaty of Machilipatnam, surrendering the coastal region to the East India Company for a fixed annual rent.

From the 1720s the Nizams fought the Marathas at Palkhed, Bhopal, Rakshasbhuvan and Kharda, losing each time, and paid them chauth, a regular tax. In 1805, after the Company's victory in the Second Anglo-Maratha War, the Nizam came under British protection. The title His Exalted Highness and Faithful Ally of the British Government rewarded the Nizams' role in the Second and Third Anglo-Mysore Wars and the rebellion of 1857. The Berar region was separated in 1903.

The seventh Nizam, Mir Osman Ali Khan, was crowned in 1911. During his reign the state gained railways, electricity, roads, reservoirs and Osmania University, and 80,000 men raised by him served in the Second World War. In 1947 he chose to join neither India nor Pakistan and sought to be an independent monarchy within the Commonwealth, which India and George VI rejected. The Razakars, who wanted accession to Pakistan, are described as committing atrocities against the Hindu population, and in Operation Polo the Indian Army invaded on 13 September 1948, an operation in which massacres of Muslims are also recorded. The Nizam capitulated on 17 September 1948.

The dynasty had only seven recognised rulers. The Nizams founded hospitals, schools and colleges teaching in Urdu, a Hyderabad Civil Service, and reservoirs such as Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar. Mir Osman Ali Khan became Rajpramukh after accession and died on 24 February 1967. The seventh Nizam also gave grants to temples, churches and gurdwaras. The title is now held by his great-grandson, a pretender.
nizami-ganjavi: Born into a Persian family of urban background in Ganja, Nizami was named Ilyas and chose the pen-name Nizami. He is believed to have spent his whole life in the South Caucasus. Because he was not a court poet he does not appear in the annals of the dynasties, and the biographical compilations called tazkerehs rest largely on legends and hearsay, so that his own work is the only real source and says little about his personal life. He was orphaned early and raised by his maternal uncle Khwaja Umar, who gave him an excellent education. His mother, Ra'isa, was of Kurdish origin.

He married three times. His first wife was an enslaved Kipchak woman, sent to him by Fakhr al-Din Bahramshah, the ruler of Darband, as part of a larger gift, and she bore his only son, Mohammad. She died after Khosrow and Shirin was completed. His two other wives also died young, and each death coincided with the completion of an epic. His poems show wide learning, from Arabic and Persian literature to astronomy, alchemy, medicine, law, philosophy, music and the visual arts, and he is often called Hakim, the Sage.

Nizami's main work is the Khamsa, or Panj Ganj, five long narrative poems in masnavi, double-rhymed verse. They are Makhzan-ol-Asrâr, dated 1163 or 1176, Khosrow o Shirin, 1177–1180, Leyli o Majnun, 1192, Eskandar-Nâmeh, 1194 or 1196–1202, and Haft Peykar, 1197. The first was influenced by Sanai's Garden of Truth, and the other four are medieval romances. Khosrow and Shirin, Bahram-e Gur and Alexander the Great all have episodes in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, and Layla and Majnun derives from Arabic sources. In every case Nizami reworked his material substantially. He dedicated his poems to various rulers of the region, as was the custom, but avoided court life, and little is known of his relations with his patrons.

Only a small body of his lyric poetry survives, mainly odes and ghazals, and ten of his quatrains are recorded in the anthology Nozhat al-Majales, compiled about 1250. His influence on later literature was great. The Khamsa became a pattern that poets emulated in Persian and other Islamic literatures, among them Amir Khusro, and his stories, with Ferdowsi's, are the most frequently illustrated in Persian miniature painting. A Khamsa was made for the Mughal emperor Akbar in the 1590s. Nizami's mausoleum stands outside Ganja.
nizamuddin-auliya: Nizamuddin Auliya was born in 1238 into a Sayyid family at Badayun. At five, after his father's death, he came to Delhi with his mother, Bibi Zulekha. When he was sixteen or seventeen he first heard the name of Fariduddin Ganjshakar, known as Baba Farid, and love and respect arose in his heart. At twenty he went to Ajodhan and became Baba Farid's disciple, but kept studying theology in Delhi and visited Ajodhan each year for Ramadan. On his third visit Baba Farid made him his successor, and soon after he learned that Baba Farid had died.

Nizamuddin lived at several places in Delhi before settling at Ghiyaspur, a neighbourhood away from the noise of the city, where he built a khanqah. People from all walks of life were fed and taught there, rich and poor alike. He had more than 600 khalifas, disciples authorised to take disciples of their own, among them Nasiruddin Chiragh Dehlavi, his spiritual successor, the singer and poet Amir Khusro, and Hasan Sijzi, who compiled his discourses as Fawaid ul Fuad. He did not marry.

Sultan Qutbu'd-Din Mubarak Shah, angered that Nizamuddin had made Khizr Khan his disciple, forbade his nobles to visit Ghiyaspur and ordered Sufis to pray at the mosque he built. The Shaikh refused, and sent a servant to the monthly gathering at the palace in his place. The sultan was assassinated on 8 July 1320, before the first day of the next month.

Like his predecessors, Nizamuddin stressed love as a means of realising God, and for him love of God implied love of humanity. He emphasised renunciation and trust in God, the unity of mankind without distinctions of status, helping the needy and feeding the hungry. He strongly disapproved of mixing with sultans, princes and nobles. He held sema, devotional listening, permissible only without musical instruments and dancing, and he discouraged displays of miracles.

He died on 3 April 1325. His shrine, the Nizamuddin Dargah in Delhi, was built in its present form in 1562 and is visited by people of all faiths. Amir Khusro, who died within a few months of his master, is buried at his feet. Nizamuddin is regarded as the founder of the Chishti Nizami order.
nizar-ibn-al-mustansir: Abu Mansur Nizar was born on 26 September 1045 to the caliph al-Mustansir, then about 15 years old. He was most likely the eldest son, although another son, Abu Abdallah, is sometimes listed as the senior. When the caliphate fell into crisis in the late 1060s, with the Seljuk Turks advancing in Syria and fighting between the army's Turkish and black African troops in Egypt, al-Mustansir sent his sons away for safety. A proclamation of 1122 by the caliph al-Amir says Nizar was sent to the port of Damietta.

As the eldest son Nizar was expected to succeed, but no formal designation seems to have been made. The historian al-Maqrizi describes a deep enmity between him and al-Afdal Shahanshah, vizier since June 1094: Nizar had once ordered al-Afdal to dismount in the palace and called him a dirty Armenian. On the caliph's death al-Afdal seated al-Musta'li, who had just married his sister. Summoned to do homage, Nizar refused, claimed a written document naming him heir, and fled. Historians such as Farhad Daftary see the later stories of al-Musta'li's nomination as attempts to justify what was in effect a coup.

At Alexandria the governor Nasr al-Dawla Aftakin, the qadi, the townspeople and the nearby Arab tribes joined him, and he took the title al-Mustafa li-Din Allah; a gold dinar bearing it was found in 1994. He repulsed al-Afdal's attack in February 1095 and raided to the outskirts of Cairo, but al-Afdal won back the tribes with gifts. In November his commander Ibn Masal left the besieged city with most of the treasure, and Nizar and Aftakin surrendered under a guarantee of safety. Taken to Cairo, Nizar was immured and Aftakin executed.

The schism was permanent. Al-Musta'li was recognised in Egypt, Syria and Yemen, but most Isma'ilis of Persia and Iraq followed Nizar, and the chief da'i of Persia, Hassan-i Sabbah, set up his own hierarchy. The Order of Assassins he founded killed al-Afdal in 1121 and al-Amir in 1130. Sons of Nizar or claimants to that descent rose against the Fatimid caliphs until 1162. Alamut Castle minted coins in Nizar's name until 1162, and from Hassan II on its rulers claimed descent from him, a claim the Aga Khan continues to hold.
nizari-ismaili-state: The state grew out of the split among Ismaili Shias over the succession to the Fatimid imamate, when most Ismailis of Persia and Syria accepted the claim of Nizar ibn al-Mustansir upheld by Hassan-i Sabbah. Expelled from Egypt, Hassan drew on resentment of the Sunni Seljuks, who had divided farmland into fiefs and taxed heavily. Wanted by the vizier Nizam al-Mulk, he hid in Qazvin, sent supporters to settle in the Alamut valley and entered the castle in disguise. In 1090 he took it from its Zaydi lord, Mahdi, without violence; Mahdi was spared and later paid 3,000 gold dinars.

Hassan and his successors repeated this covert capture at fortresses across Persia and Syria, creating a state of unconnected strongholds in hostile country, with its own coinage that called Alamut the Capital of Daylam. In the mid-12th century the Nizaris acquired fortresses in the Nusayriyah Mountain Range of coastal Syria, among them Masyaf and al-Kahf.

Below the imam stood a hierarchy of chief da'is, great da'is and ordinary da'is, with companions, sworn adherents and fida'is, mostly peasants and artisans. Each territory had a chief da'i appointed from Alamut but free to act locally. Their opponents called them Assassins, and they did kill selected leaders in public, beginning, it is widely held, with Nizam al-Mulk; yet almost any political murder of the period was attributed to them. Most of what is known about them comes from hostile sources.

In 1238 the Nizari imam and the Abbasid caliph sent a joint embassy to the kings of Europe, Louis IX of France among them, seeking an alliance against the Mongols, without result. The young imam Rukn al-Din Khurshah surrendered Maymun-Dizh to Hulagu Khan on 19 November 1256 after hard fighting. Möngke Khan then ordered the massacre of all Nizari Ismailis of Persia, and Rukn al-Din was killed by his Mongol guard in Mongolia. Gerdkuh, the last stronghold in Persia, fell in 1270, and the Mamluk sultan Baibars annexed the castles in Syria in 1270-73. A son of Rukn al-Din recaptured Alamut in 1275, though only for a few years.
nizhny-novgorod: Nizhny Novgorod stands at the confluence of the Oka and the Volga in central Russia, 420 km east of Moscow. The Oka divides it into two parts: the Upper City on the hilly right bank, which includes the Kremlin, the historical and administrative centre, and the Lower City on the low western side, built up around the Gorky Automobile Plant. Originally the name was just Novgorod, meaning Newtown. To tell it from the older Novgorod to the west, it was called Novgorod of the Lower Lands, lower because it lay downstream of cities such as Moscow, Vladimir and Murom.

The city began as a small wooden hillfort founded by Grand Prince Yuri II of Vladimir in 1221 at the confluence of two of the most important rivers of his principality. It was the easternmost Russian settlement until 1372. After its incorporation into the Grand Principality of Moscow in 1392, the local princes took the name Shuysky and settled in Moscow. The Crimean Tatar chief Edigu burned the city in 1408; it was restored and regarded by the Muscovites as a great stronghold against the Tatars of Kazan.

The red-brick Kremlin, built in 1508-1511 under Pietro Francesco, withstood Tatar sieges in 1520 and 1536. In 1612 Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky organised an army in the city for the liberation of Moscow from the Poles and Lithuanians.

In 1817 the Makaryev Fair was transferred to Nizhny Novgorod and began to draw millions of visitors a year, so that by the middle of the 19th century the city was the trade capital of the Russian Empire. At the All-Russia exhibition of 1896, Alexander Popov's radio receiver and Vladimir Shukhov's hyperboloid tower were demonstrated. In the Soviet period the city became an important industrial centre, known as Gorky and nicknamed the Russian Detroit after the Gorky Automobile Plant. Shortly before the dissolution of the Soviet Union it took the name Nizhny Novgorod again.

Nizhny Novgorod is the administrative centre and largest city of Nizhny Novgorod Oblast and of the Volga Federal District, with about 1.2 million residents at the 2021 census. Its metro opened in 1985, and the city marked its 800th anniversary on 21 August 2021.
nizwa: Nizwa is the largest city in Ad Dakhiliyah Governorate and lies about 140 km from Muscat, at the base of the western Hajar Mountains.
