It acquired its importance as a meeting point amid a spread of date palms, at the crossroads of routes linking the interior with Muscat and the lower reaches of Dhofar. Historians cannot agree on the origin of its name: some derive it from an Arabic verb meaning being alone, others from an old water spring. It is a centre of date growing and the market place of the area.

Tradition holds that in 630 a handwritten letter from the Prophet Muhammad asked the people of Nizwa to convert. They sent a delegation to Medina and embraced Islam, and Muhammad sent a tutor to teach them the fundamentals of the religion. The city's Jama, its grand mosque, was long a centre of Islamic learning, and the So'al Mosque dates from the 2nd century AH (9th century CE). In the 14th century the traveller Ibn Battuta described a city at the foot of a mountain, enveloped by orchards and streams, with fine bazaars and splendid clean mosques.

Nizwa Fort was built in 1668 by Imam Sultan Bin Saif Al Ya'rubi. The main bulk took about twelve years to complete, and it stands above an underground stream. It served as the administrative seat of the imams and walis and as a stronghold against raiders. In the early 1950s the fort's large round tower was bombed and rocketed by the British Royal Air Force, called in to help Sultan Said bin Taimur suppress a revolt by leaders of the interior Imamate of Oman, a conflict driven by a struggle for a share of the country's newly found oil wealth.

Since 1970 Nizwa has been modernised, with a road link to Muscat, a hospital and educational institutions including the University of Nizwa. The fort, the mosque and the traditional souq stand next to one another in the centre and were renovated in the 1990s with traditional materials. The souq is known for silver jewellery and khanjars, the curved daggers made by local craftsmen. Falaj Daris, the largest falaj, or irrigation system, in Oman, was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006, and palm farms stretch for eight kilometres along the wadis Kalbouh and Al Abiad.
nkosi-sikelel-iafrika: Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika, literally Lord Bless Africa, is a Christian hymn composed by Enoch Sontonga at a Methodist mission school near Johannesburg. It consisted of a single stanza in Xhosa, written in B-flat major, with a four-part harmony supporting a repetitive melody that combined features of Western hymn composition and indigenous South African melodies. It was first sung in public at the ordination of John Hlengani Mboweni as a pastor in 1899. In 1927 the poet Samuel Mqhayi added seven further Xhosa stanzas.

The choir of Ohlange High School took up the hymn, and its co-founder served as the first president of the South African Native National Congress. The hymn closed the Congress meeting of 1912, and by 1925 it was the official closing anthem of the organisation now known as the African National Congress. Solomon Plaatje, a founding member of the Congress, had it recorded in London in 1923, and John Langalibalele Dube's Ohlange Zulu Choir popularised it at concerts in Johannesburg. It became a popular church hymn and an anthem at political meetings.

During the apartheid era it was the African National Congress's official anthem and a symbol of the anti-apartheid movement; the regime banned it because of that connection, and many regarded it as the unofficial national anthem, representing the suffering of the oppressed.

The melody and versions of the words were later adopted as national anthems in Africa. A Swahili translation, Mungu ibariki Africa, was first officially performed on 8 December 1961, at the Tanganyika independence celebration in Dar es Salaam, when the Union Jack was lowered and a band played the new anthem. Tanzania still uses it. Zambia used the hymn from independence in 1964 until 1973, when the melody was kept with new words. Zimbabwe used a Shona and Ndebele version from 1980 until 1994, and Namibia used it at independence in March 1990 and replaced it in 1991.

In 1994 President Nelson Mandela declared that both Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika and Die Stem van Suid-Afrika would be national anthems of South Africa. A shortened, combined version was released in 1996 and adopted in 1997, with its first stanza in Xhosa and Zulu, its second in Sesotho, a third in Afrikaans taken from Die Stem and a fourth in English. The anthropologist David Coplan wrote that the hymn symbolised, more than any other expressive work, the struggle for African unity and liberation in South Africa. It has been recorded by Paul Simon, Miriam Makeba and Ladysmith Black Mambazo, among others.
nkvd: After the February Revolution of 1917 the Provisional Government dissolved the tsarist police, and after the October Revolution the Bolshevik government turned the Ministry of Internal Affairs into the People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs, the NKVD. Overwhelmed by its inherited duties, the government set up a secret political police, the Cheka, on 20 December 1917 under Felix Dzerzhinsky, with the right to hold quick non-judicial trials and executions. The Cheka was reorganised in 1922 as the State Political Directorate and then as the OGPU. In 1934 the NKVD became an all-Union body and absorbed the OGPU as its Main Directorate for State Security, taking over the Gulag camps and the regular police.

Genrikh Yagoda headed the NKVD from 1934 to 1936, Nikolai Yezhov from 1936 to 1938 and Lavrentiy Beria from 1938 to 1946. Under Yezhov the Great Purge reached its height: in 1937 and 1938 alone at least 1.3 million people were arrested and 681,692 were executed for crimes against the state, and the Gulag population grew by 685,201. Most of those executed were formally convicted by troikas, special tribunals, on very low standards of evidence, and the use of torture was sanctioned. Secret plans set quotas of victims by region, and under Order no. 00486 of 1937 the families of the repressed, including children, were also repressed. The Polish Operation of 1937 and 1938 alone resulted in the execution of 111,091 Poles.

During World War II the NKVD deported hundreds of thousands of Poles, Balts and Romanians and millions of people of ethnic minorities from the Caucasus, causing millions of deaths. Its Internal Troops, which grew from 15 rifle divisions to 53 divisions and 28 brigades, defended the rear and fought at Stalingrad. It also killed Polish prisoners in 1940, including in the Katyn massacre, and assassinated Leon Trotsky in Mexico City in 1940. In March 1946 the commissariats became ministries and the NKVD became the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the MVD.

After Stalin's death in 1953 Nikita Khrushchev halted the NKVD purges, and from the 1950s to the 1980s thousands of victims were rehabilitated, often with the formula that evidence of a crime was lacking rather than that they were cleared of all charges. Very few NKVD agents were ever convicted of violating anyone's rights. The labour of the Gulag contributed to the Soviet planned economy, and the NKVD also ran sharashkas, special prisons where imprisoned scientists and engineers such as Sergey Korolev and Andrei Tupolev continued their work.
nkvd-order-no-00447: The order set up troikas at the level of the republics and of the krai and oblast regions, and named their members personally. The chairman was the chief of the local NKVD, such as the People's Commissar of a republican NKVD; the prosecutor of the republic or region usually sat on the troika, or could attend its sessions; the third member was usually the regional Communist Party secretary. Operative groups were to investigate in a speedy and simplified way and deliver their results to the troikas, whose protocols went back to the operative groups for the sentences to be carried out.

The order also set upper limits for each territory and each category of social class. The Byelorussian SSR, for example, was given 2,000 people in Category I and 10,000 in Category II, 12,000 anti-Soviet elements in all. Article III of the order fixed the start of the operation for 5 August 1937 and gave it a term of four months.

The limits were described as estimates that could not be exceeded without Yezhov's personal approval, but that approval was easy to obtain, and the first limits were overrun by orders of magnitude. By 15 August 1937, 101,000 people had been arrested and 14,000 convicted. On 23 July 1938 the Omsk NKVD chief, Gorbach, asked for a higher limit of thousands more executions because his men had already fulfilled their plan; Stalin approved it personally and promoted him to a larger district. By the autumn of 1937 the pressure for arrests was such that interrogators picked names from the telephone directory, or chose married men with children, who were known to confess quickest.

After the order, First Category and Second Category became standard abbreviations in NKVD documents for the highest measure of punishment and for placing in corrective labour camps. The operation was part of the wider Great Purge, in which the system of repression was by 1939 bursting at the seams.
nkvd-troika: The first troika, set up in 1918 under the Cheka, was made up of Felix Dzerzhinsky, Yakov Peters and the Left SR Vyacheslav Aleksandrovich. Its three members acted as ad hoc judges, and defendants were usually not entitled to legal aid or the presumption of innocence. Members reached their verdicts by common sense and socialist revolutionary principles, convictions recorded little more than the charge and the sentence, and the outcome was often fixed in advance by target numbers of people to be executed or sent to the Gulag camps.

A troika for West Siberia, decreed by the Politburo on 28 June 1937 to look for a plot linked to the ROVS, a group of White officers based in Paris, was a first step towards NKVD Order No. 00447, signed by Nikolai Yezhov by 30 July 1937. It set up troikas at the level of republic, krai and oblast. Operative groups investigated in a speedy and simplified way and passed the cases to the troika, chaired by the regional NKVD chief and usually including the prosecutor and the regional party secretary.

The order named every member, but many were themselves repressed during the purge, so the troikas' staff changed over time. Sentences went back to the operative groups to be carried out, and the times and places of executions were kept secret. The troikas were set up for four months but worked for about a year.

Order No. 00485 of 11 August 1937, against the Polish Military Organization, became the model for the National Operations against the Soviet Union's German, Finnish, Latvian, Estonian, Romanian, Greek and Chinese diasporas, and from 15 September 1938 special troikas took over cases that two-man commissions had left unheard. By NKVD figures, troikas sentenced 335,513 people in these operations from July 1937 to November 1938, of whom 247,157, or 73.6%, were shot. Troikas also tried most of the around 60 senior staff of the Agro-Joint who were arrested, and the Jewish party leadership of Birobidzhan.

In 1940 a troika of Vsevolod Merkulov, Bogdan Kobulov and Leonid Bashtakov authorised the Katyn Massacre, the shooting of around 15,000 Polish officers. In 1941 a troika was made responsible for deporting thousands of Germans from the Volga German Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic.
nlakapamux: The Nlakaʼpamux, also written Nlakapamuk, have been known by many names. Besides Thompson, Thompson River Salish and Thompson River people, frontier-era histories and maps wrote the name as Hakamaugh or Klackarpun, and the people were also called the Kootomin, the Couteau or Knife Indians. Their traditional territory, in southern British Columbia, also takes in parts of the North Cascades region of Washington.

They speak an Interior Salishan language, Nlakaʼpamuxtsn, known in English as the Thompson language. The Ashcroft Indian Band uses the variant name Nlʼakapxm, while the Nlakaʼpamux of the Nicola Valley call themselves Scwʼexmx and speak a dialect of that name. With the Spaxomin, a branch of the Okanagan people (Syilx) of the upper Nicola Valley, they are known together as the Nicola people.

In the nineteenth century the Nlakaʼpamux were the object of both Anglican and Roman Catholic missions, and by the beginning of the twentieth century the great majority belonged to one of the two churches. Among their traditional foods, blueberries are used in pies, and the leaves of sedge served as brushes for cleaning and as forage for livestock.

Their communities are organised as bands grouped in tribal councils. The Nlakaʼpamux Nation Tribal Council, which despite its name does not include all Nlakaʼpamux, brings together bands such as Boothroyd, Boston Bar, Spuzzum and Skuppah. The Scwʼexmx Tribal Council, originally the Nicola Tribal Association, includes the Shackan, Nooaitch and Coldwater bands, together with the Upper Nicola Band, a Syilx community of the Okanagan Nation Alliance. Other bands, among them Ashcroft, Kanaka Bar, Lower Nicola, Siska and Cook's Ferry, belong to neither. The Lytton First Nation, centred on the town of Lytton, called Camchin or Kumsheen in their language, is one of the largest Nlakaʼpamux communities.
nnamdi-azikiwe: Nnamdi Azikiwe was born on 16 November 1904 at Zungeru in Northern Nigeria. His first name is Igbo and means my father is alive. His father, a clerk in the British administration, came from Onitsha, and his mother was descended from a royal family there. He grew up speaking Hausa, learned Igbo in Onitsha and Yoruba in Lagos. In the United States, where he was known as Ben Azikiwe, he studied at Storer College, Columbia University, the University of Pennsylvania and Howard University, and he competed in athletics, boxing and other sports.

He returned to Africa in 1934 and worked as a journalist in the Gold Coast, advocating Nigerian and African nationalism. After he backed the general strike of June 1945, publication of his paper, the West African Pilot, was suspended for a month. He warned of an assassination plot and went into hiding, and his circulation rose, though some Yoruba politicians doubted the story. When Herbert Macaulay died, Azikiwe took over the NCNC, the nationalist party, and led its delegation to London against Governor Arthur Richards's constitution. He became premier of the Eastern Region in 1954, and his government founded the African Continental Bank, the first indigenous Nigerian bank.

Parliament passed the Nigerian Independence Act on 29 July 1960, and Azikiwe served as governor-general until 1963. When the Federal Republic was established on 1 October 1963, the constitution deemed him elected president, a ceremonial head of state beside Prime Minister Abubakar Tafawa Balewa. The census dispute and the December 1964 election, marked by boycotts, rigging and violence, broke the coalition of the NPC and the NCNC, and for several days Azikiwe refused to call Balewa to form a government.

In 1966 a military coup on 29 July brought Yakubu Gowon to power. Azikiwe died on 11 May 1996. He is widely regarded as the father of Nigerian nationalism, and his ideas, called Zikism, rest on five canons: spiritual balance, social regeneration, economic determinism, mental emancipation and political resurgence.
nobel-peace-prize: Alfred Nobel died in 1896 and left no explanation for adding a peace prize. According to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, his friendship with the peace activist Bertha von Suttner, herself later a recipient, profoundly influenced the decision. Some Nobel scholars suggest it was his way of compensating for developing destructive forces: his inventions included dynamite and ballistite, and he helped turn Bofors into an armaments company.

A well-known story that a French newspaper printed a premature obituary in 1888 calling him the merchant of death is reportedly apocryphal. His will says the prize goes to whoever has done the most or the best work for fraternity between nations, for the abolition or reduction of standing armies and for the holding and promotion of peace congresses.

The Norwegian Parliament appoints the five-member Norwegian Nobel Committee, which chooses the laureate. Each year the committee invites qualified people to nominate, among them members of national assemblies and governments, certain university professors and previous laureates. The statutes bar publication of information about nominations for 50 years, so the label 'Nobel Peace Prize nominee' has no official standing; in 1939 a Swedish parliamentarian made a satirical nomination of Adolf Hitler, mocking a serious one of Neville Chamberlain.

The prize is presented on 10 December, the anniversary of Nobel's death, in the presence of the King of Norway, and is the only Nobel Prize not presented in Stockholm. The 1901 prize was 150,782 Swedish kronor. The medal, designed by Gustav Vigeland, shows three men in a fraternal bond.

The International Committee of the Red Cross has won three times, in 1917, 1944 and 1963, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees twice, in 1954 and 1981. Lê Đức Thọ is the only person to have declined the prize. The 1973 award to Henry Kissinger and Lê Đức Thọ may have been the most disputed: two members of the selection committee resigned in protest.

Mahatma Gandhi was nominated in 1937, 1938, 1939, 1947 and just days before his assassination in January 1948, but never won; in 1948 the committee made no award, on the grounds that there was no suitable living candidate. When the Dalai Lama received the prize in 1989, the chairman called it in part a tribute to Gandhi's memory.
nobel-prize: Alfred Nobel was born on 21 October 1833 in Stockholm into a family of engineers. He was a chemist, engineer and inventor who amassed a fortune from 355 inventions, dynamite among them. In 1894 he purchased the Bofors iron and steel mill, which he made into a major armaments manufacturer. A popular story holds that in 1888 he read his own obituary, titled The Merchant of Death Is Dead, in a French newspaper, when it was in fact his brother Ludvig who had died, and that this inspired him to change his will. Historians have been unable to verify the story, and some dismiss it as a myth.

Nobel died on 10 December 1896 in his villa in San Remo, Italy, of a cerebral haemorrhage, aged 63. His last will was signed in Paris on 27 November 1895. To widespread astonishment it specified that his fortune be used for prizes to those who confer the most benefit on mankind in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and peace. He left 94 per cent of his assets, 31 million SEK, to establish the five prizes. Because of scepticism about the will, the Storting in Norway did not approve it until 26 April 1897, and its executors, Ragnar Sohlman and Rudolf Lilljequist, formed the Nobel Foundation.

The prizes were first awarded in 1901. A sixth prize, in Economic Sciences, was established in 1968 by Sveriges Riksbank in memory of Alfred Nobel and has been awarded since 1969. Except in special circumstances such as war, all are given annually. Each laureate receives a medal, a diploma and a monetary award. No more than three individuals may share a prize, though the Peace Prize can go to organisations. Prizes are not awarded posthumously, but one is presented if its winner dies after being named.

The process is similar for all prizes. Nomination forms go to about 3,000 individuals, generally prominent academics, with the deadline on 31 January. The committee nominates about 300 potential laureates, and nominees are not named publicly or told, and all nomination records are sealed for 50 years.

Four institutions choose the laureates by majority vote, and their decision cannot be appealed: the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences for chemistry, physics and economics, the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute for physiology or medicine, the Swedish Academy for literature and the Norwegian Nobel Committee for peace. Winners are announced during the first two weeks of October.
nobi: Nobi status passed mainly by inheritance, but people also became nobi as a legal punishment for a crime or for failing to pay a debt. Some entered it of their own will to escape crushing poverty in poor harvests and famines, or to be released from taxation and military service, most of all in the late 18th century, when Joseon suffered severe poverty. Nobi were made within Korean society, not through the conquest of other peoples, and were of the same ethnicity as their owners. Their status was justified by a supposed moral stain, often the idea that they descended from criminals.

Nobi were divided into kongnobi, owned by the state, and sanobi, owned privately. Household nobi served as personal retainers and domestic servants, and most received a monthly salary that they could add to by work outside their hours; non-resident nobi, far more numerous, lived at a distance and differed little from tenant farmers. Under the chakkae system a nobi was given two pieces of land, the produce of one going to the master and of the other to the nobi. Freedom could be bought, earned through military service or granted by the government. Some nobi owned nobi of their own.

Most nobi had no surname, a great stigma in Joseon society, and some bore degrading names symbolising dogs, pigs or excrement. At the same time the owner, as the legal father of his nobi, was responsible for feeding and clothing them, and the bond between a yangban master and his nobi was likened to the Confucian relation of ruler and subject, or father and son; nobi were called the yangban's sujok, hands and feet. Because some had property and civil rights, some scholars argue that they should not be called slaves, while others describe them as serfs. The Korean word for a slave in the European and American sense is noye.

In 1426 Sejong the Great granted kongnobi women 100 days of maternity leave after childbirth, lengthened in 1430 by a month before the birth, and in 1434 he granted their husbands 30 days of paternity leave. The Annals of King Taejong state that the nobi is also a human being and should be treated generously. During the Imjin War (1592–1597) sanobi carried out important and dangerous tasks, searching for their owners' separated family members and carrying news of the war to their masters.
nobles-of-the-robe: As a rule an office of the robe did not itself carry a title such as baron or viscount, though a holder might have one, and it was almost always tied to a particular function. Together with the older nobility, the Nobles of the Robe formed the Second Estate. Nobles of the Sword, whose rank rested on their families' knightly past and on fiefs held for military service, often considered them inferior, and commoners mocked them as the nobility of the pen and ink.

By the mid-17th century the two groups had blended so far that a single family often had both kinds of noble. A common strategy was to send a second or third son into the church while the elder sons pursued a career in the robe or the army. A new untitled noble who wanted to become a baron or viscount had to buy a fief and add its name to his own: Antoine Crozat, from a wealthy family of commoners, bought the barony of Thiers in 1714 for 200,000 livres.

Because the offices were sold, they were at first relatively easy to obtain. In the 17th century a councillor's seat in a parlement cost 100,000 livres, but by the mid-18th century its value had halved as the offices multiplied. The descendants of those first ennobled for service fought to limit entry to the class, and they protested strongly whenever the crown, short of money, created large numbers of new posts in the bureaucracy to raise revenue.

In the 18th century nobility through a judicial office became practically closed. Other offices were still for sale: a secrétaire-conseiller du roi gained first-degree nobility at once and hereditary nobility after 20 years. The post cost 120,000 livres in 1773 but was a sinecure with no conditions or duties, and the old nobility scorned it as a savonette à vilain, a soap for washing away common birth.

The Nobles of the Robe had key roles in the French Enlightenment, Montesquieu among its earliest figures. The elite of the class, above all the members of the parlements, had long struggled to keep their standing beside the Nobles of the Sword, and the abolition of the parlements and the lower courts in 1790, during the French Revolution, ended the basis of their rank.
nobody-knows-the-trouble-ive-seen: The Child at Home presented the song as a specimen of the hymns sung by the freedmen of the South, sent in by a teacher working at Charleston, South Carolina. Its chorus ran: Nobody knows de trubble I see, Nobody knows but Jesus; Nobody knows de trubble I see, Sing, Glory, Halleloo! In May 1866 The Pennsylvania Freedmen's Bulletin reported it sung at a school near Beaufort, South Carolina, and in 1867 it appeared with four verses as Nobody Knows The Trouble I've Had in Slave Songs of the United States.

The text sets private suffering against faith. Its verses turn on the lines Sometimes I'm up, sometimes I'm down and I have my trials here below, each answered by Oh, yes, Lord, and the singer asks anyone who reaches Heaven first to tell his friends that he is coming. The second line of the chorus, often sung today as Nobody knows my sorrow, reads Nobody knows but Jesus in the earliest versions, and that form is the one most often printed in American church hymnals. The Jubilee Singers sang a different song with a similar chorus, first published in 1872.

The spiritual entered concert music through arrangements by Black composers. J. Rosamond Johnson set it for voice and piano in 1917, while directing the New York Music School Settlement for Colored People, and for violin and piano in 1919 at the suggestion of the violinist Maud Powell. Hugo Frey used the 1867 version in a collection published by Robbins Music in 1924, and Florence Price quoted it in her Mississippi River Suite of 1934.

Marian Anderson had her first successful recording with it on the Victor label in 1925, and Louis Armstrong, Paul Robeson, Mahalia Jackson, Lena Horne and Sam Cooke were among the many who recorded it. Michael Tippett made it one of the five spirituals of his oratorio A Child of Our Time, first performed in 1944, and it was sung in films from Roberto Rossellini's Paisan of 1946 onwards.
nocera-inferiore: At an early date the city became an episcopal see named Nuceria Christianorum, meaning Nocera of the Christians. In the 12th century it sided with Pope Innocent II against Roger II of Sicily and suffered severely for the choice; the castle on the hill of Sant'Andrea was destroyed by Roger's troops in 1138. In the 13th century the town became known as Nocera dei Pagani, Nocera of the pagans, because Frederick II introduced a colony of Muslim Saracens into the annexed territory of present-day Pagani. One account describes it as a Muslim town with its mosques and minarets, and it is said that the townsfolk's complexion and features preserve the settlers' heritage.

The castle held several prisoners and guests. Helena, the widow of Manfred of Sicily, was imprisoned there and died after the Battle of Benevento in 1268. In 1385 Pope Urban VI was besieged in the castle by Charles III of Naples, and he imprisoned there the cardinals who favoured the Antipope Clement VII. The writers Dante Alighieri and Boccaccio were also guests.

From the end of the 15th century until 1806 the town carried the epithet Nuceria Paganorum. In 1806 Nocera dei Pagani, which had been divided into seven boroughs, was split into five separate comuni: Nocera Inferiore, Nocera Superiore, Pagani, Sant'Egidio and Corbara. The two Noceras were distinguished by their height above sea level, and Inferiore, the lower one, took its name from this.

Nocera Inferiore is a town and comune in the province of Salerno, in Campania, lying west of Nocera Superiore at the foot of Monte Albino, some 35 km east-southeast of Naples by rail. Some of the necropoleis of the ancient city of Nuceria Alfaterna lay in its area.

Its monuments include the cathedral of San Prisco and San Marco, the Church of San Matteo, the Convent of San Giovanni in Parco, the Church of Sant'Angelo in grotta, the monastery of Santa Chiara and the sanctuary of Santa Maria dei Miracoli. The city's arms show a walnut tree with golden fruits and the words Urbs Nuceria. Its notable people include the poet Jacopo Sannazzaro and the Baroque painter Francesco Solimena.
nodira: Nodira, also spelled Nadira, was a poet of the Khanate of Kokand. Her birth name was Mahlar-ayim. Nadera was her pen name, used along with Kamila in her Chagatai poems, and in her Persian poems she wrote as Maknuna.

She was born in Andijan, which was governed by her father Rahmanqulibi, the uncle of the sixth ruler of Kokand, Alim Khan, who reigned from 1801 to 1810. In 1808 she was married to Alim Khan's brother Muhammad Umar Khan, and the couple had two children, Muhammad Ali Khan and Sultan-Mahmud.

Her writings, numbering nearly 10,000 verses, include a divan, a collection of poetry, with 136 poems in Chagatai and 44 in Persian. She taught the works of authors such as Ali-Shir Nava'i, Fuzuli and Abd al-Qadir Bedil. The modern historian Scott C. Levi names Nadira as the best known of Khoqand's women poets. At the court of Kokand she brought together other prominent poets, among them Jahonotin Uvaysiy, Mahzuna and Dilshad Barna.

After the death of her husband in 1822 she played an important role in court politics and state affairs during the reign of her son Muhammad Ali Khan. She also promoted cultural and social development by sponsoring mosques, madrasas and bazaars. In 1842 the Emirate of Bukhara captured the capital, Kokand, and its ruler had Nodira and her sons executed.
noe-zhordania: Noe Zhordania was born on 15 January 1868 into a family of petty landowners in the village of Lanchkhuti in Guria, western Georgia, then part of the Kutais Governorate of Imperial Russia. His father Niko was the village scribe, a lawyer and a court mediator, and his mother, Kristine Chikovani, was Mingrelian. He studied at the Ozurgeti Orthodox Theological Academy and then at the Georgian Orthodox Theological Seminary in Tbilisi. His parents hoped he would become a priest, but from an early age he disbelieved in God, and he came to regard the tsar's claim to rule by divine appointment as groundless.

In the 1890s Zhordania became a leader of the first legal Marxist organisation in Georgia, the Mesame Dasi, which in 1894 published a programme in the journal Moambe. Fearing arrest, he left for Europe in May 1893. In Geneva he met Georgi Plekhanov, Leo Deutsch and Vera Zasulich, and he later studied in Paris, Stuttgart, where he met Karl Kautsky, and Munich. He wrote for the journal Kvali.

Back in the Russian Empire during the revolution of 1905, he edited the clandestine newspaper Social Democrat and the legal Skhivi. He took part in the congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in Stockholm in 1906 and was elected to the State Duma, where he led the Social Democratic faction until the Duma was dissolved after about a month.

After the February Revolution of 1917 he chaired the Tbilisi soviet. On 3 September 1917 he urged workers not to yield to Bolshevik sentiment but to fight for a parliamentary republic. From 26 November 1917 he chaired the Presidium of the National Council of Georgia, and in May 1918 he headed the parliamentary session that declared the independent Democratic Republic of Georgia.

Zhordania headed the government from 24 July 1918 until 18 March 1921, when the invasion of the Red Army forced him into exile in France. In Istanbul he met French ambassadors, who invited him to settle the government in exile in France, but he was not warmly welcomed there in April 1921, and later appeals in Brussels and London found no interest. He lived in Paris and then in Leuville-sur-Orge, where he helped prepare the Georgian revolt of 1924. He criticised the Soviet Union in books and founded the journals Battle and Our Flag. He led the government in exile until his death on 11 January 1953.
noemvriana: Greece stayed neutral when the First World War began, but its leadership was divided. Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos favoured Britain and the Allies, while King Constantine I, educated in Germany and married to Sophia of Prussia, sister of Kaiser Wilhelm II, wanted a neutrality that suited the Central Powers. In May 1916 the border fortress of Roupel was surrendered to German and Bulgarian forces, and the Allies suspected a secret understanding between Athens and the Central Powers. After a military uprising of pro-Venizelos officers in Thessaloniki, Venizelos, Admiral Pavlos Kountouriotis and General Panagiotis Danglis formed a provisional government there in October 1916, splitting the country in two.

The king secretly agreed on 23 October with the French deputy Paul Bénazet to hand over war materiel, but abandoned the agreement under pressure from his military advisers. On 24 November Vice Admiral Louis Dartige du Fournet gave Athens seven days to surrender at least ten mountain artillery batteries.

A French and British force of 2,500 marines under Captain Henri Pugliesi-Conti, ordered to avoid violence, landed at Piraeus and found its positions around Athens already held by Greek troops. After a rifle shot of unknown origin, fighting spread through the city, and the Allied squadron at Phaliron shelled areas near the stadium and the palace. The king agreed to give up six batteries, and by the early morning of 2 December the Allied troops had gone. Historian George Leon counts 194 Allied and 82 Greek dead and wounded, not counting civilians.

Royalist reservists, with arrests ordered under Generals Konstantinos Kallaris and Anastasios Papoulas, then ransacked the homes and shops of Venizelists: Leon gives 35 murdered and 980 expelled from Athens, Giannis Mourelos 14 civilians killed and 922 imprisoned across Greece, among them the mayor of Athens, Emmanuel Benakis.

On 2 December Britain and France recognised Venizelos's government as the only lawful government of Greece, and on 25 December the Archbishop of Athens, under pressure from the palace, anathematised Venizelos. Du Fournet was relieved of his command, and in Britain H. H. Asquith gave way to Lloyd George, an admirer of Venizelos. Venizelos returned to Athens on 25 June 1917, and a united Greece joined the war; by autumn 1918 its 150,000 soldiers were the largest part of the Allied army on the Macedonian front, which earned Greece a seat at the Paris Peace Conference.
nogais: The Nogais are a Turkic people who speak Nogai, a language of the Kipchak branch. Their name comes from Nogai Khan, who died in 1299 or 1300, a general of the Golden Horde and a great-great-grandson of Genghis Khan, who was de facto ruler and kingmaker of the Horde and briefly proclaimed himself khan. The Nogais descend from Mongolic and Turkic tribes that formed the Nogai Horde, of which a Mongol tribe called the Manghits was the core. They originated as nomadic tribes in Central Asia and moved west after the Golden Horde conquered them in the 13th century.

The Nogai Horde supported the Astrakhan Khanate, and after the Russians conquered Astrakhan in 1556 it turned to the Crimean Khanate. The Nogais guarded its northern borders and, through raids into the Wild Fields, hindered Slavic settlement. A split came when Yusuf Mirza favoured the Ottomans while his brother Ismail Mirza, Bey of the Nogai Horde from 1555 to 1563, allied with the Russians. Yusuf's followers went to Crimea and Yedisan, and about 1630 the Kalmyks reached the Volga and expelled the Nogais from their homeland.

After the Russian annexation of Crimea in 1783, settlers occupied Nogai pastures. Catherine the Great resettled about 120,000 Nogais in the 1770s and 1780s, and the general Alexander Suvorov slaughtered thousands of rebellious Kuban Nogais in 1783. The government forced the rest to settle by burning their tents and limiting their movement. The great exodus came in 1860, when 50,000 of some 70,000 Nogais of Kuban and Stavropol left Russia for the Ottoman Empire.

The Nogais raised herds and migrated seasonally in search of pasture, and were proud of nomadic traditions that they thought superior to settled farming. There are nine main groups, among them the Ak Nogai, Karagash and Bug-Nogai. Most live in northern Dagestan and Stavropol Krai, with others in Karachay-Cherkessia, Chechnya and Astrakhan Oblast and smaller communities in Dobruja, Turkey and Kazakhstan. Those in Turkey have kept dishes such as üken börek and a tea boiled with milk, butter, salt and pepper.
nogent-le-rotrou: Nogent-le-Rotrou was the former capital of the Perche. The count lived in the Château Saint-Jean, which still dominates the town from the plateau that bears its name; its keep dates from the first half of the 11th century. The second part of the town's name comes from Rotrou I, Count of Perche.

Early in the 17th century the overlordship of the town was acquired by the Duke of Sully, financial minister of Henry IV. A small building in the courtyard of the hospital, which was originally founded at the end of the 12th century, holds the tomb of Sully and his wife.

Nogent-le-Rotrou is a commune and sub-prefecture of the department of Eure-et-Loir, on the river Huisne, 56 kilometres west of Chartres and 150 kilometres south-west of Paris, to which it is linked by rail and motorway. It lies in the Perche, at the heart of a large agricultural zone, and until the late 1970s many of its jobs were tied to farming. Industrial employment in the 1980s and 1990s owed much to the motor industry, and since 1978 the town has been the base of one of France's three civil defence units.

Besides the château, the town preserves three Gothic churches and the remains of the old priory of St Denis. Statues honour General St Pol, killed at the siege of Sevastopol, and the poet Rémy Belleau, a native of the town. Others connected with it include the painter and children's writer Clara Filleul (1822–1878), the social psychologist Gustave Le Bon and Mathilde Mauté, the wife of the poet Paul Verlaine.
noin-ula: The site lies by the Selenga River in Batsumber sum of Töv Province and holds more than 200 large mounds, roughly square and some 2 m high, over timber burial chambers. The Russian geologist Andrei Ballod came upon it in the spring of 1913 while surveying for a gold-mining company and sent finds to the Imperial Russian Geological Society, but the First World War and the revolutions in Russia and Mongolia delayed further work. In 1924 a member of Ballod's team told Pyotr Kozlov, who, after Sergei Kondratiev confirmed the find, opened eight mounds. Most of the objects are now in the Hermitage Museum, and later Mongolian finds are in the National Museum of Mongolian History in Ulaanbaatar.

The tombs were opened in antiquity and the bodies taken out. Han chronicles relate that leaders of a nomad people once oppressed by the Xiongnu desecrated the tombs of the chanyus about 100 years after the Xiongnu decline, removing their remains with clothing, weapons and symbols of rule. Kurgan No 6 was the tomb of Wuzhuliu, who reigned from 8 BCE to 13 CE and freed his people from a Chinese protectorate that had lasted from 47 BCE to 9 CE. His burial is dated to 13 CE by the inscription on a cup the Chinese emperor gave him at a reception in the Shanlin park near Chang'an in 1 BCE.

Like some graves of the Pazyryk culture, the chambers had flooded and then frozen, preserving organic material. The robbers left Xiongnu weapons, household goods and art in the Scythian animal style, Chinese bronze, nephrite and lacquered wood, and textiles, some of them Greek in their weaving and embroidery. Four kurgans held lacquer cups inscribed, it is believed, with the names of Chinese craftsmen, dated between 9 and 2 BCE. One richly furnished tomb had a coffin apparently made in China and a saddle threaded with wool clipped to look like velvet. Sergey Yatsenko holds that the embroidered portrait carpets were made by the Yuezhi in Bactria.
nokalakevi: Nokalakevi, locally Nokalaku in Mingrelian, is a village and archaeological site in the Senaki municipality of the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region. Georgian chroniclers of Kartli called it Tsikhegoji, the fortress of Kuji, a Colchian ruler or eristavi. The ruins cover about 20 hectares on the Tekhuri River at the northern edge of the Colchian plain, 15 km from Senaki on the Martvili road, where they commanded a crossing of the river and a route through the hills to Chkhorotsqu. The defences use a loop of the river, which has cut a limestone gorge to the west, and the steep ground to the north made the citadel there almost unassailable.

A wall joined this upper town to a lower town, where excavations have revealed stone buildings of the 4th to 6th centuries. Beneath these late Roman layers lie several earlier phases of occupation and abandonment from the 8th to the 2nd centuries BCE. In the 6th century the fortress was one of the keys to the defence of Lazika, modern Mingrelia, against Sasanian Persian and Iberian attack. In the war of 540 to 562 the Persians' failure to take it from the Byzantines and the Laz eventually cost them control of Lazika.

The Swiss philologist Frédéric Dubois de Montpéreux visited in 1833-4, identified the ruins as Archaeopolis and argued that they were also Aia, the Colchian capital of the Argonaut myth. In the winter of 1930-31 a German-Georgian team under Alfonse-Maria Schneider of Freiburg University traced the walls and dug about 40 trenches; a hoard of gold solidi of Emperor Maurice confirmed the identification with Archaeopolis but not with Aia, which most scholars still place at Kutaisi.

A state expedition under Parmen Zakaraia excavated and conserved the site from 1973 until the early 1990s, when the collapse of the Soviet Union and the civil disturbances that followed Georgian independence cut its funding. Large-scale work resumed in 2001 with a joint project founded by David Lomitashvili of the S. Janashia State History Museum and Ian Colvin of Cambridge University; the Anglo-Georgian Expedition to Nokalakevi marked its twentieth anniversary in 2020.
nokia: Nokia's history dates from 1865, when the mining engineer Fredrik Idestam established a pulp mill on the shores of the Tammerkoski rapids near Tampere, then in the Grand Duchy of Finland under Russian rule. A second mill opened in 1868 near the neighbouring town of Nokia, where hydropower was better. In 1871 Idestam and his friend Leo Mechelin formed a shared company and called it Nokia Ab, after the site of the second mill.

In 1967 three companies, Nokia, Kaapelitehdas and Finnish Rubber Works, merged to create a new Nokia Corporation, organised in four businesses: forestry, cable, rubber and electronics. In the early 1970s it entered the networking and radio industries, and it also made military equipment for Finland's defence forces.

After Simo Vuorilehto became chief executive in 1988, units judged not strategic were sold. Nokian Tyres split away in 1988 and Finnish Rubber Works followed in 1990. Finland was then in its worst recession in living memory, and the collapse of the Soviet Union, a major customer, made matters worse. Since the 1990s the company has focused on telecommunications infrastructure, and it helped develop the GSM, 3G and LTE standards.

For a decade from 1998 Nokia was the largest vendor of mobile phones and smartphones in the world. At its peak, in 2000, it accounted for 4 per cent of Finland's gross domestic product and 21 per cent of the country's exports, and Finns viewed it with national pride. In the later 2000s it lost market share sharply after a series of poor management decisions. On 10 September 2010 Olli-Pekka Kallasvuo was dismissed as chief executive and Stephen Elop of Microsoft took the post, the first non-Finnish head in the company's history.

In 2014 Microsoft bought Nokia's mobile phone business. Nokia then concentrated on network equipment through Nokia Networks and took over Alcatel-Lucent, including its Bell Labs research organisation, in 2016. In the same year the Nokia brand returned to phones through a licensing arrangement with HMD Global, a company in Espoo founded by former Nokia employees. Nokia is the oldest company listed under the same name on the Helsinki stock exchange, where it has been listed since 1915.
noman-celebicihan: Noman Çelebicihan was born in 1885 in the village of Büyük Sonaq, in the Chonhar region of Crimea near the present-day city of Dzhankoy; the village no longer exists. His father, İbraim Çelebi, belonged to a well-to-do Crimean Tatar family, as did his mother, a daughter of Cihanşah Çelebi. After his first schooling in the village, his uncles helped send him to the Gülümbey Medrese, and later he went on to Constantinople to continue his education.

He arrived in Istanbul in 1908, attended the Vefa Lisesi and then law school, and lived in the Karagümrük quarter among a small group of Crimean Tatar students. In 1910 he and his friend Abibulla Temircan founded the Young Tatar Writers' Association, and he published early works such as Qarılğaçlar Duası (Swallows' Prayer) and Altın Yarıq (Golden Light). He was among the founders of the Crimean Tatar Student Association and of Vatan (Homeland), which became the seed of the Milliy Fırqa, the National Party.

Back in Crimea after his law studies, he was elected to represent the Or region in the Crimean Tatar Qurultay, where his youth and Istanbul education made him one of the most popular delegates. In 1917 he founded the Milliy Fırqa. He was also Mufti of Crimea, Lithuania and Poland, and a poet: besides Ant Etkenmen (I've Pledged), which became the words of the national anthem, his best-remembered poem is Savlıqman Qal Tatarlıq! (Farewell Tatarness!), which he wrote on the walls of the Simferopol railway station on his way to military service in the First World War.

In January 1918, barely two months after the Qurultay had chosen him to lead the Crimean People's Republic, Bolshevik forces invaded Crimea. He was arrested and imprisoned in Sevastopol, and on 23 February 1918 a firing squad of the Black Sea Fleet executed him and threw his body into the sea, without the Islamic burial rites. Crimean Tatars still remember him as a hero, and his death during the Russian Civil War is commemorated among them. The Noman Çelebicihan Battalion is named after him.
nomenklatura: Vladimir Lenin wrote that appointments should weigh reliability, political attitude, qualifications and administrative ability. Joseph Stalin, the party's first general secretary, was known as Comrade File Cabinet (Tovarishch Kartotekov) for his attention to appointments. In 1922, under his direction, the party created departments of the Central Committee and lower organs, known as uchraspred, to register and appoint party officials. The historian Richard Pipes argued that the system mainly continued the old Tsarist regime, since many former Tsarist officials joined the Bolshevik government during and after the Russian Civil War of 1917–1922.

Every party committee, from Moscow down to the district and city levels, prepared two lists. The basic list (osnovnoi spisok) detailed the posts in the political, administrative, economic, military, cultural and educational bureaucracies that it was responsible for filling, and the registration list (uchyotny spisok) named the people suitable for them. At the all-union level the Party Building and Cadre Work Department supervised appointments and kept records on party members. Virtually all members of the nomenklatura belonged to a communist party.

According to the American Sovietologist Seweryn Bialer, the party considerably expanded its appointment authority after Leonid Brezhnev took power in October 1964, while in the late 1980s some official statements indicated an intention to reduce it, particularly in economic management, in line with Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms.

Milovan Đilas, in The New Class, wrote that ordinary citizens saw the nomenklatura as a bureaucratic elite with special privileges that had supplanted the earlier capitalist elites. China adopted the system from the Soviet Union in the 1960s. A plan of 1983 proposed halving the number of centrally managed cadres from 13,000 to 7,000, and since 1984 two lists have divided the Central Committee's control: about 5,000 senior positions needing its approval, and tens of thousands of lower ones reported to it.
nominoe: Nominoe was the second son of Count Erispoe of Poher, and his elder brother was Count Riwallon of Poher. After a general rebellion in the Carolingian Empire was put down, an assembly was held at Ingelheim in May 831, where Louis the Pious probably appointed him to rule the Bretons, which meant almost all of Brittany. His power base was the Vannetais, and two charters call him Count of Vannes. He remained a staunch ally of Louis until the emperor's death in 840 and backed Redon Abbey.

The title Duke of Brittany is mainly a chronicler's invention of the tenth century. The emperor called him only fidelis or missus imperatoris, and Breton charters gave him many titles, among them master, prince and duke.

Relations with Charles the Bald were at first friendly. In spring 841 Nominoe agreed to submit to him, and later that year he rebuffed Lothair I, who claimed Neustria. Breton soldiers took part in the Oaths of Strasbourg. In summer 843, however, Lothair or his supporter Lambert II of Nantes persuaded him to change sides, and he became an enemy of Charles. In June 844 he raided Maine while Charles besieged Toulouse. At the synod of Yutz in October 844 the bishops ordered him to renew his fealty to Charles. Lambert and Pepin II of Aquitaine complied, but Nominoe did not, and Charles was defeated at the battle of Ballon on 22 November 845.

In summer 846 Charles marched into Brittany and made peace with Nominoe, and the chronicler Prudentius of Troyes calls him duke for the first time in this context. Nominoe soon resumed raiding Neustria, probably with Lothair's backing. In 849 he held a synod at Coitlouh that deposed five Breton bishops, those of Alet, Saint-Pol, Vannes, Quimper and Dol, and replaced them with his own men. Later popes, among them Nicholas I, held the depositions invalid, and a Frankish synod of 850 accused him of simony. He also sacked Rennes and Nantes, and the Breton church thereby became independent in practice of its metropolitan at Tours.

In 850 Nominoe and Lambert raided Maine together and defeated the garrisons that Charles had placed at Rennes and Nantes. Nominoe died on 7 March 851 near Vendôme while ravaging the Nantais and Anjou, and was buried at Redon Abbey. His son Erispoe, by his wife Argentaela, succeeded him. He founded a political tradition in Brittany that had not existed before, and his successors imitated Carolingian language in their charters. To Breton nationalists he is Tad ar Vro, father of the country.
nonantola-abbey: The abbey stands in the commune of Nonantola, about 10 km north-east of Modena in the Emilia Romagna region. King Aistulf endowed it richly, making it one of the main landowners of northern Italy. Pope Stephen II appointed Anselm its first abbot and gave it relics of Saint Sylvester, to whom it was dedicated as S. Silvestro de Nonantula. After Aistulf's death in 756 the new king, Desiderius, banished Anselm to Monte Cassino, but Charlemagne restored him seven years later.

Its abbots served the emperors: Peter of Nonantola was imperial ambassador to Constantinople in 813, and his successor Ansfrid held the same post in 828. In 883 Charles the Fat and Pope Marinus I met there. In 900 invading Hungarians destroyed the monastery and church and killed everyone who had not fled, but rebuilding began almost at once. Until the 11th century it was an imperial monastery, and emperors and popes contended for control of its abbatial elections.

In the Investiture Conflict it first sided with the emperor, until Matilda of Tuscany forced it to submit to the pope in 1083, and in 1111 it declared openly for the papal party; that year the monk Placidus of Nonantola wrote De honore Ecclesiæ, an important defence of the papal position. Decline began in 1419 under commendatory abbots, among them Giuliano Della Rovere and Carlo Borromeo. Pope Clement XIII suppressed the abbey in 1768, Pope Pius VII restored it as a monastery on 23 January 1821, and the Italian government appropriated the buildings in 1866.

The church, built under Abbot Damian and restored in the early 20th century to its early 12th-century form, has a nave, two aisles and a crypt of sixty-four columns dating from the 8th century. The crypt holds the relics of Saint Anselm, who died on 3 March 803, of Saint Sylvester, Saint Adrian III and other saints. The church is a basilica and the co-cathedral of the Diocese of Modena-Nonantola, formed in 1986. The surviving buildings house the town hall, where 11th-century frescoes were found, a museum of sacred art and the abbey's archives and library.
nongqawuse: Nongqawuse was born near the Gxarha River in independent Xhosaland, close to the border of the newly established colony of British Kaffraria, at a time when European settlers were encroaching on Xhosa lands. Little is known of her parents, who died during the Waterkloof campaigns of the Eighth Frontier War (1850–1853). In a deposition she named her father as Umhlanhla. The orphan was raised by her uncle Mhlakaza, son of a counsellor of the Xhosa King Sarili kaHintsa, a diviner who had spent time in the Cape Colony, learned of Christianity there and returned to Xhosaland in 1853.

In April 1856 Nongqawuse, then 15, went with her friend Nombanda, a girl of between 8 and 10, to scare birds from her uncle's crops in the fields by the mouth of the Gxarha. On her return she told Mhlakaza that she had met the spirits of two ancestors. He doubted her at first, but when she described one of the men he recognised his own dead brother. He became the interpreter and organiser of her visions and carried the prophecy to Sarili. The spirits demanded that all cattle be slaughtered, as reared by contaminated hands, that cultivation cease, that new houses, enclosures and milk sacks be made, and that people abandon witchcraft, incest and adultery.

At the time many Xhosa herds were suffering from lung sickness, possibly brought by European cattle. The killing spread from Sarili's Gcaleka to the whole Xhosa nation, and historians estimate that the Gcaleka killed between 300,000 and 400,000 head of cattle.

Nongqawuse foretold that the promise would be fulfilled on 18 February 1857, when the sun would turn red. When it was not, her followers first blamed the minority who had refused to kill, the amagogotya, then turned against her. By early 1858 about 40,000 people had starved, and the population of British Kaffraria had fallen from 105,000 to fewer than 27,000. The chief of the Bomvana handed her to Major Gawler, at whose home she was photographed with the Mpondo prophetess Nonkosi. She later lived on a farm in the Alexandria district and died in 1898. The valley where she said she met the spirits is still called Intlambo kaNongqawuse.
noor-mahal: Noor Mahal, the Palace of Light, was designed for the princely state of Bahawalpur by its state engineer, an Englishman named Heennan. When the foundation was laid in 1872, a map and coins of the state were buried in it as a good omen. Most of its materials and furniture were brought from England and Italy, and it was finished in 1875 at a cost of Rs. 1.2 million. Nawab Sadiq Khan IV commissioned it for his wife, Noor, but she spent only one night there and would not return, because the Basti Malook Shah graveyard was visible from her balcony; she lived in Darbar Mahal instead.

The palace covers 4,140 square metres and has 32 rooms, 14 of them in the basement, as well as six verandas and five domes. Its design joins Corinthian and Islamic styles with a touch of the subcontinent's own: the Corinthian in the columns, balustrade, pediments and the vaulted ceiling of the Durbar Hall, the Islamic in the five domes, and the subcontinental in its angular elliptical shapes. In 1906 Nawab Muhammad Bahawal Khan the fifth added a mosque to the palace at a cost of Rs. 20,000.

Prince Albert Victor visited the palace on 11 January 1890, and Sir McOrth Beck, a senior finance commissioner of Punjab, stayed there with his family from 22 to 24 December 1892. When Bahawalpur State was merged into Pakistan in 1956, the Auqaf department took the building over. It was leased to the army in 1971 and bought by it in 1997, and in September 2001 the Department of Archeology of the Government of Pakistan declared it a protected monument, open to visitors and school and student trips.
noorbakhshia: The Noorbakhshia, also called Sufia Nurbakhshia, is an offshoot of the Kubruwiya order. Its spiritual lineage, the Silsila-e-Zahab Sufia Nurbakhshia or Golden Chain, is held by its followers to reach back to the Prophet Muhammad through Imam Ali and Ali al-Rida, with Ma'ruf al-Karkhi as the first Qutb of the order. Nurbakhshis believe that their practices are not the personal views of Muhammad Nurbakhsh Qahistani but came to him from the Prophet through the masters of the chain. Although Nurbakhsh had many scholar-disciples, such as Shaikh Asiri Lahiji, none of them wrote down his life or preserved his teachings in full.

Besides a Sufi order, the Noorbakhshia is a school of Islamic jurisprudence. Its basic tenets come from a short treatise by Nurbakhsh, Kitab al-Itiqadiyya, and its law follows his Al-Fiqh al-Ahwat; a third work, Dawat-e-Sufia, is associated with Sayyid Amir Kabir Ali Hamadani, known as Shah-e-Hamadan. Its jurisprudence stresses Muslim unity, discourages declaring other Muslims unbelievers over questions of creed and practice, and aims to remove innovations. Its followers hold Ali to be the first of the saints and the Mahdi the last, and its principles rest on the teachings of the twelve imams.

In Iran the order moved towards Twelver Shi'ism several decades after the Safavid dynasty made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion in 1501. A similar change took place in Kashmir, either in the lifetime of Shams ud-Din Iraqi, who died in 1527, or in the following decades, during the brief rule of the Chak dynasty. There the order declined from the mid-16th century, and persecution by Sunni authorities brought it to an end, its followers absorbed into mainstream Twelver Shi'a Islam.

In Kurdistan, Turkey, Afghanistan and Tajikistan other traditions, mostly the Naqshbandis and Twelver Shias, replaced it. In Baltistan and in Purig in the Kargil district it survived as a distinct sect blending Shi'a and Sunni elements, and its adherents live in Baltistan and in villages of Kargil and the Nubra Valley.
norcia: Norcia was a city of the Sabines, situated very close to Umbrian territory, and tombs in the area contain Italic funerary objects, among them bronze swords, shield disks and fibulae of the 7th century BCE from a necropolis at Ancarano. Its people became Roman citizens toward the middle of the 3rd century BCE, though without full rights until after the Social War. The earliest historical mention is in 205 BCE, when Norcia was one of three Sabine cities that voluntarily supplied soldiers for the army of Scipio. Octavian later punished its citizens for aiding Lucius Antonius in the Perusine War. In the later Roman Empire the town declined and was devastated by the Lombards.

Norcia formed as a free municipality in the 13th century and in the 14th became the leading municipality of the Sibillini Mountains, building its walls in this period. In 1398 Pope Boniface IX granted it the castle of Mevole with the title of marquisate. In the 16th century the Castellina, designed by Vignola and laid out in 1554, was built as the fortified residence of the papal governor after violent unrest, and in 1569 Pope Pius V founded the Prefecture of the Mountain. In the early 17th century the town had a major renewal in building and the arts. It passed to the French Empire in 1809, and papal rule was restored in 1820.

Norcia stands at 603 metres on a plateau near the Monti Sibillini in the province of Perugia, Umbria. Pigs fed on its oak woods made pork processing the chief industry of the inhabitants, and the term norcino for a pork butcher spread as far as Rome; Italian norcineria still names such products.

Tradition holds that the site of the Basilica of San Benedetto, built between 1290 and 1338 over an older crypt, was the birthplace of the twin saints Benedict and Scholastica. A Benedictine monastery stands on the site of their house, with a chapel corresponding to the room where Benedict was born. Pope Gregory I spoke of Benedict as born in the province of Nursia. Earthquakes struck near Norcia on 24 August 2016 and 30 October 2016, causing heavy damage to the city. The Roman cryptoporticus, probably part of the forum, dates from the second half of the 1st century BCE.
nordalbingia: Nordalbingia, in German Nordelbingen, takes its name from Alba, the Latin name of the Elbe, and was one of the four regions of the medieval Duchy of Saxony, beside Angria, Eastphalia and Westphalia. It is the earliest known dominion of the Saxons. According to Adam of Bremen, writing in 1076, it held three tribal districts: Dithmarschen, along the North Sea coast from the mouth of the Elbe to the Eider; Holstein proper, on the Stör, a tributary of the Elbe; and Stormarn, on the north bank of the Elbe.

Its tribes were allied with the Saxons of Land Hadeln south of the river. To the east the Limes Saxoniae, an inaccessible stretch between the Elbe and the Kiel Fjord, divided it from Wagria, where the Slavic Obotrites lived.

Charlemagne began the Saxon Wars in 772. According to the Royal Frankish Annals, the Westphalian noble Widukind refused to attend the assembly at Paderborn in 777 and fled across the Elbe to Nordalbingia, or perhaps on to the court of the Danish king Sigfred. Even after Widukind submitted and was baptised in 785, the Nordalbingian tribes held out until the Battle of Bornhöved in 798, where the Franks and their Obotrite allies under Prince Drożko defeated them. The Saxons lost 4,000 people, and 10,000 Saxon families were deported to other parts of the Carolingian Empire.

Danish invasions followed the handing of the land to the Obotrites, and Charlemagne's son Charles the Younger drove the Danes back across the Eider in 808. The next year the emperor had Esesfeld Castle built near present-day Itzehoe, and the whole region was taken into the Frankish realm. The Danish March, from the Eider to the Danevirke, was probably set up against King Gudfred, and in 811 his successor Hemming agreed in the Treaty of Heiligen that the Eider should be the border. Quarrels went on until Henry the Fowler defeated King Gnupa at Hedeby in 934.

After Charlemagne's death in 814 the Nordalbingian Saxons were pardoned and their land was taken back from the Obotrites and restored to them. Some sources say the emperor had meant to found a diocese of Nordalbingia under the priest Heridag, a plan dropped at Heridag's death. Under Louis the Pious the region was assigned to the dioceses of Bremen and Verden, and Ansgar became archbishop at Hamburg in 831.
norddeutscher-lloyd: The Bremen merchants Hermann Henrich Meier and Eduard Crüsemann founded the company on 20 February 1857, after the dissolution of the German-American Ocean Steam Navigation Company. Meier chaired the supervisory board and Crüsemann became its first director. Its first ship, the Adler, sailed from Nordenham to London on 28 October 1857, and a year later regular services ran from Bremerhaven to New York with the steamships Bremen and New York. The company lost money until 1859, then added Baltimore, in partnership with the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, and New Orleans, and bought waterfront facilities at Hoboken, New Jersey, in 1869.

Under Johann Georg Lohmann, director from 1877, the company built fast liners, and in 1885 it won the German imperial mail contract to Australia and the Far East. By 1890 it was the second largest shipping company in the world after P&O and carried more transatlantic passengers to New York than any other, mostly emigrants in steerage. The Kaiser Wilhelm der Große of 1897, then the largest and fastest ship afloat, won the Blue Riband, as did the Kronprinz Wilhelm and Kaiser Wilhelm II in 1902 and 1904. On 30 June 1900 over 300 dock workers and others died in a fire at Hoboken. By 1914 it employed about 22,000 people.

The Treaty of Versailles took every ship over 1,600 GRT, leaving the company with 57,000 GRT. It rebuilt, helped found Deutscher Aero Lloyd, a forerunner of Lufthansa, and in 1929 and 1930 launched the Bremen and Europa, both Blue Riband winners. Hit by the Depression, it was placed in trusteeship with HAPAG in 1932, and under the Nazi regime the National Socialist Rudolph Firle headed it. The whole fleet was lost in the Second World War or handed over as reparations; the Steuben was sunk in the Baltic in 1945 with the loss of some 4,000 lives.

Relicensed by the American military administration on 29 November 1945 with 350 employees, the company built a new fleet from 1951, resumed North Atlantic passenger service in 1955 and opened a container service to the United States in 1968. Already doing three quarters of its freight business with HAPAG, it merged with it on 1 September 1970 to form Hapag-Lloyd, based in Hamburg. The Lloyd Werft in Bremerhaven, the Lloyd Passage in Bremen and the Bremer Bank, founded by Meier, keep its memory.
nordlinger-ries: The Nördlinger Ries is an impact crater and large circular depression in western Bavaria and eastern Baden-Württemberg, north of the Danube in the district of Donau-Ries. The city of Nördlingen lies within it. The name derives from Raetia, since the Raetians lived in the area in pre-Roman times. The floor lies 100 to 150 m below the eroded remains of the rim. In 1960 Eugene Shoemaker and Edward C. T. Chao showed that it was a meteorite impact, the key evidence being coesite found in suevite from the Otting quarry; Shoemaker had been encouraged by St George's Church in Nördlingen, built of local suevite.

An asteroid about 1.5 km in diameter, travelling at about 20 km/s, struck the area about 15 million years ago. Molten surface material was thrown up to 450 km away and came to rest in what is now Bohemia and Moravia, where the solidified droplets are found as moldavites. About two seconds after impact the main excavation began, producing a transient crater about 8 km across and 4 km deep. Its steep walls then slid inwards, enlarging it to about 24 km, and crater growth ceased after about three minutes.

About 150 km3 of rock were ejected and an area of about 5,000 km2 around the crater was buried metres deep. The impact triggered an earthquake estimated at magnitude 8, and ejecta blocked the courses of the ancestral Main and Altmühl rivers, damming a lake of up to 500 km2. The crater itself filled with a lake of about 400 km2, which silted up after about two million years.

Stone buildings in Nördlingen contain millions of tiny diamonds, all under 0.2 mm, formed when the impact struck a graphite deposit. The Ofnet Caves on one edge of the Ries held thirty-three Mesolithic human skulls found in the early 20th century, and the Battle of the Ries took place on 13 May 841. Apollo 14 astronauts, including Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell, trained at the Ries in August 1970, as did Apollo 17 astronauts.
nordwestmecklenburg: Nordwestmecklenburg, meaning Northwestern Mecklenburg, is a district in the north-western part of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Germany. It lies on the coast of the Baltic Sea, which includes the small island of Poel, and borders Schleswig-Holstein to the west. Its neighbours are the districts of Rostock and Ludwigslust-Parchim, the district-free city of Schwerin, and, in Schleswig-Holstein, the district of Lauenburg and the district-free city of Lübeck. The district is roughly situated in a triangle between Lübeck, Rostock and Schwerin, and its seat is the town of Wismar.

Two large lakes lie partly within it: the eastern half of the Schaalsee, of 23 square kilometres, on the western border, and the northern half of the Schweriner See, of 63 square kilometres, in the south. The smaller Bibowsee and Mechower See also lie within it.

The district was established in 1994 by merging the former districts of Gadebusch, Grevesmühlen and Wismar, together with smaller parts of the districts of Sternberg and Schwerin-Land. In the district reform of 2011 it was merged with the town of Wismar, which until then had not belonged to any district. A referendum on 4 September 2011 decided the district's name.

Its coat of arms, designed by Heinz Kippnick and granted on 1 July 1996, shows the half crowned bull's head of Mecklenburg on one side and a bishop's staff on the other. The staff stands for the diocese of Ratzeburg, which became the Principality of Ratzeburg in 1648, and also for the diocese of Schwerin. The red and white of the Hanseatic city of Wismar are also represented.
noreia: Noreia's importance came from the iron of Noricum. The ore mined in Carinthia, in the south of the region, was rich in manganese and almost free of phosphorus, and around 500 BCE the Celtic peoples of Noricum, chiefly the Taurisci, found that it made superior steel. A major production and trading centre grew up at Magdalensberg, where specialised blacksmiths made weapons that were mostly exported south to Aquileia, a Roman colony founded in 180 BCE. The steel known as chalybs Noricus supplied Roman swords from the mid-Republic onwards.

From about 200 BCE the tribes of Noricum appear to have been gradually united in a Celtic kingdom, the regnum Noricum, with Noreia as its capital according to Julius Caesar. It became a key ally of the Roman Republic, trading weapons and tools for military protection without a formal treaty. When invaders entered Noricum in 113 BCE, the Norici made a desperate appeal and the Roman consul Gnaeus Papirius Carbo led an army over the Alps, but he was heavily defeated near Noreia. Strabo and Appian both report this battle against the Cimbri and Teutoni. By the time of Pliny the Elder in the 1st century CE, Noreia was already spoken of as a lost city.

It is not known whether the battlefield and the capital were the same place. On the basis of ancient distances, 18th-century writers placed Noreia near Murau or Neumarkt in Styria, an identification that has repeatedly been questioned. The recorded distance of 1,200 stadia from Aquileia points rather to Carinthia, and scholars have proposed the settlements on the Magdalensberg or the nearby Zollfeld plain, a sanctuary of the mother goddess Noreia near Liebenfels in the Glan valley, the Gurina settlement near Dellach, and the mining area of Hüttenberg.

The Tabula Peutingeriana, a 12th-century copy of a late Roman road map, seems to show both an older and a new Noreia, which may mean the name simply meant a Noric city, though a copyist's error is thought more probable.

The site has still not been verified. The view favoured today places it on the Gracarca mountain beside Lake Klopein in Carinthia, where a prehistoric hilltop settlement and several graves of Celtic princes have been found. After excavations at Sankt Margarethen near Mühlen in Styria, the villagers renamed their village Noreia in 1930, although the finds there proved to be medieval.
norfolk: Norfolk is a ceremonial county in the East of England. It borders Lincolnshire and The Wash to the north-west, the North Sea to the north and east, Cambridgeshire to the west and Suffolk to the south, and covers 2,074 square miles (5,370 square kilometres). The centre is gently undulating lowland. To the east lies the northern half of the Broads, a network of rivers and lakes that extends into Suffolk; the west contains part of the Fens, and the south part of Thetford Forest. Clay and chalk deposits make the coast susceptible to erosion, and the most recent major erosion event occurred during the North Sea flood of 1953.

The area was settled before Roman times; there were Palaeolithic settlers as early as 950,000 years ago, with camps along the higher land in the west, where flints could be quarried. A Brittonic tribe, the Iceni, emerged in the 1st century BCE. The Iceni revolted against the Roman invasion in 47 CE and again in 60 CE under Boudica. The crushing of the second rebellion opened the area to the Romans, who built roads and ports and spread farming. The Angles settled the area in the 5th century, after which it became part of the Kingdom of East Anglia.

In the later Middle Ages the county was prosperous and heavily involved in the wool trade, which paid for the construction of many large churches. Norwich was one of the largest settlements in England in the Norman era. In 1549 Norfolk was the scene of Kett's Rebellion, an unsuccessful protest against the enclosure of land. The county was not heavily industrialised during the Industrial Revolution, and Norwich lost its status as one of the largest cities in England.

Norfolk is predominantly rural, with a population estimated at 940,359 in 2024. Its only city is Norwich, the county town and main business and cultural centre; the other principal towns are the port of King's Lynn and the seaside resort of Great Yarmouth. For local government it is a non-metropolitan county with seven districts. The economy is largely based on agriculture and tourism. The county is one of the few in England without a motorway.
norfolk-four-course-system: Before the four-course system, livestock farming in Britain depended mainly on the natural grasses of pastures, and English farmers faced a problem that fed on itself. Manure was the usual fertiliser, supplying organic matter and nutrients to the fields, but without enough pasture to feed more animals farmers could not enlarge their herds, and without larger herds they could not produce more manure to keep their land fertile. Earlier rotations such as the three-field system also left part of the land fallow each year.

Turnips, the fodder crop of the rotation, gave plentiful feed for livestock and so more animal products and more manure. Their roots reach deeper than those of wheat and barley, so they drew nutrients from lower in the soil; when the crop was eaten and returned as manure, or its remains were left in the ground, those nutrients became available to the crops that followed.

Clover, the grazing crop, likewise reduced farmers' dependence on pasture and let them expand their herds more freely. As a legume, clover fixes nitrogen, and nitrogen compounds in the soil are essential for plant growth; in the rotation it replaced the nitrogen used by the cereal crops before it, raising yields and reducing the risk of exhausting the soil. The use of legumes was not itself new: older rotations, including the three-field system, relied on other legumes for the same benefit.

By growing fodder and grazing crops on the arable land itself, the system allowed continuous production of feed through the year and greater year-round productivity of livestock, which is why it is counted among the key developments of the British Agricultural Revolution.
norfolk-island: Norfolk Island lies in the Pacific Ocean between New Zealand and New Caledonia, 1,412 kilometres directly east of Australia's Evans Head and about 900 kilometres from Lord Howe Island. It covers about 35 square kilometres, with 32 kilometres of coast and no large internal bodies of water. Together with the neighbouring Phillip Island and Nepean Island it forms the Territory of Norfolk Island. The climate is humid subtropical, with warm summers and mild, rainy winters. The evergreen Norfolk Island pine is native to the island and appears on its flag.

Archaeological investigation suggests that East Polynesian seafarers settled the island in the 13th or 14th century, either from the Kermadec Islands or from the North Island of New Zealand. Both Polynesian and Melanesian artefacts have been found. Occupation had ceased at least a few hundred years before Europeans arrived, probably because the island was isolated and poor for horticulture. Captain James Cook, on his second voyage, was the first European known to have landed, on 10 October 1774, and named it after Mary Howard, Duchess of Norfolk.

The island served as a convict settlement from 6 March 1788 until 5 May 1855, except for an interval between 15 February 1814 and 6 June 1825, when it lay abandoned. In 1824 the British government instructed the Governor of New South Wales, Thomas Brisbane, to reoccupy it as a place for what it called the worst description of convicts. The landing of 6 June 1825 brought 104 people, of whom 57 were convicts.

On 8 June 1856 permanent civilian settlement began, when 194 descendants of Tahitians and of the HMS Bounty mutineers, including those of Fletcher Christian, arrived from the Pitcairn Islands, which had become too small for their growing number. They occupied many of the buildings left by the penal settlements and established farming and whaling. Some families returned to Pitcairn in 1858 and 1863. Norfolk Island was part of New South Wales from 1788 to 1844, then of Van Diemen's Land, and was transferred from the United Kingdom to Australia in 1914.

Norfolk Island is an external territory of Australia, with its capital at Kingston and its largest town at Burnt Pine. The 2021 census counted 2,188 inhabitants. About half of the islanders trace their roots to Pitcairn Island. English and a creole called Norfuk, a blend of 18th-century English and Tahitian based on Pitkern, are both spoken. Tahitian influence survives in the hula dance and in dishes such as mudda, green banana dumplings. Tourism is the main economic activity.
noria: The English word noria comes through Spanish from the Arabic nā‘ūra, from a verb meaning to groan or grunt, after the sound the wheel made in turning. The term noria is commonly used for devices turned by moving water; those driven by animals are usually called saqiyah, though in Spain noria is used for both.

Paddle-driven water-lifting wheels had appeared in ancient Egypt by the 4th century BCE. The oldest archaeological evidence of a water wheel, a saqiyah of the 3rd century BCE, comes from the Faiyum. Hellenistic engineers used undershot and overshot wheels between the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE. Around 300 CE the Romans tied separate ceramic pots to an open-framed wheel, creating the noria.

A noria is a large, narrow undershot water wheel whose rim carries containers or compartments. They lift water from a river to an aqueduct at the top of the wheel, which discharges it sideways into a channel, for irrigation or to supply cities and villages. Unlike the wheel of a watermill, it supplies no mechanical power to any other process, and its principle is similar to the modern hydraulic ram.

Muslim engineers adopted norias from classical antiquity and improved them. Ibn Bassal of al-Andalus, active between 1038 and 1075, pioneered the flywheel in the noria, and in 1206 Ismail al-Jazari introduced the crank. The norias of Hama are 20 metres in diameter, and the largest has 120 compartments. The Marinid sultan Abu Yaqub Yusuf built a Grand Noria, 26 metres across, begun in 1286, to water the Mosara Garden at Fez.
