In Spain the Albolafia at Córdoba and a large noria at Toledo were well known, and the rice plantations of Valencia were said to have 8000 norias. The Alcantarilla Noria near Murcia, built in the 15th century, survives.
norman-architecture: Vikings arrived at the mouth of the river Seine in 911, and over the following century the people of the territory ceded to them, now called Normans, adopted Frankish customs, Christianity and the langue d'oïl. Norman barons built timber castles on earthen mounds, beginning the development of the motte-and-bailey castle, and great stone churches in the Romanesque style of the Franks; by 950 they were building stone keeps. Caen was the centre of the style, with its castle and two wealthy ducal abbeys, the Abbaye aux Dames and the Abbaye aux Hommes, whose large churches with three-storey elevations and towered façades became models for the English cathedrals.

The buildings show massive proportions in simple geometries with small bands of sculpture. Arches are semicircular, early ones plain and square-edged, later ones enriched with zig-zag and roll mouldings. Massive piers are either clusters of shafts or cylinders, sometimes incised, notably at Durham Cathedral. Windows are small and narrow, usually a single round-headed light. Main doorways have a succession of receding arches, often with chevron mouldings, and sometimes a tympanum carved with a Biblical scene. Churches were cruciform, often with a deep chancel and a square crossing tower. Though now mostly bare stone, the buildings would have been plastered and painted.

Edward the Confessor, brought up in Normandy, brought masons in 1042 to build Westminster Abbey, the first Romanesque building in England. After the Conquest of 1066 the Normans replaced every English bishop but one, rebuilt every cathedral, starting with Canterbury after a fire in 1067, and almost every monastic church, and built hundreds of parish churches and a chain of castles. Durham Cathedral, begun in 1093, was the first to use a ribbed vault with pointed arches. The style spread to Wales, to Scotland under David I and, after 1169, to Ireland with Anglo-Norman settlers.

After a fire at Canterbury in 1174 William of Sens introduced Gothic architecture, and Romanesque had virtually disappeared in England by the early 13th century, after decades of overlap known as the Transitional Style.

The word Norman for the architecture may come from eighteenth-century antiquarians, and Thomas Rickman gave it a place in a sequence of styles in 1817. Earlier writers often mistook Norman buildings for Saxon. In the nineteenth century a Neo-Norman revival used the style for buildings needing heavy massiveness, such as Lewes Prison, and also for Penrhyn Castle and the Natural History Museum.
norman-conquest: In 911 Charles the Simple allowed Vikings under Rollo to settle in Normandy, and they adopted Christianity and the Old French language. William's claim to the English throne rested on his family relationship with the childless Edward the Confessor, who may have encouraged his hopes. Edward died in January 1066 and was succeeded by his brother-in-law Harold Godwinson.

In September 1066 the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada, another claimant, invaded northern England and won the Battle of Fulford on 20 September, but Harold defeated and killed him at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September.

William gained the support of the Norman aristocracy at the Council of Lillebonne and gathered an army from Normandy and across France, with large contingents from Brittany and Flanders. Modern historians estimate it at 7,000 to 12,000 men. The Normans landed at Pevensey in Sussex on 28 September and built a wooden castle at Hastings.

The Battle of Hastings began at about 9 am on 14 October 1066 and lasted all day. The English formed a shield wall along a ridge and at first threw back the Normans with heavy casualties. When some Breton troops fled and some English pursued them, Norman cavalry cut the pursuers down, and William rallied his men, who twice more used feigned withdrawals to draw the English out. Harold was killed. William faced revolts in the following years, among them risings in Northumbria in 1069, aided by a Danish fleet sent by Sweyn II. The Fenland rebellion led by Hereward the Wake ended with the storming of the Isle of Ely in 1071.

William dispossessed the resisting English elite and gave their lands to his continental followers, to be held from the king in return for military service. The Domesday Book of 1086 shows that only about 5 per cent of the land south of the Tees remained in English hands. After 1075 all earldoms were held by Normans, and after the death of Wulfstan in 1095 no bishopric was held by an Englishman. Historians estimate that around 8,000 Normans and other continentals settled in England. Many Anglo-Saxons fled abroad.

Anglo-Norman, a dialect of Old French, became the language of the ruling classes. Government changed little, since the Normans took over many Anglo-Saxon forms, including the shires and writs. Slavery disappeared by the mid-12th century. Historians have argued over the conquest since its own time, and the theory of a Norman yoke arose in the 17th century.
norman-kirk: Kirk was born in Waimate in South Canterbury to a poor family; his father was a carpenter and his parents were Salvationists. He left school shortly before turning thirteen, when his father lost his job, and worked as a roof-painter's assistant and a stationary engine driver; in 1941 the army found him medically unfit. In 1943 he married Ruth Miller and joined the Labour Party in Kaiapoi, where he built his own house. In 1953, at 30, he became the country's youngest mayor, and at the 1957 election he won the Lyttelton seat.

At the end of 1965 a group of mostly younger MPs helped him unseat Arnold Nordmeyer as party leader. After Labour won the election of 25 November 1972 with a majority of 23 seats, Kirk became prime minister and minister of foreign affairs. He withdrew all New Zealand troops from Vietnam, abolished compulsory military training and widened links with Asia and Africa. With Australia his government took France to the International Court of Justice over its Pacific nuclear tests, and in 1973 he sent the frigates HMNZS Canterbury and Otago into the test zone at Mururoa. He refused a visit by a South African rugby team because of apartheid.

At home his government introduced the Domestic Purposes Benefit for sole parents in 1973, began the Ohu scheme of rural communes, made Māori an optional subject in state schools and kept Lake Manapouri from being raised. Rising oil prices and spending brought soaring inflation, and price controls followed in 1974. In March 1974 the government began the Dawn Raids, police raids on overstayers that primarily targeted Pasifika peoples, and stopped them with an amnesty in April.

Kirk kept an intense schedule and ignored doctors' advice to rest. By 1974 he had difficulty breathing, eating and sleeping, and an examination on 27 August found an enlarged heart weakened by embolisms. He died of a pulmonary embolism at the Home of Compassion Hospital in Wellington on the evening of 31 August 1974. His biographer Michael Bassett compared the grief that followed to that after the death of M. J. Savage in 1940. After a lying-in-state in Parliament House and services in Wellington and Christchurch, he was buried at Waimate. Bill Rowling succeeded him.
norman-manley: Norman Washington Manley was born on 4 July 1893 to parents of mixed race in Roxborough, in Manchester Parish. His father, Thomas Albert Samuel Manley, a small businessman, died in 1899, and his mother moved her four children to the Belmont estate near Spanish Town. At Jamaica College he won six medals at the schoolboy championships of 1911, running the 100 yards in 10 seconds, a record unbroken until 1952. A Rhodes Scholarship took him to Jesus College, Oxford, where he took a Bachelor of Civil Law with First Class Honours.

He served in the Royal Field Artillery in the First World War and was awarded the Military Medal. Called to the bar in England in 1921, he returned to Jamaica in 1922 and became one of its leading lawyers. In 1921 he married his cousin Edna Swithenbank.

During the troubles of 1938 Manley gave his time and advocacy to the workers, and in September he co-founded the People's National Party, which at first supported Alexander Bustamante's trade union. Bustamante left in 1943 to form the Jamaica Labour Party, which won the first elections under full adult suffrage in 1944 and again in 1949, when the PNP took more votes but fewer seats. In 1954 the party expelled Richard Hart and three others, the four H's, for alleged communist views. The PNP won in 1955, and Manley became chief minister and, on 14 August 1959, the first premier.

His governments passed a Housing Law in 1955, aid to small businesses and farmers, new protections for workers in factories, shops and quarries, and a pension scheme for sugar workers, and founded the Common Entrance Examination and the Jamaica Broadcasting Corporation. When Bustamante pledged to take Jamaica out of the West Indies Federation, Manley called a referendum, and in 1961 Jamaica voted 54% to leave.

Manley chaired the committee and led the team that negotiated independence, then called an election for April 1962 and lost it, so that Bustamante became the first prime minister when Jamaica became independent on 6 August 1962. As the first Leader of the Opposition, Manley lost again in 1967. He retired through respiratory illness on his birthday in 1969 and died on 2 September 1969. On 18 October 1969 he and Bustamante were proclaimed National Heroes, and he appears on the five-dollar coin and the thousand-dollar note.
normandy-landings: After Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, Joseph Stalin pressed his new allies to open a second front in western Europe. Winston Churchill persuaded Franklin D. Roosevelt to postpone the invasion, since even with American help the Allies lacked adequate forces. Planning began in 1943. In the months before the landings the Allies carried out Operation Bodyguard, a deception meant to mislead the Germans about the date and place. Its part Fortitude South used a fictitious First United States Army Group under George S. Patton to suggest that the main attack would fall at Calais. Erwin Rommel commanded the German forces and the work on the Atlantic Wall, and Dwight D. Eisenhower the Allied forces.

The planners needed a full moon, a tide midway between low and high and a landing shortly before dawn, which fit only a few days a month. Eisenhower tentatively chose 5 June, but high winds and low cloud forced a delay of 24 hours. The invasion began shortly after midnight on 6 June with bombing and the landing of 24,000 American, British and Canadian airborne troops. Amphibious landings followed at about 06:30 along an 80-kilometre stretch of coast divided into five sectors: Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword.

Strong winds blew the landing craft east of their targets, particularly at Utah and Omaha. At Omaha, the most heavily defended beach, 27 of 32 amphibious tanks sank, and casualties were highest. At Pointe du Hoc, men of the 2nd Ranger Battalion scaled 30-metre cliffs and disabled guns found some distance away. At Gold, Juno and Sword several fortified towns were cleared house by house.

The Allies established beachheads at all five sites on the first day, though Caen, a major objective, was not captured until 21 July. All five beachheads were not joined until 12 June. Allied casualties on the day were at least 10,000, with 4,414 confirmed dead, and German casualties are estimated at 4,000 to 9,000. Nearly 160,000 troops crossed the Channel on D-Day, and 875,000 had landed by the end of June. The Germans never achieved Hitler's stated aim of throwing the Allies back into the sea.
norn-language: Norn was a North Germanic language spoken in Orkney and Shetland, off the north coast of Scotland, and in Caithness on the Scottish mainland. Norse settlement in the islands probably began in the early 9th century, and the settlers are believed to have arrived in very substantial numbers, most of them probably from the west coast of Norway. Shetland place-names resemble those of northwest Norway, while Norn vocabulary points to links with more southerly Norwegian regions. Norn belonged to the West Scandinavian group with Faroese, Icelandic and Norwegian and is generally considered to have been fairly similar to Faroese, perhaps even mutually intelligible with it.

Orkney and Shetland were pledged to James III in 1468 and 1469, and the replacement of Norn by Scots is most associated with these pledges. The decline of Norse speech in Orkney probably began in 1379, when the Earldom of Orkney passed to Henry Sinclair, and Scots had become the language of prestige there by the early 15th century. By the end of the 15th century both island groups were bilingual, but most natives of Orkney and Shetland probably spoke Norn as a first language until the late 16th and early to mid 17th centuries respectively. One of the last documents written in Norn was a mortgage of 1597. In Caithness it had probably become extinct by the 15th century.

It is not known exactly when Norn died out. A source of 1670 says that only three or four parishes in Orkney spoke it, chiefly at home, and another of 1701 mentions a few monoglot speakers, with more speakers in Shetland than in Orkney. In 1750 James Mackenzie wrote that it was retained by old people. It is more likely that the language was dying out in the late 18th century.

Almost no written Norn survives, but the little that does includes a version of the Lord's Prayer and the ballad Hildina. Songs in Norn lasted long enough in oral tradition to be recorded: in the 1940s and 1950s John Stickle of Unst and Kitty Anderson of Lerwick were recorded singing the Unst Boat Song and the ballad of Orfeo with a Norn refrain. Fragments of vocabulary survive in place-names and in terms for nature, mood and fishing, such as voe, an inlet. The present-day Shetland dialect evolved from Middle English and is distinct from Norn. Norn words are still used for the colours and patterns of the native sheep of Shetland and Orkney.
norodom-of-cambodia: Norodom was born Ang Voddey on 3 February 1834, the eldest son of King Ang Duong, whom a peace treaty between Siam and Vietnam had recognised as king after decades of war fought largely on Cambodian soil. In 1850 his father sent him and his half-brother Prince Sisowath to study in Bangkok, where they grew up near members of the Siamese royal family. In 1857 he served in the Royal Siamese Army as a military adviser. He was elected to the throne in 1860.

In 1861 another half-brother, Si Votha, rebelled, and Norodom abandoned the capital of Oudong and fled to Bangkok. The Siamese court returned him to Phnom Penh early in 1862. He could not be crowned, because Siam held the royal regalia, which a Khmer monarch needed to be a legitimate ruler. After French military pressure, including a steamboat sent up the Chao Phraya river to Bangkok, the Siamese reluctantly gave the regalia back, and it was the French who crowned him in 1864.

The treaty of 1863 gave France control of Cambodia's foreign relations in exchange for his personal protection against his enemies. On 17 June 1884, with French gunboats anchored outside the Royal Palace, he was forced to sign a treaty giving up control of public revenue, customs taxes and public works. The anger this caused led in 1885 to a revolt against French rule under Si Votha; the French suspected Norodom of supporting it in secret. It ended when he assured Cambodians that the French had offered him concessions, and for a time afterwards the French were less inclined to press him. In October 1887 Cambodia became part of French Indochina.

He reduced the number of provinces to cut administrative costs and, following King Chulalongkorn of Siam, abolished commercial monopolies, slavery and the civil lists of the royal family. Under his supervision Wat Oudong was consecrated on 6 June 1875 and the Silver Pagoda built in 1892. Classical dance recovered prestige at his court, and after a visit to Manila in 1872 he brought Filipino musicians to Cambodia to teach modern music.

Norodom named his son Prince Norodom Yukanthor heir apparent, but Yukanthor fell out with the French and did not succeed. The king died in the palace at Phnom Penh on 24 April 1904 and was cremated in the traditional Buddhist fashion in 1906; his half-brother Sisowath followed him on the throne. His reign of 43 years and 188 days is the longest in Cambodian history that can be dated exactly.
norodom-ranariddh: Norodom Ranariddh was born on 2 January 1944 in Phnom Penh to Norodom Sihanouk and his first wife, Phat Kanhol, a ballet dancer attached to the royal court. When she remarried he was three years old, and he grew up mostly in the care of his aunt Norodom Ketkanya and grandaunt Norodom Sobhana, close to his grandparents but distanced from his father. In 1958 he was sent to a boarding school in Marseille with his half-brother Norodom Chakrapong. He planned to study medicine but was persuaded by his grandmother Sisowath Kossamak to study law, and in 1961 he enrolled at the University of Paris. He later became a law researcher and lecturer in France.

Ranariddh declined to join FUNCINPEC when Sihanouk formed it in 1981, disagreeing with its association with the Khmer Rouge, but joined in June 1983 and took charge of its diplomatic activities in Asia from Bangkok. He became commander-in-chief of its army in 1986, secretary-general in 1989 and president in February 1992. He signed the Paris Peace Accords in October 1991 as a member of the Supreme National Council.

After FUNCINPEC won the 1993 election it formed a coalition with the Cambodian People's Party, and Ranariddh became First Prime Minister with Hun Sen as Second. Benny Widyono observed that although Ranariddh was nominally senior he held less executive power. Relations deteriorated from early 1996 over the distribution of authority and rival approaches to the Khmer Rouge. In October 1994 he and Hun Sen had dropped Sam Rainsy as Finance Minister, and in May 1995 Ranariddh expelled Rainsy from FUNCINPEC.

Clashes between FUNCINPEC and CPP troops on 6 July 1997 amounted to his effective ouster. The Foreign Ministry called him a criminal and a traitor and accused him of conspiring with the Khmer Rouge, and Ung Huot replaced him as First Prime Minister in August. Ranariddh returned on 12 November 1998 and was nominated President of the National Assembly on 25 November.

Ranariddh resigned as President of the National Assembly on 14 March 2006 and left for France. He founded the Norodom Ranariddh Party in November 2006 and was convicted of embezzlement in March 2007, fleeing to Malaysia before his sentence. He was pardoned in September 2008 and returned to FUNCINPEC, which he led again from January 2015. A car accident during the 2018 election campaign killed his second wife. He died on 28 November 2021 in Aix-en-Provence, where he had gone for medical treatment.
norodom-sihanouk: Norodom Sihanouk was the only child of Prince Norodom Suramarit and Princess Sisowath Kossamak, daughter of King Sisowath Monivong. His parents followed the advice of the Royal Court Astrologer, who warned that he risked dying young if raised under parental care, and placed him with Kossamak's grandmother. When Monivong died in 1941, Sihanouk became king under French colonial rule. After the surrender of Japan in August 1945, nationalist forces loyal to Son Ngoc Thanh staged a coup; when the French returned in October, Thanh was dismissed, and a modus vivendi of January 1946 granted Cambodia autonomy within the French Union.

On 2 March 1955 Sihanouk suddenly abdicated in favour of his father, saying he wished to escape the intrigues of palace life and reach ordinary people. According to Osborne, the step freed him to pursue politics while keeping the deference he had enjoyed as king. His party, Sangkum, won the elections that year and he became prime minister. His changes included votes for women, Khmer as the sole official language, and policy-making powers vested in the prime minister rather than the king. In 1956 he began a national programme of Buddhist socialism. After Suramarit died on 3 April 1960, a referendum approved a new post of Head of State, to which Sihanouk was appointed on 14 June 1960 while remaining Sangkum's leader.

In March 1970, while Sihanouk was abroad, a coup brought a military government under Lon Nol. He announced a resistance movement on 23 March and encouraged Cambodians to fight; revered by the peasantry, his endorsement of the Khmer Rouge had immediate effects. He returned as figurehead head of state after their victory in 1975, resigned in 1976 and was kept under house arrest until the Vietnamese invasion of 1979. Refusing Deng Xiaoping's proposal to co-operate with the Khmer Rouge, as he opposed their genocidal policies, he founded FUNCINPEC in 1981 and in 1982 headed the Coalition Government of Democratic Kampuchea. He signed the Paris Peace Accords on 23 October 1991, and a new constitution restored him as king on 24 September 1993.

On 6 July 2004 Sihanouk announced in an open letter that he would abdicate again, citing the disregard of his suggestions by Hun Sen and Norodom Ranariddh. His son Norodom Sihamoni succeeded him. Sihanouk died of a heart attack in Beijing on 15 October 2012. He produced about 50 films, beginning with Apsara in 1966, and wrote at least 48 songs. He held more state roles than any other modern royal, and is remembered for leading Cambodia to independence, although his reputation was damaged by his association with the Khmer Rouge in the 1970s.
norse-gaels: The name Gall-Goídil means foreigner Gaels. Though it could in theory mean any Gael of foreign origin, it was used of Gaelic speakers with some kind of Norse identity. The Norse–Gaels arose in the Viking colonies of Ireland and Scotland, where from as early as the 9th century Norse settlers, except those in Cumbria, married Gaels, took up the Gaelic language and many Gaelic customs, and left the worship of the Norse gods for Christianity. They called themselves Ostmen or Austmen, the East-men, and called the Gaels Vestmenn, the West-men.

The Norse are first recorded in Ireland in 795, when they sacked Rathlin Island. After sporadic raids until 832 they built fortified settlements and set up kingdoms at Dublin, Waterford, Wexford, Cork and Limerick, which did not survive the Norman invasions, though the towns prospered. Gaelicised Scandinavians dominated the Irish Sea until the Norman era of the 12th century, founding the Kingdom of the Isles, the Kingdom of Dublin and the Lordship of Galloway, and briefly ruling the Kingdom of York from 939 to 944. Their most powerful dynasty was the Uí Ímair.

Among the English in Ireland between the 12th and 14th centuries the Ostmen were a group apart, given legal protections the Irish lacked for their place in the economy as merchants, fishermen, craftsmen and cattle raisers. In Dublin they lived north of the River Liffey in Ostmentown, now Oxmantown, and others in Limerick and Waterford, until they merged with the English settlers. Norse–Gael settlers also took part in the settlement of Iceland and the Faroe Islands, where Grímur Kamban, seen as the founder of the Norse Faroes, may have been one of them.

Most place names of the Isle of Man and the Outer Hebrides are of Norse–Gaelic origin, and the Hebrides are still called Innse Gall, the islands of foreigners, in Scottish Gaelic. The Lords of the Isles traced their descent to Norse–Gaelic settlements, as do Clan MacQueen, Clan MacDonald, Clan MacDougall and Clan MacLeod. The gallowglass mercenaries came from these clans, the Viking longship shaped the Gaelic birlinn, and surnames such as MacIvor and MacAskill survive.
north-africa: There is no single accepted scope for North Africa. The most common definition includes Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Tunisia and Western Sahara, while the United Nations also counts Sudan. Its southern boundary is sometimes placed at the Sahel, south of the Sahara.

The region has three main geographic features: the Sahara in the south, the Atlas Mountains in the west, and the Nile and its delta in the east. The Sahara covers more than 75 percent of the region. Fertile farmland lies in the sheltered valleys of the Atlas, in the Nile Valley and Delta, and along the Mediterranean coast, where olives, figs, dates and citrus fruits grow.

Finds at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco contain some of the oldest Homo sapiens remains known. The cave paintings of Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria depict daily life in the Neolithic Subpluvial period, about 8000 to 4000 BCE, before the Sahara dried rapidly around 3500 BCE. The northwest has been inhabited by Berbers since the beginning of recorded history, and the east was the home of the Ancient Egyptians and Nubians.

Phoenician and Greek colonies were founded on the coast in the 7th century BCE. Carthage, a Phoenician foundation, built a commercial empire, and its North African territories became the Roman province of Africa in 146 BCE. The kingdom of Mauretania was annexed by Emperor Claudius in 42 CE. In the early fifth century the Vandals crossed the Strait of Gibraltar, and the loss of Africa, an important grain province, weakened the Western Roman Empire.

The early Muslim conquests reached North Africa by 640, and by 700 most of it was under Muslim rule. Arab migrations followed, among them the westward movement of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym in the eleventh century, which historians regard as a critical moment in the Arabization of the countryside. Much of the area later came loosely under the Ottoman Empire, with the Barbary states on the coast. In the 19th century France, the United Kingdom, Spain and Italy brought the whole region under European occupation, and the North African states gained independence in the 1950s and 1960s.

Modern Standard Arabic is the official language of all the countries of North Africa, and Algeria and Morocco also recognize Berber as official. French serves as an administrative language in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia. The region is predominantly Muslim, with Jewish communities in Morocco and Tunisia and a significant Christian minority, the Copts, in Egypt.
north-african-elephant: The North African elephant (Loxodonta africana pharaohensis) is an extinct subspecies of the African bush elephant, or possibly a separate species, that lived north of the Sahara until it died out in Roman times. It has been formally described but is not widely recognised by taxonomists. Its natural range probably extended along the coast of the Red Sea, in what is now Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea, and may have reached further across northern Africa. Carthaginian frescoes and coins show very small elephants, perhaps 2.5 m at the shoulder, with large ears and a concave back, and contemporary writers noted that they were smaller than the Indian elephant.

The animal was significant in Nubian culture, depicted on temple walls and Meroitic lamps. Kushite kings used war elephants, believed to have been kept and trained at the Great Enclosure at Musawwarat al-Sufa, and Kush supplied them to the Egyptians, Ptolemies and Syrians. The elephants with which Hannibal crossed the Pyrenees and the Alps in the Second Punic War (218-201 BCE) belonged to this group, with the possible exception of his personal animal Surus, who has been speculated to be a Syrian elephant, though little direct evidence suggests it.

Polybius, writing in the 2nd century BCE, described their inferiority in battle against the larger Indian elephants of the Seleucid kings. About 3,500 elephants were killed in Roman circus games during the reign of Augustus, and this long use in baiting games, together with hunting, would drive the species to extinction by the 4th century CE.

Ansell (1971) classified it as a distinct taxon closely related to the African forest elephant, but this is not universally accepted. Its small size could instead reflect a small population of bush elephants, a population of forest elephants, or the capture of young bush elephants. Ancient DNA may settle the question if specimens of definite North African origin are found; remains from Tetouan, Morocco, dating to the time of the Roman Republic and identified as elephant by collagen fingerprinting, probably belong to this taxon.
north-america: North America is bordered to the north by the Arctic Ocean, to the east by the Atlantic Ocean, to the southeast by South America and the Caribbean Sea, and to the south and west by the Pacific Ocean. Its only land connection to South America is at the Darien Gap on the Colombia and Panama border. Some geologists place its southern limit instead at the Isthmus of Tehuantepec in Mexico. The Caribbean islands are considered part of it, and so is Greenland, which lies on the same tectonic plate. The Gulf of Mexico is the largest body of water indenting the continent, followed by Hudson Bay.

It is unknown exactly how and when the first human populations reached North America. People are known to have lived in the Americas at least 20,000 years ago, and some evidence points to earlier dates. The traditional theory is that hunters crossed the Bering Land Bridge between eastern Siberia and present-day Alaska; a growing view is that the first inhabitants sailed from Beringia some 13,000 years ago. Before European arrival the peoples of North America were divided into many polities, from small bands of a few families to large empires, and lived in cultural regions such as the bison-hunting Great Plains and farming Mesoamerica.

Norse exploration and colonization began in the late 10th century, with several settlements in Greenland and at least one in Newfoundland. From 1492 the voyages of Christopher Columbus began a transatlantic exchange, including migrations of European settlers. Present-day patterns reflect interactions among early European colonists, indigenous peoples, enslaved Africans and later immigrants from Europe and Asia. The Spanish Empire called its American territories Las Indias and governed them through a body named the Council of the Indies.

The name America comes from Amerigo Vespucci, through the German cartographers Martin Waldseemüller and Matthias Ringmann, who placed it on a world map in 1507. Most North Americans speak English, Spanish or French, and significant indigenous populations keep their pre-colonial cultural and linguistic traditions. The continent includes the subregions of Northern America and Middle America, and the term is sometimes used for Northern America alone.
north-american-free-trade-agreement: The idea of a North American free trade zone began with Ronald Reagan, who made it part of his campaign when he announced his candidacy for the presidency in November 1979. Canada and the United States signed the Canada–United States Free Trade Agreement in 1988. Soon afterwards Mexican president Carlos Salinas de Gortari approached President George H. W. Bush to propose a similar agreement, to bring in foreign investment following the Latin American debt crisis. The Canadian government under Brian Mulroney feared that its gains from the 1988 agreement would be undermined by a bilateral deal between the United States and Mexico, and asked to join the talks.

After diplomatic negotiations dating back to 1990, the leaders of the three countries signed the agreement in their capitals on 17 December 1992. It sought to eliminate barriers to trade and investment. On 1 January 1994 tariffs ended at once on more than half of Mexico's exports to the United States and more than a third of United States exports to Mexico, and almost all other tariffs between those two were to go within ten years; most trade between the United States and Canada was already duty-free. It also sought to protect intellectual property.

Freedom of movement for goods, services and capital did not extend to labour. Chapter 11 allowed corporations or individuals to sue a government for compensation when its actions violated international law, and Chapter 19 sent antidumping and countervailing duty disputes to binational panels. Two side agreements, on labour and on the environment, were added before ratification; the environmental one created the Commission for Environmental Cooperation in 1994.

Ratification was contested. In Canada the 1993 election swept away Kim Campbell's Progressive Conservatives in favour of Jean Chrétien's Liberals, who had promised to renegotiate or abrogate the agreement. President Bill Clinton inherited the task of ratifying it, and all three countries did so in 1993.

Its effects on jobs, the environment and growth were disputed. Most economic analyses held that it benefited the three economies but harmed a minority of workers in industries exposed to competition, and a Congressional Research Service review found its overall effect on the United States modest. On the day it came into force, 1 January 1994, the Zapatista Army of National Liberation rose in Chiapas, calling the agreement a death sentence for indigenous communities; preparations for it had included repeal of Article 27 of Mexico's constitution, which protected communal landholdings. NAFTA was replaced by the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement, which took effect on 1 July 2020.
north-brabant: North Brabant borders South Holland and Gelderland to the north, Limburg to the east, Zeeland to the west and the Belgian provinces of Antwerp and Limburg to the south. Its northern border follows the Meuse westward to its mouth in the Hollands Diep strait. The land is mostly flat but almost everywhere above sea level, so it has fewer canals than lower parts of the Netherlands. In the south lies De Kempen, a sandy heathland of infertile soil, and in the east the Peel, a moorland that has almost entirely been brought into cultivation. The Biesbosch, southeast of Dordrecht, was formed by the St. Elizabeth's floods of 19 November 1421, which inundated over 40,000 hectares.

The Duchy of Brabant was a state of the Holy Roman Empire established in 1183 or 1190, developing from the Landgraviate of Brabant. It formed the heart of the historic Low Countries and was part of the Burgundian Netherlands from 1430 and of the Habsburg Netherlands from 1482, until the Dutch revolt split it up. Until the 17th century the area of North Brabant was mostly part of the duchy, whose southern part is now in Belgium. The 14th and 15th centuries were a golden age there, above all for Brussels, Mechelen, Leuven and Antwerp, and for Breda, Bergen op Zoom and 's-Hertogenbosch.

The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 assigned present-day North Brabant, known as Staats-Brabant, to the Generality Lands of the Dutch Republic, while the reduced duchy remained with the Southern Netherlands until French Revolutionary forces conquered it in 1794. After the War of Independence, Catholics were systematically and officially discriminated against by the Protestant government of the north until the second half of the 19th century, which strongly influenced the economic and cultural development of the southern Netherlands. When Belgium broke away in the Belgian Revolution, the old pre-1790s borders of the Dutch Republic were adopted, so North Brabant and Limburg stayed in the Netherlands.

North Brabant has about 2,626,000 inhabitants. Its capital is 's-Hertogenbosch, and its largest cities are Eindhoven, Tilburg and Breda. The four cities of the Brabantse Stedenrij form a kite-shaped urban centre, and the rest of the province is more rural. The province has been divided into 56 municipalities since 2022. Brabant dialects and traditions such as Carnival keep the character rooted in the Duchy of Brabant, and Catholicism, a dominant social force for centuries, shaped its distinct identity. It has national parks at the Biesbosch, the Loonse and Drunen Dunes and De Groote Peel.
north-caucasus: The North Caucasus, or Ciscaucasia, is the northern part of the wider Caucasus region, which separates Europe and Asia. It is bordered by the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea to the west, the Caspian Sea to the east and the Caucasus Mountains to the south, and shares land borders with Georgia and Azerbaijan. Mount Elbrus, in the southern part, is the tallest peak in Europe. The term also refers to the northern slope and western extremity of the Greater Caucasus range. The Pontic-Caspian steppe is often included, with the Manych River generally regarded as the northern boundary of the Forecaucasus steppe. Because of its mild climate compared with much of Russia, the region has been described as Russia's sunbelt.

Ancient cultures of the North Caucasus are known as the Klin-Yar community, and one of the most notable is the Koban culture. The Ciscaucasus was historically covered by the Pontic-Caspian steppe, largely fertile calcareous chernozem soils that have since been extensively tilled and grazed.

The region came under Russian control in the 19th century, following the Caucasian War between the Russian Empire and the various regional powers; the conquest was completed by 1864. From the 1850s to the early 20th century about a million North Caucasian Muslims, including Circassians, Chechens, Ingush and Ossetians, became refugees in the Ottoman Empire, which settled them in territories of present-day Turkey, Syria, Jordan, Lebanon, Bulgaria, Serbia and other states, creating a large diaspora.

In 1918, taking advantage of the instability of the Russian revolutions, much of the North Caucasus seceded as the Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus, a minor participant in the Russian Civil War. Its troops fought the invading Volunteer Army of the White general Anton Denikin until the latter's defeat by the Red Army. Soviet Russia occupied the region informally soon afterwards, and the republic was compelled to accept annexation in January 1921. It was reformed as the Mountainous Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, dissolved in October 1924 and replaced by a series of autonomous okrugs and oblasts.

The North Caucasus is the southernmost part of Russia and is divided between Krasnodar Krai, Stavropol Krai and the republics of Adygea, Karachay-Cherkessia, Kabardino-Balkaria, North Ossetia-Alania, Ingushetia, Chechnya and Dagestan, with Kalmykia to the north. It is extremely diverse ethnically and linguistically. The local population is predominantly Sunni Muslim, except the Ossetians. In the western half pagan traditions remain, closely connected with Islam, while in the east, in Chechnya, Dagestan and Ingushetia, Sufism dominates. The region is known for a large number of centenarians.
north-china-plain: The North China Plain is a downfaulted rift basin formed in the late Paleogene and Neogene and later modified by Yellow River deposits. It is the largest alluvial plain of China. The Yanshan Mountains bound it on the north, the Taihang Mountains on the west and the Dabie Mountains on the south, while the Yellow Sea and the Bohai Sea lie to the east. It covers about 409,500 square kilometres, most of it less than 50 metres above sea level, and takes in much of Henan, Hebei and Shandong. The part around the middle and lower Yellow River, the Central Plain, formed the cradle of Chinese civilisation.

The plain runs largely uninterrupted by mountains, so communication by horse is rapid and its spoken language is relatively uniform; historians connect this with the tendency of China's political centre to lie here. Imperial capitals stood on it, among them Luoyang, at various points the capital of the Han, Jin, Sui and Tang dynasties, and Kaifeng, capital of the Northern Song. Confucius lived and taught in the State of Lu, on the plain, from 551 to 479 BCE.

The fertile soil merges with the steppes and deserts to the north, so the plain was open to nomadic invaders, which prompted the building of the Great Wall. Its weather is unpredictable, and the flat land floods massively when river works are damaged. Many historians propose that these conditions encouraged a centralised state able to manage granaries, hydraulic works and fortifications. In the winter of 1957 to 1958 the first project of the Great Leap Forward was the speeding up of waterworks here.

Beijing lies on the north-eastern edge of the plain, Tianjin near its coast, and Jinan and Zhengzhou on the Yellow River. It is one of the most densely populated regions in the world and a major farming region, producing wheat, maize, sorghum, millet, cotton and vegetables. Because of its yellow soil it is nicknamed the Land of the yellow earth.
north-east-frontier-agency: In 1914 tribal-majority areas were separated from the Darrang and Lakhimpur districts of Assam Province of British India to form the North-East Frontier Tract, divided into a Central and Eastern Section and a Western Section, each under a political officer. In 1919 these were renamed the Sadiya and Balipara Frontier Tracts, and from 1937 they were grouped with the Lakhimpur Frontier Tract as the Excluded Areas of the Province of Assam under the Government of India Act, 1935. The Tirap Frontier Tract was formed in 1943, and the Assam Frontier (Administration of Justice) Regulation, 1945 proved a landmark in the region's history.

After independence in 1947 the tracts became part of Assam state. In 1948 the Sadiya Frontier Tract was split into the Abor Hills and Mishmi Hills districts, and in 1950 their plains were transferred to the Assam government while the rest became one of the Tribal Areas under the sixth schedule of the constitution. In 1954 the territory was reorganised into the Kameng, Subansiri, Tirap, Siang and Lohit frontier divisions, with a Tuensang Frontier Division for a Naga tribal area that in 1957 joined the Naga Hills district.

The agency had its headquarters at Shillong and remained constitutionally part of Assam, administered by the Governor of Assam as agent of the President of India. On 1 August 1965 its administration passed from the Ministry of External Affairs to the Ministry of Home Affairs, and on 1 December 1965 the five divisions became districts, each under a deputy commissioner instead of a political officer. An Agency Council was set up in 1967.

Under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971, the agency became the Union Territory of Arunachal Pradesh on 21 January 1972, under a Chief Commissioner. It was governed from Shillong until its capital moved to Itanagar in 1974.
north-india: North India is a loosely defined region rather than a fixed administrative unit. It extends from the Himalayan mountain range in the north to the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the Thar Desert and the Central Highlands, and several major rivers cross it, among them the Indus, the Ganges and the Yamuna. Official bodies draw its limits differently: the Northern Zonal Council, created in 1956 by the States Reorganisation Act, and the Ministry of Culture's North Culture Zone, established in Patiala on 23 March 1985, include different states.

Its landscape ranges from the Trans-Himalayan ranges such as the Karakoram, Ladakh and Zanskar, through the Greater Himalayas with Nanda Devi and the Gangotri Glacier, to the forested Shiwalik hills. The plains have a humid subtropical climate with hot summers, cool winters and monsoon rains, while the Thar Desert in the west is arid and can reach temperatures as high as 50 °C.

After 6500 BCE farming and permanent settlements appeared at Mehrgarh and other sites in Balochistan, and these developed into the Indus Valley Civilisation, which flourished from 2500 to 1900 BCE. Kalibangan in Rajasthan and Rakhigarhi in Haryana were among its prominent cities. The region was later the centre of the Vedic culture, the Mahajanapadas, the Gupta Empire and the Pratihara dynasty.

In 1206 Qutub-ud-din Aibak declared his independence and founded the Sultanate of Delhi, which came to control much of North India. By repulsing Mongol raiders in the 13th century it spared India the devastation suffered in West and Central Asia, and refugees from those lands brought about a syncretic Indo-Islamic culture in the north.

By the early 18th century Mughal authority had weakened, and the Marathas, Rajputs and Sikhs asserted control in its place. The East India Company took much of North India by the early 19th century, annexing Delhi in 1803 and Oudh in 1856. The partition of India caused upheaval and violence in Punjab and Delhi. The princely states of the Rajputana Agency were merged into Rajasthan in 1949, and in 1966 Punjab was reorganised along linguistic lines, creating Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and the present Punjab. Uttarakhand was carved out of Uttar Pradesh in 2000.

The people of North India mostly belong to the Indo-Aryan ethno-linguistic branch, with Tibeto-Burman groups along the Himalayan states. Hinduism is the dominant religion, and Punjab is the homeland of Sikhism. The region holds the Hindu pilgrimage centres of Varanasi, Haridwar and Ayodhya, the Buddhist sites of Sarnath and Kushinagar, and the Golden Temple at Amritsar, as well as World Heritage Sites including the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort, Fatehpur Sikri, the Qutb Minar and the Khajuraho temples. The composite culture produced by contact between Hindu and Muslim traditions is known as Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb.
north-korea: In the late 19th century Korea came under the influence of Japan, which had won the First Sino-Japanese War against Qing China and the Russo-Japanese War against the Russian Empire. Japan compelled Korea to become its protectorate in 1905 and formally annexed it in 1910. A period of forced assimilation followed, in which Korean language, culture and history were suppressed. It led to the March First Movement protests in 1919 and to resistance groups in exile, primarily in China.

In the 1930s Japan developed mines, hydro-electric dams and steel mills in northern Korea and neighbouring Manchuria, so that 65% of Korea's heavy industry but only 37% of its agriculture lay in the north. A Korean guerrilla movement emerged in the mountainous interior and in Manchuria, and one of its most prominent leaders was the Communist Kim Il Sung.

After the Japanese surrender in 1945 the peninsula was divided into two occupation zones along the 38th parallel, the Soviet Union holding the north and the United States the south. Negotiations on reunification failed. Kim Il Sung became chairman of the Provisional People's Committee of North Korea, established in February 1946. The South declared its statehood in May 1948, and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea was established in the North on 9 September 1948, with Kim Il Sung as premier.

Shtykov and Kim lobbied Joseph Stalin to support a quick war against the South, and it began in 1950 as the Korean War. The Korean Armistice Agreement of 1953 brought a ceasefire and established the Korean Demilitarized Zone. Kim Il Sung consolidated power and promoted his philosophy of Juche as the state ideology. The loss of Eastern Bloc trading partners and natural disasters in the 1990s brought a famine from 1995 to 1998, which an estimated 240,000 to 420,000 North Koreans did not survive.

North Korea occupies the northern part of the Korean Peninsula, covering 120,540 square kilometres. About 80 percent of it is mountains and uplands, and the highest point is Paektu Mountain at 2,744 metres, a sacred place in Korean culture. Pyongyang is the capital and largest city. The Workers' Party of Korea is the sole ruling party and the state owns almost all means of production. The Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong and the Complex of Koguryo Tombs are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
north-macedonia: North Macedonia has an area of 25,436 square kilometres and borders Serbia, Kosovo, Bulgaria, Greece and Albania. It constitutes approximately the northern third of the larger geographical region of Macedonia. A central valley formed by the Vardar river defines the country, framed by mountain ranges; the tallest is Mount Korab in the Šar Mountains, at 2,764 metres. Lake Ohrid, Lake Prespa and Dojran Lake lie on the southern borders, and Ohrid is considered one of the oldest lakes in the world. The region is seismically active, and an earthquake in 1963 heavily damaged Skopje and killed over 1,000 people.

In antiquity most of the area corresponded to Paeonia, a kingdom immediately north of ancient Macedonia, and Pelagonia. The Achaemenid Persians under Darius the Great conquered Paeonia in the late 6th century BCE and withdrew after 479 BCE. Philip II of Macedon absorbed Lynkestis, Pelagonia and the southern part of Paeonia into his kingdom in 356 BCE, and Paeonia became his vassal.

Rome conquered the region by the mid-2nd century BCE. Slavic tribes raided and settled it from the 6th century CE, and after contention between the Byzantine and Bulgarian empires it passed to the Serbian Empire in the mid-14th century and to the Ottoman Empire from the late 14th century.

The Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913 brought Serbian rule. Bulgaria ruled the territory during the First World War and again during the Second. After the Second World War it was established as a constituent state of communist Yugoslavia, and it seceded peacefully in 1991. The Socialist Republic of Macedonia had first adopted the name Macedonia officially at the end of the Second World War; the interwar Kingdom of Yugoslavia had prohibited its use.

The country took the name North Macedonia in 2019 under the Prespa Agreement. Many citizens still call it Macedonia. It joined the United Nations in 1993, has been a candidate for European Union membership since 2005 and is a member of NATO.

The 2021 census counted 1,836,713 people. The largest group is ethnic Macedonians, followed by Albanians, who dominate much of the north-west. Tensions over the balance of power between the two communities led to a brief war in 2001 and a power-sharing agreement. Macedonian is the official language, and Albanian is also co-official at state level.
north-maluku: Historically the name Maluku referred to four royal centres, Ternate, Tidore, Bacan and Jailolo, a confederation that most likely emerged in the 14th century and was called Moloku Kie Raha, the Four Mountains of Maluku. Ternate began to grow in the early 13th century and, by traditional chronology, elected its first kolano, or king, in 1257. Islam was adopted by the leading families from the mid-15th century, and the title of sultan replaced kolano. Tidore adopted Islam as its official religion only at the end of the 15th century.

The Portuguese reached Ternate in 1512 under Francisco Serrão and were allowed a trading post. Tidore received the survivors of the Magellan expedition in 1521. The Portuguese interfered in Ternatan succession disputes, and a Portuguese captain later murdered Sultan Hairun inside their fort. His successor Sultan Baabullah expelled them from northern Maluku in 1575 after five years of war, and Ternate's influence then reached from Sulawesi to the Papuan Islands. After Baabullah's death the sultanate weakened. On 26 June 1607 Sultan Mudafar Syah I signed a contract giving the Dutch East India Company a monopoly on buying spices in return for help against Spain, and the Dutch built Fort Oranje on Ternate.

Ternate became a vassal of the company in 1682 and Tidore in 1780, although the Tidorese prince Nuku led a rebellion across much of Maluku and western Papua between 1780 and 1805. The sultanates remained self-ruling territories under the Dutch until the Indonesian Revolution.

The islands are mostly volcanic: Gamalama on Ternate and Dukono on Halmahera are active volcanoes, and the whole of Tidore is one large stratovolcano. Halmahera is the largest of the province's 1,474 islands. Its rainforests, in the Wallacea transition zone, hold many endemic species, including Wallace's standardwing and the invisible rail.

Japan occupied the region in 1942, and Allied forces took Morotai in 1944. The province of North Maluku was established on 12 October 1999 by separation from Maluku. Its economy rests on agriculture, fisheries, and commodities such as copra, nutmeg, cloves, gold and nickel. Most of the population is Muslim, with a significant Christian minority, and the people speak languages of the Austronesian and Papuan families.
north-ossetia-alania: The republic lies in the North Caucasus and covers about 8,000 square kilometres. Its northern part is on the Stavropol Plain, and about 22 per cent of its territory is forested. It borders Georgia, including South Ossetia, to the south, and Kabardino-Balkaria, Stavropol Krai, Chechnya and Ingushetia. Its highest point is Mount Kazbek, at 5,033 metres.

The region traces its history to the ancient Alans, who founded the Kingdom of Alania in the 8th century and adopted Christianity in the 9th. Alania profited from the Silk Road, which passed through its territory. In 1220 Genghis Khan sent his commanders Subutai and Jebe on a campaign that reached Alania, and in 1239 the Mongols destroyed its capital, Maghas, and other cities. The Alans were forced to flee to the mountain gorges and leave the flat lands. Islam was introduced in the 17th century by Kabardians.

Pressed by conflicts between the Khanate of Crimea and the Ottoman Empire, Ossetia entered an alliance with Russia in the 18th century, and Vladikavkaz became the first Russian-controlled area in the northern Caucasus. The Georgian Military Road was built in 1799, and by 1830 Ossetia was under complete Russian control. An estimated 50,000 Ossetians left the Caucasus in the early 1860s, as part of a wider migration of Muslims from the region to the Ottoman Empire. After 1917 North Ossetia was merged into the Mountain Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic in 1921, became an autonomous oblast on 7 July 1924 and an autonomous republic on 5 December 1936.

When the Soviet Union dissolved, the Ossetians were divided between North Ossetia, in the Russian republic, and South Ossetia, in the Georgian one. In 1992 a brief ethnic war between Ossetians and the Ingush took place in the Prigorodny District, and 30,000 to 60,000 Ingush were forced to leave North Ossetia. The name Alania, revived by Ossetian intellectuals in the last years of the Soviet Union, was added to the republic's title in November 1994.

The republic's capital is Vladikavkaz, at the foot of the Caucasus Mountains, and its population was 687,357 at the 2021 census. Ossetians form 68.1 per cent of it. Ossetian is an east Iranian language descended from the medieval Alanic and ancient Sarmatian languages. Most Ossetians are Eastern Orthodox Christians, and almost 30 per cent of the population follows the Ossetian ethnic religion, Uatsdin.
north-rhine-westphalia: North Rhine-Westphalia is a landlocked state in western Germany. It covers the plains of the Lower Rhine region and parts of the Central Uplands up to the gorge of Porta Westfalica, and it borders Belgium, the Netherlands, Lower Saxony, Rhineland-Palatinate and Hesse. The Rhine flows through it, and its banks are heavily populated and industrialised, particularly around Cologne and Düsseldorf. The state is not culturally uniform: customs differ significantly between the Rhineland and the regions of Westphalia and Lippe, and its flag combines their arms.

The first written account of the area is by Julius Caesar, who conquered the tribes on the left bank of the Rhine; the Eburones lived west of the river, and east of it he reported the Ubii and the Sugambri. Augustus established fortified posts on the Rhine, but the Romans never won a firm footing on the right bank. The Battle of Teutoburg Forest took place near Osnabrück, and Charlemagne is thought to have spent considerable time in Paderborn, with his Saxon Wars partly fought in Westphalia.

The British military administration established the state on 23 August 1946 by merging the Prussian province of Westphalia and the northern part of the Rhine Province. The former state of Lippe was added on 21 January 1947, and the state joined the Federal Republic in 1949. Bonn served as federal capital until the reunification of Germany in 1990 and as seat of government until 1999. A coal crisis began in 1958 and a steel crisis around 1967, ending the era in which the state was known as the land of coal and steel.

North Rhine-Westphalia has more than 18 million inhabitants and is the most populous German state. Düsseldorf is the capital and Cologne the largest city. Aachen Cathedral, Cologne Cathedral, the Zeche Zollverein in Essen, the Augustusburg Palace in Brühl and the Imperial Abbey of Corvey are World Heritage Sites. The University of Cologne, founded in 1388, is the oldest of its universities, and Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770.
north-sea: The North Sea lies on the European continental shelf and connects to the Atlantic Ocean through the English Channel in the south and the Norwegian Sea in the north. It is more than 970 kilometres long and 580 kilometres wide, covering 570,000 square kilometres, and has a mean depth of 90 metres; only the Norwegian trench, up to 725 metres deep, is much deeper. In the east it reaches the Baltic Sea through the Skagerrak and Kattegat.

Its coasts were shaped by glaciers: deep fjords in Norway and cliffs in Scotland in the north, and sandy beaches, estuaries and mudflats in the south. Its southern coasts were originally flood plains and swamp, and from about 1200 their people joined single ring dikes into a dike line along the coast.

There is little documentary evidence for the North Sea before the Roman conquest of Britain in 43 CE, but archaeology shows cultures and technologies spreading across it and some prehistoric peoples relying on fishing, whaling and seaborne trade. When the Romans left Britain in 410, the Angles, Frisians, Saxons and Jutes began the next great migration across the sea. It was the centre of the Vikings' rise, and the Hanseatic League, the Dutch Republic and Britain all later sought command of it. Flemish whalers worked the sea from the 9th until the 13th century, and were replaced in the 16th century by Dutch, English, Danes and Germans.

In the 17th century the Dutch Golden Age brought Dutch maritime power to its zenith, until England challenged it in the first three Anglo-Dutch Wars between 1652 and 1673, which ended in Dutch victories. After the Glorious Revolution of 1688 put the Dutch prince William on the English throne, power shifted from Amsterdam to London, and Britain faced no challenge in the North Sea until the 20th century.

In 1904 Russian ships on their way to the Far East fired on British fishing boats near the Dogger Bank, nearly bringing Britain into the Russo-Japanese War. As Germany's only outlet to the ocean, the sea was strategically important in both world wars.

The sea is bordered by Great Britain, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, and carries key north European shipping lanes. Offshore drilling began in 1966, and the Ekofisk field, found in 1969, began commercial production in 1971. The sea is Europe's main fishery, mostly by trawling. Until the First World War English also called it the German Ocean.
north-sea-canal: The North Holland Canal, built in 1824 to link the harbour of Amsterdam with the North Sea, was long and narrow and soon too small for the growing traffic. A few decades later it was decided to dig a new canal across the narrowest point of Holland, the shortest route to the sea. Digging began on 8 March 1865 at the dunes of Breesaap. No Dutch company was willing to take on the work, so it was awarded to an English contractor.

The builders dug a channel through the old IJ Bay and lined it with dikes; the rest of the bay was then reclaimed and turned into polders, and a new cut was made through the dunes at Velsen. Nine side canals were dug so that the tributaries of the IJ, among them the Spaarne, the Zaan and the Nauerna Canal, could still drain and carry shipping. The work was done by hand, and the labourers lived in huts of twigs, driftwood, sod and straw, where disease, fights and heavy drinking were common.

At the eastern end the Oranje Locks were built in 1872, closing the IJ off from the Zuiderzee so that a fixed water level could be kept. A small set of locks, the Zuidersluis, was built at the western mouth in 1876, where the new town of IJmuiden grew up. King William III opened the canal on 1 November 1876. The Middle Locks followed in 1896 and the North Locks in 1929, then the largest canal lock in the world, and the canal has been widened and deepened several times.

The canal ends at Amsterdam in the closed-off IJ, which joins the Amsterdam-Rhine Canal. Its water is drained to the sea through the sea lock at IJmuiden and the largest pumping station in Europe, a system vital to the groundwater management of the western Netherlands. Jetties built out into the sea, designed after research by the Waterloopkundig Laboratorium that began in 1957, keep the entrance from silting up. Tunnels for road, rail and metro, among them the IJ Tunnel and the Coen Tunnel, pass under it, and ferries cross it at Amsterdam.
north-west-company: After the British conquest of New France in 1763, English speakers took over the management of the fur trading posts, and the high cost of outfitting canoes for the far west pushed these pedlars to combine. The standard histories trace the company to a 16-share organisation of 1779 that included Isaac Todd, Simon McTavish and James McGill. It was put on a long-term footing in the winter of 1783–1784, and in 1787 it absorbed its rival Gregory, McLeod and Co., which brought in Alexander Mackenzie. From then the firm of McTavish, Frobisher and Company effectively controlled it.

Under the company's auspices Mackenzie descended the river now named after him to the Arctic Ocean in 1789 and crossed overland from Peace River to the Pacific in 1793, while David Thompson and Simon Fraser explored the Rocky Mountains and the Interior Plateau. Dissident partners formed the XY Company, which Mackenzie soon joined; after McTavish died on 6 July 1804 his nephew William McGillivray merged the two firms that year. In 1813 the company bought Fort Astoria from John Jacob Astor's Pacific Fur Company and renamed it Fort George.

The Hudson's Bay Company's charter gave it a virtual monopoly in Rupert's Land, and the rivalry turned violent after Thomas Douglas, Lord Selkirk, obtained the Selkirk Concession. After the Battle of Seven Oaks in 1816 Selkirk arrested McGillivray and other proprietors, seized Fort William and charged them with the deaths of 21 people. Ordered by Henry Bathurst, Secretary of State for War and the Colonies, to stop the hostilities, the partners signed a merger in July 1821, bringing 97 trading posts to the Hudson's Bay Company's 76.

The masters, or bourgeois, were mostly of Scottish descent, often related by blood or marriage: 77 of 128 leading figures were of Scots descent. Montreal agents hired staff, bought goods and exported furs, while wintering partners, each holding a share or two, ran the inland districts and met the agents every July at Grand Portage on Lake Superior, later at Fort William. Clerks served five to seven years as apprentices in hope of a partnership.

The servants, or engagés, were mostly Canadiens, peasants' sons from around Montreal. Seasonal voyageurs who paddled between Montreal and the Great Lakes were called pork-eaters, and wintering servants worked the interior posts. In 1799 the company employed nearly 2,500 people.
north-west-frontier-province: The East India Company annexed the north-western frontier after the Second Sikh War of 1848–49, and the region remained part of the Punjab until the province was created from its north-western districts in 1901. Commonly known as Sarhad, the frontier, it served with the Frontier Tribal Areas as a buffer with Afghanistan. Until 1947 it bordered five princely states to the north, the minor states of the Gilgit Agency to the north-east, the Punjab to the east and Balochistan to the south. It covered 70,709 square kilometres in six divisions, Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan, Hazara, Kohat, Mardan and Peshawar, to which Malakand was later added.

In a referendum held in July 1947, before the Partition of India, the province voted overwhelmingly to join Pakistan, and it acceded on 14 August 1947. The chief minister, Dr Khan Sahib, with his brother Bacha Khan and the Khudai Khidmatgars, boycotted the vote because it offered neither independence nor union with Afghanistan.

In 1955 the province was merged into the new province of West Pakistan under the One Unit policy announced by Prime Minister Chaudhry Mohammad Ali, and its offices of governor and chief minister ended on 14 October 1955. It was recreated in 1970, when the One Unit system was dissolved, and kept its name until 2010, when the Eighteenth Amendment to the Constitution of Pakistan renamed it Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

At independence there was a clear Muslim Pashtun, Hindkowan and Punjabi majority, with significant Hindu and Sikh minorities scattered across the province. Most people spoke Pashto or Western Punjabi, chiefly Hindko and Saraiki, and Kohistani was also spoken; before the British, Persian had been the official language. The tribal areas were counted separately in the colonial censuses.

The census of 1911 described Islam as less strictly observed in the southern districts, such as the Derajat, than in the north, through which the Khyber and Kurram routes had long carried conquerors, and found the Hindus of the province less particular about caste than those further east. Colonial census reports also noted how hard it was to tell Hindus and Sikhs apart.
north-west-rebellion: After the Red River Rebellion of 1869–1870, many Métis moved from Manitoba to the Fort Carlton region of the North-West Territories and founded the Southbranch settlements of Fish Creek, Batoche, St. Laurent, St. Louis and Duck Lake along the South Saskatchewan River. Their farms were laid out as narrow river lots, but from 1882 the Dominion Land Survey divided the new District of Saskatchewan into square townships. The 36 families of St. Louis found that the Crown had sold their farms and village to the Prince Albert Colonization Company, and with the buffalo gone they feared losing their main means of living.

Of about 5,400 Métis in Saskatchewan, most stayed neutral, as their priests advised; about 350 armed men supported Riel, and a smaller group opposed him under Charles Nolin. His supporters were mostly older, less assimilated Métis with close ties to the First Nations, while his opponents were younger, better educated and wanted to be part of Canadian society rather than a separate domain.

Riel, Gabriel Dumont, Honoré Jackson and others proclaimed the Provisional Government of Saskatchewan on 18 March 1885. On 26 March Dumont's fighters turned back a force of Prince Albert Volunteers and North-West Mounted Police under Leif Newry Fitzroy Crozier at Duck Lake. Ottawa sent Major General Frederick Middleton, whose force grew to about 5,500, including militia from Ontario and Quebec carried west by train through snow and breaks in the line.

Cree fighters took Fort Pitt on 15 April, and Métis held Middleton's column at Fish Creek on 24 April. Middleton captured Batoche on 12 May after three days of battle and siege, by which time the Métis had run out of ammunition, and Riel surrendered on 15 May while Dumont escaped to Montana. The Cree conflict went on: Poundmaker surrendered at Battleford on 26 May, and Big Bear's band, after a victory at Frenchman's Butte, fought the last engagement at Loon Lake on 3 June.

The campaign was Canada's first independent military action and cost about $5 million. It lost the Conservative Party much of its support in Quebec and secured anglophone control of the Prairies. Poundmaker and Big Bear were imprisoned, and eight men, among them the Plains Cree war chief Wandering Spirit, were hanged for murders at Frog Lake and Battleford, the largest mass hanging in Canadian history. Many Métis, who had no treaty status, were left on poor land or road allowances. Batoche, where the provisional government was formed, is now a National Historic Site.
north-yorkshire: North Yorkshire covers 8,654 km2 in Northern England and is bordered by County Durham, the North Sea, the East Riding of Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, West Yorkshire, Cumbria and Lancashire. The centre holds a wide plain, called the Vale of Mowbray in the north and the Vale of York in the south. The North York Moors rise to the east, and the Yorkshire Dales, in the west, contain the source of the River Ure, which becomes the Ouse and drains most of the county into the Humber estuary. Whernside, at 736 m, is the highest point. The Moors and most of the Dales are national parks.

The Local Government Act 1888 reconstituted the three ridings of Yorkshire as administrative counties, with Middlesbrough and York as county boroughs. The Local Government Act 1972, in force from 1974, created the non-metropolitan county of North Yorkshire from the majority of the North Riding, the northern part of the West Riding, the county borough of York, and parts of the northern and eastern edges of the East Riding, including Filey and Norton-on-Derwent. The area around the lower Tees, including Middlesbrough, became the new county of Cleveland, and North Yorkshire was divided into eight districts.

Cleveland was abolished in 1996, and Middlesbrough, Redcar and Cleveland, and the part of Stockton-on-Tees south of the Tees became part of North Yorkshire for ceremonial purposes, while York became a unitary authority. In 2023 the non-metropolitan county of North Yorkshire itself became a unitary authority, and the seven remaining districts were abolished.

Transport shaped the county's later history. The Tees Transporter Bridge opened in 1911 and is one of few surviving transporter bridges worldwide. The Beeching cuts of the 1960s took passenger services from places such as Richmond, Ripon, Tadcaster, Helmsley and Pickering, and the Larpool Viaduct near Whitby, opened in 1885, closed in 1965. The North Yorkshire Moors Railway, a heritage line, opened in 1973.

The county has a population of more than a million. Middlesbrough and Redcar lie in the north-east, forming part of the Teesside conurbation, and the city of York in the south; the rest is largely rural, with Harrogate, Ripon and Scarborough among its settlements. About 85% of the county is classed as rural or super sparse, and agriculture is the main source of employment over large areas. Tourism is a significant part of the economy, drawn by the Dales, the Moors, the coast and York.
northern-black-polished-ware: The ware gives its name to an urban Iron Age culture that succeeded the Painted Grey Ware and Black and red ware cultures. It developed in the late Vedic period and peaked from about 500 to 300 BCE, when the 16 great states, the Mahajanapadas, emerged in northern India, followed by the rise of the Mauryan Empire. According to Geoffrey Samuel, following Tim Hopkins, its centre in the Central Gangetic Plain was culturally distinct from the Painted Grey Ware culture of Kuru-Pancala to the west and developed towards cities and the use of iron on its own.

A transitional phase, proto-Northern Black Polished Ware, was first reported by Giovanni Verardi and his team at Gotihawa in the Terai of Lumbini, Nepal. It has a lustrous black surface with red spots left by problems in high-temperature firing, thick walls and the typical thali shape.

The period of the ware saw the first large cities of the subcontinent since the decline of the Indus Valley Civilisation, with massive embankments and fortifications, population growth, sharper social ranks, wide trade networks and crafts such as the carving of ivory, conch shell and semi-precious stone. Writing appeared in the Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts, including inscribed stamp seals, alongside a system of weights. Scholars note likenesses to the Harappan cultures, such as ivory dice and combs, though rice, millet and sorghum became more important. The culture may reflect the first state-level organisation in the subcontinent.

Around 200 BCE the ware gave way to red ware decorated with stamped and incised designs, but the same cities stayed inhabited and prosperous under the Shunga and Satavahana dynasties and the Kushan Empire.

The ware has been found at sites linked to the Mahajanapadas from Charsada and Taxila in Pakistan through Delhi, Hastinapura, Mathura, Ayodhya, Sravasti, Varanasi, Vaishali and Pataliputra to Ujjain and Vidisha, and east to Mahasthangarh and Wari-Bateshwar. Finds at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka show contact with the Gangetic valley. Shards from southern Thailand were once reported as the ware, but the archaeologist Phaedra Bouvet regards them as local KSK-Black Polished Wares, alike only in shape and style.
northern-cape: The Northern Cape holds 30.5 per cent of South Africa's land area, a size just short of the American state of Montana and slightly larger than Germany, and distances between towns are enormous. The province is dominated by the Karoo Basin, mostly sedimentary rock with some dolerite intrusions. The south and south-east are high-lying, at 1,200 to 1,900 metres, the west coast on the South Atlantic is dominated by Namaqualand, known for its spring flowers, and the north is primarily Kalahari Desert with parallel red sand dunes. The Orange River drains the interior westwards and forms the border with the Free State and with Namibia; near Upington it irrigates vineyards.

The precolonial past is reflected in a rich, mainly Stone Age, archaeological heritage. Wonderwerk Cave near Kuruman has a uniquely long sequence, reaching more than a million years in its basal layer, where stone tools may be Oldowan. Iron Age sites such as Dithakong lie in the north-east, because the westward spread of Iron Age farming was constrained mainly to the area east of the Langeberg Mountains. The copper mines of Namaqualand and the diamond rush to the Kimberley area created industrial landscapes that herald the modern era.

The province was created in 1994, when the Cape Province was divided into three, the others being the Western Cape and the Eastern Cape. In 1999 the government settled more than 1,000 San at Platfontein; they had served as trackers and scouts for the South African Defence Force in the Border War and had left Namibia after its independence, fearing reprisals.

Kimberley is the capital and the seat of the provincial government. The province has four official languages, Afrikaans, Tswana, Xhosa and English, and is the only one in which native Afrikaans speakers form a majority. The 2022 census counted 1,355,629 people, the fewest of South Africa's nine provinces. Mining and agriculture dominate the economy: diamonds around Kimberley, manganese and iron ore, sultana vineyards on the Orange River and sheep in the southern Karoo. It includes the Kalahari Gemsbok National Park, part of the Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park shared with Botswana, and the Augrabies Falls.
northern-circars: The region was a narrow strip along the western side of the Bay of Bengal, between 15° 40′ and 20° 17′ north. Circar is an English spelling of sarkar, a Mughal term for a district of a province, in use since the time of Sher Shah Suri. The Subah of Deccan had 22 circars, and these five northern ones were the most prominent: Chicacole (Srikakulam), Rajmandri (Rajahmundry), Ellore (Eluru), Mustaphanagar (Kondapalli) and Murtuzanagar (Guntur). Together they covered about 78,000 square kilometres.

The Bahmani Sultanate invaded the region in 1471, and from 1541 the Qutb Shahi dynasty extended its conquests over Guntur and Masulipatnam, wresting the country from Balram Dev I of Jeypore and completing the conquest in 1571 under Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah. In 1674 Vishwambhar Dev of Jeypore defeated the Qutb Shahi faujdar of Chicacole. Aurangzeb conquered Golconda in 1687 and annexed the Circars, but Raghunath Krishna Dev of Jeypore defeated and killed the first two Mughal faujdars and held the region until his death in 1708.

The fourth Nizam, Salabat Jang, who owed his throne to the French East India Company, granted the French the district of Kondavid and then the other circars. When the British took the fortress of Masulipatnam in 1759, they kept the port and left the rest under the Nizam's administration. After the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II's grant to Robert Clive in 1765, the British seized the fort of Kondapalli. The Nizam Ali Khan received an annuity of £50,000, and Guntur, the estate of his brother Basalat Jang, came under British administration only in 1788. In 1823 the company bought out the Nizam's remaining claims.

The loss of the Circars left Hyderabad State landlocked, bounded on all sides by British India. The region was governed as part of the Madras Presidency until independence in 1947. In 1953 its Telugu-speaking districts became part of Andhra State, which was joined with the Telugu-speaking parts of Hyderabad State as Andhra Pradesh in 1956; that state was divided again in 2014 into Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
northern-crusades: The Northern Crusades were military campaigns by Catholic kingdoms and military orders to convert the Balts, Finns and West Slavs around the southern and eastern shores of the Baltic. Some were explicitly called crusades, such as the war on the Estonians authorised by Pope Alexander III's bull of 1171, and some, like the Wendish Crusade, partly aimed at control of rich resources. Pope Celestine III's call in 1195 is counted as the official start, though the kingdoms of Scandinavia, Poland and the Holy Roman Empire had begun earlier. Conflict between Finnic, Baltic and Slavic peoples and their Saxon and Danish neighbours had been common for centuries, and the crusades gave it a papal sanction.

The Wendish Crusade of 1147 ran alongside the Second Crusade against the Polabian Slavs. Sweden campaigned against the Finns, Tavastians and Karelians between 1150 and 1293, and Denmark made crusades to Finland and Estonia, including one by Canute VI in 1191.

In Livonia, Bishop Albert of Buxhoeveden landed at the Daugava in 1200, and the Livonian Brothers of the Sword were founded in 1202. The Livonians, Latgallians and Estonians were subdued in turn, and Estonian resistance ended after a defeat near Viljandi in 1217 in which the leader Lembitu was killed. Denmark landed at Lindanisse, later Tallinn, in 1219, and Saaremaa accepted Christianity in 1227 after an army of 20,000 crossed the frozen sea. The Semigallians were conquered only in 1289 and 1290.

In Prussia, Duke Konrad I of Masovia called in the Teutonic Knights in 1226 after his own attempts failed. The Brothers of the Sword were crushed by the Samogitians and Semigallians at the Battle of Saule in 1236 and were absorbed into the Teutonic Order in 1237 as the Livonian Order. The Order failed to conquer Lithuania, though King Mindaugas accepted baptism around 1251. Against Orthodox Novgorod the Livonian branch was defeated at the Battle of the Ice in 1242.

Lithuania began its official conversion with Jogaila's baptism in 1386 and his marriage to Jadwiga of Poland. Fighting continued until the Battle of Grunwald in 1410, in which Poland and Lithuania decisively defeated the Teutonic Knights.
