The pagan peoples suffered forced baptism and military occupation, while the Teutonic Order and German merchants profited greatly. Livonia, also called Terra Mariana, remained under the complex control of the Livonian Order and prince-bishops.
northern-dobruja: Northern Dobruja is the part of Dobruja within Romania. It lies between the lower Danube and the Black Sea and is bordered on the south by Southern Dobruja, which belongs to Bulgaria. It now forms the counties of Constanța and Tulcea, with an area of 15,570 square kilometres and a population slightly under 900,000. Its cities include Constanța, Tulcea, Medgidia and Mangalia, and the Danube Delta, with its many lakes, belongs to it.

Around 600 BCE the Greeks colonised the Black Sea shore and founded fortresses and trading towns, among them Tomis, today's Constanța, Callatis and Histria, trading with the Dacians of the mainland. After the Roman conquest of the Dacian tribes Dobruja became a Roman province; the fortress of Capidava is among the best preserved remains. From the 7th to the 14th century it was part of the First and the Second Bulgarian Empire, for a long period in the 14th and 15th centuries it belonged to Wallachia, and from the mid-15th century it was Ottoman.

In 1878 Romania was given Northern Dobruja for its role in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-78 and as compensation for the transfer of a region partly overlapping Southern Bessarabia, while Bulgaria received the smaller southern part. After the Second Balkan War in 1913 Romania also annexed Southern Dobruja, and ruled it until the Treaty of Craiova in 1940. That treaty, approved by Britain, Vichy France, Germany, Italy, the Soviet Union and the United States, provided for a population exchange: the Bulgarian minority of Northern Dobruja moved south, and Romanians, including Aromanians and Megleno-Romanians, were brought north.

Alongside its Romanian population Northern Dobruja has a Csángó Hungarian village, Oituz, in Constanța County. Since 2015 Romania has observed Dobruja Day on 14 November, marking the incorporation of Northern Dobruja into the Kingdom of Romania after the Treaty of Berlin in 1878.
northern-england: Northern England mainly corresponds to the historic counties of Cheshire, Cumberland, Durham, Lancashire, Northumberland, Westmorland and Yorkshire. For statistical purposes it is the three northernmost regions of England: the North East, the North West, and Yorkshire and the Humber. Its northern boundary is the border with Scotland, its western the Irish Sea and a short border with Wales, and its eastern the North Sea. Its southern border is often debated.

The Pennines, sometimes called the backbone of England, run through most of the area, from the Tyne Gap to the Peak District. Other uplands are the Lake District, which has England's highest mountains, the Cheviot Hills and the North York Moors. The Pennines hold peat, large coalfields and millstone grit. The major cities are all as recent as the Industrial Revolution, while older cities such as Chester, Durham, Lancaster and York are comparatively small.

Roman histories name the Brigantes, whose name probably means highlanders, as the Celtic tribe that held most of the region, which the Romans called Brigantia. After Roman rule ended and the Angles arrived, the Old North, Yr Hen Ogledd, divided into the rival kingdoms of Bernicia, Deira, Rheged and Elmet. Aethelfrith of Bernicia conquered Deira around 604 and united the two as Northumbria, which saw a golden age of scholarly and monastic activity centred on Lindisfarne with the help of Irish monks. Cumbric, a Celtic language, was spoken mainly in Cumbria until about the 12th century.

The Northumbrian and Danish aristocracy resisted the Norman Conquest, and in the winter of 1069 to 1070 William the Conqueror ordered the Harrying of the North, in which towns, villages and farms were systematically destroyed across much of Yorkshire and northern Lancashire and County Durham. Famine followed. Chroniclers reported a hundred thousand deaths, while modern estimates are in the tens of thousands out of a population of two million. After the English Reformation the North saw Catholic risings against Henry VIII, including the Pilgrimage of Grace, and the Rising of the North against Elizabeth I.

At the start of the Industrial Revolution the North had plentiful coal and water power and cheap labour. Textile manufacture, iron and then steel, and shipyards on Tyneside and at Barrow-in-Furness grew up. The First World War was the turning point for the economy. In 1937 unemployment in the North, Scotland and Wales was 16.1 per cent against 7.1 per cent in southern England, and the period saw unrest including the general strike of 1926 and the Jarrow March.

The three regions together covered about 37,331 square kilometres and had a population of 15.5 million at the 2021 census, with 18 cities. Traditional dialect areas follow the historic counties, among them Cumbrian, Lancastrian, Northumbrian and Tyke, and urban speech includes Geordie, Mancunian and Scouse.
northern-europe: The northern region of Europe has several definitions. A restrictive one places it roughly north of the southern coast of the Baltic Sea, about 54°N, while others rest on climate and ecology. It may include the British Isles, Fennoscandia, the peninsula of Jutland, the Baltic plain to the east and the many islands offshore, and in some cases Greenland, which is politically European as part of the Kingdom of Denmark but not geographically in Europe. The area is partly mountainous, with Iceland, Jan Mayen, Scotland and the western seaboard of Scandinavia, and the whole region is at least mildly affected by the Gulf Stream.

The vegetation varies with the climate, from sparse tundra in the north and the high mountains, through boreal forest in the north-east and centre, to temperate coniferous and broadleaf forests in the south and west.

During the Early Middle Ages the Roman Catholic Church expanded into northern Europe and spread Christianity among the Germanic peoples. Christianity reached the peoples of Scandinavia and the Baltic region in later centuries. The Latin alphabet travelled north from Rome with Western Christianity, and led to the writing of English, German, Dutch, Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, Icelandic, Irish, Scottish, Welsh, Lithuanian, Latvian, Estonian, Finnish and Sámi languages. The Sámi were the last of the peoples to be converted, in the eighteenth century.

Every definition includes the Nordic countries, and many add the British Isles and the Baltic states. The United Nations geoscheme lists Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom, while EuroVoc and the CIA World Factbook place the British Isles in Western Europe. North Germanic languages are the most common first languages in Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark and the Faroe Islands. English is the most common in the British Isles, Finnic languages in Finland and Estonia, and Baltic languages in Lithuania and Latvia. Celtic languages are spoken in the British Isles, and the Sámi languages in the transnational region of Sápmi.
northern-expedition: In the 1920s the Beiyang government in Beijing was internationally recognised as the legitimate Chinese government, yet much of the country was ruled by a patchwork of warlords. The Kuomintang (KMT), based in Guangzhou, aspired to be the party of national liberation and spent the years after 1922 strengthening itself politically and militarily. Before his death in March 1925, Sun Yat-sen had supported Sino-Soviet co-operation, which produced the First United Front with the Chinese Communist Party. Chiang Kai-shek, Sun's protégé, was appointed commandant of the Whampoa Military Academy in 1924 and emerged as a contender to succeed him.

The nationalist government appointed Chiang commander-in-chief of the National Revolutionary Army on 5 June 1926, and he accepted the post in a ceremony on 9 July, the formal start of the expedition. The strategy, devised largely by the Soviet advisers Mikhail Borodin and Vasily Blyukher, was to defeat Wu Peifu while appeasing Sun Chuanfang. KMT forces took Changsha on 11 July, and Jiujiang and Nanchang by 19 September, but Sun Chuanfang counter-attacked and killed hundreds of students, teachers and suspected KMT members. On 22 March 1927 the army entered Shanghai after a communist general strike there, which is said to have caused 322 deaths.

In April 1927 the KMT split between Chiang's Nanjing faction and the left-leaning Wuhan faction under Wang Jingwei, partly after Chiang's Shanghai Massacre of Communists, which ended the First United Front. Chiang stepped down in August 1927 and went into exile in Japan. After Sun Chuanfang's attempt to retake Shanghai failed in the battle at Longtan, ending on 31 August, Chiang resumed command and in February 1928 was given the title Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Expeditionary Forces. With allied warlords including Yan Xishan and Feng Yuxiang, the army advanced north. Zhang Zuolin left Beijing by train and was killed on 4 June 1928 by a bomb planted by the Japanese Kwantung Army. The Third Collective Army entered Beijing on 6 June, ending the Beiyang government.

In December 1928 Zhang Xueliang, who succeeded his father, announced that Manchuria would accept the authority of the nationalist government in Nanjing, which was launched on 10 October 1928 with Chiang at its head. China remained in practice divided among five realms controlled by military leaders, and the proposals to centralise finance and military power depended on former warlords giving them up. The expedition also divided Stalin and Leon Trotsky in the Soviet Union. Stalin encouraged the Chinese Communist Party to co-operate with the KMT, while Trotsky opposed it, and the failure of the United Front left Stalin vulnerable and moved him towards Socialism in One Country.
northern-ireland-assembly: From 1921 to 1972 the devolved legislature for Northern Ireland was the Parliament of Northern Ireland, set up by the Government of Ireland Act 1920 and meeting at Stormont from 1932. It always had an Ulster Unionist Party majority, and the UK Government suspended it on 30 March 1972. Direct rule followed until 1999. An Assembly of 1973 with a power-sharing Executive was brought down by the Ulster Workers' Council strike in May 1974, and another set up in 1982 was dissolved in 1986.

The Northern Ireland (Elections) Act 1998 set up the Assembly under the Good Friday Agreement. The first election was on 25 June 1998 and it first met on 1 July, but it was a shadow body until full powers were devolved on 2 December 1999. It has been suspended six times, the longest from 14 October 2002 to 7 May 2007, when unionist parties withdrew from the Executive after police raided Sinn Féin's offices at Stormont. After the St Andrews Agreement of 2006, Ian Paisley and Martin McGuinness took office on 10 May 2007, and powers over policing and justice were transferred in April 2010.

A suspension followed from 9 January 2017 to 11 January 2020, after McGuinness resigned over the Renewable Heat Incentive scandal. Another began on 3 February 2022, when First Minister Paul Givan resigned. After the May 2022 election, in which Sinn Féin became the largest party, the Democratic Unionist Party refused to assent to the election of a speaker in protest against the Northern Ireland Protocol. Devolved government was restored on 3 February 2024, with Michelle O'Neill as First Minister and Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy First Minister.

The Assembly is a unicameral body of 90 members, known as MLAs, elected by single transferable vote. It selects most ministers of the Executive by the D'Hondt method, so that unionist and nationalist blocs both take part, and certain contentious motions need cross-community support. It may legislate on transferred matters, meaning anything not excepted or reserved to the UK Parliament; while it is suspended, the UK Government exercises its powers. It is one of two institutions of the Good Friday Agreement, the other being the North/South Ministerial Council.
northern-mariana-islands: The Northern Mariana Islands are the 14 northern islands of the Mariana Archipelago, whose southernmost island, Guam, is a separate United States territory. Their area is about 475 square kilometres. The southern islands are limestone, with level terraces and fringing coral reefs, while the northern islands are volcanic, with active volcanoes on several, including Anatahan, Pagan and Agrihan. Mount Agrihan is the highest point, at 965 m. The climate is tropical rainforest, with a dry season from December to June and a rainy season, which can bring typhoons, from July to November.

The Mariana Islands were the first islands settled by humans in Remote Oceania, around 1500 to 1400 BCE, by people from the Philippines. Ferdinand Magellan, sailing under the Spanish flag, reached Guam in 1521 and claimed the archipelago for Spain, which made the islands part of the Spanish East Indies in 1565 and in the 18th century forced the people of the northern Marianas to relocate.

After the Spanish–American War, Spain ceded Guam to the United States and sold the rest of the Marianas to Germany under the German–Spanish Treaty of 1899. After the First World War they became part of the Japanese Mandate under the League of Nations. The Battle of Saipan in 1944 ended Japanese rule, and afterwards the islands were administered by the United States as part of the United Nations Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. In 1975 nearly 80% voted to become a commonwealth of the United States, and in 1977 over 93% approved the constitution of the commonwealth.

The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands is an unincorporated territory of the United States whose residents are United States citizens. The 2020 census counted 47,329 people, most of them on Saipan, Tinian and Rota, the only permanently populated islands. The administrative centre is Capitol Hill on Saipan. The northern islands were evacuated because of volcanic threat, and Pagan has been largely uninhabited since a 1981 eruption.
northern-nigeria-protectorate: The Berlin Conference of 1884 and 1885 assigned the area to the British, and the Royal Niger Company, formed in 1886 with George Taubman Goldie as vice governor, moved inland and made trade and political agreements, sometimes coercive, with local chiefs. In 1897 Frederick Lugard was appointed head of the West African Frontier Force, raised against Fulani resistance and possible French incursions. On 1 January 1900 the company's charter was revoked: it received £865,000 and half of the mining revenue of a large area for 99 years, and Lugard read the proclamation of British rule.

Military operations began in 1902 and went on in sporadic fighting for about five years. The remnants of the Bornu Empire were conquered in 1902, the Sokoto Caliphate was defeated at the Battle of Kano, and fighting continued in Bassa in 1904. In 1906 a Mahdist rising at the village of Satiru, outside Sokoto, was put down by the Royal West African Frontier Force together with 300 Sokoto cavalry and infantry under Mallam Isa, sent by Muhammadu Attahiru II: it was the last major armed resistance to British rule in the region.

Lugard left for Hong Kong in 1907 and was followed as High Commissioner by Percy Girouard, a railway builder, and in 1909 by Henry Hesketh Bell. In 1912 the protectorate was estimated at about 660,000 square kilometres with some 10 million people. Lokoja was the capital from 1900, and from 1902 Zungeru, the most northerly town reached by river transport.

Chiefs and emirs, among them the emir of Bornu, were fitted into the administration as native authorities. Necessity drove the arrangement as much as design: Lugard's poll taxes were foiled by the emirates, powerful merchants opposed taxes on trade, the budget ran a deficit covered by imperial grants, and British staff were short before 1907. Those difficulties led Lugard to press for union with the Lagos Colony and the Southern Nigeria Protectorate, paid for in part by the south's customs revenue. On 1 January 1914 the protectorate became the Northern Province of the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria, whose northern administration stayed largely separate and relied still more on native authorities.
northern-qi: Northern Qi was the successor of the Xianbei state of Eastern Wei. Its founder, Gao Yang, had a Han father of largely Xianbei culture, Gao Huan, and a Xianbei mother, Lou Zhaojun. Gao Huan was the powerful minister of Eastern Wei and was succeeded by his sons Gao Cheng and Gao Yang, who took the throne from Emperor Xiaojing of Eastern Wei in 550 and established Northern Qi as Emperor Wenxuan. Though of mixed descent, the Qi rulers strongly asserted a Xianbei identity, and they referred to the surviving Tuoba and to literati of all ethnicities as near Han, calling them Han'er. Gao Huan was said to have told Han and Xianbei different things about each other.

Northern Qi was the strongest of the three main states in China when the Chen dynasty was established, the others being Northern Zhou and Chen itself. It was plagued by violent or incompetent emperors, in particular Houzhu, by corrupt officials and by deteriorating armies. In 571 He Shikai, an important official who had guided the emperors Wucheng and Houzhu, was killed, and Houzhu tried to strengthen the throne, instead setting off a series of purges that turned violent in late 573.

In 577 Northern Zhou, a northwestern kingdom with poorer resources, attacked, and the leaderless Qi disintegrated within a month amid large-scale defections of court and military personnel. Houzhu and the last emperor, Youzhu, were captured and both died in late 577. Gao Shaoyi, Prince of Fanyang, protected by the Tujue, later declared himself emperor in exile but was handed to Northern Zhou in 580 and exiled to what is now Sichuan. Historians dispute whether he counts as a Northern Qi emperor, but generally take 577 as the end of the dynasty.

Faced with the threat of the Göktürks, the Qi built long stretches of wall from 552 to 556 and rebuilt the Northern Wei wall in 555; the Northern Zhou repaired the Qi walls in 580, and the later Ming wall west of Gubeikou mostly follows their route. Two stretches of earth-and-stone Qi wall still stand in Shanxi.

Buddhist sculpture reached a stylistic peak under the Qi, moving from the linear drapery of the Northern Wei towards rounded, cylindrical bodies influenced by Indian Gupta styles. The court sponsored the Xiangtangshan Caves near Handan. Tombs have yielded ceramics, including a jar in a tomb closed in 576 seen as a forerunner of Tang sancai, and wares with Sasanian-style figures, which point to exchange with Western Asia.
northern-region-nigeria: British involvement in the north began with the trade of the Royal Niger Company, whose territory spread north from the meeting of the Niger and Benue rivers at Lokoja. Frederick Lugard proclaimed the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria at Ida, on the basis of the Treaty of Berlin of 1885. War with the Sokoto Caliphate followed: the emirates of Kontagora and Ilorin were conquered first, the fort of Kano was taken in February 1903, and Sokoto soon gave in. Lugard governed through local rulers by a policy of indirect rule, and in 1914 merged the protectorate with Southern Nigeria. The Richards constitution of 1945 gave the north wide autonomy.

The region's government followed the Westminster system. A premier led the government, while a governor acted as viceroy, commanded the constabulary and appointed the House of Chiefs, an upper house of unelected emirs of the Native Authority Councils; the elected House of Assembly sat beside it. The region was divided into thirteen provinces, among them Kano, the largest in population and economy, and Zaria, where the capital Kaduna stood. Groundnuts and cotton from Kano were its main source of revenue, and tin was mined in Plateau Province. The Hausa, Fulani and Kanuri, chiefly Muslims, dominated the north-west and east, while the Yoruba, Nupe, Tiv, Igala and Idoma were strongest in the north-central areas.

Under Sir Ahmadu Bello, its first premier, the Northern Peoples Congress dominated the regional parliament, and the Northern Elements Progressive Union formed the main opposition. After British rule ended in 1960, a governor continued to be appointed as representative of the federal administration in Lagos. In 1962 the British Northern Cameroons voted to become a province of the region. In 1967 the Federal Military Government of General Yakubu Gowon broke up Nigeria's four regions into twelve states, and the north became the North-Eastern, North-Western, Kano, Kaduna, Kwara and Benue-Plateau states, each with its own governor. The name Northern Nigeria is still used loosely for the same area.
northern-rhodesia: Northern Rhodesia was formed in 1911 by joining two earlier protectorates, Barotziland-North-Western Rhodesia and North-Eastern Rhodesia. The name Rhodesia comes from Cecil John Rhodes, who pushed British influence north of the Limpopo by obtaining mineral rights from local chiefs under questionable treaties. His main interest lay south of the Zambezi, and when Mashonaland's expected wealth did not appear, little was spent on the north. Lewanika granted concessions in Barotziland, and Joseph Thomson and Alfred Sharpe negotiated treaties with chiefs in the north-east in 1890 and 1891.

An Order-in-Council of 9 May 1891 placed the area under the British South Africa Company, though no Administrator went to Barotseland until 1895. The Orders-in-Council of 1899 and 1900 confirmed both territories as protectorates, with the Colonial Office responsible for the welfare of Africans. The Company's railway reached the Congo border and the Katanga copper mines in 1911.

The territory drew few European settlers, but they pressed for white minority rule and opposed the Company, which refused them elected representatives. After Southern Rhodesia received responsible government in 1923, the Company negotiated with the British government, and on 1 April 1924 Northern Rhodesia became a protectorate under the British government with a Legislative Council. Copper was the main economic factor. Large firms stayed profitable through the economic crash, and by the end of the 1930s mining was booming. During the Second World War Northern Rhodesian units served in the East African Campaign, at Madagascar and in Burma, and the Ministry of Supply bought the copper the armed forces needed.

Policy towards Africans was direct rule by District Officers, followed from 1930 by Indirect Rule that differed little in practice. Reserves created in 1928 and 1929 left about half the land by the main railway for European farming, and in 1938 the reserves were reported overcrowded. Africans organised through welfare associations, the Northern Rhodesia Congress, formed in 1948, and a miners' union.

The Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, formed in 1953, was intensely unpopular with the African majority and hastened calls for majority rule. A state of emergency in March 1959 led to the arrest of 45 Zambia African National Congress members, including Kaunda, who received a 19-month sentence. Northern Rhodesia became independent as Zambia on 24 October 1964. It entered the 1964 Summer Olympics under its old name and left the closing ceremony as Zambia, the only country to have changed its name and flag between the two.
northern-seven-years-war: The Kalmar Union of Sweden, Norway and Denmark lasted on and off from 1397 to 1523 and collapsed after Swedish resentment of Danish domination. Under Gustav Vasa, who claimed the Swedish throne in June 1523, Sweden began to rival Denmark–Norway, but its access to the North Sea was limited to a short stretch of the Kattegat near Älvsborg, and Denmark controlled the Baltic. In 1544 Gustav Vasa used the old Scandinavian levy to establish one of Europe's first native standing armies.

After the deaths of Christian III in 1559 and Gustav Vasa in 1560, both realms had young monarchs. Frederick II of Denmark envisioned reviving the Kalmar Union under Danish leadership, while Eric XIV of Sweden wanted to end Denmark's dominant position. Disputes over the Three Crowns insignia and Eric's failed marriage negotiations in 1563 added to the tension. Lübeck, upset by Eric's obstacles to the Russian trade, joined Denmark, and Poland–Lithuania joined to gain control of Baltic trade. War was declared on 13 August 1563.

The Danes advanced from Halland with about 25,000 professional mercenaries and took the Älvsborg fortress on 4 September 1563 after three days of bombardment, cutting Sweden off from the North Sea. Later, the Danish commander Daniel Rantzau defeated the Swedish army at the Battle of Axtorna on 20 October 1565. The Swedes fared better at sea, where the admiral Klas Horn destroyed much of a Danish–Lübeck fleet, levied a toll on ships in the Öresund and secured the eastern Baltic in 1565.

In the north, Swedish forces occupied Jämtland, Härjedalen and Trøndelag, including Trondheim, but were repelled from Bergenhus. A Swedish column in 1567 captured Hamar, reached the Skiensfjord and burned Skien before being repelled from Oslo. The Danish army, though superior, would not fight until its pay was current. Eric turned insane, paralysing the Swedish effort. In 1568 his brother John staged a coup and was enthroned as John III.

John III opened negotiations, and a draft peace at Roskilde on 18 November 1568 was rejected by the Swedes, so fighting resumed in 1569. With both armies exhausted, a meeting began at Stettin in September 1570, and peace was reached on 13 December 1570 in the Treaty of Stettin. The Swedish king withdrew claims to Norway, Skåne, Halland, Blekinge and Gotland, the Danes withdrew claims to Sweden, and the Kalmar Union was declared dissolved. Sweden ransomed Älvsborg for 150,000 riksdaler and returned captured warships. The Three Crowns dispute stayed unresolved. Historians disagree on whether the war ended in a Danish victory or inconclusively.
northern-thai-language: Lanna, also called Kam Mueang, Tai Yuan or Northern Thai, is a Southwestern Tai language spoken by the Lanna people of Thailand. It has about six million speakers, most of them in northern Thailand, with a smaller community in north-western Laos. Its speakers generally regard the name Tai Yuan as pejorative and call themselves Khon Mueang, Lanna or Northern Thai. Kam Mueang means city language, and Central Thai speakers call it phasa thin phayap, the speech of the north-western region.

Most linguists classify it in the Chiang Saen branch with Central Thai and Southern Thai, and consider it closer to Central Thai than to Lao, though it has been heavily influenced by both. Some modern scholars question this grouping, arguing that it may reflect political Thaification and that Lanna has closer historical ties with the Lao-Phutai branch. The language has six tones in the Chiang Mai dialect. Its verbs do not inflect, and word order is subject, verb, object.

The ancestors of the Lanna people spoke Southwestern Tai dialects and migrated from what is now Guangxi and northern Vietnam. Small-scale movement into Southeast Asia took place mainly between the eighth and twelfth centuries, and the ancestors of the Lanna followed the Mekong. They founded the early kingdom of Ngoenyang and smaller states such as Phayao beside the Mon kingdom of Hariphunchai. The Mon writing system was eventually adapted for the language as the Tai Tham script.

In the 13th century King Mangrai consolidated these lands as the kingdom of Lan Na. Under King Tilokkarat in the 15th century a golden age of Northern Thai literature produced many palm-leaf manuscripts in Tai Tham, written in the vernacular and mixed with Pali and Buddhist Indic vocabulary.

After the Burmese were driven out in 1775, the northern principalities were vassals of Siam, which annexed them in 1899. The Compulsory Education Act of 1921 banned schools and temples from using any language other than Central Thai, and Khruba Srivichai and other religious leaders were jailed for preaching in Lanna. Thai cultural mandates of the 1940s reinforced the prestige of Central Thai.

Today Lanna is often mixed with standard Thai in urban areas, while remoter areas use it alone. The traditional script is largely limited to Buddhist temples, where old sermon manuscripts are still used, and Thai script is used for writing the language, though it cannot show all of its tones. There is a renewed interest in writing it in the traditional way.
northern-zhou: The Northern Zhou was a Xianbei-led dynasty founded by members of the Yuwen tribe, of Xiongnu origin. It succeeded the Western Wei and was overthrown by the Sui. Its name came from the title Duke of Zhou held by its founder, Yuwen Jue, before his accession, and it reflected the Yuwen family's admiration for the Rites of Zhou. Claiming to have carried out reforms on the Zhou model was meant to show that the dynasty was the heir of the Ji-clan Zhou and to add legitimacy to the abdication from the Wei.

Its power was laid by Yuwen Tai, paramount general of the Western Wei. After his death in 556 his nephew Yuwen Hu forced Emperor Gong of Western Wei to yield the throne to Yuwen Tai's son Yuwen Jue, who became Emperor Xiaomin.

Yuwen Hu dominated the reigns of the first three emperors until Emperor Wu ambushed and killed him in 572 and took power himself. Emperor Wu destroyed the rival Northern Qi in 577. His death in 578 doomed the state, since his son Emperor Xuan was an arbitrary and violent ruler. After Xuan died in 580, his father-in-law Yang Jian took power, put down a rebellion by regional commanders led by Yuchi Jiong, and had five sons of Yuwen Tai put to death. On 4 March 581 Emperor Jing abdicated in favour of Yang Jian, who renamed the state Sui. The Northern Zhou had lasted twenty-four years.

Yuwen Tai encouraged agriculture and sericulture and restored the equal-field system, which returned land to farmers who had lost it to annexation, war and disaster. He raised the age for corvée service from fifteen to eighteen and limited it to one person per farming household. A Confucian, he founded the Imperial Academy at Chang'an under the scholar Lu Dan.

Buddhism and Buddhist art flourished, and the dynasty contributed narrative paintings of the Buddha's life in Cave 428 at Dunhuang. Tombs such as that of An Jia show contact with resident Sogdian merchants, whose main trading partners were the Turks of the First Turkic Khaganate. Emperor Wu married a Turkic empress, Ashina, daughter of Muqan Qaghan.
northumberland: Northumberland is low and flat near the North Sea coast and becomes increasingly mountainous towards the north-west. The west contains part of the Cheviot Hills and the North Pennines, and the Cheviot, at 815 metres, is the highest point. The Cheviot Hills consist mainly of Devonian granite and andesite lava, and the Whin Sill, an intrusion of dolerite on which Hadrian's Wall runs, forms a second ridge. The North Tyne and South Tyne join near Hexham, and the Tweed forms part of the Scottish border. Because of its latitude and high ground it is one of the coldest areas of England, though rainfall is relatively low.

The name is recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle as norð hẏmbra land, the land north of the Humber, and the kingdom of Northumbria took its name from the Old English for the people or province north of the Humber. The county has a rich prehistory, with rock art, hillforts such as Yeavering Bell and stone circles such as the Goatstones and Duddo Five Stones. Most of the area was occupied by the Brythonic Celtic Votadini, with the Brigantes to the south. In the Roman era most of the county lay north of Hadrian's Wall.

Much of the county's history was defined by its position on a border. The region was contested between England and Scotland into the early modern era, which led to the building of many castles, peel towers and bastle houses and to the early modern fortifications at Berwick-upon-Tweed. The earldom was held by the Scottish royal family by marriage between 1139 and 1157 and again between 1215 and 1217, and Scotland gave up all claims to the region in the Treaty of York of 1237. As lords in the Scottish Marches, the earls of Northumberland held the task of protecting England from Scottish retaliation for English invasions, and wielded significant power in English affairs.

Northumberland is also associated with Celtic Christianity, particularly the tidal island of Lindisfarne. Coal mining in the county goes back to Tudor times, and during the Industrial Revolution the area had significant coal mining, shipbuilding and armaments industries.

Northumberland is the northernmost county of England, a ceremonial county in the North East bordering Scotland. It is largely rural, and its administrative centre is Morpeth. It contains Northumberland National Park and the Farne Islands, known for their bird life. It has its own traditions, among them the rapper sword dance, the clog dance and the Northumbrian smallpipe, and its own tartan.
northwest-indian-war: By the Treaty of Paris of 1783 Great Britain ceded the lands north-west of the Ohio River to the United States, though the Native peoples living there had no part in it. As American settlers moved in, a Wyandot-led confederacy formed in 1785 to resist them; its members called themselves the United Indian Nations and are better known as the Northwestern Confederacy. In 1786 the Kentucky militia invaded Native land: George Rogers Clark's march along the Wabash achieved nothing, but Benjamin Logan's men burned the Shawnee towns on the Mad River, and the elderly chief Moluntha was executed. The confederacy then declared the recent treaties invalid because they had not been made with all its members.

Once the Constitution took effect, President George Washington directed the army to enforce American sovereignty. In autumn 1790 General Josiah Harmar led 1,100 militiamen and 320 regulars from Fort Washington against Kekionga, the Miami capital, and was defeated. The Natives followed up with raids such as the attack on Big Bottom on 2 January 1791, which killed eleven settlers. Arthur St. Clair, governor of the Northwest Territory, then led a second expedition, whose defeat in 1791 destroyed most of the United States Army.

In March 1792 Congress enlarged the army to more than 5,000 men under Major General Anthony Wayne, who reorganised it as the Legion of the United States and drilled it hard, flogging offenders and hanging deserters. Peace envoys sent to the Natives in 1792 were killed, and talks in 1793 failed. In 1794 Lord Dorchester told an Iroquois delegation that Britain might soon be at war with the United States, and John Graves Simcoe built Fort Miami on the Maumee. Wayne advanced up the Great Miami and Maumee valleys and won a decisive victory at Fallen Timbers.

The Jay Treaty with Britain required its withdrawal from the Great Lakes forts, which it left in 1796. By the Treaty of Greenville the confederacy also gave up tracts around forts in the Illinois Country, recognised the United States rather than Britain as the ruling power and surrendered ten chiefs as hostages until all prisoners were returned. Settlement and removals followed into the 1830s. Little Turtle lamented that more of his people had died since Greenville than in the war, and contributors to the Journal of Genocide Research describe the campaigns as attempted genocide, citing Henry Knox's orders to extirpate the Natives he called banditti.
norway: Norway's core territory comprises the western and northernmost portion of the Scandinavian Peninsula, together with the island of Jan Mayen and the archipelago of Svalbard. Its total area is 385,207 square kilometres, or 323,808 without Svalbard and Jan Mayen. The rugged coastline is broken by huge fjords and thousands of islands, and the mainland coastline including fjords stretches 28,953 kilometres. Sognefjorden is the world's longest fjord at 204 kilometres. The Scandinavian Mountains form much of the border with Sweden, and about 400,000 lakes lie within the country.

The earliest traces of human occupation lie along the coast, where the ice shelf of the last ice age melted between 11,000 and 8000 BCE. The oldest finds are stone tools dating from 9500 to 6000 BCE, and between 3000 and 2500 BCE Indo-European farmers of the Corded Ware culture arrived in eastern Norway. Bronze was introduced around 1500 BCE, and the oldest known Norwegian runic inscription dates from the third century. By about the 8th century several small political entities existed, and it has been estimated that there were nine petty realms in Western Norway in the early Viking Age.

According to tradition, Harald Fairhair unified them into one kingdom in 872 after the Battle of Hafrsfjord, becoming the first king of a united Norway; according to the sagas, many Norwegians left the country to live in Iceland, the Faroe Islands, Greenland and parts of Britain and Ireland. From 1537 to 1814 Norway was part of Denmark–Norway, and from 1814 to 1905 it was in a personal union with Sweden. Its Constitution was adopted on 17 May 1814. Norway was neutral during the First World War, and was invaded and occupied by Nazi Germany from April 1940 until the end of the Second World War.

Norway has about 5.6 million inhabitants, with Oslo as its capital and largest city. It is a unitary constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system, and its unicameral Parliament, the Storting, has 169 representatives. The Sámi people are indigenous to the Far North, and the Sámi Parliament gives them a certain amount of self-determination. From the 19th century up to the 1970s the government tried to assimilate both the Sámi and the Kven through what is called the Norwegianization process.
notion-ancient-city: The name means southern in Greek. The city stood on a hill within sight of the sea on the Gulf of Kuşadası, about 50 kilometres south of İzmir, and pilgrims bound for the oracle of Apollo at Claros often passed through it. Remains of its defensive walls, necropolis, temple, agora and theatre survive east of the modern town of Ahmetbeyli, in the Menderes district of İzmir Province.

Herodotus lists Notion as the southernmost city of Aeolis, and its Aeolian Greeks were uneasy neighbours of Ionian Colophon. The historian Robin Lane Fox links their rivalry to the story of a quarrel between two prophets at Claros, in which Mopsus, linked with the Aeolian Greeks of Notion, outwitted Calchas, linked with the Ionian Greeks of Colophon. Herbert William Parke suggests that in the seventh century BCE Notion controlled Claros but remained a small town dominated, and protected against Lydia, by Colophon.

Persia conquered both cities in the mid-sixth century BCE. Freed in the Greco-Persian Wars, they joined the Delian League separately, Notion paying a third of a talent a year against Colophon's three. Early in the Peloponnesian War, when one faction called in mercenaries under Persian command, the Athenian admiral Paches restored the pro-Athenian party, and Thucydides records that settlers were sent from Athens and the place was organised under Athenian laws; it then served as an Athenian base. By the late fourth century BCE Notion was joined with Colophon in a sympoliteia, a federal league, and by the Roman period its own name had fallen out of use.

Archaeological work, carried out in part by the University of Michigan, resumed in 2022. In July 2023 excavators found a hoard of 68 gold Persian darics buried beneath the walls of a house; the archaeologist Christopher Ratté suggested that a soldier may have hidden it for safekeeping.
notitia-dignitatum: The Notitia dignitatum et administrationum omnium tam civilium quam militarium, Latin for 'List of all dignities and administrations both civil and military', details the administrative organisation of the Western and Eastern Roman empires. It is one of very few surviving documents of Roman government, and it describes several thousand offices, from the imperial court to provincial governments, diplomatic missions and army units. The text is not dated and names no author. It is usually considered accurate for the Western Empire in the 420s and for the Eastern Empire in the 390s.

For each half of the empire the Notitia lists the major dignities it could bestow, often with the location and the staff, or officium, of each, except for the most junior members. The offices are arranged in three groups: court officials, including the most senior dignitaries such as the praetorian prefects; vicars and provincial governors, arranged by praetorian prefecture and diocese; and military commanders, the Comites Rei Militaris and Duces, with the full titles and stations of their regiments.

It does not record the numbers of personnel, so the size of units and of the army cannot be worked out. The late 4th-century army may have equalled that of the 2nd century, over 400,000 men, or been far smaller.

Several 15th- and 16th-century copies survive, and an illuminated one made in 1542 for Otto Henry, Elector Palatine, is kept in the Bavarian State Library. All derive from the Codex Spirensis, which was in the library of the chapter of Speyer Cathedral in 1542 but was lost before 1672. The most important copy was made for Pietro Donato in 1436 and illuminated by Peronet Lamy, and is now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford.

As a source it has limits. The two sections were compiled at different times and may rest on data up to twenty years older, so units are often listed twice. Parts are missing through copying losses. Roger Collins calls it an archaising text written about 425 and unreliable on the presence of units in Britain and Spain.
noto-province: Noto bordered Etchū and Kaga provinces to the south and was surrounded by the Sea of Japan on the east, north and west. Its abbreviated name was Nōshū. It was made up of four districts: Hakui, Noto (also called Kashima), Fugeshi and Suzu. Under the Engishiki classification system Noto was ranked as a middle country, both in importance and in its distance from the capital.

The province was created in 718, when its four districts were separated from Echizen Province. It was abolished in 741 and merged into Etchū Province, then re-established in 757. After that it disappears from the record until the Wamyō Ruijushō of 930, which names Minamoto no Shitagō as kokushi, or governor, of the province. In the Nara period the provincial capital and provincial temple stood in what is now the city of Nanao, while the Ichinomiya, Keta Shrine, lay in present-day Hakui.

In the Sengoku period Nanao Castle was a major stronghold of the Hatakeyama clan and was contested by the Uesugi and Maeda clans. Under the Tokugawa shogunate the province belonged to Kaga Domain, apart from some scattered small holdings that the shogunate kept as tenryō territory, administered by hatamoto for strategic reasons.

After the Meiji Restoration and the abolition of the han system in 1871, Noto Province was renamed Nanao Prefecture, and Imizu District of Etchū was added to it. In 1872 Nanao was merged with Kanazawa Prefecture, the former Kaga Province, to form Ishikawa Prefecture, and Imizu was returned to Niikawa Prefecture. The name Noto Province still appeared in official documents for some purposes, and it is named in treaties of 1894 between Japan and the United States and between Japan and the United Kingdom.
nottingham: Nottingham stands on an area of low hills along the lower valley of the River Trent, 42 miles south-east of Sheffield and 54 miles north-east of Birmingham. It is surrounded by Sherwood Forest in the north, the Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire and Yorkshire Coalfield in the west, and the Trent and Belvoir Vales in the east and south. The name comes from the Old English Snotingaham, meaning the homestead of the Snotingas, the family or followers of a man called Snot.

The written history of the settlement begins with Edward the Elder, who captured it and built a fortress on the south bank of the Trent. After the Norman Conquest William the Conqueror built a castle there and entrusted it to William Peverel. From around 1100 it was part of the Diocese of Lichfield, and from 1884 of the Diocese of Southwell. Nottingham is historically associated with the lace-making, bicycle and tobacco industries, and the Lace Market keeps streets of red brick warehouses. It was designated a city only in 1897, in celebration of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, although it has no Anglican cathedral.

Nottingham is a city and unitary authority area and the county town of Nottinghamshire, with a population of 323,632 at the 2021 census. Its centre is the Old Market Square, dominated by the Council House built in the 1920s. Ye Olde Trip to Jerusalem, partly built into the cave system beneath Nottingham Castle, is a contender for the title of England's oldest pub, supposedly established in 1189. Notts County, formed in 1862, was a founder member of the Football League in 1888. In 2015 UNESCO named Nottingham a City of Literature, citing links with Lord Byron, D. H. Lawrence and Alan Sillitoe.
nottinghamshire: Nottinghamshire is a ceremonial county of 2,160 km2, bordered by South Yorkshire, Lincolnshire, Leicestershire and Derbyshire. The River Trent forms a wide valley that crosses it from south-west to north-east, and north of it, in the centre of the county, lies Sherwood Forest, the remnant of a large ancient woodland. The county sits on extensive coal measures, largely in the north. Nottingham, in the south-west, is the largest settlement, followed by Mansfield, Worksop and Newark-on-Trent.

The county lies on the Roman Fosse Way. Angles settled it around the 5th century, and it became part of the Kingdom, and later Earldom, of Mercia. The name first occurs in 1016, and until 1568 the county was administratively united with Derbyshire under a single sheriff. In 1066 William the Conqueror made Sherwood Forest a Royal Forest for hunting. King John died at Newark Castle in 1216.

Coal and iron ore made the county important in the Industrial Revolution. The Wollaton wagonway of 1603 to 1616, among the first experimental waggonways in the world, carried minerals from bell pits at Strelley and Bilborough, and it led to canals and railways. The lace and cotton industries grew, and in the 18th and 19th centuries deeper mechanised collieries opened. Nottingham became synonymous with lace after the invention of the knitting frame by William Lee.

In the 17th century Mansfield and its surroundings became a centre of nonconformism, and George Fox, who lived in the town, made it a birthplace of the Quakers. Christopher Saxton mapped the county in 1576, and John Chapman produced the first fully surveyed map in 1774. In 1974 Blaxton, Finningley and part of Auckley passed to Doncaster in South Yorkshire.

Nottinghamshire has a population of more than a million and is closely tied to the Robin Hood legend through Sherwood Forest. Newstead Abbey, the ancestral home of Lord Byron, who sold it in 1818, is open to the public, and the author D. H. Lawrence came from Eastwood. In the north, William Brewster of Scrooby, who was linked to the Pilgrim Fathers, was influenced by Richard Clyfton, who preached at Babworth. Notts County, formed in 1862, is described as the world's oldest professional football club.
nouakchott: Nouakchott lies in the southwest of Mauritania, on the Atlantic coast of the Sahara Desert, and is one of the largest cities in the Sahara. The ground is largely flat, and some of the city lies below sea level. Sand dunes advancing from the east pose a daily problem, and the coastal strip is mostly left empty and allowed to flood, apart from a small fishing port and the deepwater port. The city is built around the tree-lined Avenue Gamal Abdel Nasser, and other major streets are named for figures of the 1960s, among them Charles de Gaulle, Kennedy and Lumumba.

The site held a small fishing town, a fortified fishing village (ksar) in pre-colonial times and under French rule, inhabited by the Bouhoubainy, a tribe of Amazigh origin. Moktar Ould Daddah, the first President of Mauritania, and his advisers chose it because he wanted a capital that symbolised modernity and national unity, which ruled out the towns of the interior. It lay centrally between Saint-Louis in Senegal, from which the colony was governed, and Nouadhibou, and avoided the question of whether the capital stood in an area dominated by Arabs and Amazigh or by Sub-Saharan Africans.

The basics were completed by the time the French granted independence on 28 November 1960. The city was planned for 15,000 people, with broad streets in a grid and without the expectation that commerce would take place in it. The Polisario Front attacked it twice in 1976, causing little damage. From the 1970s drought and desertification drove hundreds of thousands to the city, many settling in overcrowded slums. It had only 20,000 people in 1969; censuses counted 134,000 in 1977 and 393,325 in 1988, probably below the reality, and 958,399 in 2013.

Nouakchott is the capital and largest city of Mauritania and the centre of its economy, with a deepwater port built by China that opened in 1986, an international airport and the University of Nouakchott, opened in 1981. It is divided into nine arrondissements and three regions, and holds the National Museum of Mauritania, the National Library and the National Archives. Most residents are Sunni Muslim, and it is a principal selling place of Saharan meteorites.
noumea: Nouméa stands on an irregular, hilly peninsula near the south-east end of Grande Terre, the main island of New Caledonia, in the south-west Pacific Ocean. It lies on a protected deepwater harbour that serves as the chief port of the territory. The climate is tropical savanna, with hot summers and warm winters: average highs are around 30 degrees Celsius from January to March and about 23 degrees in July and August. September and October are the dry months, and the city receives roughly 1,100 mm of rain a year.

The first European to establish a settlement in the vicinity was the British trader James Paddon, in 1851. Eager to assert control of the island, the French founded a settlement nearby three years later, moving from Balade in the north. The area served first as a penal colony and later as a centre for the export of the nickel and gold mined nearby. From 1904 to 1940 the city was linked to Dumbéa and Païta by the Nouméa–Païta railway, the only railway line that ever existed in New Caledonia.

After the 1940 coup that installed a Free French governor, the United States Navy built Naval Base Noumea, and the city became the headquarters of the United States military in the South Pacific. After the war the five-sided headquarters complex became the base of a new regional intergovernmental development organisation, the South Pacific Commission, later the Secretariat of the Pacific Community and then the Pacific Community. The wartime presence survives in the names of districts such as Receiving, Robinson and Motor Pool.

Nouméa is the largest Francophone city in Oceania and the home of most of the island's European, Polynesian, Indonesian and Vietnamese residents, together with many Melanesians and Kanaks. Greater Nouméa covers the communes of Nouméa, Le Mont-Dore, Dumbéa and Païta; at the 2019 census it had 182,341 inhabitants, 94,285 of them in Nouméa proper. The University of New Caledonia traces its origin to the Université française du Pacifique, created in 1987, and became a separate institution in 1999.
noumea-accord: The accord, named after New Caledonia's capital and largest city, was the second agreement on the territory's future, after the Matignon Agreements of 1988. For the French Republic it was signed by Lionel Jospin, the prime minister, and Jean-Jack Queyranne, secretary of state for overseas affairs. Jacques Lafleur, Pierre Frogier, Simon Loueckhote, Harold Martin, Jean Lèques and Bernard Deladrière signed for the anti-independence Rally for Caledonia in the Republic (RPCR), and Rock Wamytan, Paul Néaoutyine, Charles Pidjot and Victor Tutugoro for the pro-independence Kanak and Socialist National Liberation Front (FLNKS).

The accord promised New Caledonia and its indigenous people, the Kanaks, greater political power over a transition of twenty years, while France kept control of the military, foreign policy, immigration, police and currency. If the presidency of New Caledonia is held by an opponent of independence, the vice-president must be a supporter of it. Later referendums were to decide whether the territory would remain a special collectivity of France or become an independent state, the last of them to be called by a vote of the Congress of New Caledonia.

The accord was put to a popular consultation in New Caledonia on 8 November 1998, and 72% voted in favour. Both signatory parties campaigned for it, the RPCR promising "at least 20 years of peace and stability" and a "future in the Republic", together with the Socialist Kanak Liberation Party of Nidoïsh Naisseline and the Federation of Committees Coordinating Independents. Against it stood the dissident anti-independence party Une Nouvelle-Calédonie pour tous, which saw it opening the way to a "banana republic", Guy George's local section of the National Front, Claude Sarran's Movement for France, and the union USTKE of Louis Kotra Uregi, which wanted immediate independence.

In the referendums that followed, in 2018 and 2020, majorities chose to remain French. The third, held in December 2021 after a vote of the Congress, widely rejected independence amid a boycott by the independence movement. The accord thus ran its full course of three votes, each of which kept New Caledonia within the French Republic.
nova-gorica: Nova Gorica arose from the border drawn by the Paris Peace Treaty of 1947, which gave most of the Slovene-inhabited areas of the Province of Gorizia to Yugoslavia while the town of Gorizia itself stayed under Italian rule. The new border ran just west of the Bohinj Railway and cut the city off from its northern and eastern suburbs. About 40% of the municipality's territory passed to Yugoslavia, including Solkan, Šempeter, Kromberk, Rožna Dolina and Pristava, with around 10,000 people, almost all of them Slovenes. These areas lacked a cohesive structure and were poorly connected.

To remedy this, the Communist authorities of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia decided to build a new settlement joining the suburbs into one urban space. The project had the personal backing of Marshal Tito and was commissioned from the Slovenian architect Edvard Ravnikar, a former pupil of Le Corbusier. The first plans were laid out in the winter of 1947 and construction began early in the following year.

The town was formally established as an urban municipality in 1952 and absorbed Solkan, Kromberk and Rožna Dolina. Building continued through the 1950s and 1960s, reaching its present extent by the mid-1980s. In the early 1990s the older suburbs regained the status of independent settlements. Since 1948 the town has replaced Gorizia as the principal urban centre of the Gorizia region, Goriška.

The name means new Gorizia, and locals commonly call the town simply Gorica and the Italian neighbour Stara Gorica, old Gorizia. Since May 2011 Nova Gorica has formed a cross-border metropolitan zone with Gorizia and Šempeter-Vrtojba, run by a joint administration board. The two cities shared the title of European Capital of Culture for 2025.

The town has one of Slovenia's three national theatres, and the Goriška Museum stands in Kromberk Castle. The University of Nova Gorica is in Rožna Dolina. South of the town on Kostanjevica Hill, a Franciscan monastery of the 17th century and the Church of the Annunciation hold a crypt in which Charles X of France, who fled the revolution of 1830 and died in exile at Gorizia, is buried with members of his family. To the north, Holy Mount rises to 682 metres and has drawn pilgrims for 450 years.
nova-scotia: Nova Scotia is a province on the east coast of Canada, in the Maritimes. It consists of the Nova Scotia peninsula, Cape Breton Island and some 3,800 other coastal islands, and is joined to the rest of Canada by the Isthmus of Chignecto, where its only land border, with New Brunswick, lies. Nowhere is more than 67 km from the ocean. The name is Latin for New Scotland, first given in the 1621 Royal Charter that granted Sir William Alexander the right to settle lands as a Scottish colony, including present Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and the Gaspé Peninsula.

The Mi'kmaq, of the Algonquian-language family, inhabited the land when Europeans arrived, as part of Mi'kma'ki, their territory across the Maritimes. In 1604 the French sailed into the Annapolis Basin but settled first at Saint Croix Island in Maine. In 1605 they founded Port Royal, which grew into Annapolis Royal: the first permanent European settlement in what later became Canada and the founding settlement of Acadia, France's first New France colony.

The Scots, English and then British fought France for the territory for over a century. Britain gained it in the Peace of Utrecht of 1713, which ended the War of the Spanish Succession, and Annapolis Royal remained the capital until Halifax was founded in 1749. The British then began settling foreign Protestants in the region and deported the French-speaking Acadians en masse. The Halifax Gazette, printed on 23 March 1752, was the first newspaper in Canada. Nova Scotia was ambivalent about joining the Americans, and thousands of Loyalists settled there during the American Revolutionary War.

In 1848 it became the first British colony to achieve responsible government. On 1 July 1867 the pro-Confederation premier Charles Tupper led it into Confederation with New Brunswick and the Province of Canada. The Anti-Confederation Party under Joseph Howe then won 18 of 19 federal seats and 36 of 38 provincial seats.

Nova Scotia is a Canadian province with a parliamentary system within a constitutional monarchy. Halifax is its capital and largest city, with over 45 per cent of the population at the 2021 census. It has the largest Scottish Gaelic-speaking community outside Scotland, and its Celtic music is kept alive each year at the Celtic Colours International Festival on Cape Breton Island.
november-uprising: The Congress of Vienna created the Kingdom of Poland in 1815 under Russian control, in personal union with the tsar as king. It had its own constitution, Sejm, courts, army and treasury, but the freedoms were gradually taken back. Alexander I introduced censorship in 1819, Russian secret police persecuted Polish clandestine organisations, and sessions of the Sejm were held in secret after 1825. Grand Duke Constantine Pavlovich, the de facto viceroy, abolished Polish social and patriotic organisations and replaced Poles with Russians in important posts. The final spark was a Russian plan to use the Polish army against the July Revolution in France and the Belgian Revolution, in violation of the constitution.

On 29 November 1830 a group led by the cadet Piotr Wysocki took arms from their garrison and attacked the Belweder Palace, but Constantine escaped. Armed civilians forced the Russian troops to withdraw the next day. General Józef Chłopicki was proclaimed dictator on 5 December 1830. He hoped to negotiate, but Tsar Nicholas I demanded unconditional surrender, and radicals around Joachim Lelewel took power. On 25 January 1831 the Sejm passed the Act of Dethronization of Nicholas I.

On 4 February 1831 a Russian army of 115,000 under Field Marshal Hans Karl von Diebitsch crossed the border. Polish cavalry won at Stoczek, and the bloody battle of Olszynka Grochowska on 25 February saved Warsaw for a time. Frequent changes of command, and hopes of foreign help that never came, weakened the Polish side. France and Britain did not intervene, and Austria and Prussia closed their frontiers to supplies. After Diebitsch died, Ivan Paskevich moved against Warsaw, and its suburb of Wola fell on 6 September 1831. On 5 October the remaining army of over 20,000 men crossed into Prussia and laid down its arms.

In 1832 Nicholas I issued the Organic Statute, under which Russian-occupied Poland lost its autonomy and became an integral part of the Russian Empire. Warsaw became little more than a military garrison, and its university closed. Thousands of insurgents were executed, imprisoned or forced into exile in what became known as the Great Emigration, which included many prominent intellectuals and artists.

Russia had sent over 180,000 trained men against about 70,000 Poles, yet the war lasted eight months. Critics at the time and later blamed divided leadership, hesitation and the failure to move the fighting to Lithuania. Popular sympathy for Poland was strong in Western Europe, but governments held to the Vienna system and the Polish cause remained diplomatically isolated.
novempopulania: The land that became Novempopulania lay in the triangle formed by the River Garonne, the Pyrenees and the Bay of Biscay. Julius Caesar, in his Commentarii de Bello Gallico, called it Aquitania after the Aquitani who lived there, and described them as different in language and body type from their northern neighbours and closer to the Celtiberians. Augustus later enlarged the province of Aquitania to cover a much larger and more diverse territory, so that the old name no longer meant the land of the Aquitani alone.

Between the 2nd and 4th centuries the nine peoples of the original territory seem to have won from the emperor the right to separate from the Gauls proper, through the magister pagi Verus; an altar dedicated to the deity of the pagus, found at Hasparren, commemorates it. The new status may have affected taxes and conscription, since separate Cohortes Aquitanorum were raised for the old Aquitanians. The peoples later numbered twelve, each with its civitas: Auch, Dax, Lectoure, Comminges, Couserans, Buch and Born, Béarn or Lescar, Aire-sur-l'Adour, Bazas, Tarbes, Oloron and Eauze. Inscriptions across the province name deities, persons and places resembling present-day Basque, a basis of the theory that Aquitanian was a form of proto-Basque.

In 418 Emperor Honorius allotted Aquitania to the Visigoths as foederati. They settled along the Garonne as far as Toulouse, their seat, but their hold on Novempopulania may have been more nominal than real, and after the Battle of Vouillé in 507 the Franks drove them out. Late antiquity brought unrest: documents mention bagaudae and later raids by the Vascones, a name that by then had widened to cover all the Basque-language tribes.

Novempopulania became the core of the Duchy of Vasconia, set up by the Franks early in the 7th century to hold back the Basques, which later split into the Duchy of Gascony and the County of Vasconia. Traces of Basque survive in the Gascon language, especially in its Béarnese dialect.
novgorod-first-chronicle: The chronicle is written in Old East Slavic and is also known by the title of its English edition of 1914, The Chronicle of Novgorod, 1016–1471. Its oldest copy, the Synod Scroll, was written in stages by several hands. Its oldest parts are dated palaeographically to the second half of the 13th century, while later passages, such as the account of the Battle of Lake Peipus of 1242, date from the middle of the 14th century, when monks of the Yuriev Monastery in Novgorod continued it.

The beginning of the Synod Scroll is lost, and its text opens in mid-sentence in 1016, during the succession crisis between Yaroslav and Sviatopolk. The younger copies, the Academic Scroll and the Commission Scroll, both of the 1440s, and the Tolstoi copy, run from 854 to 1447; the Commission copy opens with two genealogies and a regnal list of princes, all beginning with Rurik. The chronicle records the accession of princes, the election of officials such as the tysyatsky and posadnik, the building of churches and monasteries, epidemics and campaigns, and it legitimises a prince by saying that he sat on the throne of his father.

The Synod Scroll was first printed in 1841 and is kept in the State Historical Museum. The Academic copy belonged to Vasily Tatishchev and was acquired in 1737 by the Library of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Saint Petersburg. Oleg Viktorovich argued in 1987 that the later copies reflect a lost Primary Kievan Code of the late 11th century; Tetyana Vilkul, in her dissertation of 2015, showed that the younger text had been contaminated by the Primary Chronicle, which must therefore be older.

The historian Igor Froyanov studied the chronicle's account of two Magi in Novgorod in 1071, who told Yan Vyshatich that the devil made man and God put a soul into him. He noted its likeness to a Mordovian-Finn legend of the creation of man by God and the devil, and concluded that the Magi held a blend of Christianity and folk belief.

Later Novgorod chronicles drew on its text again and again. It was one of the main sources of the Novgorodsko-Sofiysky Svod, the protograph of the Novgorod Fourth and Sofia First Chronicles, which passed into the all-Rus' chronicle of the 15th and 16th centuries, and it was reflected independently in the Tver chronicle.
novhorod-siverskyi: Novhorod-Siverskyi lies on the bank of the Desna River, 330 kilometres from Kyiv. Late Paleolithic remains have been found near the town, including a site with three gigantoliths, a modified mammoth rib and the bones of a rich fauna. The town has kept many architectural monuments despite historic disasters, and its centre stands on two high capes divided by ravines. A historical reserve established in 1990 is named after the Tale of Igor's Campaign.

The town was first mentioned by Volodimer Monomakh as Novyi Horod, in connection with events of the winter of 1078-1079. After the Council of Liubech in 1098 it became the capital of an appanage duchy, the Novhorod-Siverskyi Principality, which served as a buffer against incursions by the Cumans and other steppe peoples and was a base of the Kyivan princely dynasty of the Olhovychi. A campaign of one of its princes against the Cumans produced the Tale of Igor's Campaign, a great monument of early East Slavic literature.

The Mongols destroyed the town in 1239. It then passed to the princes of Bryansk and to the Grand Dukes of Lithuania, and was ruled by Kaributas, son of Algirdas. Muscovy obtained the area after the Battle of Vedrosha in 1503 but lost it to Poland after the Time of Troubles. King Sigismund III Vasa granted it Magdeburg city rights in 1620, and it became the easternmost county seat of Poland. From 1648 it was a sotnia town of the Cossack Hetmanate and later a regimental town, and it came under the Tsardom of Russia after the Russo-Polish War of 1654-1667.

The town became a cultural centre of Left-bank Ukraine. Archbishop Lazar Baranovych set up a printing house in its monastery between 1674 and 1679, and the first public school in the region opened there in 1788-1789. It was the capital of a separate viceroyalty from 1782 to 1796, after which its importance steadily declined.

The Savior-Transfiguration Monastery, the former residence of the Chernihiv metropolitans, is the main monument. It has a neoclassical cathedral of 1791-1796 designed by Giacomo Quarenghi, 17th-century stone walls and church foundations from the 16th century. Other landmarks include the Cossack Baroque Assumption Cathedral, a triumphal arch for a visit by Catherine II in 1787 and the wooden Church of St Nicholas of 1760. The town is a centre of the food, hemp-processing, textile and construction industries.
novi-sad: Novi Sad lies in the southern part of the Pannonian Plain, on the border of the Bačka and Syrmia regions, on the banks of the Danube and facing the northern slopes of Fruška Gora. The main part of the city is on the left bank in Bačka, while the smaller settlements of Petrovaradin and Sremska Kamenica lie on the right bank in Srem. At Petrovaradin the river is only 350 metres wide. The name means 'new plantation' in Serbian; its Latin name, Neoplanta, stems from the grant of Habsburg city rights, and in German it was Neusatz.

Human habitation on the site has been traced to the Stone Age, and settlements and necropolises dating to about 5000 BCE were found during the building of a boulevard in Avijatičarsko Naselje. The modern city began in 1694. The Habsburg authorities, who had taken over the area near the end of the 17th century and favoured the Roman Catholic faith, forbade Orthodox Christians to live in Petrovaradin. The Serbs of the area therefore founded a new settlement across the Danube, first called the Serb city. In 1718 the inhabitants of the village of Almaš were resettled there.

For much of the 18th and 19th centuries Novi Sad was the largest city inhabited by Serbs. Vuk Stefanović Karadžić wrote in 1817 that it was the largest Serb municipality in the world, and its cultural and political influence earned it the name Serbian Athens. In 1843 it had 17,332 inhabitants, of whom 9,675 were Orthodox Christians, 5,724 Catholics, 1,032 Protestants and 727 Jews. The city was heavily bombed in the 1848 revolution: a third of its houses were destroyed and its population was halved. It was later rebuilt.

On 25 November 1918 an assembly in Novi Sad proclaimed the union of Vojvodina with the Kingdom of Serbia. From 1 December 1918 the city belonged to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and in 1929 it became the capital of the Danube Banovina of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.

Novi Sad is the second-largest city in Serbia and the administrative centre of the autonomous province of Vojvodina. The 2022 census counted 260,438 people in the city proper. Matica srpska, the oldest cultural and scientific institution in Serbia, moved there from Budapest in 1864, and the Serbian National Theatre was founded in the city in 1861. The University of Novi Sad was established in 1960. The Petrovaradin Fortress, across the river, holds the Museum of Novi Sad.
noviomagus-reginorum: The town lay in the land of the Atrebates, 7 kilometres north of Chichester Harbour on the English Channel. Its name is a modern construction from five pieces of evidence: Ptolemy's Noiomagos, a town of the Regnoi, which he may have placed at the tidal limit of the Arun rather than at Chichester; Regno at the end of the seventh route of the Antonine Itinerary; and Navimago regentium in the Ravenna Cosmography, both of which may refer to Fishbourne. The people's name is often taken as Regni, people of the kingdom.

The settlement began shortly after the Roman invasion of 43 as a winter fort of the Second Augustan Legion under Vespasian, whose timber barracks and stores have been excavated. After a few years the army left and a civilian town grew up. It had kilns, a bronze works and a dedication to Nero dated to 58, and the River Lavant was diverted to supply water. The town was the capital of the Civitas Reginorum, a client kingdom ruled by Tiberius Claudius Cogidubnus, who is named on the dedication stone of a temple to Neptune and Minerva and may have lived at Fishbourne Roman Palace.

It became a residential, market and industrial centre making fine tableware and enamelwork. In the second century a bank and timber palisade were built round it, later rebuilt in stone, with bastions added in the early fourth century along with new roads and a sewer. By the 380s it seems to have been largely abandoned, perhaps because of Saxon raids. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says Ælle of the South Saxons took it late in the fifth century and named it after his son Cissa, but archaeology shows no Anglo-Saxon settlement of the centre until the ninth century.

Little of the Roman town survives above ground. Part of a mosaic lies beneath the floor of Chichester Cathedral, a bastion stands in the gardens of the Bishop's Palace, and the city's museum, The Novium, holds finds from across the city and the remains of a Roman bathhouse in place.
novo-brdo: The name means New Hill. The town was Novus Mons or Novamonte in Latin, Nyeuberghe in Saxon texts and Novar or Novaberde in Ottoman Turkish, and its Albanian names are Novobërdë and Artanë. It is named in documents from 1326. Mining began under King Stefan Milutin of Serbia, who built the fortress to house Saxon miners; they brought efficient techniques and a legal system that gave them greater autonomy. Within about 50 years the mine was the most prosperous in medieval Serbia and housed a state mint.

In the 15th century some four to five thousand people lived inside the walls and eight to ten thousand in satellite settlements, a large town for medieval Europe. Iron, lead, gold and silver ores were mined and smelted, and its glam silver was an alloy of silver with a sixth to a third of gold; in 1450 the mines produced about 6,000 kg of silver a year. Merchants of the Republic of Ragusa ran the trade in precious metals. Albanians came to work the mines from the 13th and 14th centuries, and a Ragusan merchant's book of debtors lists 150 Albanian household heads in the 1430s.

The town fell to the Ottomans in 1441 and was restored to the Serbs by treaty in 1443. In 1455 it was besieged for forty days and capitulated on 1 June. The senior Serbian officials were executed, young men and boys were taken for the Ottoman army, among them Konstantin Mihailović, who described the siege, and some 700 young women and girls were given to Ottoman commanders. The scribe Vladislav the Grammarian was born in the town.

By the early 20th century most inhabitants had moved to the more accessible area of Gjilan. Novo Brdo is now a municipality of the Pristina district of Kosovo with its centre at the village of Bostane, and the census of 2011 counted 6,729 inhabitants. Two lead and zinc mines, Kišnica and Novo Brdo, operate in the municipality.
novocherkassk: Novocherkassk, whose name means New Cherkassk, stands near the confluence of the Tuzlov and Aksay rivers in Rostov Oblast, Russia. The Aksay is a distributary of the Don. The city is best known as the cultural capital of the Cossacks and the official capital of the Don Cossacks. It lies on a hill known as the Wolf's Lair, north of the older centre of Cherkassk.

Matvei Platov, Ataman of the Don Cossacks, founded the city in 1805 as the administrative centre of the Don Host Oblast. Cherkassk was judged unsuitable: it lay low on the Don and was repeatedly flooded, and its wooden buildings made it prone to fires. Ten of the eleven representatives of its villages refused to move, but Tsar Alexander I granted permission by a decree of 23 August 1804. Platov and the engineer François Sainte de Wollant planned a city with wide avenues and squares, which De Wollant called a little Paris.

Building was slow, since most Cossacks were reluctant to leave their homes and the new capital was far from the Don. In 1837 Tsar Nicholas I inspected it and another site and ordered the capital kept where it was. During the Russian Civil War the city was the centre of the Don Army counter-revolution under General Alexey Kaledin, until the Red Army drove the White-aligned Don Army out on 7 January 1920. German forces occupied it from 24 July 1942 to 13 February 1943. On 1 and 2 June 1962 food riots and a strike at the locomotive factory led to the Novocherkassk massacre, in which Soviet troops killed 26 protesters and wounded 87.

In 1991 a meeting of Don Cossack organisations confirmed Novocherkassk as the capital of the Don Cossacks, and in 1993 it was proclaimed the world capital of the Cossacks. It has a large neo-Byzantine cathedral, the palace of the ataman and monuments to Platov and to Yermak Timofeyevich. A monument opened in 2005 is dedicated to the reconciliation of White and Red Cossacks.
novorossiysk: Novorossiysk, in Krasnodar Krai, sprawls along the shore of Tsemes Bay, which does not freeze and has been recognised since antiquity as one of the superior bays of the Black Sea. The climate is borderline between humid subtropical and Mediterranean. The area is one of the main wine-growing regions of Russia: the wineries of Abrau-Dyurso, established by Tsar Alexander III in 1870, produce table and sparkling wines. The resorts of Anapa to the north and Gelendzhik to the south lie nearby.

In antiquity the shores of the bay held Bata, a Greek colony that specialised in the grain trade and is mentioned by Strabo and Ptolemy. After brief periods of Roman and Khazar control, the area belonged from the 9th century to the Byzantine province of Cherson. In the 11th century nomads from the steppe led by the Cumans overran it. Later in that century Anglo-Saxon refugees who had left England after the Norman Conquest approached the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who offered them land in the province if they could recapture it, and there is evidence that a Byzantine-English colony was founded. In the 13th century Genoese merchants of the Ghisolfi family kept a trade outpost in the area.

Novorossiysk developed rapidly in the 19th century. It received city status in 1866, and in 1896 it became the capital of the Black Sea Governorate, the smallest in the Russian Empire. In December 1905 it was the seat of the short-lived Novorossiysk Republic. From August 1918 to March 1920 it was the principal centre of Denikin's White Army in the Russian Civil War, and in 1920 many Whites escaped from it to Constantinople with the help of Allied warships.

German and Romanian armies occupied most of the city on 10 September 1942. A small unit of Soviet sailors held one part of it, Malaya Zemlya, for 225 days from 4 February 1943 until the Red Army liberated the town on 16 September 1943. Their defence kept the Axis from using the port for supply shipments. Novorossiysk was awarded the title of Hero City in 1973.

Novorossiysk is a port on the Black Sea and an industrial city, with steel, food processing and metal goods, and limestone quarries that supply cement factories. It is the terminus of the pipeline from the Tengiz Field in Kazakhstan. Its population was 262,293 at the 2021 census.
novosibirsk: Novosibirsk stands on the banks of the Ob River in the West Siberian Plain, in the southwest of Siberia, about 2,811 kilometres from Moscow. Its southern boundary runs through the Novosibirsk reservoir, formed by the dam of the Novosibirsk Hydroelectric Station, which cuts through the Ob Plateau. The nearest major cities are Omsk, Barnaul, Kemerovo and Tomsk. The climate is typical of Siberia, with dry winters and temperatures far below freezing, since there is no ocean nearby and no tall mountains to the north to hold back the Arctic winds. It is the second-farthest substantially populated city from the ocean, after Ürümqi in China.

The Russian town began on 30 April 1893 on the right bank of the Ob, near an area traditionally inhabited by the Chat Tatars, at the future site of a Trans-Siberian Railway bridge. In 1895 it became known as Novonikolayevsk, in honour both of Saint Nicholas and of the reigning tsar, Nicholas II. It superseded the village of Bolshoye Krivoshchyokovo on the opposite bank, founded in 1696, which was resettled in 1893 because of the bridge. The bridge was completed in the spring of 1897 and made the settlement a regional transport hub.
