Its importance grew with the completion of the Turkestan-Siberia Railway in the early 20th century, which linked it directly with Central Asia and the Caspian Sea.

Before 1917 Novonikolayevsk had no traditional centre: the railway management buildings, the station, the chief cathedral and the city government were spread across the town. After the revolution Lenin House was built in 1925 on Krasny Prospekt, and the first Lenin monument stood near the station. The city was ravaged by the Russian Civil War but recovered in the early Soviet period and took its present name, Novosibirsk, in 1926. Work on the Opera House began in 1931 on the former market square, and under Stalin the city became one of the largest industrial centres of Siberia. After the outbreak of the Second World War it received many factories moved from the Russian core.

Novosibirsk is the administrative centre of Novosibirsk Oblast and the Siberian Federal District, and the third most populous city in Russia, with 1,633,595 people at the census of 2021. Its landmarks include the neo-Byzantine Alexander Nevsky Cathedral and the Novosibirsk Opera and Ballet Theatre, and Tolmachevo Airport is the busiest in Siberia. The metro, opened in 1985, was the first in Siberia.
now-thank-we-all-our-god: Rinkart lived through the worst of the war at Eilenburg. During the height of a severe plague in 1637 he was the only surviving pastor in the town, conducting as many as 50 funerals in a day and more than 4,000 in that year, among them his wife's. A prolific hymn writer, he included Nun danket alle Gott in his Jesu Hertz-Büchlein, printed at Leipzig in 1636, under the title Tisch-Gebetlein, a short prayer to be said before meals. The exact date of its writing is debated.

The hymn spread quickly, and it was widely sung by the time the Peace of Westphalia was signed in 1648. Johann Crüger published it with its tune, Zahn No. 5142, in the 1647 edition of his Praxis pietatis melica. The melody is sometimes credited to Rinkart but is usually considered Crüger's, and a modified form of it is more often used when the hymn is sung in English, in the 19th-century translation by Catherine Winkworth, Now thank we all our God.

A story holds that after the Battle of Leuthen in 1757 the whole assembled Prussian army took up the hymn, and from it the melody is sometimes called the Leuthen Chorale. Historians and musicologists question the account and identify it as a later invention of Prussian propaganda.

J.S. Bach used the chorale in cantatas such as BWV 79 and 192, harmonised it for four voices in BWV 252 and 386 and set it as the chorale prelude BWV 657, one of the Great Eighteen. Felix Mendelssohn devised the harmonisation now standard in 1840, when he made the hymn, in G major and with its German words, the chorale of his Lobgesang, or Symphony No. 2. Later settings include Max Reger's chorale prelude of 1902 in his Op. 67, Sigfrid Karg-Elert's Marche Triomphale, John Rutter's version for choir and brass of 1974 and Václav Nelhýbel's concertato of 1977 for brass, organ and congregation.
nripendra-narayan: Nripendra Narayan was still an infant when his father, Narendra Narayan, died in 1863, and he was crowned maharaja the same year. The administration passed to a commissioner appointed by the British Governor General. He studied at the Wards Institute at Benaras, at Bankipur College in Patna and then law at Presidency College, Calcutta. Immediately after his marriage to Suniti Devi in 1878 he left for higher studies in England.

He abolished slave-keeping, Kritadas Pratha, in his state by a law of 1884. In the name of his queen he founded a girls' school in 1881, later the Suniti Academy, and in 1888 he set up Victoria College, now A.B.N. Seal College. He built the Nripendra Narayan Hall in Jalpaiguri in 1883, granted land for the Lowis Jubilee Sanitarium in Darjeeling in 1887, opened the Anandamayi Dharmasala to feed the poor of Cooch Behar in 1889 and laid out the Narendra Narayan Park, a botanical garden, in 1892. In Calcutta he founded the India Club in 1882 and was the first president of the Calcutta Club in 1907.

A keen promoter of cricket, he kept a ground at his palace, invited leading players from abroad and fielded a Cooch Behar team whose rivals were the team of the Maharaja of Natore; he also supported the football club Mohun Bagan. He was made a Knight Grand Commander of the Order of the Indian Empire in 1887. Of his four sons and three daughters, Rajendra and Jitendra later became maharajas of Cooch Behar.

Nripendra Narayan died at the English coastal resort of Bexhill-on-Sea in September 1911, where he had come to convalesce, and his funeral was held there on 21 September. His son Jitendra opened a memorial drinking fountain in the town in 1913; moved to Egerton Park in 1934, it was taken away for restoration in 1963 and later disappeared. Jitendra also founded the Nripendra Narayan Memorial High School in his memory in 1916.
nsukka: Nsukka is a city and a Local Government Area in Enugu State, Nigeria. It shares borders with Edem, Opi (an archaeological site), Ede-Oballa and Obimo. Its people speak central Igbo and the Nska dialect. It is an agricultural trade centre for the yams, cassava, maize, taro, pigeon peas, and palm oil and kernels produced by the local Igbo people, and weaving is a traditional local craft. Coal deposits have been found east of Nsukka around Obolo, on the main Onitsha-Makurdi road.

According to oral history, a man named Asadu Ideke Arụmọna had three sons, Nsukka, Ọbụkpa and Okpuje, who settled in their own territories and formed their communities. Nsukka in turn had three sons, Nkpụ̀naanọ́, Nru Nsukka and Ihe_N_Owerre, whose descendants make up the villages of the town. The name was later applied widely, perhaps because Nsukka housed the headquarters of the colonial Nsukka province. The British also created a colonial division named Nsukka, and a Nsukka Senatorial Zone was one of three in Enugu State until 1996, when General Sani Abacha created Ebonyi State. The zone was then renamed Enugu North, though the cultural zone is still known as Nsukka.

In the 18th and 19th centuries Nsukka had one of the best fighting forces in what is now Enugu North, each of its communities stationing its own, and it waged war on its neighbours to gain territory for its rising population. Some surrounding communities asked it for protection. In one war it annexed part of Ejuona-Obukpa, almost wiping out one village, Umugboguru. According to D. C. Ugwu this was a war with the community of Ejuona, which refused the help of the rest of Obukpa. The Achadu Oko Attah clan in Idah historically migrated from Nsukka.

Nsukka is the home of the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, the first indigenous university in Nigeria. The headquarters of the local government stand on Ugwu Ashọ́, a hill dedicated to the deity Ashọ́. Most indigenes follow traditional religion, and each year they celebrate the Omabe masquerade festival, which shows reverence for the Chi, the personal god, and strengthens ties between the communities.

The masquerade has different names in different communities: Akatakpa in Obollo Afor, Odo in Igbo Etiti, Ogede in Orba, and Oriokpa or Omaba in Nsukka. In earlier times masquerades served for entertainment, peacemaking, social control and security. In every village the oldest man, the onyishi, is respected and represents it; the title is not political and passes to a new holder when the current one dies.
ntare-v-of-burundi: Charles Ndizeye was born on 2 December 1947, the son of King Mwambutsa IV and Queen Baramparaye Ruhasha, and was educated at the Institut Le Rosey in Switzerland. His half-brother Prince Louis Rwagasore was assassinated in 1961 while prime minister. After a Hutu-led coup attempt in October 1965 his father went into exile in Switzerland, leaving Burundi in effect without a head of state, while Tutsi officers under Michel Micombero purged Hutu figures from the security forces and the political leadership.

In March 1966 Mwambutsa named his only surviving son heir and entrusted him with overseeing the government. On 8 July Ndizeye dismissed Prime Minister Léopold Biha and suspended the constitution, and on 12 July Micombero presented a government with himself as prime minister and minister of defence. Ndizeye was crowned mwami on 3 September as Ntare V. Tension between the soldiers and the monarchy soon grew: on 7 November soldiers turned him away from the radio station when he tried to broadcast a decree dismissing the government, and on 28 November, while he was on a state visit to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Micombero abolished the monarchy. His was the shortest rule of any Burundian mwami.

He lived in exile in West Germany and later Uganda, and returned in March 1972 in a helicopter provided by the Ugandan president Idi Amin, who said Micombero had guaranteed in writing that he could live in Burundi as a private citizen. Within hours he was under house arrest in the former palace at Gitega, and the government accused him of preparing a mercenary invasion; whether he meant to return peacefully remains unclear.

On 29 April 1972, the day a Hutu uprising began, he was killed by soldiers in circumstances still unexplained. The government said he was shot trying to escape, while his supporters say he was shot by a firing squad and thrown into a common grave. The researcher Nigel Watt argued that the government feared monarchists would back the rebellion. Between 80,000 and 210,000 people died in the mass killings of Hutus that followed.
nuapada-district: Nuapada district lies in the west of Odisha, between latitudes 20° and 21° 5' north, and covers 3,407.5 square kilometres. It is bounded on the north, west and south by Mahasamund district of Chhattisgarh and on the east by Bargarh, Balangir and Kalahandi districts. Its plains are fringed by rugged hill ranges stretching southward that belong to the main line of the Eastern Ghats and contain plateaus about 1,200 metres high. The district has one subdivision, Nuapada, and five blocks: Khariar, Sinapali, Boden, Komna and Nuapada.

Until March 1993 the area was part of Kalahandi district, which was divided by a state notification of 27 March 1993. Its early history is that of Kalahandi. It is believed to have formed part of the ancient territory of Mahakantara, where a king named Vyaghraraja ruled when Samudra Gupta campaigned in the region in the 4th century CE. The Nala kings ruled to about 500 CE, and the Sarabhapuriya dynasty, known from copper-plate records and gold coins, held the Nuapada area in the 6th century. The Somavamsis of South Kosala held it from the 8th century until Rajendra Chola's invasion of 1022, after which came the Telugu Cholas and the Eastern Gangas.

Khariar had a separate story. The Chauhans of Patna ruled it, and in 1590 Gopal Ray founded a line of semi-independent kings there. The Marathas took Khariar in 1741 and the British occupied it in 1818. When the province of Orissa was formed in 1936 Khariar became the Nuapada subdivision of Sambalpur district. Kalahandi merged with Orissa on 1 January 1948, and on 1 November 1949 the Nuapada subdivision was added to a reformed Kalahandi district, from which the present district was cut in 1993.

The district headquarters is the town of Nuapada, and Khariar and Khariar Road are the other towns with notified area councils. In the 2011 census Nuapada district had a population of 610,382, of whom 33.8 per cent belonged to Scheduled Tribes and 13.46 per cent to Scheduled Castes. About 58 per cent spoke Odia as a first language, 24 per cent Sambalpuri and 15 per cent Chhattisgarhi. The economy rests on agriculture, with rice the main crop, supported by irrigation projects including the Upper Jonk and the Sunder dam.
nuba-mountains: The Nuba Mountains, also called the Nuba Hills, lie in South Kordofan, Sudan. They cover an area roughly 64 by 145 kilometres and rise 450 to 900 metres above the surrounding plain. Their rocks form part of the south-western fringe of the Arabian-Nubian Shield and consist chiefly of metamorphic rock of Precambrian age, with some igneous rock. The largest hills, in the central area, are inselbergs of igneous rock, because the metamorphic rock has eroded to lower ground.

The climate is green and lush compared with the hot, semi-arid country around. A rainy season runs from mid-May to mid-October, with 300 to 800 millimetres of rain a year, supporting grazing and rain-fed farming, though water is often short at the end of the dry season. There are almost no roads, and most villages are joined by old paths that vehicles cannot use.

The mountains are home to a group of indigenous peoples known together as the Nuba. They are not the same as the Nubians of northern Sudan, and their name derives from that of the mountains. In antiquity the area was part of the Kingdom of Kush, and in the Middle Ages part of the Nubian kingdom of Alodia. The kingdom of Taqali later controlled the hills until its defeat by the Mahdi, Muhammad Ahmad. After the British defeated the Mahdi's army, Taqali was restored as a client state.

In the war in Sudan that began in 1983 the Nuba, who were not aligned with the north's sharia law or the Arabic language, suffered bombing, attacks on civilians and mines at the entrances to the mountains. Samuel Totten described the government's campaign as genocide by attrition, using starvation as a weapon. In 2002 an interim ceasefire allowed food and medical supplies into the area, and the SPLA agreed not to attack the pipeline to Port Sudan.

The Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 9 January 2005 did not give the Nuba Mountains the right to join South Sudan in its vote for independence in July 2011, and offered residents only a popular consultation. In June 2011 the governor of South Kordofan suspended that process, and fighting began between the Sudan armed forces and Nuba fighters of the SPLM-N.

Up to 1.5 million people live in the mountains, mostly Nuba, with a small minority of Baggara Arabs. The movement of Baggara groups such as the Messiria and Muraheleen into the region has been influential in later conflicts. The mountains also hold phosphate deposits containing uranium, vanadium and phosphorus that may be of economic interest.
nuba-peoples: The Nuba are made up of some 50 indigenous ethnic groups, and over one hundred languages counted as Nuba languages are spoken in their mountains. Most belong to the Kordofanian group, which falls mainly within the Niger–Congo family and may be the oldest group of languages in the region; several others are Nilo-Saharan, and many Nuba also speak Sudanese Arabic. They are not to be confused with the Nubians of northern Sudan and southern Egypt, although the Hill Nubians of the Nuba Mountains are also counted among the Nubian people.

In antiquity the Nuba Mountains were part of the Kingdom of Kush, and in the Middle Ages of the kingdom of Alodia. Remote and hard to reach, the area became a refuge for people of many tongues fleeing oppressive governments and slave traders. In the Second Sudanese Civil War (1983–2005) the SPLA's Volcano Battalion, under the Nuba commanders Yousif Kuwa Mekki and Abdel Aziz Adam al-Hillu, recruited Nuba volunteers, many of whom died walking to training camps in Ethiopia and back. The governments of Sadiq al-Mahdi and Omar al-Bashir armed Baggara Arab militias against the Nuba and moved many into camps by force, and attacks by the Popular Defense Force on Nuba villages have been cited as crimes against humanity.

An internationally supervised ceasefire in early 2002 became the foundation of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of January 2005, but fighting in South Kordofan was renewed in 2011, the year South Sudan seceded.

There is no political unity among the hill groups. Villages often have no chiefs and are organised into clans or extended families under their elders; where Islam has not deeply penetrated, ritual specialists who control rain and the crops hold as much authority. A family compound encloses two round mud huts thatched with sorghum stalks, a yard for goats and donkeys and tall conical granaries. Families typically keep three farms: a garden by the house, quick-growing red millet on the hills and white millet farther out. Traditional wrestling between villages is a central contest. Most Nuba in the east, west and north of the mountains are Muslims; in the south many are Christians or follow traditional religions.
nubia: Nubia lies along the Nile between the confluence of the Blue Nile and White Nile, near Khartoum, and the First Cataract, south of Aswan. It was divided into three regions named by their position along the river. Lower Nubia lay between the First and Second Cataracts, within the present borders of Egypt, Middle Nubia between the Second and Third Cataracts, and Upper Nubia south of the Third Cataract. Languages called Nubian, among them Nobiin, descended from Old Nubian, and Dongolawi and Kenzi, were prominent along the Nile, though other languages were used as well.

Fishing, hunting and gathering, and later herding, are attested throughout the Nile Valley. By 5000 BCE the inhabitants took part in the Neolithic Revolution, domesticating sheep, goats and cattle as the Sahara dried. Around 3500 BCE the A-Group culture arose in Lower Nubia: semi-nomadic herders who traded with the Egyptians and exported gold. It ended between 3100 and 2900 BCE, apparently destroyed by rulers of Egypt's First Dynasty, and there are no records of settlement in Lower Nubia for the next 600 years.

In Upper Nubia the Kerma culture, named for its capital at Kerma, was one of the earliest urban centres in the Nile region. By 1650 BCE its kings could organise labour for monumental town walls and large mud-brick buildings such as the Deffufas, and they were buried in rich tombs. Kerma lasted from about 2500 BCE until its conquest by the New Kingdom of Egypt under Thutmose I around 1500 BCE, and Egyptian heirs then ruled much of Nubia for four centuries.

The Kingdom of Kush conquered Egypt in the eighth century BCE under Piye, ruling as its 25th Dynasty. Meroë later became its southern capital, and its rulers controlled the Nile Valley over more than 1,000 km. Around 350 CE the Kingdom of Aksum invaded and the Meroitic kingdom collapsed. Three Christian kingdoms replaced it: Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia, the last two enduring for roughly a millennium. In the 16th century Nubia was partitioned, the north coming under the Ottoman Empire and the south under the Sennar sultanate, and it was reunited under Egypt in the early 19th century.

Nubia is now divided between Egypt and Sudan. In the early 1970s many Egyptian and Sudanese Nubians were forcibly relocated to make room for Lake Nasser, after dams were built at Aswan. Nubian villages stand north of Aswan on the west bank of the Nile and on Elephantine Island, and many Nubians live in cities such as Cairo and Khartoum.
nubians: The Nubians descend from the early inhabitants of the central Nile valley. Neolithic settlements in the central Nubian region date back to 7000 BCE, and by about 6000 BCE peoples in the region had developed an agricultural economy. Lower Nubia was at times part of Pharaonic Egypt and at times a rival state, and by the Twenty-fifth Dynasty (744 to 656 BCE) all of Egypt was united with Nubia. The ancient Nubians were known as archers of great skill and precision.

The modern name is debated. An older view derives it from the Egyptian word for gold, but this has no support in Egyptian texts, and the University of Chicago's Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures traces it instead to Greek forms of the name of the Noba or Nobatae.

The Kingdom of Kush remained a major power until the fourth century CE, when it weakened amid worsening climate, internal rebellion and invasion, notably by the Noba, who introduced the Nubian languages and gave their name to Nubia. Aksumite forces took Meroë, and the Kushite realm broke into the three kingdoms of Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia. Their people gradually became Christian, and frescoes made between 800 and 1200 CE in cities such as Faras followed the Byzantine style.

Islam reached Nubia from the eighth century. In 651 the Rashidun Caliphate invaded Makuria and was repulsed twice, and a treaty known as the Baqt barred further invasions in return for 360 slaves a year and required the Nubians to maintain a mosque for Muslim visitors. Sufi preachers settled in Nubia from the late fourteenth century, and by the sixteenth century most Nubians had converted.

Nubians speak Nubian languages of the Nilo-Saharan family as their mother tongue, and Arabic as a second language. The main Nile groups, from north to south, are the Kenzi, Faddicca, Halfawi, Sukkot, Mahas and Danagla. In Egypt they live mainly in Aswan Governorate, and in Sudan in the Northern State. Today Nubians practise Islam, with some syncretism of Islam and traditional folk belief.

The building of the Aswan High Dam in the 1960s flooded much of Lower Nubia and forced many Nubians to move, some to villages in New Nubia near Kom Ombo and others from Wadi Halfa to Khashm el Girba and New Halfa. Nubians share an identity expressed in poetry, novels, music and storytelling.
nuclear-fission: In fission the nucleus of an atom splits into two or more smaller nuclei, usually with neutrons and gamma rays, and gives off a very large amount of energy. The energy released by the fission of one uranium-235 atom is about 100 million times that of burning one carbon atom in air. Most fissions are binary, with two fragments of unequal size, typically in a mass ratio of about 3 to 2. Three fragments appear in two to four events per thousand. Because the fragments are different elements from the parent atom, fission is a form of nuclear transmutation. Spontaneous fission, with no neutron to start it, was discovered in 1940 by Georgy Flyorov, Konstantin Petrzhak and Igor Kurchatov.

The discovery was made in 1938 in the buildings of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society for Chemistry in Berlin. The chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann proved on 19 December 1938 that a fission reaction had taken place. The physicist Lise Meitner and her nephew Otto Robert Frisch explained it in theory in January 1939, and Frisch named it by analogy with the division of living cells. In February 1939 Hahn and Strassmann predicted that further neutrons were set free, which opened the way to a chain reaction.

The Hungarian physicist Leó Szilárd had first thought of a chain reaction driven by neutrons in 1933. On learning of Hahn's result from Eugene Wigner in January 1939 he urged Fermi and Frédéric Joliot-Curie not to publish, lest the Nazi government take notice. Fermi agreed to hold back, but Joliot-Curie's team reported in April 1939 in the journal Nature that uranium gave off 3.5 neutrons per fission.

Uranium-233, uranium-235 and plutonium-239 can sustain a chain reaction. In a controlled form it runs power reactors, research reactors and breeder reactors, which make more fissile fuel than they use. An uncontrolled form is the basis of the atomic bomb. The United States began an all-out effort to make such weapons in late 1942, and the Manhattan Project, led by General Leslie R. Groves, with J. Robert Oppenheimer directing its science, worked at Hanford, Oak Ridge and Los Alamos. The first device was fired in the Trinity test in July 1945, and in August 1945 a uranium bomb and a plutonium bomb were used on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
Fission also occurred in nature. At Oklo in Gabon sixteen sites show self-sustaining chain reactions about 2 billion years ago, found by Francis Perrin in 1972 and suggested by Paul Kuroda in 1956.
nueces-river: The Nueces is about 315 miles (507 km) long and is the southernmost major river of Texas north-east of the Rio Grande. It rises north-west of San Antonio on the Edwards Plateau in Real County and flows south through the Texas Hill Country, past Barksdale and Crystal City, coming within 35 miles of the Rio Grande. East of Carrizo Springs it turns east across the scrub plains of South Texas. At Three Rivers it is joined by the Atascosa and Frio rivers, and near Mathis it is dammed to form the Lake Corpus Christi reservoir.

Coahuiltecan-speaking groups called the river Chotilapacquen. Alonso de León named it Nueces, Spanish for nuts, after the many pecan trees along its banks, and the captain Blas María de la Garza Falcón was among the first settlers to scout the area, in 1766. Two missions were founded in the region in the mid-1700s, San Lorenzo de la Santa Cruz and Nuestra Señora de la Candelaria, and since the early 1800s they have fed rumours of lost Spanish mines nearby.

Mexico held that the Nueces had long been the border between its states of Coahuila y Tejas and Tamaulipas. The Republic of Texas instead claimed the Rio Grande, citing the Treaty of Velasco signed by the Mexican President Santa Anna after his defeat at the Battle of San Jacinto. The land between the two rivers became known as the Nueces Strip, and the dispute continued after the annexation of Texas by the United States. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo settled it, with Mexico, then under American occupation, accepting the Rio Grande as its northern border.
On 10 August 1862 pro-Union Germans from the Hill Country who were trying to flee to Mexico were ambushed and killed by Confederates on the river, in what is known as the Nueces massacre.
The river enters Corpus Christi Bay on the Gulf of Mexico at Corpus Christi. Its clear upper reaches hold largemouth, smallmouth and the native Guadalupe bass, and the American alligator lives in it.
nueva-planta-decrees: The decrees were signed between 1707 and 1716 by Philip V, the first Bourbon king of Spain, during and shortly after the War of the Spanish Succession, which ended with the Treaty of Utrecht. Philip was angered by what he saw as sedition by the realms of the Crown of Aragon, which had supported the claim of Charles of Austria to the Spanish thrones, and he took his native France as his model of a centralised state. He suppressed the institutions, privileges and ancient charters (fueros in Spanish, furs in Catalan) of almost all the territories of the Crown of Aragon.

The Basque territories and Navarre, which had at first supported Philip, kept their home rule after he backed down from his intent to suppress it following a military campaign against a Basque uprising.

The decrees ruled that all the territories of the Crown of Aragon except the Aran Valley were to be governed by the laws of Castile, described in the 1707 decree as the most praiseworthy in all the universe. The acts were promulgated in 1707 in Valencia and Aragon and in 1715 in Majorca. The decree for Catalonia was issued on 9 October 1715 and sent out from 16 January 1716.

They ended the Courts of Aragon, Catalonia and Valencia, whose members were summoned to the Cortes of Castile, now the Cortes of Spain. Internal borders and tariffs were erased, except in the Basque territory, and all subjects gained the right to trade with the American and Asian colonies. Top civil servants were appointed from Madrid, and Castilian became the sole language of government, displacing Latin, Catalan and others, with one exception: Basque could be used in the Vizcaya Chamber of the Valladolid court.

In Catalonia the decree abolished the Generalitat, the General Court, the Consell de Cent of Barcelona and most royal officers. A Captain General replaced the viceroy, the principality was divided into twelve corregimientos on the Castilian model, and the sometents, popular militias, were banned. A cadastre taxed property, labour, commerce and industry, multiplying the tax burden sevenfold in a land already devastated by the war.

The six Catalan universities were closed and replaced by a royal university at Cervera. Catalan private law survived, and was later codified in the Civil Code of Catalonia, but its criminal and mercantile law eroded through royal ordinances during the 18th century. The Aran Valley and the Valleys of Andorra escaped the decree. Secret instructions told new officials to introduce Castilian by temperate and disguised measures.
nuevo-leon: Nuevo León, officially the Free and Sovereign State of Nuevo León, lies in north-eastern Mexico. It borders Tamaulipas, Coahuila, Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí, and has an extremely narrow international border with Texas. It covers 64,156 square kilometres. Monterrey, the capital, is its largest city. Luis Carvajal y de la Cueva named the region the New Kingdom of León after the Kingdom of León, noting similarities in their mountainous terrain, and after independence the name was shortened.

Before European colonisation there was no established state. Historians estimate that about 250 nomadic groups lived in the territory, which the Spaniards called chichimecas. Four main groups can be identified: the Coahuiltecans to the west, the Alazapas to the north, the Borrados to the east and the Guachichiles to the south. A colonisation attempt under Alberto del Canto in 1577 founded Santa Lucía on the site of present-day Monterrey but failed because of raids by the indigenous people, whom the colonisers labelled Indios Bárbaros.

Luis Carvajal y de la Cueva, who had been with del Canto, returned to Spain and negotiated with Philip II to establish a new territory in northern New Spain. He founded the New Kingdom of León in 1582, with its capital San Luis Rey de Francia on the site of Santa Lucía. Colonisation failed again in 1588, when Carvajal was reported to the Inquisition as a descendant of New Christians, and the region remained mostly uninhabited by the Spaniards. Permanent settlement did not occur until 1596.

News of the Cry of Dolores of 16 September 1810 reached the region only on 29 September. Governor Manuel de Santa María first prepared to defend it, but after the insurgent General José Mariano Jiménez advanced he changed sides and proclaimed the insurgency in Monterrey on 17 January 1811. Nuevo León became a state of Mexico in 1824. Las Siete Leyes of 1835 replaced the state with a department, and in reply a secessionist movement set up the unrecognised Republic of the Rio Grande in 1840, with its capital at Laredo, Texas. It ended after defeat at the Battle of Saltillo, and statehood returned by August 1846 with the restoration of the 1824 constitution.

Under the Porfiriato, Bernardo Reyes was governor from 1885 to 1887 and from 1889 to 1909. In 1892 he negotiated a land swap with Coahuila that gave Nuevo León access to the border with Texas. His policies industrialised the state: the Cuauhtémoc brewery was founded in 1900, the Monterrey Foundry in 1904, Cementos Hidalgo, later Cemex, in 1905 and Vidrios y Cristales de Monterrey in 1909. Industrialisation continued through the 20th century.
nuku-of-tidore: Nuku was born into one of the four branches of Tidore's royal family; his father became sultan in 1757 as Jamaluddin. By then the Dutch East India Company (VOC) had dominated the formally autonomous sultanate, with its lands on Halmahera, Seram and New Guinea, for a century. In 1768 the Dutch forced Jamaluddin to give up his rights to Seram, and in 1779 they arrested and exiled him and two of Nuku's brothers on suspicion of misrule and dealings with the British East India Company. A treaty of 1780 reduced Tidore to a Dutch vassal.

Nuku left Tidore in 1780 for Patani in Halmahera, where he was proclaimed King of the Papuans. Raiding communities of south-eastern Halmahera and the Papuan Islands joined him, and to many Biaknese he was the leader who would bring Koreri, a utopian realm. After defeating the Dutch in 1783 he was welcomed on Tidore, but a Dutch and Ternatan force crushed the island, killing more than a thousand Tidorese, and set up Kamaluddin as a vassal sultan. Nuku fought on from the Raja Ampat and Seram islands.

From 1791 his following grew, and after the French occupied the Dutch Republic in 1795 British ships based themselves at Gebe, his headquarters. Ambon and the Banda Islands fell in 1796, and Nuku restored the old kingdom of Jailolo under Muhammad Arif Bila. In April 1797 his fleet took Tidore, and he became its de facto sultan as Muhammad al-Mabus Amiruddin. With the British governor of Ambon, William Farquhar, he took Ternate in June 1801, and Farquhar proclaimed him sultan; a treaty gave him 6,000 Spanish dollars a year for cloves.

After the Peace of Amiens the British left in May 1803. Nuku kept flying the Union Jack and demanded that the Batavian authorities recognise Jailolo and treat him as a brother rather than a child. He died on 14 November 1805 with his kingdom close to war. Called Jou Barakati, Lord of Fortune, he drew Tidorese, Halmaherans, Ceramese, Papuans and Aru islanders to his cause, but his realm did not outlast him: a Dutch attack drove his brother and successor Zainal Abidin from Tidore in 1806.
nukualofa: Nukuʻalofa lies on the north coast of Tongatapu, in the southernmost island group of Tonga. Its harbour is the only deep-water harbour of the island, which determined the choice of the area as the capital, and it is the central hub for maritime transport in Tonga. The city has a tropical climate of about 1,700 millimetres of rain a year, with almost constant trade winds and cyclones that are not rare.

On 10 June 1777 Captain James Cook anchored in the bay, in ten fathoms of water, between the shore of Tongatapu and two small islands. He never used the name Nukuʻalofa. The first written record of the name is in the book of George Vason, an English missionary of the London Missionary Society who arrived in 1797 and spelled it Noogollefa, since the standard Tongan alphabet was not developed until 1826 and 1827.

Methodist missionaries arrived in 1827, and Christians persecuted in Hihifo and Hahake took refuge in Nukuʻalofa. With the encouragement of its chief Tupou, the settlement grew into the major centre of Christianity in Tonga. Taufaʻahau later moved his capital from Pangai in Haʻapai to Kolofoʻou, the new town of Nukuʻalofa. He issued the Constitution of Tonga there on 4 November 1875, which formalised Nukuʻalofa as the capital, and Article 38 of the constitution says that Parliament meets there except in time of war.

As Nukuʻalofa grew, it was divided into three districts: Kolomotuʻa, the old town round the original fort, Kolofoʻou, the new town, which holds the palace of King George Taufaʻahau Tupou I and the seat of government, and Maʻufanga, in the east, an old village of the Haʻa Takalaua that sheltered refugees in the civil wars. Riots in 2006 burned down much of the central business district.

Nukuʻalofa is the capital and largest city of Tonga and the economic hub of the country. The national government is based there, the parliament meets there and the Royal Palace stands near the city. It has markets, a central business district and tourist hotels, and it is the hub of land transport on Tongatapu. Boats to the outer islands, including ʻEua, Haʻapai and Vavaʻu, leave from its wharves.
nukus: Nukus is the capital and largest city of the autonomous Republic of Karakalpakstan and the sixth-largest city in Uzbekistan. The Amu Darya passes west of it. The name comes from the tribal name of the Karakalpaks, literally New Kath, in Persian Nūkās; the root kus derives from Kath, the name of the past capital of Khwarazm, now called Beruniy. The city has a cold desert climate, with long, dry and very hot summers and short, cold and snowy winters. Because the Aral Sea and the Amu Darya have dried up, the climate has become much hotter and drier since 1960, and health conditions resulting from salt and other chemicals in the air have become more common.

In its modern location Nukus began as a fortress built in the 17th century. It grew slowly within the Khivan Khanate and later the Russian Empire, and was a mid-sized city before the Soviet era. When the Karakalpak Autonomous Oblast was established, Toʻrtkoʻl became its administrative centre. In the 1920s, however, Toʻrtkoʻl was threatened by flooding of the Amu Darya, whose banks lay about 12 kilometres away, and most of the institutions of Karakalpakstan moved towards Nukus. The city was officially founded in 1932 and eventually received capital status. By the 1950s further development and industrialisation had made it a city of broad avenues and big public buildings.

The city's isolation made it the home of the Red Army's Chemical Research Institute, a major research and testing centre for chemical weapons. In 2002 the United States Department of Defense dismantled the institute, which had been a major research and testing site for the Novichok agent, under a Cooperative Threat Reduction programme costing six million dollars.

Nukus is the centre of Karakalpakstan's economy, government, politics and culture. It is best known for the Nukus Museum of Art, named after Igor Savitsky, which is noted for its collection of modern Russian and Uzbek art from 1918 to 1935. Both Savitsky and the collection survived because the city's remoteness limited the reach of the Soviet authorities. The State Museum holds archaeological finds, traditional jewellery, costumes and musical instruments, and displays on the Aral Sea. The Berdakh museum, built in 1998, honours the Karakalpak poet Berdakh. Near the city lie the Zoroastrian structure of Shylpyk, raised in the 2nd to 4th centuries as a dakhma, and the settlement of Tok-kala.
numa-pompilius: Numa Pompilius is the second king of Rome in tradition, of Sabine origin. According to Plutarch he was the youngest of the four sons of Pomponius and was born on the day of Rome's founding, traditionally 21 April 753 BCE. He lived a severe life of discipline. Titus Tatius, king of the Sabines, gave him his only daughter Tatia in marriage, and after 13 years she died, which led Numa to retire to the countryside. Livy places him at Cures immediately before his election. Livy and Plutarch both mention the story that Pythagoras instructed him, and both discredit it as chronologically and geographically implausible.

After the death of Romulus there was an interregnum of one year, in which senators exercised royal power in rotation, each for five days. In 715 BCE, after bickering between the Roman and Sabine factions, the Senate elected Numa, then about forty years old. He refused at first, arguing that Rome was still a country of war and needed a leader of armies, until his father, Sabine kinsmen and two senators persuaded him. He asked that an augur consult the gods, and the omens from Jupiter were favourable.

Plutarch says his first act was to disband the personal guard of 300 celeres that Romulus had kept. He built a temple of Janus whose doors stayed shut throughout his reign, a unique case in Roman history. Livy calls Romulus a king of war and Numa a king of peace. Numa died of old age and, at his own request, was buried in a stone coffin on the Janiculum rather than cremated. Tullus Hostilius succeeded him.

Many of Rome's religious institutions are attributed to Numa, among them the Roman calendar, the Vestal Virgins, the cult of Mars, the cult of Jupiter and the office of pontifex maximus. He is said to have created the flamines of Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus and the Salii, who carry the sacred shields called Ancilia, and to have introduced the cult of Terminus, god of boundaries. By tradition he divided the year into twelve months and introduced January and February.

Legend gave him a close relationship with the nymph Egeria, who taught him to be a wise legislator. He was said to have written sacred books, buried with him. According to Livy, stone coffers found at the foot of the Janiculum in 181 BCE held two bundles of seven books each, in Latin on pontifical law and in Greek on philosophy. The praetor judged them dangerous to religion and the Senate ordered them burnt in the Comitium.
numantia: Numantia was an Iron Age hill fort, called an oppidum in Roman terminology, that controlled a crossing of the river Duero. Pliny the Elder counts it as a city of the Pellendones, but Strabo and Ptolemy place it among the Arevaci. The Arevaci were a Celtiberian tribe, formed by the mingling of Iberians and migrating Celts in the 6th century BCE, who inhabited an area near Numantia and Uxama. The remains lie on a hill known as Cerro de la Muela in the municipality of Garray, in the province of Soria.

The first serious conflict with Rome came in 153 BCE, when Quintus Fulvius Nobilior was consul. Numantia had taken in fugitives from Segeda, a city of another Celtiberian tribe, the Belli, whose leader Carus of Segeda defeated a Roman army. The Romans besieged Numantia and used a small number of war elephants, but were unsuccessful. In 137 BCE 20,000 Romans surrendered to the Celtiberians of Numantia, whose population was between 4,000 and 8,000. The young officer Tiberius Gracchus, as quaestor, saved the Roman army from destruction by signing a peace treaty with the Numantines, an action generally reserved for a legate.

The final siege began in 134 BCE. Scipio Aemilianus, commanding 30,000 soldiers, besieged the city behind a 9 km barrier supported by towers, moats and impaling rods. The Numantians refused to surrender and famine quickly spread. After eight months most of the inhabitants chose to kill themselves rather than become slaves, and a few hundred burned the city before surrendering after 13 months. Occupation continued in the 1st century BCE with a regular street plan but without great public buildings. The site declined from the 3rd century, was still settled in the 4th, and later remains from the 6th century hint at a Visigoth occupation.

The exact location of Numantia vanished from memory, and some theories placed it in Zamora. In 1860 Eduardo Saavedra identified the correct site at Garray. The ruins were declared a national monument in 1882. From 1905 the German archaeologist Adolf Schulten excavated and located the Roman camps around the city, and in 1999 those camps were included in a zona arqueológica. Many finds are in the Numantine Museum of Soria, while some objects taken by Schulten are in the Romano-Germanic Central Museum in Mainz.

Roman historians recorded the siege and admired the sense of freedom of the ancient Iberians and their fighting skill. Miguel de Cervantes wrote the play El cerco de Numancia about it, and the expression numantine resistance is used of particularly obdurate resistance. The Horse of Numantia, a copper fibula showing a horse, is an emblem of the province of Soria.
nunavut: Nunavut covers 1,836,993.78 square kilometres of land and 160,930 square kilometres of water in Northern Canada. It includes a substantial part of the mainland, most of the Arctic Archipelago, and the waters and islands of Hudson Bay, James Bay and Ungava Bay, among them Ellesmere Island in the far north, parts of Victoria Island and the distant Belcher Islands and Akimiski Island. The highest point is Barbeau Peak, at 2,616 metres, on Ellesmere Island. Its boundary with the Northwest Territories roughly follows the tree line. Most regions have a polar climate, and the more southerly continental areas a very cold subarctic one.

The mainland was first populated about 4,500 years ago by the Pre-Dorset, a Paleo-Eskimo culture that moved east from the Bering Strait region, and the Dorset culture, which developed from it, followed about 2,800 years ago. The Thule people, ancestors of the modern Inuit, began to migrate from Alaska in the 11th century, and by 1300 their settlement covered most of modern Nunavut. They replaced the Dorset genetically and culturally after 1300. The earliest written account of the area dates from 1576, when the English explorer Martin Frobisher, seeking the Northwest Passage, made the first recorded European contact with the Inuit in what is now Frobisher Bay. Henry Hudson, William Baffin and Robert Bylot followed in the 17th century.

In the 1950s, as part of the High Arctic relocation, the federal government moved Inuit from Nunavik, in northern Quebec, to Resolute and Grise Fiord, where they faced starvation but were forced to stay. A 1994 report led to compensation. Debate on dividing the Northwest Territories along ethnic lines began in the 1950s, and a plebiscite on division was held on 14 April 1982. The land claims agreement was completed in September 1992 and ratified by nearly 85% of voters in Nunavut. Parliament passed the Nunavut Act and the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act on 9 July 1993, and the territory was established on 1 April 1999, the first major change to Canada's political map since Newfoundland joined in 1949.

Nunavut's capital is Iqaluit, on Baffin Island, chosen in a plebiscite in 1995. Other major communities are Rankin Inlet and Cambridge Bay. The 2021 census counted 36,858 people, of whom 84.3% identified as Inuit. The official languages are the Inuit language, Inuktut, which includes Inuktitut and Inuinnaqtun, English and French. Alert, on Ellesmere Island, is the world's northernmost continuously inhabited place. Nunavut is Canada's only geopolitical region not connected to the rest of North America by the Pan-American Highway.
nung-people: The Nùng live mainly in north-eastern Vietnam and south-western Guangxi, and sometimes call themselves Thổ, meaning native to the land. Vietnam's census counted 968,800 in 2009 and 1,083,298 in 2019, the third largest Tai-speaking group after the Tày and the Thái. In China they are classed with the Tày as Zhuang, and many scholars of the Tai peoples consider the Zhuang and Nùng a single people known by different names in the two countries. The historian Keith Taylor calls the Vietnamese terms categories of French colonial knowledge.

Under the early Song dynasty the Nong clan rose to rule an area called Temo, reaching south to Guangyuanzhou, now Cao Bằng province. Its leader Nùng Trí Cao, known in Chinese as Nong Zhigao, founded a Kingdom of the Great Succession in 1042, was captured by Đại Cồ Việt and released, then proclaimed the Kingdom of the Southern Heavens in 1048. He was defeated by the Song in 1055, and many rebels fled into Vietnam around Cao Bằng and Lạng Sơn. There hereditary thổ ty officials governed the frontier, paying tribute to both Chinese and Vietnamese courts, and most Nùng communities ruled themselves until the Viet Minh took the Việt Bắc region in 1953.

Sun Yat-sen recruited fighters from Nùng villages on the Vietnamese side of the border, and the French of the Tonkin Protectorate saw Nùng strength as a threat while also courting them. After 1975, as tension grew with China, Hanoi doubted the loyalty of the Nùng. The Viet Bac Autonomous Zone was revoked, schooling was conducted in Vietnamese, and in the 1980s an estimated 250,000 ethnic Vietnamese were settled along the Chinese border.

The Nùng farm terraced hillsides, growing rice with water wheels for irrigation, along with vegetables, corn, peanuts, tangerines, persimmons, anise and bamboo. Like the Tày they are known for silversmithing, weaving, papermaking and embroidery, often in indigo. Society is patrilineal and grouped in clans named after the regions of China they came from. Their language was written in Sawndip, a script based on Chinese characters. Many follow an indigenous religion led by village shamans, influenced by Buddhism and Confucianism, and worship Quan Âm and their ancestors.
nuno-alvares-pereira: Nuno Álvares Pereira was born on 24 June 1360 in Cernache do Bonjardim, the illegitimate son of Álvaro Gonçalves Pereira, prior of Crato, and Iria Gonçalves do Carvalhal. His grandfather Gonçalo Pereira was archbishop of Braga from 1326 until 1349. About a year after his birth he was legitimised by royal decree and so received a knightly education.

At 13 he became page to Queen Leonor and began military service in 1373, helping to stop an invasion from Castile. At 16 he married Leonor de Alvim, a rich young widow. Of their three children, two sons died early, and their daughter Beatriz married Afonso, a son of King John I.

When King Ferdinand I of Portugal died in 1383, his only heir was Beatrice, married to King John I of Castile. To preserve independence, the nobles supported John, Master of Aviz. After his first victory over the Castilians at the Battle of Atoleiros in April 1384, John named Nuno protector and constable of Portugal, in practice supreme commander of the army, and count of Ourém. He was 24. He used guerrilla tactics against the Castilian army besieging Lisbon in 1384, until plague drove it away.

After the Cortes recognized John as king in April 1385, Castile invaded. On 14 August 1385 at Aljubarrota Nuno led 6,500 volunteers to victory over a Castilian force of more than 30,000. He attributed the victory to the Virgin Mary, whose name was inscribed on his sword. He was made count of Arraiolos and Barcelos and the realm's major majordomo, and the Portuguese defeated another larger Castilian army at Valverde. At his own expense he fed the hungry populations of his Castilian opposition, built churches and monasteries, among them the Carmelite church in Lisbon and the church of Our Lady of Victories at Batalha, and when hostilities ended gave the bulk of his wealth to the veterans.

After his wife's death he joined the Carmelite order in 1423 at the Carmo Convent in Lisbon, which he had founded in fulfilment of a vow, and took the name Friar Nuno of Saint Mary. He lived there until his death on 1 November 1431, noted for prayer and penance and suffering from arthritis. In his last year King John I visited and embraced him, weeping, as his closest friend. His tomb was lost in the 1755 Lisbon earthquake.

He is known as the Saint Constable. Pope Benedict XV beatified him on 23 January 1918. In July 2008 Pope Benedict XVI promulgated the decrees recognizing his heroic virtues and a miracle, and the canonisation was marked in Saint Peter's Square on 26 April 2009. His feast in Portugal is 6 November.
nuno-da-cunha: Born about 1487, Nuno da Cunha was the son of Antónia Pais and of Tristão da Cunha, the navigator, admiral and ambassador to Pope Leo X. He first proved himself in the fighting at Oja and Brava and at the capture of Panane, under the viceroy Francisco de Almeida. King John III of Portugal, to whom he had been close since the king was a prince, named him ninth governor of the Portuguese possessions in India, with orders to end the government of Lopo Vaz de Sampaio and send him to Portugal in chains.

The pirates he subdued at Mombasa on the passage out had been harassing the coast of Portuguese Mozambique, whose watering stations were essential to the route to western India. His brothers Pero Vaz da Cunha and Simão da Cunha were to have served as his second and third in command, as was expected in the Estado da Índia, but both died on the voyage, and during his long rule he had to rely on local networks of clientage in Goa. He took office in April 1529 and held it for nine years, longer than any other governor of Portuguese Asia in the sixteenth century.

In 1529 he sent an expedition that sacked and burned Damão in Gujarat. On 20 January 1533 forces under his control captured Baxay, the later Bassein and present Vasai, from Bahadur Shah. The next year it became the capital of the Portuguese province of the North, and its citadel of black basalt was begun; the citadel was completed in 1548 and still stands. In 1538 an army of the Sultanate of Gujarat under Khadjar Safar, aided by Ottoman forces, besieged the Portuguese in Diu.

Court intrigues forced his return to Portugal. He was shipwrecked at the Cape of Good Hope on the way and drowned; his death is dated 5 March 1539. He had married first Maria da Cunha and then Isabel da Silveira. The main source for his career is the history of the Portuguese in the East by João de Barros, who lived from 1496 to 1570.
nuno-de-guzman: He was born in Guadalajara, Spain, to an old noble family; his father, Hernán Beltrán de Guzmán, was a wealthy merchant and a high constable of the Spanish Inquisition. The family backed Prince Charles during the Revolt of the Comuneros. Guzmán studied law without taking a degree and served as one of the 100 royal bodyguards of Charles V, going with him to Flanders in 1522. The crown made him governor of Pánuco in 1525 as a counterweight to Hernán Cortés, and he took up the post in May 1527.

In Pánuco he stripped Cortés's supporters of property and had some tried and executed, and he organised a trade in Indian slaves: on a raid along the Río de Las Palmas in 1528 every horseman could take 20 slaves, and in eight months he issued more than 1,500 slaving licences. The slaves were branded on the face and shipped to the Caribbean. As president of the Audiencia he banned direct letters to Spain, so that Bishop Juan de Zumárraga hid one sealed in wax inside a cask, and on 7 March 1530 Zumárraga placed the Audiencia under interdict.

On 21 December 1529 Guzmán set out west with 300 to 400 conquistadors and 5,000 to 8,000 Nahua allies. At Tzintzuntzan the cazonci Tangáxuan II received him peaceably with gifts of gold and silver, but was tortured for hidden treasure, dragged by a horse and burned alive on 14 February 1530. The campaign, which has been called a genocidal enterprise, razed villages and tortured their leaders through Jalisco, Zacatecas, Nayarit and Sinaloa, where he founded San Miguel de Culiacán on 29 September 1531. His captain Cristóbal de Oñate founded Guadalajara, and his raids were a main cause of the Mixtón rebellion. He lost Pánuco in 1533 and New Galicia in 1534.

After an inquiry by Diego Pérez de la Torre he was sent to Spain in fetters and released from the castle of Torrejón in 1538. In a memorial of 1552 he called the cazonci's execution the most just carried out in New Spain. His will of 1558, found in 1973, shows him poor and in debt, leaving most of his belongings to Sabina de Guzmán, who had nursed him. He probably died in Valladolid on or soon after 16 October 1558. Bernal Díaz del Castillo called him the most foul and evil man in New Spain; his biographer Donald Chipman calls him the personification of the Black Legend, a reputation shaped largely by his opponents, Cortés, Zumárraga and Vasco de Quiroga.
nur-jahan: Mehr-un-Nissa was the second daughter of the Persian aristocrat Mirza Ghiyas Beg and his wife Asmat Begum. Her family's fortunes reversed in 1577, and Ghiyas Beg moved to Mughal India in the hope of service at the court of Akbar. Robbers took the family's remaining possessions on the way. Ghiyas Beg later became diwan of the province of Kabul and received the title Itimad-ud-Daula, Pillar of the State. He ensured his daughter a thorough education in Arabic and Persian, art, literature, music and dance.

In 1594 Akbar arranged her marriage to Ali Quli Istajlu, a Persian soldier given the title Sher Afgan. Their only child, a daughter named Ladli Begum, was born in 1605. Sher Afgan was killed in 1607, and Mehr-un-Nissa and her daughter were summoned to Agra, where she served for four years as lady-in-waiting to Ruqaiya Sultan Begum, a widow of Akbar.

Jahangir met her in 1611 at the palace's Meena Bazaar during the spring festival of Nowruz, and they married on 25 May that year. She was thirty-four, and his twentieth and last legal wife. He gave her the titles Nur Mahal and Nur Jahan. He also trusted her with his imperial seal, so that no document had legal force without her consent. Jahangir's addiction to opium and alcohol and his poor health eased her rise.

She obtained a pardon for her father and had him appointed prime minister, and made her brother Asaf Khan grand wazir. She married her daughter Ladli Begum to Jahangir's youngest son, Shahryar. Relations with Prince Khurram, the future Shah Jahan, were uneasy, and in 1622 he rebelled. In 1626 the rebel Mahabat Khan captured Jahangir on the road to Kashmir. Nur Jahan led an attack from a war elephant, failed, and was held captive with her husband, but she then organised an escape and raised an army.

Jahangir died on 28 October 1627 without naming an heir. Nur Jahan backed Shahryar, but her brother Asaf Khan, father of Mumtaz Mahal, sided with Shah Jahan and confined her. Shah Jahan defeated Shahryar's troops and ordered his execution, and became emperor in 1628. Nur Jahan lived under house arrest in Lahore with her daughter and granddaughter on an annual allowance of 200,000 rupees from Shah Jahan.

She oversaw the completion of her father's tomb at Agra, begun in 1622, one of the earliest examples of pietra dura in India, and built the Pattar Masjid at Srinagar and sarais for travellers. She died in 1645 at the age of 68 and was buried at the tomb she had built herself at Shahdara Bagh in Lahore. Its epitaph asks that there be neither lamp nor rose on the grave of this poor stranger.
nur-mountains: The Nur Mountains, in Turkish Nur Dağları, meaning Mountains of Holy Light, are a range in Hatay Province in south-central Turkey. They were formerly called Alma-Dağ, were the ancient Mount Amanus, were known in the Middle Ages as the Black Mountain and are called Jabal al-Lukkam in Arabic. The range begins south of the Taurus Mountains and the Ceyhan river, runs roughly parallel to the Gulf of İskenderun and ends on the Mediterranean coast between the gulf and the mouth of the Orontes.

It is about 200 kilometres long and rises to 2,240 metres, and it divides the coastal region of Cilicia from Antioch and inland Syria, forming a natural border between Anatolia and the rest of West Asia. The Belen Pass, the Syrian Gates, lies near the town of Belen, and the Amanic Gates farther north. The Amanos Mountains are recognized as a biodiversity hotspot and as one of nine environmental hotspots of Turkey, with typical Mediterranean flora and many endemic species.

Monks had lived solitary lives in the mountains since the fourth century, and in the 10th and 11th centuries the Black Mountain became a major centre of Byzantine monasticism, comparable for the Byzantine East to Athos in the West. Armenian, Melkite, Jacobite, Georgian and Catholic monasteries and hermits were established there, and the Turks called the range Gâvur Dağ, Mount of Infidels. In 1028 Emperor Romanos III, troubled by the number of heretical monks, tried to draft them for his campaign against Aleppo.

In 1066 the Seljuk general Afshin Bey devastated the monasteries and killed many monks, and in 1098 the monks gave provisions to the Crusader army besieging Antioch. The monasteries were plundered again after the Battle of Ager Sanguinis in 1119, when the Artuqids of Aleppo slew many monks.
nur-muhammad-taraki: Nur Muhammad Taraki was born on 14 July 1917 into a Ghilji Pashtun peasant family in the Nawa district of Ghazni Province. At fifteen he left for Bombay, where he worked as a clerk and met members of the Communist Party of India. Back in Afghanistan he became deputy head of the Bakhtar News Agency and known as an author. His best-known book, the novel De Bang Mosaferi (1957), treats the hardships of Afghan workers and peasants, and the Soviet Union hailed him as Afghanistan's Maxim Gorky.

In 1952 he was sent to the Afghan embassy in the United States, where he denounced the royal government as autocratic and was recalled. At a congress held in his own house in Kabul he was elected general secretary of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan on 1 January 1965, with Babrak Karmal as second secretary. He failed to win a seat in the parliamentary election of September 1965, and his paper Khalq was banned within a month. In 1967 the party split into the Khalq faction, led by Taraki, who favoured a Leninist state, and the Parcham faction under Karmal, who wanted a broad democratic front.

After the Saur Revolution of 27 April 1978, in which Mohammad Daoud Khan was killed, Taraki became Chairman of the Revolutionary Council and head of government, and the country was renamed the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan. He sent prominent Parchamites abroad as ambassadors, and his government's repression killed thousands, mostly at Pul-e-Charkhi prison. A land reform begun on 1 January 1979 proved unpopular and was abandoned; other reforms banned forced marriage and bride price. Unrest spread, and a revolt broke out at Herat in March 1979. He signed a treaty of friendship with the Soviet Union on 5 December 1978, but Soviet leaders refused his requests for troops.

His deputy Hafizullah Amin, who had built up a personality cult around him, fell out with him. Taraki was arrested on 14 September 1979 and, on Amin's orders, suffocated, according to most accounts, in October. Afghan media reported that he had died of illness. His death was one of the factors behind the Soviet intervention of December 1979.
nuraghe: The word nuraghe is the native name of the structure, with the plurals nuraghes in Logudorese Sardinian, nuraxis in Campidanese and nuraghi in Italian. The Oxford English Dictionary calls its etymology uncertain and disputed.

A typical nuraghe stands near alluvial plains, where earlier prehistoric Sardinian cultures had lived, and has the outer shape of a truncated conical tower with a tholos-like vault inside. Its walls have three parts: an outer layer tilted inwards and built of stones that shrink with height, an inner layer of smaller stones forming a corbelled dome, and an intermediate layer of small pieces and soil. It stands only by the weight of its stones, each of which may weigh several tons. Some are about 20 metres high, and the tallest known, Nuraghe Arrubiu, reached 25 to 30 metres.

The entrance leads into a corridor, often with open niches, and then to the round chamber. A spiral stair within the thick walls led to upper floors or a terrace, lit by embrasures, and a tower might hold as many as three corbelled chambers one above another. The commonest type is the single-tower nuraghe; the polylobed nuraghe, also called a Nuragic royal palace, has several towers linked by high ramparts.

There is no consensus on their function. They could have been rulers' residences, military strongholds, meeting halls, temples, ordinary dwellings or a combination. Some stand on hills that command important passages. Small models of nuraghes have been excavated at religious sites such as the Su Romanzesu site near Bitti. They were not the tombs of princes, as was once believed from human remains found in them, which belong to later Carthaginian and Roman strata.

The nuraghes were built between the middle of the Bronze Age, in the 18th to 15th centuries BCE, and the Late Bronze Age. The only buildings widely accepted as related are the torri of southern Corsica and the talaiots of Menorca and Mallorca. According to the archaeologist Massimo Pallottino, the architecture of the Nuragic civilization was the most advanced in the western Mediterranean in its period.

Nuraghes are inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list, with Su Nuraxi di Barumini in the south chosen to represent all the Nuragic heritage. One of the highest and most complex is Nuraghe Santu Antine near Torralba in the north.
nurek-dam: The Nurek Dam stands in a deep gorge on the Vakhsh River in western Tajikistan, about 75 kilometres east of the capital, Dushanbe. The Soviet Union built it between 1961 and 1980, when Tajikistan was a republic within the Soviet Union, and when finished it was the tallest dam in the world. A town near the dam, also called Nurek, houses the engineers and other workers employed at the power plant. An estimated 5,000 people were resettled from the area its reservoir flooded.

The dam is an earth-fill embankment, and its primary purpose is the generation of hydroelectric power. It is uniquely built, with a central core of cement forming an impermeable barrier inside a rock and earth fill about 300 metres high; at 304 metres it was the tallest in the world at the time.

The mound has a volume of 54 million cubic metres. The power station has nine Francis turbine-generators, the first commissioned in 1972 and the last in 1979. Each was built with a capacity of 300 MW, 2,700 MW in all, and they were redesigned and refitted between 1984 and 1988 to 335 MW each, giving an installed capacity of 3,015 MW.

The reservoir, known simply as Nurek, is the largest in Tajikistan, with a capacity of 10.5 cubic kilometres. It is more than 70 kilometres long and covers 98 square kilometres. Its stored water drives the hydroelectric plant and is also used for irrigation. The Dangara irrigation tunnel carries water 14 kilometres to about 700 square kilometres of farmland. It is suspected that the filling of the reservoir may have caused induced seismicity.
nuremberg: Nuremberg is the largest city of the cultural region of Franconia and the second-largest city of Bavaria, on the Pegnitz river. It forms a continuous conurbation with Fürth, Erlangen and Schwabach. Its location on key trade routes, and later at the junction of railways, highways and the Rhine–Main–Danube Canal, shaped its rise as a commercial centre.

The first documentary mention of the city, in 1050, names it as the location of an imperial castle. King Conrad III established the Burgraviate of Nuremberg, and Frederick I of the House of Hohenzollern inherited it in 1193. The city became a Free Imperial City in the 13th century, imperial diets were frequently held there, and the Imperial Regalia were kept in the city from 1424 until the end of the empire. Its cultural flowering in the 15th and 16th centuries made it the centre of the German Renaissance; Albrecht Dürer, a native, produced the first printed star charts in 1515. It accepted the Reformation in 1525.

The Nazi Party chose the city as the site of its large conventions, the Nuremberg rallies, held in 1927, 1929 and annually from 1933 to 1938, with the Rally Grounds designed by Albert Speer. At the 1935 rally Hitler ordered the Reichstag to convene at Nuremberg to pass the Nuremberg Laws, which revoked German citizenship for all Jews and other non-Aryans. Between 1945 and 1946 an international tribunal tried German officials for war crimes and crimes against humanity there; the Soviet Union had wanted Berlin, but Nuremberg had symbolic value.

Nuremberg has 546,397 inhabitants (2024) and is a centre of transport, education and commerce in northern Bavaria. It is known for its well-preserved medieval heritage, including Nuremberg Castle, the Old Town and the city walls, much of it rebuilt after the Second World War. The Heilig-Geist-Spital, founded in 1332, stands on the Pegnitz, and its museums show the world's oldest globe, built in 1492. Gingerbread known as Lebkuchen and grilled sausages are its traditional foods.
nuremberg-laws: The Nazi Party's programme included radical antisemitism and stripping Jews of their citizenship. After it took power, a national boycott of Jewish businesses was declared on 1 April 1933, the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service of 7 April forced non-Aryans out of the legal profession and the civil service, and books were burned on 10 May.

In 1935 assaults and boycotts increased again. On 25 July the Interior Minister, Wilhelm Frick, announced a law against marriages between Jews and non-Jews. The Economics Minister, Hjalmar Schacht, complained of the economic damage, and on 8 August Hitler ordered a stop to individual actions against Jews. On 20 August he insisted that the matter be settled by legislation.

The seventh Nazi Party rally, held in Nuremberg from 10 to 16 September 1935, included the only Reichstag session of the Nazi period held outside Berlin. On 13 September Hitler summoned the Reichstag and instructed officials of the Interior Ministry to draft a law on sexual relations and marriage. On the evening of 14 September he also ordered a citizenship law for the morning. He chose the mildest of four new drafts of the Blood Law and left the definition of who was a Jew vague.

The Reichstag passed both laws unanimously on 15 September. The Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honour prohibited marriages and extramarital intercourse between Jews and Germans and forbade the employment of German women under 45 in Jewish households. The Reich Citizenship Law made only those of German or related blood Reich citizens and classed the rest as state subjects without citizenship rights.

A decree of 14 November 1935 defined a Jew as a person with three Jewish grandparents, or with two if they practised the faith or had a Jewish spouse, and brought the Citizenship Law into force. Jews lost the vote, and A decree of 26 November extended the marriage law to Gypsies, Negroes and their bastards. Those accused of racial defilement were prosecuted in the regular courts; 1,911 people were convicted between the end of 1935 and 1940, and from 8 March 1938 many were re-arrested by the Gestapo after their sentences and sent to concentration camps. Prosecutions were delayed until after the 1936 Olympics.

Jewish firms closed, Jews were pushed out of regulated professions, and emigration was burdened by a Reich Flight Tax of up to 90 per cent of a person's wealth. By 1939 around 250,000 of Germany's 437,000 Jews had left. From mid-1941 the government began the mass murder of Europe's Jews, whose total dead is estimated at 5.5 to 6 million.
nurhaci: Nurhaci was born in 1559 into the Gioro clan of the Suksuhu River tribe and claimed descent from Mentemu, a Jurchen headman who lived some two centuries earlier. He grew up as a soldier in the household of the Ming general Li Chengliang in Fushun, where he learned Mandarin Chinese and read the novels Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Water Margin, from which he learned all he knew of Chinese military and political strategy.

In 1582 a rival Jurchen chief, Nikan Wailan, led Ming forces against Fort Gure, and Nurhaci's grandfather Giocangga and father Taksi were killed in the fighting. The Ming returned his father's remains, granted him trade patents and recognised him as Giocangga's successor, but refused to hand over Nikan Wailan. Nurhaci began to build his own power from thirteen sets of armour inherited from his father, attacked Nikan Wailan at Turun in 1584 and beheaded him in 1587.

In 1593 the Yehe called on a coalition of nine tribes against the Jianzhou Jurchens, and Nurhaci defeated it at the Battle of Gure. From 1599 to 1618 he campaigned against the four Hulun tribes, conquering the Hada in 1603, Hoifa in 1607 and Ula in 1613, and finally the Yehe at the Battle of Sarhu in 1619. In 1599 he had two translators, Erdeni Baksi and G'ag'ai Jargūci, adapt the Mongolian script to write Manchu. In 1606 the Mongols granted him the title of Kundulun Khan.

In 1616 he declared himself khan and founded the Jin dynasty, called the Later Jin after the Jurchen Jin dynasty of the 12th century. He appointed five trusted companions as chief councilors. He consolidated the Eight Banners, the military system that later formed the backbone of the Qing army. In 1618 he issued the Seven Grievances against Ming rule, most of them concerning Ming favour to the Yehe, and took Fushun, whose commander Li Yongfang surrendered and received a granddaughter of Nurhaci in marriage. His conquest of the Ming region of Liaodong laid the groundwork for the Qing conquest by his descendants.

In 1626 Nurhaci was defeated by the Ming general Yuan Chonghuan at the Battle of Ningyuan, the first serious military defeat of his life. He was wounded there by Portuguese gunners using cannons made at Macau, and he died two days later, on 30 September 1626, aged 67. His tomb, the Fu Mausoleum, lies east of Shenyang.

His son Hong Taiji renamed the Later Jin as Qing, and Nurhaci is usually regarded as the founder of the Qing dynasty, with the temple name Taizu. Accounts of his life come partly from later, propagandistic works such as the Manchu Veritable Records and partly from contemporary Korean sources, including the Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty.
nuri-al-said: Nuri al-Said was born in Baghdad to a middle-class family of Arab origins from the Qaraghouli tribe of Zubaid. His father was a minor government accountant. He graduated from the Ottoman Military College in Istanbul in 1906 and trained at the staff college there in 1911 as an officer in the Ottoman Army. In 1912 he was among the officers dispatched to Ottoman Tripolitania to resist the Italian occupation, and was captured by the British during the First World War. Converted to the Arab nationalist cause, he fought in the Arab Revolt under Emir Faisal ibn Hussain of the Hejaz. In 1918 he headed the Arab troops that took Damascus for Faisal.

After the French deposed Faisal in 1920, Nuri followed him to Iraq and in 1922 became the first director general of the Iraqi police. Faisal appointed him deputy commander in chief of the army in 1924. In 1930 the British were persuaded to drop their objections, and he became prime minister for the first time. Among his first acts was the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty of 1930, an unpopular measure that confirmed Britain's permanent military prerogativesand paved the way to nominal independence. He served eight terms as prime minister. After the Bakr Sidqi coup of 1936 he was exiled to Egypt, and he returned to office after a coup on 24 December 1938.

He fled the 1941 coup of Rashid Ali al-Kaylani and was reinstalled by the British. In the early 1950s he negotiated a fifty-fifty profit-sharing agreement with the Iraq Petroleum Company and set up the Development Board. The Baghdad Pact of 1954 and 1955 tied Iraq to the Western powers and Turkey and added to discontent, which grew after the Suez invasion of 1956. He became the first prime minister of the Arab Federation of Iraq and Jordan, formed in 1958 in reaction to the union of Egypt and Syria.

On 14 July 1958 Brigadier Abd al-Karim Qasim and Colonel Abdul Salam Arif seized control of Iraq, and King Faisal II, Prince 'Abd al-Ilah and others of the royal family were shot in the courtyard of the Rihab Palace. Nuri went into hiding but was captured the next day while trying to escape, shot dead and buried. A mob later disinterred his body and dragged it through the streets of Baghdad.

He was a controversial figure, and his detractors believed his blend of Iraqi nationalism, conservatism, pro-Western sentiment, anti-communism and anti-Nasserism had failed to adapt to Iraq's changed social circumstances. The Iraqi Jewish community left the country in large numbers under his rule.
nuruddin-ar-raniri: His full name was Nur al-Din Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Hasanji al-Hamid al-Shafi'i al-Ash'ari al-'Aydarusi al-Randeri, the last part naming his home town of Rander, in the Surat province of Gujarat. He was born into a Gujarati Muslim family of Hadhrami lineage that claimed descent from the Quraysh, and his mother was said to be Malay. After his first schooling at home he went to the Hadramaut and then to the Hejaz, where he performed the Hajj in 1620 or 1621, before returning to Gujarat and later sailing for Southeast Asia.

In Aceh he served Sultan Iskandar Thani first as mufti, a jurist giving legal opinions, and later as Shaykh al-Islām, the highest religious office of the court. He was both a Sufi, practising the mystical path, and a faqih, applying sharia to daily life. His charge against Hamzah Pansuri and Syamsuddin of Pasai was that their teaching broke the Islamic belief that God is unchanged by his creation, and his own many works set out what he held to be orthodox standards. He was the most prolific author of the Acehnese court and helped give it an international name as a centre of learning. He lost favour under Iskandar Thani's widow and successor, Taj ul-Alam.

His best-known work, the Bustan as-Salatin, or Garden of Kings, was begun in 1638 and written in Malay from Arabic sources. In seven volumes it covers the history of the world from the creation through the prophets of Islam to the Muslim kings of the Middle East and the Malay lands, together with several sciences. His writings were translated into other Indonesian languages and had considerable influence on Malay literature.
nusantara: Nusantara lies on the east coast of Borneo, in the East Kalimantan regencies of Penajam North Paser and Kutai Kartanegara, next to the port city of Balikpapan. Its coast stretches east to the Makassar Strait and south to Balikpapan Bay. The landscape is hilly and was previously an industrial forest. The designated area covers 2,560 square kilometres, of which 68.56 square kilometres form the Main Governmental Zone. The climate is tropical rainforest, with no real dry season and about 3,229 millimetres of rain a year.

Nūsāntara is an Old Javanese term meaning archipelago or islands, formed from the native nūsa, island, and a Sanskrit loanword, antarā. The earliest evidence dates from the 1200s, in the Mula Malurung inscription from the time of Singhasari, the predecessor of Majapahit. It was chosen as the city's name to express the national vision called Wawasan Nusantara and the country's status as an archipelagic state.

A move of the capital from Jakarta had been proposed since the presidency of Sukarno, who in 1957 inaugurated Palangka Raya with the idea that it might become the capital. In April 2017 President Joko Widodo ordered the national planning ministry to assess sites outside Java, as part of a strategy to reduce inequality between Java and the other islands. The minister of national development planning announced the name Nusantara on 17 January 2022, and construction began that year, delayed until after the vaccination campaign against COVID-19. The plan has five phases, lasting until the hundredth anniversary of Indonesian independence.

Soil and water from historically significant sites in all 34 provinces were brought to the new capital, among them water and soil from Kutai Lama in East Kalimantan and from former Majapahit sites in East Java.

Nusantara is administered not by an elected council but by the Nusantara Capital City Authority, an agency directly accountable to the central government, whose head is appointed by the president. It is planned as a national capital region at the provincial level, replacing Jakarta, which suffers from overpopulation and sinking land. The design aims at sustainability, with most journeys by public transport, cycling or walking, renewable energy and a tenth of the area given to food production.
nutmeg: The earliest evidence of use is 3,500-year-old residue on potsherds from Pulau Ai, one of the Banda Islands in eastern Indonesia. The Banda Islands, eleven small volcanic islands in the Maluku group, were the only source of nutmeg and mace until the mid-19th century, and the spice was traded over the Austronesian maritime network since at least 1500 BCE. By the 13th century Arab traders had pinpointed its origin in the Banda Islands but kept the location secret from European traders.

In August 1511 Afonso de Albuquerque conquered Malacca for the king of Portugal, and in November he sent three ships under António de Abreu to find Banda. Malay pilots guided them, and they arrived in early 1512, the first Europeans to reach the islands, buying nutmeg, mace and cloves. The Portuguese never gained full control of the trade or a foothold in the islands.

The English took the island of Run in 1616 under Nathaniel Courthope, but after his death in 1620 abandoned it to the Dutch. In 1621 the Dutch East India Company waged a bloody battle with the Bandanese to obtain a monopoly.
