Historian Willard Hanna estimated that the islands' population of about 15,000 fell to about 1,000, the rest killed, starved while fleeing, exiled or sold as slaves. By the Treaty of Breda the British ceded Run to the Dutch in exchange for New Amsterdam, modern Manhattan.

Nutmeg is the seed, or the ground spice made from the seed, of the fragrant nutmeg tree, Myristica fragrans, a dark-leaved evergreen native to the Moluccas. The tree also yields mace, made from the reddish aril that covers the seed. Nutmeg has a pungent fragrance and a warm, slightly sweet taste, and mace a similar but more delicate flavour. Nutmeg is also cultivated on Penang, in Kerala and in the Caribbean, especially Grenada.

Nutmeg flavours baked goods, puddings, sausages, sauces and drinks such as eggnog and mulled wine; in Dutch cooking it is added to vegetables, in haggis in Scotland, and in Italian stuffings for filled pasta. In large doses nutmeg has psychoactive and toxic effects, and it has no proven medicinal value. During the Napoleonic Wars the British took the Banda Islands for a time and transplanted nutmeg trees, with soil, to Sri Lanka, Penang, Bencoolen and Singapore, and from there to Zanzibar and Grenada, whose flag, adopted in 1974, shows a split-open nutmeg fruit.
nuuk: Nuuk stands at the mouth of the Nuup Kangerlua fjord on the south-western coast of Greenland, about 240 kilometres south of the Arctic Circle. At 64°11′ N it is the northernmost capital in the world, a few kilometres farther north than Reykjavík. The mountain Sermitsiaq, 1,210 metres high, can be seen from almost everywhere in the town. The climate is a maritime-influenced tundra, with long, cold, snowy winters and short, cold summers. Nuuk is the Greenlandic word for cape.

The Paleo-Eskimo Saqqaq culture lived in the area as far back as 2200 BCE, and Norse settlers lived there from about 1000 until their settlement disappeared, for uncertain reasons, in the 15th century.

The city proper began in 1728, when the royal governor Claus Paarss moved the missionary Hans Egede's Hope Colony, founded in 1721, to the mainland, at the Inuit settlement of Nûk. The fort was named Godt-Haab, good hope. Paarss's colonists were mutinous soldiers, convicts and prostitutes, and most died of scurvy and other ailments within the first year. A smallpox epidemic in 1733 and 1734 killed most of the native population as well as Egede's wife, and Egede returned to Denmark in 1736.

In 1733 Moravian missionaries received permission to found a mission, which became the nucleus of present-day Nuuk as many Greenlanders moved to it. In 1861 Hinrich Johannes Rink began Atuagagdliutit, Greenland's first newspaper, with a Greenlander as editor. The city grew rapidly in the 1950s, when Denmark began to modernise Greenland.

Nuuk is the capital and largest city of Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, and the seat of its government, with 20,113 inhabitants, more than a third of the territory's population. The Greenland Home Rule government renamed Godthåb as Nuuk on 1 May 1979.
nuzi: Nuzi, also known by its Akkadian name Gasur, stood at the modern site of Yorghan Tepe in Iraq, 12 kilometres south-west of Arrapha, modern Kirkuk, near the Tigris. It was occupied from the Ubaid period in the 5th millennium BCE until late in the 2nd millennium BCE, and again, after a period of abandonment, in the Parthian era. The main mound, about 200 metres square, was protected by a city wall with gates, and a well-drained main road ran between the central temples and the palace. Houses lay on two rises to the north, within an outer town with its own wall, now destroyed by modern farming.

Under the Akkadian Empire the city was probably known as Gasur and was the seat of a governor, known from a clay sealing found at Tell Brak. Of 222 cuneiform tablets of this period, written in Old Akkadian, most date to the reigns of Naram-Sin and Shar-kali-sharri. They show a thriving commercial centre with trading contacts with Assur, Susa and Akkad. The Nuzi map, found here, is the oldest known map. About 6 by 6.5 centimetres, it shows a canal or river, two mountain ranges and a city called Maskan-dur-ebla, but it is unknown exactly what it depicts. After a sack the site was occupied less densely under the Ur III, Isin-Larsa and Old Babylonian periods.

In the middle of the 2nd millennium BCE the Hurrians took control of the town and renamed it Nuzi. A sealing found there names Saustatar, son of Parsatatar, king of Mitanni. In the 15th and 14th centuries BCE it was a small provincial town of Arrapha in an area populated mostly by Hurrians, its central complex holding two temples, to Šawuška or Ištar and to Teššub, and a palace administered by a governor. Most worship was in the household, with elements of ancestor worship in which the eldest son inherited the family cult statue. After the fall of the Mitanni kingdom Nuzi went into gradual decline. The excavators dated its destruction to about 1500 BCE, but later work proposes about 1430 to 1330 BCE.

Tablets from Yorghan Tepe appeared as early as 1896, and serious excavation began in 1925 after Gertrude Bell noticed tablets in the markets of Baghdad. Work continued through 1931. About 5,000 tablets are known, mostly in the Oriental Institute, the Harvard Semitic Museum and the Iraq Museum. Those from Nuzi are in a dialect of Akkadian influenced by Hurrian, and about a quarter concern the business of a single family, that of Tehip-tilla and Surki-tilla.
nyai-roro-kidul: The legend of the Queen of the Southern Sea is traced to the Sundanese kingdom of Pajajaran in the 15th century. Anthropological research suggests it may come from a much older animistic belief in a pre-Hindu-Buddhist goddess of the southern ocean, inspired by the fierce waves, storms and tsunamis of Java's south coast. One Sundanese tale tells of Kadita, the only daughter of King Munding Wangi of Galuh Pakuan. Her stepmother, Dewi Mutiara, had a shaman curse her with boils so that she was exiled; after nearly seven days and nights she reached the Southern Sea, leapt in, and was healed and made its immortal queen.

She is shown sometimes as a very beautiful woman and sometimes as a mermaid whose lower body is a fish or snake, and she is believed to take the soul of anyone she wishes. In coastal villages it is believed that she claims fishermen and bathers, preferring handsome young men. Her favourite colour is sea green, gadhung m'lathi in Javanese, and people on the southern coast are warned not to wear it, lest she take them as soldiers or slaves. Sultan Hamengkubuwono IX of Yogyakarta wrote in his memoir that she appeared as a young woman at the full moon and as an old woman at other times.

Parangkusumo, near Yogyakarta, is believed to be the place of her first spiritual encounter with Panembahan Senopati. Her love for Senopati and for Sultan Agung of Mataram is recounted in the Bedhaya dance of the royal line of Surakarta, and her place is held to lie on the Merapi-Kraton-South Sea axis. When Hamengkubuwono IX died on 3 October 1988, palace servants reported seeing her pay her final tribute.

Along the coast she is patron of the gatherers of edible birds' nests, whose harvests at Karang Bolong are marked by wayang performances and offerings. At Palabuhanratu fishermen send offerings out to sea in an annual sedekah laut ceremony, and the town's Samudra Beach Hotel, whose site Sukarno helped choose, keeps room 308 for her.
nyangwe: Nyangwe was founded around 1860 as an Arab trading depot on the right bank of the Lualaba, in what is now the territory of Kasongo. It traded in ivory, gold, iron and slaves, and it later became part of the Sultanate of Utetera, ruled by the Swahili slave trader Tippu Tip and tied to the slave trade of the Sultanate of Zanzibar. It remained one of the main slave-trading centres until the Congo Arab war. According to David Livingstone, the first European to visit it, in 1871, the traders had driven away the Wagenya who lived there, who had since become distrustful of strangers.

On 15 July 1871 Livingstone, standing beside the leading trader Dugumbe, watched Arab slavers kill around 400 to 500 Africans at the market on the river. His diary records it as revenge for the deeds of Manilla, a head slave who had sacked villages of the Mohombo people at the urging of the Wagenya chief Kimburu; the attackers fell on Kimburu's people and anyone else at the market.

Researchers at the Indiana University of Pennsylvania who scanned the diary found that in writing up his notes Livingstone left out his fear that some of his own followers, slaves of Banyan merchants hired by John Kirk, acting British consul at Zanzibar, might have helped start the killing. The edited version in his Last Journals of 1874 also dropped the villagers' earlier armed resistance to the slavers, presenting them as passive victims, though the account of the massacre itself was barely changed.

For travellers from the east Nyangwe was the last known town, and Livingstone took the Lualaba for the upper Nile. Verney Lovett Cameron came in 1874, and in 1877 Henry Morton Stanley followed the river downstream from Nyangwe with Tippu Tip's support, reaching Boma and showing that it fed the Congo. Hermann Wissmann visited in 1883.
nyanza-rwanda: Nyanza, also known as Nyabisindu, is a town in Nyanza District in the Southern Province of Rwanda. The palace of the last umwami, the traditional king of Rwanda, stands within walking distance of the town centre, and the town was a royal capital of the Kingdom of Rwanda. The palace is the town's main tourist attraction.

In 1994, in the late stages of the genocide against the Tutsi, the Rwandan Patriotic Front fought the Rwandan Armed Forces at Nyanza for several days, and the town was partly destroyed. Many Tutsi were killed there by government forces as part of the genocide.

Nyanza is the capital of the Southern Province, on a turn-off from the road linking Kigali and Butare, about two and a half hours from Kigali by bus. Its main attraction is the king's palace. Visitors see the king's traditional palace and, close by, the modern palace that the Belgian colonial authorities built for him. Much of the traditional palace remains as it was when the king lived in it, though some furniture was stolen or destroyed in 1994 and replicas have been installed. A guide in the traditional dress, the umushanana, takes visitors round. The palace is also known for its Inyambo cattle, which have heavy horns and decorations and are sung to by a herdsman.

A second site is the former Rwesero Art Museum, a large building put up as a residence for the king, who left Rwanda before he lived in it; its art was moved to Kigali and it has been turned to other uses. Nyanza is known for ikivuguto, a fermented milk drink, and has two dairies. It also has the Institute of Legal Practice and Development, a stadium used for the harvest festival Umuganura and for National Heroes Day on 1 February, and a monthly community work day, Umuganda, on the last Saturday of each month.
nyatapola-temple: Most of what is known of the building comes from a palm-leaf ledger in Nepal Bhasa, the siddhāgni koṭyāhuti devala pratiṣṭhā, now in the National Archives of Nepal, which records the name, wage and working time of every person employed, the cost of every ritual and the timeline of the work. Sal timber was cut from November 1701 by groups of workers from towns across the Kingdom of Bhaktapur, and citizens of Bhaktapur and the Kingdom of Lalitpur donated timber and stone. A smaller five-roofed temple on the site, the ṅātapula, was demolished, and houses were taken; one owner, Dūkhi Bhāro, wrote a Ramayana to console himself for the loss of his ancestral home.

On 4 January 1702 Bhupatindra Malla laid the first three bricks of the foundation, carrying them on his shoulder. The ledger counts 1,135,350 bricks for the temple, 1528 stones, a golden pinnacle made by 40 smiths in 99 days and 529 wind bells. The image of the deity was carved in three months by thirty artisans led by Tulasi Lohakarmi.

Its name means five roofs in the Bhaktapur dialect of Nepal Bhasa, and it is one of the few temples named for its form rather than its deity. With the Kumbheshvara in Lalitpur it is one of only two five-storey temples in the Kathmandu Valley. The stairway up its five-level plinth is lined with pairs of stone guardians, each pair said to be ten times stronger than the one below: the wrestlers Jai and Pratap, elephants, lions, griffin-like sārdūlas and, at the top, the goddesses Simhanī and Vyāghranī.

The temple is held to be dedicated to the Tantric goddess Siddhi Lakshmi, ancestral deity of the Malla kings of Bhaktapur, though the building ledger does not name the deity and the image is kept from public view. Only Karmacharya priests may enter, and the gates open once a year in July, on the anniversary of its founding.

The temple stands with the Bhairava temple in Tamārhi square, the heart of the city, which divides Bhaktapur into an upper and a lower town. Its outline appears on the municipality's coat of arms. Its stepped plinth acts as a base that isolates the tower from the ground's shaking, and its roofs throw debris outward.
nyau: A cave painting in Zaire shows Kasiya Maliro, a type of Nyau mask that may date to 992 CE, and local tradition says Nyau came from Malomba, a place in what is now the DRC. Members who revealed its secrets faced heavy punishment, even death, so the first missionaries and colonial officials in Maravi could not learn its origin. Nyau continued through the Ngoni invasions of the mid-1800s and the arrival of Portuguese and British colonists.

Missionaries working from the 1920s banned it in Chewa communities, and open conflict followed, but the society survived British rule by adapting and taking in some Christian elements. Many Chewa today belong both to a church and to Nyau, and Malawian migrants keep its rites in suburbs of Zimbabwe such as Mabvuku, Highfield and Tafara.

Nyau societies work at village level within a network across central and southern Malawi, eastern Zambia and western Mozambique. Men and women are initiated separately; men's initiation begins with a stay in the wooded grove where the dead are buried, and boys in Zambian villages may join novice groups called kalumbu from the age of five or six. The Chewa hold that God is both male, Chiuta in the sky, and female, Namalango in the earth, and Nyau communicates with the dead in what is called the Great Prayer.

In performance the masked men are understood to be spirits of the dead, and uninitiated women and children run indoors; such performances have at times ended in attacks and deaths. Senior women take part with clapping, song and dance. There are feathered net masks, wooden face masks of ancestors and characters such as Maliya, Mfiti the witch and Simoni, a caricature of an Englishman, and large basketry animals such as Njobvu, the elephant, seen only at the funerals of chiefs.

Gule Wamkulu, the Big Dance, is the best known and longest Nyau dance, and may date to the Chewa Empire of the 17th century. It is also called the great prayer to our ancestors and is a religious rite rather than a folk dance. UNESCO listed it in 2005 among the Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. Over 400 masks associated with it are shown at the Chamare Museum in Dedza District, Malawi.
nyaungyan-min: He was born Shin Thissa on 8 November 1555, a son of King Bayinnaung by Lady Khin Pyezon, a minor queen. As one of 91 children of minor queens, ranked below those of the senior queens, he waited until he was 25 for a post: on 8 February 1581 he succeeded his elder brother Shin Ubote as governor of Nyaungyan, a small town south of Ava, and so became known as Nyaungyan Min, Lord of Nyaungyan. He sided with King Nanda when Thado Minsaw, Viceroy of Ava, revolted in 1584.

When Nanda withdrew central administration from Upper Burma in 1594 without naming a new viceroy, a power vacuum opened. Nyaungyan's forces halted an invasion by Thado Dhamma Yaza III of Prome at Pakhan in 1596, and in 1597 his court orders show him taking over Ava and, in the words of the historian Than Tun, virtually declaring himself king. The assassination of Thado Dhamma Yaza III on 15 September 1597 spared him a two-front war with Prome and Toungoo.

On 14 November 1598 he proclaimed himself king of all the lands of his father, and on 25 February 1600 he was crowned with the reign name Thiha Thura Maha Dhamma Yaza. Rather than fight in the low country, he took the cis-Salween Shan states one by one: Mohnyin and Mogaung in 1599, Nyaungshwe in 1601, where his musketeers decided the battle, Bhamo in 1602, Mone in 1603 and 1604, and Momeik, Hsipaw and Hsenwi in 1605. His eldest son Anaukpetlun led many of these campaigns.

Taken ill during the last campaign, he died south of Hsipaw on 5 November 1605, and his ashes were buried beside the Sandamuni Pagoda. On his deathbed he asked Anaukpetlun to spare Yan Naing of Prome, whose coup had broken up the attack of 1597.

His royal orders sorted the people into their traditional groups, among them the ahmudan who owed service to the Crown, repaired irrigation works, standardised taxes and set out the earliest known Burmese rules on military unit formation. Several were reissued by later kings until the end of the dynasty in 1752. Historians credit his decision to secure the Shan states before the coast with giving his successors the men and supplies to restore the empire.
nyaya: The word nyaya means justice, rules, method or judgment, and in philosophy it covers propriety, logic and method. Its historical development is unclear. The Nasadiya hymn of the Rigveda puts spiritual questions in logical propositions, and in the early centuries BCE the first Nyaya scholars began compiling a science of rational, coherent inquiry. The foundational text is the Nyaya Sutras, attributed to Aksapada Gautama and composed by the 2nd century CE. The people of Mithila ascribe the school to Gautama, husband of Ahalya, and name a village, Gautamasthana, north-east of Darbhanga as his birthplace.

Nyaya is listed among the fourteen principal branches of learning in an early text, and the Matsya Purana says knowledge of it came from the mouth of Brahma. Commentaries clarified the Sutras and defended the school against misreadings by scholars of other traditions, and later scholars refined and applied them to spiritual questions.

Nyaya holds that human suffering results from errors produced by activity under wrong knowledge, and that liberation, moksha, comes from right knowledge. For this reason the school concerned itself with epistemology, the reliable means of gaining correct knowledge. It accepts four of the six pramanas: perception (pratyaksha), inference (anumana), comparison or analogy (upamana) and testimony of reliable experts (shabda). Its followers, the Naiyayikas, approached philosophy as a direct realism, holding that whatever really exists can in principle be known. Its metaphysics lists sixteen categories, from the means of valid knowledge and doubt to forms of debate such as truth-directed debate, victory-directed debate and destructive debate, and it stands closer to the Vaisheshika school than to others.

Nyaya posits a self distinct from the mind and the body, a nonphysical substance. It shares part of its method and its view of suffering with Buddhism, but unlike Buddhism it affirms a soul and self. Inference, one of its main contributions, is set out in a five-step procedure for arguing to others, and its authors analysed how inference can go wrong.

Nyaya treatises on epistemology influenced other schools of Hinduism, each of which fixed its own number of pramanas: the Charvaka school accepts only perception, and Advaita Vedanta six. On God, the early Naiyayikas wrote very little, and the evidence suggests they were non-theistic or atheist. Later scholars applied the school's methods to the question. Udayana, in the Nyayakusumanjali, gave nine arguments for a creator God and answered objections from the Carvaka, Mimamsa, Buddhist, Jain and Samkhya systems, while other Nyaya scholars argued against God's existence.
nyenskans: The name Nyenskans joins Nyen, the Swedish name for the Neva, to skans, a bastion; in Finnish the place was Nevanlinna. Excavations in 1992–2000 found the remains of three medieval fortresses on the site. The only one known from the records is Landskrona, a large wooden fortress with eight towers built in 1300 by Tyrgils Knutsson, Lord High Constable of Sweden. A Russian army besieged it in the spring of 1301, captured the last defenders and burned it.

Sweden built the fortress during the Ingrian War, which began in 1610 when Russia, recovering from the Time of Troubles, tried to win back Ingria; Sweden claimed the province because Russia had broken the Treaty of Viborg of 1609. The fort held 500 people. The Treaty of Stolbovo of 1617 ceded the territory to Sweden. In 1632 the settlement of Nyen grew up across the Okhta, and it received town privileges and became the administrative centre of Swedish Ingria in 1642. By the mid-17th century it had about 2,000 people, mostly Finns, then Swedes and some Germans. Its governor, John Geselia the Younger, barred Orthodox subjects from settling there, which drove out its Russian, Izhorian and Karelian inhabitants.

A Russian attack led by Pyotr Potemkin in 1656 was repelled but badly damaged Nyen. New outworks were added in 1677, and late in the century the engineer Heinrich von Soylenberg rebuilt the fort as a star fort for 600 people, with five bastions of timber and earth and a half-fort across the Neva. In October 1702, fearing invasion, the Swedes reportedly evacuated Nyen and burned it. After Peter the Great took the fortress, he renamed it Schlötburg; it served as a Russian garrison for only some weeks. Its last Swedish commandant was Colonel Johan Apolloff.

Nothing of the fortress stands above ground; its fate after 1703 is uncertain, and its central works were still known in 1849. The site lies in the Krasnogvardeysky District of Saint Petersburg, where a monument by V. A. Reppo was opened on 15 June 2000 and a museum in May 2003. Excavations in 2007 found the remains of its bastions, and the planned Gazprom tower was moved to Lakhta.
nymphenburg-palace: The palace was designed by the Italian architect Agostino Barelli, who was replaced in 1674 by Enrico Zuccalli. The scholar Emanuele Tesauro of Turin supplied the concept for the mythological decorative programme, and the ceiling paintings were by Antonio Triva and Antonio Zanchi. The central pavilion, built of limestone from Kelheim, was completed in 1675. The palace quickly replaced Blutenburg Castle as the court's main hunting lodge and rivalled Schleissheim Palace.

From 1701 Maximilian Emanuel extended it systematically. Zuccalli and Giovanni Antonio Viscardi added two pavilions to the south and two to the north, joined to the centre by gallery wings. In 1716 Joseph Effner redesigned the central facade in French Baroque style, and court stables were added in 1719. The orangery, built for balance, was finished only in 1758. Under Charles VII Albert a circle of Baroque mansions, the Schlossrondell, was built along the driveway.

The palace served as the main summer residence of the Wittelsbach rulers of Bavaria. Its frontal width of 632 metres is greater than that of Versailles. In the central pavilion the Stone Hall rises through three floors, with ceiling frescoes by Johann Baptist Zimmermann and decoration by François de Cuvilliés. Some rooms keep their Baroque ceilings, while others were redone in Rococo or neoclassical style. In the southern pavilion hangs the Gallery of Beauties commissioned by King Ludwig I, in which Joseph Karl Stieler painted 36 women from all ranks of Munich, among them the shoemaker's daughter Helene Sedlmayr and Lola Montez.

The park of 200 hectares began as an Italian garden in 1671 and was recast in French style by Dominique Girard, a pupil of Le Notre. In the early 19th century Friedrich Ludwig von Sckell redid it in the English manner for Elector Charles Theodore, keeping main elements such as the Grand Parterre. A long canal leads from the palace to the Grand Cascade, built by Joseph Effner in 1717. Elector Charles Theodore opened the park to the public in 1792.

The Treaty of Nymphenburg, signed in July 1741, allied Charles Albert with France and Spain against Austria. Charles Albert lived at the palace as Holy Roman Emperor and died there in 1745. King Max I Joseph died there in 1825, and in 1863 King Ludwig II met Otto von Bismarck there for the only time.

In 1747 Elector Max III Joseph founded the Nymphenburg Porcelain Manufactory, still housed in one of the cavalier's lodges, whose Rococo figures by Franz Anton Bustelli and Dominik Auliczek made the name widely known. The palace is open to the public and also houses a carriage museum, a porcelain collection and the Museum of Man and Nature, and it remains the home and chancery of the head of the House of Wittelsbach.
